a twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.
Therefore, one should avoid the new moon day and so forth, as well as four nights starting from the appearance of the menses. || 1.79 ||
Furthermore:

proceeding in this manner, a man should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the Maghā and Mūla constellations. When the moon is in its favorable state, a man shall once produce a son endowed with auspicious marks.

In the manner thus described, one approaching a woman should approach her when she is "emaciated" (*kṣāmā*). Her emaciation at that time occurs precisely through the observances prescribed for a woman during her menses. If, however, such emaciation does not occur, then it must be induced for the sake of producing a son by means of eating little, avoiding oily foods, and so forth. A male child is born when the male seed (*śukra*) is in excess; a female child is born when the female seed is in excess.
According to this statement:
when there is an excess of blood even on an even night, then a female alone is born with a male form;
likewise, when there is an excess of semen even on an odd night, a male alone is born with a female form.
Because time serves as the efficient cause (*nimitta*),
and because the semen and blood serve as the material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and thus possess predominance;
therefore, the *kṣāma* [observance] must be performed.
One should avoid the Maghā and Mūla constellations.

When the Moon is situated in an auspicious place such as the eleventh house and so forth—and by the word "and" (ca), when there is the excellence of male constellations, auspicious yogas, and favorable ascendants—one should procreate only once in a single night, not twice or thrice.
Thereby, one gives birth to a son endowed with auspicious marks.
A man whose virility is unimpeded. || 1.80 ||
Having thus stated the rule regarding the fertile period (*ṛtu*), he now states the rule for other times:
"Or he may act according to his desire, remembering the boon granted to women;
yet he must remain devoted to his own wife, since women are declared to be protected."
One should be "acting according to her desire" (yathākāmī), meaning that one's conduct proceeds without transgressing the wishes of his wife.
The word "or" (vā) is intended to include another restrictive rule; it does not signify the cessation of the preceding rule.

Recalling the boon granted to women by Indra—that he who frustrates their desire shall be a sinner—it is as they said: "We choose this boon: let us obtain offspring during our fertile season (*ṛtu*), and let us unite according to our desire until childbirth. Therefore, women obtain offspring during their fertile season and unite according to their desire until childbirth; for the boon chosen by them is thus established. This is connected [to the rule]. By the use of the particle *eva* (only), he excludes intercourse with other women, because of the traditional injunction regarding penance (*prāyaścitta*) for such acts.
In both cases, he states the observed purpose with the words, "since women are traditionally held to be protected.
This means that because women are traditionally held (*smṛtāḥ*)—that is, declared—to be protected, they must be well-guarded (*surakṣitāḥ*).
And in this regard, according to the NSP edition, their state of being well-guarded is achieved by [the husband] satisfying her desires and by preventing her from approaching other men.
Regarding this, it is asked: "In that regard, one should approach her during the even nights.
Is this an injunction (*vidhi*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*), or an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)? It is replied:
It is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because its purpose has already been attained;
nor is it an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), because that would entail the threefold fault.
Therefore, those learned in logic have established it as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
What, then, is the distinction between these?
An injunction (*vidhi*) is that which brings about what has never before been attained, such as: "One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," or "The *aṣṭakā* rites are to be performed.

A restrictive rule (*niyama*) is that which brings about an alternative not previously attained for something already partially established, such as: "One should sacrifice on level ground" or "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* [rites]"; here, the sacrifice is enjoined as something to be performed.
And since that [sacrifice] cannot be performed without a location, by implication a location is obtained.
That [location] is of two kinds: level and uneven (as stated in the NSP edition: "It is of two kinds, namely level and uneven").
When the sacrificer desires to sacrifice on level ground, the injunction "one should sacrifice on level ground" remains silent, because its own purpose has already been established.

When, however, one intends to sacrifice on uneven ground, the injunction "then one should sacrifice on level ground" prescribes what is for one's own benefit, because at that time [sacrificing on level ground] has not been previously established. The exclusion of uneven ground, however, follows as a matter of course; for since the sacrifice is accomplished only by means of the prescribed location, by adopting an unprescribed location, the sacrifice would not be performed in accordance with the scripture.
"Likewise, one should eat food facing the east. This example from the Smṛti is also explained by the preceding [definition].
*Parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is the restatement of something that has already been obtained in multiple places for the purpose of excluding it from those other instances.

For example, the mantra "Taking this rein of the cosmic order" (*imām agṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya*) is applied by its own inherent capacity to the grasping of both the horse's halter and the donkey's halter; yet, when it is further enjoined specifically for the horse's halter by the rule "he takes the horse's halter," it is excluded from the donkey's halter.

For instance, in the case of the rule "five five-nailed animals are edible," eating [any animal] among dogs and the like was already possible by default, whereas eating among rabbits and the like was also possible; thus, when the mention of rabbits and the like is heard again, it excludes dogs and the like.
What, then, is appropriate here?
He says: it is *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusionary specification).
For instance, since one who has taken a wife is already entitled to approach her during her season according to his own will, this is not the subject matter of an injunction (*vidhi*).
Nor is it the subject matter of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), because that would contradict the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*.
For the authors of the *Gṛhyas* record as follows: "After taking a wife, one should remain a celibate student for three nights, twelve nights, or a year."

In that case, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating "one must indeed approach [the wife] during her season," the traditional teaching on celibacy (*brahmacarya*) would be contradicted if intercourse were possible even before twelve nights or a year had passed.

Furthermore, when the core action (*bhāvārtha*) is already established, it is logical for the statement to be intended as a qualification; and since approaching one's wife during her season is already established by mere desire, the verbal formulation "if he should approach, he must do so only during her season" is appropriate.

Moreover, since approaching during the season is already established as a constant requirement by the very injunction for the procreation of sons (*putrotpatti-vidhi*), the restrictive rule "he must indeed approach during her season" would be purposeless.
Furthermore, in the case of a restrictive injunction (*niyama*), an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated.

Moreover, if it were a restriction that one "must go" during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), then for one who is absent, incapacitated by illness or the like, or lacking desire, an impossible matter would have been taught.
Additionally, there is a contradiction between injunction and restatement (*vidhi-anuvāda-virodha*) in the case of a restriction.
For indeed, a single word uttered once both restates that very same meaning in one case and conforms to it in another.
Therefore, the restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) alone—that "one should go only during the proper season and not at other times"—is logical.
This, however, Bhāruci, Viśvarūpa, and others do not accept.
Therefore, a mandatory rule alone is logical, because the injunction for one’s own purpose is possible within that context, and because a fault is heard [in scripture] regarding non-approach:
"But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt in this."
Thus:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; there is no doubt in this."

Nor is there a contradiction between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), because there is no restatement here and the statement serves the purpose of an injunction. For a contradiction between injunction and restatement occurs only where that very thing which serves as the basis for the injunction must be restated, and yet it must also be enjoined with respect to another object because it has not [otherwise] been established—as, for example, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Vājapeya* section, where the sacrifice must be restated as the basis for enjoining the quality characterized by the *vājapeya*, while that same sacrifice must also be enjoined with respect to the fruit characterized by sovereignty (*svārājya*). Thus: "One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*. In such a case, there is a conflict between the status of being the basis for an injunction and the status of being the object of an injunction. Here, however, since the *soma* is already established by the sentence "He presses the *soma*," there is no need to restate it; rather, the sentence is intended solely for the injunction of the quality of drinking. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the rule regarding the non-repetition of mantras does not apply here, because the repetition is not of the mantra itself, but of the action (*kriyā*) associated with it. Nor is there a contradiction with the principle of the non-repetition of what is already known, because the action is not previously known in this specific context. Consequently, the drinking of *soma* is indeed enjoined. This is the conclusion. || 10 || *Taittirīya-saṃhitā* 6.2.11.4: *tasmāt somam prāpya rājānam na camasa-bhakṣam bhakṣayet*. "Therefore, having obtained the *soma* king, one should not drink it as a cup-drinking (*camasa-bhakṣa*). || 11 || *Taittirīya-saṃhitā* 6.2.11.5: *na somam rājānam camasa-bhakṣam bhakṣayet*. "One should not drink the *soma* king as a cup-drinking. || 12 || *Taittirīya-saṃhitā* 6.2.11.5: *somam rājānam camasa-bhakṣam bhakṣayet*. "One should drink the *soma* king as a cup-drinking. || 13 || *Taittirīya-saṃhitā* 6.2.11.5: *somam rājānam camasa-bhakṣam bhakṣayet*. And there is no purpose here for a mere restatement (anuvāda).
As for what was said— that an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) must be postulated in the case of a restrictive injunction (niyama)— that applies equally to an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā),
because a fault is postulated for one who engages in intercourse outside the prescribed season.
As for the claim that because the obligatory rule for procreating a son implies the necessity of approaching one's wife during her fertile season, there can be no further restriction—
that is incorrect;
for this very [rule regarding the fertile season] is itself the obligatory injunction for procreating a son.

It might be thought: "In this way, one going [to his wife] would procreate a son who is emaciated yet endowed with auspicious marks. However, this is not so, because of the specific qualification: "He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present," and "He who, being healthy, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses.
Thus, there is a specific restriction.
The cessation of what is not desired follows precisely from the injunction of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*).
Nor does it follow that [the text] has the status of a mere qualifier, because an injunction regarding the meaning of the verbal root is possible in certain cases.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the *Gṛhya-smṛtis*.

If one engages in sexual union even before the appearance of the menses within the year, there is no fault of violating the vow of celibacy, just as in the case of acts such as those performed out of faith.

Therefore, a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*)—which would entail the three faults of abandoning one's own purpose, assuming a purpose for another, and resulting in the sublation of what has already been obtained—is not tenable.

Thus, regarding the rule "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," although both a restrictive injunction (*niyama*)—since eating is optionally established for rabbits and the like—and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)—since eating is established for both rabbits and the like as well as dogs and the like—are possible, nevertheless, the restrictive injunction is not accepted. This is because, under the restrictive view, the non-eating of rabbits and the like would entail a fault, while the eating of dogs and the like would entail no fault, thereby contradicting the Smṛti texts on expiation. Therefore, only the exclusive specification is adopted. By this, the restrictive injunction in the Smṛti statement, "Twice-born men have their meals prescribed for morning and evening," is also explained.
Furthermore, the statement "one should not eat in between" would be redundant if it were intended as an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).

And since this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the repetition "at every season, at every season" is obtained, according to the principle that when the occasion recurs, the occasional duty also recurs.
The phrase "he may act according to his desire" is likewise a restrictive rule.
"Even outside the fertile period (*ṛtu*), if there is a desire for a woman, one should certainly gratify her;
or one should approach her during the fertile period, or at all times except when forbidden"—these two *sūtras* of Gautama also concern only restrictive rules (*niyama*).

"One should approach her during the fertile period; even outside the fertile period, if there is a desire for a woman, one should indeed approach her, provided it is not forbidden. Enough of this digression. (1.81)
Furthermore:
"Women are to be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, paternal kinsmen, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and relatives, with ornaments, clothing, and food."
Virtuous women, such as those previously mentioned by Bhartṛ and others, should be honored according to one's ability with ornaments, garments, food, flowers, and so forth;
for when they are thus honored, they cause the increase of dharma, artha, and kāma. (1.82)
Furthermore, as to what kind of woman she should be once the household duties have been entrusted to her,
he says: "With utensils kept in order, skillful, cheerful, averse to wasteful expenditure,
and devoted to her husband, she should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law."

She is described as such because her household utensils and implements are kept restrained and placed in their proper locations— such as the mortar, pestle, and winnowing basket in the place for threshing, and the lower and upper grinding stones in the place for grinding, and so forth. She is also "dexterous," meaning she is skillful in domestic affairs.
She should always be joyful and have a smiling face;
she should be averse to expenditure and not wasteful—
this is to be understood as the remainder in every instance.
Furthermore:
*śvaśrūś ca śvaśuraś ca* (the mother-in-law and the father-in-law) becomes *śvaśurau* by means of the rule of single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*),
according to the rule *śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā*.

She should constantly perform the salutation of their feet. The mention of "father-in-law" is intended to include other venerable persons. Being devoted to her husband and remaining under his control, she should perform what was previously described. || 1.83 ||
It was stated [previously] regarding what should be done when the husband is present; now, as to what she must do when the husband is away on a journey, he says:
"A woman whose husband is away from home should abandon play, bodily adornment, attendance at social gatherings and festivals, laughter, and visiting the houses of others."

A woman whose husband has gone abroad should abandon playing with balls and other such games; the adornment of the body with ointments and the like; social gatherings, which are assemblies of people; festivals, such as weddings and the like, and the sight of them; laughter and yawning; and going to the houses of others.
The word "should abandon" is to be connected with each of these items. 1.84.
Furthermore:
A father should protect a maiden; her husband, when she is married; and her sons in old age. In their absence, her kinsmen shall protect her; a woman never possesses independence.
Before the taking of the hand in marriage, the father shall protect the maiden from committing improper acts;
thereafter, the husband;
and in his absence, the sons, during her old age.
In the absence of those aforementioned [relatives], the kinsmen (jñātis) [are entitled].
In the absence of kinsmen, the king; for there is the scriptural statement: "At the conclusion of both sides [of the family], the king is the lord and protector of the woman.
Therefore, women never possess independence in any circumstance whatsoever. || 1.85 ||
Furthermore:
She should not be deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles; for without her husband, she would become an object of reproach.
She should not be without a husband— meaning either husbandless or deprived of her father and other guardians—
for she who is deprived of them would be censurable and blameworthy;
and this applies to the case of lifelong celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
For Viṣṇu records: "When the husband has died, [the wife shall observe] either celibacy or ascension after him (anvārohaṇa).
Regarding ascension after him, there is great spiritual merit;
thus Vyāsa demonstrated this by means of the allegory of the female pigeon.
The devoted wife entered the blazing fire,
and there she was reunited with her husband, who wore variegated armlets.
Then the bird, having gone to heaven and reunited with his wife,
was honored there for his deeds and rejoiced together with his wife.
Thus,
the devoted wife entered the blazing fire;
there she was reunited with her husband, who wore variegated armlets.
Then the bird, having gone to heaven and reunited with his wife,
was honored there for his deeds and rejoiced together with his wife.
And likewise, Śaṅkha and Aṅgiras state:
"As many hairs as there are on a human being— three and a half crores—
for that much time shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven."
Having thus established this, [the author] demonstrates their inseparability:
"Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
even so that woman, having rescued him, rejoices together with him."
There, devoted supremely to her husband and being praised by hosts of apsarases,
she sports with her lord for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Thus:
"Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
even so that woman, having extracted [her husband], rejoices together with him."
There, devoted supremely to her husband and being praised by hosts of apsarases,
she sports with her lord for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
Likewise:
"Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or a slayer of a friend,
the non-widowed woman who dies taking him with her purifies him."
The woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral pyre,
is equal in conduct to Arundhatī and is glorified in the heavenly world.
As long as a woman does not cause herself to be cremated when her husband has died in the fire,
she is by no means released from that female body.
Thus it is said:
"Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or a betrayer of friends,
the woman who dies following him in death purifies him, provided she is not a widow."
The woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral pyre,
being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world.
As long as a woman does not cause herself to be consumed by fire when her husband has died in the flames,
she is by no means released from her female body.
Hārīta also says:
"She who follows her husband purifies three lineages— those of her mother, those of her father, and that of the one to whom she is given."
Thus it is said:
"She who follows her husband purifies three lineages— her mother's, her father's, and that of the one to whom she is given."
Likewise:
"She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away on a journey,
and who dies when her husband dies— she is to be known as a woman devoted to her husband."
Thus it is said:
"She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away from home,
and who dies when her husband dies— she is to be known as a devoted wife."

And this entire rule—that she follows her husband—is a common duty for all women, from the highest down to the Cāṇḍāla, provided they are not pregnant and their children are no longer infants; for it is stated without qualification that "she who follows [her husband]. Furthermore, as for those statements intended to prohibit following [the husband] in death regarding a Brāhmaṇa woman: "There is no following in death for a Brāhmaṇa woman, by the command of Brahmā."
But among the other castes, austerity is said to be supreme.
A woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste who follows her deceased husband [to death] would incur the sin of self-destruction; therefore, she should remain alive and perform the prescribed meritorious acts.
By taking her own life, she would lead neither herself nor her husband to heaven.
These and other such [passages] concern the subject of ascending separate funeral pyres;
for there is a specific traditional injunction stating: "Having ascended a separate pyre, a Brahmin ought not to depart [from it]."
By this, it is understood that separate funeral pyres are permitted for women of the Kṣatriya and other castes.

As for what has been said by some—that because suicide is prohibited for women just as it is for men, this instruction for following [the husband] applies to one who, having an excessive desire for heaven, transgresses the prohibitory scripture;

and just as the instruction for the Śyena sacrifice applies to one whose mind is overcome by intense anger and who thus transgresses the prohibitory scripture, as in "one practicing malevolent magic should sacrifice with the Śyena"—[that is incorrect].
That is incorrect.

For those who describe the Śyena sacrifice as being an evil (anartha) by way of its result—on the grounds that the violence (*hiṃsā*), which is the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) having the Śyena as its instrument, lacks contact with an injunction and is instead touched by a prohibition—in their view, the act of following [the husband in death] (*anugamana*) is clearly distinct from the Śyena. This is because, according to the scripture, it is the very act of violence that is enjoined for the sake of attaining heaven; thus, since it lacks contact with a prohibition, it stands in clear contrast to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

As for the view that violence (*hiṃsā*) is an activity conducive to death, and that the *śyena* sacrifice is indeed violence because it consists of an activity conducive to the death of another—given that in rites governed by desire (*kāma-adhikāra*), the injunction (*vidhi*) does not impel one toward the instrumental aspect of the act, since engagement there occurs through passion (*rāga*).

Because it takes the form of violence motivated by passion (*rāga*), the *śyena* sacrifice is prohibited as being harmful in its very nature. In that case as well, since the scriptural injunction for following [the husband] prescribes death itself as the means to attain heaven, even though one engages in death out of passion, the engagement in the specific procedure—such as entering the fire—which is conducive to death, occurs solely due to the injunction; thus, there is no room for the prohibition [of suicide], just as in the case of the rule: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu. Therefore, the difference between following [the husband] and the *śyena* sacrifice is quite clear.

As for the claim that following [the husband in death] is improper because it contradicts the Śruti passage, "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his life," and the further point that "one desiring heaven should not depart before the end of his life"—

meaning that a seeker of liberation (*mokṣārthin*) should not exhaust his lifespan prematurely for the sake of attaining the fruit of heaven— this is because, provided there is a remainder of life, liberation characterized by the attainment of Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss through self-knowledge, becomes possible once the stains of the internal organ have been cleansed by the performance of obligatory and occasional duties (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), and when the perfection of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) has been achieved.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should not squander one's life for the sake of heaven, which consists of impermanent and meager pleasure;

and consequently, for one who does not desire liberation but seeks heaven consisting of impermanent and meager pleasure, following [the husband] in death is appropriate, just like the performance of other optional rites—thus everything is beyond reproach. 1.86.
Furthermore:
Devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to her husband, well-conducted, and having conquered her senses,
she attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death.
"Priya" means agreeable to the mind by virtue of being irreproachable; "hita" is that which brings about welfare in the future. That which is both "priya" and "hita" is "priyahita.
"Patipriyahita" refers to what is dear and beneficial to the husband; she is "yuktā," meaning devoted, to that.
"Of good conduct" (*svācārā*) means she whose conduct (*ācāraḥ*) is beautiful (*śobhana*); such is she described.
And beautiful conduct has been demonstrated by Śaṅkha: "She should not go out of the house without speaking;
she should not walk quickly without an upper garment."
She should not speak with a stranger, except for merchants, renunciants, elders, and physicians;
she should not expose her navel;
and she should wear her garment down to the ankles.
She should not expose her breasts;
she should not laugh uncovered;
she should not harbor ill-will toward her husband or his kinsmen.

One should not stay in the same place with courtesans, rogues, women who go to meet their lovers, female renunciants, female fortune-tellers, those who practice deception through illusions or roots of magic, those of immoral conduct, and so forth;
for by such association, the character of noble women is corrupted.
Thus it is said.

She by whom the senses—the ears and so forth, as well as the speech and so forth, together with the mind—have been conquered, subdued, and restrained, attains renown and fame in this world and the highest state in the next world. Furthermore, this entire duty of women is to be understood as beginning from marriage; for there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating: "Prior to initiation (*upanayana*), [women may engage] in acting according to desire, speaking according to desire, and eating according to desire. And it is also said: "The rite of marriage is declared to be the initiation for women. (1.87)

Regarding one who has many wives, he says: "If there is another wife of the same caste (savarṇā), he should not have religious duties performed by anyone else. Among wives of the same caste, according to the rule of dharma, no other wife may act without the eldest."
While a wife of the same caste exists, he must never cause another woman of a different caste to perform religious duties.

Even when there are many wives of the same caste, in accordance with the righteous rule for the performance of dharma, he must not employ any other—whether the middle or the youngest—excluding the eldest. (1.88)
Having stated the rule for a woman whose husband has died, he now speaks concerning a man whose wife has died:
"Having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire, the husband shall,
without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule."

Having cremated a deceased wife—who possessed the conduct previously described and was observant of proper custom—either with the *śrauta* fire of the *agnihotra* or, in its absence, with the *smārta* fire, the husband (the supporter) shall, if he has not procreated a son, or if his sacrifices have not been completed, or if he is ineligible for other stages of life (*āśrama*), take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule without delay; for it is remembered by Dakṣa: "A twice-born man should not remain without a stage of life even for a single day."
And this [rule] applies only to a wife who was authorized at the time of the *ādheya* (the establishment of the sacred fires), and not to any other.
As for the statement:
"He who should cremate a second wife with the *vaitānika* fires..."
For as long as the first wife is alive, that [act] is indeed equal to the drinking of liquor.
Thus it is said:
"If one should cremate a second wife with the sacrificial fires while the first is still living, that act is indeed equal to the drinking of liquor."
Likewise: "If the second wife has died, he who should abandon the *agnihotra*—
or he who should abandon it out of desire— one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin."

Such passages as these are to be understood as referring to the act of providing fire to one who is not authorized [to maintain the sacred fires], along with the formal installation [of the fires]. || 1.89 ||

It has been stated that a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives, a Kṣatriya three, a Vaiśya two, and a Śūdra one; and it has also been stated that sons should be procreated upon them. Now, in order to distinguish which son belongs to whom and from whom he is born, [the author] says:
"From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of equal birth (sajātayaḥ)."
In blameless marriages, sons are born who increase the lineage.

From Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes] who are of the same class (*savarṇa*), sons of the same lineage—meaning those belonging to the same caste as their mother and father—are born from wives (*brāhmaṇī* and so forth) who are of the same class.
Because of the concluding summary, "this rule is prescribed for married women" (*vinnāsu*), which applies to all [the preceding cases], it is connected with the phrase "from wives of the same class.
Since the word *vinna* (married) is a relative term, it is understood that [the husbands] must also be of the same class as the fathers.
The word *savarṇa* (of the same class) is clear in its meaning. Consequently, this is the established sense:

those born from a woman of the same class (*savarṇā*) who has been wedded according to the prescribed rule are of the same caste (*samānajātīya*) as the husband because they are born from one of the same class.
And from this it follows that the Kuṇḍas, Golakas, Kānīnas, Sahoḍajas, and so forth, are declared to be of a different caste (asavarṇa).

Since they are distinguished from those of the same caste (savarṇa) and from those born in the direct (anuloma) and inverse (pratiloma) orders, they are entitled to perform common duties such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the like; for the Smṛti declares: "All those born of a violation of the marriage rules (*apadhvaṃsaja*) are recorded as having the same dharma as Śūdras."
Those born of *apadhvaṃsa* (debased unions) or born of illicit intercourse are entitled even to the duties of Śūdras, such as service to the twice-born and so forth.
But surely, since the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are not Brāhmaṇas, their exclusion from the *śrāddha* rite is untenable and contradicts logic:
whatever is produced from a man of a certain caste by a woman of a certain caste belongs to that very same caste, just as from a cow and a cow comes a cow, and from a horse and a mare comes a horse.
Therefore, it is not contradictory to say that one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is a Brāhmaṇa.

Likewise, there would be a contradiction with the statement to be made later, which follows an enumeration of the *kānīna*, *paunarbhava*, and others: "This rule has been declared by me regarding sons born of women of the same caste."
This is not the essential point.
The prohibition regarding the *śrāddha* is intended to remove the misconception that one born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is necessarily a Brāhmaṇa;
it is just as there is a prohibition against the outcast (*patita*) at a *śrāddha*, even though such a person is absolutely ineligible [for other reasons].
And there is no contradiction with logic:
where a genus (*jāti*) is perceivable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is so;
however, the genus of a Brāhmaṇa and the like is characterized by tradition (*smṛti*), and thus exists according to that tradition.

Just as, despite the commonality of *brāhmaṇya*, there are clans (*gotra*) characterized by tradition such as Kuṇḍina, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Gautama, so too, despite the commonality of being human, there are castes (*jāti*) such as *brāhmaṇa* and others characterized by tradition.
And this very same thing is the definition of caste for both mother and father.
Nor is there an infinite regress.
"Because saṃsāra is beginningless, like the conventional usage of words and their meanings;
this rule has been declared by me for [sons] who belong to the same class.
Since this is a restatement of what was already said, it will be explained according to the requirements of the context.
The *kṣetraja* son, however, belongs to the same caste as his mother, according to the traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) on *niyoga* and the practice of the learned;
for example, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura, though *kṣetraja* sons, were of the same caste as their mothers. Enough with this digression.

Furthermore, in the blameless forms of marriage such as the *brāhma* and others, the sons increase the lineage and are free from disease, long-lived, and endowed with both righteousness and progeny. (1.90)
Having spoken of those of equal caste, he now describes those born in the direct order (anuloma): "From a Brāhmaṇa, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born from a Kṣatriya woman; from a Vaiśya woman, an Ambaṣṭha;
and from a Śūdra woman, a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava."
A son born to a Kṣatriya woman married to a Brāhmaṇa is called a Mūrdhāvasikta;
one born to a Vaiśya maiden married [to a Brāhmaṇa] is called an Ambaṣṭha;
and a son born to a Śūdra woman married [to a Brāhmaṇa] is called a Niṣāda.

There is a certain person born of inverse union (pratiloma) who lives by killing fish and is named Niṣāda; lest he [be confused with the other], this one is designated as a Pāraśva-Niṣāda—this is the distinction in terminology.
The word "from a Brāhmaṇa" (viprāt) applies everywhere.
As for that which is produced by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Kṣatriya woman, he becomes a Kṣatriya indeed.

The Smṛti of Śaṅkha states: "One begotten by a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman becomes a Vaiśya; one begotten by a Vaiśya on a Śūdra woman becomes a Śūdra. This is intended for the purpose of attaining the duties (*dharma*) of the Kṣatriya and so forth, and not for the purpose of negating the caste (*jāti*) of the Mūrdhāvasikta and others, nor for the purpose of attaining the *jāti* of the Kṣatriya and so forth.

Consequently, for the Mūrdhāvasikta and others, the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites must be performed using the very same staff, deerskin, sacred thread, and so on, as prescribed for the Kṣatriya and the rest.
Prior to initiation, his conduct may be according to his own will and so forth; this is to be understood as being exactly as before. 1.91.

From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother, the Māhiṣya and Ugra are recorded as the two sons; from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, the Karaṇa is born. This is the rule declared for women who have been duly wedded.
From a Kṣatriya father, upon a married Vaiśya woman and a married Śūdra woman, the sons Māhiṣya and Ugra are born respectively.

From a Vaiśya father, upon a married Śūdra woman, a son named Karaṇa is born. This entire rule regarding the designations such as Mūrdhāvasikta and the rest is to be understood as prescribed for women who have been married [by their own fathers].
And these six—the Mūrdhāvasikta, Ambaṣṭha, Niṣāda, Māhiṣya, Ugra, and Karaṇa—are to be known as the sons born in the inverse order. || 1.92 ||
He speaks of those born in the inverse order: from a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
but from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all religious duties.
Sons begotten by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras upon a Brāhmaṇa woman are respectively known as Sūtas, Vaidehakas, and Caṇḍālas;
among these, the Caṇḍāla is excluded from all religious duties. (1.93)
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Māgadha was born; and from a Śūdra father, a Kṣattṛ was likewise born.
Furthermore, a Vaiśya woman gave birth to a son known as an Āyogava from a Śūdra father.
Furthermore,
a Kṣatriya woman bears to a Vaiśya a son named Māgadha;
that same woman bears to a Śūdra a son who is a Kṣattṛ.

A Vaiśya woman bears to a Śūdra a son called Āyogava. These six—the Sūta, Vaidehaka, Caṇḍāla, Māgadha, Kṣattṛ, and Āyogava—are born from inverse unions (pratiloma). Their occupations are to be found in the works of Uśanas and Manu. || 1.94 ||
He now describes another mixed caste born from a mixture of mixed castes:
"From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born.
Those born from the inverse and the natural orders are to be known as 'unrighteous' (asat) and 'righteous' (sat) respectively."
A *māhiṣya* is one begotten by a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman.
A *karaṇī* is one begotten by a Vaiśya on a Śūdra woman; a son begotten by a *māhiṣya* on her becomes by caste a *rathakāra*.
And for him, all rites such as the initiation (*upanayana*) are to be performed because of a specific scriptural injunction.
As Śaṅkha says:

"The son born from the union of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya woman in the direct order (ānulomya), who is a Rathakāra, is entitled to the rites of sacrifice, giving, and marriage-consecration; his livelihood consists of the study of the *Aśvapratiṣṭhā*, the *Ratha-sūtra*, and the science of architecture (*vāstu-vidyā*).

In this same way, it should be understood that for the Mūrdhāvasikta born from a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya woman, and the Māhiṣya born from a similar union in the direct order, there is the attainment of a distinct caste and the eligibility for initiation (*upanayana*) and other sacraments, because those two possess the status of the twice-born (*dvija*).
The specific designations, however, are to be understood from other Smṛti texts;
this has been stated merely as an illustration,
for it is impossible to enumerate them all due to the infinity of mixed and further mixed castes.

Therefore, this much is intended here: it should be understood that those born in the reverse order (pratilomaja) are non-existent [in the true sense], while those born in the direct order (anulomaja) are existent. || 1.95 ||
By stating "they are born from all [castes] through all [women]," and so forth, the cause for attaining a caste has been explained.
Now, he states another cause:
"An elevation of birth is to be known as occurring in the seventh or even the fifth generation."
Upon the reversal of karmas, there is equality, as before, with the lower and higher states.

The "castes" (*jātayaḥ*) refer to those such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others; their "elevation" (*utkarṣaḥ*) is the attainment of a caste such as that of a Brāhmaṇa. This elevation of caste (*jātyutkarṣaḥ*) should be understood as occurring in the seventh or, by force of the word "also" (*api*), in the fifth or sixth generation (*janmani*) within a lineage (*yuge*). And this option is fixed. The rule for this determination is as follows: a Niṣādī is produced when a Brāhmaṇa begets a child upon a Śūdra woman. She, having been married by a Brāhmaṇa, gives birth to a daughter. That daughter also, having been married by a Brāhmaṇa, gives birth to another [daughter]. In this manner, the sixth [descendant] produces a Brāhmaṇa in the seventh generation.
An Ambaṣṭha is one begotten by a Brāhmaṇa on a Vaiśya woman;
she too, in this manner, as the fifth generation, produces a sixth-generation Brāhmaṇa.
Likewise, a Mūrdhāvasikta, as the fourth generation, produces a fifth-generation Brāhmaṇa in this very same way.

In this manner, an *ugrā* woman married to a Kṣatriya, and a *māhiṣyā* woman [married to a Vaiśya], produce a Kṣatriya as the sixth and fifth [sons] respectively. Likewise, a *karaṇī* woman married to a Vaiśya produces a Vaiśya as the fifth; in this way, the principle should be inferred for other cases as well.

Furthermore, regarding the "reversal of occupations"—that is, when those occupations intended for one's livelihood are inverted—there is a secondary rule (*anukalpa*), such as: "If a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his primary occupation, he may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya."
If he cannot subsist by that [brahminical] occupation, he may subsist by the occupation of a Vaiśya; if he cannot subsist even by that, he may subsist by the occupation of a Śūdra.
A Kṣatriya also, if unable to subsist through his own duty for the sake of livelihood, may subsist by the occupation of a Vaiśya or the occupation of a Śūdra.
A Vaiśya also, if unable to subsist by his own occupation, may subsist by the occupation of a Śūdra. Thus there is a transposition of the occupations.

When that transgression has occurred, if he does not abandon that mode of livelihood even when released from the calamity, then in his seventh, sixth, or fifth birth, he attains equality—that is, birth in the same caste as the low-caste person by whose occupation he lives.

For example: if a Brāhmaṇa, living by the occupation of a Śūdra and not abandoning it, fathers a son who likewise lives by that same occupation, and that son fathers another son, and so on in succession, he produces one who is indeed a Śūdra in the seventh birth.
One living by the occupation of a Vaiśya should invite a Vaiśya on the sixth day;
one living by the occupation of a Kṣatriya should invite a Kṣatriya on the fifth day;
and even a Kṣatriya living by the occupation of a Śūdra should invite a Śūdra on the sixth day.
Living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, he produces a Vaiśya in the fifth generation.
Likewise, a Vaiśya living by the occupation of a Śūdra, without abandoning it, produces a Śūdra in the fifth birth through the succession of sons;
as before, this constitutes a lower and higher status.
The meaning of this is as follows: those born of the intermixture of castes—both those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*)—have been shown.
Furthermore, those born from the further intermixture of mixed castes have been shown by way of the example of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*).
Now, those born from the further intermixture of mixed castes are being demonstrated.

The term *adharottara* refers to both the lower and the higher classes. For example, those born from a *mūrdhāvasiktā* woman by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras; likewise, those born from an *ambaṣṭhā* woman by Vaiśyas or Śūdras, and those born from a *niṣādī* woman by a Śūdra—these are the lower *pratiloma* (inverse-order) castes. Similarly, those born from a Brāhmaṇa father on *mūrdhāvasiktā*, *ambaṣṭhā*, or *niṣādī* women; those born from a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya father on a *māhiṣyā* or an *ugrā* woman; and those born from a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya father on a *karaṇī* woman—these are the higher *anuloma* (direct-order) castes.
In this manner, the same principle should be inferred for other cases as well.
This inversion of the superior and the inferior should be understood as "non-existent" and "existent," respectively, as explained previously. || 1.96 ||
Intending to demonstrate those rites prescribed by revelation (śrauta) and tradition (smārta) which are to be accomplished with fire, [the author] states in which fire each should be performed:

"A householder should perform the smārta rite daily in the marriage fire, or else in the fire brought at the time of inheritance; he should perform the śrauta rite in the sacrificial fires (vaitānika)."

The householder should perform the rituals prescribed by the Smṛti, such as the Vaiśvadeva, as well as worldly activities characterized by daily cooking, in the marriage fire consecrated at the time of marriage.
At the time of inheritance or partition, or when fire has been brought from a Vaiśya household, he should bring that fire and perform the duties of a householder.
Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the rules of purification, the twice-born man—
One should perform the morning twilight devotion preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.

Having performed the bodily needs, such as the daily obligatory rites (*āvaśyaka*), during the daytime and at the twilights according to the prescribed method—namely, with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) placed over the ear and facing north—the twice-born (*dvija*), having completed the rules of purification according to the method stated beginning with "that which removes odor and stain," should perform the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥsaṃdhyā*) preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
And the rule for the cleansing of the teeth is as follows:
[it should be] made from a thorny or milky tree, twelve finger-breadths in length.
"The tooth-stick is prescribed as being as thick as the tip of the little finger, with a brush made from half a joint;
likewise, there is the tongue-scraper.
Thus it is said.
A tooth-stick produced from a thorny or milky tree, twelve finger-breadths in length,
as thick as the tip of the little finger, with its end fashioned into a brush-like tuft,
is prescribed for cleaning the teeth; likewise, a tongue-scraper is also prescribed.
Here, by the phrase "arising from a tree," the prohibition of grass, clods of earth, fingers, and so forth is intended;
furthermore, the prohibition of *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and other such trees should be understood as stated in other *smṛtis*.
And the mantra for cleaning the teeth is: "May life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, and wealth [be granted]."
O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us sacred knowledge, wisdom, and mental power.
Thus: "O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us long life, strength, glory, luster, progeny, cattle, and wealth, as well as sacred knowledge, wisdom, and mental acuity."

The repetition of the *saṃdhyāvandana*, although already mentioned in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), is for the purpose of establishing that it must be preceded by the cleaning of the teeth; for there is a prohibition stating, "A religious student should avoid cleaning the teeth, dancing, singing, and so forth. (1.98)
Having offered oblations into the fires dedicated to the Sun, he should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras,
master the meaning of the Vedas, and study various treatises.

After performing the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥsaṃdhyāvandana*), having offered oblations into the *āhavanīya* and other fires according to the prescribed rule, or into the domestic fire (*aupāsanāgni*),
he should thereafter mutter the mantras dedicated to the deity Sūrya, beginning with "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam," while remaining composed and with an undistracted mind.
In the interval between those [periods], he should acquire and understand the meanings of the Vedas as well as Nirukta, grammar, and so forth by means of listening;
and by the use of the word "ca" (and), he should also practice what has already been studied.
Furthermore, he should acquire various treatises such as Mīmāṃsā and others that establish dharma, artha, and health. 1.99.
And one should approach the Lord for the sake of attaining security and prosperity.
Having bathed, one should likewise gratify and worship both the gods and the ancestors.

Immediately thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing *yoga* and *kṣema*, one should approach (*upeyāt*)—that is, serve—a lord (*īśvara*) endowed with qualities such as consecration, or another illustrious person who is irreproachable.
*Yoga* is the acquisition of what has not been obtained; *kṣema* is the preservation of what has been obtained. For that purpose, one should approach and attend upon him.
By the word "approach" (*upeyāt*), he prohibits [mere] servitude.
Service consists of carrying out orders for the sake of receiving wages;
since that is prohibited as being the "way of a dog," as the Smṛti of Manu states: "Service is declared to be the way of a dog; therefore, one should avoid it.

Then, at midday, having bathed in a river or similar body of water according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, one should satisfy the gods, the ancestors as specified in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, and—by virtue of the word "and"—the sages, using the *tīrtha* sacred to the gods and others.

In that interval, one should worship any one among Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others, according to one's own inclination, with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), using the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas that reveal them, or by their own names in the dative case followed by "namaḥ," according to the prescribed ritual. 1.100.
To the extent of one's ability, one should recite the Vedas, the Atharva-veda, the Purāṇas, along with the Itihāsas,
for the successful accomplishment of the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña), as well as the knowledge concerning the supreme self.

Immediately after that, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), he should recite according to his capacity and according to the prescribed rule the Vedas, the Atharva-veda, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas—either collectively or individually—as well as spiritual knowledge (ādhyātmikī vidyā). || 1.101 ||
The rites for the ancestors (balikarma), the svadhā-oblations, the study of sacred texts, and the hospitable reception of guests constitute the great sacrifices to the spirits,
the ancestors, the gods, Brahmā, and human beings.
The *balikarma* is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*);
the *svadhā* offering is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*); and the burnt oblation (*homa*) is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*).
The private recitation of the Veda is the sacrifice to Brahman;
the hospitable reception of guests is the sacrifice to humans.
These five great sacrifices must be performed day after day because they are obligatory.
Furthermore, the mention of the fruits of these [rites] is for the purpose of proclaiming their purifying nature, not for the purpose of establishing that they are optional (kāmya). || 1.102 ||
From the remnants of the food offered to the gods, one should offer the *bali* to the spirits;
one should also place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows.
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva oblation according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, one should offer the *bali* to the spirits with the food remaining from that.
The mention of "food" (*anna*) is for the purpose of excluding uncooked items.
Immediately thereafter, one should place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows, according to one's ability.
By the word "and" (ca), [the list includes] worms, those afflicted by sinful diseases, and the fallen (patita).
As Manu says:
"Of dogs, of the fallen, of outcastes (śvapaca), and of those afflicted by sinful diseases..."
One should slowly place them on the ground for the crows and the worms.
Thus: "And for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases,
crows, and worms, one should gently place [the food] upon the ground."

And this must be performed both evening and morning, because of the traditional teaching of Āśvalāyana: "Then one should offer [portions] of the prepared sacrificial food (haviṣya) in the evening and in the morning.

Here, some maintain that the rite called Vaiśvadeva serves the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha) as well as being a rite for the consecration of food (anna-saṃskārakarma), since its status as a rite for the consecration of food is understood from the statement: "Then one should offer [portions] of the prepared sacrificial food in the evening and in the morning."

Now, having begun with "Next, therefore, the five sacrifices," and having stated their obligatory nature by saying "one should perform these sacrifices day after day," it is understood that they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
This is incorrect;
for if they were for the purpose of the person, it would be untenable for them to be acts of consecrating food (*anna-saṃskārakarma*).

For instance, in the view that it is a substance, a preparatory rite, or a primary action, the Vaiśvadeva rite would have food as its purpose; whereas if it were for the sake of the person, the substance would have the Vaiśvadeva rite as its purpose. Because of this mutual contradiction, it is more reasonable that it is indeed for the sake of the person, as it is said:
"By the great sacrifices and by the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman."
This body is made fit for Brahman through the great sacrifices and the ritual offerings;
likewise, if another guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has already been completed.
Therefore, one should give food according to one's ability, but one should not offer the bali-oblation.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu, if the rite known as the Vaiśvadeva were for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha), it would not need to be repeated at every cooking.

Therefore, by the passage beginning "Now, morning and evening," both the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi) and the performance injunction (prayoga-vidhi) are shown; and the injunction of qualification (adhikāra-vidhi) is expressed by the statement, "One should perform these sacrifices day after day. Thus, everything is beyond reproach. 1.103.
Food should be given daily to the ancestors and to men, as well as water;
one should constantly perform the private recitation of the Vedas, and one should not cook food for oneself alone.
Every day, food should be given to the ancestors and to human beings according to one's ability;
in the absence of food, roots, tubers, fruits, and so forth;
and in the absence of even those, water should be given, as indicated by the word "api" (even/also).
One should constantly engage in the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) for the purpose of not forgetting it. One should not cook food for one's own sake alone.
The mention of "food" (*anna*) is intended to illustrate all kinds of things that are to be received.
How then? Precisely by aiming at the deities and so forth. 1.1.04.
Having first fed the children, the daughters living in the household, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick,
young girls, guests, and servants, the husband and wife may eat what remains.
A married woman who remains in her father’s house is a *svavāsinī*;
the others are well known.
Having fed the children and so forth, as well as guests and servants, the husband and wife should eat the remaining food.
In times of non-distress, one should eat food according to the procedure for the Prāṇāgnihotra sacrifice;
it is ordained that cooked food should be consumed with a sense of joy. 1.105.
In times of non-distress, one should eat food according to the procedure for the Prāṇāgnihotra sacrifice;
it is prescribed that cooked food should be consumed with a sense of joy.
A twice-born man eating food should likewise perform the *āpośana* rite both before and after; thus, the food must be made neither naked nor dead.
While eating, a twice-born man must ensure that his food is neither "unclothed" nor "not nectar" by performing the rite known as *āpośana* both before and after;
the mention of "twice-born" applies to all stages of life (*āśrama*) from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) onwards. (1.106)
To those of the various classes who have arrived as guests, one should give according to one's ability and in due order.
A guest must not be turned away even in the evening, even if only with kind words, a place to sit, grass, or water.

After the Vaiśvadeva offering, when members of the various classes—beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—arrive simultaneously as guests, one should give according to one's ability in the order of the classes, starting with the Brāhmaṇas.
Even in the evening, if a guest arrives, he must not be turned away nor refused;
even if there is nothing edible to offer, one should still show hospitality with kind words, a seat, grass, and water.
As Manu said:
"Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous."
Thus [ends verse 1.107].
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous.
O monks, alms should be given with respect to one who observes virtuous vows;
and one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time.
Alms should be given to monks in general.
To one who observes the vows, a celibate student, and an ascetic, alms should be given with due respect and after pronouncing a blessing; this is the unprecedented method for giving alms.
Furthermore, the alms should be measured by mouthfuls.
A morsel (grāsa) is the size of a peacock’s egg; an alms-meal (bhikṣā) consists of such morsels; four times that is a puṣkala;
four of those make a hanta, and three times that is an agra.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Śātātapa:
at the time of eating, one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen who have arrived;
"friends" (sakhāyaḥ) refers to companions.
Relatives are those from whom a daughter has been taken or given; they are the kinsmen connected through the mother and the father. 1.108.
One should provide a large bull or a large goat to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya),
along with hospitable treatment, a seat, delicious food, and pleasant, truthful speech.

One should present a large bull, a draft animal, or a great goat to a *śrotriya* who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, saying, "This has been prepared by us for your sake"; this is for the purpose of pleasing him, not for the purpose of giving as a gift or for slaughter.

This is because it is said, "All this belongs to you," and because a bull is not available for every *śrotriya*; furthermore, because of the prohibition: "One should not practice even a duty that leads away from heaven or is loathed by the world."
Therefore, one must indeed perform hospitable treatment (*satkriyā*).
Hospitable treatment consists of welcoming words, the offering of a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and so forth.
Once he has sat down, sitting behind him is "sitting in attendance" (*anvāsana*).
"Delicious food" means sweet eating;
"pleasant speech" refers to such words as, "We are blessed today by your arrival," and so forth.

However, in the case of one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), it should be understood that the rule stated by Gautama applies: "For one who is not learned in the Vedas, [the offering consists of] water and a seat. (1.109)

However, every year the following are worthy of the guest-offering (arghya): a Snātaka, a teacher, a king, a dear friend, one for whom one’s daughter is being married, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice.
There are three types of *snātaka*: the *vidyā-snātaka*, the *vratasnātaka*, and the *vidyāvratasnātaka*.

He who returns home (*samāvartate*) after completing the Veda but without completing his vows is a *vidyā-snātaka*. He who returns home after completing his vows but without completing the Veda is a *vratasnātaka*.
He who returns home after completing both is a *vidyāvratasnātaka*.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit "samāpya... vratasnātakaḥ. The teacher (*ācārya*) has been defined by the aforementioned characteristics; the king (*pārthiva*) will have his characteristics described later.
A dear friend, a kinsman by marriage, and a son-in-law; by the word "and" (ca), the inclusion of fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others is intended.

"Having chosen the officiating priests (ṛtvij), one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka) to a Snātaka who has arrived, to a king, and to an Ācārya, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle"—so says the Smṛti of Āśvalāyana.
These individuals, beginning with the Snātaka, when they come to the house every year, are worthy of the Arghya offering; they are to be honored with the madhuparka and saluted.
The word *argha* here indicates the madhuparka.

And the officiating priests, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, are to be honored with the madhuparka offering at each sacrifice, even if it occurs within a year [of a previous one]. (1.110)
A traveler on the road and a *śrotriya* who has mastered the Vedas should be known as guests;
these two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahman.
A guest should be recognized as one who is traveling on a road.
Two śrotriyas who have mastered the Vedas and are traveling on a road, desiring to reach the world of Brahman, should be recognized as guests to be honored by a householder.
Even though one may be a śrotriya merely by virtue of Vedic study, here the term "śrotriya" refers specifically to one who is perfected in both learning and Vedic recitation.
One who has mastered the Vedas and is capable of teaching even a single branch [of the Veda]. || 1.111 ||
One should not take pleasure in food prepared by others, except when invited by those beyond reproach; one should avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating.
"One whose taste is for the cooking of others" is what is meant by "parapākaruci.
One should certainly not have a taste for the cooking of others.
[This applies] except when addressed by one who is beyond reproach.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "One should not depart when invited by one who is blameless.

Regarding "restlessness of speech, hands, and feet": *vāk-pāṇi-pāda* refers to speech, hands, and feet; one should avoid their restlessness. Restlessness of speech consists of speaking indecorous, false, and so forth.
Restlessness of the hands includes leaping, clapping, and so forth;
restlessness of the feet includes jumping and bounding, and so forth;
by the word "and" (ca), one should also avoid restlessness of the eyes and other senses.
"One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, the eyes, or speech," according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Gautama.
Likewise, one should avoid overeating, because it is a cause of ill health. (1.112)
One should follow a guest who is a learned Vedic scholar as far as the boundary of the village once he is satisfied;
for the remainder of the day, one should sit together with refined persons, beloved friends, and kinsmen.
One should follow as far as the boundary the aforementioned *śrotriya* guest and the guest who has mastered the Vedas once they have been satisfied with food and other offerings.

Then, after the meal, one should spend the remainder of the day sitting together with learned men (*śiṣṭa*) who know the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, with beloved ones who are adept at the elaborations of poetry and storytelling, and with kinsmen who are skilled in agreeable conversation. 1.113.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions, having offered oblations into those fires and attended to them,
and having eaten with his dependents until he is moderately satisfied, he should then go to rest.

Then, having performed the evening twilight devotion (*saṃdhyā*) according to the previously stated rule, and having offered oblations into the *Āhavanīya* and other fires or into a single fire, and having worshipped and approached them, he—surrounded by his dependents as mentioned before, such as his wives and others—should eat until he is not overly satiated; and by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), having settled the household concerns such as income and expenditure, he should thereafter retire and sleep. 1.114.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate what is beneficial for oneself;
one should not neglect virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) at their proper times, according to one's ability.

Then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and awakened during the final half-watch of the night, he should reflect upon his own welfare—both what has been accomplished and what is yet to be done—as well as doubts regarding the meaning of the Vedas;

for at that time, due to the mind's lack of agitation, it is fit for the discernment of reality (*tattva*). Thereafter, he should not abandon virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) according to his capacity, at their appropriate times.
The meaning is that one should pursue them as far as possible, because they constitute the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

As Gautama says: "One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; among dharma, artha, and kāma, one should give priority to dharma. Although here their pursuit is stated in general terms, nevertheless, desire (*kāma*) and wealth (*artha*) should be practiced without contradicting dharma, precisely because those two are rooted in dharma. Thus, this should be performed every day. (1.115)
They are to be honored according to their sequence by virtue of knowledge, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, if he possesses these in abundance, deserves honor on account of his old age.

Knowledge is that previously mentioned; ritual action consists of both Śrauta and Smārta rites; age is that which exceeds seventy years for oneself; kinship is the excellence of one's own people; wealth consists of villages, jewels, and so forth. Those endowed with these qualities are to be honored and worshipped in their respective order. Even a Śūdra, if endowed with these—knowledge, ritual action, kinship, and wealth—whether all of them or some of them, in abundance and fully developed, deserves honor in old age, that is, beyond eighty years, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Even a Śūdra is superior at eighty. (1.116)

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed the ritual bath, women, the sick, ascetics, and holders of the discus; among these, O King, the one who has performed the ritual bath is to be honored even by the king.
An "old man" (vṛddha) is one whose hair has turned grey; this is well known.
A "burdened man" (bhārī) is one overcome by a heavy load.
A "king" (nṛpa) is a lord of the earth, not merely a member of the Kṣatriya caste.
A "snātaka" is one who has completed his studies, his vows, or both. A "woman" is well known. A "sick person" is one afflicted by disease.
A bridegroom intent on marriage;
a potter; and a cartwright.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), those who are intoxicated, insane, and so forth are included, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "One should not [accept gifts] from children, the elderly, the intoxicated, the insane, those whose bodies are afflicted, those burdened by heavy loads, women, Snātakas, and renunciants."
The way must be yielded to these. When they approach from the opposite direction, one should step aside from the path oneself.
In the event that the elderly and others encounter the king on the road, the king is to be honored; therefore, the way must be yielded to him.
Even for a king, a *snātaka* is to be honored.
The mention of the *snātaka* is intended to include any *snātaka* whatsoever, not specifically a Brāhmaṇa, because the latter is always [automatically] venerable.
As Śaṅkha says: "Now, some say that the way should first be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, and then to the king."
And that is undesirable; for a teacher, an elder, and a Brāhmaṇa surpass even a king, [to whom it is said] "the way belongs to him.

When elders and others meet one another on the road, the distinction should be understood as being based on those who are more advanced in age and so forth, or by means of learning and other such qualities. || 1.117 ||
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are for the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
for the Brāhmaṇa, there is additionally the receiving of gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching.
For the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya—and by the word "and," for the Brāhmaṇa and those born in the direct order (anuloma) from the twice-born—sacrifice, study, and giving are the common duties.
For the Brāhmaṇa, there are additional [duties]: receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and teaching.
The phrase "likewise" includes the means of livelihood mentioned in other Smṛtis.

As Gautama has stated: "Agriculture, trade, or money-lending performed by oneself. However, teaching for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas occurs only when prompted by a Brāhmaṇa and not by their own will; for in times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, provided he follows him and serves him, and once it is completed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes his teacher—so says the Smṛti of Gautama.
These are the six duties of a Brāhmaṇa in times of non-distress.
Among those, three—sacrificing for others and so forth—are for the sake of dharma;
three—receiving gifts and so forth—are for the sake of livelihood. Of these six occupations, however, three are his means of subsistence:
sacrificing for others, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts.
Thus, according to the traditional law (smṛti) of Manu, sacrifices and the like must necessarily be performed, but not the acceptance of gifts and so forth.

For the Gautama-smṛti states: "For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving; for the Brāhmaṇa, additionally teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts; there is a restriction regarding the former [three]. (GDhS 10.1–3) || 1.118 ||
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;
for a Vaiśya, it is traditionally held to be moneylending, agriculture, trade, and animal husbandry.
For a Kṣatriya, the primary duty is the protection of the subjects, both for the sake of dharma and for the sake of livelihood.
For a Vaiśya, the duties for the sake of livelihood are moneylending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing;
moneylending is the application of capital for the purpose of interest.
Trade consists of buying and selling for the sake of profit;
the rest is well known: bearing weapons and missiles is the duty of the Kṣatriya, while commerce, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya.
However, the righteous means of livelihood consist of giving, study, and sacrifice.
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Manu [1.119].
The Śūdra’s duty is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born.

For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is the primary duty, both for the sake of merit and for the sake of livelihood. Among these, service to Brāhmaṇas is the supreme duty; indeed, service to the Vipras alone is proclaimed as the distinguished task of a Śūdra, according to the traditional teaching of Manu.
When, however, he is unable to live by serving the twice-born, then he may live by the occupation of a merchant,
or by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born;
the meaning is that he should perform such works as do not render him unfit for the service of the twice-born.

And those duties of the Śūdra spoken by Devala are: service to the twice-born, avoidance of sin, the maintenance of one's wife and others, agriculture, cattle-rearing, carrying burdens, trade in merchandise, the arts of painting, dancing, singing, and playing the flute, lute, drum, mṛdaṅga, and other instruments. 1.120.
Moreover:
Delighting in his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha),
he should not neglect the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation (namaskāra).
One who finds pleasure and approaches only his own wife, and not common women or the wives of others, is so described.
He is pure, endowed with both external and internal cleanliness like a twice-born (brahmin),
and is a supporter of his dependents and others.

Devoted to the performance of *śrāddha* rites—namely, the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddhas*—and to those non-contradictory actions which are the vows of a *snātaka*, he should not neglect, but should perform day after day the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) previously mentioned by means of the mantra "Namaḥ.
And some [mention] the mantra of salutation: "To the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis..."
Salutation to Svāhā and to Svadhā; salutation, salutation always.
Thus they describe it;
others say "namas.
Regarding this, the teachers maintain that the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should be performed in the common (laukika) fire, not in the nuptial fire. 1.121.
Now he states the common duties:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
charity, self-control, compassion, and patience are the means for the practice of dharma for all.

Himsā is the infliction of suffering upon living beings; its non-performance is ahiṃsā. Satya is speech that is truthful and does not cause suffering to living beings. Asteya is the non-appropriation of what has not been given.
Purity is both external and internal. Restraint of the senses consists in the sense organs and organs of action engaging only with their prescribed objects.
Charity consists in the removal of the suffering of living beings by giving food, water, and so forth, according to one's ability.
Self-restraint is the control of the internal organ;
compassion is the protection of those in distress;
and patience is the absence of mental fluctuation even when faced with injury.
Thus, all these [duties] are the means for accomplishing dharma for all persons, from the Brāhmaṇa down to the Caṇḍāla. || 1.122 ||
One should likewise conduct oneself with a behavior that is consistent with one’s age, intelligence, wealth, speech, dress, learning, birth, and actions— straightforward and free from deceit.
Age refers to childhood, youth, and so forth;
intellect is the innate capacity for worldly and Vedic affairs;
and wealth consists of property, houses, fields, and the like.
Speech is the act of speaking; dress is the arrangement of garments, garlands, and so forth;
learning is the hearing of the treatises on the goals of human life.
*Abhijana* means family lineage;
*karman* refers to activities such as receiving gifts for the sake of livelihood.
One should practice—that is, adopt—the conduct appropriate and fitting for these [categories], beginning with age.

Just as an elder [acts] in a manner appropriate to his own age, and not in a manner appropriate to youth; so too should this be applied to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties. "Straight" (*ajihmām*) means not crooked.
Free from deceit and free from envy. || 1.123 ||
Having thus enumerated the Smārta rites in sequence, he now enumerates the Śrauta rites:
"A twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of food may drink Soma;
one who has an annual supply of food should perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice."

Only he who possesses food sufficient for three years, or more than that, for the maintenance of his livelihood according to the three aims of life, should perform the Soma sacrifice, and not one with less wealth than that; therefore, the twice-born who drinks Soma when his resources are very meager does not obtain its fruit, even though he has previously drunk Soma.
Because such faults are heard [in the scriptures].
And this refers to optional rites (*kāmya*);
as for the obligatory rite (*nitya*), since it must necessarily be performed, there is no restriction (*niyama*).

He who possesses food sufficient for a year's livelihood should perform the rites prior to the Soma sacrifice—namely, the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Āgrayaṇa, the Paśu, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, as well as their modifications. These are the "prāksaumikī" (pre-Soma) rites. Which are they? They are these aforementioned rituals. || 1.124 ||
Having thus described the optional rites prescribed by the Śruti, he now states the obligatory ones: "The Soma sacrifice is to be performed every year, as is the animal sacrifice at each solstice;
likewise, the Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be performed."
The Soma sacrifice is to be performed every year.
The Nirūḍhapaśuyāga is to be performed at each solstice, known as the southern and northern courses (*ayanāyanayoḥ*).
Likewise, it may be performed every year; for Baudhāyana is heard to say, "One should sacrifice with an animal every year, or every six months" (NSP edition omits *baudhāyana*).
The Āgrayaṇa sacrifice must be performed upon the emergence of the grain harvest, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must be performed every year. || 1.125 ||
In the absence of these, the twice-born should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
one should not perform a rite with deficient materials when the necessary substances are available, for it yields no fruit.

If, for some reason, it is impossible to perform these aforementioned obligatory rites beginning with the Soma sacrifice at that time, one should instead perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice. Furthermore, this deficient rite (hīnakalpa) which has been described should not be performed when the proper materials are available;
and that optional rite (kāmya) which yields specific fruits—one should not perform it in a deficient manner, nor should it be performed as such. Thus reads the NSP edition. || 1.126 ||
One becomes a Caṇḍāla by performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra;
if one does not give what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one will become a vulture or even a crow.
