By begging for the wealth of a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice, one is born as a Caṇḍāla in another birth.
Furthermore, he who begs for the sake of a sacrifice but does not give away everything that was requested—nor relinquishes it—shall become a Bāsa bird or even a crow for a hundred years.
As Manu has said: "He who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all..."
That Brahmin goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.
Thus:
"The Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not give it all away, goes to the state of a vulture or a crow for a hundred years."
Bhāsa is a bird;
the crow is well known. || 1.127 ||
"Or one who possesses grain in a *kuśūla* or a *kumbhī*, or one who has provisions for three days, or even one who does not have enough for tomorrow.
A *kuśūla* is a granary; a *kumbhī* is a small jar. One whose grain is measured by both a *kuśūla* and a *kumbhī* is called a *kuśūladhānya* or a *kumbhīdhānya*.
Among these, one who possesses grain sufficient for the nourishment of his own family for only twelve days is a *kuśūladhānya*.

One who has grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*) is one who possesses enough grain to sustain his own family for exactly six days. One who has grain sufficient for three days is called *tryāhika*. One who has grain that will last until tomorrow is called *śvastana*.
One for whom there is no provision for tomorrow is called "ashvastana."
He states the means for accumulating stores such as grain in a granary:
"Or one may live by gleaning ears of corn or picking up single grains; among these [means of livelihood], each subsequent one is superior."
*Śila* is the gathering of fallen and discarded stalks of rice and other grains.

*Uñcha* is the picking up of individual, scattered grains. By means of this *śila* or *uñcha*, a householder may live according to one of four modes, such as possessing grain sufficient for a single granary (*kuśūladhānya*) and so forth.
Among these four types of Brāhmaṇa householders—beginning with those who possess grain in a granary—the one mentioned later and later is superior and more praiseworthy.

And although the "twice-born" (dvija) is the subject under discussion, this [distinction] must apply to the Brāhmaṇa alone, because of his possession of learning, tranquility, and other such qualities.
Thus it has been said by Manu: "By not harming living beings, or at least by causing them very little harm..."
Adopting that mode of livelihood, a Brahmin should live in times of non-distress.
Thus, having introduced the Brahmin specifically, [the text] states: "He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or even grain sufficient for a jar," and so forth.
This is said with reference to the *yāyāvara* who is not excessively restrained, and not with the intention of referring to the Brahmin in general.

If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with the statement: "That twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain may indeed drink Soma. Furthermore, the twofold nature of householders has been stated in various places.
As Devala said: "The householder is of two kinds: the *yāyāvara* and the *śālīna*.
Of these two, the *yāyāvara* is superior because he avoids officiating at sacrifices, teaching, accepting gifts, and the accumulation of inheritance.
The *śālīna*, however, is established in the six duties; he possesses servants, quadrupeds, a house, a village, wealth, and grain, and he conforms to worldly ways."
The *śālīna* is also of four kinds: one lives by the six means of livelihood—officiating at sacrifices, teaching, receiving gifts, agriculture, trade, and animal husbandry;
another by three, beginning with officiating at sacrifices;
and another by two, namely officiating at sacrifices and teaching.
But the fourth [type of Brahmin] exists solely through teaching.
Thus Manu says:
"One among these performs six duties; another proceeds by means of three."
One lives by two [of these], while the fourth lives by the Brahma-sattra.
Thus:
"One among these performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the *brahmasattra*."
And here, by the passage beginning "In this regard, acceptance [of gifts] is additional for a Brahmin," the modes of livelihood for the *śālīna* are shown;
likewise, for the *yāyāvara*, they are "by gleaning ears of grain" (*śiloñcha*). || 1.128 ||

Having thus described the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis, he now sets forth the observances of a Snātaka—a Brāhmaṇa who must perform them as mandatory duties—which consist of injunctions and prohibitions and take the form of mental resolves:
"He should not strive for wealth that conflicts with Vedic study, nor from whatever source it may come;
he should not engage in forbidden pursuits, and he should always remain content."
The means for a Brahmin to acquire wealth, such as receiving gifts and so forth, have been shown.
Regarding this, a specific rule is stated: he should not pursue, nor seek after, wealth that is contrary to his Vedic study, even if it is not otherwise forbidden.
"Not from here and there" means not from any source whatsoever whose conduct is unknown.

"By way of forbidden pursuits (*viruddhaprasaṅgena*)," where "forbidden acts" (*viruddha*) refers to officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice (*ayājyayājanādi*), and "pursuits" (*prasaṅga*) refers to dancing, singing, and so forth; "forbidden pursuits" is a compound of both "the forbidden" and "pursuits.
This is to be connected with the phrase "one should not seek wealth thereby."
The negation (nañ) is a restrictive exclusion (paryudāsa) with respect to each [term].
Throughout this entire section concerning the *snātaka*, the word "not" (nañ) serves exclusively as a restrictive exclusion for each individual item.
Furthermore, even when one's desires are not fulfilled, one should be content and remain fully satisfied.

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that he should also be self-restrained; for the *Manusmṛti* states: "Seeking happiness, one should become self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment. (1.129)
From whom, then, should he seek wealth? To this he says:
"One who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from kings, pupils, and those for whom he performs sacrifices;
but he should avoid those who are hypocritical, those who rely on mere reasoning, heretics, and those who act like herons."

A *snātaka* who is sinking and being oppressed by hunger may take wealth from a king whose conduct is known to him, from a pupil possessing the characteristics to be described, or from a sacrificer worthy of officiating at sacrifices.

By the phrase "sinking through hunger," it is understood that one who possesses sufficient wealth for the maintenance of his family—obtained through inheritance and other means—should not seek wealth from anyone else.
Furthermore, he should avoid hypocrites, sophists, and the like in all matters, whether worldly, Vedic, or scriptural.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), those who persist in improper actions, those who follow the "vow of the cat," and the deceitful are included,
as Manu has said: "Heretics, those who persist in improper actions, those who follow the 'vow of the cat,' and the deceitful..."
One should not honor, even with mere words, those who rely on fallacious reasoning and those who act like herons.
Thus:

"One should not honor with even a mere word those who follow heretical paths, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats, the deceitful, the rationalists, and those who behave like herons."
The hypocrite is one who performs ritual actions solely for the sake of pleasing the world.
The rationalist is one who casts doubt everywhere by means of logical reasoning.
The heretics are those who have embraced stages of life that are contrary to the three Vedas.
"Baka-vṛtti" (the crane-like mode of life) refers to one whose conduct is like that of a crane.
As Manu says:
"One who looks downward, who is deceitful, and who is solely intent on achieving his own ends..."
One who is deceitful and falsely humble is described as having the conduct of a heron.
Thus:
"One who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends,
crafty, and falsely humble, is described as one who behaves like a heron."
Those who practice what is forbidden are established in improper conduct.
A *biḍāla* is a cat; one whose vow (*vrata*) or nature (*svabhāva*) is that of a cat is a *baiḍālavratika*.
Manu has stated its defining characteristic:

One who carries the banner of Dharma while being always greedy, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world; one who is violent and intent on deceiving all—such a person should be known as a "cat-vowed" hypocrite.

Thus, one who always carries the banner of righteousness while being greedy, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world; who follows the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratika), is violent, and intent on deceiving everyone—such a person should be known as a hypocrite.
The "deceitful" (śaṭha) is crooked in all respects.
From the very prohibition of association with these [types of people], it is understood that one should not become such oneself. 1.130.
Furthermore: Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails kept short, and being pure,
he should not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing.
One who wears two garments of white, washed cloth is called "white-robed" (*śuklāmbaradhara*).
One whose hair, beard, and nails are short—that is, cut down—is so described.
One should be pure both internally and externally, and fragrant through bathing, unguents, incense, garlands, and the like.
As Gautama says: "A *snātaka* should always be pure, fragrant, and accustomed to bathing. From this very injunction regarding fragrance, the prohibition of scentless garlands follows.
And so Gobhila states: "One should not wear a scentless garland, except for garlands made of gold or jewels."
One who has completed his studies (snātaka) should always be such as this;
and this applies when it is possible [to do so], for there is a traditional teaching (smṛti) stating: "He should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes if he possesses the means."

Furthermore, one should not eat while seeing his wife standing before him, for fear that the offspring born will lack vigor. Thus says the Śruti: "One should not eat in the presence of his wife; [otherwise] the offspring will be lacking in vigor."
Therefore, eating together with her is rejected from afar;
nor should one eat while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing, nor while rising—thus the rule is connected. 1.131.
Furthermore:
one should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is untrue, nor should one be a thief or a usurer.
At no time whatsoever should one undertake or perform an action that brings about doubt or entails the risk of loss of life—

such as, for example, entering a region infested by tigers, thieves, and the like. Nor should one, without cause or provocation, speak unpleasant or distressing words to any person, whether man or woman.
Nor should one speak what is harmful, nor what is false, even if it is pleasant;
by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is connected that one should not suddenly speak what is vulgar, uncivilized, or loathsome.
And this applies except in cases such as jesting.
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "One should even laugh together with one's teacher, provided it is not crooked.
Furthermore, he would not be a thief, for a thief is one who takes what belongs to another without it being given.
He shall not be a usurer;
a usurer is one who lives by interest that has been forbidden. 1.132.
Furthermore: A woman of the Dakṣas, one wearing the sacred thread, one carrying a bamboo staff, and one carrying a water-pot—
these should perform circumambulation around a deity, a mound of earth, a cow, a Brahmin, and a large tree.
One who possesses gold in the form of a *dākṣāyaṇa* ornament is called *dākṣāyaṇī*. One who possesses the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) or sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*) is called *brahmasūtrī*.
[He is] one who possesses a bamboo staff (*vaiṇavayaṣṭimān*).
"He shall possess a water-pot"—
this should be connected everywhere.
And here, although the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) has already been mentioned in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), it is stated again for the purpose of obtaining a second one.
As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"For those who have completed their studentship (snātakas), there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper garment,
two sacred threads (yajñopavītas), a staff, and a water-pot with water."
Thus it is said.
And here, although there is the general designation "Dākṣāyaṇī," the wearing of earrings specifically is intended, as in: "One should carry a Vaiṣṇava staff and a water-pot with water;
a sacred thread, a Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu:
likewise, one should circumambulate the deity—that is, the image of a divinity—clay taken from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, and trees such as the Aśvattha;
the meaning is that one should set these to one's right and then proceed on one's way.
In this same way, one should also circumambulate crossroads and the like, as well as earth, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroad, and well-known trees.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu. 1.133.
But one should not urinate in a river, in shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one face fire, the sun, cows, the moon, the twilight, water, women, or the twice-born.
One should not urinate in rivers and similar places, nor should one discharge urine or feces there;
the same applies to cremation grounds and the like.

As Śaṅkha says: "One should not urinate on cow-dung, ploughed land, sown fields, grassy plots, funeral pyres, cremation grounds, anthills, paths, threshing floors, cow-pens, holes, mountains, or riverbanks, because these are the abodes of living beings."
Likewise, one should not urinate facing fire and other such things, nor while looking at them.
As Gautama says: "One should not cast away urine, feces, or impurities while facing the wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows; nor should one extend one's feet toward them."
Apart from these places, one should void urine and feces after covering the ground with grass unfit for sacrifice;
as Vasiṣṭha says: "Having covered his head and having covered the ground with grass unfit for sacrifice, he should void urine and feces. (1.134)
One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one who is impure look at urine, feces, or the stars during an eclipse.

Although it is stated here in general terms that "one should not look at the sun," nevertheless, it is only the looking at the sun when it is rising, setting, eclipsed by Rāhu, reflected in water, or at midday that is forbidden, and not at all times.
As Manu has said:
"One should never look at the sun as it is rising, nor as it is setting."
Neither afflicted by portents, nor situated in water, nor gone to the middle of the sky.
Thus it is said:
"One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky."
One should not look at a naked woman except during sexual intercourse;
"one should not look at a naked woman except for the purpose of mating," so says Āśvalāyana. This refers to one with whom sexual union has been engaged in, or whose enjoyment has already taken place.

One should not look at her even when she is not naked at the end of a meal; by the use of the word "and" (ca), [the text implies] one should also not look at her while she is engaged in eating and so forth.
And thus says Manu:
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease.
A twice-born man who desires his own welfare should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth.
Thus it is said: He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
nor when she is sneezing or yawning, nor when she is seated at her ease.
A twice-born man who desires his own welfare should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her eyes, nor one who is anointed with unguents, nor one who is uncovered, nor one giving birth.
One should not look at urine or feces.
Likewise, being impure, one should not look at Rāhu or the stars.
By the use of "and" (ca), it is implied that one should not see one's own reflection in water, nor should one gaze at one's own form in water; such is the dhāraṇā.
Because of this statement. 1.135.
One should recite every mantra thus: "This is my vajra.
One may go about unsheltered during rain, and one should not sleep with the head facing west.
While it is raining, he should recite the mantra: "May this vajra of mine drive away evil.

While it is raining, he should not go out, nor run, nor rush about uncovered or unsheltered, because of the prohibition: "one should not [do so] while it is raining. Nor should he sleep with his head toward the west.

From the word "and" (ca), it follows that one should not sleep naked; for there are the traditional injunctions of Manu stating, "nor should one sleep alone in an empty house," and "one should not sleep naked," and "one should not sleep alone in an empty house. (1.136)
One should not cast spittle, blood, feces, urine, or semen into water;
nor should one warm one's feet over a fire, nor step over it.
Spittle is saliva; blood is *asṛj*; feces is *śakṛt*; the remainder is well known.
One should not throw these into water.
The same applies to chaff and so forth.

As Śaṅkha says: "One should not throw husks, hair, excrement, ashes, bones, phlegm, nails, or body hair into water; nor should one strike the water with the foot or the hand. And one should not warm one's feet over fire, nor should one step over the fire.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that one should not cast spittle and other such things into the fire,
nor should one perform actions such as blowing on the fire with the mouth.
And so says Manu:
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor should one look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor should one warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it underneath anything, nor should one step over it;
one should not treat it with one's feet, nor should one commit the killing of living beings.
Thus [ends verse 1.137].
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it underneath anything, nor should one step over it;
one should not treat it as if it were beneath one's feet, nor should one commit the slaughter of living beings.
One should not drink water from one's cupped hands, nor should one awaken a sleeping person;
one should not play with dice, nor should one lie down with those who destroy dharma or those who are afflicted by disease.
One should not drink water with the hands joined together in the *añjali* gesture;
the mention of "water" here is an illustration for any liquid fit for drinking.
One should not awaken—that is, rouse from sleep—a person who is superior to oneself in learning and other qualities.
One should not wake Śreyāṃsa, according to the specific traditional injunction;
one should not play with dice and the like,
nor should one play with those who have violated the Dharma by means of animal sacrifices and similar acts.
One should not sit or lie down in one place together with those who are diseased or overcome by fever and other ailments. (1.138)
One should avoid forbidden actions, the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river [by swimming],
and staying upon hair, ashes, chaff, charcoal, or a skull.
One should avoid actions contrary to the customs of the country, the village, or the family.
It is understood that one should also avoid the smoke from a funeral pyre and crossing a river by means of one's arms.
One should avoid remaining among hair and other such impurities.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), [the rule applies] also to bones, cotton, and impure substances. || 1.139 ||
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter a place by a side door;
one should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures.
One should not point out to another a cow suckling milk from another, nor should one turn her away.
One should never enter a city, a village, or a temple by an improper gate or by a wrong path.
Furthermore, one should not accept gifts from a miserly king who transgresses the sacred scriptures.
Regarding the acceptance of gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, the prostitute, and the king are wicked;
each of these is ten times more wicked than the one preceding it, respectively.
When the act of receiving [gifts] is to be established, the five beginning with the butcher (*sūnī*) are each ten times more blameworthy than the preceding one.
A *sūnī* is one who possesses *sūnā*, which is the slaughter of living beings; thus, he is one intent on the slaughter of living beings.
A *cakrī* is an oil-presser.
The "banner-bearer" is a liquor-seller;
the "prostitute" is a woman for sale; the "lord of men" is the one mentioned immediately above. || 1.141 ||
Now he states the rules for the study of the Veda:

"The commencement of the term for the recitation of the chapters (adhyāya) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the constellation Śravaṇa; or under the constellation Hasta when the medicinal herbs have appeared, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa."

The term *adhyāya* refers to the Vedas, which are to be studied. Their *upākarma*—the commencement of study—should be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* when the herbs have appeared, either on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, or on a day joined with the *Śravaṇa* asterism, or on the fifth lunar day joined with the *Hasta* asterism.
However, when the herbs do not appear in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform it in the month of Bhādrapada under the *Śravaṇa* asterism.
Thereafter, one should study the Vedas for four and a half months.
And so Manu says:
"Having performed the Upākarma ceremony according to the rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brāhmaṇa, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months."

Thus: "Having performed the *upākarma* ceremony according to the rule on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedic hymns for four and a half months. || 1.142 ||
The time for the Utsarga ceremony:
on the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
one should perform the formal Utsarga of the Vedas outside [the village] near water according to the prescribed rule.

On the Rohiṇī asterism of the month of Pauṣa, or on the Aṣṭakā day, one should perform the Utsarga (the ritual suspension) of the Chandas (Vedas) outside the village near water, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
However, when the Upākarma is performed in the month of Bhādrapada, then one should perform the Utsarga on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
as stated by Manu:
In the month of Pauṣa, a twice-born man should perform the external suspension (utsarjana) of the Vedic hymns;
or, when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, he should do so in the forenoon.
Thus:
"In the month of Pauṣa, however, a twice-born man should perform the external Utsarjana of the Vedas;
or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, he should do so in the forenoon."
Immediately after that, having ceased for a day and night, he should study the Vedas during the bright fortnights and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) during the dark fortnights.
As Manu has said:
"Having thus performed the ritual dismissal (*utsarga*) of the Vedic hymns outside [the village] according to the scriptures..."
One should cease [the practice] for a night with two watches, or even for one day and night.
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and one should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.
Thus [ends the verse]. 1.143.
Having thus performed the formal dismissal of the Vedic hymns outside according to the scriptures,
one should cease [the study] for a night with its two flanking days (pakṣiṇī), or else for a single day and night.
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and one should study all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas during the dark fortnights.
He states the occasions when study is forbidden: "There is a three-day suspension of study upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative;
likewise at the commencement (upākarma) and the conclusion (utsarga) of the Vedic term, and when a person learned in one's own Vedic branch (śrotriya) has died."

For a twice-born student studying according to the prescribed rule, there is a three-day suspension of study—meaning he should avoid recitation for three days and nights—when his pupils, officiating priests, teachers, or relatives have died.
When the rites of *upākarma* and *utsarga* have been performed, there is likewise a three-day suspension of study.
Regarding the *utsarga*, however, this [three-day rule] is optional with the *pakṣiṇī* (a day-and-night flanked by two days) mentioned by Manu.
When a learned scholar of one's own Vedic branch or a student of one's own Vedic branch has died, there is a suspension of study for three days. (1.144)

In the event of thunder at twilight, a lightning strike, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor, one should remain fasting for a day and a night; likewise after completing the study of the Veda or having studied the Āraṇyaka.

At twilight, when there is the sound of clouds; during a thunderclap or an ominous sound in the sky; during an earthquake; at the fall of a meteor; and upon the completion of the recitation of a mantra or a Brāhmaṇa text, as well as during the study of the Āraṇyakas, there shall be no study for a day and night (ahorātra). 1.145.
On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, or the eighth lunar day; during an eclipse of Rāhu; at the junctions of the seasons; or having eaten, or having accepted a gift at a Śrāddha ceremony.

On the fifteenth day, the new moon, the full moon, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during the birth of Rāhu (an eclipse), and during an eclipse of the moon or sun, there is a suspension of study for a day and night. As for the statement, "One should not recite the Veda for three days during the birth of a king or of Rāhu," that refers to the period when [the sun or moon] has been eclipsed and has set. (Pāṇḍeya and Setlur read: *grastāstamayaviṣayam*).

On the first days following the junctions of the seasons (*ṛtusaṃdhi*), there is a suspension of Vedic study for a day and night regarding the eating of food at a *śrāddha* and the acceptance of such gifts. This rule applies to cases other than the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; however, in that case, the period is three nights: "Having accepted an invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa*, a learned twice-born man [must not study for three nights]."
"One should not recite the Veda for three days," according to the traditional legal text (smṛti). 1.146.

When an interval is created by a domestic animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a rat, it constitutes a day and night; likewise when there is the falling or the rising of Indra's banner.

When animals or the like pass between students while they are studying, there is a suspension of study for a full day and night (ahorātra) on the day the staff of Indra (Śakradhvaja) is lowered and on the day it is raised.

Although "day and night" (dyuniśam) was already established as the context, the explicit mention of "day and night" (ahorātra) here is intended to indicate that the suspension lasts until the same time the following day in the event of thundering at twilight, a atmospheric crash (nirghāta), an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor (ulkā); for Gautama states: "A meteor, an earthquake, a thunderous crash, and the sight of Rāhu [eclipse] last until the same time [the next day]. Starting from the time of the occurrence of the cause, the period until the same time on the following day is called "non-time" (akāla); the suspension of study occurring during that interval is "until the same time" (ākālika).
And this [penance] applies when there is thunder during the morning twilight;

however, when there is thunder during the evening twilight, it lasts for the night alone, and when there is thunder during the morning twilight, it lasts for a full day and night, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Hārīta: "But when there is thunder during the evening twilight, it is for the night; when during the morning twilight, it is for a day and night.

As for what was stated by Gautama—"Upon the passage between [the teacher and the student] of a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a cat, there shall be a three-day fast and staying away from home"—that refers specifically to the first lesson [of Vedic study]. (1.147)
In the presence of the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, the *sāman* chants, or the cry of the wounded;
or near impure substances, a corpse, a *śūdra*, an outcaste, a cemetery, or one who has fallen from his caste.
A dog is a *śvā*;
a jackal is a *kroṣṭā*;
a donkey is a *gardabha*.
The owl is the *ghūka*;
the *sāman* is the *sāmans*;
the arrow is the bamboo flute.
A person seeking wealth is one who is suffering.
There is a suspension of study for as long as the barking of these animals, such as dogs, continues;
likewise, even when there is the sound of lutes and similar instruments.
"Regarding the sounds of flutes, lutes, kettledrums, clay drums, and carts," according to the statement of Gautama;
"cart" (gantrī) means a wagon.
In the proximity of impure substances and the like, there is a temporary suspension of study (anadhyāya). 1.148.
In an impure place, or when one is oneself impure; during a flash of lightning or a clap of thunder;
after eating while the hands are still wet; within water; at midnight; or during an excessive windstorm.
In an impure place and when one is oneself impure;

likewise, during a flash of lightning—when lightning flashes repeatedly—and during a peal of thunder, there is a suspension of study for two watches (six hours) as long as the sound of the clouds continues.
Having eaten, one should not study while the hands are still wet.
And in the midst of water;
at midnight, known as the "great night," during the two middle watches; and when there is excessive wind—even during the day—at such times one should not study. || 1.149 ||
When there is a dust storm, a conflagration, a journey, fear of mist,
running, a foul odor, or when a learned man has arrived at the house.
During a sudden dust storm;
when there is a conflagration of the quarters where the directions appear as if ablaze;
during the two twilights; in mist and fog; and during fears caused by thieves, kings, and the like—there is no study at those times.
There is no study while running or moving quickly;

nor when there is a foul odor, such as the smell of impure substances, wine, and the like; nor when a learned man, such as a *śrotriya*, has arrived at one's house, until he has given his permission. (1.150)
When there is the sound of donkeys, camels, vehicles, elephants, horses, or boats, or when trees are being uprooted from a barren field—
these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interruptions for study.
A vehicle refers to a chariot and the like. A barren tract refers to saline soil or a desert region.
Upon mounting these, as well as donkeys and similar animals, there is a suspension of study for that duration of time.

Thus, those who know the rules for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) understand these thirty-seven suspensions—beginning from "the barking of dogs, jackals, and donkeys"—to be temporary, coinciding with the specific occasion.
By the word "understand" (viduḥ), he includes others mentioned in other Smṛtis;
as Manu says:

One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor while sitting with a cloth wrapped around the knees; nor after eating meat, nor after consuming food from a house where a birth or death has occurred. 1.151.
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor while using a cloth between the knees; nor after eating meat or food from a house where a birth-impurity (sūtaka) has occurred.
And so forth.

Having thus stated the occasions when study is prohibited, he now declares the established observances for a *snātaka*: "One should not step upon the shadow of a god, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a *snātaka*, a teacher (*ācārya*), or a king, nor that of another's wife,
nor blood, excrement, urine, spittle, ointments, and the like."

One should not intentionally step upon, stand upon, or cross over the shadow of the gods, of images of the gods, of officiating priests, of those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātaka), of teachers, of kings, or of another man’s wife.
As Manu has said:
"Of the deities, of one's guru, of the king, and likewise of the snātaka and the teacher..."
One should not intentionally step on the shadow of a tawny person or of one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
Thus:

"One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a guru, a king, a *snātaka*, a teacher, nor likewise that of one who is tawny (babhru) or one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*)."

One should not step upon anything that is brown or the color of a mongoose—whether it be a cow, or any other animal such as a dark-colored one; for the word "brown" (*babhru*) is used here in the neuter gender. Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), water used for bathing and similar substances are also included among those things one should not step upon.
One should not intentionally step upon a body-scrub, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
Thus [ends verse] 1.152.
One should not intentionally step upon body-unguents, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
Brahmins and those whose nature is that of kṣatriyas should never be treated with contempt;
until death one should desire prosperity, and one should not touch anyone in their vital parts.
A learned Brahmin, a snake, and a Kshatriya king—these should never be despised.
Nor should one's own self be despised.
Until death, throughout one's life, one should desire prosperity.
One should not strike at the vital point of any person whatsoever, nor should one disclose the misconduct of anyone else that strikes at their vital point. (1.153)
One should cast away remnants of food, feces, urine, and water from the feet from a distance;
one should always properly practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
One should discard food scraps and the like, as well as feces, urine, and water used for washing the feet, far from the house.
One should always properly observe the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti. 1.154.
One who is impure from eating should not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food with his feet;
nor should he revile or strike them. However, he may strike his son or his pupil [for the sake of correction].

One who is impure shall not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food—especially that which is cooked—with his foot, even if he is not rendered impure by remnants of food. However, when he touches these through negligence, then after performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he must always touch his vital organs with water, according to the rule: "Having touched these while impure, one should constantly touch the vital organs with water."
And likewise all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.
Thus, one should perform the duties as stated by Manu.
In this manner, one should touch the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth;
furthermore, one should not engage in reviling or striking anyone at all.

And this applies even when no harm has been done: "By causing blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting, a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death."
Thus:
"By causing blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting,
a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death."
One should strike a son or a pupil solely for the purpose of instruction;
by the use of the word "and" (ca), this includes slaves and others as well.

Furthermore, the striking must be performed with a rope or similar implement, avoiding the head; for Gautama states: "The correction of a pupil is without corporal punishment; if that is impossible, it may be done with a thin rope or a split bamboo cane; one who strikes with anything else is to be punished by the king. Moreover, it should be on the back of the body and never on the head.
Thus, according to the statement of Manu (1.155).
One should practice dharma with effort through deed, mind, and speech;
however, one should not practice even that which is consistent with dharma if it leads away from heaven or is despised by the world.
One should practice the Dharma through action with the body according to one's ability, contemplate that very same Dharma with the mind, and speak it with speech.

However, one should not perform even a prescribed act that is consistent with the Dharma if it is hated by the world or causes public censure—such as the slaughter of a cow for the *madhuparka* offering—because such an act does not lead to heaven, unlike the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice which is a means to attain heaven. || 1.156 ||
With mother, father, guests, brothers, paternal and maternal kinsmen,
maternal uncles, the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and relatives;
By avoiding disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, children, wives, slaves, and kinsmen, a householder shall conquer all the worlds.
Mother is the progenitress;
father is the progenitor;
a guest is one who travels on the road.
Brothers, even those born of different wombs;
female relatives (jāmayah), namely women whose husbands are living; and kinsmen by marriage (saṃbandhinaḥ).
A maternal uncle is the brother of one's mother.
An elder is one whose age is over seventy. A child is one up to sixteen years of age.
The patient is the sick person;
the teacher is the one who initiates [the student];
the physician is the learned man or the healer.
A dependent is one who lives off another.
"Relatives" refers to those on the father's side and those on the mother's side.
The separate mention of the maternal uncle is for the sake of showing respect.
An *ṛtvij* is a sacrificial priest;
a *purohita* is one who performs rites for pacification and so forth;
and *apatya* refers to offspring, such as sons and the like.
The wife is the partner in the practice of dharma;
the slave is the laborer.
The mention of "kinsmen" (sanābhayaḥ) as distinct from "brothers" (bhrātṛbhyaḥ) is for the purpose of including sisters who are not uterine.
By abandoning verbal quarrels with these [elders], such as one's mother and others, one attains all the worlds beginning with that of Prajāpati. || 1.157 || 1.158 ||
One should not bathe in the waters of others without first removing five lumps [of earth];
however, one may bathe in rivers, natural pools, lakes, and springs.

In waters belonging to others—that is, in reservoirs such as ponds and the like which have not been relinquished for the sake of all beings—one should not bathe without first removing five lumps [of earth]. By this, bathing even without the removal of lumps is permitted in cases that are one's own, abandoned, or authorized.
As to how it should be in rivers and the like, he says: "One may bathe in a river."
Rivers are streams that flow toward the ocean, either directly or indirectly.
A "devakhāta" (divine excavation) refers to a place such as Puṣkara, created by the gods.
A "hrada" (lake) is a deep depression filled with water, formed by the impact of flowing currents.
A spring (*prasravaṇa*) is water flowing from a high place such as a mountain.
One should bathe in these [five types of water] by means of drawing out five handfuls (*pañcapiṇḍa*).
And this refers to the obligatory daily bath (*nityasnāna*), provided it is possible; [otherwise, one should bathe] in rivers, in pools dug by the gods (*devakhāta*), in lakes, and in ponds.
One should always perform one's bath in natural pools or at springs.
This is because of the mention of "constantly" [in the preceding rule].

However, for the purpose of purification, there is no prohibition against drawing five lumps of earth from other waters as far as possible, nor even when drawing from the entire body of water. (1.159)
One should avoid another's bed, seat, garden, house, and vehicle;
one should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress.
A bed is a mattress;
a seat is a stool and the like;
a garden is a grove of mango trees and so forth.
A house is well known.
A vehicle refers to a chariot and so forth.
One should avoid—that is, one should not make use of—these things belonging to another that have not been given or authorized.
Regarding those whose food is not to be eaten, [the author] says "of one who has lost the sacred fires" (agnihīnasya).

One should not, except in times of distress, eat the food of, nor accept gifts from, one who has lost the sacred fires—that is, a Śūdra who is devoid of the entitlement to the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, or even one of mixed caste (*pratiloma*) who possesses such entitlement but lacks the fires; for there is the statement of Gautama: "A Brāhmaṇa should eat and accept gifts from those who are praiseworthy and pure by birth through their own duties. (1.160)
[The food] of misers, bound thieves, eunuchs, actors,
flute-players, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated into a guild;
A miser is one who is greedy; he is known as a miser who, out of greed, causes suffering to himself, his religious duties, and his children and wife,
as well as to his parents and dependents.
Thus it was said.
"Bound" means fettered with shackles and the like, or restrained by speech.
A "thief" is one who steals the property of another, excluding the gold of a Brahmin.
A *klība* is a eunuch.
A stage-player (*raṅgāvatārī*) refers to an actor, a bard, a wrestler, and so forth.
One who lives by cutting bamboo is a *vaiṇa*.
One who is accused is one who has been charged with actions that cause loss of caste.
A usurer is one who lives by forbidden interest.
A courtesan is a woman for sale.
One initiated into a *gaṇa* (a group) and one who performs sacrifices for many;
the phrase "one should not eat their food" carries over from the previous verse. 1.161.
[One should not accept gifts] from physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, and enemies;
nor from the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātya, the hypocritical, or those who eat the leavings of others.
A physician is one who lives by the profession of medicine.
A patient is one afflicted by a major disease.
[Major diseases are: wind-disorders, urinary stones, leprosy, diabetes, abdominal dropsy, and fistula-in-ano.
Hemorrhoids and dysentery—these eight are proclaimed as the great diseases.
Thus it is said: "Dyspnea (vātavyādhi), urinary calculi (aśmarī), leprosy (kuṣṭha), diabetes (meha), abdominal dropsy (udara), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi),
and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī)— these eight are proclaimed as the great diseases."
*Kruddhaḥ* means angry;
*puṃścalī* means an unchaste woman;
*mattaḥ* means one who is arrogant due to knowledge and so forth.
A *vidviṣ* is an enemy;
a *krūra* is one whose internal anger is firm;
an *ugra* is one who causes agitation through the activities of speech and body.
An outcast is one who has killed a Brahmin and the like; a Vrātya is one whose Sāvitrī initiation has lapsed;
a hypocrite is a deceiver.
One who eats leftovers, one who eats what has been abandoned after being tasted by another—one should not eat the food of these people, such as physicians and the like. 1.162.
[The impurity lasts for one day] for those who have no heroic sons, for women, for goldsmiths, for women who have conquered their husbands,
for village-priests, for sellers of weapons, for blacksmiths, for weavers, and for those who subsist by keeping dogs.

A woman without a protector is one who is independent, even in the absence of misconduct; others say she is one who is devoid of husband and sons. A goldsmith is one who produces various transformations of gold.
One conquered by women is one who is everywhere under the control of women.
A village-priest is one who performs propitiatory rites and so forth for a village, or who initiates many people.
A seller of weapons is one who subsists on the sale of weapons.
A blacksmith is one who fashions the world, as well as a carpenter and the like. A weaver is one who subsists by the craft of the needle.
One whose livelihood, maintenance, or way of life consists of dogs is called "dog-livelihood" (śvavṛtti).
One should not eat the food of these persons. 1.163.
[One should avoid the food] of a cruel man, a king, a dyer, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter,
a washerman, a vintner, and those who live in the same house as a paramour.
The food of slanderers and liars, as well as that of wheelmen, bards,
and sellers of Soma, must not be eaten.
Cruel means pitiless;
"king" refers to the lord of the earth,
and by association, also the domestic priest.

As Śaṅkha says: "One should avoid the food of those who are frightened, censured, weeping, crying out, shouting, hungry, having already eaten, astonished, insane, or rejected, as well as the food of a king and his domestic priest.
A washerman is one who applies blue and other dyes to clothes and the like.
An ungrateful person is one who destroys what has been done for them in return for a favor.
A "livelihood-by-killing" is one who subsists by the slaughter of living beings;
a "cloth-washer" is one who performs the cleansing of garments;
a "liquor-livelihood" is one who subsists by the sale of intoxicants.
An *upapati* is a paramour.
One whose house is together with a paramour is "one whose house is with a paramour" (*sahopapativeśma*).
A slanderer (*piśuna*) is one who proclaims the faults of others.
An *anṛtī* is a liar;
a *cākrika* is an oil-presser;
some say it refers to a cartwright.
Because they are designated separately as "the accused," "the outcaste," "the wheelwright," and "the oil-presser";
"bandhins" are panegyrists;
and "somavikrayī" is the seller of the soma creeper.
The food of these persons must not be eaten.

All these individuals, beginning with the miser (kadarya), are indeed twice-born (dvija) who, being defiled by faults such as miserliness, have their food forbidden; for a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility of access, and there is no possibility of access for others [in this context].
Regarding the statement, "One should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire except in times of distress," the fact that the food of a Śūdra is forbidden has already been stated.
Regarding this, he states the exception:
"Among Śūdras, the slave, the cowherd, the family friend, the partner in tillage, and the barber— these,
as well as one who offers himself [as a servant], are those whose food may be eaten."

"Slaves" refers to those born into slavery and the like. A "cowherd" is one who lives by the tending of cattle. A "family friend" is one who has come down through the succession of fathers, grandfathers, and so forth.
An *ardhasīrin* is one who takes a share of the fruits of agriculture characterized by the plow (*hala*) and the yoke (*sīra*).
A barber (*nāpita*) is one who causes household tasks to be performed and is himself a barber.
And he who offers himself through the actions of speech, mind, and body, saying, "I am yours."

These, beginning with the slaves, are among the Śūdras whose food may be eaten; by the use of the word "and" (ca), the potter is also included, according to the statement: "The potter, the cowherd, the barber, the family friend, the partner, and one who has offered himself—these are those whose food may be eaten. (1.166)
Having begun with the words "not for the sake of contradicting Vedic study" and having thus set forth the observances of a *snātaka* Brahmin, he now declares the duties of the twice-born:

Meat that has not been honored, meat not intended for sacrifice, meat containing hair or insects, food that has turned sour, stale food, the leavings of another, food touched by a dog, or food looked upon by an outcaste; [these one should avoid].
One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, food announced [beforehand], and food served in turns;
as well as food smelled by a cow, the leavings of birds, and food intentionally touched with the foot.
That which is given with contempt to one worthy of honor is "unhonored.

"Vain meat" refers to meat prepared for one's own sake, excluding cases such as the imminent loss of life that will be mentioned later, and that which does not remain as an offering-remnant from the worship of the gods and so forth. It is also "endowed with" or "containing" hair, insects, and the like.

That which is not sour by itself but becomes sour solely through the passage of time with crows present, or through the passage of time due to contact with other substances—apart from curd and the like—is called *śukta*. This is because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "One should not eat food that is impure, nor what has been cooked twice, nor what is *śukta*, nor what is stale (*paruṣita*), except for *rāga-khāṇḍava*, *cukra*, curd, molasses, and preparations made from wheat or barley flour. *Paryuṣita* means that which has been kept overnight.
*Ucchiṣṭa* means that which has been left over after eating.
"Śvaspṛṣṭam" means touched by a dog.
"Patitekṣitam" means looked upon by outcasts and the like. "Udakyā" refers to a woman in her menses; "tathā spṛṣṭam" means touched by her.

The mention of a *udakyā* (a woman in her courses) is intended as an illustration for *caṇḍālas* and others, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "One should avoid food touched by impure substances, outcasts, *caṇḍālas*, *pulkasas*, women in their courses, those with deformed nails, or those afflicted with leprosy.
That which is given after proclaiming "Who is eating? is called *saṃghuṣṭānna*.
That which is given under one person's name when it actually belongs to another is *paryāyānna*, as for example: [the following verse].
"A Śūdra giving food to Brāhmaṇas, and a Brāhmaṇa giving food to Śūdras—both of these are persons whose food should not be eaten; having eaten [their food], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus it is said.

A Śūdra giving food to Brāhmaṇas, or a Brāhmaṇa giving food to Śūdras—both of these are persons whose food should not be eaten; having eaten [their food], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Regarding the reading *paryācāntam*, it means that in which the *ācānta* (the rinsing of the mouth) has been performed all around—that is, the taking of mouthfuls of water for rinsing has occurred—it is *paryācānta*, and such food must not be eaten.

This is what is meant: one should not eat after taking a mouthful of water until one has performed the ritual sipping (ācamana). Regarding the reading *pārśvācāntam*, it means that if someone sitting in the same row has sipped water while standing at one's side, one must not eat until there is an interruption by ashes, water, or the like. The verb *varjayet* ("one should avoid") is to be connected with each [term].

Likewise, one should avoid what has been smelled by a cow (*goghrāta*), that which is the leavings of a bird (*śakunocchiṣṭa*)— meaning that which has been tasted or eaten by a crow or other such bird— and that which has been touched by a foot (*padā spṛṣṭa*), meaning that which has been intentionally touched with the foot. || 1.167 || 1.168 ||
He states an exception regarding stale food:
"Stale food that has been kept for a long time may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or ghee;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil."
Food that is fit to be eaten, even if it has stood overnight, may be consumed if it is mixed with fats such as ghee and has remained for a long time.

Preparations of wheat, barley, and cow’s milk—such as *maṇḍaka*, *saktu*, *kilāṭa*, *kūrcikā*, and so forth—may also be eaten even after a long period, provided they have not undergone a change in their essential nature (*vikārāntara*), according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "One should avoid cakes, fried cakes, *karambha*, parched grain flour, barley-meal, oil, milk-rice, and vegetables if they have turned sour. (1.169)

One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, of one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, or of one that has no calf; likewise, the milk of camels, of single-hoofed animals, of women, of wild animals, and of sheep.
A cow that is joined with a bull is a *saṃdhinī*.
One should know that a barren cow is a *vaśā*, and one joined with a bull is a *saṃdhinī*, according to the *Trikāṇḍī* lexicon.
Furthermore, a cow that is milked after having passed over her [proper] time, or one that is joined with another calf, is also a *saṃdhinī*.
One who has recently given birth and whose ten-day period has not yet passed is called *anirdaśā*.
One whose calf is dead is called *avatsā*.

A cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*), one whose ten-day period has not passed (*anirdaśā*), and one whose calf is dead (*avatsā*)—these are "the cow in heat, the one whose ten-day period has not passed, and the one whose calf is dead. One should avoid drinking the milk (*kṣīra*) of these cows.
The mention of *saṃdhinī* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both *saṃdhinī* and *yamalasū*.
As Gautama says: "Of those that are *syandinī*, *yamalasū*, and *saṃdhinī*. [The NSP edition reads *yamalasū ca*. A *syandinī* is one whose udder flows with milk.
A *yamalasū* is one who gives birth to twins.

Likewise, one should avoid the milk of goats and buffaloes that have not passed ten days [since giving birth], because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Vasiṣṭha: "The milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats within ten days [of calving]."
By the inclusion of the term "payas" (milk), there is also a prohibition of its derivatives such as curd and the like;
for it is not logical that when meat is prohibited, its derivatives remain unprohibited,
whereas when a derivative is prohibited, the primary substance remains unprohibited.

From the prohibition of milk, there follows no prohibition of dung, urine, and so forth. "Austre" refers to that which is produced from a camel, such as milk, urine, and so on. "One-hoofed" refers to mares and the like; "aikaśapha" refers to what originates from them.
*Strībhava* means "produced by a female.

The mention of "female" (*strī*) is intended as an illustration for all animals with two teats, excluding the goat, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "The milk of all animals with two teats is unfit to be eaten, with the exception of the goat.
*Āraṇyaka* refers to that which exists in the forest; its milk is [unfit], except for that of the buffalo.
And because of the statement: "Of all wild animals,
except for the buffalo," that which is born from a goat is *āvikam*.
The word "should avoid" (*varjayet*) is connected to each [term].

Because of the use of the suffix denoting a derivative (*vikāra-pratyaya*) in "auṣṭram" and so forth, there is a prohibition at all times of every derivative, such as milk, urine, and the like; for the Smṛti of Gautama states: "The milk of sheep, of camels, and of one-hoofed animals is always unfit for drinking. (GDh 17.24) [1.170]
One should avoid sacrificial oblations intended for the gods, the śigru plant, red exudations from incisions,
meat that has not been consecrated with ritual formulas, substances produced in dung, and mushrooms.

The sacrificial oblation (*havis*) prepared for the purpose of an offering to the deities is ready prior to the *homa* for the sake of the oblation. *Śigru* is the *sobhāñjana*; [one should avoid] red exudations from trees.
Even those tree-exudations that are not red, provided they arise from felling— that is, are produced by cutting down trees—
as Manu has said: "Likewise, [one should avoid] red exudations of trees and those arising from felling."
Thus:
"Red tree-exudations and those originating from incisions"—
by the inclusion of the word "red," there is no prohibition of asafoetida, camphor, and the like.
Meat that has not been ritually prepared refers to the flesh of an animal that has not been offered in sacrifice.
"Born from excrement" refers to plants such as *taṇḍulīyaka* and others produced from the dung of humans and other creatures who have consumed seeds.
"Mushrooms" refers to *chatrāka* fungi.
The word "one should avoid" is to be connected with each [item] individually. 1.171.
Flesh-eating birds, the dātyūha, the parrot, pecking birds, the ṭiṭṭibha,
the sārasa crane, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds.
Carnivores are those whose habit is to eat raw flesh;
these include birds such as vultures and the like,
as well as the gallinule and the cātaka.

The parrot (*śuka*) is a *kīra*. Those that feed by pecking with their beaks are called "peckers" (*pratuda*), such as hawks (*śyenādi*) and the like. The *ṭiṭṭibha* is so named because it imitates that sound.
The *sārasa* is the *lakṣmaṇa* crane;
the single-hoofed animals are horses and the like;
and the *haṃsas* are well known.
Village-dwellers include pigeons and the like; one should avoid these and other carnivorous animals. 1.172.
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, baka, and viṣkira birds;
and kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī prepared in vain.
The *koyaṣṭi* is the *krauñca* crane;
the *plava* is the water-fowl (*jalakukkuṭa*);
the *cakrāhva* is the ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*).
The *balākā* and the *baka* are well known.

As for the *viṣkira* (scatter-feeders), since they are those that eat by scattering [food] with their claws, only the *cakora* and similar birds are intended here; for while birds such as the *lāvaka* and peacock are fit to be eaten, the village cock is already prohibited simply because it dwells in villages.
One should avoid these, such as the *koyaṣṭi* and others.
One should avoid *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, *apūpa*, and *śaṣkulī* when they have been prepared "in vain," that is, without being dedicated to a deity or other such purpose.
*Kṛsara* is rice cooked with sesame and mung beans.
*Saṃyāva* is a specific kind of cooked preparation known as *utkarikā*, made from milk, molasses, ghee, and so forth;
*pāyasa* is rice boiled with milk;
and *apūpa* is a wheat product fried without oil.

*Śaṣkulī* is a preparation of wheat cooked in oil. Although the prohibition of *kṛsara* and other such foods is already established by the rule "one should not cook food for oneself," this further mention is intended to impose a heavier penance. (1.173)
The *kalaviṅka*, the *kākola*, the *kurara*, the *rajjudālaka*,
web-footed birds, the *khañjarīṭa*, and wild animals or birds that are otherwise unknown [should not be eaten].
The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow (*grāmacaṭaka*).
Since its exclusion would already be established by virtue of being a resident of a village, it is mentioned again because it frequents both [the village and the forest].
The *kākola* is the *droṇakāka* (the raven).
The *kurara* is the osprey (*utkrośa*).
The *rajjudālaka* is the woodpecker (*vṛkṣakuṭṭaka*).
The *jālapāda* is one whose feet have the shape of a net.
The repetition of the word "swans" (*haṃsa*) is because there are indeed swans that do not have webbed feet (*ajālapāda*).
A *khañjarīṭa* is a *khañjana*.
As for "wild animals and birds unknown through their species," these are those wild animals and birds that are not recognized by their specific class.
One should avoid these, such as the kalaviṅka and others. || 1.174 ||
Having intentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, dog meat, dried meat, or fish, one shall dwell for three days observing a fast.
The blue jay (*cāṣa*), the *kikīdivi*, the red-footed birds, the *kādamba* and others;
the *sauna* meat—meat from a slaughterhouse or from a place of execution—even if it belongs to animals otherwise fit for consumption;
and *vallūra*, which is dried meat.

"Matsya" refers to fish. One should avoid these, beginning with the *cāpa* [fish], as well as—by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*)—the *nālikā*, *śaṇa*, *chatrāka*, *kusumbha*, and so forth; that is, those produced from the *nālikā*, *śaṇa*, *chatrāka*, *kusumbha*, and *alābu* gourds, as well as those produced from fermented grain (*viḍbhava*).
One should avoid the kumbhī, the kanduka, the vṛntāka, and the kovidāra.

Thus: One should avoid the nālikā, the hemp-plant, the chatrāka mushroom, safflower, the bottle-gourd, those growing from excrement, as well as the kumbhī, the kanduka, the eggplant, and the kovidāra.
Likewise, one should carefully avoid flowers and fruits that have blossomed out of season, as well as anything that appears unnatural.
Likewise, according to the Smṛti: "One should avoid the fruits of the *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, *kapittha*, *nīpa*, and *mātuluṅga*.
Having intentionally consumed these aforementioned items, such as the milk of a cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*), one should fast for three nights;
however, if unintentionally, one should fast for a day and a night.
"One should fast for a day for the remaining [animals]," according to the statement of Manu.

As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha—"In the case of eating a crane, a heron, a swan, a *plava* duck, a ruddy goose, a *kāraṇḍava* duck, a house sparrow, a pigeon, a dove, a white parrot, a maina, a crane, a *ṭiṭṭibha*, an owl, a heron, a red-footed bird, a blue jay, a vulture, a crow, a cuckoo, a *śāḍvalika*, a cock, or a *hārīta* bird, one should remain without food for twelve nights and drink cow's urine mixed with barley"—that is to be understood as applying to habitual practice over a long period or to intentional consumption of all such birds together. (1.175)
Having eaten onions, a village pig, a mushroom, a village cock,
garlic, or leeks, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Onion (palāṇḍu) has a thick bulb and stalk and resembles garlic.
The village pig (viḍvarāha) is a domestic swine. The mushroom (chatrāka) is the serpent’s umbrella.
The village cock is well known. Garlic (*laśuna*) is *rasona*, characterized by its small, white bulb and stalk.
The *gṛñjana* is a small red bulb that resembles garlic.
Having eaten these six at once intentionally—that is, having consumed them—one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, the characteristics of which will be described later.

The mention here of the village cock and the mushroom (*chatrāka*), though previously prohibited, is for the purpose of establishing that they share the same expiation as the onion and other such items. However, in the case of intentional and long-term habitual practice, [the following applies]: "The mushroom, the village pig, garlic, and the village cock..."
Having intentionally eaten onions or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Thus it was stated by Manu.
Regarding habitual consumption without prior intention: "Having unintentionally eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra;
or else the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa, which will be described in the third chapter. This is how it should be understood.

But in the case of habitual consumption without prior intention, it is stated by Śaṅkha that one should drink milk for twelve nights after eating garlic, onion, leeks, village pigs, village cocks, or mushrooms. 1.176.
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the iguana, the tortoise, the pangolin, and the hare may be eaten;
and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita may likewise be eaten.
Likewise, the *pāṭhīna*, the *rājīva*, and the scaled fish may be eaten by the twice-born;
as well as the *sedhā*, the *śvāvit*, the *godhā*, and the large lizard that resembles a chameleon.
*Kacchapa* means a tortoise;
*śallaka* means a porcupine;
*śaśa* is well known [as a rabbit].
Among the five-nailed animals, such as dogs, cats, monkeys, and so forth, these—namely the porcupine and others—are edible; by the use of the word "and" (ca), the rhinoceros is also included.
As Gautama says: "The five-nailed animals [that may be eaten] are the hare, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise."
As Manu also said:

"Among five-toed animals, they declare the porcupine, the iguana, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare to be edible; likewise, those with only one row of teeth, excluding the camel."
Thus it is said: "The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—
these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel."

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha—that "they dispute regarding the rhinoceros"—and that it is inedible, that refers to occasions other than the *śrāddha*, because one observes the declaration of rewards in the context of the *śrāddha*: "That which is offered in the rite for the ancestors with the flesh of the rhinoceros becomes inexhaustible. Likewise, among fish, those such as the *siṃhatuṇḍa* and others are edible.
Siṃhatuṇḍa means lion-faced.
Rohita means red-colored.
Pāṭhīna is known as the candraka.
The *rājīva* is lotus-colored.
It is called *saśalka* because it exists together with scales that have the shape of oyster shells.

These, beginning with the *siṃhatuṇḍa*, are edible only when specifically prescribed; the *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* are the first two [of these] prescribed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
The Rajīvas, Siṃhatuṇḍas, and Śalkas are found everywhere.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu;
the mention of "twice-born" (dvijāti) is for the purpose of excluding the Śūdra. 1.177.
Having begun with "unhonored meat is meat eaten in vain" and thus stated the duties of the twice-born, he now declares the duties of the four social orders:
"Therefore, listen to the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat."

O sages, listen to the injunction in the form of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) such as "I shall not eat meat except that which has been consecrated by sprinkling (*prokṣita*) and the like," which prescribes the eating of meat that has been consecrated and so forth, while forbidding the consumption of all other prohibited meat—this is what Sāmaśravas and others have taught. (1.178)
In that regard, he shows the rule for eating:
"When life is at risk, at a śrāddha, when it has been consecrated with sprinkling (prokṣita), or at the desire of a twice-born;
having duly honored the gods and the ancestors, one who eats meat incurs no fault."

When there is a threat to life due to lack of food or being overcome by disease, one should eat meat as a rule; for it is prescribed that "one should protect oneself from all [harm]," and because death is forbidden by the injunction, "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the full span of his life.
Likewise, one invited to a *śrāddha* feast should eat meat as a rule, since a fault is heard of in the scriptures regarding its non-eating:
"But that man who, being duly appointed, does not eat meat..."
Having died, he goes to the state of a beast for twenty-one successive births.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu:

one may eat the consecrated meat (*prokṣita*)—that is, the meat remaining from the sacrifice of an animal such as the *agnīṣomīya*, which has been purified by the Vedic rite known as *prokṣaṇa* and intended for the sacrifice—since the sacrifice would not be accomplished without its consumption.

Furthermore, one does not incur any fault by eating the remains of food prepared for the purpose of feeding Brahmins, for the sake of the gods, or for the ancestors, after having first honored those [guests] with it.
Likewise, even what remains after supporting one's dependents [may be used].
Praśasta animals and birds are to be killed by Brāhmaṇas for the sake of sacrifice;
indeed, in ancient times, Agastya himself practiced this for the sake of maintaining his dependents.

Thus, from the recollection of Manu [in the verse], "he does not partake of the fault," it is shown by stating the mere absence of fault that there is only a permission for what remains after honoring guests and others, and not a restrictive rule (niyama) like that regarding consecrated food (prokṣita) and so forth.

Likewise, since even animals such as the hare, which are not prohibited, are understood to be unfit for consumption except in cases of life-threatening distress, it is understood that for a Śūdra as well, there exists an entitlement to all injunctions and prohibitions pertaining to meat. 1.179.

Now, he states a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the eating of that which is prohibited by the term "meat not for sacrifice" (*vṛthāmāṃsa*), namely meat other than that which has been consecrated (*prokṣita*):
"That man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal."
He who kills animals without following the prescribed rite and without dedicating them to a deity or the like shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on that animal.
By the word "kills," all eight types of slaughterers are included,
as Manu has stated:
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are slayers.
Thus [ends verse 1.180].
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— these are all slayers.
Now he states the rule for avoidance:
"By abstaining from meat, a brahmin becomes a sage even while dwelling at home; he attains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice."

He who possesses a firm resolve, thinking, "I must not eat meat except when it has been consecrated by sprinkling and the like," attains all his desires without obstacle once he engages in their accomplishment, because of the purity of his intention.
As Manu said:
"Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherein one fixes one's attachment..."
He who harms nothing attains that [result] without obstacle.
Thus:
whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherein one fixes one's delight—
that one attains without obstacle, provided that one harms nothing whatsoever.
And this is a secondary result.
He states the primary result: "likewise the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.
And this refers to the resolve made for a year-long period.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu:
likewise, even while living in a household, a member of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa becomes worthy of honor like a sage by virtue of abstaining from meat.

And this does not refer to meat that is prohibited, nor does it refer to meat that has been consecrated (*prokṣita*) and so forth; rather, by process of elimination, it refers to meat that is permitted as a remnant after the honoring of guests and others. (1.181)
Now he speaks of the purification of substances:
[The purification] of gold, silver, lotuses, upper vessels,
cups, stones, vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and leather.
The purification of bowls and cups is prescribed with water;
however, vessels for the *caru* oblation, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and those containing oily substances are purified with hot water.
*Sauvarṇa* means made of gold;
*rājata* means made of silver;
*abja* refers to pearls, conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and so forth.
The "upward-facing vessel" refers to sacrificial items such as the mortar and so forth, because of their association with the *grahas* and other such vessels.
The *grahas* are the sixteen cups beginning with the *ṣoḍaśin*.
The "stone" refers to the grinding stone (*dṛṣad*) and similar implements.
Śākta refers to items such as the site-plan (vāstuka) and so forth. A cord (rajju) is one made from balvaja grass and the like.
Root (mūla) refers to ginger (ārdraka) and similar substances.
Fruit refers to mangoes and the like; clothing refers to garments; and split bamboo refers to items made from bamboo and the like.
"Leather" refers to that of goats and other animals.
The mention of "wickerwork and leather" is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for their derivatives, such as umbrellas, thongs, and so forth.
"Vessels" refers to the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and others of that kind.
The *camasa* vessels refer to the *hotṛcamasa* and others.

For these, such as those made of gold and so forth, when they are free from adhering residue (*lepa*), purification is achieved merely by washing with water upon contact with food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*).
The *caru* refers to the sacrificial porridge and its cooking vessel.

The *sruva* and *sruc* ladles are well known. Vessels containing oily substances, such as the *prāśitraharaṇa* and others, are purified with hot water provided they are free of residue; a golden vessel that is free of residue is purified by water alone.
One made of lotus-wood, one made of stone, and one made of silver, provided it is unadorned.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu:
"Unadorned" means not filled by digging.
But for those [vessels] that are coated, as well as for metallic ones, gems, and everything made of stone—
Purification by means of ashes, water, and earth has been declared by the wise.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Manu.
Since earth and ashes serve the same purpose, there is an option between them;
however, water is to be used in conjunction with both.

However, in the case of defilement by the mouth of a crow or similar bird, one should scrape out the vessel that has been touched by the mouth of a black bird; it should be understood that a vessel touched by the mouth of a beast of prey must not be used at all.
And this [rule] applies except in the case of a cat, for:
"The cat, the ladle, and the wind are always pure."
"A cat, a ladle, and the wind are always pure"—
so it is remembered from the *Manusmṛti* (1.182–183).
The purification of sacrificial vessels and the like is by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

For the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the skin (*ajina*), grain, the pestle (*musala*), the mortar (*ulūkhala*), the fire-drills (*araṇi*), and for many solid objects such as grain and garments, purification is by sprinkling.
The *sphya* is a vajra, a component of the sacrifice;
the *anaḥ* is a cart;
the remainder is well known.
Their purification is by means of hot water.

The mention of "antelope skin" (*ajina*) again is for the purpose of including skins used as parts of a sacrifice. "Aggregated things" refers to many composite objects made from impure materials, such as grains and clothes.
The mention of "clothing" (*vāsa*) is intended as an illustration for the aforementioned pure substances.

For many of the aforementioned pure items—such as grain, clothing, and so forth—when they are heaped together in large quantities, purification occurs by sprinkling alone. And this "largeness" (*bahutva*) is relative to what has been touched.

This is what is meant: when grains, clothes, or similar items are heaped together, and among them a few have been touched by a *caṇḍāla* or others while many remain untouched, the purification for those that were touched is as already stated, while for the others it is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
And so it is said in another *Smṛti*:
"When a single part of a heap of clothes, grain, or the like is defiled..."
Having extracted that much [of the grain], the remainder deserves the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Thus:
"When a portion of a heap of clothing, grain, or the like is defiled, one should remove only that much; the remainder deserves sprinkling."
Furthermore, when there is a great quantity of touched items and a small quantity of untouched ones, then all of them must be washed.
As Manu says:
"The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling with water."
However, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed.
Thus it is said:
"The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed."
Even when there is equality between what has been touched and what has not been touched, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) alone is prescribed.

Since washing (*kṣālana*) is established for a small number of items by virtue of the rule prescribing sprinkling for many, the repeated mention of washing for a small number is intended to preclude washing in cases where [the degree of contact] is equal. However, when there is no distinction such as "this much is touched" and "this much is untouched," washing alone is required.

Since even a partial defect must be avoided, the authors of the legal digests maintain that for grains, clothing, and similar items being carried by many people—whether touched or untouched—sprinkling with water (*prokṣaṇa*) alone is the required purification. (1.184)

Having stated the purification for items that are unsullied by contact alone, he now describes the purification for those with stains: "The scraping of wood, horn, and bone; the wiping of vessels made from fruits with cow-hair;
and the cleansing of sacrificial vessels with the hand during a sacrificial rite."
[This refers to] wood, the horns of sheep, buffaloes, and so forth, and the bones of elephants, boars, conchs, and the like.
By the mention of "bones," the inclusion of teeth is also intended.

Regarding those smeared with food-leavings, oils, and so on—meaning those from which the smear has not been removed by means of earth, ashes, water, and so forth—Manu says: "As long as the odor and the smear caused by contact with impure substances do not depart from that which has been touched by them..."
In all purifications of objects, earth and water should be employed accordingly.
Thus, because purification is prescribed in general terms:
*takṣaṇa* (scraping) is purification consisting of the removal of a certain amount of material from the surface;
