for vessels made from fruits—such as those produced from the *bilva*, *alābu*, or coconut—the purification is by scrubbing with cow-hair.

The cleansing of sacrificial vessels—such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles—when they are being employed in a sacrifice, must be performed with the right hand using *darbha* grass or a *daśāpavitra* (a fringed filter), according to the scriptures, as an integral part of the ritual act.

This is a Vedic example intended to demonstrate that other vessels as well, such as those made of gold, possess the status of being valid ritual implements (*aṅga*) only when they have been purified in Smārta or worldly rites.

Furthermore, for sacrificial implements that have already undergone purification, this cleansing with the *daśāpavitra* and so forth is for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*); this is the implied meaning. (1.185)
Woolen and silken fabrics are purified with saline water and cow’s urine;
aṃśupaṭṭa cloth with bilva fruits, and likewise kutapa wool with ariṣṭa fruits.
It is purified by cow urine mixed with saline earth or by water, depending on the degree of the stain.
That which is made of wool (*āvikam*) and that which originates from a cocoon (*kauśikam*), such as silk cloth and the like, is purified when washed.
The plural "with water and cow urine" (udakagomūtraiḥ) is used for the purpose of obtaining water even later on.
*Aṃśupaṭṭa* is made from fibers of bark.
"With *śrīphala*" means together with *bilva* fruits.
A *kutapa* is a blanket made from the hair of mountain goats.
It is purified by water mixed with cow’s urine and *ariṣṭa*; this [rule] continues to apply. And this should be understood to hold when there is contact with food remnants, oil, and so forth.

However, when the damage is slight, sprinkling and similar methods are prescribed because the material cannot withstand washing; for it is desired that purification be accomplished everywhere without destroying the substance.
And so says Devala:
"Those made of wool, silk, *kutapa* wool, bark-cloth, linen, and fine cotton cloth..."
These [beings] possess only slight purity through methods such as drying and sprinkling.

Having said this, he continued: "One should wash those very items, when defiled by impurities, with their own respective purifying agents—namely, with pastes of grains, with juices derived from fruits, or even with alkaline substances."
Thus it is said:
"Those very [objects] joined with impurities one should wash with their own respective purifiers— namely,
with pastes of grains, with juices derived from fruits, or even with alkaline substances."
The case of linen applies equally to hemp because they share a common origin.
The mention of wool and so forth is intended to include mattresses and other items made from them.
Therefore, when there is only slight defilement, no washing should be performed—except in the case of contact with impure substances—for mattresses, pillows, and likewise for flower-dyed garments.
Having dried it slightly in the sun, one should repeatedly wipe it with the hands.
And afterwards, having sprinkled them with water, one should employ them in ritual action;
even those that are extremely defiled, one should purify according to the rule.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Devala.
"Red with flowers" means dyed with saffron, safflower, and so forth.
The mention of "red with flowers" is intended to include other substances as well, such as turmeric and the like, which cannot withstand washing.
Not [the case] for madder and the like, because they can withstand washing. It has also been stated by Śaṅkha: "Dyed substances, when sprinkled with water, are pure. (1.186)
Linen cloth is purified by white mustard seeds; earthenware by firing;
the hand of an artisan, merchandise, alms-food, and likewise the mouth of a woman, are pure.

Linens—namely cloth and other items made from *kṣumā* (hemp) or *atasī* (flax)—are purified with water and cow urine mixed with white mustard seeds. Earthenware, such as jars and the like, is purified by re-firing. This rule should be understood to apply when there is a smear of impure oil or food leavings.
Manu: An earthen vessel that has been touched by intoxicants, urine, feces, saliva, pus, or blood cannot be purified even by re-firing.
This is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).
However, in the case of defilement by *caṇḍālas* and the like, there must be total abandonment [of the water].
As Parāśara has said:
Grain or even clothing that has been touched by Caṇḍālas and others is purified by washing;
however, an object made of earth is purified by discarding it.
Thus:
"But grain or even clothing touched by Caṇḍālas and others is purified by washing;
however, that which is made of earth is purified by discarding it."

Artisans—such as dyers, laundrymen, cooks, and so forth—their hands are always pure. This purity pertains to the work they perform; thus, even when birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or similar conditions occur, their hands remain pure for tasks such as washing clothes.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female slaves,
male slaves, as well as kings and royal servants, are declared to be pure immediately."
Thus: artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female slaves,
male slaves, as well as kings and royal servants, are declared to be immediately pure.
Merchandise, which is fit for barter and sale, such as barley, rice, and so forth,
does not become impure even when handled by many buyers and sellers; nor does it become so for merchants on account of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like.

Alms (bhaikṣa) is a collection of begged food; that which has come into the hands of a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) and others is not defiled even by such causes as being given by a woman who has not sipped water for purification, or by being stepped over on a road made impure [by excrement].
Likewise, the mouth of a woman is pure at the time of sexual union, according to the traditional law (smṛti): "And women are pure during the contact of passion. (1.187)
Now he speaks of the purification of the ground:
"The purification of the ground is by sweeping, by burning, by time, and likewise by the treading of cows;
by sprinkling, by scraping, and by smearing; and the house [is purified] by sweeping and smearing."
Sweeping (*mārjana*) is the clearing away of dust, grass, and so forth by means of a broom (*mārjanī*).
Burning (*dāha*) is [the removal] by means of grass, wood, and the like.
Time (*kāla*) is that duration of time by which the disappearance of smears and such occurs.
Treading by cows, trampling by the hooves of cattle,
sprinkling with milk, cow-urine, cow-dung, or water— or alternatively, showering them down;
scraping, planing, or digging.

Smearing with cow dung and other substances—whether these, such as sweeping and so forth, are used collectively or individually—the ground defiled by impurities and the like, as well as that which is merely dirty, becomes purified.
Accordingly, Devala states: "Where a woman gives birth, dies, or is even cremated..."
Wherever there is a dwelling of Caṇḍālas, or wherever there is a heap of excrement and the like.
Thus, the earth is proclaimed to be impure when it is abounding in filth;
it becomes defiled when touched by dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, and the like.
It becomes defiled by charcoal, husks, hair, bones, ashes, and so forth.

Having thus stated the threefold classification of ground to be purified—namely, as impure (*amedhya*), defiled (*duṣṭa*), and soiled (*malinā*)—he now demonstrates the specific methods of purification: "Ground that is impure is purified in five ways or four;
that which is associated with defilement is purified in three or two ways; and that which is merely soiled is purified in one way."
Thus, ground that is impure is purified by five or four methods;
that which is defiled by contact with the wicked is purified by three or two methods; and that which is merely soiled is purified by one method.

Where humans are cremated, and where Caṇḍālas dwell, purification occurs through five acts: burning, treading by cows, sprinkling, and scraping. Where humans are born, where they die, and where there is a constant accumulation of excrement and the like, purification occurs through those same four acts, excluding burning. For ground long inhabited by dogs, pigs, or donkeys, purification occurs through three acts: treading by cows, sprinkling, and scraping.

Ground that has been occupied for a long time by camels, village cocks, and the like is purified by sprinkling and scraping. Ground that has been occupied for a long time by charcoal, husks, hair, and the like is purified by scraping.
Sweeping and anointing, however, are to be combined with these in all cases.
In this way, the house is purified by sweeping and smearing.
The separate mention of the "house" is for the purpose of ensuring that sweeping and smearing are performed every day. (1.188)
When food has been smelled by a cow, or is defiled by hair, flies, or insects,
water, ashes, or even earth should be sprinkled upon it for the sake of purification.
When food is defiled by the breath of a cow, it is unfit for consumption even if it is merely a small amount;
likewise when it is defiled by hair, flies, or insects.
The mention of "hair" is intended to include body hair and the like.
Insects refer to ants and the like.
For the sake of purification, water, ashes, or earth should be sprinkled as appropriate.

As for what was stated by Gautama—that food containing hair or insects is always unfit to be eaten—that refers specifically to cases where the food has been cooked together with hair, insects, and so forth. (1.189)
The purification of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, water, or water; that of bell-metal and iron is by ashes and water; but for liquids, it is by immersion.
Pearls and the other items are well known.
Their purification—whether by alkaline water, acidic water, or plain water—should be performed using these substances either collectively or individually, depending on the degree of defilement.
For bell-metal and iron, purification is achieved with ash-water.
By the mention of copper (*tāmra*), brass (*rītikā*) and bell-metal (*pittala*) are also included, because they share a common origin.

Furthermore, this prescription regarding the purification of copper and other metals with acidic liquids and the like is not intended as a restrictive rule. For it is said: "That [impurity] which arises from contact with dirt is removed by that very substance with which the object is defiled."
That is declared to be the general purification for it, which effects the cleansing of substances.
Because of this general injunction regarding recollection,

one should not, as a rule, perform purification with sour liquids or water when the stains of food remnants, water, and so forth on copper and other materials can be removed by other means. For this very reason, it was stated generally by Manu:
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, or water.
Thus:
"The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water."

As for the statement, "Bell-metal is purified by ash; copper is purified by acid," that is intended to establish the ultimate limit of purification for copper and the like, not to prohibit other methods. However, when there is an excessive degree of defilement, then there is a repetition of acid, water, and so forth, in the case of bell-metal vessels smelled by cows or those left over as the leavings of a Śūdra.
And things defiled by dogs or crows are purified by ten alkaline substances.
Thus it is from the Smṛti. An additional passage in the NSP manuscript *ka* states: "He mentions ten [plants] that cause cauterization: sesame, *muṣkaka*, *śigru*, *kokilākṣa*, and *palāśa*."
Likewise, [the roots] of kāka-jaṅghā, āvajña, ciñcā, aśvattha, and vaṭa.
However, purification of bell-metal occurs by means of these ten cleansing agents.

Regarding the rule "but for a liquid, purification is by overflowing": for a liquid substance such as ghee and the like, exceeding one *prastha* in measure, which has been defiled by dogs, crows, and so forth, or touched by impure substances (*amedhya*), "overflowing" (*plāva*) means filling the vessel with a liquid of the same kind until it overflows; "purification" is understood to continue [as the result] until the [impurity] exits.
After that, there is the discarding of what remains if it is small in quantity.
Whether something is "much" or "little" is to be understood in relation to factors such as place and time.
As Baudhāyana has said:
"Of sesame, muṣkaka, and śigru; of kokilākṣa and palāśa; likewise of kākajaṅghā, avajñā, ciñcā, aśvattha, and vaṭa."
However, by means of these ten purifying agents, purification occurs for bell-metal.
Having understood the place, the time, as well as the measure, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the justification, and the state, one should determine the purification.
Having understood the place, the time, as well as the measure, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the justification, and the state, one should determine the purification.
However, for that which has been defiled by insects and the like, purification is by straining;
as Manu says:
"For all liquid substances, purification is traditionally held to be by straining."
Thus it is said:
"And for all liquid substances, purification is traditionally held to be straining."
In this context, "purifying by winnowing" (*utpavana*) means placing [the liquid] into a vessel separated by a cloth; otherwise, the removal of insects and other impurities would be impossible.

Regarding honey, water, and the like contained in a vessel belonging to a Śūdra, purification occurs by transferring them into another vessel, because of the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana: "Honey, water, milk, and their derivatives are purified when transferred from one vessel to another."
Honey, ghee, and other such substances, having been received from the hand of one of the lowest castes, must be transferred to another vessel and purified again.
As Śaṅkha says: "For edible foods that have been sprinkled with ghee, purification is achieved by re-purifying them; likewise for oily substances and liquids containing oil. (1.190)

Having thus stated the purification for all items made of gold, silver, and so forth mentioned in this section when they are defiled by food-leavings, oily substances, and the like, he now states the purification for those same items when defiled by impure matter (amedhya): "The purification of that which is smeared with impure matter is by means of earth and water, through the removal of odor and other such qualities. That which is commended by word, that which is washed with water, and that which is unknown [to be defiled] are always pure."
The impurities born of the body are fat, semen, and so forth:
fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nails, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of men.
Likewise: human bone, a corpse, feces, semen, urine, menstrual blood,
fat, sweat, tears, rheum of the eyes, phlegm, and wine are called impure.
Thus: human bone, a corpse, excrement, semen, urine, menstrual blood,
fat, sweat, tears, rheum of the eyes, phlegm, and wine are called impure.

Impurities such as excrement and the like have been set forth by Manu, Devala, and others; that which is smeared with fat and other such substances is "contaminated by impurity" (*amedhyākta*). Its purification must be performed with earth and water by means of removing the odor.
By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the removal of stains (*lepa*) is also included.
As Gautama has said: "The purification of that which is smeared with impurity is by means of removing the stain and the odor."
In all cases of purification, first the removal of stains and odors must be performed using earth and water alone.

If the odor and so forth do not depart by means of earth and water, then it should be done by other means; for, as the Smṛti of Gautama states: "If one is unable [to remove them], then by other means, first with earth and then with water. Furthermore, the mention of *vasā* (fat) and the rest is intended to establish the impurity (*amedhya*) of all these substances, and not to indicate that they cause an equal degree of defilement; for [the text continues]: "By liquors, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears, and blood..."
An earthen vessel that has been defiled by contact with impurity cannot be purified even by baking it again.

This is because specific exceptions are stated regarding defilement. Furthermore, their impurity is established by the scriptural statement: "And they are impure when they have fallen from the body as excretions. This refers only to those that have fallen from the body, not to those remaining in their own place.
For a person, if any limb other than the hands is touched by something else that is impure, bathing is required above the navel.
As Devala has said: "Having touched the bone of a human, fat, excrement, menstrual blood, urine, semen, marrow, or blood belonging to another, one should perform a bath."
Thus:
having touched the human bone, fat, feces, menstrual blood, urine, semen, marrow, or blood of another, one should perform a bath.
Having touched those very [limbs] of one's own, washed them, and sipped water, one becomes pure.
Thus,
having touched those very parts of his own body, washed them, and sipped water, he becomes pure.
Likewise:

"If any part of the body above the navel, excluding the hands, is defiled, one should bathe; but for that which is below, one becomes pure by washing it and performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)."
Thus:

"Except for the two hands, whatever part of the body above the navel is defiled, one becomes pure by bathing; but for that which is below, one is purified by washing it and performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)."

Even when the aforementioned purification has been performed, if there is dissatisfaction of the mind such that doubt regarding purity arises, that which is "declared pure by word" (*vākśasta*) is pure;
the meaning is that it becomes pure through the declaration of Brahmins, saying, "May this be pure.
That which is "washed with water" (*ambunirṇikta*) refers to an object for which no specific method of purification is prescribed; its purification is achieved through washing.

That which cannot withstand washing is purified by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Furthermore, that which is "unknown" (*ajñāta*)—meaning that which has been defiled by crows and the like but is never known to have been so used—is always pure.
The meaning is that no unseen fault (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*) arises from its use.

But is this not contradicted by the following: "The best of the twice-born should perform at least one *kṛcchra* penance for a year for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly, and especially so for that which was known?"

This is not so, because although a penance is prescribed even for that which is seen to be free from defects, the penance pertains to the act of eating, whereas the absence of defect pertains to its use for other purposes. (1.191)
Water on the ground that is naturally pure and sufficient for one's thirst is clean;
likewise is meat fallen from a dog, a caṇḍāla, a carnivorous beast, or the like.

Water situated on the earth—that is, standing on the ground—which is sufficient to satisfy the thirst of a single cow, untouched by *caṇḍālas* and others, remaining in its natural state, and not having undergone any change in its color, taste, smell, or touch, is pure and fit for sipping (*ācamana*) and other uses.
The phrase "situated on the earth" is intended to exclude water located on impure ground from being considered pure; it does not, however, exclude the purity of atmospheric water.
Nor does it apply to water that has been drawn up, for it is said: "And those [waters] that have been drawn up are also purified when drawn up in clean vessels."
Water that has stood for even one night must be discarded, even if it is pure by itself.
Thus, according to the statement of Devala:

"Likewise, there is no fault regarding a tank or similar water source constructed by Caṇḍālas and others; for even when a well, a dam, a step-well, or similar structure has been built by those of the lowest castes, there is no penance required for bathing or drinking there."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śātātapa:
"Meat killed by dogs, Caṇḍālas, carnivorous beasts, and the like, is pure.
By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (ādi), there is also the inclusion of Pulkasas and others.
The inclusion of the term "struck down" (nipātita) is for the purpose of excluding that which has been eaten. || 1.192 ||
A ray of light, fire, dust, shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth, and the wind;
droplets, flies, a calf at the time of suckling, and [the shadow] on contact are pure.
Rays belong to luminous substances such as the sun;
fire is well known;
and dust exists apart from its connection with goats and the like.

In this regard, because the following fault is heard in scripture— "Through contact with the dust of dogs, crows, camels, donkeys, owls, pigs, domestic birds, goats, sheep, and deer, one's lifespan and fortune decline"— one must perform sweeping and other purificatory acts upon touching them.
The shadow of a tree and so forth;
a cow; a horse.
Vasudhā is the earth;
anila is the wind;
and *vipruṣaḥ* are droplets of dew, since those produced from the mouth will be described later.
And flies:
these are pure upon contact even when touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and others. A calf is pure when it is discharging its milk, that is, while drawing away the milk situated in the udder.
The mention of "calf" is intended as an illustration for a child; the rule is that whatever is surrounded by children, whatever is handled by women, and whatever is unknown, is always pure.
Because of this statement. 1.193 ||
The mouths of goats and horses are pure, but those of cows and humans are not;
roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.
The mouths of goats and horses are pure; not so the mouth of a cow,
nor the impurities originating from humans.
The word *nara* denotes the body by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The impurities produced from it, such as fat and the like, are not pure.
Paths—that is, roads—even when touched by dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and others, become purified at night by the rays of the moon and by the wind.
But during the day, [it is purified] by the rays of the sun and by the wind. || 1.194 ||
Droplets from the mouth are pure, as are the drops from the act of sipping water (ācamana).
Likewise, the beard that enters the mouth and what adheres to the teeth becomes pure after one has removed it.

Drops of phlegm produced in the mouth are called *mukhaja*; they are pure and do not cause one to become ritually impure (*ucchiṣṭa*), provided they do not fall upon the body—according to the statement of Gautama: "Drops from the mouth do not cause impurity unless they fall on the body. Likewise, drops of water from the rinsing of the mouth that touch the feet are pure. Furthermore, a beard that has entered the mouth—that is, gone inside the mouth—does not cause impurity.
Food and such that have become stuck between the teeth becomes pure once it has fallen out of its own accord;

that which does not fall out is considered equal to the teeth. And so Gautama says: "But what is stuck to the teeth is like the teeth, except when touched by the tongue; some say [it remains so] until it falls out; but once they have fallen out, one should know they are like saliva; it is pure as soon as one swallows them."
Furthermore, this swallowing is presented as an alternative to the renunciation mentioned by Yājñavalkya.
The word "even" (*eva*) in the phrase "swallowing indeed" (*nigirann eva*) [indicates the restriction]. However, one should always rinse the mouth after chewing, except for the chewing of betel;
likewise after touching the lips when they are covered with hair, and after changing one's garment.
Thus, this is for the purpose of prohibiting the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) mentioned by Viṣṇu.
The mention of betel (*tāmbūla*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for fruits and the like.
As Śātātapa has said:
After consuming betel-leaf and fruit, or when there is a residue of oil,
or upon contact with something stuck to the teeth, a twice-born man does not become impure from the remnants of food.
Thus [ends verse 1.195].
When betel, fruit, or the residue of oily substances has been consumed,
or when there is contact with something stuck to the teeth, a twice-born man does not become impure by leavings.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, walked upon a road,
or changed one's garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
When bathing, drinking, sneezing, sleeping, eating, walking on a road, or putting on a garment has been performed, one who has already sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again;
that is to say, he should sip water twice.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), [the rule applies] also to weeping, beginning Vedic study, agitation, speaking untruths, and so forth.
And likewise Vasiṣṭha says: "Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again. Manu also says:
"Having slept, sneezed, eaten, spat, or spoken a false word..."
Having drunk water, and when about to study, one should sip water (ācamana), even if already pure.
Thus: having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruthful words,
having drunk water, and when about to study, one should sip water (ācamana) even if already pure.
Regarding eating, however, there is sipping twice even at the beginning, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "One who is about to eat, even if already pure, should sip water twice.
At the beginning of bathing and drinking, it is once;
but at the commencement of Vedic study, it is twice.
In the remaining cases, the twice-sipping of water (dvirācamana) is performed only at the end, as previously stated.
The muddy waters of a street, even when touched by outcasts, dogs, or crows, are purified by the wind alone; and likewise, structures built of baked bricks are purified by the wind.
A *rathyā* is merely a road;
*kardama* is mud and *toya* is water.
Mud and water situated on a road, when touched by outcastes such as *caṇḍālas*, or by dogs and crows, become pure—that is, they attain purification—by the wind alone.
The plural number is used for the purpose of including the attainment of cow-dung, gravel, and so forth found therein.
Temples, white palaces, and the like, constructed with baked bricks and such materials, are purified by air alone even when touched by Caṇḍālas and others.
Furthermore, this sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is intended to preclude the previously mentioned prohibition of sprinkling regarding solid objects.
But for objects made of grass, wood, leaves, and so forth, sprinkling alone is prescribed. || 1.197 ||
Now, intending to establish the dharma of self-restraint, he speaks in praise of the alms-bowl as a constituent part of that discipline:
"Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brahmins for the protection of the Vedas,
for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of dharma."
At the beginning of the kalpa, Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha, having performed austerity and meditation, first created the Brāhmaṇas, thinking, "Whom shall I create?
For what purpose?
For the protection of the Vedas, that is, for the sake of guarding the Vedas.

For the sake of satisfying the ancestors and the deities, and for the sake of preserving the Dharma by means of instructing its practice; therefore, the intention is that what is given to them yields inexhaustible fruit. 1.198.
The Brahmins who are devoted to sacred learning and study are the source of all;
among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior, and even more excellent than they are those who possess the highest knowledge of the supreme self.

Among all [classes], beginning with the Kṣatriyas, the Brāhmaṇas are the source and the most excellent, both by birth and by action. Even among the Brāhmaṇas, those who are habituated to hearing and studying the Vedas, being perfected in hearing and study, are superior. Among them, those devoted to ritual action—those whose nature is the performance of prescribed duties—are the most distinguished.

Even more excellent than those are the ones most skilled in knowing the inner self, who, through the yoga of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, according to the path to be described, are devoted to the knowledge of the reality of the Self; this is to be supplied as the conclusion. 1.199.

Having thus described the state of being a worthy recipient through each individual factor—namely birth, learning, performance of rites, and austerity—by way of praise, he now declares that the state of being a complete recipient arises from their combination:
"Neither by learning alone, nor even by austerity, is one a worthy recipient;
where conduct and both of these exist together, that indeed is proclaimed a worthy recipient."
Full qualification does not arise through learning alone— that is, through the mere accomplishment of hearing and studying the scriptures—

nor through austerity alone, such as tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth. By the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that full qualification does not arise through ritual performance alone, nor through caste alone.
How then?

That person in whom conduct—that is, the performance of duties—and both of these, namely knowledge and austerity (the word "and" implying also the Brāhmaṇa caste), exist, is proclaimed by Manu and others as a "full vessel. For there is no recipient more excellent than him.

In this regard, one should observe the gradation of results according to the increasing excellence of the combination of birth, knowledge, performance of rites, and austerity, each succeeding one being more praiseworthy than the preceding. || 1.200 ||
A gift of cows and other such things should be given to a worthy recipient.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be bestowed upon a worthy recipient with due honor;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise person desiring his own welfare.

The aforementioned gift, such as a cow and so forth, should be given to a worthy recipient (pātra) along with the prescribed ritual procedures, including the offering of water as enjoined by the scriptures.

However, regarding an unworthy recipient (apātra)—such as a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa who is fallen (patita)—a wise person who understands the specific fruits resulting from specific recipients and who desires the highest good (śreyas), that is, the full fruit, must not give even the slightest thing.
By the use of the term "highest good," it is indicated that even in the case of giving to an unworthy recipient, there is some kind of tamasic fruit.
As Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana has said:
"That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients,
and which is offered without respect and with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa)."
Thus:
"That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients,
without respect and with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa)."

By stating that "it should not be given to an unworthy recipient" (*apātra*), it is indicated that when a distinguished place, time, or substance is present, but a worthy recipient (*pātra*) or the substance itself is not, one may either perform a renunciation (*tyāga*) intended for that recipient or make a formal promise (*pratiśravaṇa*) to him and then deliver it; however, it is not meant that one should give to an unworthy recipient.

Likewise, even what has been promised should not be given later if it is subsequently discovered that the recipient is associated with sin or other such faults, because of the prohibition: "Even having made a promise, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness" (1.201).
Having stated the prohibition against giving to an unworthy recipient, he speaks with regard to the receiver:
"A gift must not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward."
One who is devoid of learning and austerity should not accept gifts such as gold and the like;
for by accepting them while lacking learning and other virtues, he leads both the donor and himself downward, bringing them to hell. || 1.202 ||
It has been stated that [gifts] such as cows should be given to a worthy recipient; regarding this, he states a specific rule:
"One should give daily to a worthy recipient, and especially on auspicious occasions."
Even when requested, one should give what is purified by faith, according to one's own ability.

Every day, according to one's capacity and following the prescribed rule, gifts such as cows and the like should be given to a worthy recipient without detriment to one's own family. On special occasions, such as lunar eclipses and others, one should especially give more with great effort.
Even when requested, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith and cleansed by freedom from malice.

By stating that "one should give even when requested," it is taught that a gift given by going oneself to the aforementioned worthy recipient, or by inviting them, yields great fruit. And so says the traditional scripture: "The gift which is given after having gone [to the recipient] is remembered as having infinite fruit."
When summoned, he should pay a thousandfold; but when requested, only half of that.
Thus [ends the section]. 1.203.
A gift that is given after having gone [to the recipient] is said to have infinite fruit;
one given after summoning [the recipient] has a thousandfold fruit, but when requested, it is half of that.
It has been stated that cows and other such items are to be given; regarding that, he states the specific details for the gift of a cow:
"A well-behaved cow with horns plated in gold and hooves in silver, provided with a cloth."
A milch cow, accompanied by a bronze vessel and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given.
That cow which has horns made of gold is called *hemaśṛṅgī*.

She should be provided with silver hooves (*raupya*), covered with cloth, accompanied by a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), yielding much milk, and of good temperament; she should be given according to one's ability along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). || 1.204 ||
He states the fruit of the gift of a cow:
"The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs [on her body];
if she is tawny (kapilā), she further delivers his lineage up to the seventh generation."

The donor attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on this cow—that is, equal in number to the hairs. If she is tawny (kapilā), then she not only rescues the donor, but also the family up to the seventh generation, encompassing six ancestors beginning with the father and oneself as the seventh.
The word *bhūyas* is used in the sense of "also" (*api*). 1.205.
The Fruit of the Gift of a Cow with Calf Facing Both Ways:
A donor who gives a cow facing both ways according to the previously mentioned rite attains heaven for as many eons as there are hairs on the bodies of the cow and her calf.

One who gives a "two-faced" cow according to the previously mentioned rite attains and enjoys heaven for as many ages—as many as the hairs on the body of that cow together with her calf; for "with her calf" (*savatsā*) means she who exists together with her calf, and "equal to the hairs" means for a number of ages equal to the total number of hairs on both the calf and the cow, such as the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages. || 1.206 ||
What, then, is the "two-faced" [cow], and how is that gift of such great fruit? To this he says:
"As long as both the calf's two feet and its face are seen within the womb, for that long the cow is to be known as the earth, until she releases the fetus."

As long as the two feet and the face of the calf emerging from the womb are visible within the birth canal, she is called "two-faced" (*ubhayatomukhī*), because at that time she possesses faces on both sides.
As long as she does not release the fetus, that cow should be known as equal to the earth;
therefore, it is appropriate that there be an excellence of fruit [from such a gift]. || 1.207 ||
The fruit of the general gift of a cow: Having given a cow in whatever manner possible— whether it be a milch cow or even one that is not milch—
the donor, provided the animal is healthy and free from affliction, is glorified in heaven.

In any case, even if golden horns and the like are absent, by giving a cow—whether one that yields milk or not—that is non-barren, free from disease, unafflicted, and not excessively weak, according to the previously mentioned procedure as far as possible, the donor is honored and exalted in heaven. || 1.208 ||

He states that these are equal to the gift of a cow: massaging one who is fatigued, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away the remnants of their meal; these are like the gift of a cow.
Relieving the fatigue of the weary by providing seats, beds, and so forth, is "massaging the weary.
Attending to the sick consists of serving them according to one's ability and providing medicine and other necessities.
Worshiping the gods is the propitiation of Hari, Hara, Hiranyagarbha, and others with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Washing the feet of twice-born men who are equal or superior [to oneself],
and wiping away their food-leavings—
these are equal to the gift of a cow mentioned immediately above. (1.209)
By giving land, lamps, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter, a house, gold, and draft animals,
one is glorified in heaven.
The earth yields fruit;
lamps [are offered] in temples and other such places;
and shelter is a refuge for travelers.
That which is given for the purpose of settling [the bride]—that is, for the sake of the householder’s life—is *naiveśika*.
Gold is *suvarṇa*.
A draft-ox is a bull capable of bearing a burden.
The rest is well known.
Having given these—the earth, the islands, and so forth—one is glorified and honored in the heavenly world.
Furthermore, the mention of heaven as the fruit of giving land and other gifts is not intended to exclude other fruits; for it is said: "Whatever sin one commits, whether knowingly or unknowingly..."
One is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cowhide.
Likewise, Manu says: "The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision."
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of an ox attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun.
This is because other such fruits are heard [in scripture].
Furthermore, the definition of a *gocarma* has been shown by Bṛhaspati:
"A *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas* measured by a staff seven cubits long."
Having given ten of those very same cow-hides, one is glorified in heaven.
Thus [ends the verse]. 1.210.
A *nivartana* consists of thirty *daṇḍas*, each *daṇḍa* being seven cubits long; ten such *nivartanas* constitute a *gocarma*. By giving this much land, one is glorified in heaven.
By giving a house, grain, fearlessness, shoes, an umbrella, garlands, ointments, a vehicle, a tree, a favorite object, or a bed, one becomes supremely happy.
A house is well known. Grains refer to rice, wheat, and so forth. Fearlessness is the protection of those who are afraid.
Sandals, an umbrella,
a garland such as that of jasmine and other flowers,
and an ointment such as saffron and sandalwood.
A vehicle refers to chariots and the like;
a tree refers to those such as mango trees that provide sustenance;
and "that which is dear" refers to whatever is dear to someone, such as dharma and so forth.
By giving a bed, one becomes exceedingly and supremely happy.

Nor is it the case that the gift of Dharma is impossible because, like gold and other such things, it cannot be placed in the hand; for this difficulty applies equally to the gift of land and so forth, and because the gift of Dharma is heard of in another Smṛti: "One should diligently bestow merit upon the gods, the gurus, and likewise upon one's mother and father; it is nowhere enjoined that one should give demerit."

In the case of giving what is not meritorious, that very [demerit] increases for the recipient as well, who proceeds out of greed and other such motives; for the evil-minded person who accepts [a gift] knowing it to be harmful, sin shall cling to him in proportion to his reprehensible conduct.
Among donors, [the merit] increases twofold at each stage up to a thousandfold, and it becomes infinite.
Thus it is from the traditional law (smṛti).

And here, in all cases, the gradation of the fruit for both the giver and the recipient is to be understood from the specific nature of the place, time, and recipient; from the specific nature of the gift to be given; from the specific nature of the giver; and likewise from the specific nature of the conduct of the recipient—as it has been declared by me: "In giving, there is a fruit; in harming [by not giving], there is indeed the same. || 1.211 ||
The fruit of giving has been explained. Now, he states the causes for attaining the fruit of giving even apart from the act of giving itself:
"Since Brahman, which consists of all dharmas, is superior to all gifts..."
By giving that, one attains the world of Brahmā, from which there is no falling away.
Since Brahman consists of all phenomena (*sarvadharmamaya*) by virtue of being their manifestor, therefore that gift is superior even to all other gifts.
Consequently, one who gives it attains the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) through means such as teaching,
and does not fall away— that is, so that there is no falling away.
The meaning is that he remains in the world of Brahmā until the dissolution of all beings (*bhūtasaṃplava*).

And in this case, "giving" (*dāna*) regarding the gift of Brahman consists merely in the transfer of ownership to another, since it is impossible to effect the cessation of one's own ownership. (1.212)
The fruit for the donor has been explained. Now, he states the reason why one may obtain the fruit of giving even without the act of giving itself:
"He who, though capable of receiving, does not accept a gift..."
Whatever worlds belong to those who are generous and virtuous, he attains those abundant realms.

He who, though being a worthy recipient, does not accept or take possession of gold and other such gifts that have been offered—if he does not take what has not been offered, he attains all those worlds belonging to those whose nature is generosity. || 1.213 ||
Now, in the context of the prohibition against accepting all gifts, he states the exception: "Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth,
meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water— these should not be refused."
*Dhānāḥ* are roasted barley grains;
*kṣitiḥ* is earth;
the rest is well known.

And this *kuśa* grass and so forth, when brought by oneself, must not be refused; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), [other items such as] the house and so forth are included: "One should not reject a bed, a house, *kuśa* grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, and even vegetables."
Likewise:
"One may accept from anyone fuel, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered, honey, and the gift of safety."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu (1.214).
To the question "Why should it not be rejected?", he says:
Even that which is brought unasked may be accepted from one of evil deeds,
except in the case of an unchaste woman, a eunuch, or an outcast, O twice-born one.
Since even this grass and such, brought unasked, which belongs to one who has committed evil deeds, is to be accepted— how much more so that belonging to one who acts as prescribed?
Therefore, it must not be refused,
except in the case of unchaste women, eunuchs, the fallen, and enemies.
A *kulaṭā* is one who wanders from family to family, such as an unchaste woman;
a *ṣaṇḍha* is the third gender (*tṛtīyā prakṛtiḥ*). || 1.215 ||
He states another exception to the prohibition against accepting gifts:
"For the sake of honoring gods and guests, or indeed for the purpose of maintaining one's teachers and dependents,
as well as for one's own subsistence, one may accept [gifts] from anyone."

Because of the necessity of honoring the gods, guests, and so forth, for that purpose he may accept gifts from all sources—excluding those who are fallen or otherwise utterly contemptible—even if they lack spiritual self-restraint (*anātman*).
"Gurus" refers to the mother, father, and others; "dependents" (*bhṛtyāḥ*) refers to those to be supported, such as wife, sons, and so forth. (1.216)
Now the section on *śrāddha* is commenced.
*Śrāddha* is defined as the relinquishment (*tyāga*) of food or a substance serving as its substitute, dedicated with devotion (*śraddhayā*) to the deceased (*preta*).
It is of two kinds: *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa*.
Among these, that which is performed with reference to three ancestors is the *pārvaṇa*;
that which is performed with reference to a single ancestor is the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
Furthermore, it is of three kinds: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*).

In this context, that which is enjoined with reference to the constant condition of fixed times—such as every day, the new moon, or the *aṣṭakā* days—is called *nitya*. That which is enjoined with reference to an occasional condition is *naimittika*, such as [rites performed] upon the birth of a son and so forth. That which is prescribed with reference to the condition of a desire for a result is *kāmya*, such as [rites performed] when there is a desire for heaven and so forth on specific lunar mansions like Kṛttikā or on particular lunar days (*tithi*).
Furthermore, it is of five kinds: the daily *śrāddha*, the *pārvaṇa*, the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, the *ekoddiṣṭa*, and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
Among these, the daily *śrāddha* is that which has been described in such passages as "food for the ancestors and humans," and so forth.
And likewise, Manu says:
One should offer the Śrāddha daily with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, to bring about inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors.
Thus it is said.
One should offer the Śrāddha daily with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, to bring about inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors.
Now, intending to demonstrate the *pārvaṇa* and *vṛddhi* śrāddhas, he states their times: "The new moon (*amāvāsyā*),

the *aṣṭakās*, the *vṛddhi*, the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*), the availability of materials, the excellence of Brahmins, the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and the sun's passage into a new sign (*sūryasaṃkrama*)."
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the times for Śrāddha.

The day on which the moon is not visible is the new moon (amāvāsyā). When that [new moon] spans two days, the one occurring during the afternoon (aparāhṇa) is to be accepted, according to the statement: "The afternoon belongs to the ancestors. And the afternoon is the fourth part of the day divided into five parts, consisting of three muhūrtas.
Regarding the four Aṣṭakās, Āśvalāyana stated: "The Aṣṭakās are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons."
*Vṛddhi* refers to occasions such as the birth of a son;
the *kṛṣṇapakṣa* is the latter fortnight;
and the two *ayanas* are those designated as southern and northern.
The substance consists of *kṛsara*, black gram (*māṣa*), and so forth.
The excellence of the Brahmins will be described later.
The two equinoxes are the sun’s passage through Aries and Libra.

The *sūryasaṃkrama* is the Sun’s transition from one zodiac sign (*rāśi*) to another. Although the solstices (*ayana*) and equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) are already established as types of *saṃkrānti*, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of demonstrating their superior results. A *vyatīpāta* is a specific type of astronomical conjunction (*yoga*).

Regarding *gajacchāyā*: when the moon is in the constellation presided over by the ancestors (Maghā) and the sun is situated in Hasta, whichever lunar day that may be, it is indeed proclaimed as *gajacchāyā*.
Thus it is defined.
Some say it means "the shadow of an elephant," but that is not accepted here because the context concerns time.
An eclipse is the seizing (grahaṇa) of the moon and the sun;
and when the performer has a desire for the śrāddha, then also—
by the word "and" (ca)— the beginnings of the yugas and so forth are included.

These are the times for the *śrāddha* ceremony. Although there is a prohibition against eating during an eclipse, as stated in the rule "one should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun," nevertheless, while the eater incurs a fault, the giver gains spiritual merit. (1.217–1.218)
He now describes the excellence of the Brahmins required for the four types of śrāddhas to be mentioned hereafter, excluding the daily (aharahaḥ) śrāddha:
"The foremost among all those learned in the Vedas is one who is a śrotriya, a knower of Brahman, and young;
one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, a reciter of the Trimadhu, and a reciter of the Trisuparṇa."
Those who are capable of constant and unerring study of all the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, by means of undistracted attention, are the foremost.
A *śrotriya* is one perfected in the hearing and study of the scriptures.
One who knows the Brahman that is about to be described is a *brahmavid*.
"Youth" refers to one in middle age;
this qualifies everyone.
One who knows the meaning of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is called a "knower of the meaning of the Veda."

The *jyeṣṭhasāman* is a specific *sāman* chant and the vow that is its auxiliary study; one who studies it by performing that vow is a *jyeṣṭhasāmā*. The *trimadhu* is a portion of the *Ṛgveda* and the vow associated with it; one who studies it by performing that vow is a *trimadhu*. The *trisuparṇa* is a portion of both the *Ṛgveda* and the *Yajurveda* and the vow associated with it; one who studies it by performing that vow is a *trisuparṇika*.
"These Brāhmaṇas" is to be connected with what will be stated as "the perfections of the Śrāddha. (1.219)
A sister’s son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, a person for whom one performs sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle,
one who has mastered the Triṇāciketa rite, a daughter’s son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman;
A sister's son is a *svastrīya*;
an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is defined by the previously stated characteristics;
a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*) is the husband of one's daughter.
The *triṇāciketa* is a portion of the *Yajurveda* as well as its associated vow; one who studies that [portion] by performing that vow is a *triṇāciketa*.
The rest is well known.

These [types of persons] are to be understood as [eligible recipients] in the absence of those previously mentioned, such as the foremost *śrotriya* and others; for this is indeed the primary rule (*kalpa*) regarding the offering of *havya* and *kavya* oblations.
This secondary rule has been proclaimed by the virtuous as one that is never to be censured.
Having stated this, [it is so] because Manu has prescribed [the performance of rites] for one's sister's sons and others. 1.220.

Those Brahmins who are devoted to ritual action, devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, lifelong celibates, and those dedicated to their fathers and mothers, bring perfection to the Śrāddha rite.
Those devoted to action (*karmaniṣṭhāḥ*) are those intent upon the performance of prescribed duties.
Those devoted to austerity (*taponiṣṭhāḥ*) are those whose character is defined by ascetic practice.
One who possesses the *sabhya*, *āvasathya*, and the three sacrificial fires (*tretāgni*) is a "five-fire" practitioner (*pañcāgni*), as well as one who studies the *Pañcāgnividyā*.
The *brahmacārins* are both those who have returned home (*upakurvāṇaka*) and those who remain lifelong (*naiṣṭika*).
They are devoted to their father and mother, intent upon their worship; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), those devoted to knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭha*) and others are also included.
The Brahmins, not the Kṣatriyas and others, are the causes for the attainment of imperishable fruit in the Śrāddha rites; they are the ones who bring about the perfection of the Śrāddhas. (1.221)
He states those who are to be avoided: "One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, one born of a remarried woman,
one who has broken his vow of chastity, a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth."
A "sick person" (rogī) is one afflicted by a major disease. One whose limb is deficient or redundant is "one with deficient or redundant limbs" (hīnātiriktāṅgaḥ).
One who sees with only one eye is "one-eyed" (kāṇaḥ).
For this very reason, those who are blind, deaf, impotent, bald, afflicted with skin diseases, and so forth, are excluded.
A *paunarbhava* is one born from a *punarbhū*, whose characteristics have been previously described.
An *avakīrṇin* is one who has faltered in his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) while still in that state.
The Kuṇḍa and the Golaka: two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from the wives of others.
The son born while the husband is alive is a Kuṇḍa; when the husband is dead, he is a Golaka.
These two possess the characteristics thus described.
A "kunakhī" is one with deformed nails;
a "śyāvadantaka" is one whose teeth are naturally black.
"These are censured at a śrāddha" is the connection with what is to be stated hereafter. || 1.222 ||
One who teaches for wages, a eunuch, one who corrupts a maiden, one accused of a grave sin, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother;
One who teaches for the sake of receiving wages is a "wage-teacher" (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*);
likewise, one who studies by giving wages [to the teacher] is also [one to be avoided].
A "eunuch" (*klība*) is a hermaphrodite (*napuṃsaka*).
One who defiles a maiden with false or true faults is a "defiler of maidens" (*kanyādūṣī*).
One who is accused of a crime such as the killing of a Brahmin, whether falsely or truly, is "accused" (*abhiśasta*).
A betrayer of friends is a "friend-betrayer" (*mitradhruk*).
A slanderer is one who habitually proclaims the faults of others.
A seller of soma is one who sells the soma used in a sacrifice.
A "parivindaka" is a younger brother who marries before his elder brother.

If an elder brother has neither taken a wife nor established the sacred fires, and a younger brother should take a wife or establish the sacred fires, he is called a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder),
while the elder brother is a *parivitti* (the one superseded).
As Manu says:
He who enters into the union of marriage and the agnihotra while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivetta*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.
Thus:

"He who, while his elder brother remains, enters into marriage and the *agnihotra* sacrifice, is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*."

In this way, both the giver and the officiating priest, as well as the elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him, and she by whom he is married— all these go to hell, with the giver and the priest as the fifth.
Thus, from the statement of Manu: 1.223.

One who abandons his mother, father, or teacher; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*; the son of a *vṛṣala*; the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and those whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.

He who abandons his mother, father, or guru without a valid reason is one who has abandoned his mother, father, and guru. Likewise is he who abandons his wife or son. Manu declared: "An aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be supported even if they have committed a hundred improper acts."
This is because of the identical designation.
One who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* is called a *kuṇḍāśin*.
Likewise for a *golaka*: he who eats the food of those two is proclaimed a *kuṇḍāśin*.
According to this statement: a *vṛṣala* is one devoid of dharma; his son is a *vṛṣalātmaja*. A *parapūrvā* is a remarried woman (*punarbhū*); her husband [is also excluded].

One who takes what is not given is a thief. Those corrupted by their actions are those who act in contravention of the scriptures. By the use of the word "and" (ca), gamblers, temple-priests, and others of that sort are included.
These are censured and prohibited in the *śrāddha*.

Although the unfitness of those other than the ones described is already established by the definition of Brāhmaṇas fit for the *śrāddha*—beginning with the words "foremost in all the Vedas" and so forth—the repeated prohibition of certain individuals such as the sick and others is intended to ensure that, in the absence of Brāhmaṇas possessing the aforementioned characteristics, those who are free from the [other] prohibitions may be accepted. (1.224)
Having thus described the times for the *śrāddha* and the Brahmins [to be invited], he now states the procedure for the *pārvaṇa* rite:
"On the day before [the rite], one who is self-possessed and pure should invite the Brahmins;
they too must remain restrained in their mental, vocal, and physical actions."

On the day before [the rite], or on the following day, or when the Śrāddha ceremony is at hand— on either the previous day or the next— he should invite the previously mentioned Brāhmaṇas with the words, "May a moment be granted for the Śrāddha," and by means of this request, he should cause them to accept the invitation. He should properly invite at least three Brāhmaṇas who possess the qualities already described.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu,

one who possesses self-control (*ātmavān*), being free from grief, madness, and other such afflictions, does not become possessed of faults. Alternatively, "possessing self" means that one should have the senses restrained.
He should be pure and self-restrained; and those invited Brahmins, too, must remain disciplined and controlled in their mental, vocal, and physical activities. 1.225.
Having honored those who have arrived with a welcome in the afternoon,
he— holding the purifier (pavitra) in his hand and having offered them water for sipping (ācamana)— should cause them to sit upon their seats.

In the afternoon, having honored those invited Brahmins according to the previously described characteristics, having summoned them and greeted them with words of welcome, and having performed the washing of their feet, one should seat them—once they have sipped water (ācamana) and are seated on prepared seats—with the *pavitra* grass held in one’s own hand, while they likewise hold the *pavitra* in their hands.

Although it is stated here generally as "in the afternoon," nevertheless, it is most auspicious to begin at the *kutapa* hour and complete the rite within the five *muhūrtas* following it; for fifteen *muhūrtas* are always renowned in a day, and among them, that which is the eighth *muhūrta* is remembered as the *kutapa* time.
Since the sun always becomes dim at midday,
therefore an undertaking begun at that time is distinguished by yielding infinite fruit.
The four muhūrtas that follow the Kutapa muhūrta—
this group of five muhūrtas is indeed desired as the abode of Svadhā.
Thus it is stated. Likewise, another item useful for the *śrāddha* rite, known as the *kutapa*, has been mentioned:
"Midday, a sword-vessel, and likewise a Nepalese woolen blanket."
Silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and a daughter—these are recorded as the eight [purifiers].
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; since these eight cause torment (saṃtāpa) for one who possesses such [sin], they are therefore renowned as "kutapa."
Thus [ends verse 1.226].
Midday, a sword, a vessel, as well as a Nepalese blanket,
silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth.
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; because these eight cause torment for one who possesses such [sin], they are therefore renowned as "kutapas."
One should invite an even number of guests for the rite to the gods according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number for the rite to the ancestors;
this should be done in a pure place that has been strewn [with grass] and slopes toward the south.
In a *daiva* or *ābhyudayika* śrāddha, one should seat an even number of Brāhmaṇas. How? According to one's capacity, without exceeding that capacity.
Therein, for the Vaiśvadeva rite, there are two; for the three beginning with the mother, two for each individual, or two for all three together.
In this manner, for each individual among the father and others, there are two [seats], or for three, there are two.
Likewise, for the maternal grandfather and others, in each of the three groups, the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed either separately or as a single common procedure (*tantra*).
In the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha for the ancestors, one should seat an odd number—that is, an uneven number—of [invited guests]; thus the connection is made.

And this [rite] should be performed on a site that is strewn all around, covered over, purified by being smeared with cow dung and the like, and sloping toward the south—that is, inclined toward the south. (1.227)

Regarding the rule "an odd number for the ancestors," since there is a possibility of using an odd number even in the Vaiśvadeva rite which is an ancillary part of the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, this [next verse] is commenced: "Two for the gods.
Two for the gods, three to the east for the ancestors, or one each;
likewise for the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common procedure (tantra).

In the *daiva* rite for the Viśvedevas, two Brāhmaṇas should be seated facing the east. Regarding the statement "an odd number in the *pitrya* rite," since this would otherwise apply without distinction, a specific rule is stated: "three in the *pitrya*.
In the *pitrya* rite—that is, at the place for the ancestors and others—three should be seated facing the north.
He states another alternative: "Or indeed one by one.
One should seat one [guest] each at the Vaiśvadeva and the Pitrya rites;
this is an option according to the circumstances.
The invitation and other rites for the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*) in the *śrāddha* are likewise performed.

Two [seats] are for the gods (*daiva*) to the east, and three to the north for the ancestors (*pitrya*), or else one for each; this should be done according to the procedure for the paternal *śrāddha*.
Both the paternal *śrāddha* and the maternal grandfather *śrāddha*, including the *vaiśvadevika* rite, should be performed either separately or by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).
The word *tantra* denotes a collective performance.
However, when only two Brāhmaṇas are obtained, then, having prepared a single vessel for the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should appoint one Brāhmaṇa at each [of the two rites].
As Vasiṣṭha has said:
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed? Having set aside a portion of food from all that has been prepared into a vessel—
Having performed [the rites] in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the śrāddha;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (brahmacārin).
Thus [ends the verse]. 1.227.
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed? Having set aside a portion of food from all that has been prepared into a vessel—
Having performed [the rites] in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the śrāddha;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (brahmacārin).
Having given water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for the seats, he should, being authorized, invoke the Viśvedevas with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas... (*viśvedevāsaḥ*).

Immediately thereafter, having given water into the hands of the Brahmins intended for the Vaiśvadeva rite and having placed double-folded *kuśa* grass for their seats on the right side of their sitting places, he should ask the Brahmins, "Shall I invite the Viśvedevas? Being permitted by them with the words, "Invite them," he should invoke them with this Ṛgvedic verse, "O Viśvedevas, come hither," and with this Smṛti mantra, "May the illustrious ones arrive.

This should be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) and moving clockwise; then, having turned the thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), he should perform the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) counter-clockwise.
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) regarding this specific rule for rites for the ancestors (pitrya). 1.229.

Then, having scattered barley grains [into the vessel], and having poured water into the vessel containing the *pavitra* blades while reciting "śaṃ no devīr," he likewise pours barley grains while reciting "yavo 'si."
One should pour the *arghya* water into their hands with the mantra beginning "yā divyā."

Then, having strewn barley grains around the ground in a clockwise direction near the Brāhmaṇas invited for the Vaiśvadeva rite, he should next pour water into a vessel made of metal or other materials that contains a *pavitra* and is lined with a pair of *kuśa* blades, reciting the verse, "May the divine waters be for our aid" (*śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye*). Then, having poured barley grains with the mantra beginning, "Thou art barley, the king of grain," and subsequently adding perfumes and flowers, he should pour the *arghya* water into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas—which are covered by the *pavitra* from the *arghya* vessels—reciting the mantra beginning, "The celestial waters on earth," followed by, "O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*. || 1.230 ||
Having offered water, perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps;
Likewise, there is the gift of a garment and water for the purpose of washing the hands.
Now, having given water for the purpose of washing the hands, one should perform the offering of fragrance, flowers, incense, and lamps in due order, as well as the gift of a garment.
Regarding the specific details of the fragrances and other items, the distinctions stated in another Smṛti should be observed.

Viṣṇu has stated that sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka are for the purpose of anointing. As for flowers, in a śrāddha ceremony, jasmine, mallikā, white yūthikā, all water-born flowers, and the campaka are recommended.
Thus they have been described.
And those to be avoided are: flowers with pungent odors, those that are odorless, those growing from trees at a *caitya*, and those that are red in color. These flowers are to be rejected.
Not that which grows on thorns.
Even if it grows on thorns, one should offer that which is white and fragrant;
one should not offer that which is red.
One should also offer red substances such as those derived from saffron or lotus; these and other such items are to be understood [from the scriptures].
Regarding incense (*dhūpa*), a specific rule has been stated by Viṣṇu: one should not offer any part of a living being for the purpose of incense.

One should offer guggulu, śīkhaṇḍa, agaru, devadāru, sarala, and so forth, combined with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and honey. Śaṅkha has stated: "A lamp should be offered with clarified butter or, alternatively, with sesame oil."
One should carefully avoid a lamp produced from fat or marrow.
Thus it is said:
A lamp should be offered with clarified butter or, alternatively, with sesame oil;
one should carefully avoid a lamp produced from fat or marrow.
And one should give a bright, new, unwashed garment with its fringe intact.
All this section concerning the performance of the Vaiśvadeva rite should be done facing north;
the section concerning the ancestors (pitrya) should be done facing south.
As Vṛddha-Śātātapa said: "Facing north for the gods and facing south for the ancestors, one should offer everything according to the rules in the Pārvaṇa rite, beginning with the deities."
Thus [ends verse 1.231].
Facing north for the gods and facing south for the ancestors,
one should offer everything according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the rites for the gods in the Pārvaṇa ceremony.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should perform the circumambulation for the ancestors in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having offered double-folded *kuśa* grasses while reciting the verse "uśantas tvā," he should invoke the ancestors; then, permitted by them, he should mutter the verse "āyantu naḥ."

Then, immediately after the Vaiśvadeva section, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) so that it hangs across the chest (prācīnāvīta), the author indicates by the use of the word "tataḥ" (then) that the performance follows the *kāṇḍānusamaya* order. Having offered water first, one should place an odd number of *kuśa* blades—folded double and turned counter-clockwise—from left to right for the purpose of the seats (*viṣṭara*) upon the seats for the three ancestors beginning with the father; then one should offer water again, for the *Āśvalāyana-smṛti* states: "Having offered water, having provided the seat with *darbha* blades folded double, and having offered water again..."

This offering of water at the beginning and the end should be understood as being for the sake of introducing and concluding each individual rite, both in the *vaiśvadeva* and the *pitrya* ceremonies.

Then, having asked the Brahmins, "I shall invoke the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers," and being permitted by them with the words, "Invoke [them]," he should invoke the ancestors and so forth with this verse, "uśantas tvā nidhīmahi," and then worship them with the mantra beginning, "āyantu naḥ pitaraḥ. (1.232–1.233)
Having scattered sesame seeds all around while reciting "apahatāḥ," one should perform the functions of barley with sesame seeds and offer the *arghya* and other rites as before.
Having offered the *arghya* water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down with the words, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors."
Tasks to be accomplished with barley, such as the scattering [of grain] and so forth, should be performed with sesame seeds.
Then, one should perform the rites from the placement of the *arghya* vessels up to their covering, as previously described.

In this regard, the specific procedure is as follows: having scattered sesame seeds around the Brāhmaṇas in a counter-clockwise direction while reciting the mantra beginning with "The Asuras and Rakṣasas have been struck down by the sesame seeds," and having poured water into three vessels made of silver or other materials—each containing a *kūrca* (a bundle) made of an odd number of *kuśa* grass blades—while reciting the mantra "May the Goddesses be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*); and having thrown sesame seeds and fragrant flowers into them while reciting the mantra beginning with "Thou art sesame, Soma is thy deity" (*tilo 'si somadaivatya*); and having placed the *arghya* vessels before the Brāhmaṇas while saying "Svadhā, worthy of honor" (*svadhā-arghyāḥ*); he should then offer the *arghya* into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas at the conclusion of the mantra "That which is divine" (*yā divyāḥ*), saying: "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*."
Even in this alternative view—that one may offer to each [deity] in both [the *arghya* and *tarpaṇa* rites]—three vessels must be prepared.

Having thus offered the *arghya*, one should take the remnants (*saṃsrava*) of those *arghya*s—the water from the *arghya* offerings that has flowed from the hands of the Brahmins—and place them into the vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*). Then, having placed a bunch of *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south upon the ground, one should turn that vessel face down (inverted) over it with the mantra: "Thou art the seat for the ancestors.
Upon that, one should place the strainers (*pavitra*) from the *arghya* vessels.

Immediately thereafter, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garments using the formula: "Father, this is your perfume; Father, this is your flower," and so forth. || 1.234 || 1.235 ||
He states the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) with two verses:
"Intending to offer into the fire, he takes up the food soaked in ghee and asks [the permission].
Having been granted permission with the words 'Do so,' he offers it into the fire as in the *pitṛyajña*."
With a concentrated mind, one should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels,
especially those made of silver, as they may be available.
Immediately thereafter, intending to offer it into the fire, he should take food soaked in ghee and smeared with ghee and ask the Brāhmaṇas, "I shall offer into the fire.
The mention of ghee is for the purpose of excluding soup, vegetables, and the like.

Then, having been authorized by them with the words "Do so," wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), and having placed pure food near the fire, he should take a portion with a stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa) according to the rules for taking sacrificial portions and offer it with the mantra: "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, svadhā! Homage!"

Having offered into the fire with the formula, "To Agni Kavyavāhana, Svadhā! Homage! according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and having cast the stirring-ladle (mekṣaṇa) into the fire, he should give the remains of the oblation—excluding anything made of clay—into vessels for the ancestors and others that are available, especially those made of silver, but not into the vessels used for the Vaiśvadeva offering. He should do so with a concentrated mind, his attention fixed on nothing else.

In this context, although it is stated without qualification that "in the fire," nevertheless, for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) according to the *sarvādhāna* method, there is no *aupāsana* fire. Consequently, in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* which occurs immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the oblation is offered in the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire), because that fire is present and because we observe an exception to the rule that "Smārta rites are performed in the marriage fire" (*vivāhāgni*).
As Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"But one who has maintained the sacred fires, being composed, should offer the oblation in the *dakṣiṇāgni*."
"But one who has not maintained the sacred fires [should offer] on the *aupāsana* fire; in the absence of fire, [he may offer] in a twice-born man or in water.
However, one who has maintained the sacred fires should, with a concentrated mind, offer the oblation in the *dakṣiṇāgni*.

However, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the fire-offering (*agnaukaraṇahoma*) is performed either in the *aupāsana* fire, or in the absence of fire in a twice-born man, or in water.

But in the case of one who maintains half of the fires (*ardhādhāna*), since the *aupāsana* fire is present, the fire-offering is performed in that very *aupāsana* fire, just as it is for one who has not maintained the fires.
This applies likewise to the three occasions beginning with the *Anvaṣṭakā*, because the ritual procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is extended to them by analogy.
In the four rites beginning with the *kāmya*, the oblation is offered into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa alone.
As the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras have said:
"The *ānvaṣṭakya*, that on the day before, the monthly, and then the *pārvaṇa*."
The optional rite for prosperity on the eighth day, and then the eighth is the Ekoddiṣṭa.
For those who maintain the sacred fires, the oblation is prescribed to be offered into the fire during the first four [rites];
for the latter four, it should be placed into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors.
The meaning of this is as follows:
the *aṣṭakās* are prescribed for the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons (*hemanta-śiśira*).
Among these, that which is performed on the ninth day is called the *anvaṣṭakya*.

That which is performed on the seventh [lunar day] is done on the preceding day. That which is prescribed by extension from the *anvaṣṭakya* rite—on whichever lunar day one chooses among those beginning with the fifth of the dark fortnight month after month—is as follows:
that which is prescribed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) immediately following the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is the *pārvaṇa*.
That which is prescribed for specific desires, such as the attainment of heaven, under asterisms like Kṛttikā and others, is called *kāmya* (optional).
That which is prescribed on occasions of prosperity—such as the birth of a son, or the consecration of tanks, gardens, and deities—is called *ābhyudayika* (prosperity-related).
The *aṣṭakās* are prescribed for the eighth lunar day.

Regarding the term *ekoddiṣṭa*: here, by the word *ekoddiṣṭa*, the author indicates the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, because the *ekoddiṣṭa* is also present therein, whereas it is absent in the direct *ekoddiṣṭa*.

Alternatively, according to the view of the commentator on the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, since the *pāṇi-homa* (offering into the hand) exists even in the direct *ekoddiṣṭa*, it refers to that very direct *ekoddiṣṭa*.

Of these eight [offerings], in the first four, the oblation is made into the fire by one who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*); in the latter four, it is made into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors (*pitrya*).

Even for a twice-born man who lacks a sacred fire because his father has died, the *pārvaṇa* rite is obligatory; therefore, even for him, the oblation is made only into the hand. "The twice-born man whose father has died who does not offer the *śrāddha*... [is censured].
But he who does so at the end of the month, when the mother's milk has ceased, must perform an expiation every month.
Because of this statement;
