likewise, in the case of rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the *aṣṭakā*, and the *ekoddiṣṭa*, the oblation is offered directly into the hand. For it is recorded in the *Manusmṛti*: "In the absence of fire, however, one should offer [the oblation] into the hand of the Brahmin alone."
The prohibition against taking separate mouthfuls from food given by hand is stated as follows;
as the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras say:
"Foolish people eat separately the food that has been placed upon the palm of the hand."
By that [offering], the ancestors are satisfied; they do not receive the remaining food.
That which is placed in the palm of the hand and that which has been prepared otherwise should be enjoyed as one; no distinction exists.
Thus [ends the section]. 1.236 || 1.237 ||
The unintelligent eat the food given in the palm of the hand separately;
by that the ancestors are satisfied, but they do not receive the remaining food.
That which is placed upon the palm of the hand and that which has been prepared otherwise should be enjoyed as one; no distinction exists between them.
The offering of food:
having offered the food, one consecrates the vessel with the mantra, "The earth is the vessel";
then, having recited "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should cause the thumb of the twice-born to rest upon the food.

Having placed food—such as boiled rice, soup, milk-rice, ghee, and so forth—into the vessels, one should consecrate the vessels with the mantra beginning "The earth is your vessel" (*pṛthivī te pātram*). Then, with the verse "Viṣṇu strode across this" (*idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame*), one should cause the thumb of a twice-born guest to touch the food.
Furthermore, during the *vaiśvadeva* rite, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), one says, "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering for the gods" (*viṣṇo havyaṃ rakṣa*).
During the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one says, "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering for the ancestors" (*viṣṇo kavyaṃ rakṣa*).
"One should say 'O Viṣṇu, protect the offering to the gods and the offering to the ancestors' respectively," according to the recollection of Manu (1.238).
Having recited the Gāyatrī with the Vyahṛtis and the three verses beginning with "madhuvātā," they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as much as necessary for comfort.

Immediately thereafter, having offered the food to the gods with water containing barley, saying: "To all the Viśvedevas, this food has been served and shall continue to be served until they are satisfied," and likewise having offered it to the father with the offering of water containing sesame seeds, saying: "To the father, belonging to the [such-and-such] gotra and named [such-and-such], this food has been served and shall continue to be served until he is satisfied," and having similarly offered it to the grandfather and the great-grandfather; then, having given the *āpośana* water, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* together with the previously mentioned *vyāhṛtis*, the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," and the mantra "madhu madhu madhu" three times. Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should say, "Enjoy it as you please," and perform the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* and the honey-verses for the sake of the ancestors and the gods.
Having offered the *śrāddha* and the *apośāna*, there follows the invitation to partake (*juṣapraiṣa*) and then the meal.
Likewise: one should recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the Vyāhṛtis either three times or even once; and likewise the triplet beginning with "madhu vātā" and that triplet beginning with "madhu."

Thus, according to the statement beginning with "Pāraskara": "They too should eat while restraining their speech. Those Brāhmaṇas also, restraining their speech—that is, remaining silent—should eat. 1.239.
Free from anger and without haste, he should give the desired food;
and having recited the purificatory texts as well as the previously mentioned prayers until they are satisfied.
Food consists of five types—edible, chewable, lickable, suckable, and drinkable—and it should be that which is desired by the Brāhmaṇa, the deceased, or the performer.

*Haviṣya* (sacrificial food) is that suitable for the *śrāddha* oblation; it should be understood as comprising rice, *śāli*, barley, wheat, mung beans, black gram, the "hermit's food" (*munyanna*), black nightshade, large-scaled fish, cardamom, ginger, black pepper, asafoetida, jaggery, sugar, camphor, rock salt, *sāṃbhara* salt, *panasa*, coconut, plantain, jujube, products of the cow such as milk, curd, ghee, milk-rice, honey, meat, and so forth, as established in other *smṛtis*.

By the term "fit for oblation" (*haviṣya*), there is the exclusion of everything unfit that is prohibited by other Smṛtis, such as *kodrava*, *masūra*, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), *kulattha*, *pulāka*, flat beans (*niṣpāva*), *rājamāṣa*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), the two types of *bṛhatī*, water-cress (*upodakī*), bamboo shoots, long pepper (*pippalī*), *vacā*, *śatapuṣpā*, herbs, biḍ-salt, buffalo milk, yak-milk, curd, ghee, milk-porridge (*pāyasa*), and so forth.
"Free from anger" means even when a cause for anger arises;
"not hurried" means undisturbed.
The connection is that one should give until satisfaction.

By the word "but" (tu), it is meant that one should give such that something remains as leavings, because the portion of the group of servants consists of the leavings; for the group of servants, that which has fallen on the ground at a rite for the ancestors is declared to be their share, provided they are straightforward and not deceitful.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu:

likewise, having muttered purifying hymns (*pavitra*) such as the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Pāvamānī* verses until satiety, and having recognized that they are satiated, one should mutter the previously mentioned recitation, namely the *Sāvitrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*, as has been stated. (1.240)
Having taken food and being satisfied, and having obtained permission regarding the remainder,
one should scatter that food on the ground and offer water once, then once again.

Immediately thereafter, having taken all the food and asked them, "Are you satisfied? and being told by them, "We are satisfied," he asks, "Is there any remainder? What should be done with it? Having accepted the response, "Let it be enjoyed together with those you love," he places that food on the ground before the Brahmin representing the ancestors, near the remains of the meal, upon which Darbha grass with its tips pointing south has been spread; having first sprinkled water mixed with sesame seeds while reciting the verse beginning with "ye agnidagdhāḥ," he should again sprinkle water mixed with sesame seeds.
Immediately after that, one should give water once in each hand of the Brahmins for the purpose of rinsing the mouth. || 1.241 ||
Before this, the NSP adds: "The offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍapradāna):
having taken all the food together with sesame seeds, facing south, one should offer the rice-balls near the remains of the meal, just as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña)."

By virtue of the extension of the ritual rules for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, if there is the cooking of sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should take all the food together with the remainder of the *caru* left over from the *agnaukaraṇa* offering and offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) in the vicinity of the fire.

In the absence of that, one should take all the food prepared for the Brahmins, mix it with sesame seeds, and facing south, offer the funeral cakes in the vicinity of the leavings according to the ritual rules of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. (1.242)

Before this, NSP and Pāṇḍeya add: "The offering of inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka). One should likewise offer it for the maternal grandfathers; then one should provide water for sipping (ācamana), and thereafter perform the recitation of 'svasti' and the offering of inexhaustible water."
For the maternal grandfathers as well, the ritual—from the invocation of the Viśvedevas up to the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas)—should be performed in exactly this same manner.
Immediately thereafter, one should give the Brāhmaṇas water for sipping (ācamana).
Then one should perform the recitation of the Svasti; one should cause the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce the Svasti by saying, "Pronounce the Svasti."
When they have said, "May it be well," he should offer water into the hands of the Brahmins, saying, "Say, 'May it be inexhaustible'";
and they should say, "May it be inexhaustible. 1.243.
Before this NSP and Pāṇḍeya add: *svadhāvācanam* | "Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should utter the word *svadhā*.
Being authorized with the words 'Let it be recited,' [the priest says] 'Let *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors.'"

Immediately thereafter, having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) such as gold or silver according to his ability, and having said, "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be uttered," and being permitted by those Brahmins with the words, "Let it be uttered," he should pronounce the exclamation *svadhā*, saying, "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors beginning with the father, and for the maternal ancestors beginning with the maternal grandfather. || 1.244 ||
When they have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," one should pour water on the ground;
then, when the Brahmins have said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," one should mutter this:
And those Brahmins should say, "So be it; svadhā.
When they have spoken thus, one should immediately sprinkle water on the ground from a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Then one should say, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased."
When the Brahmins have said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should mutter this which is now being stated immediately hereafter. || 1.245 ||
Before this NSP and Pāṇḍeya add: *Brāhmaṇaprārthanā* (The Prayer to the Brahmins):
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may our faith not depart, and may we have much to give."

May givers of gold and other riches flourish in our family; may they become numerous. May the Vedas increase through the means of study, teaching, understanding their meaning, and their practical application. And may our lineage flourish through the succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
"May our faith in the ancestral rites (pitrya-karma) not depart; let it not go.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "na māṅyoge.
The meaning is that one should mutter: "May there be for us much and boundless wealth, such as gold and the like, to be given. (1.246)
Having spoken thus and having uttered kind words, he should prostrate and dismiss [the guests],
saying "Vāja-vāja" with joy, performing the dismissal beginning with the ancestors.

Having thus recited the previously mentioned prayer-mantra and having spoken kind words—such as, "We are blessed; our home has been purified by the dust of your two feet; disregarding the hardship of eating only vegetables and the like, we have been graced by you"—one should bid them farewell after prostrating and performing a circumambulation preceded by salutation.

As for how one should perform the dismissal, he says: with this verse, "O strong ones, come to our offerings at every offering," one should, preceded by the ancestors—that is, beginning with the great-grandfather and ending with the Viśvedevas—perform the dismissal while holding onto the *darbha* grass, saying, "May the ancestors rise," being pleased and with a well-pleased mind. (NSP 1.247)
But having turned face upwards that vessel of the ancestors into which the remnants were previously placed in the *arghya* vessel, one should dismiss the Brahmins.

In that arghya vessel into which the *saṃsravas*—the water from the arghya offerings that have flowed from the hands of the Brahmins—were previously poured and placed, one should turn that arghya vessel upside down and then turn it face upwards; having done so, one should dismiss the Brahmins. This should be understood as occurring after the recitation of the blessing mantras (*āśīrmantra*) but before the verse beginning with "vāje vāje"; for this is evident from the use of the absolutive suffix (*ktvā*) in the word "having done" (*kṛtvā*) in the phrase "having done, one should dismiss. (1.248)
Having circumambulated [the vessel] clockwise, he should eat what was served to the ancestors;
he should remain celibate for that night together with the Brahmins.

Immediately thereafter, having followed the Brahmins as far as the boundary, and being permitted by them with the words "Please sit down," he should circumambulate them and return; then, together with his loved ones, he should eat the remnants of the *śrāddha* meal enjoyed by his ancestors.
This is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) and not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).
Regarding meat, however, it is said [in the verse] "according to one's taste" and "with the desire of the twice-born."
On the night connected with the day on which the *śrāddha* was performed, the performer shall remain celibate (*brahmacārī*) together with the invited Brahmins who have eaten.
By the use of the word "but" (*tu*), it is further implied that he should also abstain from eating a second meal and so forth;
for the performer of the *śrāddha* should avoid these seven: cleaning the teeth, betel-leaf, anointing the body, bathing with oil, eating, sexual intercourse, medicine, and food provided by others.

Furthermore, one who has eaten at a funeral feast (śrāddha) should avoid these eight things: eating again, traveling on a journey, carrying a load, Vedic study, sexual intercourse, giving a gift, receiving a gift, and performing a fire sacrifice (homa).
Because of this statement. 1.249.
Having thus described the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, he now speaks of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*:
"In this manner, proceeding in a clockwise direction, one should worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors at a rite of prosperity (*vṛddhi*);
the offerings should consist of balls of rice mixed with curd and *karkandhū* fruits, and the ritual acts should be performed with barley."

At a *śrāddha* performed on occasions such as the birth of a son or other family increases (*vṛddhi*), one should worship—that is, honor—the ancestors in the manner thus described. Regarding this, he states a specific rule: "one who proceeds clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇāvṛtka*).
One whose method of performance (*anuṣṭhānapaddhati*) is clockwise is called *pradakṣiṇāvṛtka*, which means one whose movement is from left to right.
The term *nāndīmukhān* is an epithet of the ancestors (*pitṛs*).
Therefore, in the invocation and other rites, one should observe the following usage: "I shall invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors," "the Nāndīmukha grandfathers," and so forth.
To the question of how one should sacrifice, he says: "mixed with curd and jujube fruits."
*Karkandhu* is the fruit of the *badarī*.
Having offered balls (*piṇḍa*) mixed with curd and *badarī* fruits, one should sacrifice—this is how the connection is made.
All rites that are to be accomplished with sesame seeds should be performed with barley.
And here, the number of Brahmins has already been shown in the passage, "an even number for the rite to the gods (daiva) according to one's ability.
The enumeration of circumambulation from left to right (*pradakṣiṇāvṛt*) and so forth is for the purpose of indicating other specific duties mentioned in other Smṛtis.

As Āśvalāyana says: "Now, in the *abhyudayika* (prosperity) rite, the Brahmins are an even number; the *darbha* grass is rootless; he should face east and wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*); the procedure is from left to right; barley takes the place of sesame seeds; the offering of scents and so forth is done twice each; and he should give straight *darbha* blades for the seats."
"Thou art barley, having Soma as thy deity, created by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice;
offered by the ancients for the sake of prosperity, do thou gratify these Nāndīmukha ancestors and these worlds for us, svāhā!"—this is the sowing of barley.
"O Viśvedevas, this is your arghya; O Nāndīmukha ancestors, this is your arghya"—thus the offering of the arghya water is performed according to the respective gender.
The oblation in the hand is offered with the words: "Svāhā to Agni Kavyavāhana! Svāhā to Soma Pitṛmat!
In place of the triplet beginning with "madhu vātā ṛtāyate," he should cause [the priests] to recite the five verses beginning with "upāsmai gāyata.
He should recite the sixth verse with "akṣann amīmadanta."

When they have sipped water, one should smear the area where they ate with cow-dung, spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward, and upon those [blades] offer two *piṇḍas* each for every individual using the remains of the meal mixed with *pṛṣadājya*, and so forth.
Although it is stated in general terms that "one should sacrifice to the ancestors," nevertheless, the three types of *śrāddhas* and their sequence are to be understood from other *smṛtis*.
As Śātātapa says:
The Śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed by that for the paternal ancestors;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—thus, at a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi), three Śrāddhas are prescribed.
Thus [ends the section]. 1.250.
The Śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed by that for the paternal ancestors;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—thus, at a Vṛddhi ceremony, three Śrāddhas are prescribed.
He speaks of the *ekoddiṣṭa*:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the gods; it has a single *arghya* offering and a single *pavitraka*;
it is indeed devoid of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa*, and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*)."
The *ekoddiṣṭa* is that śrāddha in which one [deceased] is designated; thus, *ekoddiṣṭa* is the name of the rite.

This is because of the concluding statement, "one should perform the remainder as before. Since the entire ritual procedure of the *pārvaṇa* would otherwise apply by default, the specific particulars are now stated.
"Devoid of gods" means lacking the Viśvedevas; "a single arghya-vessel" and "a single darbha-strainer"; "devoid of invocation and the fire-oblation" (agnaukaraṇahoma);
"with the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (apasavyavat) means with the brahmasūtra worn as prācīnāvīta.
By this, he indicates that in the previously mentioned *abhyudayika* rite, the sacred thread is worn in the *yajñopavīta* manner. 1.251.
Furthermore:
at the dismissal of the Brahmins, while they are standing in the place of imperishability (*akṣayya-sthāna*), he should say, "May you be delighted," and they should reply, "We are indeed delighted."

Regarding what was stated: "Then one should recite the benediction (*svastivācana*) and likewise offer the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*)," in that context, at the place where *akṣayya* is normally used, one should say, "May [the ancestors] be present. When the dismissal of the Brahmins is to be performed, at the end of the recitation of "vājaś ca me," while touching darbha grass, one should say, "May you be pleased."
And they should say, "We are delighted.
Indeed, this is well-known.
The remainder is as before; such is the meaning.
And this should be performed at midday.
As Devala has said:
"Rites for the gods are to be performed in the forenoon, but those for the ancestors in the afternoon."
The ekoddiṣṭa rite is performed at midday, while that occasioned by prosperity (vṛddhinimittaka) is performed in the morning.
Thus:
rites for the gods are performed in the forenoon, those for the ancestors in the afternoon;
the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is at midday, while that occasioned by prosperity is in the morning.
Regarding the injunction "one should eat what was consumed by the ancestors," a prohibition is observed in the case of a specific *ekoddiṣṭa* rite:
"One should never eat that which remains from the *navaśrāddha* offerings, nor that which has been kept overnight in the house, nor the remnants of what has been eaten by a married couple."
Thus:
"One should never eat what remains from the nine types of śrāddha offerings, nor what has been left over in the house overnight, nor the remnants of what has been eaten by a married couple."
And the *navaśrāddha* (the rite for the newly deceased) is thus shown:
"On the first day, the third day, the fifth, the seventh,
as well as the ninth and the eleventh— this is called the *navaśrāddha*."
Thus [ends the section]. 1.252.
On the first day, the third day, the fifth, the seventh,
as well as the ninth and the eleventh— this is called the *navaśrāddha*.
He describes the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite:
One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
With the two verses beginning "ye samānā," one should perform the remainder as previously described;
this Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for a woman is also performed as an Ekoddiṣṭa.
One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds for the purpose of accomplishing the *arghya* offering, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
By stating "four vessels containing sesame seeds," it is indicated that there are four Brahmins for the group of ancestors (*pitṛvarga*).
Two remain for the *vaiśvadeva* rite.

In this rite, one should divide the water remaining in the vessel for the deceased (preta) into three parts and pour it into the vessels for the ancestors (pitṛs) with the two mantras beginning, "Those who are equal, of one mind...
The remainder of the ritual, from the invocation of the Viśvedevas up to the dismissal, should be performed as before, according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure.

Having offered the *arghya* water from the remainder of the *arghya* vessel of the deceased into the hand of the Brahmin representing the deceased's station, one should conclude the rest according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
In the three rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), it is performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rule.
This *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* mentioned immediately above, as well as the *ekoddiṣṭa* mentioned prior to that, must be performed for a woman—that is, for one's mother as well.
By stating this, it is implied that in the *pārvaṇa* rite, the śrāddha for the mother must be performed separately.
In this context, some explain the word *preta* as referring to the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) of the father;
for it is logical that, since he is included within the [three ancestors], the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) and other rites cease after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony.
However, inclusion is not appropriate for one who has died most recently, because the offering of rice balls and water continues for him thereafter.
For this very reason, Yama said:

"He who offers a separate funeral ball (piṇḍa) to a deceased person for whom the sapindikarana has been performed becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunctions and is born as a slayer of his ancestors."
Thus:
"He who should offer a separate rice-ball to a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is born as a slayer of his ancestors."

The term *preta* applies even to the fourth [state] because they have departed (*preta*) in an excellent sense (*prakārṣeṇa*), and because we observe its usage in such injunctions as "one should offer to the *pretas* alone.
Furthermore: "One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha preceded by the gods;
one should feed the ancestors (*pitṛs*) there, but should not designate the deceased (*preta*) again."

Thus, a prohibition of *śrāddha* and other rites for the deceased is observed for the period following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*; however, this would not be possible for one who has died immediately [before the rite], because the performance of *śrāddha* is prescribed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions. Furthermore, the statement, "Sapiṇḍatā ceases with the seventh person," is only consistent if the fourth person is included within the three; for the fourth person pervades three *piṇḍas*, the fifth pervades two *piṇḍas*, the sixth pervades one *piṇḍa*, and there is cessation at the seventh.

The phrase "into the vessels of the fathers" (*pitṛpātreṣu*) also fits only this particular view because the father is the primary [ancestor], and not otherwise, since the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) is the primary one [in that other view].

Therefore, the interpretation that "one should pour that vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the fathers"—meaning one should pour the great-grandfather’s vessel into the vessels of the father and so on—is incorrect.

For here, the joining of the *piṇḍas* does not serve the purpose of terminating the subsequent offering of *piṇḍas* and so forth; rather, it is for the sake of the deceased father attaining the status of a *pitṛ* by ceasing his state of being a *preta*.
And the state of being a *preta* is a condition characterized by the experience of extreme suffering produced by hunger and thirst.
As Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The residence of humans in the world of *pretas* is proclaimed to last for one year."
"Hunger and thirst shall occur there every day, O descendant of Bhṛgu;
the residence of men in the world of the departed is proclaimed to last for one year."
O descendant of Bhṛgu, hunger and thirst shall afflict him there every day;
yet he attains the status of a *pitṛ* (ancestor) through his connection with the deities of the *śrāddha*, such as the Vasus.

It is understood that one attains the state of a *pitṛ* by the cessation of the state of a *preta* (departed spirit) through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite performed together with the previous *ekoddiṣṭa* rites—provided those sixteen *preta-śrāddhas* have been offered for him. If these sixteen *preta-śrāddhas* have not been given, [he remains a *preta*].
His state as a preta remains firmly established, even by hundreds of funeral offerings (śrāddha) performed for him.
Thus it is said:
"For him to whom these sixteen *śrāddhas* for the deceased have not been offered,
his state as a *preta* remains firmly established, even if hundreds of other *śrāddhas* are performed."
Likewise: "One should offer four rice-balls; one should place [the deceased's portion] among them first.
From that time forth, the deceased indeed partakes in the commonality of the ancestors."
Because of such statements as these,

and because by the phrase "the deceased whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed," the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is prohibited through the separate procedure of the *ekoddiṣṭa*, it is understood that the offering of the rice-ball occurs according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure;
and that [offering] is set aside by the rule for the annual or occasional *ekoddiṣṭa*.

Furthermore, as for the statement that one should not designate [the deceased] as a *preta*, its purpose is to indicate that one should not utter the word *preta*, but rather the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) alone.
Moreover, the term *preta* does not apply there simply because of having gone to a superior state;
for it has been stated that the term *preta* is used by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) to denote the specific state of experiencing particular suffering.
Even the application of the term *preta* to one who has merely died occurs by way of what was previously the case.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "sapiṇḍatā ceases with the seventh person," this is also consistent because the first *piṇḍa* extends to the fourth, the second extends to the fifth, and the third extends to the sixth; thus, it ceases at the seventh.

Moreover, it has been stated that *sāpiṇḍya* does not arise from the connection of the *piṇḍas* to be offered, as that would be non-pervasive, but rather from the connection of the constituent parts of a single body.

Furthermore, the word *pitṛ* (father/ancestor) applies to those who have attained the status of deities of the *śrāddha* through the cessation of their state as *preta*s; thus, the expression "in the vessels of the ancestors" (*pitṛpātreṣu*) is not contradictory.
Therefore, the meaning is that the immediate predecessor [Bhāṣyakāra] has presented the view of another school by way of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
It is established that there is a mixing (*saṃsarjana*) of the water from the vessel of the deceased and of his *piṇḍa* into the vessels and *piṇḍas* of the ancestors.
The Teacher, however, has merely presented the opinion of another.
And this *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father is to be understood as occurring only when the three ancestors beginning with the grandfather have died.
When the father is deceased but the grandfather is still living, there is no *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* at all.
"Because of the scriptural statement: 'And for those who have died out of their natural order, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite must not be performed at all.
As for the statement of Manu: 'He whose father has passed away, whether his grandfather still lives or not...'"
Having proclaimed his father's name, he should proclaim his great-grandfather's name.

Thus, that [offering] is also for the purpose of establishing the rule for the use of the word "father" (pitṛ), not for the purpose of giving two rice-balls (piṇḍa). How so? "But while the father is living, one should offer to the ancestors alone; however, for one whose father has passed away but whose grandfather is still living..."
The syntactical connection is that he too should offer [the oblation] to the ancestors alone.
To the question of how one should offer it in either of the two cases, he says:
"Having pronounced the name of the father, he should mention the great-grandfather."

By including "beginning" and "end" in this manner, the formula *pitṛbhyaḥ pitāmahebhyaḥ prapitāmahebhyaḥ* (to the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers) is to be used in all cases; never, however, should the grandfather or great-grandfather occupy the position of the beginning, nor the great-great-grandfather or his father occupy the position of the end.
Consequently, because words such as "father" (*pitṛ*) and so forth denote relative relationships, even while the father is living, one says: *pitṛbhyaḥ pitāmahebhyaḥ prapitāmahebhyaḥ*.
While the grandfather is living, one says: *pitāmahasya pitṛbhyaḥ pitāmahebhyaḥ prapitāmahebhyaḥ*.
Consequently, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the mantras beginning with "May the ancestors be purified" (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*) in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*.
As for the statement of Viṣṇu— "He whose father is deceased should, having placed the *piṇḍa* for his father, offer [the other two] to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather"—
its meaning is as follows:

While the grandfather is still living, or when the father has died, one should offer a single rice-ball for the father according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure; then, one should offer [rice-balls] to the two ancestors beyond the father’s own grandfather.
Since the grandfather remains as the recipient for oneself [the performer], one should offer to the great-grandfather and the two ancestors beyond him.
The rule regarding the employment of words is exactly as previously stated.
In this same way, it should be understood that there is likewise an absence of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for one who has been killed by a *brāhmaṇa* or others.
As Kātyāyana said:
"When a father has been killed by a *brāhmaṇa* or others, or has fallen [from his caste], or has abandoned all social ties..."
And when he has died out of order, the inheritance should be given to those very persons to whom he himself would have given it.
Thus:
"When one's father has been killed by a Brāhmaṇa or others, has fallen from his caste, has abandoned all attachments,
or has died through an unnatural course, the funeral offering should be given to those very persons to whom he himself would have given it."

Since it is impossible to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a father who has been killed by a cow or a Brahmin, it would be illogical to bypass him and perform the *pārvaṇa* rite for the grandfather and others; thus, the absence of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is understood.
Furthermore, in another *smṛti*:
"For those men whose lineage is severed, there is no *sapiṇḍatā*."
"And the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites should not be performed together with these [other ancestors]. Thus,
for those men whose lineage is severed, there is no *sapiṇḍatā*."
Furthermore, the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites should not be performed together with these [other ancestors].
Regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so forth for the mother, there is a disagreement concerning the lineage (*gotra*):
because scriptural statements are seen in both cases, it may be offered either by the husband’s lineage or by the father’s lineage.
A woman falls from her own lineage at the seventh step of the marriage ceremony;
her rites of offering rice-balls and water must be performed by the lineage of her husband.
This statement concerning the husband's lineage and so forth [is as follows]:
"One should not abandon the father's lineage and adopt the husband's lineage;
for women, the paternal family remains [the primary one] both at birth and in times of misfortune."
This refers to the paternal lineage (*pitṛgotra*) and so forth.

Thus, in cases of conflicting views regarding Āsura and other types of marriage, as well as in the practice of appointing a daughter (*putrikākaraṇa*), the paternal lineage alone applies, because of specific statements to that effect in each instance and because the act of giving (*dāna*) has not ceased.

In the case of Brāhma and other types of marriage, however, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*), just like the choice between rice and barley, or like the choice between the Bṛhat and Rathantara Sāmans.

And in that regard: "By the path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that, he does not incur fault. By the path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone.
"By that one should travel the path of the virtuous; traveling by that path, one does not incur fault.

Because of this statement, there is a settled rule (*vyavasthā*) based on the practice handed down through family lineage, since there is no other scope for this statement apart from such a subject matter.

However, where there is neither a settled rule from scripture nor established practice, then according to the statement "but [one's] own satisfaction," one's own satisfaction alone is the determining factor, as in the case of the rule: "in the eighth year after conception, or in the eighth year [after birth]."
Regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a mother as well, contradictory statements are observed; therein, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with the paternal grandmother and others is recorded in the Smṛtis.
Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi states that the husband must also perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of his wife together with his own mother and others:
"But when a woman dies without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍatā*."
Her sapindikarana rite should be performed together with those of her mother-in-law and the others.
Thus it is said: "But when she dies childless, the husband shall perform the sapinda-rite;
her sapindikarana shall take place together with her mother-in-law and the others."
Yama has declared that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a woman must be performed together with her husband alone: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a woman must be performed by her husband alone;
for even when she has died, she has attained oneness with him through mantras, oblations, and vows."
Thus it is said:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a woman must be performed by her husband alone;
for even in death, she has attained unity with him through mantras, oblations, and vows."
But Uśanas has declared that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite with the maternal grandfather should be performed:
"Just as the sons perform the *sapiṇḍatā* for the father's paternal grandfather when a full year has elapsed,
so too should this *sapiṇḍatā* be performed for the mother's maternal grandfather."
Likewise, the Lord Śiva has declared: "When a full year has passed, sons should join their father with the grandfather, and likewise their mother with the maternal grandfather."
Thus, when there are various such statements, if a wife dies without a son, the husband should perform the *sapiṇḍana* for her with his own mother alone.
However, in the case of *anvārohaṇa* (the widow ascending the funeral pyre), the son should perform the mother’s *sapiṇḍana* with his own father.
A son born of an *āsura* or other such marriage, as well as the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*), should perform it with the maternal grandfather alone.

One born of a *brāhma* or other [approved] form of marriage may perform [the rite] optionally with the father, the maternal grandfather, or the paternal grandmother. Even here, if there is a fixed family tradition (*vaṃśasamācāra*), one should act accordingly. If the family tradition is not fixed, then one should act according to one's own preference, following the principle that "one's own satisfaction is the authority."

And in that regard, even when there is *sāpiṇḍya* with the mother by any means whatsoever, where the Śrāddha for the mother is specifically prescribed separately—as in the Anvaṣṭakās and so forth—it is said:

"On the Anvaṣṭakā days, on the occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), at Gayā, and on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), one should perform the Śrāddha for the mother separately; elsewhere, it should be performed together with the husband."

Thus, on the Anvaṣṭakā days, at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), at Gayā, and on the anniversary of death, one should perform the Śrāddha for the mother separately; on other occasions, it is performed together with the husband.
In that case, the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* should be performed by the daughter herself with her paternal grandmother and the others;

however, in other instances, it is performed together with her husband, because she shares in his portion through *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with him. Likewise, in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with her maternal grandfather, she shares in his portion and therefore performs it together with him alone.
As Śātātapa has said:
"When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed, the wife attains a single form with the ancestors of her husband; therefore, she is entitled to a share of their portion."
Thus,
once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed, she attains a single form with her husband’s ancestors; therefore, the wife is a sharer in their portion.

This being the case, when the mother’s *sāpiṇḍya* is with her maternal grandfather, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is obligatory (*nitya*), just like the *śrāddha* for the paternal ancestors.
When the mother’s *sāpiṇḍya* is with her husband or her paternal grandmother, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is not obligatory.
The settled conclusion is that if it is performed, there is prosperity; if it is not performed, there is no transgression. 1.253–1.254.
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has taken place before the completion of a year,
one should provide food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of that year.

For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year, one should give food along with a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa every day or every month for the duration of that year, according to one’s ability, with that person as the intended recipient.
By stating "before the year," it is shown that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* may take place either when the year is complete or prior to it.
As Āśvalāyana says: "Now, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*: at the end of the year or on the twelfth day."

Kātyāyana also said: "Then, when a year has elapsed, or after three fortnights, or whenever an auspicious occasion (vṛddhi) occurs before that time—the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa should be performed on the twelfth day if the performer possesses the sacred fires, or if the deceased (preta) also possessed the sacred fires.
Regarding the father's sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, it should be performed on the twelfth day.
Because of this statement:
"But one who maintains no sacred fires (niragnika) should perform it at the end of three fortnights, upon the occurrence of an increase [in lunar days], or after a year.

A doubt arises as to whether, when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed before the completion of a year, one should first perform the sixteen *śrāddhas* and then the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, or whether one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and then perform those [sixteen *śrāddhas*] at their respective times; for scriptural injunctions are seen to support both views.
One should not perform the sapindikarana rite until the sixteen śrāddhas have been offered;
having completed the sixteen śrāddhas, one should then perform the sapindikarana.
Thus it is said:
"One should never perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite without having first offered the sixteen *śrāddhas*;
having completed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should then perform the *sapiṇḍana*."
And there are sixteen śrāddhas: on the twelfth day, at the three-fortnight mark, at six months, monthly, and the annual;
these sixteen śrāddhas are remembered by the wise.
Thus they have been shown. Likewise:
"Even for one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs before a year has passed..."
A monthly offering and a water-pot should also be given for him for a year.
Thus it is said:
"Even for one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs before the end of the year,
the monthly offerings and the water-pot (*udakumbha*) must be given throughout that year."

In that regard, the primary rule is that after performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, these [rites] should be performed at their own proper times, because prior to that there is no entitlement due to the time not having arrived.
As for the statement that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed even before the end of the year only after completing the sixteen *śrāddhas*, this is a rule for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*).
However, when one performs the *preta-śrāddhas* before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* by virtue of being in a state of distress, one should perform them according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

But when one performs [the rites] according to the primary method at their own proper time, then one should perform the monthly *śrāddhas* in the same manner as one performs the annual *śrāddha*, whether it be the *pārvaṇa* or the *ekoddiṣṭa*. However, while performing the sixteen *śrāddhas* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform all of them according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
After the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, whenever one performs [the annual rites] again,
one should perform those as well in the same manner as one performs them every year.
Thus it is from the Smṛti.

And this Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, together with the Śrāddha for the deceased (preta-śrāddha), even when there are many brothers who have divided the wealth, is sufficient when performed by only one; it need not be performed by all. As it is said: "The Navaśrāddha, the Sapiṇḍatva, and also the sixteen Śrāddhas—these should be performed by only one, even among those who have divided the wealth."
Thus it is from the Smṛti.

Furthermore, this Sapindikarana, together with the Śrāddha for the deceased (preta-śrāddha), must necessarily be performed by sons and others for those who have not renounced the world (asaṃnyāsin), because its purpose is the liberation from the state of being a preta; however, it need not be performed for one who has renounced the world (saṃnyāsin).
As Uśanas said:
One should never perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for ascetics (*yatins*);
rather, when the eleventh day arrives, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed.
The sapindikarana rite for them should not be performed by sons or others;
indeed, through the mere taking up of the triple staff (tridanda), the state of being a preta never arises.
Thus it is said:
"One should never perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* for ascetics (*yatis*);
rather, when the eleventh day arrives, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed."
The sapindikarana rite for them should not be performed by their sons and others;
indeed, upon the taking up of the triple staff (tridanda), the state of being a preta never arises.

In the absence of a son, the funeral rites (preta-karma) up until the end of the tenth day must be performed by that very person of the same lineage (sagotra) or others who performed the cremation; whether he be of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man—whoever performs the offering on the first day shall complete it throughout the ten days.
This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).

This [rite] must also be performed for Śūdras on the twelfth day without mantras; for Viṣṇu has taught: "In this manner, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for Śūdras, excluding mantras, is to be performed on the twelfth day.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the annual rites, the *pārvaṇa* offerings, and so forth, must necessarily be performed by the son; for others, they are not mandatory. (1.255)
He states the times for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite:
"It should be performed on the day of death every month for a year;
likewise, it should be performed annually, and the first [rite] on the eleventh day."
On the anniversary of the day of death, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed every month for a year.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone should be performed annually.
The first *ekoddiṣṭa*, which serves as the archetype for all *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, is performed on the eleventh day.
If the day of death is unknown, the rite should be performed on the day of hearing the news, or on the new moon (amāvāsyā).
This is because of the traditional legal authority (smṛti) stating: "When the day of death is unknown, [the rite is performed] on the new moon day or on the day of hearing the news.

Regarding the phrase "on the new moon day," it refers to the new moon day associated with the month of departure; it should be given on the day of departure, or even on the waning of the moon (indukṣaya) of that month.

Thus it is from the Smṛti. Regarding the phrase "on the day of death," a specific rule for one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) has been stated by Jātūkarṇya: "The śrāddha that occurs after three fortnights [of the death] should be performed on the very day of death;
however, for a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires, one should cause it to be performed before the cremation."
Thus:
"The śrāddha that occurs after three fortnights should take place on the very day of death;
however, for a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires, one should perform it before the cremation."
In that regard, whatever rites for the deceased are performed within three fortnights should be carried out for one who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) starting from the day of cremation;
whereas the meaning is that whatever *śrāddha* is performed after three fortnights, it should be on the very day of death.
For one who did not maintain the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), however, everything is to be done on the anniversary of death itself.

Some maintain that the phrase "on the eleventh day" is an indication for the period of impurity (*āśauca*), because purity is a prerequisite for performing rites, as in the rule "a rite must be performed by one who is pure," and because Viṣṇu has prescribed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite after generally introducing the removal of impurity for all social classes (*varṇas*).
That is incorrect; for the *śrāddha* performed on the eleventh day is declared to be the general [rite].
And for all four castes, the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) is distinct for each.
Thus, because this contradicts the traditional teaching of Paiṭhīnasi: "One who is impure may perform the first śrāddha on the eleventh day;
his purity for that occasion belongs to the performer alone, yet he remains impure [for other purposes]."
Furthermore, because this contradicts the statement of Śaṅkha,
the statement of Viṣṇu— which begins with general rules— is applicable even to the context of ten-day impurity (*daśāhāśauca*).
And as for the rule "and likewise every year," the Lord of Yogins has prescribed that every year, on the anniversary of the day of death, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Every year, an honoring of one's mother and father must be performed;
one should feed those not invited for a deity at the Śrāddha and offer a single rice-ball."
Thus:
"Every year, an honoring of one's mother and father must be performed;
one should feed those who are not deities at the śrāddha and offer a single pinda."
Yama also said:
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, every year on the anniversary of death, the sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* offering separately for the mother and the father."
Thus:
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, every year on the anniversary of death, sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for their mother and father separately.
Vyāsa, however, prohibits the pārvaṇa rite:
"If a man performs the pārvaṇa rite while abandoning the ekoddiṣṭa, one should know that it is as if unperformed; he becomes a slayer of his ancestors."
Thus:
"If a man performs the *pārvaṇa* rite while abandoning the *ekoddiṣṭa*, one should know that it is as if unperformed; he becomes a slayer of his ancestors."
Jamadagni, however, has declared that it is the *pārvaṇa* rite:

"Having performed the *sapiṇḍana*, the legitimate son (*aurasa*) shall duly perform the *śrāddha* for his mother and father on the anniversary of their death, according to the rules for the new moon."
Thus it is said:

Having established the sapinda relationship according to the rule, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall perform the śrāddha for his mother and father on the anniversary of their death, just like the darśa-śrāddha.
Śātātapa also said:
"Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the wise man should always perform [the rite] according to the *pārvaṇa* method;
this is the rule proclaimed by Chāgaleya for every year."

Regarding this contradiction in scriptural statements, the Southerners indeed maintain this settled rule: "On the anniversary of the death of the parents, the *pārvaṇa* rite alone must be performed by the *aurasa* (legitimate) and *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife) sons; the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is to be performed by the *dattaka* (adopted) and other such sons," because of the statement of Jātūkarṇya: "The *kṣetraja* and *aurasa* sons should perform [the rite] every year according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure alone;
the other ten types of sons should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*."
Thus:
"Every year, the *kṣetraja* and *aurasa* sons should perform [the rite] according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure alone;
the other ten types of sons should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*."
That is incorrect;
for in this context there is no mention of the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*), but rather of "every year" (*pratyabdam*).
Furthermore, there exist annual *śrāddhas* distinct from the anniversary of death, such as those performed on the Akṣayyatṛtīyā, Māghī, Vaiśākhī, and other such occasions.
Therefore, this is not sufficient to establish a fixed rule regarding the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites for the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*).
As for the statement of Parāśara: "When the father has attained divinity, the three-generation rite applies to the legitimate son;
in all cases, even for those of different lineages, it is performed on the single day of death for one person alone."
Thus, even that [statement] does not establish [the rule],
because its meaning is as follows:
for a father who has attained divinity and whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, the *pārvaṇa* rite for three generations must be performed by the legitimate son (*aurasa*) in all cases.
The śrāddha performed on the anniversary of death for maternal uncles and others who belong to various or distinct lineages is indeed a single-ancestor *ekoddiṣṭa* rite alone.
Furthermore, Paiṭhīnasi has stated that even after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed by the legitimate son (*aurasa*) as well:
"For the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed by the legitimate son on the anniversary of death."
After the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, there is no pārvaṇa śrāddha for one's mother and father.
Thus [it is said].
For on the anniversary of death, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite must be performed by the legitimate son;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *pārvaṇa* rite is not to be performed for the mother and father.

The Northerners, moreover, establish the following rule: on the anniversary of death occurring on the new moon day, or during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the *pārvaṇa* rite is performed; on any other anniversary of death, it is exclusively the *ekoddiṣṭa*. As it is said: "If one's death occurs on the new moon day, or again during the fortnight of the departed (*pretapakṣa*), the *pārvaṇa* must be performed there; never the *ekoddiṣṭa*."

Thus it is from the traditional Smṛti. Yet the elders do not respect even that, because it is improper to excessively restrict many statements—which have well-established foundations and concern only the *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death) and the *pārvaṇa* (monthly śrāddha)—to the occasion of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the days of death during the fortnight following it, on the basis of this statement whose root is uncertain; furthermore, it would render the general statements purposeless.

For in that case, there is a restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) of a general statement by a specific statement where both statements become meaningful through the knowledge of the relationship between the general and the specific.

For example, there is a restriction of the sentence "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," which is studied as an isolated rule (*anārabhyādhīta*) and thus pertains to all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), by the sentence concerning the seventeen verses found within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Mitravinda sacrifice; for while the former becomes meaningful by making known the connection with the *sāmidhenīs* as its medium, the latter becomes meaningful by making known the connection with the new transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the Mitravinda sacrifice.
But here, since both [texts] would have as their sole object the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), they would lack purposeful application.
Therefore, it is logical that the restrictive injunction for the *pārvaṇa* rite is intended here to result in the exclusion of the optional *ekoddiṣṭa*.

Nor is it appropriate to establish a fixed rule whereby the statements concerning the *ekoddiṣṭa* apply specifically to the anniversary of the death of a mother or father, while the statements concerning the *pārvaṇa* apply to anniversaries other than those.

Since the mention of mother, father, and son exists in both cases: "After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, every year on the anniversary of death, the sons should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite separately for the mother and the father."
Thus:
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
every year on the anniversary of death, the sons must separately perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* for their mother and father.

Likewise: Having established the status of sharing the funeral rice-ball (sahapiṇḍatva) according to the rule, the legitimate son (aurasa) should perform the Śrāddha for his mother and father on the anniversary of their death, as prescribed for the Darśa sacrifice.

Thus: Having established the status of being offered the same funeral rice-ball (*sahapiṇḍatva*), the legitimate son (*aurasa*) shall perform the *śrāddha* for his mother and father on the anniversary of their death according to the rule, as if it were the new-moon day.

As for what is said by some—that on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father, one who maintains the sacred fires (sāgni) should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite, while one without such fires (niragni) should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*—[it is countered by: "Every year, the son who is a twice-born man possessing the sacred fires should perform the *pārvaṇa*;
the wise man without such fires should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the day of their death."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Sumantu;
yet even that [argument] is to be disregarded because it is countered by an opposing argument:
"Those Brahmins who maintain many sacred fires (bahvagni), as well as those who maintain only one fire (ekāgni)..."
For them, after the sapindikarana rite, the ekoddista ceremony is performed, not the parvana.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.

On this point, the settled conclusion is as follows: on the anniversary of the death (kṣayāha) of renunciants (saṃnyāsins), the son must perform only the Pārvaṇa rite; for an ascetic (yati), there is no Ekoddiṣṭa here because of his taking up the triple staff (tridaṇḍa).
Due to the absence of the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, the Pārvaṇa rite is always prescribed for him.
Thus, according to the *Smaraṇa* of Pracetas:

on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) occurring on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), as well as on the anniversary of death occurring during the fortnight of the departed (*pretapakṣa*), the *pārvaṇa* rite alone is prescribed. This is because the scriptural statement beginning with "for whom the anniversary of death falls on the new moon day, or again during the fortnight of the departed," is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) according to the manner previously explained.

Except on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) and for the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, there is indeed an option between the two, like that between rice and barley. Nevertheless, when a settled custom of the lineage exists, the option is restricted; in its absence, it is optional according to one's preference. Enough of this digression. 1.256.
This is stated as the remainder of all *śrāddhas* other than the daily (*nitya*) *śrāddha*:
"One should give the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to a cow, a goat, or a Brahmin, or else throw them into fire or water;
while Brahmins are present, one must not wipe away the remnants of the twice-born's meal."
This is the procedure for the balls of food (*piṇḍas*) previously offered: one should give those *piṇḍas* to a cow, a goat, or a Brāhmaṇa who seeks them;
or one may cast them into fire or deep water.
Furthermore, while learned Brāhmaṇas remain in the place of eating, one must not sweep away nor remove the remnants of the twice-born. 1.257.
He states the specific results according to the specific food offered:
"By means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
[the same result is obtained] by fish, deer, goat, bird, or the meat of the black antelope."
The ancestors, when offerings are made here, are satisfied for increasing periods of one month each by the meats of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively.
*Haviṣya* refers to sacrificial materials suitable for oblation, such as sesame, rice, and so forth.
As Manu has said:
"With sesame, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits..."
When given according to the prescribed rules, the ancestors of men are satisfied for one month.
Thus:
"By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits according to the prescribed rule,
the ancestors of men are satisfied for one month."
That food is sacrificial food (*haviṣya*); with that, the ancestors are satisfied for a month—this is the syntactical connection with what follows.

With milk-rice (*pāyasa*) prepared from cow's milk, they are satisfied for a year; for it is stated in the traditional law (*smṛti*): "But for a year, [they are satisfied] by cow's milk and by milk-rice."
Fish that are edible include the *pāṭhīna* and others; this [meat] belongs to them, thus it is called *mātsya*.
The *hariṇa* is the copper-colored deer (*tāmramṛga*).
The *eṇa* is black; the *eṇa* should be known as the black deer, while the copper-colored one is called the *hariṇa*.
Thus, according to the recollection of Āyurveda:
"Of this [meat], that which comes from the deer is *hāriṇaka*;
that which belongs to the sheep (*avi*) or the ram (*urabha*) is *aurabhra*."
*Śakuni* is the partridge; *śākuna* is that which relates to it. *Chāga* is the goat; *chāga* is its [meat]. *Pṛṣat* is the spotted deer; *pārṣata* is its meat.

The *eṇa* is the black antelope; its flesh is *aiṇa*. The *ruru* is the *śambara* deer; what originates from it is *raurava*. The *varāha* is the wild boar; that which is produced from it is *vārāha*.

This belongs to the hare, thus it is "śāśam. Because it has been stated that "by these months of sacrificial food (haviṣya) given to the ancestors, [they are satisfied] for a month," thereafter the ancestors are satisfied by an increase of one month each in successive order. 1.258–1.259.
Furthermore:
rhinoceros meat, large-scaled fish, honey, or even the food of ascetics;
iron-flesh, great vegetables, and the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa crane.
Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
The rhinoceros is the *gaṇḍaka*; its meat [is prescribed].
The *mahāśalka* is a species of fish. Honey is that produced by bees (*mākṣika*).

"Hermit-food" (munyanna) refers to all forest-grown produce such as wild rice (nīvāra) and the like. "Lauhāmiṣa" means the meat of a red goat; "loha" means red, and "āmiṣa" means meat. "Mahāśāka" refers to black pot-herbs (kālaśāka).

A *vārdhrīṇasa* is an old white goat; however, those learned in the sacrificial rites call that old, white lord of goats who drinks with three [parts of its body] and whose senses are decayed a *tripiba*, used in the performance of the *śrāddha* ceremony.

Thus it is well known among the ritualists (*yājñika*). A "three-drinker" (*tripiba*) is one whose two ears and tongue touch the water as he drinks; he is called "three-drinker" because he drinks with three [parts]. This refers to the meat of that *vārdhrīṇasa* (the rhinoceros).
"Whatever he gives while staying at Gayā"—this means that whatever he gives while residing at Gayā, even if it be merely vegetables and the like.

By the use of the word "and," [the text includes] Gaṅgādvāra and other such places; for a Śrāddha performed at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Arbuda, Saṃnihatyā, or Gayā attains imperishability.
"He attains infinity" means he obtains the state of being the cause of infinite fruit.
The phrase "he attains infinity" is to be connected with each [preceding item].

Likewise, whatever is given specifically on the thirteenth day of the rainy season—the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada—especially when conjoined with the Maghā asterism, all that "attains infinity"; this is the connection with what has preceded.

In this regard, although foods such as those of forest hermits (*muni*), meat, honey, and so forth are generally shown to be suitable for the *śrāddha* of all castes, nevertheless, the rule stated by Pulastya should be observed: "Foods of forest hermits are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa; meat for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya;
the gift of honey for the Śūdra; and whatever is not incompatible for any [caste]."
Thus it is said: "The food of forest hermits is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa; meat for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya;
the offering of honey for the Śūdra; and whatever is not forbidden for all."

The meaning of this is as follows: the food of sages, such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like, which has been declared suitable for the *śrāddha*, is the primary offering for a Brāhmaṇa and bestows the complete fruit.
That which has been declared as meat is the primary offering for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. That which has been declared as honey is [the primary offering] for a Śūdra.

Whatever is distinct from these three categories—whether it be non-conflicting, unprohibited, such as *vāstuka* and other greens, or prescribed sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), such as *kālaśāka* and the like—all of that yields the full fruit for everyone. || 1.260 || 1.261 ||
He states the specific results arising from specific lunar days:
"A daughter, those who recognize a daughter, cattle, virtuous sons,
as well as gambling, agriculture, trade, and likewise animals with cloven and solid hooves."
The giver of a Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Brahmanic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all his desires.
On the days beginning with the first of the lunar fortnight, excluding the fourteenth day,
offerings are given there for those who have indeed been slain by weapons.
A maiden endowed with beauty, auspicious marks, and virtuous character;
sons-in-law who seek a maiden and are perfected in intelligence, beauty, and auspicious marks;
and small livestock such as goats and the like.
Good sons who walk the path of the righteous;
gambling, meaning victory at dice;
and agriculture, meaning the fruit of cultivation.
Trade refers to the profit from commerce.
"Two-hoofed" refers to cattle and the like;
"one-hoofed" refers to horses and the like.

"Endowed with spiritual luster" (*brahmavarcasvin*): spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) is the splendor produced by the study of the Vedas and the performance of their prescribed duties; they possess that.
"Gold and silver" (*svarṇarūpya*) refers to gold and silver. "Base metal" (*kupya*) is that which is distinct from those, such as tin, lead, and so forth.
"Preeminence among kinsmen" means being superior among one's relatives. "All desires" refers to those things desired, such as heaven, sons, cattle, and so forth.

The giver of the *śrāddha* obtains these fourteen fruits—beginning with a daughter and ending with the aforementioned—in sequential order on the fourteen lunar days starting from the first day of the dark fortnight until the new moon, excluding the fourteenth day.

To those who have been killed by weapons, one should offer a *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, provided they were not killed by a Brahmin or similar [high-status person]. Even for a father who has attained equality [with the gods] but was killed by a weapon, the sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the fourteenth day; this is the *mahālaya*.

Because of this traditional authority (*smaraṇa*), it is restricted that on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada during the *mahālaya*, the *śrāddha* is for one who has been killed by a weapon and whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed and who has attained equality [with the ancestors], and not for anyone else; however, it is not restricted that the *śrāddha* for one killed by a weapon must occur only on the fourteenth day.
Furthermore, on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) and other such occasions, the *śrāddha* for even one killed by a weapon is performed exactly as prescribed.

Nor should it be thought that this rule for the *śrāddha* applies only to the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada; for Śaunaka records: "On the full moon of Prauṣṭhapadī, during the latter half of the month, and likewise month by month. (1.262–1.264)
He states the specific results according to the specific lunar mansions:
heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, land, strength,
as well as a son, preeminence, good fortune, prosperity, and auspicious leadership.
As well as the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], success in trade and other pursuits,
freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly offers the Śrāddha bestows wealth, the Vedas, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī,
he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires.

He who offers a *śrāddha* to each lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī, obtains in due order all desires from heaven up to long life, provided he is a believer (*āstika*), full of faith (*śraddhādhāna*), and free from pride and envy. A believer is one who possesses conviction; one full of faith is one endowed with an excess of reverence.
Free from intoxication and envy— *mada* being pride and *matsara* being jealousy— one who is devoid of these two [attains] heaven, which is unsurpassed bliss;
and [he regards] his offspring without distinction.
*Ojas* is an excellence of one's own power;
*śaurya* is fearlessness;
and *kṣetra* is that which bears fruit.
Physical strength;
a virtuous son;
preeminence among kinsmen.
Good fortune is being beloved by the people;
prosperity is the abundance of wealth and so forth; preeminence is the state of being foremost.
Auspiciousness in general;
the state of having set the wheel of Dharma in motion; and unimpeded authority.
Trade and so forth refers to commerce, usury, agriculture, and cattle-rearing.
Health is the state of being free from illness.
Fame is renown.
Freedom from sorrow is the absence of suffering produced by such things as separation from the beloved.
The supreme goal is the attainment of the world of Brahmā;
wealth refers to gold and the like;
and the Vedas refer to the Ṛgveda and the others.
Success in medicine is the attainment of the fruits of medicinal herbs.
Base metals (*kupya*) refers to copper and other metals, excluding gold and silver.
Cows are well known.
Goats, sheep, and horses;
It has been stated that "the ancestors are satisfied by what is given here for a month's duration," implying that satisfaction of the ancestors occurs through the *śrāddha* rite.

However, this is untenable; for it is impossible for humans who have gone to heaven, hell, or other realms due to the power of their own individual good and evil karma to be satisfied by food, drink, and so forth offered by their sons and others.
Even if such satisfaction were possible, how could they bestow fruits such as heaven, when they themselves lack mastery over their own selves?
Therefore, he says:
"The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the Śrāddha;
when satiated by the Śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings."
When pleased, the ancestors bestow upon men longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness, as well as sovereignty.

For in this context, it is not Devadatta and others alone who are designated by the words "father" and so forth as the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) of the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*); rather, they are [designated] only when accompanied by their presiding deities, such as Vasu.

Just as by the words "Devadatta" and so forth neither the body alone nor the self alone is meant, but rather the self as qualified by the body, so too Devadatta and others are designated by the words "father" and so forth only when accompanied by their presiding deities.

Therefore, the presiding deities, such as the Vasus and others, being satisfied by the food, drink, and so forth offered by the sons and others, in turn satisfy those [ancestors] such as Devadatta, and they also endow the agents, the sons and others, with the fruit [of their action].

Just as a mother, being herself satisfied by consuming the food, drink, and other desired items provided for the nourishment of her fetus—items not given by others—satisfies even the offspring within her own womb and unites the provider of those desired foods with the fruit of that reciprocal service; in the same way, the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas (the sons of Aditi) who are the Pitṛs denoted by the terms *pitṛ*, *pitāmaha*, and *prapitāmaha*—and not merely individuals such as Devadatta and others who serve as the recipients (*saṃpradāna*) in the *śrāddha* rite—themselves, having been satisfied by the *śrāddha*, satisfy the human ancestors such as Devadatta through their possession of an excellence of knowledge and power.

Furthermore, they do not merely gratify the ancestors; rather, being themselves pleased, the ancestors—the Vasus and others—bestow upon those who perform the *śrāddha* rites longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, happiness, and sovereignty. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that they also grant whatever other fruits are mentioned in various scriptures for those specific occasions. (1.269–1.270)

Actions that accomplish visible and invisible results have been described and will also be described; since their accomplishment of their own nature and their efficacy as means to a result occur without obstacle, [the author], intending to prescribe a rite for the sake of removing obstacles, states the causes that produce and indicate obstacles:
"Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā to preside over the Gaṇas and to ensure the accomplishment of obstacles to ritual action."

"Vināyaka [is worshipped] for the sake of accomplishing actions and removing obstacles," and so forth; thus, through the thorough knowledge of the causes of both types of obstacles, those who act with foresight proceed either to preserve against the prior occurrence of an obstacle or to destroy one that has already arisen, just as one acts regarding a disease after understanding its two kinds of causes.

Vināyaka, the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara), was appointed and commissioned by Rudra, Brahmā—and by Viṣṇu as well, indicated by the word "and" (ca)—to ensure the accomplishment of obstacles for those actions that are means to achieve the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha), specifically to bring about the obstruction of their attainment of their own nature, results, and means; [he was appointed] to the lordship and sovereignty over the Gaṇas, such as Puṣpadanta and others. || 1.271 ||
Having thus stated the efficient cause (*kārakahetu*) of the obstacle, he speaks in order to demonstrate the indicative cause (*jñāpakahetu*): "Learn the symptoms of one who is afflicted by it:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men."
He wears saffron-colored robes and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he dwells together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels.

Even while walking, one likewise considers oneself followed by others. O sages, learn—understand—the characteristics that indicate one who has been approached and seized by that leader. The repeated address to the sages is for the purpose of commencing the section on tranquility (*śānti-prakaraṇa*).
In a dream, that is, during the state of dreaming, one plunges excessively into water, is carried away by a current, or sinks;
or one sees men with shaven heads,
and those wearing saffron robes or garments dyed red, blue, and so forth.
He mounts birds that eat raw flesh, such as vultures and others, as well as beasts of prey, such as tigers and others.
Likewise, he stands surrounded by outcastes such as Caṇḍālas, and by donkeys, mules, camels, and dromedaries.
While walking or moving about, he perceives himself as being pursued and overcome from behind by enemies who are running after him. (1.272–1.273)
Having thus described the visions in dreams, he states the signs based on direct perception:
"Dejected and with his undertakings fruitless, he sinks down without apparent cause."
Afflicted by that, the prince does not obtain a kingdom;
the maiden does not find a husband, nor does the woman conceive offspring in her womb.

The teacher does not attain the status of an ācārya, nor does the learned brahmin [attain] discipleship; likewise, the student does not obtain his studies, the merchant does not gain profit, and the farmer does not reap the fruits of his cultivation.
"Dejected" means one whose mind is distracted.
"One whose undertakings are fruitless" refers to one for whom undertakings have no result; he obtains no fruit whatsoever.
"He desponds without cause" means that, lacking a specific reason, he becomes dejected in mind.
A prince, though born into a royal family and endowed with qualities such as learning, heroism, and fortitude, does not obtain the kingdom;
nor does a maiden, though possessed of beauty, auspicious marks, and noble lineage, obtain her desired husband;
nor does a pregnant woman obtain offspring.
A woman in her season [attains] pregnancy;
even when there is study and knowledge of its meaning, one is a *śrotriya* by virtue of being a teacher;
and even if one is endowed with discipline, conduct, and so forth, one is a student by virtue of study or listening.
The phrase "does not obtain" is to be connected with every instance. A merchant, one who lives by trade, even if skilled therein, does not obtain profit from the buying and selling of grain and such;
a farmer, a cultivator, even if devoted to it, does not reap the fruit of agriculture.
Thus, if one who lives by a particular mode of livelihood finds that their undertakings therein are fruitless, they should be known as being afflicted by that [mode]. 1.274 || 1.275 || 1.276 ||
Having thus explained the causal factors of the agent and the indicator, he states the ritual procedure for the purpose of pacifying obstacles:
"His bath should be performed on an auspicious day according to the prescribed rules.
For him who is afflicted by Vināyaka, or for one desiring to avoid future affliction by Vināyaka, a bath—that is, an ablution—should be performed.
On an auspicious day, conjoined with favorable constellations and so forth,
during the daytime and not at night,
according to the prescribed ritual accompanied by the procedures taught in the scriptures.
He states the procedure for the ritual bath:
"And [for one] who has been rubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter..."

Likewise, for one whose head has been anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, virtuous twice-born men should pronounce the benediction of *svasti*.

For a person whose limbs have been massaged with a paste of white mustard (*gaurasarṣapa*) and ground *siddhārtha* mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and who has likewise had his head anointed with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadha*) such as *priyaṅgu* and *nāgakesara*, and with all fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*) such as sandalwood, agallochum, and musk, and who is seated upon the auspicious throne (*bhadrāsana*) to be described hereafter—four twice-born Brahmins, auspicious, endowed with Vedic learning, study, and good conduct, and of handsome appearance, should be addressed with the words: "May you, sirs, pronounce a blessing (*svasti*) for him."
The meaning is that at this time, one should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* according to the path prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. 1.277 || 1.278 ||
Furthermore: from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a confluence,
and a pool— one should take earth, yellow pigment (rocanā), fragrant substances, and guggulu, and cast them into the water.
Then, having placed the auspicious seat upon the hide of a red bull, one should set it down after water has been drawn from the lake by four attendants of a single caste using water-pots.

One should throw into those waters five kinds of earth brought from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, the confluence of rivers, and a lake that does not dry up; as well as *gorocana*, fragrant substances such as sandalwood, saffron, and agallochum, and *guggulu*. Then, upon the hide of a bull—red in color, with the hair facing upward and the neck toward the east—one should place an auspicious and pleasing seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood.
