The water that has been drawn from a lake that does not dry up, or from a confluence, using four jars of a single uniform color, unblemished by cracks or discoloration, and taken from the heart of the water. After that, on the hide of a bull—red, crimson-colored, with the hair turned upward and the neck pointing eastward—an auspicious and delightful seat fashioned from *śrīparṇī* wood should be established.

Then, having placed four jars—filled with water and earth, perfumes, and other substances; adorned with the sprouts of mango and other trees; their necks wound with garlands; smeared with sandalwood paste; and decorated with new, unwashed cloths—in the four directions beginning with the east, he should spread upon a pure, well-smeared sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) marked with a five-colored *svastika* a red bull-hide with the hair on the outside and the neck facing east, and place upon it a seat covered with a white cloth; this is the *bhadrāsana*.
For one seated upon it, the twice-born should pronounce blessings (*svasti*). (1.279–1.280)
Moreover:
With the thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed [water], made purifying by the seers—with that I sprinkle you; may the *pāvamānī* verses purify you.

Immediately after the recitation of the benediction (*svastivācana*), the Guru—having taken the water-pot (*kalaśa*) situated in the eastern direction, which has been consecrated with auspicious rites by well-dressed women who possess beauty and virtue and whose husbands and sons are living—should sprinkle [the disciple] with this mantra:

"I sprinkle you, who are afflicted by Vināyaka, with this water for the pacification of the affliction of Vināyaka—water that is purifying and sacred, produced and rendered holy by the seers (*ṛṣi*), Manu, and others, as thousand-eyed, possessing manifold powers, and flowing in many streams.
And may these waters, which are the *Pāvamānī* verses, purify you. (1.281)
May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune, and may the Seven Seers grant you fortune.
Immediately after that, taking the second jar situated in the southern region, one should consecrate [the candidate] with this mantra:
"May King Varuṇa grant you fortune (bhaga); may Sūrya grant you fortune; may Bṛhaspati grant you fortune; and may Indra, Vāyu, and the Seven Seers grant you fortune. || 1.282 ||
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, in your parting, or on your head; whatever is in your forehead, your ears, or your eyes—may the waters destroy it forever.
Then, taking the third jar, one should sprinkle [the person] with this mantra:

"O divine waters, may you destroy all that misfortune and ill-fortune which is in your hair, at the parting, on the crown of the head, on the forehead, and in the ears; may you pacify it forever. (1.283)
Having bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood into the head, while holding kuśa grass with the left hand.
Then, taking the fourth vessel, he should consecrate [the disciple] with the three previously mentioned mantras;
for it is indicated by the characteristic of the mantra that the fourth [consecration] is performed with all the mantras.

Having thus performed the consecration according to the stated method, the preceptor should offer mustard oil—held in his left hand and concealed by kuśa grass—upon the head of the [disciple], using a ladle made from the udumbara tree, while reciting the mantras to be described hereafter. 1.284.
And with the names Mita, Sammita, as well as Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa,
Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Rājaputra— each accompanied by "svāhā" at the end.

The connection with what has preceded is as follows: one should offer oblations with the names of Vināyaka—such as *Mitasaṃmita* and others—which are accompanied by salutations (*namaskāra*), end in *svāhā*, and begin with the *praṇava* (oṃ), along with the *bali-mantras*.
Because of the application of the term *svāhākāra*, the fourth case ending is used.

And therefore, there are six mantras: "Oṃ mitāya svāhā," "Oṃ saṃmitāya svāhā," "Oṃ śālāya svāhā," "Oṃ kaṭaṅkaṭāya svāhā," "Oṃ kūṣmāṇḍāya svāhā," and "Oṃ rājaputrāya svāhā. Immediately thereafter, having cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the rules for the *sthālīpāka* in the worldly fire, one should offer oblations into that very fire with these same six mantras. Then, one should present the bali-offering to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Ananta, using their names in the dative case followed by the word "namaḥ" as the bali-mantras. || 1.286 ||
He states what should be done immediately thereafter:
"One should place a winnowing basket at a crossroads, having strewn *kuśa* grass all around it."
Rice grains both prepared and unprepared, as well as rice mixed with minced meat,
cooked fish and likewise raw fish, and meat— only these [are permitted].
Variegated and fragrant flowers, as well as the three kinds of liquor; radishes, fried cakes, and pastries, and likewise garlands of *uṇḍeraka* flowers.
Having collected all these— curd-rice, milk-porridge, and flour-cakes with jaggery along with water— and having placed them upon the ground, he should then place his head there.

Then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka. Having presented the collection of offering materials, such as prepared and unprepared foods, before Vināyaka and because of his presence, and having likewise gone to the ground with one's head bowed before his mother, one should recite: "We meditate upon that Being; we contemplate the One with the Crooked Trunk;
may He, the Tusked One, inspire us."
With this mantra, one should pay homage to Vināyaka; and with the mantra, "We meditate upon Subhagā, we contemplate Kāmamālinī; may Gaurī impel us," one should pay homage to Ambikā.

Then, having placed the remains of the offering in a winnowing basket spread with *kuśa* grass, he should set it down at a crossroads, [saying]: "May the gods—the Ādityas, the Vasus, as well as the Maruts, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas—accept this *bali*."
Asuras, Yātudhānas, Piśācas, Uragas, Mātṛs,
Śākinīs, Yakṣas, Vetālas, Yoginīs, Pūtanās, and Śivās.
The Jṛmbhakas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Māyāvins, Vidyādharas, and men; the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds, and those who are the Vighnas and Vināyakas.
May Brahmā and the other great sages, who bring peace to the worlds,
grant that there be no obstacle for me, no sin, and no adversaries.
May the spirits and ghosts be gentle, satisfied, and bringers of happiness.
With these mantras.
Rice grains are both prepared and unprepared, and are offered all at once.
*Palala* is crushed sesame; rice mixed with that is *palalaudana*.
Fish are both cooked and uncooked.
Flesh is only this much, both cooked and uncooked.
Flower is variegated, with various colors such as red, yellow, and so forth.
Sandalwood and the like are fragrant substances.
Surā is of three kinds: gauḍī, mādhvī, and paiṣṭī.
Mūlaka is a specific kind of food, shaped like a bulbous root.
Pūrikā is well known.
*Apūpa* is a wheat product cooked without oil.
*Uṇḍerakasrajaḥ* refers to garlands made of *uṇḍeraka*, which are strings woven from flour and other such materials. *Dadhyanna* is food mixed with curd.
Pāyasa is milk-rice;
guḍapiṣṭa is flour of śāli rice and other grains mixed with molasses;
modakas are sweetmeat balls.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Vināyaka and his mother Ambikā with the mantra to be recited hereafter. || 1.286 – 1.289 ||
Having done what? He says:
having offered a full añjali of water for honor (*arghya*) consisting of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers.

Having offered the *arghya* with water containing flowers, one should first offer a handful (*añjali*) of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers, and then stand in attendance; this is the connection with what has preceded. 1.290.
He recites the mantra for attendance:
"O Blessed One, grant me form; grant me fame; grant me fortune.
Grant me sons; grant me wealth; and grant me all my desires."
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
he should feed the Brahmins and give a pair of garments even to his preceptor.
In the *ambikopasthāna*, the modification (*ūha*) is "O Blessed Lady" (*bhagavatī*); however, Pāṇḍeya and Seltur read: in the *vināyakopasthāna*, the modification is "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*).

Then, immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the patron (*yajamāna*), wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, should feed the Brahmins according to his capacity.
He should give a pair of garments to the preceptor (*guru*), who is endowed with learning, study, and good conduct, and who is knowledgeable in the ritual procedure for the bathing of Vināyaka.
By virtue of the word "api" (also), one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability to the Brahmins, dedicated to Vināyaka.
In this regard, the sequence of the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is as follows.

The preceptor, possessing the aforementioned characteristics and conversant with the mantras, together with four Brahmins, having prepared the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana), should worship Vināyaka and his mother in its vicinity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the prescribed mantras. Then, having cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru) and performed the recitation for an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) for the patron seated upon the auspicious seat, he should sprinkle him with water from four jars, offer mustard oil into the fire upon his head, and perform the oblation of the caru. Finally, in the consecration hall, he should present the ritual offering (bali) to the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, in the four directions.

The sacrificer, having bathed and put on white garlands and garments, together with the preceptor, shall present an offering to Vināyaka and Ambikā; bowing his head to the ground, he shall offer water with flowers as an *arghya*, and after offering a handful of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers, he shall worship Vināyaka and Ambikā.
The preceptor, having placed the remains of the offering in a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), shall set it down at a crossroads.
Thereafter, he shall give a pair of garments, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and a meal for a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the ceremonial bathing of Vināyaka. 1.291 || 1.292 ||
In order to demonstrate another application by way of a concluding summary of this very rite of bathing Vināyaka, he says:
"Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity."
Thus, having worshipped Vināyaka in the manner described, one obtains the fruit of actions without obstacle; this is the conclusion of what was said.
He states another application: "and one obtains the most excellent prosperity.
The meaning is that one who desires prosperity should worship Vināyaka by means of this very procedure.

Desiring to prescribe the ritual procedure for the worship of the planets and so forth for one who wishes to pacify the afflictions caused by the planets such as the Sun, and for one who desires prosperity and the like, [the author] introduces the worship of the planets with the words, "Having worshipped the planets according to the rule.
Having fully worshipped the planets, beginning with the Sun, according to the method that will be described, one attains success in one's undertakings and attains prosperity. 1.293.
He states the connection between the obligatory and the optional rites:
"By constantly performing the worship of the Sun, as well as the tilaka of the Lord (Śiva) and that of Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain success."

By constantly performing worship every day of the Blessed Āditya with red sandalwood, saffron, flowers, and so forth, and by constantly performing worship of Skanda and Mahāgaṇapati, one attains perfection and liberation through the gateway of self-knowledge; this is the obligatory connection (*nityasaṃyoga*).
By fashioning a *tilaka*—an image made of gold, silver, or other materials—of any one of Āditya, Skanda, or Gaṇapati, or of all three, one attains the desired perfection;
likewise, [the same applies] to the eyes; this is the optional connection (*kāmyasaṃyoga*). (1.294)

"Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule, one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity. By this [verse], it is stated that through the worship of the planets, there is the successful accomplishment of actions without obstacles, and prosperity is the result.
Now, he states other results:

One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, should perform the sacrifice to the planets; likewise, one who desires rain, long life, or nourishment, as well as one practicing exorcism (abhicāra).
"Desirous of prosperity" (*śrīkāma*) is a restatement of what was previously mentioned.

"Desirous of peace" (*śāntikāma*) means one who desires the pacification of calamities. "Rain" (*vṛṣṭi*) refers to the falling of rain for the sake of the growth of crops and so forth. "Longevity" (*āyuḥ*) refers to living for a long duration through victory over untimely death (*apamṛtyu*).
"Nourishment" means having a faultless body; "one who desires these" refers to one desiring rain, long life, and nourishment.
Those desiring prosperity and so forth should perform the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*), that is, the worship of the planets.
Likewise, even one practicing sorcery—sorcery being the infliction of pain upon another by unseen means—one desiring such should also perform the sacrifice to the planets. (1.295)
He speaks of the planets: "The Sun, the Moon, the Son of the Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu— these are remembered as the planets."
These are the nine planets, beginning with the Sun. || 1.296 ||
It has been stated that the planets are to be worshipped.
Having done what? He says:
from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, and gold—both [from these].
The planetary orbs should be fashioned, in order, from silver, iron, lead, and brass.

The forms of the Sun and the other [planets] should be fashioned from copper and other materials in their respective order; or, in the absence of those, they should be drawn on a cloth with pigments of their own colors, or [represented] by scents within mandalas.
Or [they are to be drawn] in mandalas with perfumes.
The grammatical connection is that they are to be painted with perfumes such as red sandalwood and so forth, according to their respective colors.
However, the specific details regarding their having two arms and so on should be understood from the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
For example: Ravi (the Sun) should always be depicted with two arms, seated upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, with his lotus-seat, lotus-hands, and a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus.
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments;
he has two arms, holds a mace in his hand, and is bestowing a boon.
Wearing red garlands and garments, holding a spear, a trident, and a mace,
the son of the Earth (Mars) shall have four arms, ride upon a ram, and grant boons.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, possessing a luster like that of the *karṇikāra* flower,
holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, and seated upon a lion, the planet Mercury bestows boons.
Likewise, the two preceptors of the gods and the Daityas should be depicted as yellow and white, four-armed, holding staffs,
granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted as having the luster of sapphire, bearing a trident, granting boons, riding upon a vulture, and holding an arrow and a bow.
With a terrifying face, bearing a sword, shield, and trident, the blue Rāhu, seated upon a lion-throne and bestowing boons, is praised here.
All smoke-colored, two-armed, bearing maces, and having distorted faces;
seated eternally upon vultures, these banners shall be granters of boons.
All the planets, which bring welfare to the world, should be depicted wearing crowns;
all of them should always be one hundred and eight in number and raised [in height] by one's own finger-breadths.
Thus:

Ravi (the Sun) should always have two arms, be seated upon a lotus-seat, have hands like lotuses, possess a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus, and be situated upon a chariot drawn by seven horses.
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments;
he has two arms, holds a mace in his hand, and displays the gesture of granting boons.
Wearing red garlands and garments, holding a spear, a trident, and a mace,
the son of the Earth (Mars) shall have four arms, ride upon a ram, and grant boons.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, possessing a luster like that of the *karṇikāra* flower,
holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, and seated upon a lion, the planet Mercury bestows boons.
Likewise, the two preceptors of the gods and the Daityas should be depicted as yellow and white, four-armed, holding staffs,
granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted as having the luster of sapphire, bearing a trident, granting boons, riding upon a vulture, and holding an arrow and a bow.
With a formidable face, bearing a sword, shield, and trident,
the blue Rāhu is praised here as the bestower of boons while seated upon a lion-throne.
All smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, and having distorted faces;
seated eternally upon vultures, these banners shall be the bestowers of boons.
All the planets, which bring welfare to the world, should be depicted wearing crowns;
they should all always be one hundred and eight in number and raised [in height] by one's own finger-breadths.
The location for their installation is also stated in that very same place:
"One should know Bhāskara in the center, Lohita to the south,
Guru to the north, and Budha to the northeast."
One should know Bhārgava to be in the east, Soma in the southeast;
one should know Śani in the west, and Rāhu in the southwest.
One should indeed establish the banner in the north-western direction with white rice grains.
Thus [it is said].
One should know Bhāskara (the Sun) to be in the center, Lohita (Mars) to the south,
Guru (Jupiter) to the north, and Budha (Mercury) to the northeast.
One should know Bhārgava to be in the east, Soma in the southeast;
one should know Śani in the west, and Rāhu in the southwest.
One should indeed place the banner in the north-western direction with white rice grains.
He states the ritual procedure for the worship of the planets:
"Garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors."
Fragrance, offerings, and incense made of guggulu should be presented;
and oblations (caru) accompanied by mantras should be performed for each respective deity.
According to the color—whatever the color of each planet is, garments, perfumes, and flowers of that same color should be offered.
As for the oblations (*bali*) and incense, *guggulu* resin should be offered to all.

And as for the sacrificial porridges (*caru*), one should offer four handfuls for each deity, preceded by the establishment of the fire (*agnipratiṣṭhāpana*) and the ritual preparation (*anvādhāna*), according to the prescribed rule beginning with: "I offer you, acceptable to such-and-such [deity]."

Immediately thereafter, having performed the ritual actions beginning with the placing of fuel on the well-kindled fire and ending with the pouring of the libations (āghāra), one should offer the oblations of cooked rice (caru) in the manner to be described, after first offering the prescribed fuel-sticks (samidh) according to the sequence and mantras to be stated, dedicated to Āditya and the other deities. 1.298–1.299.
He states the mantras for the planets: the verses "ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed in their respective order.
"Bṛhaspate atiyad aryaḥ," likewise "annāt parisrutaḥ," "śaṃ no devīḥ," likewise "kāṇḍāt," and "ketuṃ kṛṇvan imān" likewise.

The nine mantras beginning with "Moving through the black dust" (ākṛṣṇena rajasā vartamāna) are to be understood as pertaining, in their respective order, to Āditya and the other [planets]. || 1.300 || 1.301 ||
Now he speaks of the fuel-sticks:
the *arka*, the *palāśa*, the *khadira*, the *apāmārga*, then the *pippala*, the *udumbara*, the *śamī*, the *dūrvā*, and the *kuśa* grasses are the fuel-sticks in their respective order.
The *arka*, *palāśa*, and other such trees serve as fuel-sticks (*samidh*) for the Sun and the other deities respectively;
these should be prepared fresh, unbroken, with their bark intact, and measuring one span (*prādeśa*) in length. || 1.302 ||
Furthermore: for each one here, there are either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight [recitations].
They should be offered as oblations with honey and clarified butter, or combined with curd or milk.

For each of the deities beginning with Āditya, the aforementioned sacrificial fuel-sticks of *arka* and so forth—numbering either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight as appropriate—should be offered together with honey, clarified butter, curds, or milk. 1.303.
Now he describes the foods:
rice with molasses, milk-rice, sacrificial food, sixty-day rice with milk,
rice with curd, sacrificial oblation, flour, meat, and variegated rice.
The wise man should thus give food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets,
honoring them with due ceremony and according to his capacity or as it may be obtained, in accordance with the prescribed rite.
Rice mixed with molasses is *guḍaudana*; *pāyasa* (milk-rice);
and sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) such as the grains of sages (*munyanna*).
*Kṣīraṣāṣṭika* is rice from the *ṣaṣṭika* variety mixed with milk; *kṣīramiśraḥ ṣāṣṭikaudanaḥ* is *ṣaṣṭika* rice boiled with milk.
*Gardhnā miśra odanaḥ* is rice mixed with curd, i.e., *dadhyodana*.
*Haviḥ* is ghee-rice (*ghṛtaudana*).
Powder refers to rice mixed with sesame powder. Meat refers to rice mixed with edible meat. Variegated rice refers to rice of various colors.
One should give these items, such as rice with jaggery and so forth, in due order to twice-born Brāhmaṇas for the purpose of a meal, dedicating them respectively to Āditya and the other deities.
The number of Brāhmaṇas should be determined according to one's means.

However, in the absence of rice with jaggery and the like, one should give whatever rice or other food is available, having honored it with the prior performance of rites such as washing their feet, and presenting it with due respect. (1.304–1.305)
He states the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā): "A cow, a conch, likewise an ox, gold, a garment, a horse in sequence;
a black cow, iron, and a goat—these are remembered as the sacrificial fees."
A cow that yields milk;
a conch shell, which is well known;
and an ox, a draft animal capable of bearing a load.
Gold is yellow; the garment is yellow;
the horse is white.
A black cow;
iron implements such as weapons and the like;
a goat is well known.
These [gifts], beginning with a cow, are traditionally prescribed by Manu and others as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for Brahmins, intended respectively for Āditya and the other [deities].
And this applies when such [gifts] are available; however, in the absence of them, whatever else may be obtained according to one's means should be given. 1.306.

It has been stated that all the planets should be worshipped without distinction by one who desires peace; regarding this, he states the specific rule: "Whichever planet is unfavorable for whichever person at whatever time, that person should worship that planet with diligence."
A boon was granted to them by Brahmā: "When you are honored, you shall honor [others] in return."
Whichever planet belongs to a person, if at that time it is situated in an unfavorable position—such as the eighth house or other malefic locations—one should worship that planet with special effort.
For a boon was previously granted to these planets by Brahmā: "Being worshipped, you shall honor your worshipper by the attainment of what is desired and the removal of what is undesired. || 1.307 ||
Rites such as those for pacification and nourishment have been set forth generally with reference to the twice-born.
Regarding this, he says that a king endowed with the qualities of consecration has a special entitlement:
"The rises and falls of kings depend upon the planets."
Since the existence and non-existence of the world depend upon them, the planets are most worthy of worship.
One who performs this hospitality for the planets, even once every year,
shall be endowed with health and strength and live for a hundred autumns.
For kings who are consecrated kṣatriyas, the planets are most worthy of worship.
By this, it is understood that they are also to be worshipped by others. He states the reason for both cases:
Since the prosperity and downfall of living beings depend upon the planets, they should therefore be worshipped by those who possess the requisite authority.
Furthermore, the existence and non-existence— the birth and cessation— of the world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, are dependent upon the planets.
In that regard, if these [planets] are worshipped, then their arising and cessation occur at their own proper time;
otherwise, there would be no arising at the time of its occurrence, and cessation would occur out of season.

Furthermore, because kings are the lords of the world and act for its welfare and security, the planets are most worthy of worship; thus, they have a specific authority over rites such as pacification (*śāntika*).

And likewise, Gautama, having addressed the king with the rule, "The king has authority over all, except for the Brahmins," and having stated certain duties such as, "He shall protect the social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*) according to justice, and he shall establish those who stray from them in their own duty," concludes: "Furthermore, he should respect whatever the experts in divine portents (*daivotpāta*) might declare, for some maintain that even security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) depend upon them."

Having stated the reasons for performing rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), [the author] has shown the pacificatory rites (*śāntika*) and so forth by stating that one should perform in the hall-fire (*śālāgni*) those rites pertaining to prosperity (*ābhyudayika*)—conjoined with auspicious days (*puṇyāha*), blessings (*svastyayana*), longevity (*āyuṣya*), and auspiciousness (*maṅgala*)—as well as those conjoined with incantations for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), immobilization (*stambhana*), malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and the increase of enemies. (1.308)
Having described the duties common to householders, he now states the specific duties of one endowed with qualities such as royal consecration:
"He should be highly energetic, liberal, grateful, a servant of the elders,
humble, possessed of courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure."
One who is not dilatory, possessed of mindfulness, noble-minded, and likewise not harsh;
one who is righteous, free from vice, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets.

That lord of men was a guardian of his own senses, disciplined in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) as well as in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and likewise trained in the science of livelihood (vārtā) and the triple Veda (trayī).

*Utsāha* (energy) is the determination to undertake actions that accomplish the goals of human life; one who possesses great energy is *mahotsāha*. One who perceives many objects to be given is *sthūlalakṣa*.
One who does not forget benefits or harms conferred by others is *kṛtajña* (grateful).
A "servant of the elders" (*vṛddhasevaka*) is one who serves those advanced in austerity, knowledge, and so forth.
"Disciplined" (*vinīta*) means endowed with discipline (*vinaya*).

By the word "discipline," the previously mentioned collection of duties for a *snātaka* is expressed—those stated in such passages as: "One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause."
Endowed with courage, he is free from joy and dejection regarding prosperity and adversity;
he is of noble birth and well-born on both his mother’s and father’s side;
and he is truthful in speech, being habituated to speaking the truth.

"Pure" means endowed with both external and internal purity. "Not procrastinating" refers to one who does not delay in undertaking necessary tasks nor in completing those already begun. "Possessing mindfulness" means having a disposition that does not forget what has been learned.
He is not mean-spirited nor does he hate the virtues of others; he is not harsh and has the disposition not to proclaim the faults of others;
he is righteous, being endowed with the duties of his social class and stage of life.
One who has no calamities is "one free from calamities" (*avyasana*).

There are eighteen such calamities, as Manu states: "Hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and instrumental music], and idle wandering—this is the tenfold group born of desire."
Slander, violence, malice, envy, jealousy, and the spoiling of property;
along with verbal and physical harshness—this is the eightfold group born of anger.
Thus, hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication,
the triple symphony [of song, dance, and instrument], idle wandering, and [vain] talk constitute the tenfold group born of desire.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, jealousy, and the spoiling of wealth, as well as harshness of speech and punishment arising from anger— this is the group of eight born of anger.
And among those, seven are most grievous. As Manu says: "Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—in this order—one should know this tetrad to be the most grievous in the group born of desire."
The infliction of physical punishment, verbal abuse, and the embezzlement of wealth—
one should always know that this triad is most grievous, even within the group of vices born of anger.
Thus, drinking, dice, women, and hunting— in this order—
one should know that this group of four is the most grievous among the vices born of desire.
One should always know that this triad— the infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the embezzlement of wealth— is always painful, even within the group born of anger.
He is wise, capable of discerning profound meanings;
he is brave and fearless;
and he is a knower of secrets, skillful in concealing matters that must be kept hidden.

A guardian of one's own vulnerabilities (*svarandhragoptā*): that laxity in the seven constituent elements of sovereignty (*rājyaṅga*) which serves as an opening for the entry of an enemy is one's "vulnerability" (*svarandhra*); its "guardian" is the one who conceals it.
In *ānvīkṣikī*, which is the science of the self (*ātmavidyā*);
and in *daṇḍanīti*, which is applicable to the acquisition and preservation of wealth (*arthayogakṣema*).
He was trained— that is, led to proficiency— by those experts in *vārttā*, which consists of agriculture, commerce, and cattle-rearing and serves as the cause for the accumulation of wealth,
and in the *trayī* (the triple Veda), known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas (or,
according to a variant reading, consisting of the Sāman).
As Manu said: "From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple Vedic knowledge and the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti);
from those who know the self, the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī); and from the world, the various undertakings of commerce and agriculture.
Thus, from those learned in the three Vedas, [he learns] the triple Vedic knowledge and the eternal science of government.

"A king who has been consecrated for sovereignty should [study] Ānvīkṣikī from those who know the Self, and the undertakings of commerce (vārtā) from the world. This is to be connected with every [verse]. (309–311)
Having thus explained the internal qualities of one endowed with consecration, he now speaks of the external ones:
"He should appoint as ministers those who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
together with them, and then with a Brahmin, he should deliberate upon the kingdom himself."
A king endowed with qualities such as great energy should appoint ministers. Of what nature should they be? They should be wise and skilled in discerning between the beneficial and the harmful.
Those who are hereditary, having come down through their own lineage;
steadfast, remaining free from agitation even in great occasions of joy or sorrow;
and pure, being proven honest through tests concerning dharma, wealth, pleasure, and fear.
And they should be seven or eight in number.
As Manu said: "He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and well-tested."
Thus:
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.
Having thus first appointed his ministers, he should deliberate on matters of state—characterized by peace, war, and so forth—with them, both collectively and individually.

Thereafter, having ascertained their opinions and deliberated on the matter together with a Brahmin priest (*purohita*) who is skilled in investigating the meaning of all the scriptures, he should then deliberate on the matter himself through his own intelligence.
To explain what kind of priest he should appoint, [the author] says:

He should appoint as his domestic priest one who is skilled in astrology, highly distinguished by noble birth and conduct, proficient in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and likewise learned in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda].
And he should make the domestic priest (purohita) his own ally through gifts, honor, and respect in all undertakings concerning both visible and invisible matters.
Of what nature should he be?
He should be a knower of the stars (daivajña), one who understands the planets, portents, and the means for pacifying them.

"Exalted" (uditoditam) means increased by those things exalted through learning, noble lineage, religious observances, and so forth, as prescribed in the scriptures; it means prosperous. "Skilled in the science of government" (daṇḍanīti) refers to the treatise on statecraft (arthaśāstra), and also to the rites of pacification and so forth in the Atharvāṅgirasa. || 1.313 ||

For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, he should indeed choose officiating priests and should likewise perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
For the successful accomplishment of the performance of rites such as the Śrauta Agnihotra and the Smārta Upāsana, he should choose officiating priests (ṛtvij).
And he should perform sacrifices such as the Rājasūya according to the rules, that is, in accordance with the injunctions, providing abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 1.314 ||
Moreover:
He should bestow enjoyments and various kinds of wealth upon the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins constitutes an inexhaustible treasure for kings.
One should bestow enjoyments and pleasures upon the Brahmins by means of granting them their rightful shares;
likewise, various kinds of wealth, such as gold, silver, land, and so forth.
For that which is given to the Brahmins is the inexhaustible treasure and storehouse of kings.
Since giving is attained as a common duty [shared by all], this statement is made again for the purpose of demonstrating the preeminence of giving among kings. 1.315.
Furthermore:

An offering made into the fire of a Brahmin from the presence of [an ordinary] fire is said here to be superior— provided it is not spilled, is free from distress, and is untainted by the need for expiatory rites.

It is said here that what is offered into the fire of a Brahmin is superior even to offerings made into the sacrificial fire—such as the Rājasūya and other rites accomplished by fire involving abundant sacrificial fees—for this [offering] is unspilled, free from delay, painless, devoid of injury to animals, and untainted by the need for expiatory rites. (1.316)
It has been stated that one should give wealth to the learned;
by what procedure should one give it? To this he says:
One should seek what has not been obtained through righteous means, and one should protect with effort what has been obtained.
One should increase what has been protected through prudent policy, and one should bestow what has increased upon worthy recipients.
One should strive, in accordance with the treatises on dharma, to acquire what has not yet been acquired.

What has been acquired through effort should be protected by one’s own supervision. What has been protected should be guarded with diligence, and once guarded, it should be made to increase through policy such as trade routes and the like.
And he should bestow—that is, give—the surplus among the three kinds of recipients: the recipient for dharma, the recipient for artha, and the recipient for kāma. || 1.317 ||
Having cast [the water] into the vessel, what should he do? To this he says:
"Having given the land or having made a formal pledge (nibandha), the king should cause a document (lekhyam) to be prepared for the information of future virtuous rulers."

Having bestowed the land according to the prescribed rule and having effected the cessation of his own ownership, he should cause a document to be executed after establishing a fixed assessment (*nibandha*). This assessment may be formulated as: "For one load of merchandise, there are this many *rūpaka*s," or "For one load of leaves, there are this many leaves.
For what purpose?
It is for the sake of providing full knowledge to future noble and virtuous kings—those who will come—that "this was given by him" and "this was accepted by him."
"Pārthiva" means a king (*bhūpati*).
By this, it is shown that only a king has the authority to grant land or to grant an endowment (*nibandha*), and not a mere lord of enjoyment (*bhogapati*). || 1.318 ||
It was stated that "one should have a document prepared.
To explain how one should have it prepared, he says:
"Either on a cloth or on a copper plate, marked with one's own seal."
The lord of the earth, having inscribed his own lineage and himself [upon the pillar].
One should cause a firm edict to be issued, specifying the extent of the land received, describing the boundaries of the gift,
and completed with one's own hand and the date.

On a cotton cloth, a copper plate, or a wooden tablet, one should inscribe one's own ancestors—the great-grandfather, grandfather, and father—preceded by a description of their lineage, heroism, learning, and other virtues, so that the plural number may be meaningful; and having inscribed oneself as well (the word "ca" implying) the recipient, the extent of the gift, and a description of the boundaries of the donation.
"Pratigraha" means that which is received; it refers to the bond [of ownership], and its "extent" refers to the quantity of silver coins or other such measures.

That which is given is a *dāna* (gift), such as a field and so forth. Its *cheda* (demarcation) refers to that by which it is delimited; this includes rivers, boundaries, *nivartanas*, and their measurements. Its description should be recorded, such as: "To the south of such-and-such river is this village or field," or "To the east of such-and-such village is a measurement of so many *nivartanas*," and so on, including the measurement in *nivartanas*.

Thus, because the ground may undergo increase or decrease due to the shifting of pits, rivers, cities, roads, and so forth, in order to prevent that, it must be made complete and valid by the words: "This is my approval, [name] son of [name], regarding what has been written above"; it must be endowed with two kinds of time—the era of the Śaka king and the year itself—specified by lunar eclipses and the like; it must be marked and inscribed on the outside with his own seal bearing the form of Garuḍa, Varāha, or other such symbols; and it must be stable and firm. He should cause this edict to be issued, for future kings are instructed by it that the preservation of a gift is more meritorious than the act of giving itself; thus it is called an *edict* (*śāsana*).

The lord of the earth is not the master of enjoyments. He who acts as the negotiator of peace and war should not be anyone at random; rather, he should be the scribe of that very person who conducts the peace and war.
Commanded by the king himself, he shall write the royal edict.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Since the fruit of giving is accomplished by the mere act of giving itself, the execution of the legal document is for the purpose of an excellence of fruit through the increase of enjoyment. 1.319–1.320.
Now he states the king’s place of residence:

He should dwell in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the protection of his people, his treasury, and himself.
Delightful and beautiful with aśoka, campaka, and other trees;
fit for cattle (paśavya), meaning beneficial for livestock and conducive to the increase of animals;
and providing a livelihood (ājīvya), meaning a source of subsistence through bulbs, roots, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
Although a *jāṅgala* region is one where water, trees, and mountains are scarce, nevertheless, even a region possessing water, trees, and mountains is designated by the term *jāṅgala*.
One should settle in or dwell in such a place;
in such a region, one should construct a fortress for the purpose of protecting the people, the treasury consisting of gold and other wealth, and oneself.
And that is of six kinds,
as Manu has said:
"A desert-fortress, an earth-fortress, a water-fortress, or indeed a forest-fortress..."
Having taken refuge in either a human fortress or a mountain fortress, he should dwell in his city.
Thus [ends verse 1.321].
Having taken refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort,
a forest fort, a human fort, or a mountain fort, one should dwell in a city.
Furthermore:
In various matters concerning income, expenditures, and administrative tasks, he should appoint officials who are experts, supervisors, skillful, pure, and diligent.
In each respective matter concerning dharma, artha, kāma, and so forth, he should appoint capable and qualified officials as supervisors.
As it has been said:
"In matters of dharma, those who know dharma; in matters of artha, the learned."
One should employ eunuchs among women and low-born men in contemptible tasks.
Thus:
In matters of dharma, he should employ those who know dharma; in matters of wealth, the learned;
in the case of women, eunuchs; and in contemptible tasks, the low-born.
Of what kind?
Proficient, meaning those whose activities are directed toward nothing else; skilled, meaning those who are adept in their respective tasks.
"Pure" means those who have been proven honest through the fourfold tests.

"Diligent" means those who are energetic and untiring in matters of income—namely, in the places where gold and other materials are produced—and in matters of expenditure—namely, in the places where gold and other materials are disbursed.
By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that they are also endowed with qualities such as wisdom.
And it is said: "Wisdom, purity of character, vigilance, diligence, freedom from addiction to affairs, and devotion to the master— these constitute fitness."
Thus [ends verse] 1.322.
Wisdom, purity of intention, vigilance, diligence,
freedom from addiction to worldly affairs, and devotion to the master constitute fitness for office.
"One should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins"—thus has the general giving of one's own property been stated.
Now, he describes the excellence of the fruit resulting from the gift of what was acquired through valor by kings:
"There is no duty higher than this for kings, namely that which is acquired in battle."
Wealth is given to the Brahmins, and constant fearlessness is granted to the subjects.
O kings, there exists no dharma more excellent than this: that wealth acquired in battle is bestowed upon Brahmins, and that the gift of fearlessness is granted to one's subjects. 1.323.
It has been stated that what is acquired in battle must be given.

However, since misfortune can also befall one who has engaged in battle for the sake of acquiring wealth—such that it would be neither dharma nor artha—it is better to desist from it; therefore, he says:
"Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land, without turning their backs..."
With their weapons unerring, they go to heaven just like yogins.

Those who, for the sake of land and other such goals, engage in battles and are slain while facing their enemies without turning their backs— just like those devoted to the practice of yoga— they go to heaven, provided that the warriors fight with weapons that are not intended to kill and are not smeared with poison or similar substances. 1.324.
Moreover:
"The words of those who do not retreat when broken are equal to a sacrifice;
however, the king takes away the merit of those who are slain while fleeing."

When one's own forces—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—are broken, the footsteps of those who do not retreat but advance toward the enemy force are equal to sacrifices; they are equal to the Aśvamedha.
He states the fault in the opposite case: "The king takes away the merit of those who flee, turn their backs, and are slain. (1.325)
Moreover:

One should not strike one who proclaims "I am yours," a eunuch, one who is weaponless, one who has joined with another, one who has retreated, or one who is merely a spectator of the battle and so forth.

"One who says 'I am yours'—him, a eunuch, a neuter; one who is weaponless, unarmed; one who has joined with another, fighting alongside someone else; one who has turned away from battle, having retreated from the fight; and one who is a spectator of battle, a watcher of the fray—one should not kill him. This is the connection for all cases. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), horsemen, charioteers, and others are included.

As Gautama says: "There is no fault in killing in battle, except for those who are without horses, charioteers, or weapons; those with palms joined in supplication; those with disheveled hair; those with their backs turned; those who are seated; those standing on the ground; those mounted on trees; those who are insane; messengers; cows; Brahmins, and so forth. Śaṅkha also says: "A king who is not himself a king shall not kill one who is drinking water, nor one who is eating, nor one who is putting off his shoes, nor one who is without armor against one who has armor, nor a woman, nor an elephant, nor a horse, nor a charioteer, nor a herald, nor a messenger, nor a Brahmin, nor another king. (1.326)
Having performed his protective rites and risen, he should personally inspect income and expenditure;
then, having attended to legal affairs and bathed, he may eat according to his desire.
Having performed the protective rites for the city and for himself, he should rise every day at dawn and personally inspect his income and expenditures.
Then, having attended to legal affairs and bathed at midday, he should eat according to his desire and at the appropriate time. (1.327)
Gold brought by those engaged in trade should be deposited in the treasuries;
thereafter, having consulted with his ministers, he should inspect his spies and dispatch his envoys.

Immediately thereafter, having personally inspected the gold brought by those appointed to fetch it and other valuables, he should deposit it in the treasuries. Then, he should see the spies (*cāra*) and secret agents (*spasa*) who have returned;

having seen those spies who were dispatched as hidden agents in the guise of wandering mendicants, ascetics, and so forth, in order to ascertain the state of affairs in the enemy kingdom, he should station them in appropriate places.
Immediately after that, one should observe the messengers.
These messengers are those who openly engage in coming and going between different kings;
they are of three kinds.
They are: those with full authority (*nisṛṣṭārtha*), those with limited instructions (*saṃdiṣṭārtha*), and messengers carrying a royal decree (*śāsanahara*).
Among them, those with full authority are capable of explaining royal affairs themselves, as appropriate to the place and time.
Those who communicate to another exactly what has been said to them are those with limited instructions.
The messengers of the royal edict are those who carry the king's letters. Having been previously dispatched, he should see them upon their arrival in the company of his ministers.
Having seen them and deliberated upon their report, he should dispatch them again and again. (1.328)
Then he may move about at his own pleasure, or associate with his ministers;
having inspected the forces, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief.
Immediately thereafter, in the afternoon, he should remain alone at his own pleasure and as he desires, dwelling within the inner apartments;

or, surrounded by trustworthy ministers who are skilled in the arts and knowledgeable in recreation, and by women endowed with beauty, youth, and elegance, he should eat and enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments. Having enjoyed himself for the appropriate time, he should again attend to his duties.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu:

"Then, adorned with excellent garments, flowers, unguents, and ornaments, and having inspected the forces of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, he should consider with the commander-in-chief (senānī) matters such as their protection, in accordance with the requirements of place and time. (1.329)
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of his spies;
he may enjoy himself with songs and dances, and he should also recite his sacred study.
Then, having performed the evening twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at dusk,
he should— though it is generally understood that this has already been established— speak again for the sake of ensuring it is not forgotten due to the busyness of his duties.
Immediately thereafter, with weapon in hand, he should listen within the inner apartments to the secret speech of those spies whom he previously observed and stationed in various places.

And it has been said by Manu: "Having performed the twilight devotions, the king, bearing his weapons, should listen within his inner apartments to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his spies."
Thus,
having performed the twilight devotions, the king should listen within his inner apartments to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his spies.

Then, having enjoyed himself for some time with dancing, singing, and other such pleasures, he should enter another chamber and eat; having gone to yet another chamber and taken leave of those people, he should enter the inner apartments together with the women for the purpose of dining.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti;
therefore, for the sake of not forgetting it, one should recite the sacred texts according to one's ability. (1.330)
He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise wake up to that same sound;
he should contemplate the scriptures with his intellect, as well as all his duties.
Immediately after that, he should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and conchs;
likewise, he should wake up to the sound of musical instruments and the like.
Having awakened, during the final watch of the night, he should—either alone or together with trustworthy experts in the scriptures—reflect upon the scriptures, all his duties, and all his tasks.
And this is said with reference to one who is in good health;
however, one who is unwell should appoint another for all duties,
as Manu has said:
A healthy lord of the earth should carry out this conduct;
when unwell, he should entrust all of this to his chief minister.
Thus [ends verse 1.331].
A healthy lord of the earth should carry out these duties;
when unwell, he should entrust all of this to his chief minister.
Then, having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family priest, and the teachers, he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and those of others.
Having seen them, he should give cows, gold, and land to astrologers and physicians;
furthermore, he should give dwellings and houses to those learned in the Vedas.

Immediately thereafter, remaining right there, he should dispatch his own trusted spies—who have been honored with gifts, respect, and hospitality—to his own feudatories and officials, as well as to other kings, in order to ascertain their intentions.

Then, having performed the morning twilight devotions and offered the *agnihotra* sacrifice, being greeted with blessings by the domestic priest, officiating priests, teachers, and others; having consulted the astrologers and learned from them the positions of the planets and other celestial bodies; having instructed the domestic priests to perform propitiatory rites (*śāntika*) and the like; having seen the physicians and informed them of the state of his own body and directed their treatment; and having bestowed upon Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*)—Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas—a milch cow, gold, land, wedding requisites such as ornaments for the bride, and houses whitened with lime and the like.
The word "should give" (*dadyāt*) is to be connected with each [of the preceding items]. 1.332 || 1.333 ||
Furthermore:

A king should be patient toward Brahmins, straightforward toward his affectionate kin, and wrathful toward his enemies; he should behave toward his circle of servants and his subjects as a father does.
He is patient even when Brahmins revile him;
he is affectionate toward those who are affectionate, such as friends and others;
and he is wrathful toward his enemies.

"He should be compassionate toward his circle of servants and toward the subjects like a father, by practicing what is beneficial and turning away from what is harmful"—this [phrase] is to be connected with each [of the preceding]. (1.334)
He states the fruit of protecting the subjects:
"By protecting [them] according to justice, he takes a sixth part of their merit;
for the protection of subjects is superior to all gifts."
Because, by protecting the subjects according to justice and the path taught in the scriptures, he takes a sixth part—that is, a one-sixth share—from the merit produced by those protected subjects;
and because the protection of subjects yields a greater fruit than all other gifts of land and so forth;
therefore, the connection with what precedes is that he should be toward his subjects exactly as a father is. (1.335)
He shall protect the subjects from those who oppress them— such as flatterers, thieves, evildoers, and violent criminals— and especially from the scribes.
Flatterers are deceivers who, having gained someone's trust, steal their wealth;
thieves are those who take things in secret;
and the wicked include conjurors, gamblers, and the like.

*Sahasa* means force; that which is done by force is *sāhasa*. That which is both great and *sāhasa* is *mahāsāhasa*; those who act by means of it are *mahāsāhasikāḥ*, namely those who seize property by violence.
From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [are included] base practitioners of trickery and those of evil conduct.
The king should protect his subjects when they are being oppressed and afflicted by these.
Scribes, copyists, and accountants—being especially oppressed by these, one should protect [the subjects] from them;
for they are difficult to restrain due to their favoritism with the king and their extreme deceitfulness. (1.336)
Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not protected,
half of that belongs to the king, since he receives taxes from them.
If subjects, being unprotected, commit any offense whatsoever—such as theft, adultery with another's wife, and so forth—the king incurs half of that sin;
for that king receives taxes from the subjects for the purpose of providing protection. (1.337)
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed to govern the realm,
the king should honor the virtuous and put to death those who act contrarily.
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
but he should always settle there learned Vedic scholars (śrotriyas) who are honored with gifts, respect, and hospitality.

Having thoroughly ascertained through spies of the aforementioned characteristics the conduct and behavior of those appointed to the kingdom and its administrative offices, he should honor the virtuous who act rightly with gifts, marks of respect, and hospitality;
and having correctly identified those who are the opposite—those of wicked conduct—he should have them executed according to their offenses.
Furthermore, those who live by bribery, he should deprive of their wealth and banish from his own kingdom.
Having honored the Vedic scholars with gifts, food, and hospitality, he should always cause them to dwell within his own kingdom and his own country. || 1.338 || 1.339 ||
The king who increases his own treasury from the kingdom through unjust means shall, before long, lose his royal fortune and meet with destruction along with his kinsmen.

That king who, having seized wealth unjustly from his own kingdom, increases his own treasury, will very soon—indeed swiftly—be deprived of glory, his fortune destroyed, and meet with ruin along with his kinsmen. || 1.340 ||
The fire born from the suffering and oppression of the subjects does not cease until it has consumed the king's family, his fortune, and his very life.

The mass of demerit, which—like a fire arising from the distress caused by the oppression of subjects by thieves and others—is called "fire" because it produces burning heat, does not turn back nor is it extinguished until it has consumed and brought to ruin the king’s lineage, fortune, and life. (1.341)
Whatever dharma belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom,
that very same dharma he attains in its entirety when bringing another's kingdom under his control.

Whatever dharma belongs to a king in the lawful protection of his own kingdom, he obtains that entire dharma, as well as a sixth part of it, by bringing another's kingdom under his control and making it his own, according to the method to be described. || 1.342 ||
Furthermore: "In whatever region there is a particular custom, legal practice, or family tradition..."
In the same way, he must be protected once he has come under one's control.

When a foreign land has come under one's control, one should not introduce a mixture of the customs and practices of one's own country; rather, whatever custom, family tradition, or legal procedure existed in that land previously, exactly that must be maintained, provided it is not contrary to the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*).
By the phrase "when it has come under control," it is shown that prior to coming under control there was no fixed rule.
As it has been said:
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain encamped and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel.
Thus [ends verse 1.343].
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain encamped and harass his kingdom;
he should also constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel.
Since sovereignty has its root in counsel, therefore one's counsel must be well-guarded.
He should act in such a way that they do not know his actions until the emergence of their results.

Since it has been stated that one should deliberate on the kingdom together with them, and so forth—that the kingdom is rooted in counsel—therefore, one should protect the counsel with such effort that others do not know the king's plans, beginning with peace and war, until the emergence of their results, that is, until the completion of those fruits. (1.344)
Furthermore:
the enemy, the friend, the neutral, the immediate neighbor, the one beyond him, and the one beyond that.
The mandala should be visualized in due order through the means of conciliation and the other [stratagems].
An enemy (ari) is a foe; a friend (mitra) is a well-wisher;
and one who possesses neither of these characteristics is neutral (udāsīna).
And those three are of three kinds: innate, artificial, and natural.
Among them, an innate enemy is one such as a co-wife's son, a paternal uncle, or their sons;
an artificial enemy is one by whom harm has been done or to whom harm has been done.
The natural enemy (*prākṛta*) is the ruler of an adjacent territory.

A natural friend (*sahaja-mitra*) includes one's sister's son, one's father's sister's son, one's mother's sister's son, and so forth. An acquired friend (*kṛtrima-mitra*) is one who has rendered assistance or to whom one has rendered assistance.

A natural friend is the ruler of a territory separated by one intervening state. Those who lack the characteristics of both natural and artificial friends or enemies are natural and artificial neutrals. A natural neutral is the ruler of a territory separated by two intervening states.

Furthermore, the enemy is of four kinds, distinguished as one to be marched against (*yātavya*), one to be uprooted (*ucchettavya*), one to be oppressed (*pīḍanīya*), and one to be weakened (*karśanīya*).
Among these, one who is an immediate neighbor, but is in distress, weak in strength, and whose subjects are disaffected, is one to be marched against.
One who has no fortifications, lacks allies, and is weak is one to be uprooted.
One who is deficient in the power of counsel should be oppressed;
one endowed with the power of strong counsel should be weakened. They say that "oppression" (pīḍana) consists of uprooting, total destruction, causing pain, and the suppression of military force;
whereas "weakening" (karśana), on the other hand, they define as the depletion of the treasury and the army.
Thus it is said:
"Uprooting" means total eradication; "afflicting" means the suppression by force;
whereas "emaciating," they say, refers to the depletion of the treasury and the army.

A friend is of two kinds: one to be strengthened and one to be weakened. One who is deficient in treasury and military force is to be strengthened; one who excels in treasury and military force is to be weakened.

"Next to that, the one beyond, and the one beyond that"—this refers to the natural enemy (*ari*), the friend (*mitra*), and the neutral (*udāsīna*). The immediate neighbor is the natural enemy; the one beyond him is the natural friend; and the one beyond that is the natural neutral. The remaining [positions] are not mentioned because they are well known. This circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) should be considered in sequence according to the order of the directions starting from the east, and their activities must be understood.
Having understood this, one should apply oneself by means of the methods such as conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth, which will be described later.

Thus, with three kings in front, three behind, and three on each side, plus the king himself as the one in the center, this circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*) consisting of thirteen kings is shaped like a lotus.

As for the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), the ally of the rear-enemy (*ākranda*), the ally of the rear-enemy’s ally (*āsāra*), and so on, they are merely included within the categories of enemy, friend, and neutral; since only a difference in terminology is shown in other texts, they were not mentioned separately by the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*). 1.345.
It was stated [previously] that one should act by means of conciliation and the other methods; now he explains those very means:
"The means are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise force."
When applied correctly, [the other means] may succeed; however, punishment is the last resort when no other way remains.

Conciliation (*sāma*) is pleasant speech. Giving (*dāna*) is the bestowing of gold and other such things. Sowing dissension (*bheda*) is the act of creating division by instigating mutual enmity among neighboring kings and others.
Punishment consists of injury ranging from the seizure of property to execution, whether carried out secretly or openly.
These means, beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), are the instruments for overcoming adversaries and others.
Furthermore, these will achieve success when properly employed in accordance with place, time, and other relevant factors.

And among these, force (*daṇḍa*) is the last resort; it should not be employed when other means are possible. This is with regard to those who are to be oppressed or weakened. However, in the case of one who is to be attacked or destroyed, force alone is the primary means.
These means, such as conciliation (*sāma*) and the rest, pertain not only to the affairs of state but also to all worldly affairs.
For example:
"Study, my dear son! Study! I will give you sweetmeats."
Or else, if I shall give it to another, I will tear out your ear.
Thus [ends verse 1.346].
"Study, my dear son, study! I will give you sweetmeats;
otherwise, I shall give them to someone else, and I will tear out your ear!"
Furthermore:
One should properly deliberate upon these strategic qualities— peace, war, marching, encamping, seeking refuge, and duplicity— just as they are.
Peace (*saṃdhi*) is the making of an agreement;
war (*vigraha*) is injury;
marching (*yāna*) is an expedition against an enemy.
*Āsana* is indifference;
*saṃśraya* is seeking refuge with one who is powerful;
*dvaidhībhāva* is the division of one's own forces into two parts.
One should appropriately employ these qualities, beginning with the alliances, in accordance with the influence of place, time, power, allies, and so forth. 1.347.
Regarding the times for marching, he says:
One should march when the enemy's kingdom is endowed with the excellence of crops,
while one's own side is inferior, and one's own mounts and men are joyful.

When the enemy's kingdom is endowed with crops such as rice and other grains, as well as qualities such as water, fuel, and grass, and is thus prosperous; while the enemy is deficient in strength and other resources, and one’s own self has joyful mounts and men—where "mounts and men" (*vāhanapūruṣāḥ*) refers to those whose mounts, such as elephants and horses, and their men are joyful—at that time, one should march forth to bring the enemy's kingdom under one's own control. (1.348)

Since the prosperity and downfall of living beings depend upon destiny (*daiva*), one might argue: "If destiny exists, then foreign kingdoms and the like will come under one's control by themselves; if it does not exist, they will not come under control even if human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is exerted; therefore, this exertion in military expedition is entirely futile. To this, he says: "The accomplishment of action is established in both destiny and human effort.
Among these, destiny is that which was manifested as human effort in a previous life. (2.33)
The accomplishment of karma— the attainment of results characterized as desirable or undesirable—
is not established in destiny alone;
rather, it resides also in human effort (puruṣakāra), because such is observed in the world and because treatises on medicine and other sciences would otherwise be rendered useless.
Furthermore, he says "therein, destiny" (tatra daivam) to show that in the absence of human effort, destiny itself does not exist;
for it is precisely the human effort acquired in a previous body that is called destiny.
Human effort belonging to a prior life is manifested as the arising of a great fruit immediately following a small amount of [present] human effort.
Therefore, since there is no destiny in the absence of human effort, one must apply oneself with diligence to human exertion. || 1.349 ||
Now he states other views:
"Some of virtuous intellect desire that the fruit [of action] arises from destiny, or from inherent nature, or from time, or from human effort; some [desire it] from their conjunction."
Some maintain that the fruit, characterized as desirable or undesirable, arises solely from destiny;
some, from inherent nature, meaning it occurs by itself without depending on a cause;
and some, from time.
Some say that [the result arises] from human effort alone.
He states his own view: "The wise, such as Manu and others, believe that the fruit arises from the conjunction—that is, the combination—of fate and the other factors. (1.350)
Regarding the point that the result does not arise from each factor individually, he provides an illustration:
"For just as a chariot cannot move with only a single wheel,
so too destiny is not accomplished without human effort."
There is nothing hidden here. 1.351.
It has been stated that one must go to a foreign kingdom for the sake of gain. And gain is threefold: the gain of gold, the gain of territory, and the gain of allies.
Among these, the gain of allies is the most excellent.
Therefore, one should apply effort toward the means for attaining that;
and the means for attaining that is truthful speech, as he says:
"Since the acquisition of friends is better than the acquisition of gold or land."
Therefore, one should strive for its attainment and, with a concentrated mind, protect the truth.

Since the acquisition of friends is better and more excellent than the acquisition of gold or land, one should therefore strive—that is, exert effort—to attain it through means such as conciliation (sāma) and the rest;
and one should protect the truth with full concentration and vigilance, because the acquisition of friends has truth as its foundation. 1.352
Now he states the constituent elements of sovereignty:
"The sovereign, the minister, the people, the fortress, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the primary constituents; sovereignty is said to have seven limbs."
The lord of the earth, whose characteristics have been described as "possessing great energy" and so forth, is the sovereign.
The ministers consist of counselors, domestic priests, and others. The people are the subjects, such as the Brahmins and the rest.
A *durga* (fortress) refers to a desert-fortress (*dhanvadurga*) and so forth.
A *kośa* (treasury) is a heap of wealth such as gold and other valuables.
A *daṇḍa* (army) consists of the fourfold military force characterized by elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Friends are those who are innate, acquired, and natural.
These—the sovereign and the others—are the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) of the kingdom, which are its primary causes.
Thus, the kingdom is said to have seven limbs. (1.353)
Having obtained that [kingdom], the king should inflict punishment upon the wicked;
for Dharma was created by Brahmā in the form of punishment in ancient times.

Having obtained such a kingdom as this, the king should inflict and apply punishment upon those of wicked conduct—such as deceivers, rogues, scoundrels, those who seize the wives or property of others, and those who commit violence;
for indeed, Dharma itself was fashioned by Brahmā in the form of punishment in the past.

Moreover, "daṇḍa" is its etymological designation, for they say, "daṇḍa is so called because of subduing (damana)," based on the traditional teaching of Gautama: "By means of it, he should subdue those who are unsubdued," and so forth. || 1.354 ||
He cannot be led away by right means by one who is greedy, of unrefined intellect,
though that person be truthful in commitment, pure, well-supported by good companions, and wise.

That aforementioned *daṇḍa* cannot be properly administered or applied by one who is greedy, miserly, of unrefined intellect, or of fickle mind, even according to justice—that is, in accordance with the rule. By what kind of person, then, can it be administered? He says: by one who is true to his word (*satyasaṃdha*), meaning not a deceiver; by one who is pure and has conquered the six internal enemies; by one who has good assistants, being accompanied by the aforementioned helpers; and by one who is wise, being skilled in discerning right policy (*naya*) from wrong policy (*anaya*). Such a person is able to administer that *daṇḍa* according to justice—that is, in accordance with the Dharma. (1.355)
When employed according to the scriptures, it shall bring joy to the entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, it would provoke their wrath.
That punishment, when applied according to the path prescribed by the scriptures, would gladden and delight this entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans;
otherwise, if applied in violation of the scriptures, it would provoke the wrath of the world. (1.356)
It is said that not only does the world become agitated by unjust punishment, but the administrator also suffers the loss of both visible and invisible merit:
"Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world;
however, just punishment brings the king heaven, fame, and victory."
Furthermore, any punishment inflicted through greed or other such motives by transgressing the scriptures destroys heaven, fame, and the worlds, because it is a cause of sin.
However, that which is inflicted according to the path prescribed in the scriptures becomes a cause for heaven, fame, and victory, because it is a cause of dharma. || 1.357 ||
Whether it be a brother, a son, one worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle, there is no one who,
having deviated from his own duty, is not subject to punishment by the king.
The *arghya* is one worthy of the *arghya* offering, such as a teacher (*ācārya*) and others.
The rest is well known.
Since even these—brothers, sons, and so forth—are to be punished if they deviate from their own duty, how much more so others?
For there is no one whatsoever who, having deviated from his own duty (*svadharma*), is exempt from the king's punishment;
and this applies with the exception of mother, father, and so forth.

Accordingly, another *Smṛti* states: "Mother and father, a *snātaka*, the domestic priest (*purohita*), a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), and forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) who possess learning, good character, purity, and proper conduct are exempt from punishment, for they are authorities on dharma. (1.358)
Furthermore: That king who punishes those deserving of punishment and causes those deserving of death to be executed properly,
has performed sacrifices with the most excellent sacrificial fees.

But that king who properly punishes those deserving of punishment—those fit for punishment due to deviation from their own duty and the like—by means of the methods prescribed in the scriptures, such as censures, fines, and so forth, and who causes those deserving of death to be executed, by him a sacrifice has been performed with abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*);
the meaning is that he obtains the fruit of sacrifices involving many fees.

Furthermore, one should not think that the infliction of punishment is merely optional (*kāmya*) because of the mention of its reward, for there is a traditional legal rule (*smṛti*) prescribing expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for its non-performance.

As Vasiṣṭha has stated: "Upon the failure to inflict punishment, the king shall fast for one night, and the domestic priest for three nights; upon the inflicting of punishment on one who does not deserve it, the domestic priest shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance, and the king for three nights.
It has been said that punishment must be properly applied against the wicked;

however, since the identification of the wicked does not occur without the examination of legal cases (*vyavahāra*), he states that the king himself must personally conduct the examination of legal cases every day in order to identify them.
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his assessors, should personally examine the legal cases daily, each yielding fruit equal to that of a sacrifice.

Having thus reflected thoroughly—on how a result equal to that of a sacrifice follows from punishing those who do not deserve punishment, and on the destruction of heaven and other rewards following from failing to punish those who deserve it—the king himself, surrounded by assessors (sabhyas) possessing the characteristics to be described hereafter, should daily examine legal cases according to the method to be explained, in order to distinguish between the wicked and the virtuous, following the sequence of the social classes (varṇas) and so forth. 1.360.
Having disciplined those who have strayed from their own duty— whether they be families, castes, guilds, assemblies, or even provincial districts— the king shall establish them on the right path.
Families are those of the Brahmins and so forth;
castes are those such as the Mūrdhāvasiktas and others;
guilds are those of the betel-sellers and so forth.
The *gaṇas* are those such as the *helā-vukkas* and others;
the *jānapadas* are artisans and the like.
Having disciplined and punished these people—who have deviated and fallen away from their own duties—the king should establish them on the path of their own duty according to their offense.
It has been stated that one should inflict punishment upon those of evil conduct.
That punishment is of two kinds: corporal and monetary.
As Nārada says: "Punishment is indeed recorded as being twofold: corporal and monetary."
Physical punishment, such as beating and so forth, is proclaimed to extend up to the point of death.
The monetary fine, however, begins at one kākiṇī and likewise ends with the confiscation of all one's property.
Thus it is said:
"Punishment is indeed recorded as being of two kinds: corporeal and monetary.
Corporeal punishment is proclaimed to range from flogging up to the death penalty."
The monetary fine begins at one kākiṇī and likewise extends up to all one's possessions.
Although there are two types [of punishment], they become manifold according to the nature of the offense.
As it has been said: "Corporal punishment is declared to be tenfold, while monetary fine is indeed of many kinds."
Thus [ends the section]. 1.361.
The corporal punishment is declared to be tenfold, whereas the monetary fine is manifold.

In this context, fines for offenses should be expressed by means of terms such as *kṛṣṇala*, *māṣa*, *suvarṇa*, and *pala*. Since these terms denote different quantities depending on the region, [the author] says the following in order to demonstrate that in legal proceedings regarding fines, the terms *kṛṣṇala* and so forth have fixed measurements, so that even when the offense is of the same nature, there may not be a lesser or greater fine due to differences in locality: "The mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as *trasareṇu*."
