Eight of those [louse-eggs] make one nit (likṣā), and three of those are called a royal mustard seed (rājasarṣapa).
Three *gauras* make one *yava*; three medium *yavas* make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.
A pala is proclaimed to be four or even five suvarṇas.
The dust particle that rests upon a sunbeam entering through a lattice window is called a *trasareṇu* by the lords of yogis and other seers of reality.
Eight such *trasareṇus* constitute a *likṣā*, which is the egg of a sweat-born louse.
Three such *likṣās* make a *rājasarṣapa*, also known as a *rājikā*.
Three of those royal mustard seeds (rājasarṣapa) make one white mustard seed (gaurasarṣapa), also called siddhārtha. Six white mustard seeds make one medium barleycorn (yava);
"medium" means neither large nor small.
By this it is understood that white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*) are also "middling" (*madhyama*).

Likewise, from the word "middling" itself, it is understood that even black mustard seeds (*rājasarṣapa*)—and indeed words such as "mustard seed"—do not merely denote a measure, but rather denote the substance measured by that unit;
just as barley grains measured by a *prastha* are called a "prastha."
In this way, a substance measured by a mustard seed and so forth is designated by the words "mustard seed" and so on.

Since the words "mustard seed" and the like would otherwise denote only a mere measure, it would be impossible to measure by collecting *trasareṇu*s (motes of dust), and consequently, the practical usage regarding *kṛṣṇala*s and other weights would not exist. In that regard, since a difference in practical usage exists in each region due to the distinctions in the measurements of mustard seeds—ranging from the coarse, coarser, and coarsest, to the subtle, subtler, and subtlest, as well as the medium—the term "medium" (*madhya*) is fixed for the purpose of legal proceedings (*daṇḍavyavahāra*).
Three of those middle-sized barleycorns make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five of those *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*;
sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.

It is stated that four *suvarṇas* are designated as one *pala*; however, Nārada and others have also proclaimed five [suvarṇas] to be a *pala*. In that context, when a *kṛṣṇala* is calculated based on three thick barley grains, a *kṛṣṇala* constitutes the sixteenth part of a conventional *niṣka*.
Five of those [rattikas] make one māṣa;
sixteen māṣas make one suvarṇa;
and that one suvarṇa consists of five vyāvahārika niṣkas.
Those four [kṛṣṇalas] make one pala;
twenty niṣkas make one pala.
However, when a kṛṣṇala is calculated as three small barley grains, then a kṛṣṇala becomes the thirty-second part of a conventional (vyāvahārika) niṣka.
In that system, a *suvarṇa* is two and a half *niṣkas*,
and a *pala* is ten *niṣkas*. However,
when the *kṛṣṇala* is calculated according to the medium-sized barley grains, then a *kṛṣṇala* is one-twentieth of a *niṣka*, a *suvarṇa* is four *niṣkas*, and a *pala* is sixteen *niṣkas*.
Thus, five *suvarṇas* constitute a *pala*.
In the *paka* [system], twenty *niṣkas* constitute a *pala*.

In this manner, other measures as well—such as a *kṛṣṇala* being the fortieth part of a *niṣka*, two *niṣkas* being a *suvarṇa*, and eight *niṣkas* being a *pala*—should be inferred from this very sūtra according to worldly convention. 1.362–1.363.
Having thus established the measurement of gold, he now states [the measurement] for silver:
two *kṛṣṇalas* make one silver *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make a *dharaṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, and [ten *dharaṇas*] also make one *pala*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*. Two *kṛṣṇalas*—as previously mentioned—are a silver *māṣa* (a *māṣa* related to silver).
Sixteen of those silver *māṣas* make one *dharaṇa*.

"Purāṇa" is another name for this very [weight], according to the traditional teaching of Manu: "Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* shall be a *purāṇa*. Furthermore, ten *dharaṇas* are designated as a *śatamāna* or a *pala*.
Four suvarṇas of the kind previously mentioned constitute one silver niṣka. || 1.364 ||
Now he states the weight of copper:
a *kārṣika* of copper is a *paṇa*.
It is well known in the world that a fourth part of a *pala* is a *karṣa*.
That which is measured by a *karṣa* is *kārṣika*. That which is a product of copper is *tāmrika*.

An object made of copper weighing one *karṣa* is designated as a *paṇa* and is also known by the name *kārṣāpaṇa*; for it is stated in the words of Manu: "A copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be understood as a *paṇa*, a *kārṣāpaṇa*. According to the view that five *suvarṇas* constitute a *pala*, a *paṇa* consists of twenty *māṣas*.
This being the case, common practice such as "a *māṣa* is proclaimed to be the twentieth part of a *paṇa*" becomes established.
However, according to the view that four *suvarṇas* constitute a *pala*, a *paṇa* consists of sixteen *māṣas*.

And in this view, although the words *suvarṇa*, *kārṣāpaṇa*, and *paṇa* have the same meaning, the words *paṇa* and *kārṣāpaṇa* refer specifically to copper. Thus, the measurement of gold, silver, and copper has been stated first, because it is useful for legal proceedings (*daṇḍavyavahāra*). The measurement of bell-metal, brass, and so forth, which are also constituent parts of worldly transactions, should likewise be understood. (1.365)
He states the technical definitions of his own treatise:
"A fine of eighty-one thousand paṇas is called the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa);
half of that is declared the middle amercement (madhyama), and half of that is recorded as the lowest (adhama)."
A *paṇasahasra* is a thousand *paṇas*; that which has this as its measure is called *paṇasāhasra*.
That which exists together with eighty is *sāśīti*.
A fine measured by one thousand *paṇas* plus eighty should be understood as being designated the "highest amercement" (*uttamasāhasa*).

Half of that is the middle [fine]; half of those eighty-one thousand *paṇas* is five hundred and forty *paṇas*, and half of that is a fine measured at two hundred and seventy *paṇas*, which is known as the lowest *sāhasa*. This has been declared by Manu and others.
As for the statement: "Two hundred and fifty *paṇas* are known as the first *sāhasa*;
the middle is to be understood as five hundred, and the highest is indeed one thousand."
This which was stated by Manu should be understood as referring to another alternative case involving an offense committed unintentionally. (1.366)
He states the different types of punishment:
"The punishment of reproach, the punishment of words, the punishment of fines, and likewise execution—
these should be applied individually or collectively according to the nature of the offense."
The punishment of reproach (*dhig-daṇḍa*) consists of censure such as "fie! or "shame!"; the punishment of speech (*vāk-daṇḍa*) consists of harsh words and curses;
and the punishment of wealth (*dhana-daṇḍa*) consists of the confiscation of property.
The corporal punishment consists of physical restraint ending in death.
These four types of punishments—either individually, in pairs, or all four together—should be applied according to the nature of the offense.
Following the stated order, each subsequent punishment should be employed when the preceding one has failed to achieve its purpose.
As Manu said: "One should first apply the punishment of reproach, then the punishment of verbal censure;
thirdly, the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal death."
Thus [ends verse 1.367].
One should first apply the punishment of reproach, followed by the punishment of verbal censure;
thirdly, the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal punishment.
He states the grounds for determining punishment:
"Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength, as well as the age,
the occupation, and the wealth, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment."

Having ascertained the offense, one should administer punishment accordingly; that is, having ascertained the place, time, age, action, and wealth [of the offender], one should impose punishment upon those deserving of it according to those factors.
Likewise, one should act in accordance with whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and whether it was a single occurrence or a repetition.

Although this collection of royal duties has been stated with reference to the king, it should nevertheless be understood as a duty for others as well—specifically for those authorized to protect the territory, the circle of subjects, and so forth.

"I shall proclaim the duties of kings, according to which a king should conduct himself"—here, because of the separate mention of "king" and because the taking of taxes is for the purpose of protection, and protection depends upon the administration of punishment [this is established]. (1.368)

Thus ends the first chapter, on Right Conduct (*sadācāra*), in the *Ṛjumitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Vijñāneśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, son of the venerable Padmanābha Bhaṭṭopādhyāya.
This is the work of the disciple of the one with the most excellent title,
the commentary on the *Dharmaśāstra* by the yogi Vijñāneśvara.

The sections in this chapter are as follows: 1. The section on the introduction; 2. The section on the student (brahmacārin); 3. The section on marriage; 4. The section on the discernment of castes; 5. The section on the duties of the householder; 6. The section on the vows of the *snātaka*; 7. The section on what may and may not be eaten; 8. The section on the purification of substances; 9. The section on the duty of giving (*dāna*); 10. The section on ancestral rites (*śrāddha*); 11. The section on the ritual for Gaṇapati; 12. The section on the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*); 13. The section on the duties of kings. Thus, there are thirteen sections.
For what learned person is this commentary on the treatise of the sage Yājñavalkya not intended?
Though its words are few, it is rich in extensive meaning and sprinkles nectar upon the ears. (1)
For a king endowed with qualities such as consecration and the like, the supreme duty is the protection of his subjects.
And that protection is not possible without the suppression of the wicked.
Furthermore, the thorough identification of the wicked is not possible without the examination of legal cases (*vyavahāra*).
It has been stated that this administration of justice must be performed day by day: "He himself, surrounded by his assessors, shall examine the legal cases every day.
However, the nature of such a legal case, its varieties, and the entire procedure as to how it is to be conducted have not yet been set forth.
To explain that, the second chapter is commenced with the words "the legal proceedings.
The king shall examine the legal proceedings together with learned Brāhmaṇas,
in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras, free from anger and greed.
Discourse (*vyavahāra*) is the statement of something as being connected to one's own self in contradiction with another;
for example, one person says, "This field and so forth are mine," while another, in opposition to him, says, "They are mine.
He shows its manifold nature by means of the plural number.

The term "king" (nṛpa) indicates that this duty does not belong to the Kṣatriya alone, but to anyone else who is authorized to protect the subjects. The word "should look" (paśyet) is a restatement of what was previously mentioned, intended to prescribe specific duties. "By the learned" (vidvadbhiḥ) means by those who are experts in the Vedas, grammar, and the treatises on dharma (dharmaśāstra).

[The term] "by Brāhmaṇas" [is used], not by Kṣatriyas and so forth. Because of the use of the instrumental case in the expression "together with Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇaiḥ saha*), these [Kṣatriyas, etc. are subordinate; for it is recorded in the grammatical tradition: "When joined with *saha*, that which is not the primary factor [takes the third case]."
Therefore, whether through oversight or by seeing otherwise, the fault lies with the king and not with the Brahmins.
As Manu has said:
"A king who punishes those who are not deserving of punishment, and fails to punish those who are deserving of punishment..."
He incurs great infamy and indeed goes to hell.
Thus:
"A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell."
How so? According to the *dharmaśāstra*, not according to the *arthaśāstra*.
Since the local customs (*samayadharma*) of regions and so forth that do not contradict the *dharmaśāstra* also fall within the scope of the *dharmaśāstra*, they are not mentioned separately.
And thus he will say: "But that which is conventional, provided it does not conflict with one's own dharma, as well as that dharma established by the king, must also be protected with effort."
Thus:
"free from anger and greed.
Since it is already established by the phrase "in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras," the statement "free from anger and greed" is for the sake of emphasis.
Anger is intolerance;
greed is an excessive desire for acquisition. || 2.1 ||

And he said to the members of the assembly: "The king should appoint as members of his court those who are accomplished in learning and Vedic study, knowers of dharma, speakers of truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend."
Furthermore, they were perfected in learning and study; that is, they were perfected through "learning"—the hearing of Mīmāṃsā, grammar, and so forth—and through "study"—the study of the Vedas.
They were knowers of Dharma, meaning they were experts in the treatises on Dharma.
They were speakers of truth, meaning they were habituated to truthful speech.

Those who are equal toward both enemy and friend, being free from passion, hatred, and the like— such members of the assembly (*sabhāsadaḥ*), who sit (*sīdanti*) in the assembly (*sabhāyām*, i.e., the court), should be treated by the king with gifts, honors, and hospitality. Although it was stated without distinction that they must be "endowed with learning and Vedic study," nevertheless, they must be Brahmins alone.

As Kātyāyana has said: "But that [court] should be joined by stable, wise, and eminent twice-born men who are hereditary members, who are skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras and proficient in the Arthaśāstra."
Thus it is said:
"He [the king] shall be joined by stable, wise, and hereditary members of the highest caste (dvija),
who are skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras and proficient in the Arthaśāstra."

And those three must be appointed, because the plural number has significance and because of the traditional teaching of Manu: "In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit down... Bṛhaspati, however, says that there may be seven, five, or three members of the assembly.
Wherever Brahmins who know the world, the Vedas, and the Dharma— whether seven, five, or even three— are seated, that assembly is equal to a sacrifice.
Thus:
"Wherever Brahmins who know the world, the Vedas, and the Dharma— whether seven, five, or even three— are seated, that assembly is equal to a sacrifice."

Nor should it be thought that the Brahmins mentioned in the preceding verse are qualified by the attributes "endowed with Vedic study" and so forth, because a relationship of qualifier and qualified is impossible between those indicated by the instrumental case (*brāhmaṇaiḥ*) and those indicated by the nominative case (*saha*), and because it would result in the redundancy of the term *vidvadbhiḥ* ("by the learned").

Thus, Kātyāyana clearly shows the distinction between the Brahmins and the members of the court: "The King, together with the judge, the ministers, the Brahmins, the domestic chaplain, and the court members, remains in heaven according to dharma as a witness."
Thus:

"The king who presides over the court together with the judge, his ministers, his Brahman-priest and domestic chaplain, and the members of the assembly, remains in heaven by virtue of his righteousness."
In this regard, the distinction is that the Brahmins are unappointed, whereas the members of the assembly (*sabhāsada*) are appointed.
For this very reason it has been said: "Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma is qualified to speak."
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma ought to speak.
In that regard, even when those appointed state the matter exactly as it stands, if the king acts otherwise, he must be restrained; otherwise, there is a fault.
And it has been said by Kātyāyana:
Those members of the assembly who follow him even as he proceeds by unjust means share in that guilt;
therefore, they must admonish that king.
Thus:
"Those members of the assembly who follow him even as he proceeds by unjust means share in that guilt;
therefore, they must inform the king of it."

Furthermore, for those not appointed [as judges], there is fault in speaking otherwise or in remaining silent; however, there is no fault for the king in failing to restrain them. One should either not enter the court at all, or one should speak what is just. A man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner.
This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "toward an enemy and toward a friend," it is indicated that the court should be presided over by even a few merchants for the purpose of pleasing the public.
As Kātyāyana has said: "By those who possess noble lineage, good character, youth, virtuous conduct, and wealth, and who are free from envy..."
It should be presided over by a few merchants who have become like members of one family.
Thus [it is said].
It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good conduct, youth, virtuous behavior, and wealth, and who are free from envy, acting as true members of the community.
It has been stated that "the king shall examine legal cases.
Regarding this, he states the secondary rule:
"But when, due to the pressure of business, the king does not personally examine the legal cases..."
A Brāhmaṇa who knows all the dharmas should be appointed together with the members of the assembly.

When a king, being preoccupied with other affairs, does not personally oversee legal proceedings, he should appoint a Brāhmaṇa—never a Kṣatriya or others—to preside over the examination of cases along with the previously mentioned members of the court. He should be one who knows all *dharma*; that is, one who knows all the duties prescribed in the *Dharmaśāstras* as well as those established by convention (*sāmāyika*), and who investigates them.
One endowed with the qualities described by Kātyāyana should be appointed.
As he says:
One who is self-controlled, of noble birth, impartial, free from causing agitation,
steadfast, fearful of the next world, most righteous, diligent, and devoid of anger.
Thus: one who is self-controlled, of noble birth, impartial, not causing agitation, steady,
fearful of the hereafter, most virtuous, diligent, and free from anger.
In the absence of such a Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, but not a Śūdra.
As Kātyāyana has said:
"Where a Brāhmaṇa is not available, one should employ a Kṣatriya there."
Or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort.
Thus it is said: "Where a Brāhmaṇa is not available, one should appoint a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should avoid a Śūdra with every effort."
But this very [method] was shown by Nārada as the primary one:
"Having placed the Dharmaśāstra before him, he should abide by the opinion of the judge (prāḍvivāka),
not by his own opinion."
Just as a king perceives the enemy army through the eyes of his spies, so too does he;
this is his etymological designation.

He is a *prāṭ* because he questions the plaintiff and the defendant; he is a *vivāka* because, together with the members of the court (*sabhyas*), he discriminates—that is, he discerns—their statements, whether they are contradictory or consistent.
One who is both a questioner (*prāṭ*) and a judge (*vivāka*) is a *prāḍvivāka*.
And it has been said:
"Having carefully questioned those involved in the dispute, together with the members of the court..."
Because he deliberates [on the case], he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka* (judge).
Thus [ends section] 2.3.
Having diligently questioned the litigant who has come for a dispute, he deliberates together with the members of the court; because of this, he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka* (the judge).
If the judges and other members of the court deliberate on a legal case in a manner contrary to the sacred law (*smṛti*) due to passion and so forth, what should the king do? To this he says:
"Judges who act contrary to the sacred law and the like out of passion, greed, or fear shall each be punished individually with a fine double that of the amount in dispute."

Moreover, the aforementioned members of the court, being overwhelmed by passion due to its unrestrained nature, may—out of attachment (rāga), excessive affection, greed (lobha), excessive desire for gain, fear, or terror—act contrary to tradition (smṛtyapeta) or, as indicated by the word "and so forth" (ādi), contrary to established conduct (ācārāpeta). For such acts, each individually, they shall be fined double the penalty (dama) resulting from their defeat in the lawsuit, but not double the value of the property that was the subject of the dispute. If it were otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of no punishment at all in cases such as adultery with women.

The purpose of this rule is to establish that the seizure of those possessed by passion, greed, or fear, and the double punishment for those very same offenses of passion and so forth, applies only to these cases and not to ignorance, delusion, and the like.

Furthermore, one should not conclude from the statement of Gautama—"The king has authority over all except the Brāhmaṇas"—that Brāhmaṇas are exempt from punishment; for that statement is intended as a praise.

As for the statement that "one who is to be avoided by a king—though not to be killed, nor to be imprisoned, nor to be punished, nor to be banished, nor to be censured, nor to be excluded"—that too refers to one who is "learned" (*bahuśruta*), as has been explained: one who knows the *Lokaveda* and the *Vedāṅgas*, who is skilled in *Vākovākya*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*, who depends on those [scriptures] and lives according to them, who is purified by the forty-eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), and who is devoted to the three duties or well-trained in the six rules of conduct (*samayācārika*). Thus, this refers to the specific category of the learned, not to the Brāhmaṇa in general. (2.4)

He states the subject matter of legal procedure: "When one who has been oppressed by others through a course of action contrary to tradition and custom brings a complaint before the king, that indeed is a matter for legal procedure."

When one who is oppressed or overcome by others through a path contrary to the *dharmaśāstras*, traditional conventions (*samaya*), and established conduct (*ācāra*) makes a formal complaint or representation to the King or the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*), that which is thus complained about is the "subject of litigation" (*vyavahārapada*). Litigation consists of the plaint (*pratijñā*), the reply (*uttara*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the grounds for investigation (*hetu*), deliberation (*parāmarśa*), means of proof (*pramāṇa*), decision (*nirṇaya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*); this is the subject of such litigation. Its general definition is as follows: it is of two kinds—litigation based on suspicion (*śaṅkābhiyoga*) and litigation based on a factual charge (*tattvābhiyoga*).
As Nārada has said:
"A lawsuit is to be understood as being of two kinds, based on suspicion and based on factual evidence;
suspicion arises from association with the wicked, while factual evidence is established through the discovery of stolen goods."
Thus it is said:
"A lawsuit is to be understood as being of two kinds, arising from suspicion (*śaṅkā*) and from proof of fact (*tattva*).
Suspicion arises from association with the wicked; proof of fact arises from the discovery of stolen goods (*hoḍha*) or from confession."
*Hoḍha* means stolen property;
that is to say, a sign.
By means of that, "seeing"—either seeing directly or seeing [the sign]—is *hoḍhābhidarśana*; from that [reason].
Furthermore, that charge (*abhiyoga*) is also of two kinds:
consisting of a prohibition (*pratiṣedhātmaka*) and consisting of an injunction (*vidhyātmaka*).
For example: "Having taken gold and other goods from me, he does not return them."
And [the thought], "He is seizing my field and so forth.
And it was said by Kātyāyana: "He who does not wish to act justly toward his own property, or who commits what is unjust..."

He who does not wish to perform what is right regarding his own property, or performs what is unjust, is further divided into eighteen types. As Manu has said: "Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt (ṛṇādāna), followed by deposit (nikṣepa) and sale without ownership (asvāmivikraya)."
Joint undertaking, and the non-delivery of what has been given.
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen;
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these are the eighteen titles of law established here in this world.
Thus [it is said].
Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt; then the deposit, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given.
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen;
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women;
The duties of women and men, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these are the eighteen titles of law established here in this world.
These also become manifold again according to the differences in what is to be accomplished.
As Nārada said: "There is another division of these very [laws] which becomes one hundred and eight;
due to the differences in human actions, it is said to have a hundred branches."
Thus [it is said].
There is another further subdivision of these very [tantras] which consists of one hundred and eight;
due to the diversity of human activities, it is said to have a hundred branches.

By the phrase "if he reports to the king," it is shown that he reports having come of his own accord, and not being impelled by the king or impelled by the king's official. As Manu says: "The king himself should not initiate a lawsuit, nor should his official; nor should he ever swallow up a case brought forward by another."
Thus it is said.
The king himself, nor his official, should initiate a legal case;
nor should he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another.
By the word "by others" (paraiḥ), he shows that there is linguistic usage with one, two, or many others—namely, by one [other], by two [others], or by many [others].
Furthermore, it has been declared by those who know the Dharma that a lawsuit brought by a single person against many, or involving women and servants, shall not be accepted for trial.
Thus, Nārada’s statement refers to two distinct types of legal matters (*sādhya*).
By the phrase "if he reports it to the king," it is established by implication that when questioned by the king, one should report with modest attire;

and once reported, if it is appropriate, the summoning of the defendant by means of a seal or other methods, as well as the non-summoning of those who are incapacitated (*akalpa*) and so forth, are established by the sense of the matter and thus not explicitly stated.
In another Smṛti, however, it is stated for the sake of clarity:
"At the proper time, he should question the one seeking redress who stands before him speaking:
'What is your business? What is your suffering? Do not fear; speak, O man!'"

"By whom, in what place, at what time, and for what reason?"—one who asks thus is considered a member of the assembly. When questioned in this manner, he should speak together with the Brahmins who constitute the court.
Having deliberated on the matter, if it is found to be just, he should thereafter summon [the defendant] for that purpose;
otherwise, he should deposit a seal or appoint an official to represent him.

A king should not summon servants who are ignorant, childish, or aged; those distracted by improper tasks; those overwhelmed by urgent business, calamities, royal duties, or festivities; or those who are intoxicated, insane, heedless, or afflicted by illness.
A young woman born of noble family who has not yet had a child,
even if she is the most excellent of all castes, is considered to remain under the authority of her paternal kinsmen as long as she is unmarried.
The invitation of those women who are dependent on others for their livelihood, those who are wanton, prostitutes, those of low birth, and those who have fallen from their caste is prescribed.
Having ascertained the time, the place, and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should gradually summon even those who are exempt from service by means of vehicles.
Having learned of their intent, even those who have gone forth as forest-dwellers and the like,
the king should summon them for matters of great importance, provided he does not provoke their anger.
Thus:
At the proper time, he should question the one seeking redress who stands before him speaking:
"What is your business? What is your suffering? Do not fear; speak, O man!"

"By whom, toward whom, when, and for what reason should one ask? Thus should one inquire of those who are present in the assembly. When thus questioned, that which he says, together with the Brahmins who are members of the assembly,"
Having deliberated on the matter, if it is found to be just, he should thereafter summon [the defendant] for that purpose,
or else deposit a seal with him, or appoint a person to represent him.

A king should not summon servants who are ignorant, childish, aged, or engaged in improper tasks; those overwhelmed by urgent business, those distressed by calamities, or those preoccupied with royal affairs or festivals; nor those who are intoxicated, insane, heedless, or afflicted by illness.

A young woman born of a noble family who has not yet reached her youth, a woman who has recently given birth, or a maiden of the highest caste— these are declared to remain under the authority of their paternal kinsmen.

The invitation of those women who are dependent on others for their livelihood, those who are wanton, prostitutes, those from whom the family lineage has been severed, and those who are outcasted is prescribed.
Having ascertained the time, the place, and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should gradually cause even those who are incapable to come before him by means of vehicles.
Having learned of their intent, even those who have gone forth as forest-dwellers and the like,
the king should summon them for matters of great importance, provided he does not provoke their anger.

The rules regarding restraint have been stated by Nārada as being established by the very nature of the matter: "When the defendant does not abide by the matter to be stated or when he departs from those words, the plaintiff shall restrain him until the appearance for the summons."
Confinement may be of four kinds: restricted to a place, limited by time, from exile, or due to a specific task; one who is not yet acquitted must not violate such confinement.
If one who has been placed under restraint during the period of restraint violates that restraint, he should be punished;
otherwise, the one who imposed the restraint shall be liable for the penalty.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering a difficult region or calamity,
one who departs while still unaccomplished in his purpose does not incur blame for that departure.
One who desires to settle a debt, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one assailed by another, and likewise one engaged in royal service.
Cowherds [should go] to the grazing grounds for cattle, farmers to sow the crops,
artisans to their workshops, and those who bear arms to the battlefield at that time.
Regarding the matter to be stated, the plaintiff shall restrain one who stands firm or attempts to depart from that statement until the appearance for summons.
Confinement may be of four kinds: by place, by time, by exile, and likewise by work; one who is not yet released from such confinement must not violate it.
If one who has been restrained at the time of restraint violates that restraint, he should be punished;
otherwise, the restrainer shall incur the penalty.
In cases such as crossing rivers, traversing wildernesses, or encountering calamities in difficult regions,
one who departs while still unaccomplished in his purpose does not incur blame for violating that prohibition.
One who desires to settle a debt, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal business.
Cowherds [should go] when the cattle are grazing; farmers when the crops have been sown;
artisans at their respective times; and those who bear arms during a conflict.
"Seizure" is confinement by royal command.

Those who are disqualified and so forth may send their son or another friend; yet they do not speak on behalf of another, for it is said: "One who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent—whoever speaks on behalf of another in legal proceedings shall be punished for speaking falsely."
Thus, from the words of Nārada. 2.5.
When the defendant has been brought before him by any one of the seal-bearers, scribes, or messengers, what should the king do? To this he says:
"The document, as presented by the plaintiff, shall be read in the presence of the defendant, marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, and other identifying characteristics."

That which is sought is the *artha*, meaning the object to be established; one who possesses that is the *arthin* (the plaintiff); his opponent is the *pratyarthin* (the defendant). In his presence, before him, the *lekhyam*—the written document—must be composed.

It must be exactly as it was previously stated at the time of the initial petition, and not otherwise, for by stating otherwise, there would be the consequence of the failure of the legal proceeding due to perjury.

One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance of legal acts, one who does not appear, one who is unable to provide an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these are recorded as the five kinds of defeated litigants.

Thus it is said: "One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the legal procedure, one who does not appear, one who has no reply, and one who flees when summoned— these five are recorded in tradition as defeated."

Since the statement of the plaintiff has already been written down at the very time of the formal filing (*āvedana*), writing it again would be purposeless; therefore, he says "the year, month," and so forth.

[The document] is marked by the year, month, fortnight, lunar day, weekday, and so on, as well as by the names of the plaintiff and defendant and their caste (such as *brāhmaṇa*) and other such signs.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the object, its quantity, place, time, capacity, evidentiary marks (*liṅga*), and so on are included.
As it has been said: "It should possess meaning, be connected with the Dharma, be complete and unconfused, contain words capable of establishing the thesis, and be relevant to the subject at hand."
It is well-known, non-contradictory, certain, capable of proof,
concise, complete in its meaning, and not inconsistent with time or place.
It is endowed with the year, season, month, fortnight, day, time,
place, region, location, dwelling, the name of the person to be accomplished, caste, physical form, and age.
It was marked with the names of many kings, including those of his own ancestors and his enemies, just as it is marked by the number of proofs for what is to be established.
That which, accompanied by an admission of fault and self-inflicted suffering,
causes the claimant to present his case to the king, is called *bhāṣā*.
Thus:
"It should be meaningful, connected with dharma, complete, unconfused,
contain words expressive of what is to be established, and be relevant to the subject matter at hand."
It is well-known, non-contradictory, certain, capable of proving [the point],
concise, containing the entire meaning, and not inconsistent with place or time.
It is endowed with the year, season, month, fortnight, day, time, place, and region;
as well as location, dwelling, the name of the person to be accomplished, caste, physical form, and age.
It was marked with the names of many kings, including those of his own ancestors and his enemies, just as one might mark the number of proofs for a thesis.
That which one reports to the king— characterized by patience, an embrace, self-inflicted pain, or the taking or giving of something— is called *bhāṣā*.
The term *bhāṣā* is synonymous with *pratijñā* and *pakṣa*; there is no difference in meaning.

The distinction is that at the time of the initial petition (*āvedana*), only the matter of the case is recorded, whereas in the presence of the defendant, it is recorded with specific details such as the year, month, and so forth.

Although the specification of the year is not useful in all legal proceedings, it is nevertheless useful for reaching a decision in cases of pledges (*ādhi*), gifts (*pratigraha*), and purchases (*kraya*), according to the rule: "In the case of a pledge, a gift, or a purchase, the earlier one is more powerful."

Because of this statement: even in the case of a transaction involving property, if one who is being asked for a certain amount of a certain substance that was received from someone by a certain person in one year, and which was returned by that person from that source in another year, should say, "It is true that it was received and returned," [the distinction is made that] "it was received and returned in a different year, not in this year"— this is what is required.

In this same manner, [the rules] should also be applied to months and so forth. Furthermore, place, location, and the like are applicable only to immobile things: "Place, as well as location, configuration, genus, name, residence, measurement, and the name of the field."
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should record these ten things: the paternal and ancestral lineage, and the genealogy of former kings.
Thus it is from the traditional authority (smṛti).
"Region" refers to Madhyadeśa and so forth;
"place" refers to Vārāṇasī and so forth.
Location (*saṃniveśa*) is the arrangement of houses, fields, and so forth, situated properly and delimited by the divisions of the eastern and western directions.
Class (*jāti*) refers to the status of being a Brahmin and so forth for the plaintiff and the defendant.
Name (*saṃjñā*) refers to Devadatta and the like.

*Adhivāsaḥ* refers to the people living in the vicinity. *Prāmāṇam* refers to the measurement of land, such as the *nivartana* and so forth. *Kṣetranāma* (the name of the field) includes designations such as "rice field," "areca nut field," "black soil," or "white soil."
The names of the father and grandfather of both the plaintiff and the defendant, as well as the mention of the names of the three preceding kings—this is the meaning:
in whatever legal proceeding the year, month, and so forth are required, those alone should be recorded therein. This is the essential point.

Thus, since the definition of a thesis (*pakṣa*) has been established, it is already proven that those things which lack the characteristics of a thesis but appear as if they were theses are "pseudo-theses" (*pakṣābhāsa*); therefore, the Lord of Yogis did not state the pseudo-theses separately.
However, others have stated them for the sake of clarity:
"That which is unestablished, unassailable, purposeless, or useless."
One should avoid a fallacious thesis (pakṣābhāsa) that is either impossible to prove or contradictory.
Thus:
one should avoid a fallacious thesis (pakṣābhāsa) that is unestablished, unobjectionable [in its formulation], purposeless, devoid of utility,
impossible to prove, or contradictory.
"Unestablished" (aprasiddha) refers to such statements as "having taken my rabbit's horn, he does not give it back," and so forth.

"Unobjectionable" (nirābādha) refers to such statements as "this person conducts his affairs in his own home by means of the light from the lamp in our house," and so forth. "Meaningless" (nirartha), being devoid of a denotable object, refers to such strings of sounds as "kacaṭatapagajaḍadaba," and so forth.

That which is purposeless (*niṣprayojana*) is, for example: "This Devadatta recites in a beautiful voice in the vicinity of our house," and so forth. That which is impossible to accomplish (*asādhya*) is, for example: "I was mocked by Devadatta with a frown," and so forth.
This is impossible to accomplish because the means for its accomplishment do not exist.
Because of the shortness of time, there is no possibility of witnesses; because of its insignificance, neither a written document nor an ordeal is applicable.
This is contradictory, as in cases such as "I have been cursed by a mute person," and so forth;
or it may be contrary to the interests of the city, the kingdom, and so on.
He who is shunned by the king, he who creates opposition among the citizens,
or likewise among the entire kingdom and its constituent subjects;
Furthermore, those legal proceedings which involve opposition from cities, villages,
or large groups of people are all declared to be inadmissible.
Thus.
He who is shunned by the king, he who creates opposition among the citizens,
or likewise among the entire kingdom and its constituent subjects;
Furthermore, those legal proceedings which involve opposition from cities, villages,
or large groups of people are all declared to be inadmissible.

As for the claim that "a plaint (*pūrvapakṣa*) mixed with multiple points is not valid," if by this one means "mixed with multiple matters," then there is no fault; for a plaint such as, "My gold, clothing, silver coins, or other property has been stolen by him," is not defective.
If it is argued that a mixture of categories such as "non-payment of debt" (*ṛṇādāna*) and others constitutes a fallacious plaint (*pakṣābhāsa*), that too is not the case.

It is indeed accepted that such claims as "my coins were taken by him at interest," "gold was deposited in his hand," and "he is seizing my field" constitute the subject matter (*pakṣatva*) of a lawsuit.
However, because of the difference in the legal actions (*kriyā*), the litigation proceeds sequentially and not simultaneously.
As Kātyāyana has said: "When a case involves multiple plaints and is well-established in a lawsuit..."
The king may indeed accept even that, out of a desire to know the truth.
Thus:
Even a lawsuit involving many claims that has been thoroughly investigated,
the king may certainly take up if he desires to ascertain the truth.

Therefore, its meaning is that a plaint (*pūrvapakṣa*) composed of multiple, intermingled points cannot be established simultaneously. By the mention of the "plaintiff" (*arthin*), the son, father, and so forth are included, because they share a single purpose. Furthermore, even for one who is formally appointed (*niyukta*), his single-purpose status is implied by that very appointment; for it is said: "Whether he is commissioned by the plaintiff or sent by the defendant."
Between two parties who dispute for the sake of one another, victory and defeat belong to them both.
According to this traditional teaching, victory and defeat belong only to the original owner and the one who was appointed [as his representative].

And this, having been written with chalk on the ground or a wooden board and refined through the process of insertion and deletion, should subsequently be entered upon a formal document; the judge shall record the plaintiff's case as it was stated naturally:
"First on the board with chalk, then on the document, once refined."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana:
"The purification must be carried out until the defendant's reply (uttara) is seen, and not beyond that, for fear of falling into an infinite regress.
For this very reason, Nārada stated: "One should examine the plaintiff's claim (pūrvavāda) only until the defendant's reply is seen."
For one who has been seized by the latter, purification occurs through the former.

Thus, if the members of the court (sabhyas) deliver a verdict without having even examined the plaintiff's case, then the king, having punished those members with the aforementioned penalty for passion or greed, must initiate the legal proceeding anew, beginning with the formal statement of the claim (pratijñā). || 2.6 ||
One should examine the plaintiff's claim until the defendant's reply is seen;
once the claim is countered by the reply, the process of examination ceases.
When the plaint has been thus refined and recorded on the document, what should be done? To this he says: "The defendant's reply (uttara) should be written down in the presence of the plaintiff.

One by whom the meaning of the plaint (bhāṣārtha) has been heard is the "one who has heard the matter" (śrutārtha); his reply, which comes after the plaint, is the "reply" (uttara), and that must be written down.
The *uttara* (rejoinder) is that which is stated in the presence of the plaintiff who brought the initial claim, and which constitutes a refutation of what was previously asserted.
As it has been said:
"It must pervade the entire position (*pakṣa*), be essential, free from doubt, and unconfused."
Those who know that [reality] understand this to be the answer: that it cannot be understood through explanation.
Thus: "That which pervades the position, which is essential, free from doubt, unconfused,
and not requiring further explanation— this, those who know it recognize as the correct answer."
It is comprehensive of the position (*pakṣa*), capable of refutation,
essential, logical— that is, not deviating from reason—
and free from doubt, being devoid of uncertainty.

A sound reply is one that is coherent—meaning it is not contradictory between its earlier and later parts—and is not dependent upon explanation; that is, it does not require interpretation due to the use of obscure terminology, poorly constructed inflections or compounds, the necessity of supplying missing words (*sādhyāhāra*), or the employment of a regional dialect. Such a reply is valid.

And that is of four kinds: admission (*saṃpratipatti*), denial (*mithyā*), counter-pleading (*pratyavaskandana*), and the application of a prior judgment (*pūrvanyāya*). Thus said Kātyāyana: "Admission, denial, likewise counter-pleading, and the rule of prior judgment—thus the reply (*uttara*) shall be of four kinds."
Thus:
"The true reply, the false reply, likewise the counter-attack,
and the application of a prior judgment— thus the reply (uttara) is of four kinds."
In that regard, an oath (*satyottara*) is as follows: when it is said, "He owes me a hundred coins," one replies, "Truly, I owe them.
As it has been said: "The making of a truthful statement regarding the matter to be proved is declared to be the formal admission (*pratipatti*)."
Thus,
the defendant's admission of the matter to be proven (*sādhya*) has been illustrated by the statement of truth; however, a false plea (*mithyottara*) is, for example, "I do not owe it."
And so Kātyāyana says: "If one who is accused should deny the accusation, one should know that to be a false reply according to legal procedure."
Thus [it is said].
If the defendant, when charged, should deny the charge,
one should recognize that as a false reply in accordance with legal procedure.
And that false defense (mithyottara) is of four kinds:
"This is false," "I do not know [it]," "I was not present there at that time," and "I was not born at that time"— thus the false defense is fourfold.
Thus:
"This is false; I do not know it; I was not present there at that time;
and I was not yet born at that time"—thus is a false statement of four kinds.

*Pratyavaskandana* (counter-pleading) means that what was claimed as true has been returned or obtained through a formal gift. As Nārada said: "If the defendant, having accepted the matter exactly as it was written by the plaintiff, states a legal justification (*kāraṇa*), that is known as *pratyavaskandana*."
Thus:
"If the defendant, having admitted the matter as it was written by the plaintiff,
should state a legal justification for it, that is known as *pratyavaskandana* (counter-pleading)."
The plea of *prāṅnyāya* (prior judgment) occurs when the defendant himself says: "I have been accused on this matter, and in that case, I was defeated according to the course of legal procedure.

And it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "If one who has been defeated by conduct (i.e., by a prior judgment) writes [a new plaint] again, he should be declared defeated previously; that is called *prāṅnyāya*."
Thus:
"If one who has been defeated by conduct is made to write again, he is to be declared as previously defeated; that is called *prāṅnyāya* (a plea of former judgment)."

Thus, when the characteristics of a valid rejoinder (*uttaralakṣaṇa*) have been established, it follows by implication that those lacking the characteristics of a rejoinder—which nevertheless appear as if they were rejoinders—are merely "semblances of rejoinders" (*uttarābhāsa*).

This has also been clarified in another Smṛti: "Anything other than the subject under discussion, that which is doubtful, that which is too little or too much, and that which does not pervade one part of the proposition (*pakṣaikadeśavyāpin*)—such things cannot be a valid rejoinder."

An answer that consists of disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is confused, requires interpretation, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the accomplishment of one's own purpose.
Any other [reply] that is ambiguous, different from the subject matter, too little, or too much;
or any other that only covers one part of the position—such would not be a valid rejoinder.

An answer that consists of disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is confused, requires interpretation, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the accomplishment of one's own purpose.
In that regard, "ambiguous" is as follows: when it is said, "He has taken a hundred gold pieces," [the defendant replies], "It is true he took them, but a hundred gold pieces or a hundred māṣas.
"Something other than the subject matter" is, for example, when in a suit for a hundred gold pieces, one says, "I owe a hundred paṇas.
"Too little" is when in a suit for a hundred gold pieces, one says, "I owe five hundred."
*Atibhūri* (excessive): when one is charged with a debt of one hundred gold coins, one replies, "I owe two hundred.
*Pakṣaikadeśavyāpi* (covering only a part of the claim): when one is charged with gold, clothing, and so forth, one replies, "Only the gold was received, nothing else.

*Vyastapada* (separate points): when one is charged with the non-payment of a debt, one offers an answer on a different point, such as replying to a charge of a hundred gold coins, "I was beaten by him."

*Avyāpi* (non-pervasive): that which does not pervade the specific details of place, location, and so forth; for example, when the plaintiff has written in the plaint, "A field was seized by him in the eastern direction in Vārāṇasī in the Middle Country," but he subsequently writes only, "The field was seized. *Nigūḍhārtha* (of hidden meaning): for example, in a lawsuit concerning a debt of one hundred gold pieces, when asked, "Do I owe this to him?", the plaintiff indicates through intonation (*dhvani*) that he owes it to someone else, whether it be the judge, a court member, or another person; thus, it is of hidden meaning. *Ākula* (confused): that which is contradictory in its preceding and succeeding parts; for example, when a lawsuit for one hundred gold pieces has been brought, [the defendant says], "It is true it was taken, but I do not owe it."

"Accessible through interpretation" (*vyākhyāgamya*) means that it is understood through interpretation by means of expressing poorly joined case-endings, compounds, or ellipses, or by using a non-standard regional dialect (*adeśabhāṣā*).

For example, in a lawsuit regarding a debt for one hundred gold coins (*suvarṇa*), when there is an accusation of a father's debt, [the defendant] says: "I do not know [anything] about my father’s hundred gold coins," because of the statement of his father who had taken a hundred.
Here, based on the statement of the father who took the hundred, [the meaning is]: "I do not know that a hundred gold coins were taken."

*Asāra* (insubstantial) means contrary to justice; for example, when there is a legal claim that "this person took a hundred gold pieces at interest and paid only the interest, not the principal," and the defendant replies, "it is true that the interest was paid, but the principal was not taken.
By the use of the singular number in the term *uttara* (reply), the confusion of multiple types of replies is excluded.
As Kātyāyana says: "That which is true regarding one part of the claim, and [where] there is a reason regarding another part..."
Because it is both false and partial due to its confusion, that is not a valid answer.
Thus:
That which is true in one part of the thesis, a reason in another part,
and false in yet another part, is not a valid rejoinder because of its internal inconsistency.
And the reason for its being unsurpassed has been stated by that very same [author]: "In a single dispute, there cannot be a legal procedure for both disputants;
there can be no establishment of the case for both, nor can there be two procedures in one place."
Thus:
"In a single dispute, there should not be legal action for both parties;
there can be no establishment of the case for both, nor can there be two actions in one [matter]."

When there is a confusion between a plea of denial (*mithyā*) and a plea of a special defense (*kāraṇottara*), it follows that the burden of proof (*kriyā*) would fall upon both the plaintiff and the defendant; for it is stated in the legal tradition: "The burden of proof lies with the plaintiff in the case of denial, and with the defendant in the case of a special defense. However, both of these [burdens] are contradictory within a single lawsuit.

For example, in a lawsuit where the claim is that "he took both gold and a hundred coins," [the defendant may respond]: "The gold was not taken; as for the hundred coins, they were taken and have been returned.

However, when there is a confusion between a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) and a plea of justification (*kāraṇa*), the burden of proof lies solely with the defendant: "But when a plea of prior judgment or a plea of justification is stated, the defendant shall point out the means of proof (*kriyā*).
Thus it is said.
But when a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a plea of a legal cause (*kāraṇa*) has been stated, the defendant shall point out the proof (*kriyā*).
For example: "The gold was received and returned; I have been defeated according to the course of legal procedure.
And in this case of a plea of prior judgment, it must be substantiated either by the document of victory (*jayapatra*) or by those who witnessed the prior judgment.
But if a reason is stated, it must be proven by means of witnesses, documents, and so forth; thus there is a contradiction.
The same should be understood regarding the confusion of the other three types of replies.

For example, when a charge is brought that "this person received gold, a hundred coins, and clothes," the reply might be: "It is true that gold was received and returned, but the hundred coins were not received; as for the clothes, however, I have been defeated according to the previous legal principle."
The same applies even when there is a combination of four [defenses].

Furthermore, these [defenses] are not "superior" (*anuttara*) because that particular portion cannot be established simultaneously without each of those [specific conditions]; rather, they are "superior" only in sequence.
And the sequence occurs according to the desire of the plaintiff, the defendant, and the members of the court.

Furthermore, where there is a conflation of both [types of reply], there the legal proceeding should first be conducted by adopting that one which has a broader scope of subject matter, and subsequently the proceeding should be viewed as proceeding by adopting the reply with the narrower scope.

And where there is a conflation of a plea of admission (*saṃpratipatti*) and another type of reply, there the legal proceeding should be viewed as proceeding by adopting the other reply, because there is no action to be performed in a plea of admission.
As stated by Hārīta: "If both a plea of denial (*mithyā*) and a plea of a special cause (*kāraṇa*) should exist together in one case..."
Or even if it is true, what answer can be given there, especially when accompanied by another [contradictory] statement?

Having said this, he further stated: "That answer which concerns a vast range of meaning, or wherein the fruit of the action resides, should be known as the primary one; otherwise, it is considered secondary."
The word "becomes mixed" (*saṃkīrṇam*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
This means that, with respect to the remaining [claims], the order is optional (*aicchika*).

In that regard, an example of a matter involving multiple items is as follows: when there is a formal accusation (*abhiyoga*) stating, "By this person, gold, a hundred *rūpaka* coins, and garments were received," [the defendant replies]: "Neither the gold nor the hundred *rūpaka* coins were received; however, the garments were received and have been returned."

In this case, since the plea of "false" (*mithyottara*) covers a broader range of subject matter, the legal proceeding should first be conducted by taking up the claimant's action, and only afterwards the proceeding concerning the garment.
This same principle should be applied to the mixture of "false" and "prior judgment" (*mithyā-prāṅnyāya*), as well as to the mixture of "reasoning" and "prior judgment" (*kāraṇa-prāṅnyāya*).

Likewise, when that same charge is brought, if the defendant replies regarding gold and a hundred silver coins that "I will give [them back]" and regarding clothes that "they were not taken" or "having been taken, they were returned," or that "I was previously defeated in the matter of the clothes"—then, even though the subject matter is extensive, because there is no legal proof (*kriyā*) required for that part, the lawsuit must proceed by taking up the legal proof pertaining to the other pleas, such as denial (*mithyā*).

However, there are cases where both the *mithyā* (denial) and *kāraṇa* (causal) defenses pervade the entire claim (*kṛtsnapakṣavyāpitva*). For example: someone points out a specific cow, saying, "This cow is mine; it was lost at such-and-such a time, and today it was seen in his house. Another person replies, "This is false; she was already staying in my house before the time you mentioned, or she was even born in my house.
This is certainly not a non-defense (*anuttara*), because it is capable of refuting the claim; nor is it merely a *mithyā*, because a causal argument (*kāraṇa*) has been presented.

Nor is it a *kāraṇa* (ground for defeat), because there is no admission even of a single part [of the claim]. Therefore, this is a false rejoinder (*mithyottara*) that possesses a ground. And in this case, the burden of proof (*kriyā*) falls upon the defendant, according to the rule: "When the defendant is the one who possesses the ground."

Now, one might ask: why does the burden of proof (*kriyā*) not fall upon the plaintiff in the case of a "false" (*mithyā*) plea? It is because that [plea] has as its object a pure falsehood (*śuddhamithyā*).
And why does the rule "when the defendant is the one who asserts a cause" (*kāraṇe prativādini*) not apply when the object is a pure cause (*śuddhakāraṇa*)?
This is not so.

Since every *kāraṇottara* (defence based on a cause) possesses a nature associated with falsehood (*mithyā*), there is no such thing as a "pure" *kāraṇottara*. In a well-known *kāraṇottara*, because one accepts a portion of the matter asserted in the plaint, that portion is false; for example: "It is true that I received a hundred coins, but I do not owe them, because they have been returned. However, the distinction in the present example is that there is no acceptance even of a single portion of the matter asserted in the plaint.
And this has been clearly stated by Hārīta:
"Between a false plea and a plea based on a reason, that which is based on a reason should be accepted as the valid defense."
In the case of both *mithyā* (denial) and *kāraṇa* (defence based on a special cause), the answer that contains the *kāraṇa* (special cause) is to be accepted.

Where both *mithyā* and *prāṅnyāya* (confession of a prior judgment) pervade the defendant's position—as for example, when in a suit for the non-payment of a hundred coins, the defendant says, "This is false; in this very matter, he was previously defeated"—here too, the burden of proof (*kriyā*) rests with the defendant alone.
However, when a *prāṅnyāya* or a *kāraṇa* is asserted, the defendant must point out the evidence (*kriyā*).

Because of this statement, since there can be no "prior judgment" (*prāṅnyāya*) for one who is pure [of charge], it would follow that such a case lacks a formal reply. Furthermore, even in the case of "admission" (*saṃpratipatti*), its status as a reply is established precisely because it negates the character of being a "probandum" (*sādhya*) by presenting the subject under dispute—which was previously taught as a probandum—as already proven. However, when there is a conflation of "cause" (*kāraṇa*) and "prior judgment," as for example, when one accused of having received a hundred [coins] replies: "It is true I received it, but I have returned it; in this very matter, he was defeated by a prior judgment."

In that regard, since it is according to the preference of the opponent, there is no possibility of two simultaneous actions occurring for both the proponent and the opponent in a single legal proceeding; such is the conclusion.

When the plaint has been thus entered on the subsequent leaf, since the establishment of the matter to be proven depends upon the means of proof, someone may ask: "Who should provide the exposition of the means of proof? In response to this expectation, he says: "Thereafter, the plaintiff should have the proof of the matter asserted written down."
Immediately after the *uttara* (the defendant's reply), the plaintiff—the one possessing the claim (*sādhyavān*)—should have it written down at once, that is, without delay.

"The matter asserted" (*pratijñātārtha*) refers to that which is both the subject of the proposition (*pratijñāta*) and the object to be proven (*artha*). Its "proof" (*sādhana*) is that by which it is established; thus, "proof" means the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By stating here that "he should have it written down at once," it is understood that even a delay in time for the articulation of the *uttara* is permitted.
This will be analyzed further below.

By stating that "the plaintiff (arthin) shall cause the proof of the matter asserted to be written down," it is meant that whoever possesses the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven) is the one who must cause the proof of the matter asserted to be written down. Consequently, in the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya-uttara*), since the prior judgment itself is the *sādhya*, the defendant (*pratyarthin*) becomes the plaintiff; therefore, he alone shall cause the proof to be written down. Likewise, in the case of a plea of a special defense (*kāraṇa-uttara*), since the special reason itself is the *sādhya*, the party asserting the reason is the plaintiff; thus, he alone shall cause it to be written down.
But in the case of a false plea (*mithyottara*), the plaintiff alone is the claimant (*arthin*); he himself must point out the proof (*sādhana*).
Thus, by stating that "the claimant shall cause the document to be written," it is declared that the claimant alone—and no one else—shall cause it to be written.

Consequently, in the case of a plea of admission (*saṃpratipattyuttara*), since there is an absence of the matter to be proven (*sādhya*), neither of the two parties—the plaintiff nor the defendant—is a claimant; therefore, there is no pointing out of proof at all, and it is understood that the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is concluded by that much alone.
This very point has been clearly stated by Hārīta: "But when the grounds for a prior claim have been stated, the defendant shall indicate the proof;
however, in the case of a denial (mithyā), the plaintiff shall do so, and in the case of a confession (pratipatti), there shall be no such requirement."
Thus [ends the section]. 2.7.
But when the grounds for a prior judgment have been stated, the defendant shall point out the proof;
however, in the case of a denial or a confession, that [proof] need not be produced by the plaintiff.
Upon the establishment of that, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.

When there is the establishment—that is, the completion—of that means of proof (*sādhana*), characterized as witnesses, documents, and so forth which are about to be described, one attains success, namely victory, which is the characteristic of the thing to be proven (*sādhya*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: other than this manner, by another manner, when the means of proof is not established, the opposite occurs—one attains failure, which is the characteristic of defeat, regarding the thing to be proven.
Having thus explained the nature of legal procedure, he concludes:
"This fourfold legal procedure has been set forth regarding disputes."

It has been stated that "the king shall examine legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*). This very *vyavahāra*, consisting of four feet and divided into four parts, has thus been demonstrated and described in relation to disputes such as the non-payment of debts and others.
Among these, the first is the "foot of the plaint" (*bhāṣāpāda*), which consists of the written statement to be presented before the defendant.
"The answer to the meaning of what was heard should be written"—this is the second part, the *uttarapāda*.
"Then the plaintiff should have it written immediately"—this is the third part, the *kriyāpāda*.
"Upon its establishment, he obtains success"—this is the fourth part, the *sādhyasiddhipāda*.

As it has been said: "The settlement of mutual disputes among humans regarding conflicting claims to their own interests, established through the principles of speech, is declared to be legal procedure (*vyavahāra*)."
That which is characterized by speech, subsequent action, accomplishment, and success, and which proceeds in a sequence,
is called "four-footed" when its four constituent parts are implied.
Thus,
the determination of the rights of humans regarding their mutual disagreements over self-interest through the application of logical principles is declared to be judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*).
That which has its four components implied through the sequence of speech, subsequent action, accomplishment,
and success, is designated as "four-footed" (catuṣpād).

However, in the case of the *saṃpratipatti* (admission) reply, because there is no presentation of a proof (*sādhana*) and because the meaning of the speech is not something yet to be proven (*asādhya*), there is no stage characterized by the establishment of a probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*). Thus, it possesses only two stages. Furthermore, following the statement of the reply, the *pratyākalita*—characterized by the deliberation of the court members as to which of the plaintiff or defendant should undergo the legal action—is not designated as a stage of the lawsuit by the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya). Moreover, because it lacks a connection with the litigant, it is established that it does not constitute a stage of the lawsuit. (2.8)
Having thus stated the *vyavahāramātṛkā*, which is applicable to all legal procedures, he now says [the following] to show a certain specific rule regarding a particular type of legal procedure:
"Without having settled the charge (*abhiyoga*), one should not bring a counter-charge against him.
A *abhiyoga* is that by which one is charged; it is an offense.
Without having settled—that is, without having resolved—this accusation, one should not bring a counter-accusation against this accuser; one should not connect him with an offense.

Although a "counter-attack" (*pratyavaskandana*) takes the form of a counter-accusation, it does not fall within the scope of this prohibition because its nature consists in avoiding one's own offense.
Therefore, this is a prohibition specifically against a counter-accusation that consists in not refuting one's own original accusation.
This was stated with reference to the defendant; now, he speaks with reference to the plaintiff:
"One who has been accused should not be subjected to further interrogation by another, nor should one who has already spoken be brought into a state of contradiction."
Another plaintiff shall not bring a charge against one who has already been charged for a non-expansive matter.
Furthermore,
he shall not lead— that is, cause to reach— a state of contradiction or opposition to what was stated at the time of the formal complaint (*āvedana*).

This is what is meant: whatever object was presented in its specific form at the time of the oral testimony, that very same object must be recorded in writing at the time of the deposition, and not otherwise.
But is it not already stated in the rule, "The plaint shall be written in the presence of the defendant exactly as it was declared by the plaintiff," that this very point has been addressed?
Why then is it stated again that "one should not bring about a change in the nature of the claim"?
It is replied: [to clarify further].

By the phrase "as reported by the claimant," it is stated that whatever matter was presented at the time of the initial report (*āvedana*) must be written down exactly in the same way at the time of the formal plea (*bhāṣā*).
Not even a single word may differ from the original matter.

For example, having established at the time of the report that "one hundred *rūpakas* were taken as interest," one must not say at the time of the formal plea in the presence of the defendant, "one hundred pieces of cloth were taken as interest."
If that were the case, then even when one shifts to another word, because one has moved to a different object, the inferior litigant would be subject to punishment.
It is not by the rule "one should not lead [the matter] into a different state" that shifting to another word is prohibited even when the underlying object remains the same.

For example, at the time of filing the plaint, one states, "Having taken a hundred *rūpakas* as interest, this man does not repay it," but at the time of the formal statement (*bhāṣā*), he says, "He forcibly seized a hundred *rūpakas*."

In that context, moving to another subject matter was prohibited; here, however, it is the shifting to another point in the argument that is forbidden, and thus there is no tautology. This very point has been clarified by Nārada: "That man who, having abandoned his initial position, takes up another again, is to be known as a defeated litigant because of his shifting of the ground."
Thus:
"He who, abandoning the previous position, takes up another again,
should be known as a man of inferior speech because of his shifting of positions."
One who speaks falsely is subject to punishment, yet he does not lose the matter at hand.

Therefore, this instruction—beginning with "without having completed the legal proceeding"—is intended solely for the purpose of preventing negligence on the part of both the defendant and the plaintiff; it does not concern the success or failure of the matter under litigation itself.
For this very reason, the author will later state: "Having set aside frivolous objections (*chala*), the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the truth."
And this should be understood to apply to legal proceedings concerning material interests (*arthavyavahāra*).
However, in a proceeding brought on account of anger (*manyukṛta*), if one makes a statement through negligence, one is indeed defeated even in that very proceeding at hand.
As Nārada says: "In all disputes over material interests, one does not fail because of a verbal quibble (*vākchala*)."
In cases of adultery with another's wife, theft of land, or non-payment of debt, even if he is punished, he does not lose his claim to the property.
Thus:
"In all disputes concerning property, one does not fail through verbal quibble;
even if he is to be punished in cases involving another's wife, land, or the non-payment of debt, he does not lose his case."

The meaning of this is as follows: in all disputes concerning material interests—not those arising from anger—even if one employs verbal deception or speaks through inadvertence, one does not falter; that is, one is not defeated.
The sense is that one is not deprived of the subject matter at hand.
An illustration of this is provided in the passage beginning with "another's wife," and so forth.

Just as one who has falsely accused another of adultery with another's wife, theft of land, or non-payment of debt is to be punished so that he does not lose the substance of the case at hand, so it is in all disputes concerning property (*arthavivāda*).

From the use of the term "disputes concerning property," it is understood that in disputes arising from anger (*manyukṛta-vivāda*), if one makes a false statement, one loses even the substance of the case itself.

For example, having stated at the time of the formal complaint (*āvedana*) "I was struck on the head by him with his foot," but then saying at the time of the plea (*bhāṣākāla*) "I was struck by him with his hand or foot," one is not only to be punished but is also defeated in the suit. (2.9)
He states an exception to the rule that "one should not bring a counter-charge against another without having first settled one's own charge":
"And one may bring a counter-charge in cases of quarrels and acts of violence (*sāhasa*).

In the case of quarrels consisting of verbal or physical assault, and in acts of violence such as the destruction of life caused by poison, weapons, and the like—where a counter-charge is possible—one may bring a counter-charge against the accuser even without having settled one's own charge."

But surely, even here, since a counter-accusation (*pratyabhiyoga*)—being of the nature of not refuting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—is not a valid rejoinder, it constitutes a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*), and thus the impossibility of simultaneous legal proceedings (*yugapadvyavahāra*) remains the same.
True.

However, the instruction regarding the counter-accusation here is not for the sake of simultaneous legal proceedings, but rather for the purpose of obtaining a lesser penalty or for the avoidance of an excessive penalty.

For instance, when there is a formal charge such as "I have been struck or cursed by him," and a counter-charge is subsequently brought such as "I was previously struck or cursed by him," the punishment is reduced.
As Nārada says: "He who first brings a false accusation shall certainly be the bearer of the guilt."
Even he who is disrespectful later was formerly disciplined by his teacher.
Thus:
"He who first utters an accusation shall certainly be the one to bear the fault;
he who does so later is also one who acts improperly, for in the case of the former, the punishment is severe."
Furthermore, when there is a simultaneous engagement in such acts as striking against two parties, the imposition of a heavier punishment is precluded.
Regarding verbal abuse or assault, when both parties engage in them simultaneously,
if no distinction can be established, the punishment for both shall be equal.
Thus:
"In cases of verbal abuse or assault, when both parties have engaged simultaneously,
if no distinction can be found, the punishment shall be equal for both."

Thus, even though simultaneous engagement in legal proceedings is impossible, a counter-charge is meaningful in cases such as quarrels; however, in matters such as the non-payment of debts, it is entirely useless.
Having stated the procedure for the plaintiff and the defendant, he now describes the duty of the presiding judge together with the members of the court:
"A surety should be accepted from both parties who is capable of deciding the case."

In all disputes between both the plaintiff and the defendant, a guarantor (*pratibhū*) capable of performing the duty of the judgment—where "duty of the judgment" (*kāryanirṇaya*) refers to the performance of the judgment (the compound *kāryanirṇaya* following the rule for words beginning with *āhitāgni*, where the word *kārya* is placed first)—namely, the payment of the proven debt and the imposition of punishment—must be accepted by the presiding judge together with the members of the court.
In the absence of such a person, men should be appointed to protect the interests of the plaintiff and the defendant.
And they must be paid their wages by those two every day.
Thus says Kātyāyana:
"Now, if there is no surety, but the litigant has a connection to the legal matter..."
Having protected him until the end of the day, he should give the wage to the servant.
Thus [ends section] 2.10.
If there is no surety, but the plaintiff has business to attend to,
he shall, having been protected until the end of the day, pay his wages to the servant.
It has been stated that in a judicial proceeding involving a plaintiff and a defendant, a surety must be taken by the presiding judge together with the members of the court.
What is that judicial proceeding in which a surety is taken? In response to this inquiry, he says:
"If [the defendant] denies [the claim] and is subsequently proven [guilty], he shall pay the debt to the creditor and an equal amount to the king."
One who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim as a fine.
