When a defendant denies a claim presented by a plaintiff, if the defendant is made to admit it through witnesses or other means by the plaintiff, then he shall pay the principal sum to the plaintiff and an equal amount as a fine for denial to the king. If the plaintiff is unable to prove his case, then he becomes one who has brought a false suit; thus, he shall pay double the value of the claimed property to the king.
This same rule should be applied in cases of *prāṅnyāya* (judgment on prior proof) and *pratyavaskandana* (defendant's counter-claim).

In that case, if the plaintiff is indeed proven by the defendant to be one who makes a false denial, he shall pay to the king a fine equal to the subject matter of the suit. If, however, the defendant is unable to prove either a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a valid legal excuse (*kāraṇa*), then he alone, being a false accuser, shall pay double the amount to the king and the original sum to the plaintiff.
But in the case of a plea of admission (*saṃpratipatti*), there is no fine at all.

And this [rule] pertains exclusively to the subject of the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*). It does not apply to all subjects, because punishments are specified for various other categories elsewhere, and because it is impossible for it to apply to legal proceedings concerning property that is not a debt.
Although the rule "the king shall compel the debtor to pay" pertains to the subject of the non-payment of debt, we shall explain its specific details in that very context.
Or rather, this very point may also be applied to the scope of all legal proceedings.
How so?

When the defendant has denied the charge brought against him, if he is proven guilty by the plaintiff through witnesses and other means, then [the fine] shall be equal to that—exactly as prescribed for each specific case.
The word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis.
"He shall pay wealth as a fine to the king" is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

However, if the plaintiff is unable to substantiate his accusation, then he is declared a "false accuser" (*mithyābhiyogī*), and it is prescribed that he shall pay double the wealth and fine specifically mentioned in the rule.
In this case as well, the same application as previously stated should be understood for both the plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) and the plea of denial (*pratyavaskandana*). || 2.11 ||

By stating that "therefore, the plaintiff should immediately have written the proof of the matter asserted," it is shown that one must wait for the time when the writing of the defendant's reply (uttara) is due.
Regarding this, he states an exception:
"In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, a false accusation regarding cattle, a grave emergency, or matters concerning women..."
One should initiate the lawsuit immediately; in other cases, the time is said to depend on one's own wish.
Sāhasa (violence) consists of acts such as depriving life by means of poison, weapons, and so forth.
Steya is theft. Pāruṣya is harshness of speech and harshness of punishment, the definitions of which will be stated hereafter.
A cow that yields milk;
an accusation of a curse is an accusation of a sin; calamity is the loss of life or wealth; in that [calamity].

The singular number is used because of the *dvandva* compound being treated as a single unit (*ekavadbhāva*). Regarding "a woman"—that is, a woman of good family (*kulastrī*) and a female slave (*dāsī*): in the case of a dispute concerning character, it refers to the woman of good family; in the case of a dispute concerning ownership, it refers to the female slave.
One should cause her to state her defense and cause her to pay the fine.
One should act immediately and not wait for a delay;
except in other types of disputes, where the time for giving a reply is prescribed by the desire of the plaintiff, the defendant, the members of the court, and the presiding judge. (2.12)
He states the characteristics of the wicked:
"He moves from place to place, licks the corners of his mouth,
his forehead perspires, and his face becomes discolored."
With parched mouth and faltering speech, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips.
One who undergoes a change from his natural disposition through actions of mind, speech, or body,
whether during a legal proceeding or as a witness, is proclaimed to be wicked.

One who, by means of actions of mind, speech, and body, undergoes a transformation or change due to his very nature and not from signs such as fear, is declared to be wicked when faced with an accusation or a trial.
He demonstrates that transformation by dividing it [into specific behaviors]:
he goes from one place to another and does not remain anywhere.
He licks the corners of his mouth—the extremities of the lips—touching and rubbing them with the tip of his tongue; this is a distortion of action (*karman*).

His forehead perspires, becoming marked by drops of sweat, and his face undergoes a change of color (*vaivarṇya*), reaching a state of paleness or blackness; this is a distortion of the body (*kāya*).
His speech becomes parched and faltering—that is, he is one whose speech is parched, stammering, faltering, and disjointed.
To speak much that is contradictory, or inconsistent with what was said before and after, is a distortion of speech.
To fail to honor the words spoken by another by giving a reply, or to fail to honor [the speaker] by looking back at them, is a sign of a distortion of mind.
Likewise, to pucker or distort the lips is also a distortion of the body.
And this is stated merely as a suspicion of a fault, not for the sake of a certainty regarding a fault;
for it is difficult to discern the distinction between a natural modification and one caused by external conditions.
Even if some person of keen intellect were to perceive that distinction, nevertheless, it would not constitute grounds for defeat.
For people do not perform the funeral rites for one who is about to die simply because they observe the signs [of death].
Likewise, even when it is understood from a sign that "this person will suffer defeat," there is no occasion for performing actions necessitated by defeat. 2.13, 2.14, 2.15.
Furthermore: "He who,
being independent, attempts to prove a doubtful matter, he who absconds,
or he who says nothing when summoned— he is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment."

He who, being independent and regardless of further proof, establishes a doubtful matter that has not even been admitted by the debtor through means such as legal restraint (āsedha) and the like, is considered defeated and liable to punishment. Furthermore, he who, when asked for what has been admitted by himself or established by proof, flees or runs away; and he who, having been accused and summoned by the king, says nothing at all in the court—he too is recorded in the Smṛti as defeated and liable to punishment. This is how the connection [of the text] is to be understood.

Since it has been stated that "he is proclaimed as corrupt in a legal proceeding or in giving testimony," the mention of the term *daṇḍya* (one deserving punishment) is used so that it may not be understood merely as one who is defeated (*hīna*).

Furthermore, since one who is punished (*daṇḍya*) and even one who is censured (*śāsya*) does not, by implication, lose his case (*arthāt na hīyate*), the mention of the term *hīna* is used here so that this [confusion] regarding the loss of the case may not occur. (2.16)
Now, when two litigants simultaneously arrive before the judge as claimants,
it is as follows: for instance,
someone having acquired a field by means of a gift and having enjoyed it for some time, departs for another country with his family due to some business matter.
Another person also, having acquired that very same field by means of a formal gift and having enjoyed it for some time, went to another country.

Then both of them, arriving simultaneously and disputing with one another—saying "this field is mine" and "this field is mine"—approached the judge. When it was required there [by the judge] whose case should be heard first, he said: "When witnesses exist on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff."
When the prima facie position has been defeated, the proponents of the rejoinder prevail.

When witnesses are available for both disputants, the witnesses of the *pūrvavādī*—he who says, "In the earlier time, it was received by me and enjoyed by me"—are to be questioned, and not those of him who merely presents his case first.

But when another speaks thus: "It is true that he previously received and enjoyed this, however, this very field was obtained by me through purchase from the king and given to me," or "it was obtained by me through a gift and given to me"—in that case, the plaintiff's initial claim has been defeated due to its lack of proof. Once that initial claim has been defeated, witnesses must subsequently be questioned by the disputant regarding the receipt and enjoyment [of the property].
The interpretation that "when the grounds for a prior legal claim have been stated and the plaintiff's position has been defeated, the witnesses belong to the defendant" is incorrect.

This is because such a meaning has already been expressed by the rule, "Then the plaintiff shall immediately cause [the defendant] to write down the proof of the matter asserted," and thus there would be the fault of tautology.

Nārada has clarified this very first interpretation: "In a case of denial (*mithyā*), the burden of proof (*kriyā*) lies with the plaintiff; in a case of a plea of justification (*kāraṇa*), it lies with the defendant."
But when a case is established through the procedure of a prior judgment, the document of victory shall be the proof.
Having said this: "When two parties are disputing and there are witnesses for both, the witnesses shall belong to the one whose case is the first plea."
Thus it was said.
And because this differs from the previously mentioned conventional usage, it is presented as distinct. || 2.17 ||
Moreover:
If a dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay the fine,
his own wager, and the debt to the creditor.

If a dispute (*vyavahāra*) involves a wager (*sapaṇa*), where "wagering" (*paṇana*) means a stake (*paṇa*), and it is thus accompanied by such a stake, then in that case—in that wagered lawsuit—the king shall cause the defeated party to pay the previously mentioned fine, his own pledged stake, and the wealth at issue to the plaintiff. Furthermore, even where one party, under the influence of a fit of anger, pledges, "If I am defeated in this matter, I will give a hundred stakes," while the other party pledges nothing at all, there too the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) proceeds.
When that [dispute] has proceeded, if the party who made the wagered promise loses, then he alone shall be compelled to pay the fine along with the wager;
whereas the other defeated party shall be compelled to pay only the fine, not the wager, because of the specific mention of "his own wager" (*svapaṇa*).
However, in a case where one party promises one hundred and the other promises five hundred, even upon defeat, both shall be compelled to pay only the wager they themselves made.
By saying "if there should be a dispute involving a wager," it is shown that a dispute may also exist without a wager. || 2.18 ||
Furthermore:
Having set aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the facts; for even if the facts exist, one who fails to present them loses the case in the legal proceeding.

Having cast aside and abandoned deceit and negligence, the king should bring legal proceedings to their conclusion according to what has actually occurred—that is, in accordance with the reality of the facts.

For even that which is factual and the reality of the matter itself is lost—that is, it suffers defeat—through the legal process, namely by means of witnesses and other such evidence, if it is not presented or stated.
Therefore, one must pursue the actual facts.
Just as the plaintiff and the defendant speak the truth, so should the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, strive by means of conciliation and other such methods.
When this is possible, a decision is reached even without relying on witnesses and the like.
However, if it is in no way possible to pursue the actual facts, then a decision must be made based on witnesses and so forth; this is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*).
As it has been said:
"Because it follows both the real and the deceptive, it is declared to have two courses:
that which is conjoined with the true meaning is the real (bhūta), while that which is stated through negligence is the deceptive (chala)."
Thus it is said:
"Because it follows both the real and the deceptive, it is declared to have two courses:
the real (bhūta) is that which is connected with the true meaning, while the deceptive (chala) is that which is stated through negligence."
In that regard, legal procedure following the facts (*bhūtānusārī*) is primary, while that following a pretext (*chalānusārī*) is secondary.

When a lawsuit is decided by means of witnesses, documents, and so forth, it sometimes follows the actual state of affairs and sometimes does not, because witnesses and the like may also be subject to error. (2.19)
Regarding the principle that "even a fact, if not presented [in court], is lost in legal proceedings," he provides an illustration:

"If a defendant denies a written document, but is proven in one part of it, he shall be made by the king to pay the entire debt; however, what was not declared [at the outset] shall not be accepted [as evidence]."

If a defendant denies everything that has been written and claimed by the plaintiff—whether it be gold, silver, clothing, or other items—and thus disavows it all, then, once the defendant has been proven on one part regarding the gold through witnesses and other means, he must be compelled by the king to pay the entire amount previously written, including the silver and other items, to the plaintiff.

However, what was not previously declared—that which was not mentioned at the time of the plaint but is later brought forward by the plaintiff saying, "I forgot this before"—is not to be accepted; it shall not be made payable by the king.
And this is not merely a matter of literal scriptural injunction.

Because it is certain that the defendant is a liar regarding one part [of the claim], there is the possibility that he is a liar regarding the other part as well; and because it is certain that the plaintiff is truthful regarding one part, there is the possibility that he is truthful regarding the other part as well. Thus, based on this very statement of the Lord of Yogins (Yogīśvara), which is supported by a conviction of probability—otherwise known as *tarka*—the legal conclusion is that the king must cause the entire amount to be paid.
Thus, when a decision is made in accordance with logical reasoning (*tarka*), there is no fault for those who oversee legal proceedings even if the actual state of affairs is otherwise.

To this effect, Gautama states: "Reasoning is the means for attaining [knowledge of] justice; having inferred by means of it, one should lead [the case] to its proper place," and concludes, "Therefore, the king and the teacher are not to be censured.

Nor is it understood here merely that a defendant whose testimony is established in only one part is one whose word is not to be accepted, because of the statement: "One who is proven in one part must be made to pay the whole by the king."
As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana: "Even when a claim involves multiple matters, the creditor shall receive only as much wealth as he proves with witnesses; such is the wealth he recovers."
Thus:
even when multiple matters are brought forward,
the creditor receives only as much recovered wealth as he can prove by means of witnesses.
This refers to cases concerning debts owed by a father and others that are to be paid by a son and others.

For in such a case, when a son or other heir who has been charged with many matters denies them by saying "I do not know," he does not become a defendant who practices concealment (*nihnavavādī*); thus, even if he is proven on one part, he is nowhere a liar. Therefore, the scriptural rule—"one does not deny what is written"—does not apply there, because there is an absence of concealment and an absence of the required presumption (*tarka*). As for the statement of Kātyāyana, "even when there is a charge involving multiple matters," it is a general rule; it applies to the plea of ignorance (*ajñānottara*), setting aside the specific rule's subject matter, which is the plea of concealment (*nihnavottara*).
Indeed, in disputes concerning debts and the like, which are generally stable in nature, once a decision has been reached,
the matter to be proven is not established even if the amount stated is either less or more than the truth.

By stating this, Kātyāyana has declared that when a charge involving multiple matters is brought, if the witnesses establish only one part or more than one part, the entire matter to be proven (*sādhya*) is not established.
This being so, how can there be proof of the unestablished part once one part has been established?
It is said in reply:

The meaning of this is that when witnesses—who have been presented as the means for proving all the matters set forth—state only a portion or state more than [what was alleged], the entire matter to be proven (*sādhya*) is not established.

In that case too, because of the statement "that which is certain is not established," there remains doubt just as before; thus, there is certainly room for another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), in accordance with the rule "having set aside quibble" (*chala*).

However, in cases such as *sāhasa* (violent crimes), since the witnesses are designated as the means for proving the entirety of the matter to be proven, once even a single part is proven, the entire matter to be proven is indeed established.

For that much alone suffices for the establishment of [crimes such as] violence and the like, and because of the statement of Kātyāyana: "Even when only a portion of the matter to be proven has been stated by the witnesses, the entire case shall be established—[this applies] in matters of sexual intercourse with women, violence, and theft, whatever is declared to be the matter to be proven."
Thus [ends the verse]. 2.20.
Even when the portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by witnesses, the entire case shall be established;
this applies to matters concerning sexual intercourse, violence, and theft, which have been proclaimed as the objects of proof.

Now, is it not the case that the Smṛti rule stating "one does not deny a written document" is one [Smṛti], and likewise, the Smṛti rule stating "even when there is an accusation involving multiple matters" is another Smṛti?

Since these two Smṛtis are mutually contradictory, why should they not lack authority due to their mutual sublation, rather than having their scope determined by a restriction of subject matter? To this, he says:
"In the conflict between two Smṛtis, however, the principle of reasoning (nyāya) is stronger based on judicial practice."

Where there is a mutual contradiction between two traditional authorities (*smṛti*), the principle characterized as the general rule and the exception (*utsargāpavāda*)—consisting in the determination of their respective domains (*viṣaya-vyavasthāpana*) and so forth—is powerful and capable of resolving that contradiction.
As to the question of from where this principle is to be understood, he says: "from usage" (*vyavahārataḥ*).
It is understood from usage—that is, from the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Therefore, even in the present example, it is logical that there be a fixed determination of the scope [of application].
In this way, in other cases as well, the fixed determination of scope, its optionality, and so forth, should be applied according to what is possible.
Thus, regarding this universal objection, he states the exception:
"But the treatise on Dharma is more powerful than the treatise on Artha; such is the established rule."

Since the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), such as that of Uśanas, are excluded by the very phrase "in accordance with the *dharmaśāstra*," the *arthaśāstra* intended here is specifically that which is included within the *dharmaśāstra*, characterized by royal policy (*rājanīti*).
The established rule (*maryādā*) is that in the event of a conflict between the legal codes of *arthaśāstra* and *dharmaśāstra*, the *dharmaśāstra* prevails over the *arthaśāstra*.

Although there is no difference in their essential nature between the *Arthaśāstra* and the *Dharmaśāstra* due to their sharing a common agent [of composition], nevertheless, because the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—dharma—is primary and artha is secondary, the *Dharmaśāstra* is stronger; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the primacy of dharma has been demonstrated at the beginning of the treatise.

Therefore, when there is a conflict between the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra*, the *Arthaśāstra* is simply set aside (*bādha*); there is neither a restriction of scope (*viṣayavyavasthā*) nor an option (*vikalpa*).
What is the illustration for this?
It is not, for instance: "One should indeed kill an assailant who approaches, without hesitation, whether he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin."
No guilt whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an assassin;
whether done in secret or openly, it is wrath that meets that wrath.
Likewise, one should indeed slay without hesitation an assailant approaching, even if he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin.
In the killing of an *ātātāyin* (one who comes with intent to kill), no fault whatsoever accrues to the slayer;
whether done in secret or openly, it is simply fury meeting fury.

"Even if an assailant (*ātatāyin*) who has mastered the Vedānta approaches on the battlefield seeking to kill, one may kill him in return; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). Such is the *Arthaśāstra*.
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed.
Such is the Dharmaśāstra;
when there is a conflict between these two, it is logical that the Dharmaśāstra is more authoritative.

Since these two [texts] cannot have the same subject matter, there is no contradiction between them; thus, the consideration of their relative strength does not apply. For instance, having begun with the statement, "The twice-born may take up arms when dharma is obstructed," it continues: "In self-defense, and in battle for the sake of sacrificial fees..."
And one who kills for the sake of assisting a woman or a Brahmin does not incur punishment according to the law.

Having stated that one who kills an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor) with a non-deceptive weapon incurs no punishment—whether for self-defense, for protecting sacrificial materials such as the priestly fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other implements, in battle, or even when killing women or Brahmins—this [verse] is now spoken as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to that: "Or a teacher, or children and the elderly," and so forth.
The meaning is: since one may kill even teachers and others who are otherwise absolutely exempt from being killed if they become *ātatāyins*, how much more so others?

Because of the hearing of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even upon hearing the word *vā*," there is no perception of the teachers and others being subject to execution; for according to the statement of Sumantu: "There is no fault in killing an *atatāyin*, except in the case of killing a cow or a Brāhmaṇa. And from the [text]: "One should not harm a teacher, a lecturer, a mother, a father, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics."
And because of this statement of Manu:

"This statement is meaningful as a prohibition against harming Ācāryas and others who are *ātatāyins*, and not otherwise, since the prohibition of mere violence is already established by the general rule.
Even the statement 'no fault whatsoever accrues to the killer in the slaying of an *ātatāyin*' refers exclusively to those other than Brāhmaṇas and the like."
For it is said: "The arsonist, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the seizer of land or wife—these six are indeed *ātatāyin*s (assassins)."
Likewise, one who has raised a sword, one with poison or fire, one with a hand raised for a curse,
one who kills by means of Atharvan spells, and also a slanderer [are to be avoided] regarding a king.
One who violates his wife's fidelity and one who is intent on seeking out his vulnerabilities—
one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin* (assassins).

Thus, those who are not *ātatāyin*s (aggressors) have been shown in general. Consequently, it is the settled rule that if Brāhmaṇas and others—even if they are *ātatāyin*s—are being warded off for the sake of protecting themselves and so forth, and should they happen to perish through negligence because there was no intention to cause harm, then there is a light penance and an absence of royal punishment.
Therefore, another example must be stated here.
It is said: since the acquisition of a friend is superior to the acquisition of gold or land, one should strive for its attainment;
such is the science of polity (Arthaśāstra).
"According to the Dharmaśāstra, [the king should act] free from anger and greed"—
thus says the Dharmaśāstra.
In certain matters, a contradiction arises between these two.

For example: when a legal proceeding involving four parties is underway, if the victory is adjudicated in favor of one, there is the acquisition of a friend, but the treatise on Dharma (dharmaśāstra) has not been followed;
if the victory is adjudicated in favor of the other, the treatise on Dharma has been followed, but the acquisition of a friend is reversed.
In such a case, the treatise on Dharma is more authoritative than the treatise on worldly interest (arthaśāstra).
For this very reason, Āpastamba has shown the severity of the penance for one who, when a conflict arises between dharma and artha, chooses the artha, by stating "this very [penance]";
by the words "this very," the twelve-year penance is referred to. (2.21)
Then it is stated: "The plaintiff should immediately have written the proof for the matter he has asserted.
When the question arises as to what that proof is, [the author] says:
"Evidence is declared to be documentary proof, possession, and witnesses."
In the absence of any one of these, any one of the divine [means] is prescribed.
That by which something is measured or determined is called a means of proof (*pramāṇa*).
It is of two kinds: human and divine.
Among these, the human is threefold: written documents, possession, and witnesses.
It has been proclaimed by the great seers (*maharṣi*).
Among those, written documents are of two kinds: the royal edict (*śāsana*) and the deed of gift (*cīraka*).
The edict possesses the characteristics already described.
The *cīraka* (document) has the characteristics that will be described below.
"Enjoyment" (*bhukti*) means utilization.
"Witnesses" (*sākṣiṇaḥ*) refers to those whose nature and types will be described below.

Now, it may be argued that since a written document and witnesses are included within the category of "verbal testimony" (*śabda*) by way of manifesting words, their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is appropriate; but how can possession (*bhukti*) be a valid means of knowledge? It is said in reply: possession also, when accompanied by certain qualifications, either infers—due to its invariable concomitance—the actions and so forth that constitute the cause of ownership, or, being otherwise inexplicable, leads to a presumption (*arthāpatti*). Thus, because it is included within inference or presumption, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge.

In the absence of even one of these three—writing and the others—an oath from among those whose specific varieties will be described below is declared to be a means of proof, depending on the caste, place, time, object, and so forth.
From this very statement, it is understood that an oath has authority only when human evidence is absent;
for the nature and the authoritative status of an oath are to be known through traditional scripture (*āgama*).

And therefore, where two parties, having arrived at the same time before a judicial officer with a mutual dispute, one resorts to human proof (*mānuṣī kriyā*) while the other resorts to divine proof (*daivī kriyā*), in that case only the human proof is to be accepted. As Kātyāyana says: "If one should state a human proof and the other should state a divine proof, the king should accept the human proof therein, but not the divine proof."
Thus:
if one should state human evidence and another should state divine evidence,
the king should accept the human evidence there, but not the divine procedure.

Even where human proof is possible for establishing a portion of the principal claim, there too one must not resort to divine means (*daiva*). For example, in a case of denial of a legal charge (*abhiyogāpahnava*) such as, "Having taken a hundred *rūpakas* at this rate of interest, he does not repay it," if the defendant says, "I have witnesses for the taking [of the money], but none for the amount or the specific interest; therefore, I shall prove my case by ordeal," there is no room for an ordeal because the specific amount and interest can be established even by the principle of proving a part (*ekadeśavibhāvitanyāya*).
And so it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
If a human action exists even when it pervades only a single part [of the case], it should be accepted; however, for men who speak, a divine action, even if complete, is not to be accepted.
Thus it is said:
"If a human action, even though it pervades only a single part [of the truth], should exist, that is to be accepted by men who speak; but not even a complete divine action."

As for the statement, "But for those who commit secret acts of violence, examination by ordeals is prescribed," that too is intended as a restrictive rule applicable when human means of proof are impossible.
Furthermore, as stated by Nārada: "In a forest, in a secluded place, at night, or inside a house, in cases of violence..."
And when there is a denial of the deposit, a divine ordeal is applicable.
Thus, even that [divine proof] is impossible for humans;
therefore, the general rule is that a decision by divine means occurs only in the absence of human witnesses.
However, an exception to this is observed: "In cases of assault, verbal abuse, and threats involving physical punishment..."
In matters arising from force, witnesses and even divine proof [are admissible].
Thus:
"In cases of assault, verbal abuse,
and threats involving physical force, as well as in matters arising from the use of power, witnesses and even divine ordeals [are admissible]."

Likewise, a restriction is observed in certain cases regarding documents and other means of proof, as follows: "The established rule for guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like is that their proof consists of a document; neither ordeal nor witnesses [are required]."
Likewise: In matters such as gates, paths, works, enjoyment, and water-conduits, possession alone shall be the weighty proof;
neither ordeal nor witnesses are required.

Likewise: when there is a dispute between masters and servants regarding what has been given or not given, or concerning the relationship of sale and gift, or when one, having purchased property, refuses to pay the price;
In matters of gambling, dueling, and when a dispute has arisen,
witnesses are declared the means of proof, not divine ordeals nor written documents.
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, when there is a dispute between masters and servants regarding what was given or not given, or concerning the sale and delivery of goods, or when one has purchased wealth but does not wish to accept it; |||
In matters of gambling, challenges to combat, and when a dispute has arisen,
witnesses are declared the means of proof, neither divine ordeals nor written documents.

Since both [procedures] may exist as valid means of proof and there is no discernment of their relative strength or weakness, one might ask which of the two prior or subsequent actions is more powerful.
To this he says: "In all disputes concerning matters of fact, the subsequent action is stronger.
In all disputes concerning matters of fact, such as debts and the like, the subsequent action—so called because it is performed—is the stronger effect (*kārya*).
When the subsequent matter is established, the proponent of that matter becomes victorious;

even if the prior matter is proven, the proponent of that matter is defeated. For example: suppose one person seeks to establish possession through receipt, while another seeks to establish non-possession through restitution. In that case, although both the proof of receipt and the proof of restitution are established by means of evidence, restitution is the stronger argument; thus, the proponent of restitution becomes victorious.
Likewise, having previously accepted a debt of two hundred, one later agrees to three hundred; although there is evidence for both cases, the acceptance of three hundred is stronger.
Because it occurs later, it does not arise without subverting the prior [agreement]. And it has been said: "For the subsequent will be established only by not subverting the prior."
He states an exception to this:
"But in the case of a pledge, a gift, or a purchase, the prior [title] is more powerful."
Among the three—pledges (*ādhi*) and so forth—the prior act is stronger.

For example: having made a single field a pledge for one person and received something [in exchange], if he then makes it a pledge for another and receives something [else] from them as well, it belongs to the former alone, not to the latter. The same applies to gifts (*pratigraha*) and purchases (*kraya*).
But surely, since that which has been established [as sacred fire] lacks ownership at that time, a re-establishment (*punar-ādhāna*) is simply not possible.
Likewise, for that which has been given or purchased, giving and buying are not logically tenable.
Therefore, this statement is meaningless.

It is said: even if [the property] is not one's own, if someone—out of delusion or greed—performs acts such as re-consecration (*punar-ādhāna*) and so forth, the rule that "in that case, the prior [act] prevails" is based precisely on the principle (*nyāya*); thus, this statement is not to be challenged. (2.23)
Intending to demonstrate the validity of possession when it is accompanied by certain qualifications, [the author] states another legal consequence of a particular type of possession:
"For land, loss occurs after twenty years for one who sees and speaks [of the encroachment];
for wealth, it occurs after ten years while it is being enjoyed by another."

When one sees land or wealth being enjoyed by another without any connection to oneself, and remains silent—failing to object by saying, "This land is mine; you must not enjoy it"—there occurs a loss of that land due to twenty years of uninterrupted enjoyment, based on that twenty-year period of possession.
However, for wealth such as elephants, horses, and the like, the loss occurs after ten years.
But is this not untenable?
For ownership does not depart merely because it has not been denied;
for neither in common worldly practice nor in the treatises is it established that the mere absence of a denial is a cause for the cessation of ownership, just as the act of giving or selling is.

Nor does ownership arise from twenty years of possession, because possession is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding ownership, and because a means of valid cognition does not produce its object [ex post facto], and because possession is not enumerated among the causes that create ownership, such as inheritance or purchase.

For instance, Gautama enumerates exactly eight grounds for the creation of ownership—inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, finding, and so forth—as follows: "The property of a Brāhmaṇa is that which is received as a gift; that of a Kṣatriya is that which is conquered; and that of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra is that which is earned through service. He does not mention possession (*bhoga*).
Nor is it logical to claim that this very statement establishes twenty years of enjoyment as a cause for the arising of ownership.
This is because ownership and the causes of ownership are well-known in the world and are not exclusively cognizable through the scriptures.
And this will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the section on partition;
however, the statement of Gautama is for the purpose of restriction.

Moreover: "But he who enjoys property that has not been transferred to him, even for many hundreds of years, the lord of the earth should punish that sinner with the punishment prescribed for a thief."
Thus, this contradicts the view that possession without title (*anāgama*) is the cause of ownership.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that the rule "he who enjoys [property] without title" refers to enjoyment in the absence of the owner's perception, while the rule "though seeing, he does not speak" refers to enjoyment in the presence of the owner; for the statement "he who enjoys without title" is made without qualification. Furthermore, no force may be exerted by the taker or his son regarding the enjoyment [of property].
The dharma is established for cattle, women, men, and so forth.
And because of this statement by Kātyāyana, and because loss is impossible in the case of possession in the presence [of the owner] due to the absence of any cause for loss;

nor should it be thought that, by way of an exception to the superiority of the prior act in the cases of pledge, gift, and sale, this text declares the superiority of the subsequent act— characterized by twenty years of possession in the case of land and ten years of possession in the case of movable property—
for in those cases, the subsequent act simply does not truly arise, since only one's own property can be pledged, gifted, or sold.
Ownership does not exist over that which has been left as a gift, given away, or sold.

Punishment for both giving and receiving what is not one's own property is recorded in the legal tradition: "He who takes what should not be taken and he who gives what should not be given—both of them are to be punished like thieves and made to pay the highest fine."
He who takes what should not be taken and he who gives what should not be given—

both of them are to be punished like thieves and made to pay the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). Furthermore, if this verse were intended as an exception (*apavāda*) to the three types of pledges (*ādhi*) and so forth, then an exception for pledges concerning boundaries (*sīmā*) and the like in the following verse would be untenable.
Therefore, the loss of the earth and so forth is indeed untenable,
nor is there any loss of conventional usage;
for, while he remains silent and maintains equanimity, [the world continues as before].
If the aforementioned time has passed, the legal proceeding is not established.

Thus, by Nārada, loss in legal proceedings (*vyavahārahāni*) was stated as being caused by the absence of signs of negligence, and not by the absence of the object itself. Likewise, Manu also says: "If a person is neither mentally incapacitated nor a minor, and his property is enjoyed [by another], that [claim] is defeated in legal proceedings; the enjoyer is entitled to that wealth."

Thus, the defeat [of the claim] has been shown from the perspective of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*vastu*). And the breakdown of the legal procedure is as follows: the possessor indeed says, "This man is not dull-witted, he is not a minor, and he is not a child; in his presence I have possessed this property for twenty years without opposition, and there are many witnesses to that.
If I were possessing his property through injustice, why would he remain indifferent for such a long time? And in that case, the opponent becomes speechless.

In this way, even for one who is without a superior (niruttara), a factual legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) certainly takes place, according to the rule: "The king should conduct legal proceedings by means of the truth, having set aside deception. Now, if it is argued: "Even if there is neither a loss of the substance of the case nor a loss of the legal proceeding itself, nevertheless, a suspicion arises that the legal proceeding is lost because [the judge] saw [the evidence] but did not refute it; therefore, to remove that [suspicion], it is taught that one must not remain silent," [we reply: [This is not so. For the purpose of removing that suspicion, silence is indeed prohibited. However, the prohibition against silence does not establish the existence of a legal proceeding. Rather, the existence of a legal proceeding is established solely by the fact that the defendant has been summoned and has remained silent despite being questioned. Therefore, since the very basis for the suspicion—that the legal proceeding is lost—is absent, the teaching that "one must not remain silent" is merely for the sake of removing that suspicion. Furthermore, the rule "one must not remain silent" is intended to prevent the suspicion that the legal proceeding is lost due to negligence on the part of the judge. It does not, however, establish the existence of a legal proceeding where none exists. Consequently, the objection that "there is no legal proceeding for one who is without a superior" is refuted. Thus, the claim that "one must not remain silent" is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of a lost legal proceeding is untenable. This concludes the section on the "loss of the legal proceeding" (*vyavahārahāni*). Now, the section on "confession" (*svīkāra*): In this regard, confession is of two kinds: that which occurs before the judge and that which occurs before witnesses. Among these, confession before the judge is of three types: 1) confession after being summoned, 2) confession upon being questioned, and 3) confession through silence. Confession before witnesses is of two types: 1) confession upon being questioned by the witnesses, and 2) confession through silence when the witnesses have been questioned. Among these, the first two types of confession—confession after being summoned and confession upon being questioned—are considered valid as grounds for judgment. The third type, confession through silence, is not accepted as a ground for judgment. This is because it is impossible to determine whether such silence is due to a lack of memory or due to a desire to conceal the truth. As for the two types of confession before witnesses, they are both accepted as grounds for judgment. This is because, in the case of witnesses, it is possible to determine whether their silence is due to a lack of memory or due to a desire to conceal the truth. Therefore, the rule is: "One should accept the confession of a litigant before the judge and before witnesses. This concludes the section on "confession. Now, the section on "oath" (*śapatha*): In this regard, an oath is of two kinds: that which is based on a divine witness and that which is based on a human witness. Among these, an oath based on a divine witness is of four types: 1) the *kūṭa-śapatha*, 2) the *mudrā-śapatha*, 3) the *agni-śapatha*, and 4) the *kośa-śapatha*. An oath based on a human witness is of two types: 1) the *satya-śapatha* and 2) the *anṛta-śapatha*. Among these, the *kūṭa-śapatha* consists of swearing an oath by touching a sacred object such as a cow or a Brahmin. The *mudrā-śapatha* consists of swearing an oath by placing one's hand upon a seal. The *agni-śapatha* consists of swearing an oath by holding fire. The *kośa-śapatha* consists of swearing an oath by drinking water from a vessel containing consecrated substances. The *satya-śapatha* consists of swearing an oath by saying, "I swear by the truth. The *anṛta-śapatha* consists of swearing an oath by saying, "I swear by falsehood. Among these, the *kūṭa-śapatha*, the *mudrā-śapatha*, and the *satya-śapatha* are to be administered to those of low status. The *agni-śapatha* and the *kośa-śapatha* are to be administered to those of middling status. The *anṛta-śapatha* is to be administered to those of high status. This is because, for those of low status, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are easy to perform; for those of middling status, the *agni-śapatha* and others are appropriate; and for those of high status, the *anṛta-śapatha* is suitable. Furthermore, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are not habitually sinful. The *agni-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are habitually sinful. This is because, for those who are not habitually sinful, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others do not cause great suffering; whereas for those who are habitually sinful, the *agni-śapatha* and others are necessary to produce the required effect. Moreover, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are not wealthy. The *agni-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are wealthy. This is because, for those who are not wealthy, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others do not require much expense; whereas for those who are wealthy, the *agni-śapatha* and others are appropriate. Furthermore, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are not afraid. The *agni-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are afraid. This is because, for those who are not afraid, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others do not cause fear; whereas for those who are afraid, the *agni-śapatha* and others are necessary to produce the required effect. Additionally, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are not prone to anger. The *agni-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are prone to anger. This is because, for those who are not prone to anger, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others do not provoke anger; whereas for those who are prone to anger, the *agni-śapatha* and others are necessary to produce the required effect. Furthermore, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are not prone to deceit. The *agni-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are prone to deceit. This is because, for those who are not prone to deceit, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others do not induce deceit; whereas for those who are prone to deceit, the *agni-śapatha* and others are necessary to produce the required effect. Moreover, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are not prone to greed. The *agni-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are prone to greed. This is because, for those who are not prone to greed, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others do not induce greed; whereas for those who are prone to greed, the *agni-śapatha* and others are necessary to produce the required effect. Finally, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are not prone to pride. The *agni-śapatha* and others are to be administered to those who are prone to pride. This is because, for those who are not prone to pride, the *kūṭa-śapatha* and others do not induce pride; whereas for those who are prone to pride, the *agni-śapatha* and others are necessary to produce the required effect. This concludes the section on "oath. Now, the section on "ordeals" (*divya*): In this regard, an ordeal is of five kinds: 1) the *taptamāṣaka*, 2) the *phāla*, 3) the *kośa*, 4) the *taṇḍula*, and 5) the *dharma*. Among these, the *taptamāṣaka* consists of swallowing a heated ball of gold. The *phāla* consists of drawing a ploughshare. The *kośa* consists of drinking water from a vessel containing consecrated substances. The *taṇḍula* consists of chewing rice grains. The *dharma* consists of invoking the gods. Among

But that is not so, because possession (*bhukti*) belonging to a period remembered from tradition lacks the quality of being a cause for suspicion of loss; if the intention were merely to state that "one should not remain silent," the mention of twenty years would be unintended as a specific limit.
Now, it might be argued:
the mention of twenty years is for the purpose of precluding the raising of objections regarding defects in the document after that time.
As Kātyāyana has said: "When a person who is capable [of contesting] enjoys property through a document in the presence of the owner for twenty years, that document is free from defects."
Thus:
"When a person enjoys property by means of a document in the presence of one who has the power [to object],
and twenty years have elapsed, that document is free from defect."

That too is not correct; for even in the case of pledges (*ādhi*) and the like, since the refutation of the raising of defects in the document after twenty years is the same [for all], it would be impossible to apply exceptions such as "beyond the boundary" (*adhisīma*).
As Kātyāyana says: "Now, if a pledge has been enjoyed for twenty years with certainty, its validity is established by that document, free from any defects of the document."
Likewise: When a dispute over boundaries has been decided, a boundary-deed (sīmāpatra) is to be executed;
its defects must be declared for a period of twenty years.
Thus, when a dispute over boundaries has been decided, a boundary-deed (sīmāpatra) is prescribed;
its defects must be declared for a period of twenty years.
By this, the statement that "the [period for] wealth is ten years" is also refuted.
Therefore, the true meaning of this verse must be stated.
It is said:
In this context, what is intended is the loss of the fruit of the land and the wealth, not the loss of the substance itself, nor the loss of legal title.

For instance, although an owner may rightfully recover his field after twenty years of possession by one who has been free from reproach, he does not obtain the fruits [accruing therefrom] due to his own fault—characterized by his failure to object—and because of this specific textual provision.
However, in the case of possession in absentia (*parokṣabhoga*), he certainly does obtain the fruits even after twenty years, because of the expression "he sees" (*paśyate*).

And because of the statement, "if he does not speak when there is direct enjoyment and verbal abuse," one acquires [the property] before twenty years have passed even if it is witnessed and without verbal abuse, since the term "twenty" is specified.
Now, an objection: since the ownership of the fruit produced from that [property] still belongs to him, its loss is indeed untenable.
"Certainly.

When it remains exactly as it was without the destruction of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), then—as in the case of the betel-nut, jackfruit, trees, and so forth produced from it—the ownership (*svatva*) is lost only through the destruction of that [nature] which was produced from it and has perished due to enjoyment. However, 'He who enjoys what has not been lawfully acquired, even for many hundreds of years, the king should punish that sinner with the punishment for a thief.'"

By this statement, having calculated [the value] as a price of redemption, the obligation to pay an amount of goods equal to that [property], like a thief, would have resulted; however, this is set aside by the rule "loss occurs after twenty years.
Furthermore, the royal punishment certainly remains even beyond twenty years, because there is no exception for possession exceeding that period.
Therefore, it is established that due to the owner's own fault characterized by negligence, and by virtue of this statement, he does not recover the produce after twenty years.
By this, the rule that "wealth [is purified] by ten years" is also explained. (2.24)
He states the exceptions to this rule:
"Except for property placed in deposit within the boundary, that belonging to the dull-witted or children,
and likewise except for sealed deposits, and the property of the king, women, and Vedic scholars."

*Ādhi* (pledge), *sīmā* (boundary), and *upanikṣepa* (deposit) constitute "pledges, boundaries, and deposits. *Jaḍa* (the dull-witted) and *bāla* (the child) constitute "the dull-witted and the child"; their wealth is "the wealth of the dull-witted and the child. [The compound] *ādhisīmopanikṣepajaḍabāladhana* refers to pledges, boundaries, deposits, and the wealth of the dull-witted and the child; [the phrase means] "without these. A *upanikṣepa* is defined as property placed in the hand of another for the purpose of protection, after having displayed its form and number.
As Nārada said:
"When one deposits one's own property with another out of trust and without hesitation,
that is declared by the wise to be the legal title known as 'deposit' (nikṣepa)."
Thus:
"That wherein one deposits one's own property out of trust, free from apprehension, is called 'deposit' (nikṣepa) by the wise; such is the title of law."
*Upanidhāna* means a deposit (*upanidhi*).

In the case of pledges (*ādhi*) and the like, even if one sees [the property] and does not speak of it, there is no loss of interest (*upacaya-hāni*) for land after twenty years, nor for wealth after ten years; this is because such a fault on the part of the person is absent, and because the grounds for neglect exist in each respective case.
For instance, in the case of a pledge, enjoyment is conditioned precisely by its status as a pledge; thus, even if there is neglect, it does not constitute a fault on the part of the person.
Neglect is possible in the case of a boundary because it is easily established through signs such as long-standing ash or charcoal;

neglect is also appropriate in the case of deposits (upanikṣepa) and sealed trusts (upanidhi), since their consumption is prohibited, and if they are consumed in violation of that prohibition, one obtains the fruit along with interest;
furthermore, neglect is entirely fitting in the case of the mentally disabled and children, due to their lack of capacity and immaturity respectively.
Because the king is preoccupied with many affairs;
because women are ignorant and lacking in confidence;
and because the Vedic scholar is occupied with studying, teaching, investigating the meaning of those [texts], and performing rituals—neglect is indeed appropriate in these cases.

Therefore, since the grounds for indifference exist in all cases such as [the loss of] property and so forth, there is never any loss of the fruit when the enjoyment is witnessed and no protest is raised. (2.25)
In order to prescribe specific punishments for those who misappropriate deposits and the like, he says:
"The king shall cause the one who misappropriates deposits and so forth to pay the wealth to the owner,
and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or else [a fine] according to his capacity."

The phrase "ya ādhyādīnām... is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) meaning that one should cause the person who, by virtue of long-term possession, has seized wealth subject to dispute—ranging from deposits (*ādhi*) up to the property of a *śrotriya*—to restore it to its owner.
The injunction (*vidhi*) is that he should also cause him to pay a fine equal to that to the king—that is, a fine equal to the value of the disputed property.

Although a fine equal to the value of the property is not possible in the case of houses, fields, and the like, nevertheless, [the rule applies] in cases such as "in the breaking of a boundary" and "in the transgression of a limit."
The punishment to be described hereafter, beginning with these words, is to be understood.

Now, if the subduing of the thief through a penalty equal to the value of the property is not possible because he possesses great wealth, then one should cause him to pay wealth according to his capacity.

One should cause him to pay as much as will result in the subsiding of his arrogance; for they say that "punishment (*daṇḍa*) is from subduing (*damana*)," and since the purpose of taking up the staff of punishment is for the sake of subduing those who are unsubdued.

But he who does not possess even an equivalent amount of property should be made to pay as much as causes him pain. Furthermore, one who has no wealth at all should be subdued by means of a "punishment of reproach" (*dhig-daṇḍa*) and other such methods.
And so says Manu:
One should first apply the punishment of censure, followed by the punishment of verbal reprimand;
thirdly, the punishment of a fine, and after that, the punishment of corporal punishment.
Thus:
"One should first apply the punishment of reproach, then the punishment of verbal censure;
thirdly, the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal death."
Even corporal punishment for those other than Brahmins has been shown to be tenfold.
Thus Manu says:
"Manu, the son of Svayambhū, declared ten places for punishment."
Whatever wealth may belong to the three castes, a Brāhmaṇa may take it away unharmed.
The genitals, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Thus said Manu, the son of Svayambhū, regarding the ten places of punishment for the three social orders; a Brāhmaṇa, however, should depart unhurt.
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
It should be understood that if these individuals commit an offense against the *nimitta* (the ritual object), punishment must be meted out right there at the *upastha* and so forth;
they should either be made to perform labor or be cast into prison,
as stated by Kātyāyana.
Having ascertained that he is unable to pay the fine, one should compel him to perform labor under one's own supervision;
if he is incapable of even that, he should be cast into prison—with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus:
Having ascertained that [the debtor] is unable to pay the debt, one may compel him to perform labor under one's own authority;
if he is incapable of labor, he should be cast into prison, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, when there is an absence of property, punishments such as separation from ritual duties (*karmaviyoga*) and so forth are to be applied.

As Gautama says: "In the event of [the inability to pay] due to lack of livelihood, [punishments] such as separation from ritual duties, public proclamation of the offense, banishment, and branding with marks (*aṅkakaraṇa*) are to be employed. Nārada also states:
Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding,
and the amputation of limbs— this is declared to be the punishment of the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
The rule for punishment is ordained to apply without distinction to all alike.
Having said this, he spoke again: "Except for execution, a Brahmin does not deserve death; no other form of killing is appropriate for a Brahmin."
Thus:
"Except for execution, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death."
Shaving the head is his punishment, as is banishment from the city;
furthermore, he shall have the mark of his crime branded on his forehead and be made to travel upon a donkey.
Thus [it is said].
Shaving the head is his punishment, followed by banishment from the city;
furthermore, he shall have the mark of his crime branded on his forehead and be made to travel on a donkey.
And the rule regarding branding is shown: "For violating the Guru's bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the foot of a dog should be made; and for killing a Brahmin, a headless male figure."
Thus:
"In the case of violating the teacher's bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the footprint of a dog shall be made; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man."

As for the statement of Āpastamba, "The eyes of a Brāhmaṇa [should be] covered," its meaning is that at the time of his banishment from the city, the eyes of the Brāhmaṇa should be covered with a cloth or similar material; it does not mean the plucking out of the eyes, because that would contradict the statements of Manu, Gautama, and others such as, "A Brāhmaṇa shall go unhurt" and "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. Enough of this digression. (2.26)
It has been stated that possession (*bhoga*) is authoritative regarding ownership (*svatva*) because it is invariably concomitant with ownership.
Since mere possession can deviate from ownership, [the author] asks what kind of possession is authoritative; therefore, he says:
"Title (*āgama*) is more weighty than possession, except in the case of possession inherited through prior succession."
The cause of ownership is acquisition (*āgama*), such as acceptance of a gift or purchase;
it is stronger even than possession (*bhoga*), because possession requires acquisition for the cognition of ownership.
As Nārada said:
Possession acquired through pure title attains the status of valid proof;
possession with impure title never attains validity.
Thus:
Possession that is accompanied by pure title attains the status of valid proof;
possession with impure title never attains validity.

Ownership is not understood from mere enjoyment alone, because it is possible to enjoy even what belongs to another through seizure and other such means. For this very reason: "But he who asserts enjoyment alone, and never the legal title (āgama), should be known as a thief under the pretext of a fraudulent claim of possession."
Thus it is recorded in the Smṛti.

Therefore, it is stated that possession (*bhoga*) endowed with five specific qualifications—namely, being accompanied by title (*sāgama*), long-standing (*dīrghakāla*), uninterrupted (*nirantara*), free from protest (*nirākrośa*), and witnessed by the opponent (*pratyarthipratyakṣa*)—is authoritative.
And so it is recorded in the Smṛti.
Possession is fivefold: it consists of [title] with documentary evidence, long duration, uninterruptedness, non-abandonment by another, and enjoyment in the presence of the opponent.
Possession is fivefold: it must be accompanied by title, long-standing, uninterrupted, not abandoned by another, and even while the opponent is present, there must be actual enjoyment.
And in some cases, possession (*bhoga*) is authoritative even when independent of title (*āgama*); thus he says, "except for that which has come down through the succession of ancestors.

"Succession of ancestors" (*pūrvakrama*) refers to the sequence of the three preceding generations, beginning with the father; the connection is that, except for possession that has come down by such means, title is superior. Furthermore, that [possession] is superior to title.
The meaning is that scripture (*āgama*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it is independent of [prior] knowledge.
In this regard, scripture is independent of what is unknown, not independent of existence;
for it should be understood that its very existence is apprehended by that [scripture] itself.
The phrase "except for that which has come down through prior succession" is intended to demonstrate the period beyond the reach of memory (*asmārtakāla*).
Furthermore, the principle that "title (*āgama*) is superior to possession (*bhoga*)" pertains to the period within the reach of memory (*smārtakāla*).

Consequently, since the absence of title can be ascertained during a period amenable to memory through the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), possession possesses legal validity only when it is dependent upon knowledge of such title.

But in a period beyond the reach of memory (*asmārta-kāla*), since it is impossible to ascertain the absence of scriptural title due to the lack of non-perception of a competent [title], continuous possession alone, independent of knowledge of such a title, is the means of proof.
This very point has been clarified by Kātyāyana:
"In the period within the reach of memory, the legal act regarding land is required; possession is held to be [valid] only when accompanied by title."
Because there is no means of tracing [the lineage] beyond what is recorded in memory, [the impurity] lasts for three generations in succession.
Thus:
"In the period of memory (smārta-kāla), possession of land is held to require both a title and enjoyment;
in the period beyond memory (asmārta), because there is no means of tracing it back, it is established by possession passed down through three generations in succession."
And the period prescribed by traditional law (*smārta*) extends up to one hundred years, based on the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years.
The phrase "due to the absence of following" means that there is no certainty regarding the absence of title because of the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*).

Therefore, possession that exceeds a hundred years—being continuous, unopposed, and witnessed by the opponent—even when the absence of title is not certain, leads to the inference of title and establishes ownership, as it is invariably concomitant with it.

Even in a period beyond the reach of memory (*asmārta-kāla*), as long as there exists an unbroken tradition of the remembrance of [the source] scripture (*anāgama-smṛti-paramparā*), possession (*bhoga*) is not a means of valid proof.

For this very reason, it is said: "But he who possesses property without a title to it (*anāgama*), even for many hundreds of years—the king should punish that sinner with the punishment prescribed for a thief."
Thus it has been stated.

Furthermore, one should not conclude from the singular reference in the phrase "he who enjoys [property] without title" (*anāgamam tu yo bhuṅkte*) and from the use of the word "even" (*api*) in "even for many hundreds of years" (*bahūny abdaśatāny api*), that the prescription of punishment applies only to the first person who enjoys it without title for a long period. For if that were so, it would follow that the enjoyment without title of a second or third person would also be valid, which is not accepted. Indeed, it is held that in the beginning the cause is the gift (*dāna*), while in the middle it is possession with title (*bhuktiḥ sāgamā*).

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Nārada. Therefore, in all cases of possession without title, this [verse]—"But he who enjoys without title"—is to be understood as applicable. Furthermore, as for the statement: "Even that which was enjoyed through improper means by the father and three preceding ancestors..."
That which has come down through three generations cannot be taken away by force.

Thus, that too should be construed as "with the father and the three preceding ancestors. In that case as well, the phrase "transmitted through three generations in succession" serves as the defining characteristic of possession for a period beyond the scope of memory (*asmārta-kāla*). If one intended only three specific individuals, then since the passing of three persons could occur even within a single year, it would follow that possession in the second year—even if lacking a formal title—would be authoritative.
If that were the case, there would be a contradiction with the Smṛti which states: "In the period governed by the Smṛtis, possession of land is accepted as valid when accompanied by title.

Furthermore, the phrase "even that which has been enjoyed through injustice" must be explained as meaning that even what has been enjoyed unjustly cannot be taken away, let alone when the injustice is not established; for this is indicated by the hearing of the word "api" (even).
And as it was said by Hārīta:
"That which has been enjoyed for a long time by three preceding generations without a title deed cannot be taken away, having come down through the succession of three persons."
Thus, even in that case, it means "absolutely without scriptural authority" (*āgama*).
This should be explained as "absolutely without a perceivable scriptural authority," and not as "without the very nature of scriptural authority.
For it has been stated that in the absence of the very nature of scriptural authority, ownership does not arise even through a hundred enjoyments.
"Transmitted through three generations in succession"—the meaning of this has already been explained.
Now, an objection: when possession (*bhoga*) occurs at a time suitable for recollection, its validity as dependent upon title (*āgama*) is untenable.

For instance, if the title is already known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then since ownership is understood by that very [title], possession has no authority regarding either ownership or the title itself.
Now, if the title-deed has not been understood through another means of knowledge, how can possession qualified by it be a means of proof?
It is said in reply:
possession that is continuous and accompanied by a title-deed understood through another means of knowledge establishes ownership at a later time.

Even if a title deed is known, it is not capable of establishing ownership after a lapse of time if it is devoid of possession, because in the interim, ownership may have ceased through such means as gift or sale;
thus, everything is beyond reproach.
It has been stated that possession is authoritative when it depends upon title (*āgama*). In that case, title would be authoritative even independently of possession; therefore, he says:
"Even in the case of title, there is indeed no strength whatsoever where there is not even the slightest possession."
In that scriptural tradition (*āgama*) where there is not even the slightest enjoyment or use, there is no complete authority at all.
This is the intended meaning:
giving consists in the cessation of one's own ownership and the transfer of it to the ownership of another.
And the transfer of ownership to another occurs only if the other person accepts it, and not otherwise.
Acceptance is threefold:
mental, verbal, and physical.
Among these, the mental [appropriation] consists of the form of the conceptualization "this is mine.
The vocal, however, is a determinate cognition characterized by the articulation of such expressions as "this is mine" and so forth.
The physical, moreover, is of many kinds, consisting of the taking up, touching, and so on.

And in that regard, a rule is recorded in the Smṛti: "One should give a black antelope skin on the back, a cow at the tail, an elephant on the trunk, likewise a horse on the mane, and one should cause a female slave to be given on the head."
Thus it is said:
"One should give a black antelope skin upon the back, a cow at the tail,
an elephant at the trunk, likewise a horse at the mane, and one should cause a female slave to be given upon the head."
Āśvalāyana also says: "One should recite the mantras over animate things, touch them, and likewise for inanimate things and a maiden.

In that regard, since the taking [of possession] through lifting and so forth is possible immediately after the offering of water in the case of gold, clothing, and the like, all three types of acceptance are accomplished. However, in the case of fields and such, since physical acceptance is impossible apart from the enjoyment of the fruit, there must be some degree of enjoyment, even if slight; otherwise, the transfer of ownership—such as through gift or purchase—does not reach completion. Thus, a title of ownership (*āgama*) lacking physical acceptance characterized by the enjoyment of the fruit is weak compared to a title accompanied by such enjoyment.

And this applies when there is no knowledge of the prior or subsequent timing of the two; however, when the prior and subsequent timing are known, even if defective, the acquisition of the earlier time alone is stronger.
Alternatively, it has been stated that "written evidence, witnesses, and possession acquired through three generations are the means of proof.

Regarding the conflict of these, where and which one possesses greater force, this [verse] is applicable: "Acquisition is superior to possession, except in the case of possession acquired through prior succession."
Even if there is scriptural authority, it possesses no strength at all where there is not even a slight amount of possession.
Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning:
in the case of the first person, a title of ownership (*āgama*) established by witnesses is stronger even than possession, provided it is without possession inherited through prior succession.

Furthermore, possession inherited through prior succession is stronger than title derived from a written document; however, in the interim, even a title accompanied by only slight possession is stronger than a title devoid of possession.
This very point has been clarified by Nārada: "In the beginning, the cause is the gift; in the middle, possession accompanied by title."
The sole ground [of ownership] is possession itself—continuous and long-standing.
Thus [ends verse] 2.27.
In the beginning, possession is the cause; in the middle, enjoyment accompanied by title is the cause;
but in the case of long-standing, continuous enjoyment, that alone is the cause.

Regarding the statement "of one who sees but does not speak," it has been declared that after twenty years of possession for land, or ten years of possession for wealth, there can be no pursuit of the fruits [of the property].

Anticipating the objection that, just as there is no pursuit of the fruits, there will likewise be no pursuit of punishment, the author speaks as follows to demonstrate the determination of punishment based on the status of the person and the validity of the title:
"But he by whom a title-deed was made, when sued, must produce it."
Neither his son nor the son of his son [has a right there]; in that case, possession is more weighty.

When a person is challenged as to how he acquired land or other property—asking, "From where did you obtain this field and so forth?"—he must establish and demonstrate that acquisition, such as through a formal gift (*pratigraha*), by means of written documents and other evidence.
By this, it is implied that punishment shall befall the first possessor who fails to produce proof of his acquisition.
However, his son, the second in line, when challenged, need not produce proof of acquisition; rather, he must prove possession for an uninterrupted period in the presence of witnesses.

By this, it is established that for the second [successor], who does not produce a title of ownership (*āgama*), there is no punishment; rather, punishment applies to one who fails to produce a special enjoyment (*viśiṣṭa-bhoga*).
His son, the third, shall neither produce a title nor a special enjoyment, but only the mere enjoyment descended through succession (*kramāgata-bhogamātra*).

By this, it is declared that for the third, there is punishment for failing to produce the enjoyment inherited through succession, but not for failing to produce a title, nor for failing to produce a special enjoyment.
In that regard, between those two—the second and the third—possession alone is more significant.
Even there, it should be discerned that possession is weightier in the second case, while it is even weightier in the third.
The essential meaning is that although the loss of the object is exactly the same in all three cases if the title is not produced, there is a distinction in terms of the penalty.
And it has been stated by Hārīta:
"He who has made a formal agreement (āgama) but fails to deliver it shall be punished;
neither his son nor his grandson is liable for that, though for both of them there is the loss of the enjoyment [of the property]."
Thus [ends verse] 2.28.
He who has made a formal agreement (āgama) but fails to carry it out shall be punished;
neither his son nor his grandson is liable for that, though both of them suffer the loss of their right to enjoy the property.

It has been stated that possession for a period not recorded in memory is authoritative when independent of knowledge of a title; however, regarding the phrase "except for that which has come down through prior succession," he states an exception to that rule:
"If one who is accused should die, his heir shall clear him [of the charge];
in that case, possession established without a title is no ground [for ownership]."
Furthermore, when the one who initiated the suit or another party has died—having passed away before a judicial decision has been reached—then his heir, such as a son, shall produce that title.
For in such a case, possession devoid of a title, even if established by witnesses and other means, is not authoritative;
because possession is subject to challenge when it is preceded by a formal legal claim.
Nārada has also said: "The son must clear up the claim of a deceased litigant who had carried his lawsuit to such an extent; mere possession shall not bar that claim."
Thus [ends verse] 2.29.
When a deceased litigant has thus entered into a dispute, his son must clear up that matter; possession shall not overturn it.
It has been established that when a lawsuit is not yet decided and the litigant has died, the legal proceeding does not continue.

However, even when a lawsuit has been decided and the litigant remains alive, the proceeding may in some cases continue and in others it may not; therefore, in order to establish this rule, the author states the relative strength and weakness of those who oversee legal proceedings:
"Groups authorized by the king, guilds, and likewise families..."
In the legal procedure for men, each preceding one is to be known as more authoritative than the following.

"Appointed by the king" refers to those authorized by the sovereign for the administration of justice, as stated in such passages as "the king shall appoint members of the court. "Guilds" (pūga) refers to groups or associations of people of different castes and different occupations who reside in the same place, such as villages, cities, and the like.
"Corporations" (śreṇi) refers to assemblies of people belonging to various castes who subsist by the same type of craft or occupation.
As in the case of the Heḍābukas and others, or betel-sellers, weavers, leather-workers, and so forth;
"families" (kulāni) refers to the assemblies of kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
Among these four—beginning with those appointed by the king—it should be understood and known that whichever is mentioned earlier in the sequence is more significant and possesses greater authority.
This is stated regarding the procedure for legal proceedings—that is, the business of adjudicating lawsuits—for men who are litigants:

even if a person who has been defeated in a lawsuit decided upon by those authorized by the king feels dissatisfaction due to a perception based on false views, there is no further legal proceeding against him in the *pūga* (guilds) and similar bodies.
