Likewise, once a case has been decided by a *pūga*, there is no recourse to the *śreṇi* (corporations) and so forth.
Likewise, when one has been determined by a guild (*śreṇi*), there is no going to a family (*kula*). But when one has been determined by a family, there is going to a guild and so forth.
When one has been determined by a guild, there is going to a corporation (*pūga*) and so forth.
It is said that when a case has been decided by a *pūga*, one may go to the king.

However, Nārada further stated that even when a legal dispute has been decided by royal officials, one may still go to the king: "Families, guilds, assemblies, royal officials, and the king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one among these is more authoritative than the preceding."
Thus:
"Families, guilds, assemblies, and appointed officials, O King, are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one among these is more authoritative than the preceding."

And in that case, when the king has gone there accompanied by the courtiers and the legal proceeding is being decided by the former courtiers in a suit involving a wager, if that proponent of a false view is defeated, then he shall be punished;
but if he is victorious, then the authorized courtiers shall be punished. (2.30)

It has been stated that a legal proceeding seen by weak judges may be overturned, but one seen by powerful ones does not cease. Now, he says that even a proceeding seen by the powerful may in some cases be set aside: "He shall annul legal proceedings brought about through force or fraud."
Likewise, those caused by women, at night, within the house, outside the house, or by enemies; |||
He shall set aside legal proceedings that have been brought about or completed through force, compulsion, fraud, fear, or similar means;
likewise those involving women,
and even those occurring at night, even when not involving women.

The connection [of the verse] is that he should terminate legal proceedings initiated by enemies within the interior of the house—that is, inside the home—and outside of villages and other such places. (2.31)
Regarding those who do not engage in legal proceedings,
he says: "A lawsuit instigated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by illness, beset by calamity, a child, or terrified,
as well as one brought about by an incompetent person, is not valid."
Moreover:
"intoxicated" means by means of an intoxicating substance; "insane" means afflicted by the fivefold insanity arising from wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, or possession by a spirit.
The "afflicted" (ārta) is one suffering from disease and the like.
The "one in distress" (vyasanin) is one who possesses the misery (duḥkha) produced by separation from the desired or the attainment of the undesired.
The "childish" (bāla) is one unfit for worldly transaction (vyavahāra).
"Frightened" means [fearful] of enemies.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it refers to those who are hostile toward cities, kingdoms, and so forth.
This includes one who is hostile toward cities and kingdoms, as well as one who has been dismissed by the king.
The argument stated by those who know the Dharma would be unacceptable.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Manu:
"A legal proceeding (vyavahāra) conducted by these [persons] does not succeed.
The connection is that even a legal proceeding conducted by those who are unappointed or unrelated does not succeed.
As for the traditional legal maxim (smaraṇa): "In a dispute between teacher and pupil, father and son, husband and wife, or master and servant, a lawsuit between them is not valid."

Thus, even that [statement] does not intend to prohibit all worldly interaction (*atyantika-vyavahāra-pratiṣedha*) between teacher and disciple and so forth, because some form of interaction among them is indeed accepted. For it is thus stated in the *Smṛti* of Gautama: "The correction of a disciple is without corporal punishment; if that is impossible, it may be done with a thin rope or a split bamboo cane; one who strikes him with anything else shall be punished by the king"; and from the *Smṛti* of Manu: "In no way [should he strike] on the head."

If a teacher, under the influence of a fit of anger, strikes a student on the head with a severe punishment, and the student—being unassailable because he has departed from the path of mindfulness—reports this to the king, then that indeed becomes a ground for legal dispute (*vyavahārapada*).

Likewise, according to the statement beginning with "land acquired by the grandfather," when ownership over land and other property acquired by the grandfather is equal for both father and son, if the father destroys the grandfather’s acquired land and so forth through sale or other means, and the son then approaches the judicial authority, then a legal dispute arises between the father and the son as well.
Likewise, in times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction,
a husband is not required to give back the wife's property against his will.

According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), if—apart from cases such as famine—the husband, despite possessing wealth, does not give his wife's property when requested even after having spent it, then a legal dispute (*vyavahāra*) between the husband and wife is indeed recognized. Likewise, he will describe a legal dispute between a food-slave (*bhaktadāsa*) and his master.

He will also speak regarding a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*) and others, in the context of those beginning with the "slave born in the womb," [in the verse]: "And whoever among these should liberate his master from a life-threatening danger... [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.183].
From that state of servitude he shall be released, and he shall receive his share as a son.
Since this has been stated by Nārada, who can prevent a legal proceeding between a master and [his dependents] regarding their non-release or the taking of a share of the son's property?

Therefore, a legal proceeding with teachers and others does not lead to welfare in either the visible or invisible realms; thus, students and the like must first be restrained by the king together with his council. This is the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "Of the teacher, the student," and so forth.
However, if there is extreme persistence, a legal proceeding may be initiated even against students and others in the manner previously described.
Furthermore, it has been declared by those who know the Dharma that a lawsuit involving one person against many, or concerning women and servants, is not to be admitted.

This is the statement of Nārada. In that regard, because of the Smṛti texts such as, "He who misappropriates the property of a corporation, he who violates an agreement," and likewise, "One person against many," it should be understood that a legal proceeding with many parties is intended only when they have a common purpose; therefore, a simultaneous legal proceeding of one person against many who have distinct purposes does not occur.

Regarding the phrase "of women," this should be explained as follows: since women such as those belonging to cowherds, vintners, and so forth, do indeed engage in legal proceedings due to their independence, the meaning is that for all other women, while their husbands are alive, legal proceedings are inadmissible because of their dependence on them.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and of servants," this too should be explained as follows: because servants are dependent on their masters, even when conducting legal proceedings for their own interests, they may do so only with the master's permission, and not otherwise. (2.32)
Having stated that legal proceedings are subject to reversal, he now speaks of property subject to reversal:
"Lost property that has been found must be returned by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by signs, he deserves a fine equal to its value."

Gold and other property that has been lost, recovered by customs officers, local guardians, or others, and delivered to the king, must be returned by the king to the owner, provided the owner establishes his ownership through characteristics such as appearance and number.
If he does not establish it, then he should be fined an amount equal to that property because of his false testimony.
Since the discovery of lost property is a cause for ownership, this verse declares that once ownership is established, its reversal [to the finder] is prohibited.
And in this regard, he will state the time limit: "Goods lost, stolen, or recovered [by thieves] shall be reclaimed by the owner within one year; after that, the king shall take them."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, Manu has specified a period of three years as the limit: "The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
before the end of three years the owner may take it, but after that, the king may take it."
Thus:
Property whose owner has disappeared, the king shall cause to be kept for three years. Within three years the owner may take it; after that, the king may take it.
In that case, it must necessarily be protected for a period of up to three years. If the owner should arrive before the lapse of one year, then he shall give back the entire thing.
But when he arrives after one year has passed, then, having taken a sixth part as the price for protection, he shall give the remainder to the owner.
As it is said: "Then the king, remembering the duty of the virtuous, shall take a sixth part, or even a tenth or a twelfth, of goods lost and then recovered."
Thus,
remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of goods lost and then found.

In that case, in the first year one should give the whole amount; in the second year, a twelfth part; in the third year, a tenth; and from the fourth year onwards, having taken a sixth part, one should give the remainder.
A fourth part of the king’s share must be given to the finder.
However, if the owner does not appear, the king, after giving a fourth part of the entire property to the finder, shall take the remainder for himself.
Thus Gautama says: "Having found property whose owner has disappeared, it should be guarded by the king for one year; after that, a fourth part belongs to the finder, and the remainder to the king.
Here, the singular number in "one year" is not intended to be restrictive, because of the traditional legal authority (smṛti) stating, "The king should cause it to be deposited for three years.
Furthermore, the statement "after that, the king may take it" is intended to permit the king's expenditure of the property after three years have passed, provided the owner has not appeared.
After that, when the owner has arrived, even though the property has been expended, the king shall deduct his own share and give an amount equal to it.
And this refers to gold and similar items;
regarding cattle and the like, he will state later: "In the case of one-hoofed animals, he shall pay [the value] in paṇas," and so forth. (2.33)

Having stated the rule for the discovery of lost gold and other items that have fallen in a street, at a toll-house, or elsewhere, he now states the rule for the discovery of what is called a "treasure" (nidhi)—gold and the like long buried in the earth:
"The king, having found a treasure, shall give half to the twice-born;
but a learned twice-born man may take the whole, since he is the master of all."
When a treasure is found by someone other than the rightful owner, the king shall take a sixth part;
if the finder fails to report it and is subsequently discovered, he must be made to pay that [treasure] as well as a fine.
Having discovered a treasure-trove of the characteristics previously described, the king shall give half to Brāhmaṇas and deposit the remainder in the treasury.

However, if a learned Brāhmaṇa—one endowed with Vedic learning and study and possessed of virtuous conduct—should find a treasure, he may take the whole of it, because such a person is the master of the entire world. But when a treasure is found by anyone other than the king or a learned Brāhmaṇa—that is, by an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or others—the king shall give a sixth part to the finder and take the remaining treasure for himself.

As Vasiṣṭha says: "Whatever property that is not being claimed a person may find, the king shall take that; he should give a sixth part to the finder. Gautama also states: "The discovery of a treasure-trove becomes the property of the king, except in the case of a worthy Brāhmaṇa; some say that a non-Brāhmaṇa who reports it shall receive a sixth part.
In the word *anivedite*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* denotes the agent.

One who has found a treasure but neither reported it nor informed the king—having been discovered by the king after failing to report it—must be made to surrender the entire treasure and pay a fine according to his capacity.

However, if the rightful owner of the treasure arrives and establishes his ownership through its appearance, quantity, and other such characteristics, then the king, having returned the treasure to him, shall take for himself a sixth or a twelfth part.
As Manu says:
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.
Thus:
"If a man should truthfully declare, 'This treasure belongs to me,' the king shall take a sixth part, or indeed a twelfth part, of it."
However, the distinction regarding the portions (aṃśa) should be understood as depending on the [specific] phoneme, time, and so forth. 2.34–2.35.
Regarding property stolen by thieves, he says: "The king must restore to the subject property stolen by thieves;
for by not restoring it, he incurs the sin belonging to the owner of that property."

Property stolen by thieves, having been recovered from them, must be given by the king to the local inhabitant of his own country to whom that property belongs. For, by not giving it— that is, by failing to restore it— the king incurs the guilt of the person whose property was stolen,
as well as the guilt of the thief himself.
As Manu has said: "The wealth stolen by thieves must be restored by the king to people of all castes;
the king who makes use of that [wealth] incurs the guilt of the thief."
Thus:
"The king must restore to all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief."

If one takes [the property] from the hand of a thief and uses it oneself, then one incurs the guilt of the thief. If, however, one neglects what has been stolen by a thief, then one incurs the guilt of the local official.
If, despite striving to recover what was stolen by a thief, one is unable to do so, then one should give that much wealth from one's own treasury.

As Gautama says: "Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he should restore it to its proper place, or he should give it from his own treasury" (GDh 10.46–47). Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana also states: "But if one is unable to recover wealth stolen by thieves, that indeed should be given from his own treasury by the king who is incapable [of recovering it]."
Thus [ends verse] 2.36.
If wealth stolen by thieves cannot be recovered,
it must indeed be paid from the king's own treasury by the ruler who is unable to recover it.

Having explained the *vyavahāramātṛkā* (the matrix of legal procedure) in its common and uncommon forms, he now demonstrates the first of the eighteen titles of law (*vyavahārapada*), namely the title of "Non-payment of Debt" (*ṛṇādāna*), beginning with the verse "The interest shall be one-eightieth part" and ending with "the pledge shall be released when the debt has doubled through the profit derived from it.

That non-payment of debt is of seven kinds. Regarding the debtor, it is of five types: such a debt is payable; such a debt is not payable; it must be paid by this specific authority; it must be paid at this specific time; and it must be paid in this specific manner.

The procedure regarding debt consists of two types: the procedure for giving and the procedure for taking. This has been clarified by Nārada: "That which is to be given and that which is not to be given, by whom, where, and in what manner—through the rules of giving and receiving, this is known as the law of lending and borrowing (*ṛṇādāna*)."
Thus:
"That which is to be given and that which is not to be given, by whom, where, and in what manner—
through the two dharmas of giving and receiving, this is known as the title of law concerning the recovery of debts."
In that regard, he first states the rule for the creditor’s receipt of payment, because the other rules are preceded by it:
"The interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month after month when there is a pledge;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be one-hundredth, one-fiftieth, one-thirtieth, one-twentieth, or one-fifteenth."

"Month by month," that is, every month, "secured by a pledge" (sabandhaka) refers to a loan where a pledge is deposited for the sake of confidence—that is, as a mortgage (*ādhi*). In such a secured transaction, an eightieth part of the principal lent is the lawful interest.
Otherwise, in an unsecured transaction, the lawful interest for the social classes—beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—is respectively two, three, four, and five percent per hundred.

When a Brāhmaṇa is the debtor, the interest is two per cent; for a Kṣatriya, three per cent; for a Vaiśya, four per cent; and for a Śūdra, five per cent, month after month. Thus, two, three, four, or five—namely *dvitricatuḥpañca*—are given as interest on this hundred, hence it is called a *dvitricatuḥpañcaka* hundred. Following the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*, which continues from the previous sūtra, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense: "that [amount] is given as interest, profit, gain, toll, or fee on this.
Additional verse found in some manuscripts: Interest upon interest is *cakravṛddhi*; however, that which is paid monthly is *kālikā*.
That which is performed intentionally would be bodily [action] through bodily karma.
And this interest, being taken month by month, is called *kālikā*;
this same interest, when divided by a calculation of days and taken daily, becomes *kāyikā*.
And so it has been stated by Nārada: "Interest is of four kinds: *kāyikā*, *kālikā*, *kāritā*, and likewise another."
And in the treatises, its increase is described as fourfold: the increase of the wheel and the increase of the person.

Having said this, it was stated: "That increase which is not inconsistent with one's physical means, consisting of a quarter-pana or similar amounts, flowing month by month—that is considered *kālikā*."
That interest which is caused by the debtor himself is called "stipulated interest. Interest upon interest is declared to be "compound interest" (cakravṛddhi).
Thus [ends verse] 2.37.
Interest that does not conflict with the principal, which accrues as a fixed sum per month for items such as pawns or foot-wear,
and which flows forth every month— that increase is considered *kālikā* (time-based interest).
That interest which is caused by the debtor himself is called "stipulated interest. Interest upon interest is declared to be "compound interest" (cakravṛddhi).
He states another classification based on the specific recipient:

"But those traveling through the wilderness [give] ten; those traveling by sea, twenty; and [those traveling] by land, a hundred. The word *kāntāra* means a forest; those who go there are *kāntāragāḥ*.
Those who, having taken money on interest, enter a very dense forest out of a desire for excessive profit—a place where there is a risk to their lives and wealth—should pay ten per cent.
And those who go by sea should pay twenty per cent every month.

This is what is meant: the creditor may take ten per cent from those traveling through forests and twenty per cent from those traveling by sea, because there is even a suspicion of the loss of the principal.
Now he speaks of interest stipulated by agreement:
"Or they may pay the interest agreed upon by themselves, in all cases and among all classes."

Or rather, all persons, beginning with Brāhmaṇas, who are debtors—whether without collateral or with collateral—should pay the interest they themselves have agreed upon in their own contract across all castes.
In some cases, however, interest accrues even if it was not stipulated.
Thus says Nārada:
Interest on gifts made out of affection shall never accrue if they were not requested;
yet even that which was unrequested begins to increase after half a year has passed.
Thus:
"There shall be no interest on gifts made out of affection if they were not requested;
yet even that which was unrequested increases after half a year has passed."
Regarding one who, having taken a borrowed item, has gone to another country, Kātyāyana has stated: "He who, having taken a borrowed object, should depart for another region without returning it,
that property shall accrue interest for him after the lapse of one year."
Thus:
"If one who has taken a loan should depart for another region without returning it,
that debt shall accrue interest after the lapse of one year."
And regarding one who, having taken a loan, departs for another country even when requested to repay it, it has been stated by that same [author]:
"If one who has been requested goes abroad without repaying the principal,
after three months have passed, that debt shall accrue interest."
Thus:
"If one who has been asked for a loan and has made a formal agreement departs for another region without returning it,
that debt shall accrue interest after the lapse of three months."

Furthermore, if one who remains in his own country does not give back what was borrowed when requested, the king shall make him pay interest starting from the time of the request, even if he has not been formally summoned.
As it is said:
"But he who, though remaining in his own country, does not give when asked at any time..."
One should compel him to pay that interest which he had not previously agreed to, even if he is unwilling.
Thus:
"But if one who resides even in his own country does not pay when requested at any time,
the judge shall compel him to pay that interest which has accrued, even if he is unwilling."
An exception to the increase of interest has been stated by Nārada:
"The price of goods, wages, a deposit, a fine, and that which is stipulated as a gift,
as well as stakes in gambling— these do not accrue interest unless they are intended to do so."
Thus: "The price of goods, wages, a deposit, a fine, and whatever has been stipulated— these,
as well as gifts made in vain and stakes in gambling, do not increase if they are not intended to accrue interest."
"Unintended" means not being brought about by a formal invitation. || 2.38 ||
Now he states the specific increase regarding specific types of property:
"But the offspring of cattle and women.
For cattle and women, the offspring itself constitutes the interest.
The application [of interest] is possible for one who is unable to maintain livestock or women, yet desires their nourishment and progeny;
and the taking [of interest] is for one who seeks the service of milk.

Now, regarding a substance that has been lent out and remains for a long time even without the taking of interest, he speaks in response to the inquiry as to what the maximum interest may be on which substance.
The maximum interest on liquids is eightfold;
for cloth, grain, and gold, it is four, three, and two times the principal respectively.
In the case of liquids such as oil and ghee, for those that remain for a long time and increase by their own natural growth, the maximum interest is eightfold;
it does not increase beyond this.
Likewise, for clothes, grain, and gold, the maximum interest is respectively fourfold, threefold, and twofold.
Vasiṣṭha, however, has stated that there is a threefold interest on liquids: "Gold bears double interest; grain bears triple interest.
By the same rule as grain, liquids, flowers, roots, and fruits are explained.
That which is weighed on a scale bears eightfold interest."

Manu, however, has stated that for grain, flowers, roots, fruits, and the like, the rate is fivefold: "In the case of grain, fodder, wool, and beasts of burden, it does not exceed fivefold. (Manu 8.152) In the case of grain, fodder, wool, and beasts of burden, it does not exceed fivefold.
Grain refers to the yield of the field, such as flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth;
wool refers to the wool of sheep and the hair of yaks and camels, and so forth;
and draught animals refer to oxen, horses, and so forth.
Interest on grain, wool, and forest produce does not exceed fivefold.
In this regard, the determination should be understood according to the capacity of the debtor and the influence of the time, such as a famine.
And this is to be understood as applying to a single transaction and a single collection.

When another application is made by transferring the loan to a different person, or when multiple subsequent applications are made to the same person through repeated pouring [of interest] or addition, gold and other such items increase beyond doubling and so forth, just as before.

Even in the case of a single initial application, if interest is collected daily, monthly, or annually, the amount owed by the debtor may reach doubling; thus, together with the interest previously collected, it continues to increase until it exceeds the limit of doubling.
As Manu says: "Interest on a loan, even when collected all at once, does not exceed the point of doubling."
Thus:
"Interest on a loan shall not exceed doubling [the principal], even if collected at once.
There is also a reading: "even if collected at once" (*sakṛdāhitā*).

Interest (*kusīda*) is wealth employed for the purpose of accumulation; the increase thereof is "interest-increase" (*kusīdavṛddhi*). That [increase] does not exceed, nor does it surpass, doubling [the principal], provided that it has been established once or employed once.
If, however, by transferring it to another person or through other such means, a new application is made, it exceeds doubling.
However, if the reading is *sakṛdāhṛtā* (borrowed once), it should be explained as follows: "Borrowed gradually—daily, monthly, or annually—from the debtor, [the debt] exceeds doubling.
Likewise, Gautama has also stated: "In a long-standing loan, there is doubling of the principal.
Because of the singular number used in the term *prayogasya* (of the loan), what is intended is that the exceeding of doubling occurs upon the commencement of a new loan transaction.
By the instruction "for a long time," it is shown that when interest is taken gradually, the doubling of the principal may be exceeded. (2.39)

The rules regarding the lending of debt have been stated. Now, the rules regarding the recovery of the lent wealth are being declared: one who is recovering a debt that has been admitted shall not be subject to reproach by the king.
If he persists in his claim, he shall go before the king; he is to be punished and made to pay that wealth.

A creditor who recovers, by means of righteous methods such as conciliation and the like, a debt that has been admitted by the debtor or proven through witnesses and other evidence, is not to be censured by the king; that is, he is not to be restrained.

And the means, beginning with *dharma*, have been shown by Manu: "One should recover a debt through *dharma*, through legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), through trickery (*chala*), through customary practice (*ācarita*), and fifthly, by force (*bala*)."
Thus:
"One should recover a debt through dharma, through legal procedure, through artifice, through customary practice,
and fifthly, by force."
By means of dharma, that is, through truthful speech joined with affection; by means of legal procedure, such as the methods of witnesses, written documents, and so forth;
and by means of artifice, such as taking ornaments under the pretext of a festival or similar occasion.
By customary practice, by fasting,
and by the fifth means— force, such as binding with shackles and so forth— one should appropriate for oneself the wealth employed for the purpose of accumulation through these methods.
By stating that "one who is pursuing a claim already admitted need not be spoken to," he shows that one who is pursuing a claim not yet admitted must be restrained by the king.
This very point has been clarified by Kātyāyana:
"If a creditor should harass a debtor who is speaking justly,
he shall be deprived of that wealth and shall incur a fine equal to it."
Thus:
"If any creditor should oppress a debtor who speaks according to justice,
he shall be deprived of that wealth and shall incur a fine equal to its value."

However, if a debtor who has been approached with means such as *dharma* (moral persuasion) and so forth, and while his wealth is being recovered through such methods, should go to the king—approaching the sovereign and opposing one who is seeking justice—he becomes liable to punishment; furthermore, he must be made to pay that wealth to the creditor according to his capacity.
Regarding the methods for compelling payment by the king, they have been shown:
"The king, however, should cause the debtor to give the debt to the creditor by means of peaceful persuasion alone."
But others who are wicked, he should compel to pay by means of local custom after having oppressed them.
One should cause even an heir or a friend to pay by means of stratagem alone.
Thus:
"The king, however, should cause the creditor to receive payment from his debtor through conciliation alone;
but others who are wicked, he should cause to pay by means of oppression in accordance with local custom."
One may cause even an heir or a friend to pay by means of deception alone.
"One who is being prosecuted may go to the king"—this should be understood as the counter-example to the rule "one who has deviated from the Smṛti and established custom. (2.40)
When many creditors present their claims simultaneously, by what order should the debtor be made to pay by the king? To this inquiry, he says:
The debtor shall be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they received the loans;
however, having paid the Brāhmaṇas first, he shall pay the king immediately thereafter.
Among creditors of the same caste, the debtor shall be made to pay by the king according to the very order in which the wealth was received;
however, among those of different castes, it shall be according to the order beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. (2.41)

Furthermore, when the creditor is weak and, being unable to recover the admitted debt through means such as moral persuasion (*dharma*) and so forth, has the debt recovered by the king, then [the law] prescribes a fine for the debtor and the payment of a fee to the creditor:
"The king shall cause the debtor to pay ten percent of the amount recovered;
and the creditor who has obtained his property shall be made to pay five percent."
The debtor shall be made to pay ten percent of the amount recovered by the king from the admitted debt;
that is to say, the king shall take a tenth part of the admitted and recovered amount as a fine from the debtor.
However, the creditor who has obtained his due shall be made to pay five percent as a fee.
The meaning is that the king should take a twentieth part of the recovered amount from the creditor for the purpose of maintaining his servants.

However, regarding the case where the recovery of the debt is not admitted, the distribution of fines has been shown by the rule beginning with "if [the debtor] denies [the debt], he shall pay [the fine] once proven," and so forth. (2.42)
The means of recovery regarding a solvent debtor has been stated.
Now, he speaks concerning an insolvent debtor:
"One should compel a debtor of low caste who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt."
But a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his means.

A creditor who is a Brāhmaṇa or of a higher caste may, for the purpose of recovering a debt, compel a debtor of a lower caste—such as a Kṣatriya or another—to perform his own work, which is appropriate to his birth, provided it does not cause hardship to the debtor’s family.
However, a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished and destitute should be made to pay the debt gradually, according to his income and as far as possible.
In this context, the mention of a "lower caste" is also indicative of one of the same caste.
And for this reason, even one of the same caste who has become impoverished should be made to perform work as is appropriate.
Furthermore, the mention of a Brāhmaṇa is an illustration for those of superior castes;
therefore, even a Kṣatriya or others who have become impoverished should be made to pay a Vaiśya or others gradually, according to their income.
This very point has been clarified by Manu:
"A debtor of lower caste who is equal [to the creditor] should discharge the debt even through labor;
one of superior caste, however, should pay it gradually."
Thus:
A debtor of lower caste should settle his debt with a creditor even by means of labor;
however, one of equal or superior caste should repay it gradually.
The meaning is that the debtor should, by his action, make himself one who no longer bears the designations of "creditor" or "debtor" with respect to the creditor. (2.43)
That which is deposited with a neutral third party does not increase.
He who does not take his own wealth when it is being offered,
even if it has been deposited with a neutral third party, shall not have it increase beyond that point.

Furthermore, if a creditor, out of greed for interest, does not accept money being paid by a debtor that was lent for the purpose of accumulation, it shall cease to increase from the point it is deposited with a middleman by the debtor;
however, if the creditor, even when asked, does not deliver the deposited amount, then it continues to increase as before. (2.44)
Now he states when and by whom a debt is to be paid:
"But a debt that has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided,
the heirs shall pay it upon the death or departure abroad of the head of the household."
A debt contracted for the sake of the family by many members who are undivided, or by even a single one, must be paid by the head of the household.
Upon his death or departure, all his heirs shall pay it.
(2.45) He states here a counter-example regarding the rule "by whom it is to be paid."
A wife shall not pay what was incurred by her husband or son, nor shall a father pay what was incurred by his son;
likewise, a husband shall not pay what was incurred by his wife, except for the sake of the family.
A wife shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband;
a mother shall not pay a debt contracted by her son;
likewise, a father shall not pay a debt contracted by his son.
Likewise, a husband shall not pay what was contracted by his wife;
the phrase "other than for the sake of the family" applies as a supplement to all [the preceding rules].
Consequently, whatever has been contracted by anyone for the sake of the family must be paid by the head of the household.
It has already been stated that, in his absence, those who inherit his estate must pay it. (2.46)
He will state that "a debt must be paid by sons and grandsons";
prior to that, he states an exception:
[a debt] incurred for liquor, passion, or gambling, as well as the remainder of fines and taxes.
Likewise, in this world, a son should not give away his father’s property as a useless gift.

The debt incurred through drinking liquor, whether done intentionally or caused by addiction to women, that resulting from defeat at gambling, fines, and taxes, as well as "vain gifts"—that which is promised to rogues, actors, wrestlers, and the like—is distinguished [from legitimate debts]. As it is said: "A gift given to a rogue, an actor, a wrestler, a quack physician, a gambler, a cheat, a flatterer, a wandering minstrel, or a thief becomes fruitless."
Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), a son or other descendant need not pay to liquor-sellers and the like this debt incurred by the father.

In this context, because of the inclusion of the word "remainder" in the phrase "the remainder of fines and tolls," one should not think that everything must be paid; rather, [he may pay] the fine, or the remainder of the fine, or the toll, or the remainder of the toll.
But a son must not give what is not legally valid for transaction.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Uśanas;
and it has also been stated by Gautama: "The penalties for liquor, bride-price, gambling, and lust shall not descend upon the sons.
The meaning is that they do not fall upon the son.
By this, the debt that must not be paid has been described. (2.47)

He states an exception to the rule that "the husband is not liable for what is done by the wife": "The husband shall pay the debt of the wives of cowherds, vintners, actors, washermen, and hunters, because their livelihood depends upon him."
A cowherd is a *gopāla*;
a vintner is a *śauṇḍika*;
an actor is a *śailūṣa*.
A washerman is one who dyes clothes;
a hunter is a deer-stalker.
Whatever debt has been contracted by the wives of these [occupations], that must be paid by their respective husbands.

Since their livelihood—that is, their subsistence—is dependent on her, and since it is stated as a reason that "since the livelihood is dependent on her," it is understood that others as well, whose lives depend on a woman, must pay a debt incurred by that woman. (2.48)
He states an exception to the rule that "a wife shall not pay what was contracted by her husband": "What was promised by the woman, or what was contracted together with the husband,
or whatever debt she herself has incurred— other than these, a woman is not liable to pay."
When a debt has been contracted by a wife who was authorized by her husband—whether he was about to die or about to go abroad—that debt is considered contracted by the husband and must be paid.
Furthermore, a debt incurred jointly by the husband and wife must also be paid by the wife in the absence of the husband, provided she is without sons.
Likewise, a debt contracted by herself must also be paid.
[Objection: Surely it need not be stated that "the three beginning with the *pratipanna* must be given by a woman," because there is no doubt [on this point].
[Reply: It is said: "A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property.
Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong."

Because of this statement, there might arise a doubt that those such as the wife, who are recognized as being without property, are ineligible for inheritance; therefore, this is said: "What has been promised by a woman must be given," and so forth.
Nor does this statement declare the lack of property for women and others, since its purpose is merely to establish their state of dependence (*pāratantrya*).
This will be clarified in the section on partition (*vibhāga*).
"In that case, one should not say 'no other woman deserves to give [the debt],' because the prohibition regarding others is already established by the injunction itself.
It is replied: this is stated as an exception to the two cases where "what was promised by the woman" or "what was contracted together with the husband" must be paid;

[it means] that other things, such as those mentioned in the context of the desire for liquor and so forth, are not to be paid even if they were promised or contracted together with the husband. (2.49)
Furthermore, he states the triad of what debt is to be paid, by whom it is to be paid, and at what time it is to be paid:
"When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; if denied, it is established by witnesses."

If a father, having failed to pay a debt that ought to be paid, dies or has gone to a distant land, or is overcome by an incurable disease or similar affliction, then the debt contracted by him must necessarily be paid by the son or the grandson—by virtue of being a son or a grandson—even in the absence of paternal wealth. In this regard, the sequence is as follows: in the absence of the father, the son; in the absence of the son, the grandson. The syntactical connection is that if the son or grandson denies the debt, the debt, once established by the creditor through witnesses and other means, must be paid by the son or grandson.
In this context, although it is merely stated that "the father has gone abroad," the specific period of time must be understood as that which was declared by Nārada:
"A son shall not pay the debt to his uncle or even to his eldest brother before twenty years have passed since the father went abroad."
Thus:
"If the father has been away for more than twenty years,
the son shall not pay the debt to the paternal uncle or even to the eldest brother before that time."
Even in the case of a deceased person, one who has not yet reached the age of legal capacity should not give [the inheritance];
however, one who has reached the age of legal capacity should give it.
And that age has been shown by him [the author] himself.
A child is to be known as being like one still in the womb until the eighth year;
from then until the sixteenth year, he is called a *bāla*, and specifically a *paugaṇḍa*.
One who knows legal procedure may act independently on his own behalf, except against his parents.
Thus:
"A child is to be known as being like an embryo until the eighth year;
from the sixteenth year onward, one is called a youth (bāla), and until then, one is termed a paugaṇḍa."
One who knows legal procedure is independent with respect to others, except in the case of his parents.
Even though a child becomes independent after the death of the father, he nevertheless remains liable for debt.
As it is said:
"If he has not attained legal capacity, even if he is independent, he is liable for debt."
For sovereignty is traditionally held to reside in the eldest; seniority is determined by both qualities and age.
Thus:
"Even one who is independent, if he has not attained legal capacity, remains liable for debt;
for independence is traditionally held to reside in the eldest, based on qualities and age."
Likewise, prohibitions against arrest and summons are observed:
"A minor, an envoy, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and those in a precarious situation must not be arrested; nor shall the king summon them."

Thus: "A messenger, one who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and those in distress— these should not be obstructed, nor should the king summon them."
Therefore:
"For this reason, once a son is born, the father must be diligently released from his debt by the son, renouncing his own interests, so that he does not go to hell."
Thus it is said:
"Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive with effort to liberate his father from debt for his own sake,
so that the father does not go to hell."
It should be explained that [the debt is paid] by a son who has been born and has reached maturity, due to his lack of knowledge regarding legal transactions (*vyavahāra*).

However, even a minor (*bāla*) has the right to perform a *śrāddha*, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Gautama: "One should not cause a child to recite the *brahma* (Veda), except when offering the *svadhā*.

Because of the use of the plural number in the expression "by sons and grandsons" (*putrapautraiḥ*), if there are many sons who are divided, they should each pay the debt in proportion to their own shares.
If they are undivided, it is understood that among those who live together by means of joint enterprise in a relationship of subordinate and principal, the one who is the principal alone shall pay;
as Nārada says:
"From this point forward, the sons shall pay the father's debt according to their respective shares."
Whether undivided or divided, he who bears that burden [is the true heir].
Thus it is said: "From this point forward, the sons of the father shall pay his debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are undivided or divided, provided that they bear that burden."

And in this regard, although it has been stated without distinction that "debt must be paid by sons and grandsons," nevertheless, a distinction should be understood: just as the father gives with interest, so it must be given by the son; but by the grandson, only the principal (mūla) equal [to the debt] should be given, not the interest. As it is said: "Debt contracted by one's father, even if divided among sons, must be paid like one's own; but the debt of a grandfather is to be paid equally [by the son], while it is not to be paid by his [the grandson's] son."

A debt incurred by one's father, whether divided or undivided, must be paid by the sons as if it were their own; a debt of a grandfather must be paid equally [by all grandsons], but the son of such a grandson need not pay it.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati:

"In this regard, because the term 'vibhāvita' (proven) is used without qualification, the mention of 'sākṣivibhāvita' (proven by witnesses) is an illustration for all means of proof (*pramāṇa*). Whatever has been taken with interest must be returned exactly as it was taken; no further interest is due."
It is not to be given to his son’s great-grandson who has not received the wealth;
this will be made clear in the following verse. || 2.50 ||

In the discharge of a debt, three types of debtors—the debtor himself, his son, and his grandson—have been shown as the liable parties; their order of succession in the event of their simultaneous presence has also been shown.
Now, he states the order for the simultaneous presence of other liable parties:
"The heir to the estate shall be made to pay the debt, and likewise the one who takes the wife."
A son who possesses property not dependent on others is the heir to one who is sonless.
When property belonging to one person becomes the own property of another without purchase or other such means, that is "inheritance" (*riktha*).
One who takes the inheritance by way of partition is an "inheritor" (*rikthagrāha*); he must be made to pay the debt.
This is what is meant.
He who takes another's property in the form of inheritance shall be made to pay the debt incurred by that person; however, a thief or the like is not so liable.
A "yoṣidgrāha" (one who takes a woman) is one who takes a wife; he likewise shall be made to pay the debt.
He who takes another's woman shall be made to pay the debt incurred by her.
Because women are not entitled to the designation of inheritance due to their property being indivisible, they are mentioned separately.
Furthermore, a son whose wealth is not dependent on others must be made to pay the debt.

"Dependent on others" (*anyāśrita*) means property belonging to relatives of the mother or father; one whose wealth is thus dependent on others is "one whose wealth is dependent on others" (*anyāśritadravya*). One who is not such is "one whose wealth is not dependent on others" (*ananyāśritadravya*). The connection [of the sentence] is: "the heir of one who has no son must be made to pay the debt."

Regarding the order of succession among these when they are present together, it is precisely the order of the textual recitation: the heir to the estate (*rikthagrāha*) must pay the debt; in his absence, the one who takes the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*); and in his absence, the son.
But surely, their coexistence is impossible, because it is said: "Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs to the father's estate.
Since this states that while a son exists, it is impossible for anyone else to take the inheritance.
Even the seizure of a woman is not tenable, for it is stated in the Smṛti: "A second husband is nowhere ordained for virtuous women.
Likewise, the claim that "the son shall be made to pay that debt" is also improper, because it has been declared that "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons."

The qualification "not dependent on another substance" is also redundant, because as long as there is a son, it is impossible for the substance [the estate] to depend on anyone else; and even if such dependence were possible, the point would already be covered by the phrase "the heir to the inheritance.
Furthermore, the statement "of one who lacks a son, the heirs [must pay]" need not be stated either.
For it is established that as long as there is a son, the heir to the inheritance is the one to be made liable for the debt.
It is already established that if there is no son, the heir to the estate must be made to pay all the more.
To this it is replied: even when a son exists, another person may still be the heir to the estate;
for instance, the case of those who are impotent, blind, deaf, and so forth, who, despite being sons, lack the right to inherit the property.
And likewise, having enumerated the impotent and others, the author will state that "they should be maintained but without a share.
Similarly, according to the Smṛti of Gautama: "Even a son of equal caste does not receive [a share] from some authorities if he is of improper conduct.
Therefore, when sons such as the impotent exist, and when there is a son of equal caste who is of improper conduct, the one who takes the inheritance is the paternal uncle, his son, or another.

Although taking a woman as a wife is not possible without contradicting the scriptures, nevertheless, one who has transgressed the prohibition remains indeed entitled to discharge the debts incurred by his previous husband.
"Taking a woman" refers to one who marries the last of the four types of *svairiṇīs* (unfaithful women), and one who marries the first of the three types of *punarbhūs* (women remarried).
As Nārada says: "Other women who have had previous husbands are declared to be seven in number, in their respective order."
A remarried woman is of three kinds, while a wanton woman is of four kinds.
A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage,
is declared the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) by virtue of the rite of re-consecration.
A woman who, having disregarded the laws of the land, is given by her elders to another man out of impulsive passion,
is proclaimed as the second [type of wife].
One who has acted with rashness or committed adultery;
or one who, in the absence of brothers-in-law, is given by her kinsmen to a sapinda of the same caste— she is proclaimed the third [type of wife].
Whether she has borne children or not, if a woman, while her husband is still alive,
out of lust resorts to another man, she is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, has resorted to another man,
and then returns to the house of her husband, is proclaimed as the second [type].
But she who, upon the death of her husband, having rejected the brothers-in-law and others who have approached her,
approaches another out of desire, is proclaimed as the third [type of woman].
She who has come from another land, purchased with wealth, and is afflicted by hunger and thirst,
approaching you saying "I am yours"— she is proclaimed as the fourth.
The last among those who live by their own will and the first among those who are remarried—
whosoever has taken refuge with these two shall pay the debt contracted by their husbands.
Thus:
"The debt incurred by the husband of both the last among women who have lived with their own will and the first among remarried women shall be paid by whoever has taken them under his protection."
Likewise, another person who takes a woman as a wife is also authorized to discharge her debts, as shown by that very same [text]:
"But a woman who possesses property, or one who has offspring, may resort to another;
he shall pay her husband's debt, or she may likewise abandon it."
It is "sapradhanā" because it exists together with excellent wealth;
that is to say, it possesses abundant wealth.
Likewise.
For when a man dies without wealth and without a son, he who takes his wife incurs the burden of his debts; she alone is declared to be his property.
Thus it is said:
"For when a man dies without wealth and without a son, whoever takes his wife incurs the burden of his debt; she alone is declared to be his property."
The son’s statement again is for the sake of establishing the proper order.

The phrase "one whose property is not dependent on another" is intended to show that when there are many sons, even in the absence of other wealth (*riktha*), only those who are capable of receiving a share have the right to discharge the debt, and not those incapable of it, such as the blind and so forth.

The phrase "of one who is without a son, the heirs" is also intended to show that if the great-grandsons (*prapautra*) and others take the inheritance of one who is without a son or grandson, then they must be made to pay the debt, and not otherwise.
It has been stated that sons and grandsons must be made to pay even in the absence of anyone else to inherit the estate;
as Nārada says:
"The debt which was cleared by the sons, having been received in due order without interruption..."
The grandsons should give the paternal great-grandfather's share; that obligation ceases with the fourth descendant.
Thus, everything is faultless.
Alternatively, it has been stated that in the absence of a woman-seizer (*yoṣidgrāha*), the son shall be made to pay;
and in the absence of a son, the woman-seizer shall be made to pay.

Regarding the phrase "the heir of one who is childless" (*putrahīnasya rikthinaḥ*), by the word *riktha* (inheritance/property) the woman herself is meant, because of the traditional legal maxim (*smṛti*) stating, "She alone is declared to be his wealth": "He who seizes another's wife seizes his wealth."
And thus it is said.
Is it not the case that there is a mutual contradiction: [the rule] that "if the woman-seizer is absent, the son shall be made to pay the debt;
if the son is absent, the woman-seizer" implies that when both are present, neither is to be made to pay?
This is not a fault.

In the absence of one who has taken a woman for the last time, one who has taken her as a remarried wife (punarbhū) for the first time, or one who has seized her along with her property, the son shall be made to pay;
and in the absence of a son, the one who has taken a woman who is destitute and childless shall be made to pay.
This very point was stated by Nārada.
Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, the one who inherits the debt shall take the property:
the son [takes it] when there is neither a wife nor wealth; the wife when there is neither wealth nor a son; and the one who takes the wealth when there is neither a son nor wealth.
Thus it is said:
"Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who bears the debt shall take the wealth;
if both the wife and the wealth-taker are absent, the son shall take it; and if both the wealth-taker and the son are absent, the wife shall take it."
When there is a combination of those who take the wealth, the wife, and the son, he who takes the wealth is the one liable for the debt.

Regarding the phrase "the son [is liable] when the wife and the owner of the wealth are absent": "owner of the wealth" (*strīdhanin*) refers to those two who possess both the wife and the wealth; when such owners of the wealth are absent, the son alone becomes liable for the debt.
When the owner of the wealth and the son are absent, the one who takes the wife (*strīhārī*) is indeed liable for the debt.

The apparent contradiction—that "the son is liable for the debt in the absence of one who takes the wife," and "the one who takes the wife is liable in the absence of a son"—is resolved as before. There is another interpretation of the phrase "of the heir of one who has no son": when there arises the expectation of whose debt these—the taker of wealth, the taker of the wife, and the son—are to be made to pay, [the answer is] they are to be made to pay the creditor; in his absence, to his son and so forth. When there arises the further expectation of whose debt they are to be made to pay in the absence of a son and so forth, this [sūtra] applies: "of the heir of one who has no son."
The debt is to be paid by the heir—that is, the kinsman such as a *sapiṇḍa* who is entitled to inherit—the estate of a creditor who is destitute of offspring and other successors.

Accordingly, Nārada states: "If there is no one with a lineal descendant (*sānvaya*) to whom the debt of a Brāhmaṇa is owed, one should discharge it among his *sakulyas*; in their absence, among his *bandhus*."
Thus it has been stated:
"But when there are no *sakulyas*, nor any *sambandhis* or *bāndhavas*, then one should give [the property] to twice-born men; if none of these exist, one should cast it into the water."
Thus [ends verse] 2.51.
But when there are no agnatic kinsmen, nor relatives by marriage or paternal kin, then one should give [the offering] to twice-born men; if none of these exist, one should cast it into the water.
Now, while prohibiting the taking of a loan from certain specific persons, he prohibits other matters as well by way of context:
"Suretyship, debt, and witness testimony between brothers, husband and wife, or father and son are not recorded [as permissible] when they have not yet divided their property."
The state of being a surety is "suretiship" (*prātibhāvya*).

Regarding brothers, husband and wife, or father and son, when property is undivided—that is, prior to the partition of assets—suretiship, debt, and witnesshood were not prescribed by Manu and others; rather, they were prohibited. This is because the wealth is common to all, because both suretiship and witnesshood may ultimately result in the expenditure of one's own property, and because a debt must necessarily be repaid.
And this [prohibition] applies except by mutual consent;
for through mutual consent, even among those who are undivided, acts such as standing surety certainly do occur.
However, after partition, they occur even in the absence of mutual consent.

Now, an objection may be raised: the prohibition against acting as a surety and so forth prior to the partition of husband and wife is not tenable, because since there is no partition between them, such a qualification would be purposeless.
Furthermore, the absence of partition has been shown by Āpastamba: "No partition exists between wife and husband.
This is true.

Having stated that there is a distinction regarding those rites to be accomplished by the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires and their respective fruits, [the author], in response to the inquiry as to why [there is no distinction] in other cases, has stated the reason: "For from the taking of the hand [in marriage], there is joint participation (*sahatva*) in rites, and likewise in the fruits of merit.

For since joint participation in rites is heard of in scripture starting from the taking of the hand—as in the text, "The husband and wife should together establish the sacred fires" (*jāyāpaty agnim ādadhīyātām*)—therefore, because of the joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*) in the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), there is joint entitlement in those rites to be accomplished by the fires established through that *ādhāna*.

Likewise, because of Smṛti texts such as "rites pertaining to the Smṛti are to be performed in the marriage fire," there is indeed joint entitlement even for those rites accomplished in the fires established at marriage.
Consequently, regarding *pūrta* rites which do not depend on either of the two types of fires, the entitlement of the wife and husband is established as being separate.

Similarly, the companionship of the wife and husband is heard of with respect to the fruits of meritorious deeds, such as heaven and the like, in passages such as, "May they both attain undecaying light in heaven."

It should be understood that "jointness" applies to the fruits of those meritorious acts in which they have a joint entitlement, but not even to the fruits of *pūrta* (charitable works) performed with the husband's permission. [Objection: But was it not stated that jointness exists even regarding ownership of property? As it is said: "And in the acquisition of property; for they do not teach that there is theft when a gift is made on account of a specific occasion during the husband's absence.
[Response: True.
By this [verse], the wife’s ownership of property is demonstrated; however, it does not mean that there is no partition [of the estate].

For, regarding the possession of property, the reason for her authority has been stated: since Manu and others do not teach that theft occurs when a wife gives gifts during her husband’s absence—whether on account of a specific occasion or as a mandatory duty such as feeding guests or giving alms—it follows that the wife also possesses ownership over the property; otherwise, such acts would constitute theft.
Therefore, a division of property for the wife indeed takes place by the will of the husband, but not by her own will.
As he will state [later]: "If he should make equal shares, the wives are to be made sharers of equal portions. (2.52)
Now, in order to define suretyship (*prātibhāvya*), he says:
"Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment;
however, in the case of the first two [types] being rendered void, the debt must be paid by them, and in the case of the other, even their sons."
Surety (*prātibhāvya*) is an agreement with another person for the sake of trust. It is divided into three types according to the difference in their objects, as follows:
regarding "seeing" (*darśana*), it means "I shall produce him [as a witness]" when there is a requirement for seeing.
"Give him the money on my guarantee (*pratyaya*), for he will not deceive you; this man is the son of so-and-so, and he possesses excellent land and choice property.
"If he does not give it when it is time for payment, then I myself shall pay it"—thus is the surety (*prātibhāvya*) prescribed, and this applies to each [of the three types].

The first two—the guarantors for appearance and for the contingency of denial—are to be made to pay the stipulated sum to the creditor by the king in the event of a false claim, a change of circumstances, non-appearance, or breach of trust;
whereas the sons of the other—the guarantor for payment—must also be made to pay.
By stating "even the sons of the other" in reference to one who, out of deceit or poverty, does not repay a debt, it is indicated that the sons of the two former [creditors] need not be made to pay.
By using the term "sons," it is shown that the grandsons are not to be made to pay. (2.53)
To clarify this very point, he says:

"Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; [only] those who stood as sureties for payment (*dāna*) shall pay."

But when a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for trust (*prātyayika-pratibhū*) has gone to heaven, their sons shall not pay the paternal debt incurred by that suretyship. However, the sons—not the grandsons—of a surety who stood as a guarantor for payment (*dāna-sthita*) shall pay it;
and they shall pay only the principal (*mūla*), not the interest (*vṛddhi*). A grandson shall pay a grandfather’s debt, while a son shall pay a debt incurred by suretyship.
One should give [the debt] equally; however, it is certain that his two sons shall not be made to pay.
This is according to the words of Vyāsa:
a grandson shall pay his grandfather’s debt, excluding that which arose from suretyship, equally—that is, exactly as much as was received—and not with interest.
Likewise, the grandson’s son (great-grandson) shall also pay his father’s debt incurred through suretyship equally.

The sons of those two—the grandson and the son—and their grandsons and great-grandsons, shall not be made to pay the debt incurred by suretyship or that which was not a matter of suretyship, respectively, if they have not received the money from the debtor. Furthermore, as for the traditional legal maxim (*smaraṇa*): "If the debtor is devoid of wealth while the surety is wealthy, the principal alone shall be paid by him; he is not liable to pay interest."
Thus, regarding that [debt], there is the *lagnaka* (surety), the *pratibhū* (guarantor), and the *khādaka* (the debtor).
If the *lagnaka* is wealthy and has died, then his son must pay only the principal (*mūla*) and not the interest (*vṛddhi*); this is how it should be explained.

However, in a case where a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for confidence (*pratyaya-pratibhū*) becomes a guarantor after taking sufficient collateral (*bandhaka*), there the sons of that surety must indeed pay the debt incurred through the guarantee from that very collateral.
As Kātyāyana has stated: "Where a pledge has been taken and [the debtor] remains liable upon its presentation, the son shall be made to pay that debt from his own wealth, even without his father."
Thus:
"In a case where a pledge has been taken and the debtor remains under that legal view,
the son shall be made to pay that debt from the father's wealth even in the father's absence."
The mention of "seeing" is an illustration for any [means of] cognition;
as in the cases: "without the father," "the father having died," or "the father having gone to a distant land. (2.54)
Regarding how one should be made to pay when there is the possibility of multiple sureties, he says:
"If there should be many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to their respective shares;
but among those who have relied upon a single liability, it shall be as the creditor pleases."

If there should be two or many sureties for a single transaction, they shall pay that debt by dividing it among themselves according to their respective shares. Regarding sureties who have resorted to a "single shadow" (*ekacchāyāśrita*): those who have resorted to the shadow—that is, the likeness—of a single debtor are called "those who have resorted to a single shadow. Just as the debtor stands ready to deliver the entire property, so too each of the sureties stands ready to deliver the entire property upon payment. This applies likewise to sureties for appearance (*darśana*) and for confidence (*pratyaya*). When such sureties who have resorted to a single shadow exist, the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) may act according to his preference or as he desires.
And for this reason, when a creditor has need of wealth or other assets, he shall cause that very person whom he requests for his own sake to pay the entire amount, not merely a portion.
Among those who have resorted to a single source of credit, if one has gone to another country and his son is present, then the son shall be made to pay the whole by the will of the creditor.
But if someone has died, his son shall be made to pay his father’s share without interest.
As Kātyāyana has said: "Among those who have entered under a single liability, he who is seen [at the time of the debt] shall be made to pay;
if he is away on a journey, his son shall pay the whole; but if the father is dead, they shall pay equally."
Thus [ends verse] 2.55.
Among those who have entered under a single roof, he who is seen there [at the time of the debt] shall be made to pay;
if the debtor is away on a journey, his son shall pay the whole; but if the father is dead, they shall pay equally.
Having stated the rule for the payment of a debt by a surety, he now states the rule for the repayment of what was paid by the surety:
"Whatever wealth a surety is compelled to pay publicly to the creditor,
that shall be repaid double by the debtors."

When a surety or his son, being pressured by the creditor, has been made to pay the debt publicly in the presence of all people by the king—and not paid voluntarily out of a desire for the doubling of the amount—then the debtor shall repay that double amount to the surety.
As Nārada says: "Whatever sum the surety may have paid when pressured by the creditor, the debtor shall reimburse that double amount to the surety."
Thus:
Whatever amount the surety may pay when pressured by the creditor,
the debtor shall reimburse that amount to the surety twofold.
The debtors—the borrowers—must repay that property to the surety doubled;
and that must be paid as doubled immediately, without regard for any specific period of time, by virtue of the force of the commencement of the statement.
And this refers specifically to gold.

Now, it might be argued that this statement regarding the "surety" (pratibhūr) establishes only the doubling [of the debt], and that is consistent even without contradicting the previously mentioned sequence for the calculation of time—
just as the injunction for the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice is consistent with the absence of ritual purity.

Furthermore, in the case of the view that payment must be made immediately along with interest, since there can be no immediate offspring in the case of cattle and women, it would follow that one must simply pay their market value.

That is incorrect; for by the rule itself—"the maximum interest on cloth, grain, and so forth is four, three, and two-fold respectively"—the doubling and so on are established through the sequence of time and calculation. Furthermore, if this statement were intended merely to enjoin doubling, it would be redundant.
As for cattle and women, however, even under the view of a gradual sequence of time, if there is no progeny, they must be returned in their original form.
When even a guarantor meets with the debtor after some time following the payment of the debt, then a lineage certainly arises.
Or rather, there is no problem at all in the idea that cattle and women will be given along with an already established lineage.
Now, as for the guarantee, it was made out of affection.
And therefore, what is given by a surety is indeed "given out of affection" (*prītidatta*).
Furthermore, there is no interest on what is given out of affection prior to its being requested.
As it has been said: "Whatever is given out of affection does not increase, provided it is not requested."
If that which was requested is not given, it increases by five percent per month.
Thus it is said:
"Whatever is given out of affection does not increase, provided it was not requested;
however, if what was requested is not given, it increases by five percent per month."

Therefore, it is claimed that by this statement it is meant that for a loan given without affection and even without being requested, interest accrues over time at the rate of doubling from the day of the loan until it has reached twice the principal.
That too is incorrect, because this meaning is not understood from this statement; here, only this much is understood: "twice the amount must be returned.
For it is well said that, by the force of the wording itself, twice the amount must be returned regardless of the sequence of time. (2.56)
An exception to the general rule that a debt secured by a pledge becomes doubled in all cases is stated:
"In the case of livestock and females, the offspring alone [is the interest]; grain is tripled;
clothing is declared to be fourfold; and likewise, liquids are eightfold."
Just as with the doubling of gold, women, cattle, and other such items must be returned along with the stipulated interest, regardless of the lapse of time.
The verse has already been explained.

The essential meaning is this: whatever maximum interest has been declared for a particular object, that object, when delivered by the surety, must be returned immediately by the debtor together with that interest, without regard for the specific duration of time.

But when the surety for appearance is unable to produce the debtor at the agreed-upon time, then a period of three fortnights must be granted to him for searching for him. In that case, if he produces him, the surety should be released; otherwise, he must be made to pay the stipulated debt, though for the purpose of searching for one who is lost, the maximum time to be granted is three fortnights. If he should produce him during that time, the surety shall be released.
If, when the time has elapsed, the surety does not produce that person, he shall be made to pay the security deposit; this rule is declared to apply in the case of his death as well.

Thus, from the statement of Kātyāyana. And a specific prohibition regarding the surety (*lagnaka*) has been stated by him: "Neither the owner, nor an enemy, nor one authorized by the owner, nor one who is imprisoned, nor one who has been punished, nor one who is under suspicion—none of these [should act as a surety] at any time."
Neither an heir, nor a friend, nor those who reside permanently [with him],
nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants [are liable for the debt].
He who is unable to pay the creditor and an equal amount as a fine to the king, or whose father is still living and acts according to his own will; ||| 106 ||
A surety should not be accepted for his obligation unless he has been properly examined.
Thus: neither an owner nor an enemy, nor one appointed by an owner,
nor one who is restrained, nor one who has been punished, nor one who is under suspicion— none of these [should be called as a witness] at any time.
Neither an heir, nor a friend, nor those who reside permanently [with him],
nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants [are liable for the debt].
He who is unable to pay the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king,
or whose father is still living and acts as the one who directs his will, [is not liable].
A surety should not be accepted for his obligation unless he has been properly examined.
One who is suspected or accused;
lifelong residents, namely perpetual celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins).
Thus ends the rule regarding sureties. 2.57.
In the lending of wealth, there are two causes for confidence: the surety and the pledge.
As Nārada said: "In this matter, there are two causes of trust: the surety and the pledge."
In this matter, there are two causes for confidence: the surety and the pledge. Of these, the surety has been defined;
now the pledge is being defined.

A pledge (*ādhi*) is so called because, for the sake of creating confidence regarding a property that has been received, the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) places it under the authority of the creditor (*uttamarṇa*); it is that which is pledged (*ādhīyate*), hence it is called a pledge.
It is of two kinds: one with a fixed time and one without a fixed time. Furthermore, each of these is again of two kinds: to be kept in custody (*gopya*) and to be used (*bhogya*).
As Nārada said: "That which is pledged is known as *ādhi*; it is understood to be of two kinds:
that which is to be removed at a fixed time, and likewise that which remains until the debt is repaid."
Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: the secret (gopya) and likewise the enjoyable (bhogya).
Thus:
"An *ādhi* (mortgage/deposit) is that which is pledged; it should be understood as being of two kinds:
one for a fixed period to be released [upon payment], and likewise one to remain until the debt is repaid."
Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: the secret and likewise the object of enjoyment.

Regarding the "fixed time": at that very time for the pledge, such as during the Festival of Lamps (Dīpotsava) or another occasion, [the debtor] must bring it near, meaning it must be delivered; that is, it must be released. The meaning is that it should be given as a gift. "To be released" is the sense. "Deya" means a gift.

"Not exceeding what is to be given" means as much as is to be given. "Udyata" means fixed or established; "as much as is to be given, udyata" (yāvad-deyodyata) means the limit for the repayment of the money received, with no specific time determined.

The *gopya* (pledge for custody) must be protected. Thus he states the specific rule regarding the fourfold pledge (*ādhi*): "The pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, if it is not released."
That which is caused by time may perish in due time, but that which is to be enjoyed as its fruit does not perish.
When the stipulated debt has doubled over time through the interest accrued by the creditor, if the pledge is not released by the debtor through the payment of the principal, then it is forfeited;
the property of the debtor becomes the property of the lender.
The term *kālakṛta* means "one for which a time limit has been set"; the word *kāla* is placed first in the compound according to its inclusion in the *āhitāgny-ādi* group.
But that [pledge] would be lost when the stipulated time arrives, either before or after its value has doubled.

However, that which is to be enjoyed for its produce (*phalabhogya*)—meaning that whose enjoyment consists of its produce, such as a field or a grove—is never lost at any time. It has been stated that a pledge kept in custody (*gopya*) or one to be enjoyed for its produce (*bhogya*), if made for a fixed period, is lost upon the lapse of that period, according to the rule: "That which is determined by time is lost when the time passes."
It has been stated that there is no loss of a pledge that is to be enjoyed when its time has not expired, according to the rule: "That which is to be enjoyed as a fruit does not perish.
By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the statement "the pledge shall be forfeited" remains applicable to the case of a pledge given for safekeeping (*gopyādhi*) where no time limit was set.

Regarding forfeiture due to the doubling of the debt or the lapse of the stipulated time, an expectation of fourteen days must be observed, according to the words of Bṛhaspati: "When gold has doubled [in value] and the fixed period has expired..."
The creditor shall become the owner of the pledge after waiting for two weeks.
If the debtor gives the money within that interval, he shall obtain his release from bondage.
Thus [it is said].
When gold has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for fourteen days.
Having paid that amount in the interim, the debtor shall obtain his release from bondage.

Is it not the case that the statement "the pledge may be lost" is untenable? For there is an absence of any cause for the debtor’s loss of ownership, such as gift or sale; likewise, there is an absence of any cause for the creditor’s acquisition of ownership, such as acceptance or purchase; and furthermore, this contradicts the words of Manu: "There is neither transfer nor sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time. There is neither transfer nor sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time.

"Kālasaṃrodha" means confinement for a period of time; it is the state of being held for a long duration. Because of that confinement for a long duration, there is no relinquishment (*nisarga*) of the pledge (*ādhi*); other than this, there is neither its further pledging nor its sale.
Thus, from this prohibition of further pledging and selling, it is understood that the creditor lacks ownership.
