It is replied: In common worldly practice, the very act of pledging is the cause for the cessation of ownership under certain conditions (*sopādhika*).
Furthermore, the formal acceptance of a pledge (*ādhisvīkāra*) is well known to be the cause for the acquisition of ownership accompanied by conditions (*sopādhikasvatvāpatti*).

In that regard, when the doubling of the debt has occurred and the stipulated time has arrived, because the giving of the object ceases entirely, by virtue of this statement, the debtor’s ownership is terminated absolutely and the creditor’s absolute ownership is established.
Nor is there any contradiction with the text of Manu.
For Manu says: "But one shall never receive interest on a loan secured by a pledge that provides a benefit.
That is:
"But one shall never receive interest on a loan secured by a pledge that provides a benefit."
With reference to the pledge for enjoyment (*bhogyādhi*), this is stated: "There is neither alienation nor sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time.
There is neither alienation nor sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time.
Even if a pledge intended for enjoyment remains for a long period, the creditor possesses no ownership over it due to the prohibition against its alienation by way of pledge or sale.

In this regard also, it has been stated that "a pledge to be enjoyed for its fruit does not perish"; furthermore, Manu has treated the pledge for custody separately, stating: "A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest."
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
As will be stated here as well: "In the case of using a pledge for protection, there is no interest.
However, the rule that "the pledge is lost when [the debt] has doubled" refers specifically to a pledge for protection; thus, everything is consistent. (2.58)
Furthermore:
No interest accrues on a pledge that has been used; nor does it accrue when a pledge that provides a benefit is neglected.
If the pledge is lost or destroyed—except by act of God or the king—it must be replaced.
Interest accrues from the use of a pledge consisting of copper vessels and the like belonging to a female slave (*gopī*).
Even if the use is slight, a great interest must be forfeited because it constitutes a transgression of the agreement.

Likewise, in the case of a beneficial pledge (*sopakāra*)—such as a draft ox or a copper vessel—which provides a service, if it is "caused to be lost" (*hāpite*), meaning it is rendered unfit for use in transactions, there shall be no interest; this is the connection [of the sentence].
If an object such as a copper vessel has been lost or damaged, it must be restored to its former condition by repairing holes, cracks, and so forth, before being returned.
In that regard, if a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*) is lost, it must be restored to its former condition before being returned;
even if it was used, the interest (*vṛddhi*) must also be waived.
If the pledge for use (bhogyādhi) is destroyed, then it must be restored as before;
if interest has accrued, the interest must also be relinquished.
If it is ruined—that is, has reached total destruction—it must likewise be restored by means of its value or other such compensation.
If he returns it, he receives the principal value along with interest;

when he does not return it, there is a loss of the principal. As stated in the words of Nārada: "There shall be a loss of the principal if [the object] is destroyed, except in cases caused by fate or the king."
"Except for that caused by fate or the king": "fate" refers to such things as fire, water, or the ruin of one's location;
"except for destruction caused by fate," and likewise, except for that caused by the king when it is free from one's own fault.

In the event of destruction caused by a calamity from the gods or the king, the debtor must pay the value of the object along with interest, or provide another pledge. As it has been said: "If a field is swept away by a flood or confiscated by the king, another pledge must be made, or the debt must be paid to the creditor."
Thus it is said:
"If the field is carried away by a stream or confiscated by the king,
another pledge must be made, or the debt must be paid to the creditor."
In that context, "carried away by a current" is an indicative mark for what is caused by fate. 2.59.
Moreover,
if the pledge, even while being protected, reaches a state of worthlessness from the time it was accepted,
another pledge should be provided, or the debtor shall become liable for the payment of the debt.

The establishment of a pledge (*ādhi*) occurs through its acceptance and enjoyment by the creditor; it is not established by a mere witness or a mere written document, nor by a mere verbal declaration.
As Nārada says: "A pledge is declared to be of two kinds: movable and immovable.
The validity of both is established if there is enjoyment, and not otherwise."
Thus it is said:
"A pledge (ādhi) is declared to be of two kinds: movable and immovable;
the recovery of both depends upon possession, and not otherwise."
And its result is stated: "In the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is indeed more powerful.
That action which culminates in formal acceptance is the prior one and is stronger.
However, even the prior pledge is not authoritative if it is devoid of formal acceptance.

And if that pledge, despite being guarded with effort, through the passage of time becomes worthless—remaining unchanged yet insufficient to cover the value of the debt along with interest—then another pledge must be made, or the money must be paid to the creditor.
By stating "even while being guarded, it becomes worthless," it is made known that the pledge must be guarded with diligence by the creditor. (2.60)
He states an exception to the rule that "the pledge shall be forfeited when [the debt] has doubled":
"One should cause the debtor to pay the money, together with interest, for a pledge given out of confidence (*caritrabandhaka*)."
One should cause the person who made a solemn pledge to repay the object pledged at double its value.
*Caritra* means good conduct; *caritrabandhaka* is a pledge based on such conduct. By this, it is meant that wealth has been made one's own or rendered subject to another.
This is what is intended: either, because of the creditor’s upright character, the debtor has made over even a small amount of wealth as his own, having pledged an object of great value;
or, because of the debtor’s upright character, the creditor has accepted a pledge of little value and has made a large amount of wealth subject to the debtor.
That king should cause that wealth to be paid along with interest.
This is the intended meaning: in this way, even when the debt has doubled, the pledge (bandhaka) is not lost; rather, only the double amount of the principal must be paid.
The same applies to what is made by way of a formal agreement (satyaṃkāra).
*Karaṇa* means *kāra*. The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Thus, *satyasya kāraḥ* is *satyaṃkāraḥ*; by the rule *kāre satyāgadasya*, the augment *mum* is applied.
"Satyaṅkārakṛtam" means that which is made by a *satyaṅkāra* (a formal pledge).

The underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) is this: when at the very time of handing over the collateral (*bandhaka*), it was thus stipulated—"Even when the debt has doubled, I shall pay only the double amount of the principal, and not forfeit the pledge"—then one should cause that double amount to be paid.
This is another interpretation.

*Caritrabandhaka* means a pledge consisting of conduct (*caritra*). By the word *caritra*, the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā, performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and so forth, is denoted.
In a case where a person has made a certain object his own by pledging it on the basis of that very [merit], he must pay twice that amount once it has doubled; there is no forfeiture of the pledge.
Another matter is stated here as a corollary: that which is called "made under oath" (*satyaṃkārakṛta*).

For the sake of maintaining agreements regarding purchase, sale, and so forth, when a ring or similar object is placed in another's hand, it must be returned twofold if that agreement is violated. In that case as well, if it is the very person who deposited the ring or other item who violates the agreement, then he alone must return that same item.
If, however, the other person violates the established agreement, then he shall cause that very same ring or other object to be returned twofold. (2.61)
Furthermore:
A pledge must be enjoyed by one who has presented it; otherwise, he becomes a thief. If the owner is absent, one may obtain the pledge from another member of that family for the sake of the money.
When a debtor presents himself for the release of a pledge through the payment of wealth, it must be released by the creditor; he must not retain it out of greed for interest.
Otherwise, if he does not release it, he shall be punished like a thief or a robber.
Furthermore, if the lender is absent, the debtor may take back his own pledge after depositing the money, along with the interest, into the hands of a trusted person within that family. (2.62)

Now, if the borrower is not present and there are no trustworthy persons to receive the money, or if the borrower wishes to give the money through the sale of the pledge while the borrower is absent, what should be done in that case? In response to this inquiry, he says: "Or, having fixed its value at that time, the pledge shall remain there without interest.

Having determined whatever the value of that pledge was at that time, one should leave that pledge with the creditor there itself, free of interest; from that point forward, it does not increase further.
Until the creditor, having taken the wealth, releases that pledge, or until he applies the value of that property toward the debt.

But when it has been determined at the very time of contracting the debt that even if the wealth has doubled, only the double amount of wealth is to be taken and not the forfeiture of the pledge, then—when the property has doubled and the debtor is absent—what should the creditor do? To this he says:
"Or, even without the debtor, he may sell [the pledge] in the presence of witnesses."
In the absence of the debtor—the one who holds the pledge—the creditor may, with the witnesses and those trusted by him, sell that pledge and take the money, even without the debtor being present.
The word "or" (*vā*) signifies a fixed alternative.

If, at the time of contracting the loan, it was not deliberated that when the debt has doubled, only the principal is to be taken and not the forfeiture of the pledge, then the pledge is forfeited once the debt is doubled; this is what is meant by "forfeiture of the pledge."
"But when this position is examined... (2.63)
He states the specific rule regarding objects for enjoyment and the like:
"But when the debt has doubled on the pledge,
then indeed the pledge must be released once twice the amount of money has been recovered from it."

When the lent capital has doubled by means of the interest accrued by the creditor, then, provided that the pledge has been established, the pledge must be released once the property produced from it—the "pledge-produced" (ādhyutpanna) wealth—has entered the creditor's possession and reached the value of double the principal. Alternatively, if at the outset, when the pledge was given, there was an agreement stating, "The pledge must be released when the wealth has doubled," or for some other reason such as the absence of enjoyment, then when the debt has doubled and the pledge has entered the creditor's possession for the purpose of use, the pledge must be released once the property produced from it has reached the value of double the principal. If there has been excessive use, even that excess must be returned.
This statement refers to the subject of the enjoyment of a pledge for the purpose of repaying a debt together with all its interest.
Worldly people call such a pledge a "perishable pledge" (*kṣayādhi*).

However, where there is a convention that the enjoyment is solely for the sake of interest, in that case one continues to enjoy the pledge until the principal is paid back, even after the doubling of the debt has been exceeded.

This very point has been clarified by Bṛhaspati: "The debtor shall obtain his release after having delivered the property to be enjoyed for its fruit, once the full term has elapsed and the principal has been paid back in equal value."
If that [debt] were outstanding, then the creditor would not be entitled to his wealth,
and the debtor would not be subject to seizure, except by mutual agreement.
Thus:
"The debtor shall obtain release after giving back the principal together with the interest, once the full term has expired and the enjoyment of the fruit has been completed."
If that [debt] were outstanding, then the creditor would not be entitled to his wealth,
and the debtor would not be subject to seizure, except by mutual agreement.
The meaning of this is as follows: "Phalabhogya" refers to a pledge (bandha) consisting of a fruit that is to be enjoyed; it is a mortgage (ādhi).
And that is of two kinds: one for the purpose of repaying both principal and interest, and one for the purpose of repaying the interest alone.
In that regard, the debtor shall obtain that pledge which was given for the purpose of repaying both principal and interest when its time is full—that is, when its time has reached completion.
The meaning is that when the principal together with interest has entered into the creditor's possession by way of the fruits, then the debtor shall recover the pledge. However,
for the purpose of clearing off the interest alone, the debtor shall recover the pledge by giving back the *sāmaka*— that is,
the principal itself (*samam*) being called *sāmaka*.
He states an exception to this: "If that were to be excessive.
That pledge would be "excessive" (*prakarṣita*)—meaning superior—if it yielded a result even greater than the interest. In that case, the creditor does not receive his capital;
the meaning is that the debtor may retain the pledge even without having paid back the principal.
Now, if that pledge is not enhanced and is insufficient even for the interest, then the debtor shall not recover the pledge even after paying the principal;
the meaning is that he may recover it only after paying even the remainder of the interest.

Furthermore, he states an exception to both cases: "without mutual consent" means that if there is no mutual agreement between the creditor and the debtor, then what was stated regarding "enhanced [pledges]" and so forth applies.

If there is mutual agreement, even that which is mortgaged may be used by the creditor until the principal is repaid; likewise, even that which is not mortgaged, the debtor recovers upon the mere repayment of the principal. (2.64)
Regarding the sealed deposit (*upanidhi*), he says:
"When an object situated in a container is handed over into the hand of another without being described, that is a sealed deposit; it must be returned in exactly that same manner."

A *vāsana* is another object that serves as the receptacle for a deposited item, such as a box or a casket; that which is placed within it is "placed in a receptacle" (*vāsanastha*). When an object—without specifying its particular qualities such as form or number—is sealed and entrusted into the hand of another for safekeeping out of trust, that object is called *aupanidhika*.
As Nārada says: "That which is deposited in a sealed container (*samudra*) without being numbered or described, one should know as *upanidhi*; they know that which is counted as *nikṣepa*."
Thus:
"That which is deposited as an uncounted and unrecognized sea, one should know that as an *upanidhi*;
they know a counted deposit to be a *nikṣepa*."
It must be returned in exactly that same manner.
Whatever was deposited with it—just as it was previously handed over marked with a seal or other signs—it must be returned and restored to the depositor in that very same way. 2.65.
He states an exception to the rule that "it must be returned":
"But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves.
That person to whom the deposit was entrusted shall not be made to pay for that *upanidhi* which has been taken away or lost by the king, by an act of fate such as water and so forth, or by thieves.
That property belongs to the owner alone if it was not lost through the debtor's dishonest conduct.

As Nārada says: "If a loan, together with its principal, is lost to the borrower, that loss falls upon the giver, provided it was not caused by divine calamity, royal action, or the debtor’s dishonesty."
Thus [it is said].
If that which was lost together with the object is lost due to an act of God or the king, it is lost to the debtor; provided, however, that it was not caused by his own dishonesty.
He states an exception to this:
"If there is an error and [the deposit] is not returned when demanded, he shall be made to pay it back and a fine equal to its value."

If, when sought and requested by the owner, the borrower does not return the item, then even if subsequently a loss or destruction of it occurs due to the king or others, the borrower must still pay the value of that property to the owner and an equal fine to the king. (2.66)
He states the punishment regarding the one who uses [the deposit]:

"One who lives at will [on it] is to be punished and made to pay that [deposit] along with interest. He who, by his own will and without the owner's permission, lives upon—that is, uses—the deposited property, or deals with it for the sake of profit through lending and so forth, is to be punished according to the extent of the use and the extent of the profit. Furthermore, he must be made to restore that deposit to the owner along with interest; in the case of use, it is with interest (*savṛddhika*), and in the case of dealing, it is with the profit (*salābha*).
And the measure of interest has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"If one who is being asked for it does not return a deposit, the remainder of interest, or the proceeds from a purchase or sale, the debt increases by five percent per month."
Thus:
"If one who is being asked does not repay a deposit, the remainder of interest, or [the proceeds from] purchase or sale, it increases by five percent per hundred."
And this should be understood as applying when [the property] has been consumed.

However, regarding what was lost through negligence (*upekṣā*), a distinction is shown by that very same [author]: "He who consumes [the property] shall be made to pay it with interest; he who neglects it shall be made to pay it back in its original state;
he who loses the property through ignorance shall be made to pay a small portion less."
Thus:
"He who has consumed [the deposit] shall be made to pay it with interest; he who neglected it shall be made to pay the same amount;
he who has lost the property through negligence shall be made to pay a small portion less."
"Something less" means reduced by one-fourth.
He extends the rules for deposits (*upanidhi*) to items borrowed, entrusted, or placed in trust, stating:
"This same rule applies to things borrowed, those handed over for delivery, those deposited as security, and those held in trust."
*Yācita* refers to clothing, ornaments, and so forth, which have been brought after being requested at festivals such as weddings.
*Anvāhita* is that wealth which was placed in the hand of one person, and subsequently, by that same person, was placed in the hand of another with the instruction, "Give this to the owner.

*Nyāsa* is the depositing of an object in the hands of a householder's family member without showing it to the owner and behind his back, with the understanding that it is to be delivered to the owner.
A deposit (*nikṣepa*) is the handing over [of an object] in the presence [of the recipient].

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of a counter-deposit (*pratinyāsa*)—such as gold or other materials placed in the hands of a goldsmith or similar artisan for the purpose of making bracelets and the like—and of an object deposited with mutual agreement, such as: "You must protect this which belongs to me," and "I shall protect this which belongs to you.
As Nārada says: "This same rule is observed in the case of borrowed items, entrusted items, and so forth."
The same applies to craftsmen, as well as to deposits, bailments, and counter-bailments.
Thus,
this very same rule is seen to apply in cases of borrowed goods, articles held in trust, and so forth;
as well as in the case of artisans, deposits, bailments, and counter-deposits.

Regarding these items—such as those borrowed or deposited—the same rule that applies to a pledge (upanidhi), namely the rule concerning its restoration and so forth, should be understood to apply here as well. (2.67)
It has been stated that "evidence is declared to be written documents, possession, and witnesses.
Among these, possession has been defined;
now, the nature of witnesses is being defined.
A witness (*sākṣin*) becomes such by virtue of seeing or hearing directly.
As Manu has said: "Testimony is established through direct observation and likewise through hearing."
Testimony is established through seeing in person and through hearing.
It is of two kinds: formal (*kṛta*) and informal (*akṛta*). That which is designated as a witness is formal.
"Unexamined" means not made [as a witness].
In that regard, there are five kinds of "made" and six kinds of "unmade," thus making eleven kinds in total.
As Nārada said: "Eleven kinds of witnesses have been observed in the treatise by the wise."
The "made" (kṛta) is to be known as fivefold; the "unmade" (akṛta) is said to be sixfold.
Thus:
"Eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the scriptures by the wise;
five kinds are to be known as appointed, and six kinds are said to be unappointed."

And their classification has been shown by that very same [author]: "The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness, the cognizant witness, and the secret witness, as well as the subsequent witness—witnesses are declared to be of five kinds."
Thus it is said: "The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness,
the secret witness, and the counter-witness— these are declared to be the five kinds of witnesses."

The nature of written witnesses and others has been stated by Kātyāyana: "A witness who is brought by the plaintiff himself and recorded in the document is called a 'written witness' (likhita); one who is reminded [of his testimony] without a document is called a 'reminded witness' (smārta)."
Thus:

"He who is brought by the plaintiff himself and recorded in the document is called a 'written witness' (likhita-sākṣin); he is not [required] in the absence of a document, provided he has been reminded."

The explanation of the term *smārita* (one who is reminded), derived from the word *smāritaḥ*, was provided by that same author: "A witness who, for the sake of accomplishing the matter at hand, is repeatedly reminded of the case after having seen it by the plaintiff—that witness is here called *smārita*."
Thus it is said:
"A witness who, having seen the matter for the sake of establishing the case, is reminded again and again by the plaintiff— that witness is here called 'reminded' (smārita)."

A witness who is summoned by chance is one who has come voluntarily (*yadṛcchābhijña*). Although both of these types are not recorded in writing, their distinction has been shown by that very same authority: "One who is brought for a specific purpose and one who has arrived incidentally—these two witnesses, though unwritten, are effective in proving the plaintiff's case."
Thus:
"Both a witness brought for the sake of a specific purpose and one who has arrived incidentally— though neither be recorded in writing— are effective in proving the plaintiff's case."

Likewise: he who, remaining hidden, is clearly informed by the plaintiff for the sake of establishing his own case regarding the statement of the defendant, is called a hidden witness (*gūḍhasākṣin*).
Thus:
"He who, remaining hidden, is clearly informed by the plaintiff for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose regarding the defendant's statement,
is called a hidden witness."
Likewise: "That witness who gives testimony again and again, whether by hearing or by causing others to hear, is designated as an 'uttara' witness."
Thus:
"That witness who gives testimony repeatedly,
whether by hearing it himself or by causing others to hear it, is designated as an *uttara-sākṣin* (a secondary witness)."

Nārada has shown the sixfold classification of those who have not themselves committed the offense: "The village headman, the judge, the king, whoever may be authorized in the legal affairs of the litigants, and whoever has been dispatched by the plaintiff."
In disputes between families, members of those families should also be known as witnesses.
Thus:
"The village headman, the judge, the king,
whoever may be authorized in the affairs of litigants, and whoever has been dispatched by the plaintiff."
In disputes concerning families, members of those families should also be known as witnesses.
The mention of the *prāḍvivāka* (judge) is intended to include the scribe and the members of the court (*sabhyas*).
"The scribe, the judge, and the members of the court, in their proper order,
while the king looks on— that case is declared to have witnesses."
Thus [it is said].
The scribe, the judge, and the members of the court, in their respective order,
while the king observes that legal matter, are declared to be witnesses.
As to what kind of persons these witnesses should be and how many there should be,
he says: "Ascetics, those of a charitable disposition, those of noble birth, speakers of truth,
those for whom Dharma is paramount, the upright, those with sons, and those endowed with wealth."
Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rites;
they are prescribed either according to their respective caste and class, or all may serve for all.
Ascetic means those whose nature is austerity;
generous means those devoted to giving;
noble means those born of great lineages.
They were speakers of truth, habitually truthful in speech; they held righteousness as their primary concern rather than wealth or pleasure; and they were upright, free from crookedness.
"Possessing sons" means having sons currently living;

"endowed with wealth" means being possessed of abundant wealth such as gold and other assets; and "devoted to the rites prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti" means being intent upon the performance of obligatory and occasional duties.
Men who are of such a nature constitute witnesses when they number at least three.
"Tryavarāḥ" means those for whom three is the minimum; they must not be fewer than three. Beyond that number, however, they may be as many as desired—this is the meaning.
"Transcending birth according to birth":
births refer to those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others.
Among these, for those of the *mūrdhāvasikta* caste, witnesses must be of the *mūrdhāvasikta* caste.
The same should be understood regarding the Ambaṣṭhas and others as well.
"According to their class" (yathāvarṇam) means without overstepping their respective classes;
"classes" (varṇāḥ) refers to the Brāhmaṇas and so forth.
In that case, for Brāhmaṇas, only Brāhmaṇas possessing the aforementioned characteristics and the aforementioned number shall be witnesses.
The same should be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and others as well.
Likewise, women alone shall provide testimony for women.
As Manu has stated: "Women shall provide testimony for women.

In the absence of witnesses of the same caste and class (*sajātisavarṇa*), all persons—beginning with the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others, as well as the Brāhmaṇas and others—may serve as witnesses, respectively, for all classes beginning with the *mūrdhāvasikta* and for all castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as far as possible.

Since witnesses must possess the characteristics previously described, in order to establish that others who are free from prohibitions may also act as witnesses when such qualified witnesses are unavailable, those who are disqualified (*asākṣin*) must now be declared.

And those five kinds were shown by Nārada: "For even one who is not a witness is seen in the treatises to be of five kinds by the wise: through statement, through fault, through division, through self-accusation, and through death in the interval."

For even those who are non-witnesses are seen in the treatises to be of five kinds by the wise: on account of their speech, on account of their fault, on account of their separation, self-accusation, and death in the interval. But who are the non-witnesses on account of their speech? To this he says: "Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those such as renunciants."
Since you are not witnesses, no logical reason has been stated here on account of your words.
Thus:
"Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those who have renounced the world and so forth—these are not witnesses; no further reason for this has been stated here."
Ascetics (*tāpasa*) are forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those who dispute with their father and others are included.

As Śaṅkha says: "Those who dispute with their father, those living in the teacher's house, wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), and the naked ascetics (*nirgrantha*) are not witnesses."

Those who are disqualified from being witnesses have been shown on account of their defects: "Thieves, violent assailants, the fierce, gamblers, and deceivers—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; truth is not found in them."
Thus:
"Thieves, violent men, the fierce, gamblers, and deceivers—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; truth is not found in them."
The *caṇḍas* are those who are prone to anger;

the *kitavas* are gamblers. The nature of those who are disqualified from being witnesses has been shown by that same [author]: "Of witnesses, of those who have been recorded in writing, and of those designated by the plaintiff..."
If even one among them speaks otherwise, they are all not witnesses due to that discrepancy.
Thus it is said: "Of the witnesses— whether written, oral, or specifically designated by the plaintiff—
if even one among them speaks otherwise, all are not witnesses due to their disagreement."

Likewise, the nature of a self-accusation has been stated: "One who comes forward and speaks on his own initiative without being pointed out is called a 'needle' in the scriptures; he does not deserve to be a witness."
Thus it is said in the treatises: "He is called a 'needle'; he does not deserve to be a witness."

The definition of a "deceased intermediary" (mṛtāntara) has also been stated: "If the matter that ought to be heard is absent, and there is no claimant, where could one exercise witness-hood? Thus, one who is a deceased intermediary is not a witness."
Thus:
"If the matter that ought to be heard should not exist, or if there is no claimant, where could he exercise witnesshood? Therefore, one who dies in the interval is not a witness."

When a plaintiff or a defendant has caused the witnesses to hear the matter in the form, "You are witnesses in this matter," if that plaintiff or defendant is absent, deceased, or the matter has not been reported, then the witness—being separated from the deceased—is not a valid witness, for it would remain uncertain where, in what matter, or on whose behalf he should testify.

However, in a case where a father, whether on the verge of death or while in good health, has informed his sons and others, saying, "In this matter, these persons are witnesses," there even a witness separated from the deceased is admissible.
As Nārada said: "When the claimant has died, the interval between death and the hearing is lost—except in the case of one who was about to die or one who had been informed. Likewise:
'That legal matter concerning dharma which has been communicated by one who is not ill [is binding]...'"
Even upon death, one may be a witness in that case, as well as in the six instances involving entrusted deposits and the like.
Thus [ends verses] 2.68 and 2.69.

Even if one has not been made aware by a person who is not ill, if a matter connected with dharma was stated, he shall be a witness even after death; this also applies in the case of the six types of transactions, such as deposits and the like.
He shows these persons who are not competent witnesses:
women, children, the elderly, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, the accused, actors, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired senses.
An outcast, a relative, one who has a financial interest in the matter, an associate, an enemy, a thief, one who commits violence,
and one whose fault has been previously observed— these, beginning with the "expelled," are not to be admitted as witnesses.
A woman is well known;
a child is one who has not attained legal capacity for transactions;
an elder is one who is at least eighty years of age.
The mention of "the elderly" (vṛddha) is intended to include others as well, such as those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), who are otherwise prohibited by specific scriptural injunctions.
A "gambler" (kitava) is one who plays with dice;
"intoxicated" (matta) refers to one who is so from drinking and the like.
One who is insane; one possessed by a spirit;
one accused or charged with such acts as the killing of a Brahmin;
and a stage-player or actor.
Heretics include the Nirgranthas and others;
a forger is one who produces fraudulent documents and the like;
one with impaired faculties is one deprived of hearing and other senses.
An outcaste is one such as a slayer of a Brahmin and so forth.
A trusted friend is a well-wisher. One connected by a matter is one who is related to the matter under dispute.
A companion is one who shares the same purpose; a rival is an enemy;
a thief is a robber.
He is impetuous, acting with forceful arrogance;
he is one whose faults have been observed, meaning his speech is seen to be contradictory;
he is cast out, having been abandoned by his kinsmen.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of other persons declared non-witnesses in other Smṛtis—such as those who are disqualified due to defects, those disqualified due to partiality, those who testify of their own accord, and those who have died in the interim.
These individuals, such as women, children, and the rest, are not to be witnesses. (2.70–2.71)
He states an exception to the rule that witnesses must be at least three in number:
"Even a single person may be a witness if he is approved by both parties;
one who knows the Dharma is one who performs obligatory and occasional rites preceded by knowledge."
Even if he is alone, he becomes a witness if he is agreed upon by both parties;
by the force of the word "api" (even/also), this applies to two as well.

Although the quality of knowing the Dharma is common even to those fewer than three—since they are devoted to the performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites—nevertheless, their status as witnesses occurs only in the absence of mutual agreement between the disputing parties.
The inclusion of the phrase "at least three" is meaningful because the status of being a witness occurs through the consent of either one or two persons.
He states an exception to the rule that those who are ascetic and charitable are [suitable witnesses]:
"In cases of adultery, theft, verbal assault, and violence, everyone is a witness."
Regarding the offenses such as adultery whose characteristics will be described later, all those who are prohibited by their speech and devoid of qualities such as austerity become witnesses.

Because the reasons for being non-witnesses due to "fault" (*doṣa*) or "divergence" (*bheda*), as well as "voluntary recantation," exist here as well—namely, the absence of truth—even in these cases they may become witnesses.
[The offenses include] killing a human, theft, and violating another's wife.
Harshness and both [of these] constitute the fourfold category of violence.

According to this statement, although sexual intercourse with women, theft, and verbal assault are forms of *sāhasa* (violent crime), nevertheless, when these are committed by relying on one's own strength in the presence of people, they are classified as *sāhasa*.

However, when committed in secret, they are designated by the specific terms such as "sexual intercourse" (*saṃgrahaṇa*) and so forth; thus, they are mentioned separately from *sāhasa* [in verse 2.72].
He states the procedure for summoning the witnesses:
"One should cause the witnesses to hear [the charge] while they are in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant.

Because of the statement of Gautama—"Witnesses who have assembled in the presence of the claimant and the respondent shall speak when questioned; those who have not assembled [should not speak]"—one should cause them to hear what is about to be stated.

In this regard, Kātyāyana has shown a specific detail: "The presiding judge, consoling them, shall appoint all the witnesses within the court in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, according to this rule:
'In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, he shall ask the twice-born for truthful testimony.'"
Being pure himself, he should [seat] those who are pure in the forenoon, facing either northward or eastward.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are all of known conduct and who understand the matter— one should question them individually, having bound them firmly with oaths.
Thus: Within the court, the presiding judge, consoling them, shall appoint all the witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant according to this rule.

In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they are facing either northward or eastward.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are all of known conduct and who understand the matter— one should question them individually after restraining them with solemn oaths.
Likewise, regarding the proclamation [of the ordeal] to Brahmins and others, a rule was set forth by Manu: "One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons;
a Vaiśya by cattle, seed, and gold; and a Śūdra by all sins."
Thus:
"One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra by all the [great] sins."

One should pronounce a curse upon a Brāhmaṇa who speaks falsely, saying: "Your truth shall perish. Upon a Kṣatriya, one should say: "Your vehicles and weapons shall become useless. Upon a Vaiśya, one should say: "Your cattle, seeds, gold, and so forth shall become useless."
One should pronounce a curse against him who speaks otherwise regarding a Śūdra, saying: "All sins shall be yours.
An exception to this rule has been shown by that same author: "One should treat like Śūdras those Brahmins who are cattle-herders, traders, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers."
Thus:
"One should treat cowherds, merchants, as well as artisans,
actors, servants, and usurers— though they be Brahmins— as one would Śūdras."
The mention of "Brahmins" (vipra) is intended as an illustration for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well.
"Kuśīlavas" are singers.

When a defendant has offered a challenge regarding the witnesses, if the defects such as childhood and so forth are such that they can be verified through direct perception, the decision is made accordingly.

However, regarding unworthy witnesses, the determination is made through their own statements and from common worldly experience, rather than by means of other witnesses; thus, there is no infinite regress.
If the defendant is unable to prove the defect of the witnesses after having exposed it, then he shall be punished according to the gravity of the matter.
But if he does prove it, then the witnesses are not valid.
As it has been said:
"If one fails to prove [his case], he shall be compelled to pay the fine for suborning witnesses;
once the matter has been clearly established, those witnesses who have violated the rules of witnesshood are to be excluded."
Thus:
"If he fails to prove [his case], he shall be made to pay a fine equal to the damage; the witnesses must clearly be refuted.
Once [the claim] has been established, the witnesses are to be excluded if they have violated the duties of witnesses."
When all the witnesses cited have been found to be corrupt and the plaintiff has no further need for other means of proof, he then becomes defeated;

having been defeated, he shall be made to pay the fine according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, provided that the defendant remains free from doubt and established in the truth of the witnesses' testimony.

If the plaintiff is free from further desire and remains established in the truth of the witnesses, he who has been defeated shall be compelled to pay a fine according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*);
the intention is that if [the sentence] is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), it must depend upon another action.
To explain how one should cause [the text] to be heard, he says:
"Those worlds which belong to those who have committed minor sins, and likewise to those who have committed great sins..."
Whatever worlds belong to those who set fires and those who kill women and children—
all of those he attains who speaks falsehood as witness.
Whatever merit you have performed throughout hundreds of previous births,
know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood.

The connection is as follows: one should cause [the witness] to hear, "He who speaks falsehood as testimony attains all those worlds belonging to those who commit minor offenses (upapātaka), secondary offenses (mahāpātaka), arsonists, and killers of women and children;

likewise, whatever merit has been performed by him over hundreds of future births—all that belongs to the person whom he defeats by speaking untruth. And this should be understood as referring to the Śūdra, because it is prescribed for a Śūdra that all sins (pātaka) must be proclaimed: "But a Śūdra [is to be made aware of his guilt] by means of all sins."
And this [rule] concerns twice-born castes such as cowherds, because it is stated, "cowherds, merchants," and so forth.

Since it is impossible for another person's merit accumulated over many lifetimes to be transferred, nor for one to incur the fruit of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) merely by speaking a lie, this is said for the purpose of intimidating the witnesses.
As Nārada says: "By means of ancient declarations of dharma and by proclaiming the majesty of truth..."
And he should greatly terrify these people with accusations of falsehood.
Thus [it is said].
One should greatly terrify these people with ancient declarations of dharma, with praises of the greatness of truth, and with condemnations of falsehood.

But when the witnesses, having been summoned, do not speak for some reason, what should be done? To this he says: "If men do not state the testimony, the king shall cause them to pay the debt along with ten percent interest on the forty-sixth day."

He who, having accepted to give testimony, does not speak despite being exhorted, shall be compelled by the king to pay the entire debt along with interest to the creditor, as well as the pledged security together with a tenth part.
And that tenth part belongs to the king, because it has been stated: "The debtor shall be made to pay to the king ten percent of the amount recovered."

And this should be understood to apply on the forty-sixth day; speaking before that time, one is not to be made to pay [the fine], provided he is free from afflictions such as disease. As Manu says: "A man who is healthy but fails to state his testimony regarding debts and other matters within three fortnights..."
He shall incur that entire debt, as well as a fine of ten per cent in every case.
Thus:
"If a man, being healthy, does not give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a tenth part as a fine in every case."
"Free from disease" (agada) is an indicator of being free from calamities caused by kings or divine forces. || 2.76 ||
But regarding one who, though knowing the facts, refuses to give testimony out of malice, he says:
"For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows it,
is indeed equal to false witnesses in his sin and in his punishment."

Furthermore, that lowest of men who, even though he specifically knows the matter to be contested, does not give testimony nor accepts it, is equal to false witnesses in terms of his sins and his punishment. And the author will state the punishment for false witnesses later on. After punishing the false witnesses, the legal proceeding must be conducted anew.
Or, even if false testimony has been given, it should be set aside once it is discovered.
As Manu says: "In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very matter shall be reversed; what has been done shall be as if undone."
Thus.
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; even if it has been decided, it shall be as if it were undecided.

Regarding how a decision is reached when witnesses contradict one another, he says: "In case of a conflict, the testimony of the majority prevails; if the numbers are equal, that of those possessing superior qualities;
but when there is a conflict even among those with superior qualities, the testimony of those who possess the highest degree of excellence must be accepted."

In the event of a conflict or contradiction among witnesses, the testimony of the majority is to be accepted. When the number of witnesses is equal, the testimony of those who possess superior qualities is authoritative.

Furthermore, when there is a disagreement even among those with superior qualities, the testimony of those who are most excellent—endowed with learning, study, the practice of its meaning, wealth, progeny, and other such virtues—is to be accepted.

But where there are only a few endowed with good qualities and many others, even in that case, the testimony of those alone who possess the qualities must be accepted; for "even a single person may be a witness if he is learned in the Dharma and is acceptable to both parties," since the excellence of qualities is the primary factor. As for the statement that "those separated by discord are not witnesses," that refers to cases where no distinction can be discerned among all the parties. (2.78)
To address how victory or defeat is determined based on what the witnesses have said, he says:
"He whose claim the witnesses declare to be true shall be the victor;
for him who speaks otherwise, defeat is certain."

If the witnesses declare the plaintiff's proposition—qualified by substance, genus, number, and so forth—to be true, saying, "We know it to be exactly so," that plaintiff is the victor. However, if they declare the plaintiff's proposition to be otherwise, contrary, or false, saying, "This is untrue," his defeat is certain and settled.
But where the witnesses do not establish the existence or non-existence of the matter asserted due to forgetfulness or other causes, a decision must be made by means of other evidence.
Furthermore, the king should not question the witnesses again and again;
he should accept only the statement as it was spontaneously uttered.
As it has been said:
The testimony of those witnesses, which is stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted; once the witnesses have spoken, they should not be questioned again by the king.
Thus [ends verse] 2.79.
The testimony of those witnesses, which is naturally stated and free from defects, is to be accepted;
once they have spoken, the witnesses should not be questioned again by the king.
He states an exception to the rule that "he who speaks otherwise than the truth is certain to suffer defeat":
"Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous,
or twice as numerous, should testify otherwise, the former witnesses shall be deemed perjured."

When witnesses possessing the previously mentioned characteristics have testified in their own view, stating that the matter is not contrary to the claim, if others—being more virtuous than the former or even twice as many—should give testimony otherwise, being inconsistent with the nature of the claim, then the former witnesses would be *kūṭasākṣins*, that is, false speakers.

Is this not untenable? For when witnesses—who have been examined by the plaintiff, the defendant, the members of the court, and the presiding judge, and who have become authoritative—have spoken, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in seeking further means of proof; moreover, once a legal dispute has been settled, further evidence would be fruitless.
This applies unless the written document or the witnesses were previously brought forward.
Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened,
so too is evidence useless for those whose legal case has already been decided.

And because of the words of Nārada, it is said: when a claimant, considering the testimony of witnesses— even those whose faults have not been revealed— to be unreliable due to its contradiction with the facts of the case, suspects a defect in the witnesses themselves, then by whom can the search for other means of proof be prevented?
And it has been said: "That [cognition] whose instrument is defective, yet which lacks the conviction that it is false, is indeed incorrect.

Just as, even when a defect in the instruments such as the eyes is not perceived, one infers a defect in the instrument because the resulting cognition does not correspond with the object—due to its lack of validity—so too is it here. Furthermore, because the examination of the statement is taught as being distinct from the examination of the witnesses: "The statement spoken by the witnesses should be examined together with the members of the court.
Thus it is said.
One should examine the statement spoken by the witnesses together with the members of the court.
As it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "When the legal procedure is pure according to justice, then there is the purification of that statement;
and he who is purified by a pure statement is established as pure in the matter."
Thus:
when the action is pure according to the rule, then that sentence is purified;
and from a pure sentence, that which is pure is established as pure in meaning. This is the settled principle.

According to the principle that "action is characterized by witnesses, not by those connected to the object nor by those who are merely reliable," when the action is pure, then the purification of its statement—the purification of the witness's statement—must be performed.
And the purity of the statement is achieved through the presentation of the true meaning, for there is a traditional legal maxim (*smṛti*) stating, "A statement is purified by truth.

Thus, when the meaning is understood as pure from a pure action and a pure statement, that [meaning] is established as pure and being exactly so; such is the settled rule and boundary for those who know the law.
The meaning is that, provided there is an absence of defects in the cause and of subverting cognitions, the object is indeed non-erroneous.
Now, one might object: "How can another means of proof be accepted as authoritative by bypassing the witnesses whom the litigant himself has made authoritative?
This is not a fault.
For it is said: "He who, abandoning a strong means of proof, relies upon a weak one, shall not obtain that means of proof again once the case has been decided by the members of the court."

Thus, because Kātyāyana prohibits the adoption of another means of proof after the determination of victory (*jayāvadhāraṇa*), he indicates that the adoption of another means of proof is permissible prior to that determination. Nārada as well, by stating, "But when the legal proceeding has been decided, further evidence becomes fruitless," prohibits another means of proof only after the determination of victory, not before it.

Therefore, it is established that even when testimony has been given by witnesses, one who is not satisfied may resort to another means of proof. This being the case, if there exist previously designated witnesses who are more virtuous or twice as numerous as those who have already spoken, and who are currently absent, then they alone must be made the authority; for the rule "whatever they say of their own accord is to be accepted as the legal [truth]" is a general principle governing all legal proceedings, whereas once a lawsuit has been decided, further evidence would be fruitless.
Neither a written document nor witnesses are admissible if they were not previously presented.
And because of this statement by Nārada:

"In the absence of those previously specified, even unmentioned persons of that same character should be accepted as witnesses alone, and not divine proof (*divya*)," for it is stated in the Smṛti: "When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine means of proof."

In the absence of these, divine means (*divya*) must be made authoritative. Beyond this, even if the plaintiff remains dissatisfied, he must not seek another means of proof, for there is no scriptural injunction [to that effect]; thus the legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is to be concluded.

However, where the defendant—considering the testimony of the witnesses to be unauthoritative because it contradicts his own conviction—remains dissatisfied by attributing faults to the witnesses, then, since there is no further occasion for the defendant to present evidence (*kriyā*), an examination of the witnesses must be conducted through the occurrence of divine or royal calamities (*daivika-rājika-vyasana*) within a period of seven days.

In that case, if faults are established against the witnesses, they shall be made to pay the debt that is the subject of the dispute and shall be punished according to the gravity of the offense. If, however, no faults are established, then the defendant must be satisfied with that much. As Manu says:
If, within seven days of the witness having given his testimony,
disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall him, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine.
Thus: "If, within seven days of the aforementioned statement, illness, fire, or the death of a relative should befall a witness, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine."

And this [rule], "He whose witnesses declare the claim to be true shall be the victor," should be understood as an exception applicable to a case where the defendant is fully satisfied. Some, however, explain that even when the testimony has been given by the witnesses, if the witnesses designated by the plaintiff have testified in favor of the plaintiff, and the defendant corroborates other witnesses— who are more virtuous or twice as numerous— with evidence contrary to what was previously stated, then the witnesses of the plaintiff are considered false.

That is incorrect, because the legal action (*kriyā*) of the defendant is untenable. To explain: the plaintiff (*arthin*) is one who points out the matter to be proven (*sādhya*). The defendant (*pratyarthin*), on the other hand, asserts the opposite of that or its non-existence. Since the proof of a non-entity (*abhāva*) is dependent upon the proof of an entity (*bhāva*), whereas the proof of an entity is independent of the proof of a non-entity, it is logical that the entity alone is the object to be proven (*sādhya*). This is because a non-entity cannot, in its own nature, be an object of cognition through witnesses and the like.
Therefore, it is only for the plaintiff that legal action is appropriate.
Moreover, in accordance with subsequent rules, it is traditionally taught that legal action is restricted everywhere [to the claimant];
however, when the grounds for a prior judgment are stated, the defendant shall indicate the means of proof (*kriyā*).
But in the case of a false statement, that [status] would not belong to the proponent; however, in the case of a valid admission, it would not be so.
Thus:
"But when the grounds for the prior claim have been stated, the defendant shall point out the proof;
however, in the case of a denial (mithyā), the plaintiff shall do so, while in the case of an admission (pratipatti), such [proof] need not exist."
For it is stated in the legal tradition: "Two actions do not occur in a single proceeding, nor can there be two sets of evidence for both litigants in a single dispute.
Therefore, the claim that witnesses of the defendant—who are most virtuous or twice as many—might testify otherwise is untenable.

Now, suppose this is the view: where both parties are proponents of a claim regarding an existing entity (*bhāvapratijñāvādinau*), and both claimants state, "This is my inherited property," without considering the distinction between earlier and later times—then, when there is a need to determine whose witnesses are to be accepted among the witnesses present for these two disputants, [it is said]: "When two people dispute over a matter and there are witnesses for both, the witnesses belong to him whose case is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)."

Since it is established by the statement "he who first presents [his case]" that the witnesses of that person are to be accepted, there is an exception to this rule: "even when the testimony has been given by the witnesses.

Therefore, when the number and quality of the witnesses for the plaintiff and the defendant are equal, if the witnesses of the defendant are more virtuous or twice as numerous, then those witnesses of the defendant should be questioned.
And in this way, non-existence (abhāva) does not become the object to be proven.

Since both [parties] are proponents of existence (*bhāvavādin*) and because they differ from the fourfold types of responses, there is no establishment of legal action (*kriyāvyavasthā*) in the present example.

However, in a single judicial proceeding, just as one claimant may have two actions according to the opponent's view, so too there is no contradiction in the two actions of the proponent and the respondent.

The Teacher does not accept even that, because of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even when the witnesses have testified," since the meaning of this [phrase] is not understood either from the context or by implication; enough of this digression. (2.80)
False witnesses have been shown; now he states their punishment:
"The forger and the witnesses shall each be punished separately;
the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, and it is ordained that a Brāhmaṇa shall be banished."

He who makes witnesses false by means of bribes and the like is a "false-maker" (*kūṭakṛt*), as are those witnesses who are likewise false; they shall each be punished individually with double the fine prescribed for defeat in that particular lawsuit resulting from a loss in litigation. However, a Brāhmaṇa is to be banished from the kingdom—that is, exiled—and not fined.
This rule is to be understood to apply when the specific motive, such as greed, is unknown and when the act is not habitual.
Regarding the specific causes such as greed and so forth, as well as their repeated occurrence, it is not stated by Manu:
"On account of greed, one should be fined a thousand; on account of delusion, however, the first *sāhasa* [fine];
on account of fear, two middle *sāhasa* fines; and on account of friendship, four times the first [fine]."
From desire, the first [retribution] is tenfold; from anger, the latter is threefold;
from ignorance, it is two full hundreds; and from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
Thus:
"For greed, he should be fined one thousand; for delusion, however, the first *sāhasa*;
for fear, two middle *sāhasas*; and for friendship, four times the first."
Ten times more [severe] than desire is the former [retribution], but three times more than anger is the latter;
from ignorance there are two full hundreds, but from childishness there are exactly one hundred.
In this context, greed is the desire for gain;
delusion is erroneous cognition;
and fear is terror.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is an excess of affection.
Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for sexual union with women. Anger (*krodha*) is intolerance.
Ignorance is indistinct knowledge;
childishness is the non-arising of knowledge.
In the context of thousands and so forth, copper coins (paṇas) are understood.
Likewise:
"A righteous king, having punished them, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa."
Thus:
"A righteous king, having punished the three castes who give false testimony, should banish them; however, he should only exile a Brāhmaṇa."
And this refers to cases of repeated practice, because of the use of the present tense in the word "kurvāṇān" (while committing).

Having punished the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya as previously described, he should banish them or put them to death; for the word "pravāsa" (banishment) is used in the sense of execution in the *Arthaśāstra*, and this work is of the nature of an *Arthaśāstra*.

In that case as well, banishment, the cutting off of the lips, the cutting off of the tongue, and the taking of life should be understood according to the nature of the false testimony. However, a Brāhmaṇa should be punished and then exiled— that is, expelled from his own kingdom— or alternatively, "vivāsayet" means one who is stripped of his garment (*vāsasaḥ vigataḥ vivāsāḥ*).
The form [vivāsasam] is derived by adding the causative suffix *ṇic* to the root *vas*, followed by the elision of the final syllable according to the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya*.
The meaning is "one should make [her] naked.
Alternatively, *vāsaḥ* means "dwelling," in the sense that one dwells in it.
"Expel him" means he should cause the house to be demolished.
Even for a Brāhmaṇa, when no specific motive such as greed is known and there is no habitual repetition of the offense, the punishment prescribed in each respective case applies.
However, in the case of habitual repetition, there is both a monetary fine and expulsion.

In that regard as well, the legal determination should be understood as banishment from the caste, stripping of property, confiscation of the home, or expulsion from the country, depending on factors such as the specific caste, the nature of the object, and the persistence of the offense.

When false testimony is given for a minor matter due to causes such as greed, provided there is no habitual practice and the specific motive is not known, even a Brāhmaṇa shall receive only a monetary fine, just like a Kṣatriya or others;
however, in the case of a major matter, there shall be nothing but expulsion from the country.
In this regard as well, for all cases involving repetition, that which was stated by Manu is to be observed.
Nor should it be thought that there is no monetary fine (*arthadaṇḍa*) for a Brāhmaṇa;

for if the monetary fine were absent and corporal punishment (*śārīradaṇḍa*) were prohibited, then even for a minor offense, there would result either disrobing, the destruction of the house, branding, banishment, or the total absence of punishment for all four castes who fail to perform penance.
He shall prescribe lawful punishment involving both physical injury and the forfeiture of wealth.
And because of such a traditional teaching (smaraṇa):
"A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]."
This is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).

As for the statement of Śaṅkha: "For the three [lower] castes, there shall be seizure of property, execution, imprisonment, banishment, and branding; but for a Brāhmaṇa," in that context, "seizure of property" is intended to mean the confiscation of all one's possessions, due to its association with execution. However, corporal punishment is proclaimed to be anything up to the end of life, such as confinement and the like. Monetary fines range from a *kākiṇī* upwards and likewise extend to the forfeiture of all property.
Thus, because execution and the confiscation of all property are recited together [in the legal codes],

as for what was also said— "One should banish him from the kingdom, with his entire wealth intact and uninjured"— that refers to the case of a first-time offender of *sāhasa* (violent crime), not to every case.

However, for a Brāhmaṇa, corporal punishment never applies; one must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is situated in the midst of all possible crimes—so states Manu as a general rule. Likewise, Manu says:
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive of his execution in his mind.
Thus [ends verse] 2.81.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.
Moreover: [Before *api ca*, NSP and Pāṇḍeya add: "Regarding the refusal of testimony by one who knows it, he says:
He who, having been made to hear the testimony, denies it to others, being enveloped by darkness..."
He shall be made to pay an eightfold fine, but a Brāhmaṇa one should banish.

But he who, having accepted the role of a witness and being made to hear the testimony along with other witnesses, at the time of giving his deposition, being shrouded in darkness and his mind overcome by passion and the like, denies that testimony to the other witnesses, saying, "I am not a witness in this matter"—he should be made to pay eight times the fine that is prescribed for defeat in the lawsuit.
Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa who is unable to pay the eightfold monetary fine should be banished.
And "banishment" should be understood according to the circumstances of the case as consisting of making him naked, breaking his house, branding him, or expelling him from the country.

But for others, however, in the event that the payment of a fine consisting of eightfold the value of the object is impossible, one should understand that they must perform labor appropriate to their own caste, undergo fettering, or be cast into prison, and so forth.
This principle should also be applied to the preceding verse.
When all parties conceal the testimony, then all are equally culpable.
But when, having given testimony, they speak otherwise again, then they are to be punished in consideration of the circumstances, such as the gravity of the offense;
as Kātyāyana says:
"Those who, having spoken [one way], speak otherwise, being possessed of verbal deception, shall be punished."
Having spoken thus, those who speak otherwise, being possessed of verbal quibbles (*vākchala*), should be punished.
Furthermore, witnesses spoken to by one person must not be pursued in secret by another.
As Nārada said:
"One should not approach a witness in private who has been pointed out by another;
nor should one cause dissension with anyone else; by acting in this way, one surely suffers defeat."
Thus [ends verse] 2.82.
One should not approach a witness in private at the instigation of another, nor should one cause dissension by means of someone else; by acting in this way, one will surely suffer defeat.
The failure to testify and the speaking of falsehood by witnesses is prohibited in all cases.
To provide an exception to that rule, he says:
"A witness may speak untruth where the death of those belonging to the [four] castes would otherwise occur."

Where the death of members of the castes—Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Brāhmaṇas—is likely to occur through the speaking of the truth, there a witness should speak untruth and should not speak the truth.
By this prohibition of truthful speech, the previously forbidden lying and silence of the witness are hereby permitted.

Where, in cases such as a charge based on suspicion, the death of a caste-member would result from speaking the truth while no one’s death would result from speaking an untruth, there the speaking of untruth is permitted.

However, in a case where telling the truth would result in the death of either the plaintiff or the defendant, while lying would result in the death of the other, the king may permit silence if he so consents. If, for some reason, the king does not release them from speaking even when they remain silent, then they should avoid being witnesses by creating a division [among themselves]. If even that is impossible, they must speak the truth alone.
In the case of speaking untruth, there is both the fault of killing a member of the twice-born class and the fault of lying;
however, in the case of speaking truth, there is only the fault of killing a member of the twice-born class.
In that situation, one must perform penance according to the scriptures.
In that case, since there is no transgression when one remains silent regarding untruthful speech because it is permitted by the scriptures, he says:
"To purify that [transgression], a *caru* offering to Sarasvatī must be prepared by the twice-born."
For its purification—that is, for the avoidance of the transgression caused by speaking untruth—the *sārasvata* oblation (*caru*) must be offered by each of the twice-born individually.
It is called *sārasvata* because its deity is Sarasvatī.
The term *caru* is well known to refer to boiled rice cooked internally over steam without being drained off.

The intention here is as follows: that which was prohibited for witnesses—namely, speaking falsehood or remaining silent—is here permitted. However, [the prohibition remains]: "A man becomes guilty of sin by not speaking or by speaking falsely."
Thus, lying and silence have been prohibited in general; this penance is prescribed as the cause for transgressing that prohibition.

Nor should it be thought that even though lying and silence are permitted for witnesses, the injunction of permission is useless because the sin arising from the transgression of the general prohibition against lying and silence remains the same.

For the transgression resulting from lying or silence by a witness is greater, whereas the transgression resulting from general lying or silence is smaller; thus, the statement of permission is purposeful.

Although elsewhere the cessation of a minor incidental transgression follows from the cessation of a greater transgression, nevertheless, because of the explicit permission here and the prescription of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), it is understood that even a minor incidental transgression does not cease through the cessation of the greater one.

This very point should be understood as the reason for the permission to speak untruths to travelers and others when there is a fear of killing a member of the [four] classes (*varṇa*) during questioning;
for in those cases, no expiation exists, since there is no other prohibition.

It is understood from this very statement that there shall be no punishment for witnesses or others, even when the true nature of the matter is realized at a later time through a different means. || 83 ||
The two witnesses to enjoyment have been described.
Now the document (lekhya) is being described.
In that regard, the document is of two kinds: the royal edict (śāsana) and the regional document (jānapada).
The edict has been defined. It is said to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another.
In that regard, a document executed by one's own hand is without witnesses, whereas one executed by another is with witnesses;
the validity of these two depends on local custom,
as Nārada has said:

A document should be known to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another; likewise, it may be without witnesses or with witnesses. The validity of these two depends upon their established usage in the particular region.
Thus it is said:

"A document should be known to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another; likewise, there is that without witnesses and that with witnesses. Proof of these depends upon their established usage in the particular region."
Regarding that, he states what is executed by others:
"Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement according to their own will,
a document with witnesses should be prepared for it, beginning with the name of the creditor."

When a matter concerning gold or other property between a creditor and a debtor has been settled by mutual agreement as to the amount, the time for repayment, and the monthly interest rate, a document accompanied by witnesses—meaning one endowed with witnesses possessing the characteristics previously described—and preceded by the creditor (i.e., one in which the name of the creditor is written first)—must be executed for the purpose of determining the true state of affairs should a dispute arise at a later time. "Preceded by the creditor" means that it begins with the writing of the creditor's name;
that is to say, it is to be made so.

Or witnesses possessing the characteristics already described should be appointed; for the purpose of proving the deed performed by the doer, witnesses are brought forward in legal disputes, or else a document executed by himself [is produced].
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa). 2.84.
Moreover:
[A document] is marked by the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, one's own lineage (gotra),
fellow-student status, ownership, and the names of one's father and so forth.
The year is equal [to twelve months];
the month begins with Caitra;
its half is a fortnight, either bright or dark.
The day refers to the lunar date beginning with the first (pratipad).
Name refers to that of the creditor and the debtor.
Caste refers to being a Brahmin and so forth.

One's own lineage (*svagotra*) refers to lineages such as Vāsiṣṭha and so forth; it is marked by these [names] beginning with *samā*. Likewise, a name based on a quality (*guṇanāma*) derived from one's Vedic branch (*brahmacārika*), such as the *Bahvṛca* or the *Kaṭha*, refers to those engaged in the *Bahvṛca* and other branches.
The name of one's own father and the names of the creditor and debtor;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the types of property, the number, local customs, and so forth are included.
The connection with what precedes is that a document marked with these [details] must be prepared. (2.85)
Furthermore:
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall sign it with his own hand, stating:
"This which is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so."

Regarding that matter which has been settled by mutual agreement between the creditor and the debtor, once that matter is concluded and recorded, the debtor—the borrower—should, with his own hand, enter upon the document his own name and state: "This, which has been written above in this document, is my approval and intention as the son of so-and-so. He should thus inscribe it on the leaf. (2.86)
Likewise: "The witnesses, with their own hands, preceded by the name of their father, should write: 'I, so-and-so, am a witness here'; thus they are equal."

Those witnesses who are recorded in that document shall each, after first writing down their own father’s name, write by their own hand individually: "In this matter, such-and-such a person named Devadatta is a witness. They should be equal in number and in their qualities.
If the debtor or a witness is illiterate, the debtor shall have his statement written by another, and the witness shall have his stated by another witness, in the presence of all the witnesses.
As Nārada has said: "A debtor who is illiterate should record his own opinion, or a witness should do so through another witness, in the presence of all the witnesses."
Thus [ends verse] 2.87.
One who is illiterate or a debtor should have his own statement recorded by another literate person or by a witness,
in the presence of all the witnesses.
Moreover:
"Requested by both parties, this has been written by me, the son of so-and-so; thus the scribe should write at the end, 'By so-and-so'."
Then, at the request of both the creditor and the debtor, the scribe should write at the end: "This document has been written by me, so-and-so Devadatta, son of Viṣṇumitra. (2.88)
Now he states the document executed by oneself:
"A document written in one's own hand is considered valid even without witnesses, except for that which was executed through force or fraud."
A document written in the debtor’s own hand is declared by Manu and others to be valid evidence even without witnesses, provided it was not made through force or fraud.
That is, excluding what is done by force (*bala*)—meaning by compulsion—or by fraud (*upadhi*), which is characterized by deceit, greed, anger, fear, intoxication, and so forth.
Nārada also says:
A document executed under intoxication, by a woman, a child, or through force,
as well as one made under fear or fraud, is not authoritative.
Thus:
"A document executed under duress by a woman, a child, or one who is intoxicated,
as well as one executed through fear or fraud, is invalid."

Furthermore, this document—whether executed by one’s own hand or by the hand of another—in transactions involving a pledge (*sabandhaka*) as well as those without a pledge (*abandhaka*), must be written in accordance with local custom; it should be written so that the sequence of the matter is not lost and the letters of the script are not omitted. It need not, however, be composed solely in grammatically correct Sanskrit (*sādhuśabda*); it may also be written in the specific vernacular dialect (*prātisvikadeśabhāṣā*) of the region.
As Nārada says:
"That which is not contrary to local custom and possesses the clear characteristics of the rules for pledges..."
That document is considered authoritative when its sequence and characters are uncorrupted.
Thus:
"That document which is not contrary to local custom, which possesses the characteristics of a clear procedure, and whose sequence and letters are uncorrupted, is recorded as authoritative."

*Vidhāna* means procedure; *ādhividhi* is the procedure for a pledge, which is the act of pledging. Its characteristics are "the pledge may be either secret or open," "it may be for enjoyment," "it is determined by time," and so forth. That document in which these are clearly and distinctly stated is "one whose characteristics of the pledge-procedure are manifest" (*vyaktādhividhilakṣaṇa*). "With its sequence and syllables unimpaired": the sequence of the syllables and the syllables themselves are the "sequence-syllables" (*kramākṣarāṇi*); that in which these sequence-syllables are not omitted is "one with unimpaired sequence and syllables" (*aviluptakramākṣara*).
Such a document is authoritative evidence.
