The intention is that, unlike royal edicts, there is no fixed rule regarding correct words here. || 2.89 ||
In connection with written documents, he states that even a debt recorded in writing must be paid by only three persons:
"A debt incurred by means of a document must be paid by only three persons.

Just as a debt created by witnesses and so forth must be paid by only three, so too a debt created by a document must be paid by only three—the debtor, his son, and his grandson—and not by a fourth or subsequent generations; thus it is restricted.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, since "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons," it is established that every debt whatsoever must necessarily be paid by these three without distinction? [Reply: Certainly.

This statement has been commenced in order to remove the suspicion of an exception arising from another Smṛti text regarding the subject of debts recorded in a document (*patrārūḍha-ṛṇa*), which might contradict this very general rule (*utsarga*).
For thus, after defining the characteristics of a legal document (*patra*), Kātyāyana has stated: "In this manner, when the time has elapsed, the debt is made payable by the ancestors.
Thus, when the time has elapsed, the debt is made payable by the ancestors.
In this manner, a debt recorded in writing, even if the time for repayment has elapsed, is made payable by those related to the ancestors.
Here, because of the use of the plural "of the ancestors" (*pitṝṇām*) and the statement "the time has elapsed," it is understood that a fourth-generation descendant or later is the one who must pay.
Likewise, Hārīta also states: "In whose hand the document may be, to him the recovery [of the debt] should be assigned."
Thus:
"One should declare the gain to belong to him in whose hand the document is found.
This is to be applied according to the statement of Yogīśvara.
He states an exception to this:
"But a pledge is used for as long as it is not returned."

Since there is a rule that even in the case of a secured loan (*saṃbandhaka*), the debt recorded on the document must be paid by the three [generations] alone, it would follow that the fourth has no authority to discharge the debt, and thus no authority to take possession of the pledge (*ādhi*). To this, it is said: By stating that "as long as the debt is not paid by the fourth or the fifth, so long is the pledge enjoyed," the author shows that the fourth and subsequent generations also have the authority to discharge a secured debt.
But has it not already been stated that "a pledge to be enjoyed for its fruit does not perish"?
True;
even that [statement] would apply only to the three persons in the absence of this refuting statement, and thus everything is faultless. 2.90.
Having concluded the incidental matter, he returns to the subject at hand:
"If a document is located in another country, is illegible, lost, rubbed out,
stolen, torn, burnt, or otherwise destroyed, one should have another document executed."

It is ordained that when a document is unfit for legal proceedings, one should produce another document. Unfitness for legal proceedings occurs when a document is located in an extremely remote foreign land; or when it is "badly written" (*durlekhya*), meaning a document in which the written characters, letters, or words are illegible, ambiguous, or nonsensical; or when it is lost through the passage of time; or when it is "effaced" (*unmṛṣṭa*), meaning its written characters have been rubbed away due to the weakness of the ink or other causes; or when it is stolen by thieves and the like; or when it is "broken" (*bhinna*), meaning torn asunder; or when it is "burnt" (*dagdha*), meaning set on fire; or when it is "cut" (*chinna*), meaning split into two parts—in these cases, a second document is produced.
And this applies when there is mutual consent between the plaintiff and the defendant.
However, when a dispute has arisen and a lawsuit is pending, time should be granted for the production of documents located in another country, depending on the distance of the journey.
If the document is situated in a remote place or has been lost, the determination of the lawsuit must be made by means of witnesses alone.
As Nārada said:

"When a document is deposited in another country, damaged, poorly written, or lost, there shall be a determination of its validity at that time; when it is non-existent, the testimony of witnesses is required."
Thus:

"When a document has been deposited in another country, is decayed, poorly written, or stolen, there shall be a determination of its validity at that time; if it does not exist, the testimony of witnesses must be sought."

If a document exists but is located in another country, a time limit must be granted for its retrieval. However, if the document does not exist—that is, is unavailable—the case should be concluded through the testimony of those who previously saw it, namely the witnesses.
But when no witnesses are available, a decision must be made by means of divine proof; "In a legal proceeding where there is neither writing nor witness, one should prescribe divine proof."
Thus it is from the Smṛti.
And this is a local legal document;
a royal legal document is also exactly like this.

However, there is this distinction: a document issued by a king, bearing his own hand and marked with his own seal, is declared to be a royal edict (rājakīya-lekhya) and is valid for all matters when it contains witnesses.
Thus: "A royal document is declared to be one that bears the king’s own hand, is marked with his own seal, and, in all matters, contains witnesses."
Likewise, another royal decree concerning the *jayapatra* (document of victory) was spoken by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:

"A *jayapatra* is required to be joined with the matter to be proven as it was presented, accompanied by the subsequent legal procedure (*sottarakriya*), and indeed containing a definitive conclusion."
Once the matter is settled, the judge shall give the winning litigant a certificate of victory (jayapatra), marked with the hand-signature of the presiding judge and sealed with the royal seal.
Thus:

"A document of victory (jayapatraka) is desired as being connected with the matter to be proven as it was set forth, accompanied by the subsequent action, and indeed containing a definitive conclusion."

Once the matter is settled, the judge shall give a certificate of victory (*jayapatra*) to the winning litigant; it should bear the hand-seal of the judge and others, and be stamped with the royal seal.

Likewise, the members of the assembly should also place their own hands [on the document], saying, "This is my opinion," just as those members who are experts in the treatises on law (smṛtiśāstra) present there should likewise place their own hands according to the rules for writing.
And those members of the assembly who are present there, being experts in the treatises on law (smṛti),
should likewise affix their own signatures according to the rules for documentation.
For it is so stated in the Smṛti.
Furthermore, a legal proceeding does not become free from "thorns" (i.e., valid) unless there is mutual consent among the members of the court.
As Nārada says: "Where all the people in the court consider, 'This is right'..."
That dispute would be without thorns, but otherwise it would be with thorns.
Thus:
"Where all the members of the assembly consider, 'This is well done,' that dispute shall be free from thorns; otherwise, it shall be thorny."

This is indeed the fourfold judicial proceeding: that which establishes the matter to be proven, which is endowed with the four components, and which bears the royal seal—such is recognized as a document of victory (*jayapatra*).
A document that establishes the matter to be proven, which possesses four constituent parts and is endowed with the royal seal, is recognized as a *jayapatra* (a document of victory).
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
"But where there is deficiency— as when one speaks otherwise, is averse to the legal procedure, fails to appear, provides no answer,
or flees after being summoned— one is declared to be defeated in five ways."

Thus, in that case, there is no document of victory (*jayapatraka*), but rather only a document of defeat (*hīnapatraka*). And the distinction is this: the former is for the purpose of obtaining punishment at a later time, while the latter is for the purpose of establishing the validity of the prior judicial proceeding (*prāṅnyāya*). (2.91)
He states the grounds for a decision when there is doubt regarding a document:
"The purification of a doubtful document may be established by means of a signature written in one's own hand and so forth,
as well as by means of reasoning, acquisition, performance, tokens, connection, and title."
Regarding a document that is suspected of being either authentic or forged, its validity may be established through means such as a writing in one's own hand.
The meaning is that if another document written in one's own hand contains identical characters, then the validity [of the original] shall be established.
From the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it follows that purity [of evidence] results from corroboration with witnesses, written documents, one's own handwriting, and other internal consistencies.
"Attainment through reasoning" (*yuktiprāpti*) means attainment by means of logic.
Attainment (*prāpti*) is the connection between place, time, and persons with the object in question.
The attainment of reasoning (*yuktiprāpti*) is the logical conclusion that "in this place, at this time, this person possesses this object.
The presentation of action and its witness is *kriyā*.
A unique mark (*cihna*) is [a sign] such as the auspicious letter *Śrī* and so forth.

The "connection" (*saṃbandha*) refers to a prior relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant based on mutual trust, such as a transaction involving the giving or receiving of property. "Source of title" (*āgama*) refers to the probable means of acquisition for this amount of wealth.
These alone constitute the grounds [for a claim].
The syntactical connection is that by these reasons, the purification of a disputed document may occur.
However, when no determination arises regarding doubt concerning a document, then the determination must be made by witnesses.
As Kātyāyana says: "When the document has been challenged, the plaintiff shall point out those [witnesses] recorded therein."
Thus,
once the document has been refuted, the proponent should point out those matters recorded therein; this statement applies to cases where witnesses are available.
However, the statement of Hārīta concerns a case where witnesses are unavailable: "If [the defendant says], 'I did not sign this document;
it was forged by him,' then, having set aside that document, the decision shall be reached through ordeal."
Thus [ends verse] 2.92.
"This document was not made by me; it was caused to be forged by him.
Having set that document aside, let there now be a decision by means of the divine ordeal."
When the document has been thus cleared and the debt is due for payment, if the debtor is unable to pay the entire debt, what should be done? To this he says:
"Having paid the money, the debtor should write on the back of the document;
or the creditor, having received the payment, should provide a receipt marked with his own hand."
When a debtor is unable to pay the entire debt, he should, having paid according to his capacity, write upon the back of the previously executed document: "This much has been paid by me.
Or, the creditor, having received the money that was due, should give it—that is, record it—upon the back of that very same document, writing: "This much has been received by me.
How so?

The creditor shall deliver to the debtor a document marked with his own hand, characterized by letters written by his own hand; or he may give a receipt (*upagata*) marked with letters written by his own hand. (2.93)
Regarding the question of what should be done with the document once the entire debt has been paid, he says:
"Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document, or else have another one made for the sake of clearance.
Having paid the entire debt, either gradually or all at once, one should tear up the previously executed document.

But when the document is situated in a difficult location or has been lost, then the debtor, for the sake of purification—that is, for the purpose of terminating his status as a debtor—should have another document executed by the creditor.
The meaning is that the creditor should give a certificate of clearance (*viśuddhipatra*) to the debtor according to the procedure previously described.
When a debt in its entirety must be paid in the presence of witnesses, what should be done? To this he says:
"Or whatever [debt] may be accompanied by witnesses, that should be paid in the presence of witnesses."
But that debt which was contracted in the presence of witnesses must be paid in the very same presence of those former witnesses. (2.94)

The threefold human evidence, characterized by written documents, witnesses, and possession, has been described. Now, having reached its proper occasion, the author intends to explain divine evidence (*divya-pramāṇa*). With the first five verses beginning with "the balance, fire, water," he sets forth the manual of divine ordeals (*divyamātṛkā*).
Therein, he first teaches the various types of divine ordeals.
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals here for the sake of purification.

These five ordeals, beginning with the balance and ending with the sacred libation, are to be administered in this legal treatise for the sake of purification—that is, for the removal of doubt regarding a contested matter.

But surely there are other divine ordeals elsewhere as well: "The balance, fire, water, and poison, as well as the holy water (kośa), rice grains, and the heated gold coin—these are the seven divine ordeals."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Pitāmaha, one might ask: "How is it that there are only these many? To this he says:
"These [oaths] apply to serious charges."
It is restricted that these [ordeals] are for great charges (*mahābhiyoga*) alone and not for others; however, it is not restricted that these are the *only* ordeals.
Furthermore, he will state the limit of what constitutes "greatness.

But surely, the ordeal of the balance (*kośa*) is also desired in cases of minor charges, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "One should cause the balance to be administered even in a minor case"?
True.

The inclusion of the *kośa* (ordeal by sacred libation) among the ordeals such as the balance and others is not intended as a restrictive rule (niyamārtha) limiting it to major charges (*mahābhiyoga*) alone; rather, its purpose is to ensure its application even in cases of charges brought with arrogance (*sāvaṣṭambhābhiyoga*).
Otherwise, it would apply only to charges based on suspicion (*śaṅkābhiyoga*), whereas for those accused with arrogance, one should prescribe the balance and other ordeals.
Rice grains and a treasure chest [are found] only when there is suspicion; of this there is no doubt.
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa).
Since [the rules] apply without distinction to great charges, suspected offenses, and those involving defiance, he states an exception:
"When the accuser is present at the head of the court."
These [ordeals], beginning with the balance, are for the defendant when the plaintiff is "standing upon the head" (śīrṣakastha).

The "head" (śīrṣaka) refers to the fourth part of the legal proceeding, characterized by victory or defeat; since punishment is indicated by that, one who stands there is "standing upon the head," meaning one who is subject to the punishment incurred thereby. (2.95)

"Therefore, the plaintiff shall immediately have the proof of the matter asserted written down"—this rule demonstrates that the act belongs only to the one who asserts a claim based on a factual basis (*bhāvapratijñāvādī*).
He states the exception to that: "Or, by mutual consent (*rucyā*), either party may do so, while the other shall pay the fine (*śiras*)."
When there is mutual agreement between the accuser and the accused regarding their respective positions, one of them—whether the accused or the accuser—shall undergo an ordeal (*divya*).
The other—whether the accused or the accuser—shall undergo physical punishment, corporal punishment, or a fine; that is, he shall accept [the penalty].
This is the underlying intention.
Divine proof (*divya-pramāṇa*) is not like human proof; although it has existence alone as its object, it rather takes as its object both existence and non-existence without distinction.

Therefore, in the case of a false defense (*mithyottara*), a counter-attack (*pratyavaskandana*), or a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), divine proof may be employed at the will of either the plaintiff or the defendant.

It has been stated that the ordeal by *kośa* (water) applies without distinction to both minor charges and major charges, as well as to those involving suspicion and those involving *sāvaṣṭambha* (defiance). Furthermore, a restriction has been shown that the ordeals beginning with the balance (*tulā*) and ending with poison (*viṣa*) apply only to major charges and only where there is *sāvaṣṭambha*.
Regarding this, he states an exception to the rule "only in cases of defiant charges":
"One may administer [the ordeal] even without a formal charge (*śīrṣaka*) in the case of treason against the king or in the case of a mortal sin (*pātaka*)."

In cases of suspicion of treason against the king, suspicion of heinous crimes such as the killing of a Brahmin, and suspicion of great theft, one may administer the ordeal even without the balance-scale and other implements.
As it has been said: "For those suspected by kings, those pointed out by bandits, and those intent on proving their own innocence, the divine ordeal should be administered without the head."
Thus:
"For those suspected by kings, for those pointed out by bandits,
and for those intent on proving their own purity, the ordeal should be administered with the exception of the 'head' [ordeal]."

Furthermore, rice is used only when there is suspicion of minor theft; however, the settled rule is that rice is to be administered in cases of theft and not otherwise, according to the statement of Pitāmaha:
"The *taptamāṣa* (heated gold), however, is for suspicion of major theft alone; the *taptamāṣa* is ordained for those accused under suspicion of theft."

Thus it is from the Smṛti. Others, however, hold that oaths concern matters of minor importance: "Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, gold, deities, the feet of ancestors, gifts, and meritorious deeds."
In all legal disputes, one may touch the heads of one's sons, wives, and friends,
or even perform the oath of drinking from the royal treasury.
Thus have these oaths been declared by Manu for minor matters.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Nārada.

Although oaths are designated as *divya* (divine ordeals) because they determine that which cannot be determined by human means of knowledge—according to common worldly usage where whatever determines what is otherwise undecidable is called *divya*—nevertheless, they are designated as distinct from other *divya* ordeals such as the balance (*dhaṭa*) and so forth, because they serve as the cause for a determination at a later time, whereas the others serve as the cause for an immediate determination; this is like the expression "the Brahmins and the wandering mendicants" (*brāhmaṇaparivrājaka*).

As for the *kośa* (water ordeal), although it is an oath, its inclusion among the *dhaṭa* and other ordeals is due to its similarity to them in that it concerns serious charges (*mahābhiyoga*) and charges involving a formal challenge (*avaṣṭambhābhiyoga*), rather than because it serves as the cause for an immediate determination.

Although the *taṇḍula* (rice) and *taptamāṣa* (hot gold) tests are also occasions for immediate determination, they are not included among those [oaths] because they differ from the *dhaṭa* (balance) and others in having a limited scope and being subject to suspicion; thus one should be content with this [exclusion].
These ordeals (*divya*) and oaths (*śapatha*) are to be employed in disputes concerning debts and the like, as far as applicable.
As for the statement of Pitāmaha: "In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals."
Thus, even that [rule] must be interpreted to mean that one should avoid ordeals when witnesses such as neighboring landowners (*sāmanta*) and others are available.
But surely, in other types of disputes as well, there would be no occasion for ordeals whenever other means of proof are possible?
True.

In disputes concerning debts and the like, even when the plaintiff has presented witnesses possessing the aforementioned characteristics, if the defendant—relying on the support of accepting punishment—resorts to an ordeal (*divya*), then an ordeal may indeed take place.

This is because there is the possibility of a defect in the intention of the witnesses, whereas an ordeal is faultless and pertains to the true nature of the matter; for Dharma is characterized by such truthfulness.
As Nārada says: "Dharma is established in truth, but legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) rests upon witnesses."
In a matter that can be resolved by fate, one should not employ human effort or written documents.
Thus it is said:
"In that case, the legal matter rests upon truth, whereas judicial procedure rests upon witnesses;
when a matter is to be proven by divine means, one should not employ human evidence, nor a written document."

In disputes concerning immovable property, even if the defendant, relying on the threat of punishment, insists upon an ordeal (*divya*) despite the existence of visible evidence such as witnesses from neighboring villages, the rule "in disputes concerning immovable property" and so forth, spoken by Pitāmaha, is intended to exclude that option; it is not for the purpose of an absolute prohibition of ordeals.
For if there were no written documents or neighbors, there would follow the undesirable consequence of no decision being reached in disputes over immovable property. (2.96)
Furthermore: before *kiṃ ca*, NSP and Pāṇḍeya add *divye sādhāraṇavidhiḥ* | Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on...
One should cause all the divine ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and the Brāhmaṇas.

On the day prior, having fasted, the judge shall summon the one who accepts the ordeal to bathe with his clothes on at sunrise; then, in the presence of the king, the court members, and the Brahmins, he shall administer all the ordeals. The ordeals should be administered to one who has fasted for three nights or for one night, provided he is pure and wearing wet clothes.

Thus, the alternative regarding fasting mentioned by Pitāmaha is to be understood as being regulated according to the relative strength or weakness of the matter at hand—whether it be a major or minor case. Furthermore, the rule of fasting applies to the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) who causes the ordeal to be performed: "In ordeals, the judge should conduct all the proceedings, just as the *adhvaryu* priest does in sacrifices; he shall do so while fasting, by the king's command."
Thus, according to the words of Pitāmaha.

In this regard, although it is stated without qualification that "at sunrise," nevertheless, according to the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), divine ordeals should be administered on Sundays. Furthermore: "The fire-ordeal should take place in the forenoon, and the balance-ordeal should also be in the forenoon;
however, one who desires to follow the true nature of Dharma should administer the water-ordeal at midday."
The purification by means of the ordeal by balance is prescribed for the forenoon of the day;
however, poison should be administered during the final watch of the night when it is well-cooled.
Thus, the specific rule stated by the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) is to be observed.

Regarding those ordeals for which no specific time has been mentioned—such as the *taṇḍula* (rice), *taptamāṣa* (heated bean), and so forth—their administration occurs only in the forenoon; for it is stated by Nārada in general terms: "The administration of all ordeals is proclaimed to take place in the forenoon."
The day is divided into three parts: the first part is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), the middle is midday (*madhyāhna*), and the latter is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).

Likewise, another specific division of time is shown by way of both injunction and prohibition. First, by way of injunction: "For fire, the cold season, the winter, and the rainy season are prescribed."
Water in the autumn and summer, and poison in the winter and early spring.
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these months are common to all and are not in conflict with the divine [reckoning].
The treasury, however, should always be given; the balance scale may be used at all times.
Thus it is said: "The seasons of winter and late winter, as well as the rainy season, are proclaimed to belong to Agni;
water [is beneficial] during autumn and summer, while poison is [beneficial] during late winter and early winter."
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these months are common to all and are not in conflict with the celestial [reckoning].
But the treasury must always be given; the balance, however, may be used at all times.
The mention of the "treasure" (kośa) is an indicative mark for all oaths.

Furthermore, because no specific time is mentioned regarding the rice grains (taṇḍula), they may be used at all times. There is also a prohibition-based rule: "Purification by water shall not take place in the cold season, nor shall purification by fire take place in the hot season."
One should not administer poison during the rainy season, nor should one employ a scale in a strong wind.
Neither in the afternoon, nor at twilight, nor ever at midday.
Neither in the afternoon, nor at twilight, nor ever at midday.
"In the cold season, there should be no purification by water"—here, by the word "cold," the winter (*hemanta*), dewy season (*śiśira*), and rainy season (*varṣā*) are included.

"In the hot season, there is no purification by fire"—here, by the word "hot season," the summer (*grīṣma*) and autumn (*śarad*) are meant; the prohibition, even though already established by the preceding injunction, is stated again for the sake of emphasis.
The specific purpose [of this rule] will be explained later. (2.97)
He states the rule regarding those authorized [to undergo the ordeal]:
"For women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick, [the ordeal shall be] fire or water; for a Śūdra, seven barley grains or poison."

A "woman" (strī) refers to any woman whatsoever, regardless of distinctions of caste or stage of life. A "child" (bāla) is one up to sixteen years of age, regardless of distinctions of caste. An "elderly person" (vṛddha) is one who has reached at least eighty years.
The blind man is one deficient in sight;
the lame man is one deficient in feet;
the Brahmin is one by birth alone.
The sick person is one afflicted by disease.
It is ordained that for the purification of these [witnesses], the ordeal shall be the balance alone. For a Kṣatriya, the ordeals are fire, the plowshare, and the heated metal ball.
Water alone is for the Vaiśya;
the word "vā" (or) is used here in the sense of restriction.
For the Śūdra, seven barley grains of poison, measured as previously specified, serve for the purpose of purification.

Because the scale is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa and the seven barley grains or poison are prescribed for the Śūdra, it is stated that fire or water pertains to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya. This very point has been clarified by Pitāmaha: "The balance should be given to the Brāhmaṇa, fire to the Kṣatriya;
water is declared for the Vaiśya, and one should cause poison to be administered to the Śūdra."
Thus it is said:
"The balance should be administered to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya;
water is prescribed for a Vaiśya, and one should cause poison to be given to a Śūdra."

As for the traditional rule that women and others are exempt from ordeals: "For those who observe vows, those who are severely afflicted, the diseased, ascetics, and women, an ordeal shall not be administered if justice is to be preserved."
Thus, the phrase "or the other may act according to their own preference" is intended to preclude such an option.

This is what is meant: in cases of assault and the like, when women and others are the accusers, the ordeal belongs only to those being accused; even if these [women] are the ones being accused, the ordeal belongs only to the accusers. However, in the case of mutual accusations, there is indeed an option.

In that case as well, it is restricted by the statement of Kātyāyana: "For women and others, the balance alone [is used]. Thus, regarding accusations involving suspicion of major sins (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth, the rule that for women and others the balance alone is used is meaningful as a restrictive regulation when all ordeals are available during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Caitra, and Vaiśākha, which are common for all ordeals.
However, it does not mean that for women the balance is the only ordeal at all times; for it is said: "Poison is not prescribed for women, nor is water remembered [as such] for them."
One should investigate their inner reality by means of the crucible, the crucible-box, and so forth.

Thus, because purification is prescribed by means of the balance, the water-vessel, fire, and so forth—excluding poison and water—it should be applied accordingly even to children and others. Likewise, for Brahmins and the other castes as well, there is no rule mandating the balance and such at all times; rather, the purification by the water-vessel (kośa) is prescribed for all social classes (varṇas).
All these [are forbidden] for all [twice-born], except for a Brāhmaṇa who has no poison.
Thus, according to the recollection of Pitāmaha,
this statement is intended solely as a restrictive rule for the balance and other ordeals when they are performed together at a common time;
however, at other times, all [ordeals] are prescribed for each respective occasion.
For instance, during the rainy season, fire alone [is the ordeal] for all.
However, during the winter and the cool season, there is an option between fire and poison for the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriya.
But for the Brāhmaṇa, fire alone is used and never poison, because of the prohibition: "for the Brāhmaṇa, [the ordeal is] without poison."
In summer and autumn, however, it is water alone [that is recommended].

For those for whom fire and other substances are prohibited due to specific diseases, it is said: "One should avoid fire for those suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and water for those with asthma and cough;
one should always strictly avoid poison for those with an excess of bile and phlegm."
Thus, for them, even at the time of the fire ordeal and others, the common ordeals such as the balance (tulā) and so forth are applicable.

Likewise, according to the statement, "Water, fire, and poison should be administered to strong men," the ordeals based on caste, age, and physical condition must be administered to the weak as well, in every way, by neither violating the injunctions nor the prohibitions, and without transgressing the appropriate seasons. (2.98)
It has been stated that "these [ordeals] apply in cases of great charges.
Now, he explains what constitutes the greatness of a charge in that context:
One should not administer the ploughshare, nor poison, nor the balance for less than one thousand [paṇas].
One should not administer an ordeal by plowshare, poison, or the balance for a value less than five thousand paṇas;
this also applies to the ordeal by water for those of intermediate status.
As it has been said: "One should cause ordeals beginning with the balance and ending with poison to be administered in cases involving great matters."
Thus:
"One should cause the ordeals beginning with the balance and ending with poison to be administered in cases involving serious matters.

In this context, the ordeal of the *kośa* (sacred libation) is not mentioned because it is recorded in the legal tradition that one may administer the *kośa* even in minor cases, as it is prescribed for even slight accusations.
The meaning is that these four divine [treasures] occur only after fifty thousand [years], and not before.
But is it not the case that even for lesser amounts, fire and the other ordeals were shown by Pitāmaha: "One should administer the balance for one thousand [paṇas], likewise iron for half a thousand;
for half of that, water; and for half of that, poison is prescribed"?
Thus it is said:
"In a case involving a thousand [paṇas], one should administer the balance; likewise, for half of a thousand, iron;
for half of that, water; and for half of that, poison is prescribed."
True.

In this regard, the established rule is as follows: the statement of Pitāmaha refers to the case where loss of caste (*pātitya*) occurs upon the theft of a particular substance, whereas the statement of Yogīśvara refers to other substances.
Furthermore, these two statements concern the offenses of theft and violence (*sāhasa*).
But regarding denial, a specific rule has been shown by Kātyāyana: "In a case where there is a denial of what was given, one should establish proof;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value."
Having ascertained the measure of all the materials, one should fashion the gold;
then, endowed with the proper measure of gold, one should employ that divine [image].
Having calculated the number of gold coins, poison is prescribed for the loss of one hundred;
indeed, for the loss of eighty, one should offer oneself to the fire.
In the event of a loss of sixty [paṇas], water should be administered; in the case of forty, indeed, the balance ordeal;
but for a loss of twenty or ten, the oath of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) is prescribed.
Or, upon the destruction of more than five [grains], one should use rice of half that amount;
indeed, when half of that is destroyed, one should touch the heads of one's sons and others.
For when even half of that half is destroyed, worldly activities are remembered [to cease];
reflecting thus, a king does not fall away from dharma and artha.
Thus:
"Where there is a denial of what was given, one should determine the proof;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value."
Having ascertained the measure of all the materials, one should fashion the gold;
then, endowed with the proper measure of gold, one should employ that divine [image].
Having ascertained the number of gold pieces, poison is prescribed for the loss of one hundred;
indeed, for the loss of eighty, one should offer oneself to the fire.
In the event of a loss amounting to sixty [units], water should be administered; for a loss of forty, indeed, the ordeal of the balance;
but for a loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of the sacred water (kośa) is prescribed.
Or, upon the loss of more than five [coins], one should offer rice;
then, upon the loss of half of that amount, or again half of that, one should touch the heads of one's sons and others.
For when even half of that half is destroyed, worldly activities are remembered [to cease];
reflecting thus, a king does not fall away from dharma and artha.
In the passage "having ascertained the number of *suvarṇas*," the word *suvarṇa* denotes the specific measure stated as "sixteen *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.
Furthermore, the word *nāśa* here signifies concealment or denial.
However, in the rule "there shall be no legal penalty for theft below a thousand," it should be understood as a thousand copper *paṇas*.
Now, since these ordeals are prescribed for the great sin of treason against the king, how is it that one should not carry the heated ploughshare without [a fine] of a thousand? To this he says:
"In matters concerning the king and in cases of formal accusation, they should always carry [the ordeal], being pure."

In cases of treason against the king and in charges involving mortal sins (mahāpātaka), they should administer these ordeals regardless of the amount of wealth involved; being purified by fasting and other means, they should speak and perform them.
Likewise, a specific place has been stated by Nārada:
"At the royal court, at the gate of the palace, in a temple, or in a public square."
It should be placed there immovably, worshipped with incense, garlands, and ointments.
Thus,
it should be placed motionless at the gate of the royal palace, in a temple, or in a courtyard; it is to be worshipped with incense, garlands, and ointments.
The *dhaṭa* ordeal is to be administered.
And the rule has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"In the place of Indra, for men who are accused or who are great sinners (*mahāpātakin*)."
One should employ those engaged in treason against the king at the royal gate.
For those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for others besides these, the wise know that the ordeal should be administered in the midst of the assembly hall.
For those who are untouchable, the lowest of slaves, Mlecchas, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions, there is no fixed rule regarding the king;
in cases of doubt concerning them, one should prescribe the ordeals well-known among them.
Thus [ends verse] 2.99.
For those who are untouchable, the lowest of slaves, Mlecchas, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions (prātilomya), there is no fixed rule regarding the king;
rather, in cases of doubt concerning them, one should prescribe the ordeals that are well-known among them.
Having thus described the divine *mātṛkā* which is useful for all ordeals, he now states the application of the ordeals beginning with the balance (*dhata*):
"The accused, having resorted to the balance, is made equal to the counterweight by experts skilled in weighing;
having drawn a line [to mark the position], he is lowered."
O Tula, you were created by the gods of old as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward," thus he should consecrate the balance.

Those who know how to hold and weigh with a balance—such as goldsmiths and others—should, having made the person to be weighed equalized and balanced by means of a counterweight such as clay, and having had him mount or engage with the balance, mark with a white line the position in which he stood upon the surface of the scale-pan during the state of being equalized by the counterweight; then, having lowered him, one should consecrate and entreat the balance with this mantra:
"O Balance, you are the seat of truth."
In the past, at the beginning of creation, she was fashioned and brought forth by the gods, headed by Hiraṇyagarbha.
Therefore, O auspicious and beautiful one, tell me the true nature of this doubtful matter; show it to me and release me from this uncertainty.
O Mother, if I am a doer of evil or a speaker of untruth, then lead me downward.
"Then, if I am pure and a speaker of truth, lead me upward"—
this is the mantra for consecrating the scale (*tulābhimantraṇamantra*) spoken by another Smṛti for the judge,
whereas this one is for the person undergoing the ordeal.
The characteristics of victory and defeat, however, are understood from the very indications of the mantra; thus, they have not been stated separately.

Furthermore, the construction of the balance (dhaṭa), as well as its mounting and so forth, is established by the requirements of the purpose itself, and has been made clear by Pitāmaha, Nārada, and others.
For example: "Having cut down a sacrificial tree, like a sacrificial post (yūpa), preceded by the recitation of mantras..."
Having prostrated before the guardians of the world, the wise should construct the balance.
A gentle mantra dedicated to the Vanaspati (the Lord of the Forest) must be recited while cutting [the wood];
the balance-beam should likewise be made square, firm, and straight.
And rings should be provided at three places according to the requirements.
The scale-beam should be made four cubits long, and the two supports above it should be equal to that.
The distance between the two [supports] should be exactly one and a half cubits.
Two cubits, however, should be buried for both feet as well.
And likewise, the two side-arches (toraṇas) should be made on both sides,
always ten finger-breadths higher than the balance-beam (dhaṭa).
And two downward-facing supports should be made from clay,
attached by strings to the two arches, reaching up to touch the top of the balance-beam.
The balance-beam should likewise be made motionless, facing east, in a clean place;
having suspended two scales on both sides.
One should arrange darbha grass pointing eastward on both sides of the two scales;
one should weigh the performers on the western scale and auspicious earth on the other.
One should fill that cavity with brick-dust and gravel;
in this matter, there is an option between clay, bricks, gravel, and dust. Expert examiners who are skilled in the measurement of weights must be appointed.
Merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers must always have the balance-beam of their scales examined by inspectors so that it remains perfectly level.
And water should be poured upon the balance by the wise;
that balance upon which the water does not float is to be known as even.
Having first weighed the man and then having lowered him,
one should always cause the balance-beam to be made, adorned with banners and flags.
Then, the knower of mantras should invoke the deities according to this rite,
accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and drums, and with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Facing the east and with palms joined in reverence, the judge shall then say:
"Come, come, O Lord Dharma; enter into this divine ordeal!"
Having invoked Dharma into the balance along with the world-protectors, the Vasus, Ādityas, and hosts of Maruts, one should subsequently assign the limbs [of the deity].
Having first established Indra in the east, likewise Yama, the Lord of the Dead, in the south;
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Kubera in the north.
One should also place the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions:
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, and Varuṇa has the luster of crystal.
Kubera, however, has the luster of gold, and Vahni likewise has the luster of gold;
Nirṛti is dark-complexioned, and Vāyu is praised as being smoke-colored.
Īśāna, however, should be red; thus one should meditate on these [deities] in sequence.
A wise person should worship the Vasus on the right side of Indra.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna, he likewise saw the host of Ādityas:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, and Pūṣan, with Parjanya as the tenth, are recorded;
then Tvaṣṭṛ, and then Viṣṇu, who, though born last, is not the least.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names;
one should know that the abode of the Rudras is in the western part of Agni.
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly illustrious Giriśa; Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita.
Bhavanādhiśvara, Kapālī, Viśāmpati,
Sthāṇu, and the lord Bhava— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
One should designate the station of the Mothers in the midst of the lords of the pretas and the rākṣasas:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by her hosts;
they know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti.
In the northern region of Varuṇa, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located.
[The names of Vāyu are: Pavana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.
Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīva, and the eight Maruts are proclaimed [as the deities];
the wise man should invoke Durgā on the northern side of the balance.
The wise know that the worship of these deities is performed by their own names,
ending with the offering of ornaments, followed by the presentation of *arghya* and other offerings in due order for the sake of Dharma.
After the *arghya* and other offerings, one should prepare the secondary limbs (*aṅga*) ending with the ornaments;
then one should perform the service beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) and ending with the food offering (*naivedya*).
Thus:
"Come, come, O Blessed Dharma; enter into this divine [body]."
Having invoked Dharma into the balance along with the world-protectors, the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts, one should thereafter assign the limbs [of the deity].
Having first established Indra in the east, likewise Yama, the Lord of the Dead, in the south;
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Kubera in the north.
One should also place the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions:
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, and Varuṇa has the luster of crystal.
Kubera is golden-hued, and Agni is also golden-hued;
likewise, Nirṛti is dark-blue, and Vāyu is praised as smoke-colored.
Īśāna, however, should be red; thus one should meditate upon these [deities] in sequence.
On the right side of Indra, the wise man should worship the Vasus.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna, he likewise saw the host of Ādityas:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is recorded as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, who, though born last, is not the least.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names;
one should know that the abode of the Rudras is in the western part of Agni.
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly illustrious Giriśa; Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita.
Bhavanādhīśvara, Kapālī, Viśāmpati,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhava— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
One should arrange the station of the Mothers in the midst of the lords of the pretas and the rākṣasas:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by her hosts—[these are located there];
they know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti.
In the northern region of Varuṇa, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located.
[The names of Vāyu are: Pavana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.
Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīva, and the eight Maruts are proclaimed [as the deities];
the wise man should invoke Durgā on the northern side of the balance.

The wise know that the worship of these deities is performed by their own names, ending with ornaments and garments; then, having offered [the gifts] for Dharma, one should present the *arghya* and so forth in due order.
After the *arghya* and other offerings, one should arrange the secondary limbs (*aṅga*) ending with the ornaments;
then one should perform the service beginning with perfumes (*gandha*) and ending with the food offering (*naivedya*).

And here, having fashioned a scale adorned with banners and flags, one should invoke Dharma upon it with the mantra "Come, come! (*ehy ehi*). Then, using the ritual procedure beginning with "I offer the *arghya* to Dharma, obeisance" (*dharmāyārghyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*), one should present everything from the *arghya*, *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, *madhuparka*, *ācamanīya*, bath, garments, sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and *ācamanīya*, up to the ornaments such as the crown and bracelets. Next, for the deities beginning with Indra and ending with Durgā, one should offer the items from *arghya* to the ornaments, each with their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), in the dative case, and ending with "obeisance" (*namaḥ*), according to the sequence of individual substances (*padārthānusamaya*). Having offered sandalwood paste (*gandha*), flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth to Dharma, one should likewise offer the sandalwood paste and other items to Indra and the others as before.
And for the worship of the *dhaṭa*, red fragrances and flowers should be used.
As Nārada said:
"With red fragrances, garlands, curd, cakes, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth..."
One should first worship the balance, and thereafter worship the remaining [deities].
Thus:
"One should first worship the balance with red perfumes, garlands, curd, cakes, unbroken grains, and so forth; thereafter, one should worship the remaining [deities]."
As for Indra and the others, since no specific [colors] are mentioned, their worship is to be performed with red flowers or whatever else is available; such is the sequence of worship.
And all of this the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka) shall perform, as has been stated.
Then the judge shall be a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, tranquil in mind, and free from envy.
True to his word, pure, and skillful, he was devoted to the welfare of all living beings;
having fasted, wearing clean garments, and having cleansed his teeth.
And one should perform the worship of all the deities according to the prescribed rite.
Likewise, an oblation (homa) should be performed by four officiating priests (ṛtvij) in the four directions using a worldly fire (laukikāgni).
As it is said:
"In the same way, the oblation should be performed in the four directions by those who have mastered the Vedas."
With clarified butter, sacrificial oblation, and fuel-sticks as the means for the fire-offering.
Then one should perform the oblation with the Sāvitrī mantra, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā.

The meaning is that one should recite the Gāyatrī beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and then again recite the *praṇava* ending with the *svāhākāra*, and offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) one hundred and eight times each.

Having thus performed the worship of the deity ending with the oblation, one should thereafter write down the matter at hand along with the mantra to be recited on a leaf; then, having purified that leaf, one should place it upon the head.
As it has been said:
Having written down on a leaf that matter for which one is accused,
that task, together with this mantra, should be placed upon the head.
And this is the mantra: "The sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire; heaven, earth, the waters, and the heart;
Yama, day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of a man."
Thus:
"The sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire; heaven, earth, water, and the heart;
Yama, day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of a man."
And this section of the ritual procedure, beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head, is common to all ordeals.
As it has been said:
"One should apply this entire rule of mantras to all ordeals."
And one should likewise perform the invocation of the deities.
Thus:
one should apply this entire ritual procedure for mantras to all divine ordeals;
likewise, one should perform the invocation of the deities in the same manner.
Immediately thereafter, the judge should address the balance; for it is stated in the legal tradition: "The knower of the scriptures should address the balance according to this procedure.
And the mantras have been shown: "O Balance, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked-minded."
From the letter *dha*, you are the embodiment of Dharma; from the letter *ṭa*, you are the crooked man.
Because you hold and examine [the truth], you are therefore called the Balance;
you know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings.
O God, you alone know those things which human beings do not know; this man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
Therefore, you ought to deliver him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
Thus:
"O Balance, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked-minded;
from the letter *dha* you are the embodiment of Dharma, and from the letter *ṭa* [you judge] the crooked man."
Because you hold and examine [the truth], you are therefore called the Balance (Dhaṭa);
you know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings.
O God, you alone know those things which human beings do not understand; this man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
Therefore, you ought to deliver him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
The person to be cleared (the *śodhya*) should address the balance with the previously mentioned mantra beginning with "O Balance, you are... (*śodhyas tu tvaṃ tule*).

Immediately thereafter, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), having placed the document upon the head of the person to be cleared in its proper position, causes him to ascend the balance; he should cause him to ascend again, with the document still situated on his head, according to the traditional law (*smaraṇa*).
One should keep it fixed exactly as it was for five *vināḍīs*.
An expert in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) should perform the examination of that time;
a preeminent Brahmin astrologer should carry out the examination of the time.
Five *vināḍīs* should be known by those skilled in determining the time for examination.
Thus it is from the traditional authority (smṛti).
A *prāṇa* is the duration of time required to pronounce ten long syllables;
six *prāṇas* constitute a *vināḍī*.
And it is said: Ten syllables of a guru [length] constitute one *prāṇa*; six *prāṇas* make one *vināḍikā*.
Sixty of those make one *ghaṭī*, and sixty *ghaṭīs* make one day. Thirty days make a month.
Thus: ten guru-syllables constitute one breath (prāṇa); six breaths make one vināḍikā;
sixty of those make one ghaṭī; sixty ghaṭīs make one day; and by thirty days, a month.
And at that time, for the purpose of examining purity and impurity, pure men should be appointed by the king;
they shall declare the purity and impurity,
as stated by Pitāmaha:
Brahmins who speak of matters exactly as they have seen them are the best witnesses;
those who are wise, pure, and free from greed should be appointed by the king.
Then, the king shall have the best witnesses declare both purity and impurity.
Thus:
Brahmins who speak of matters exactly as they have seen them, who are wise, pure, and free from greed—these are the best witnesses; they should be appointed by the king.
Then, the king shall determine purity and impurity based on the testimony of the most excellent witnesses.
And the cause for determining purity and impurity has been stated:
"If, when weighed, he increases in weight, he shall be pure without a doubt;
if he remains equal or decreases, that man shall not be pure."
Thus it is said: "If, when weighed, he increases in weight, he shall be pure without a doubt;
but if he remains equal or decreases, that man shall not be pure."
As for the statement of Pitāmaha:
"One with a minor fault should be known as equal [to the defendant], but one with many faults is defeated."
One with a minor offense should be known as equal [to one who has not committed an offense], whereas one with a major offense is defeated.

In that regard, although it may not be possible to determine through ordeal whether the matter of the accused is small or great, nevertheless, because it was done once without prior intent, it is considered small; and because it was done repeatedly with deliberate intent, it is considered great. Thus, the smallness or greatness of the punishment and penance is determined.
Furthermore, when the tearing or breaking of the *kakṣa* (the upper garment) and so forth occurs without any visible cause being perceived, there is likewise impurity.
In the case of the cutting of the armpit-cloth, the breaking of the balance-beam, or likewise of the *dhaṭa* and *karkaṭa*,
as well as the snapping of the cord or the breaking of the axle, one should likewise declare [the defendant] impure.
Thus it is remembered [in the Smṛti].
*Kakṣa* means the surface of the scale-pan (*śikya*).
*Karkaṭau* refers to the two slightly curved iron pins at the ends of the balance-beam that support the scale-pan, resembling the horns of a crab.
The axle is a beam for supporting the scale-pan, fixed upon the pillars and the foot-rest.
However, when their breakage occurs due to a visible cause, one should have them replaced; in the event of a breakage or tear in the scale-pans and so forth, one should have the man weighed again.
In the event of a breakage or tear in the scale-pans and so forth, one should have the man weighed again.
Thus it is from the Smṛti.
And therefore:
"One should satisfy the officiating priests, the domestic chaplain, and the teachers with sacrificial fees."
Having caused this to be done, the king shall enjoy delightful pleasures.
He attains great fame and becomes fit for absorption into Brahman.

But when he wishes to place the balance, characterized as previously described, in that very manner, he should then construct a hall provided with doors and so forth in order to prevent damage by crows and other creatures; indeed, he should have a large, high, and bright hall for the balance built, where it will not be harmed by dogs, outcasts, or crows.
In that very place, one should station all the world-protectors and others in their respective directions;
one should worship them at the three junctions of the day with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
The king should cause it to be kept non-empty, provided with doors and seeds, guarded by attendants, and supplied with earth, water, and fire.
Thus it is from the Smṛti. "Seeds" refers to barley, rice, and so forth. 2.100, 2.101, 2.102.
Now he describes the fire-ordeal, which follows in sequence:
Having examined the hands from which the rice grains have been rubbed away,
one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread for that same duration.

While the common rules prescribed in the *Divyamātṛkā* exist, and while the procedure beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the placing of the leaf upon the head as stated in the *Tulāvidhāna* is being performed, there is this specific distinction in the fire-rite (*agnividhi*).

Having marked the hands of the one who has crushed the rice grains—that is, one by whom the rice grains have been crushed or rubbed between both hands—one should mark them at the locations of moles, freckles, scars, calluses, and so forth, using lac juice and the like.
As Nārada says:
"In all cases of hand-wounds, one should indeed apply *dhaṃsapada* [plasters].
Thus it is said:
"In all cases of hand-wounds, one should indeed apply *dhaṃsapada* [plasters]."

Immediately thereafter, one should place seven *aśvattha* leaves in the hollowed palms joined as an *añjali*; for it is recorded in tradition: "Having filled the *añjali* with seven equal *aśvattha* leaves. And one should wrap those leaves together with the hands with a thread for that duration.
The meaning is that one should wrap it seven times with as many *aśvattha* leaves as there are.
Furthermore, there are seven white threads, according to the statement of Nārada: "One should wrap the two hands with seven white threads."

Likewise, one should place seven *śamī* leaves, seven *dūrvā* blades, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) smeared with curd upon the *aśvattha* leaves; then one should place seven *pippala* leaves, *śamī* leaves, and unbroken rice grains, as well as seven *dūrvā* blades and unbroken rice grains smeared with curd.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
"Likewise, one should place flowers; seven leaves of the Pippala tree, unbroken grains, flowers, and curd—one should deposit these in the two hands, and likewise perform the wrapping with a thread."

Thus, according to the words of Pitāmaha: "Sumanas" means flowers. Furthermore, there is this traditional teaching: "But [the ordeal may be performed] with heated iron held in both hands, or with seven leaves of the *arka* tree."
If he steals it while it is still hidden, he is pure; if he is not burnt, he is purified upon reaching the seventh step.
Thus, in the absence of *aśvattha* leaves, it should be understood that this refers to *arka* leaves;
for the *aśvattha* leaves are known to be primary due to the words of praise from Pitāmaha: "Fire is born from the *pippala*; the *pippala* is remembered as the king of trees.
Therefore, a wise man should place its leaves upon his hands."
Thus [ends verse] 2.103.
From the *pippala* tree fire is born; the *pippala* is known as the king of trees.
Therefore, a wise person should place its leaves upon his two hands.
The author states the consecration of the fire:
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, declare the truth to me regarding my merits and sins."

O Agni, you move within the bodies of all beings—those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts—functioning as the digester of the food and drink they have consumed. O Purifier, cause of purity, O Seer who perceives all, like a witness, speak the truth regarding merits and demerits.
The ablative case in "puṇyapāpebhyaḥ" is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (meaning "with regard to").
"Having considered merit and demerit, speak the truth"—this is the meaning of "show.
When a ball of iron has been heated by three fires and brought forward with tongs, the performer, standing facing east in the western mandala, should consecrate the fire with this mantra.
As Nārada says:
Having heated a glowing iron ball, emitting sparks and well-polished,
on the third stage of heating, one should address it while preceded by an oath of truth.
Having heated a ball of iron, glowing like fire, emitting sparks,
and well-polished, on the third stage of heating, one should address it while preceded by an oath of truth.

The meaning of this is as follows: for the purpose of purifying iron, one should heat a lump of iron until it is glowing red, cast it into water, heat it again, and cast it into water once more; then, having heated it for the third time and grasped it with tongs, when it has been brought before [the judge], the performer should recite the mantra beginning with "O Agni, you who are present before all beings," accompanied by the word "truth" (satya).

The judge, however, having kindled the common fire (laukika-agni) in the southern part of the court precinct, shall offer oblations of clarified butter one hundred and eight times with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni Pāvaka," for the purpose of pacification; he shall offer ghee into the fire one hundred and eight times, according to the traditional rule: "One should offer ghee into the fire one hundred and eight times for the sake of peace."

Having offered oblations into that fire and cast an iron ball into it, while it is being heated, one should perform the previously described ritual beginning with the invocation of *Dharma* and ending with the offering; then, while the third heating is taking place, one should consecrate the iron ball with the fire using these mantras: "O Agni, you are the four Vedas, and you are invoked in the sacrifices.
You are the mouth of all the gods; you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman."
For, dwelling within the bellies of all beings, you know their good and evil;
since you indeed purify sin, you are therefore called Pāvaka.
Reveal yourself among the wicked, O Purifier; become radiant, O Fire.
Or else, toward those of pure intent, become cool, O Consumer of Oblations.
O Agni, you move within all the gods like a witness;
you alone, O God, know those things which human beings do not know. This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification.
Therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
Thus [ends verse] 2.104.
O Agni, you are the four Vedas; you are invoked in the sacrifices.
You are the mouth of all the gods; you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman.
For, dwelling within the bellies of all beings, you therefore know their good and evil;
since you indeed purify sin, you are called Pāvaka (the Purifier).
Reveal yourself among the wicked, O Purifier; become radiant, O Fire! Or else, toward those of pure intent, become cool, O Consumer of Oblations!
O Agni, you move within all the gods as a witness;
you alone, O God, know those things which human beings do not know. This man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
Therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
Moreover:
when he has spoken thus, one should place upon both his hands an iron ball weighing fifty palas, heated to the color of fire.

When he has spoken thus, "O Agni, you are the maker of all beings," and has performed the consecration with these and other mantras, [the judge] shall cause an iron ball— a product of iron weighing fifty palas, equal and free from flaws, uniform and round on all sides, smooth, and eight finger-breadths in length— to be heated in the fire after making it flawless,
equal, and eight finger-breadths long; indeed, one shall heat the fifty-pala iron ball, which is equal and free of defects, in the fire.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Pitāmaha:

the judge (prāḍvivāka) should place [the heated object], which is fire-colored—that is, resembling fire—upon both hands, which have been separated by an aśvattha leaf, curd, dūrvā grass, and so forth. (2.105)
To the question of what he should do after that, the author says:
"Taking it up, he should walk slowly for exactly seven paces.
That man, having taken hold of that heated iron ball with his cupped hands, should walk slowly for seven paces.
By the word "only" (eva), he shows that the placement of the feet must be within the mandalas themselves and that one must not step beyond the mandalas.
As the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) said:
"One should not step beyond the mandala, nor should one place a foot outside it."
Thus:
one should not step beyond the mandala, nor should one place a foot within it;
it is said that one should walk slowly for exactly seven mandalas.
Regarding that, as to what the measure of each individual mandala is, and what the measure of the interval between the two mandalas is, he says:
"The mandala should be known as sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in size, and the interval should be of the same measure."
That which has sixteen finger-breadths is "sixteen-fingered" (*ṣoḍaśāṅgulakam*).
The mandala should be understood as having a measurement of sixteen finger-breadths;
likewise, both the interval between the two mandalas and their middle [space] are exactly sixteen finger-breadths.
By saying "one should walk seven mandalas," the first, the *avasthāna*-mandala, is stated as one.
Therefore, there are eight mandalas, each sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in size; the meaning is that the intervals between the mandalas are intermediate.
The intervals between the mandalas, moreover, are seven and of that same measure.
This very point was stated by Nārada after enumerating [the measurements]:
"They say the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
thus, with eight mandalas, there are two hundred finger-breadths."
They say that the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths; thus,
with eight mandalas,
the measurement of the ground is two hundred and forty finger-breadths.
Thus, it is forty [yojanas] more than the measurement of the earth in finger-breadths.
This is the meaning:

from the *avasthāna*-maṇḍala, another maṇḍala sixteen finger-breadths away is the second; each subsequent one, including the intervening space, is thirty-two finger-breadths. Thus, the *avasthāna*-maṇḍala is sixteen finger-breadths.
And seven circles together with their intermediate spaces are to be traversed, measuring thirty-two finger-breadths each.
Thus, by means of eight circles, there are two hundred and forty finger-breadths of ground; "measured by finger-breadths" (*aṅgulamāna*) uses the suffix *tasi* in the sense of all case-endings.

In this alternative view, however, having prepared a sixteen-finger-width area for the standing mandala, one should divide each of the seven sections of the ground—including the intervening spaces—which measure thirty-two fingers in total, into two parts. Setting aside the intervening ground sections measuring sixteen fingers, one should construct seven mandalas on the sixteen-finger-wide mandala-ground sections, with each mandala being the size of a step taken by the walker.
Thus it was said by that same [author]:
"Two hundred and ten finger-breadths of the ground, measured in finger-units"—here the suffix *tasi* functions as a general case ending (*sārvavibhaktika*).

In this alternative view, however, having prepared a sixteen-finger-breadth standing mandala, one should divide each of the seven sections of ground—including the intervening spaces—measuring thirty-two finger-breadths in total, into two parts. Then, omitting the sixteen-finger-breadth intervening spaces, seven mandalas should be constructed upon the sixteen-finger-breadth sections of ground, with dimensions equal to the step of the person walking.
Thus it is said: "One should make the measurement of the mandala equal to that step."
One should make the measurement of the maṇḍala equal to that foot-measure.
As for what was stated by Pitāmaha: "One should cause eight maṇḍalas to be made in front, and likewise a ninth;
the first maṇḍala is that of Agni, and the second is remembered as that of Varuṇa."
The third has Vāyu as its deity, the fourth has Yama as its deity;
the fifth has Indra as its deity, and the sixth is said to have Kubera as its deity.
Those who know the divine [sciences] understand that the seventh has Soma as its deity, the eighth likewise belongs to Savitṛ, and the ninth has all the gods as its deities.
They say that the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
thus, with eight mandalas, there are two hundred finger-breadths.
The measurement of the ground is calculated as fifty-six [units] more; the mandala should be made by the practitioner to the same extent as his own steps according to the prescribed dimensions.
In each and every mandala, kusha grasses should be offered as prescribed by the scriptures.

Thus, in that context, excluding the ninth mandala—which belongs to all deities and measures an unlimited number of finger-breadths (aṅgulas)—there are eight mandalas and eight intervening spaces, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths; this results in a total of two hundred and fifty-six finger-breadths.
Even there, only seven mandalas are to be traversed, because it is not contradictory for one to stand at the first and cast [the flower] into the ninth.

And the measurement of a finger (aṅgula) is as follows: eight horizontal barley-grain widths, or three vertical rice grains; this is said to be the measure of a finger. Twelve fingers make a span (vitasti).
A *hasta* is two *vitastis*, a *daṇḍa* is four *hastas*,
two thousand of those is a *krośa*, and four of those is a *yojana*.
Thus it should be understood. 2.106.
Having traversed seven circles, he asks what should be done; to this, [the author] says:
"Having released the fire, having rubbed the rice grains, if his hands are unburnt, he shall obtain purification.

Having stood at the eighth circle and, at the ninth circle, having cast aside the iron ball heated by fire and having rubbed the rice grains with both hands, if his hands are indeed unburnt, he shall obtain purification.
If the hand is burned, the meaning that it is impure is established as a matter of course.
However, if one, due to fear, stumbles and is burned elsewhere by the two hands, even then one does not become impure.
As Kātyāyana has said:
If one who is accused stumbles while being led elsewhere than to his place of standing, the gods know him to be unburnt; he should be made to undergo the ordeal once again.
Thus it is said:
"If one who is accused stumbles while walking and is burned elsewhere than at that spot, the gods know him to be innocent; he should be made to undergo the ordeal once more."
If the alms-food falls midway, or if there is doubt [regarding its purity], one may take it again.

When the lump falls before reaching the eighth intermediate circle while walking, or when there is doubt as to whether it has been burnt or not, then one should take it again; this is stated as being implied by the sense.
And in that case, the sequence of performance is as follows.

Having performed the purification of the ground on the previous day and having constructed the mandalas according to the scriptures on the following day, and having worshipped the presiding deities of the mandalas in their respective places with mantras, he should kindle the fire and perform the *śānti-homa*. Having placed an iron ball into the fire and completed the worship of all the deities—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the oblation (*havanas*)—the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), after the accused has fasted, bathed, and put on wet clothes, shall perform the ritual purifications such as the crushing of rice while the accused stands in the western mandala. Then, having bound the written pledge (*pratijñāpatra*) with its accompanying mantras upon the head of the litigant, the judge, having consecrated the fire during the third heating, should take the heated iron ball with a pair of tongs and place it into the cupped hands of the litigant, who has been consecrated by mantras.
Having passed through seven mandalas, he is cast into the ninth mandala; if unburnt, he becomes pure. || 2.107 ||
Now he states the procedure for the water ordeal:
Having sworn an oath over the water with the words, "O Varuṇa,
protect me by truth," he should enter the water while standing waist-deep, having grasped the thighs of another person.

Having consecrated and empowered water with the mantra, "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth," the person to be purified—standing in water reaching up to the navel—should enter the water and submerge himself while grasping the thighs of another man who is likewise standing in water reaching up to the navel.

This is to be done provided that worship of Varuṇa has been performed first; with a concentrated mind, one should perform the worship of Varuṇa at the outset with fragrant perfumes, garlands, honey, milk, clarified butter, and other such offerings.
Thus, according to the *Smṛti* of Nārada;

likewise, when the common duties are present—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and including the worship of all deities, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the placement of the document of pledge upon the head; and furthermore:
"O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings, created as the very first of all things."
And the cause of purification for substances as well as for embodied beings has been declared.
Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
When the presiding judge has thus performed the consecration of the water with mantras, the person undergoing purification should pray to the water, saying: "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth.
And the locations for the water have been stated by Nārada:
"In rivers that flow rapidly, in oceans, and in streams..."
In lakes, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, and in ponds.
In rivers of gentle currents, in oceans and streams,
in lakes dug by the gods, and in ponds and pools;
Likewise, the Grandfather [Brahmā] has also said:
"One should immerse oneself in water that is still, not in water that is turbid, nor in water that is shallow;
it should be free from grass and moss, and devoid of leeches and fish."
One should perform purification with water found in natural excavations;
one should always avoid brought-in water as well as the waters of swiftly flowing rivers.
"One should always enter the water that is free from waves and mud.
Thus it is said:
"One should immerse oneself in still water, not in water that is turbid or too shallow."
Free from grass and aquatic moss, and devoid of leeches and fish.
One should perform purification using water from natural pools;
one should always avoid water that has been drawn up, as well as water from rivers with swift currents.
One should always enter the water that is free from waves and mud.
Water brought from ponds and other sources and placed in a copper vessel or similar container is called *āhārya*.

Standing in water reaching up to the navel and leaning against a "pillar of dharma" (*dharmasthūṇā*) made from a sacrificial tree, one should remain facing the east; indeed, standing in the water facing the east, one should grasp the pillar of dharma.
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa). 2.108.
To the question of what should be done after that, he says:
"If a swift man, having brought back the arrow shot simultaneously,
should see the body submerged when he has departed, he shall obtain purification."

At the very moment of immersion, when one swift man has gone [to retrieve the arrow], another swift man stationed at the place where the arrow fell brings back the previously discharged shaft; if he sees the person submerged in the water, then that person is proven innocent.
This is what is meant: once the three arrows have been discharged, one swift man goes to the spot where the middle arrow fell, takes it, and remains right there.
Another man, however, who is swift, stands at the base of the archway at the place where the arrows were released.
While they are thus stationed, at the third clap of hands, the one to be tested sinks down.
At that very same moment, the one standing at the base of the archway also goes much more swiftly to the spot where the middle arrow falls.
And when the arrow-receiver has reached that spot, he goes even more swiftly to the base of the archway; if he does not see the person who had gone into the water, then he is purified.
This very point has been clarified by the Grandfather (Brahmā):
"The movement and the immersion of both the runner and the archer are equal;
a swift man should go from the base of the archway to the target station."
When he had gone, the second one also, taking up an arrow,
would go with speed to the base of the archway where that man had gone.
But when the arrow-catcher, having entered [the water], does not see it clearly while it is situated within the water,
then one should declare him pure.
Thus:
"The movement and immersion of both the goer and the agent are equal;
a swift man should go from the base of the archway to the target location."
When he had gone, the second one also, taking up an arrow,
would go with speed to the base of the archway where that man had gone.
But when the arrow-catcher, having entered the water, does not see [the arrow] clearly while it is submerged within the water,
then one should declare him pure.
And Nārada made a selection between two swift men:
"Those two who are superior in speed among fifty runners should be appointed there for the purpose of fetching the arrows."
Thus:
