"Of the fifty washers, those two who are superior in speed should be appointed there for the purpose of fetching the arrows."

And a gateway (toraṇa) should be constructed at a level spot near the bathing place, raised to the height of the ear of the person undergoing purification; having gone to that body of water, one should erect the gateway on the bank, measuring only a cubit in height, upon a clean and level portion of ground.
Thus, according to the *Nāradasamhitā*:

"One should first worship the three arrows and the bamboo bow with auspicious substances such as white flowers and the like; one should first worship the arrows and likewise the bamboo bow with auspicious incense and flowers, and thereafter perform the ritual act."

Thus, according to the words of Pitāmaha, the measurement of the bow and the location of the target have been stated by Nārada: "A fierce bow is known to be seven hundred [aṅgulas], a middling one six hundred, and a mild one five hundred; this is to be understood as the rule for the bow."
But with a medium bow, the discerning practitioner should discharge three arrows, having set a target at a distance of one hundred and fifty cubits.
But there would be a fault in shooting arrows that are either too few or too many.
Thus:
A fierce bow is known to be seven hundred [inches], a medium one six hundred, and a mild one five hundred; this is to be understood as the rule for bows.
But with a medium bow,
the wise man, having set his target at one hundred and fifty cubits, should discharge three arrows.
But there would be a fault in throwing arrows that are either too short or too long.
One hundred and seven finger-breadths (aṅgulas) is the cruel bow;
likewise, there are those of six hundred and five hundred [finger-breadths].

Thus, it is stated that the measure of the cruel bow is four cubits (hastas) plus eleven finger-breadths, that of the middling is ten finger-breadths more, and that of the slow is nine finger-breadths more.

The arrows should indeed be made of bamboo with tips not of iron; for the sake of purity, one should prepare arrows with non-iron tips, and the thrower should discharge them made of bamboo stalks with great firmness.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
The thrower should be a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa following that [Kṣatriya] occupation, and he must be appointed while fasting.
As it has been said:
The one who performs the casting is declared to be a Kṣatriya, or else a Brāhmaṇa following that same occupation;
being of gentle heart and tranquil, he should cast it after having fasted.
Thus it is said: "The thrower shall be a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa following that same occupation;
he must be gentle-hearted and tranquil, and having fasted, he should then cast [the arrow]."

When three arrows have been released, the middle one is to be grasped; for according to the injunctions of the treatises regarding those discharged arrows, the middle arrow must be seized by a man of great strength.
Because of this statement:

"In that case as well, one must take [the distance] from the place where it falls, not from the place where it glides; the fall of the arrow is to be grasped, but its gliding must be avoided, since as it glides and glides, the arrow goes further and further away."
According to this statement:

"When the wind is blowing and on uneven ground, one should not discharge an arrow; a wise man should not shoot an arrow when the wind is blowing violently, nor on an uneven terrain crowded with trees."
[The ground] was covered with grass, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, mud, and stones.
Thus, from the words of Pitāmaha:

"If one should see [the thief] with his limbs submerged, he would attain purification," it is shown by this statement that there is impurity for one whose limbs have emerged. Furthermore, Pitāmaha has stated that there is impurity in moving to another location; otherwise, there would be no purification even if only a single limb were seen.
Thus it is said: otherwise, there would be no purification, because even a single factor might be seen [to be missing],
whether due to its location or because it has moved elsewhere from where it was previously established.
Thus, whether by remaining in that place or by going elsewhere, [it is] in that [place] where it was previously established.
And regarding the statement "even from the sight of a single limb," this refers to the ears and so forth; for one might see only the head, yet neither the ears nor the nose.
One should declare that person pure even if they have entered the water.

Because of this specific statement, the procedure here is as follows: Having constructed an archway (*toraṇa*) of the described characteristics near a body of water of the described characteristics, and having placed the target at the specified distance, one should worship the bow together with the arrow near the archway. Then, having invoked and worshipped Varuṇa in the body of water, and having worshipped the gods beginning with Dharma on its bank up to the end of the fire-oblation (*havana*), the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should bind the document of the defendant's oath to the head of the person to be tested and consecrate the water with the mantra beginning: "O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings."
Then, having consecrated the water with the mantra beginning with "By truth," the defendant approaches a strong man who has grasped a pillar and is standing in water reaching up to his navel.

Then, when three arrows have been discharged, the defendant takes the middle arrow at the spot where it fell; while one swift man stands at that spot and another stands at the base of the archway, the judge claps his hands three times, and simultaneously there is the running, the immersion, and then the retrieval of the arrow. || 2.109 ||
Now he describes the procedure for poison:
"O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in the law of truth;
protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me. Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison produced from the snowy mountains.
One should declare that person pure whose [poison] is digested without the effects of its potency.
Having consecrated the poison with the mantra beginning "O Poison," the performer should consume the poison produced from the Himalayan mountain, originating from a horn.
When that has been consumed, he by whom it is digested without the effects of its potency becomes pure.

The "poisonous impulse" (*viṣavega*) is the transition of one element (*dhātu*) into another element; for it is stated: "The transition of one element into another element is known as the poisonous impulse."
The bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are seven: skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
Correspondingly, there are exactly seven stages of the poison’s onset (*viṣavega*).

Their specific characteristics have been described separately in the *Viṣatantra*: "The first stage of the poison produces horripilation; following that, it causes perspiration and dryness of the mouth. The two subsequent stages produce a change of complexion and trembling in the body."
This fifth impulse renders the eater helpless and causes the breaking of the throat; the sixth brings about hiccup, labored breathing, and delusion; and the seventh brings death to the eater.
Thus:
"The first stage of the poison produces horripilation; thereafter, two subsequent stages cause perspiration and dryness of the mouth, followed by discoloration of the body and trembling.
That which is the fifth stage brings about helplessness, a breaking of the throat, and hiccups; the sixth bestows labored breathing and delusion; and the seventh brings death to the consumer."
And in this matter, the worship of Mahādeva must be performed.
As Nārada said:
"One who has fasted should administer the poison in the presence of the gods and Brahmins."
And having worshipped Maheśvara with mantras for the offering of incense,
Thus it is said: Having fasted and having worshipped Maheśvara with incense, offerings, and mantras, one should administer the poison in the presence of the gods and Brahmins.

The judge, having observed a fast and worshipped Mahādeva, places the poison before him and performs the worship of Dharma and the other deities ending with the fire-oblation (*havana*). Then, placing the written declaration of the defendant upon his head, he consecrates the poison with this mantra: "O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked;
reveal yourself to the sinful, but become nectar for the pure."
O Poison, you are indeed the embodiment of death, created by Brahmā;
protect this man from sin, and by his truth, become nectar for him.
Thus:
"O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked;
reveal yourself to the sinful, but become nectar for those who are pure."
O Poison, you are indeed the embodiment of death, created by Brahmā;
protect this man from sin, and by truth, become nectar for him.

Having thus consecrated it with mantras, one should give it to the person standing facing south, while remaining oneself facing north or east, composed in mind, in the very presence of the twice-born who are likewise situated facing south.
Thus, according to the words of Nārada;
and the poison to be taken should be *vatsanābha* and the like, or the poison of *śṛṅgin*, *vatsanābha*, or that born of snow (*himaja*).

Thus, according to the words of Pitāmaha, he has also stated those things to be avoided: "One should completely avoid all poisons that have been administered, those that are decayed, those that are artificial, and likewise those produced from the earth."
Thus,
one should avoid all poisons that have been administered, those that are decayed, as well as artificial ones, and all those originating from the earth.
Likewise, Nārada also said: "One should carefully avoid that which is fallen, moved, fumigated, mixed, as well as kālakūṭa, alābu, and poison."
Thus:
One should carefully avoid that which is fallen, as well as that which has been practiced [inappropriately], fumigated, mixed, kālakūṭa, and the alābu poison.
And the proper time was stated by Nārada: "Having weighed it, that which is desired should be given at the [proper] time, namely at the onset of winter;
for one who knows the Dharma should not give in the afternoon, nor at midday, nor at twilight."
Thus,
having weighed it at the desired time, that gift should indeed be given at the onset of winter;
one who knows the Dharma should not give in the afternoon, nor at midday, nor at twilight.

However, at other times, a smaller amount than the stated measure should be given: the dose is four barley grains in the rainy season, five barley grains in summer, seven barley grains in winter, and in autumn it is even less than that.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa).
"Small" means six barley grains.
By the mention of "winter" (hemanta), the "cool season" (śiśira) is also included.

Because of the scriptural statement, "The winter and the cool seasons [are treated] collectively," and because spring is common to all divine ordeals, even there seven *yava*s and poison soaked in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be administered, according to the words of Nārada: "That portion which is the twentieth part of a sixth part of a *pala* of poison—
one should give that, reduced by one-eighth, soaked in clarified butter, to the person undergoing purification."
Thus: "From a pala of poison, that portion which is the twentieth part—
having reduced that by one-eighth— one should administer it, saturated with clarified butter, to the person undergoing purification."
In this context, a *pala* consists of four *suvarṇas*.
Its sixtieth part is ten *māṣas* and ten *yavas*.
However, three *yavas* constitute one *kṛṣṇala*, and five *kṛṣṇalas* constitute one *māṣa*; thus, one *māṣa* consists of fifteen *yavas*.

Thus, there are one hundred and fifty barley-corns (*yava*) in ten *māṣas*. Together with the previous ten barley-corns, this makes one hundred and sixty barley-corns, which is the sixth part of a *pala*. Therefore, the twentieth part of that is eight barley-corns; the eighth part of that is one barley-corn. One should add seven barley-corns—minus that twentieth part—to the substance to be purified, having soaked it in clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
And the clarified butter should be taken as thirty times the amount of the poison. The poison should be administered to living beings in the forenoon in a cool place.
Smoothly ground and mixed with thirty parts of ghee, it is thus prepared.
Thus, according to the statement of Kātyāyana:
"The poison shall be mixed with thirty times its quantity of clarified butter;
the person undergoing the ordeal must be protected from fraud and the like, and kept under the supervision of his own men for three or five nights."
Out of fear of fraud and other such deceptions, the king should protect the one who undergoes the ordeal.
One should examine medicinal herbs, mantra-applications, and gems that neutralize poison, as well as those produced secretly within the body of the practitioner.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Pitāmaha.

Likewise, even poison must be guarded against: "The Śārṅga variety from the Himalayas is recommended, provided it possesses the proper fragrance, color, and taste; it must be natural, not confused [in its potency], and not neutralized by mantras."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Nārada:
likewise, when poison has been drunk, he should be waited for as long as five hundred hand-claps (karatālikā); thereafter, he should be treated.
As Nārada said:
When one remains free from modification for a period of five hundred tālas, then one becomes completely purified; thereafter, one should perform the medical treatment.
Thus:
when one remains free from modification for a period of five hundred tālas, then one becomes completely purified; thereafter, one should perform the medical treatment.
But the grandfather (Yājñavalkya) has stated that the end of the day is the limit, referring to cases involving only a small amount:
"When, after having consumed [the poison], he is healthy at the end of the day, free from fainting and vomiting, and shows no abnormal symptoms, one should declare even him to be pure."

Thus it is said: "But when, after having consumed [the medicine], he has become healthy, free from fainting and vomiting, and remains without any adverse symptoms at the end of the day, one should designate him as pure."

In this procedure, the judge, having fasted and worshipped Mahādeva, places the poison before him; having offered oblations to Dharma and the other deities, he places the written declaration upon the head of the person to be tested, consecrates the poison with mantras, and hands it to the one standing facing south.
That person to be tested, having likewise consecrated the poison with mantras, consumes it; such is the sequence. (2.110–2.111)
Now he describes the procedure for the treasury:
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should take the water used for their ablutions;
having poured it out, one should then have the person drink three handfuls of that water.

Having worshipped the fierce deities, such as Durgā, Āditya, and others, by honoring them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having bathed them, one should take the water used for that bathing.

Having taken that water, the judge (prāḍvivāka) should bathe himself with the mantra beginning "O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings," and then, having placed that water in another vessel, he should have the person to be purified drink three handfuls (prasṛti) after consecrating it with the mantra: "By truth, O Varuṇa, protect me.

This [procedure] takes place when the general rules—including the invocation of Dharma (dharmāvāhana), the worship of all the deities, the oblation (homa) accompanied by mantras, and the placing of the written oath upon the head—have been completed.
In this regard, the rules concerning the deity to be bathed, the rules concerning the ritual act, and the rules concerning the qualified person have been stated by Pitāmaha and others:

"Whatever deity a devotee worships, one should cause that person to drink the water used for that deity. However, if there is no specific preference among the deities, one should cause them to drink the water of the Sun."
One should cause thieves and those who live by weapons to drink the water of Durgā;
however, one should not cause a Brāhmaṇa to drink that water which belongs to Bhāskara.
One should bathe the trident of Durgā and the maṇḍala of Āditya;
likewise, one should bathe the weapons of the other gods as well.
Thus is the rule regarding the deities.
In matters of confidence, in all instances of suspicion, and likewise in the business of making peace—
in these cases, the treasury must always be bestowed for the sake of purity of mind.
Thus is the rule regarding the procedure.
In the forenoon, for one who has fasted, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes, who possesses a white garment and is free from vices, the drinking of the *kośa* (sacramental water) is prescribed.
One who possesses a sense of shame and is a believer [is worthy].
The wise should not provide a treasury to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the conduct of atheists.

One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) in the case of those who have committed a great offense, those devoid of dharma, the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, atheists, those who have neglected their sacred vows (vrātya), and slaves.
Thus it is said:

"One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) in the case of those who have committed a great offense, those devoid of dharma, the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, atheists, those who have not undergone the initiatory rite (vrātya), and slaves."
A great offense constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*).
One devoid of dharma is a heretic (*pākhaṇḍin*), being bereft of the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*).
A contemptible person is one born of an inverse union (*pratilomaja*).
The *dāśas* are fishermen;
such is the restriction regarding the eligible persons.

Likewise, it should be understood from the statement of Nārada that, having prepared a mandala with cow-dung, one should place the person to be purified there facing the sun and make him drink [the ordeal-substance].
As it is said:
"Having summoned that accused person and placed him within the circle,
one should have him face the sun and drink three handfuls [of water]."
Thus [ends verse] 2.112.
Having summoned that accused person and placed him within the circle,
one should have him face the sun and drink three handfuls [of the liquid].

Now, while in the cases beginning with the balance and ending with poison, the determination of purity or impurity occurs immediately thereafter, how is it in the case of the *kośa* (ordeal by sacred libation)? To this he says: "If, within fourteen days, no terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate befalls anyone, he shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt."

If, prior to the fourteenth day, no severe or great calamity—whether caused by a king (*rājika*), arising from a king (*rājanimitta*), or divine (*daivika*) in origin—befalls embodied beings, even if it be slight, because such things are unavoidable, he should be known as pure.
Furthermore, there is no fault after the limit [of fourteen days].
As Nārada said:
If, after two weeks have passed, a great abnormality should occur,
he should not be treated by the wise physician, because the appointed time has elapsed.
If, after two weeks have passed, a great abnormality should occur...
"He should not be subjected [to a trial] by a wise man because of the lapse of the appointed time"—
this has been stated as a matter of course.

The phrase "prior to the fourteenth day" refers specifically to the subject of major charges (*mahābhiyoga*), since this was stated after introducing the topic with "these [rules apply] in cases of major charges."

The alternative periods mentioned by the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) have a limited scope, according to the legal tradition (smṛti): "One may cause [the ordeal] of the balance to be administered even in minor cases.
And those [periods] are: "If any abnormality is observed after three nights, seven nights, twelve days, or fourteen days, that person is declared a wrongdoer."
Thus:
"If a deformity is observed after three nights, seven nights, twelve days, or fourteen days,
he is declared to be a doer of evil."

Having divided the property into three parts from among those items mentioned in the section on "Great Accusations" (mahābhiyoga), a period of up to three fortnights, beginning with three nights, should be established. || 2.113 ||
The five great ordeals (mahādivya), beginning with the balance (tulā) and ending with the sacred chest (kośa), have been explained by the Lord of Yogins according to their enumeration.
However, in another Smṛti, other ordeals as well are mentioned for cases involving minor charges.
As Pitāmaha has said:
I shall now declare the procedure for the consumption of rice as it has been prescribed:
rice should be given to a thief, and to no one else; this is the settled rule.
One who is pure should have white rice prepared from unhusked grains and not from any other kind;
having placed it in an earthen vessel, he should do so before the Sun.
One should let them remain there very night mixed with bathing water.
[Then one should approach] a person who has fasted, bathed, and had leaves placed upon his head, facing the east.
Having eaten rice grains, one should then spit them out into a leaf;
it should be from a *pippala* tree, or in its absence, from a *bhūrja* tree.
One whose blood is seen [in the stool], whose jaw and palate are wasting away,
and whose body trembles— such a person should be declared impure.
Thus [it is said]. I shall now declare the procedure for the consumption of rice grains as prescribed:
rice grains are to be given to the thief, and to no one else; this is the settled rule.
One who is pure should prepare white rice grains from *śāli* paddy and not from any other kind;
having placed them in an earthen vessel, he should do so in front of the Sun.
One should let them remain mixed with bathing water in that very place overnight;
[the recipient] should have fasted, bathed, and had leaves placed upon his head, facing the east.
Having eaten rice grains, one should then spit them out into a leaf;
it should be from a *pippala* tree, and in its absence, from a *bhūrja* tree.
One whose blood is seen [in the stool], whose jaw and palate waste away,
and whose body trembles— such a person should be declared impure.
The judge, having placed a leaf upon the head of the accused, should cause him to eat rice grains and then spit them out.
The form "bhakṣayitvā" is derived from the root with the causative suffix (ṇic).
Furthermore, the invocation of Dharma and other rites common to all divine offerings should be performed here as well, just as previously described.

The procedure for the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*) was declared by Pitāmaha (Brahmā). It is as follows: "A circular vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay, sixteen finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths deep."
The meaning is that it should be circular.
One should fill it with twenty palas of ghee and oil;
then, once it is well-heated, one should cast a māṣaka of gold into it.
By joining the thumb and finger, one should extract the heated ball;
he whose fingertips do not tremble, nor does a blister arise,
is purified by dharma, his fingers remaining unchanged.
Based on the statement "one should lift up," only the act of raising [the food] from the vessel is to be observed, not its casting outside.
Another ritual procedure: having taken cow's ghee, one who is pure should heat it over a fire in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay.
One should cast into it a well-purified ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron,
which has been washed once with water.
In that place rich with swirling ripples and waves, which is beyond the reach of the touch of a fingernail,
one should examine it with a moist leaf, listening for the distinct "curu" sound.
Then, one should consecrate that once with this mantra.
O clarified butter, you are the supreme purifier and nectar among sacrificial rites;
O Purifier, burn away my sin, be cool as snow, and be pure.
Then, having fasted, bathed, and arrived wearing wet clothes,
he should cause him to grasp that very ring placed within clarified butter.
Then the examiners should examine its ring finger;
he on whose [finger] there are no eruptions is pure, otherwise he is impure.
Thus:
Having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over a fire.
One should cast into it a well-purified ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron,
which has been washed once with water.
In that place rich with swirling ripples and waves, which is beyond the reach of the touch of a fingernail,
one should examine it with a moist leaf, listening for the distinct "curu" sound.
Then, one should consecrate that once with this mantra.
O clarified butter, you are the supreme purifier and the immortal nectar among sacrificial rites;
burn away our sin, O Purifier, be cool as snow, and be pure.
Then, having fasted, bathed, and arrived wearing wet clothes,
he should cause him to grasp that ring which is likewise placed within clarified butter.
Then, the examiners should examine its ring finger;
he on whose [finger] there are no eruptions is pure, otherwise he is impure.
In this case as well, the invocation of the deity (dharmāvāhana) and other rites are to be performed.
The consecration of the clarified butter (ghṛtānumantraṇa) is for the judge.
"O Agni, you [are the witness] of all beings"—this is the mantra for the person undergoing purification to consecrate the fire.
Because of the statement, "They should examine the ring-finger," the extraction of the seal-ring is performed with the ring-finger alone.
Furthermore, the procedure for the ordeal known as *dharmādharmā* (the test of virtue and vice) has been described by Pitāmaha (*Bṛhaspati*).
And so it is said: "Now I shall fully explain the examination of *dharma* and *adharma*."
For men who have committed murder, who are now entreating [for mercy], and who seek expiation;
Thus it is said.
Now I shall fully explain the examination of dharma and adharma for men who have committed murder, those who are entreating mercy, and those seeking expiation.

"In the case of murderers" refers to charges of violence; "of those who petition" refers to charges concerning property; "of those seeking expiation" refers to charges concerning mortal sins (*pātaka*).
"He shall have the Dharma made of silver and Adharma of lead or iron"—this is the rule for the manufacture of the images, meaning they may be made of lead or iron.
He states another alternative:
"One should draw Dharma and Adharma, white and black respectively, either on birch bark or on cloth;
having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow, one should worship them with perfumes and garlands."
Dharma shall be represented by a white flower, while Adharma shall hold a black flower;
having fashioned these two in this manner and drawn them, one should place them within the two funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Two balls should be made from cow dung or clay, perfectly symmetrical on all sides;
they should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel and remain unobserved.
In a clean place that has been smeared [with cow dung], in the presence of gods and Brahmins,
he should then invoke the gods and the guardians of the world as before.
But one should write the document of agreement preceded by the invocation of Dharma.
Then: "If I am freed from evil, may Dharma come into my hand;
if I am impure, may evil come into my hand according to the law."
Thus [it is said].
If I am free from evil, may the Dharma come into my hand;
if I am impure, may evil come into my hand according to the nature of things.
The accused, being charged, addresses [the scales]: "Of these two, let him who is joined to them grasp one without delay;
if he grasps the *dharma*, he shall be pure, but if he grasps the *adharma*, he shall be defeated."
Thus has the examination of dharma and adharma been briefly explained.
Thus [it is said].
When challenged, he should promptly accept one of the two;
if he accepts the truth, he shall be purified, but if he accepts what is false, he shall lose the case.
Thus has the examination of dharma and adharma been briefly explained.
Furthermore, other oaths concerning the smallness or greatness of an object, as well as those concerning specific castes, have been declared by Manu and others. For example:
"For a *niṣka* there is an oath of truth; for two *niṣkas*, touching a foot."
But merit arises from [the ordeal] up to three [times]; beyond that, there is the drinking of the sacred water (kośapāna).
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons;
a Vaiśya, by cattle, seed, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all sins.
And so forth.
In this regard, the purification through ordeal has been declared by Manu: "He who does not quickly meet with misfortune should be known as pure in the case of an oath.
Thus it is said.
And he who does not quickly meet with misfortune should be known as pure in his oath.
"Misfortune" (ārti) has already been defined as when a terrible calamity—whether caused by the king or by fate—befalls one.
Furthermore, there is a restriction of time, beginning from one night up to three nights, and beginning from three nights up to five nights.
The duration starting from one night and so forth should be understood by considering the relative lightness or gravity of the matter at hand.

Likewise, regarding the determination of victory or defeat through ordeals, a specific fine has also been shown by Kātyāyana: "He who is cleared [by the ordeal] shall be made to pay fifty [paṇas]; he who is not cleared shall be subject to punishment."
One should cause a pure person to pay fifty [paṇas]; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment.

He states that punishment as follows: "In the cases of poison, water, fire, the balance, the holy vessel (kośa), rice grains, and the ordeal of the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka), one should prescribe the punishment in due order."
One should arrange one thousand, six hundred, five hundred,
and likewise four, three, two, or even one, decreasing the number according to those who are inferior.
Thus [it is said].
One should prescribe punishment in due order for poison, water, fire, the balance, the holy water-vessel, rice grains, and the ordeal of the heated gold coin.
One should calculate one thousand, six hundred, five hundred,
and likewise four, three, two, and one, according to the degree of inferiority among those who are inferior.
In the case of denial, this punishment based on ordeal is to be combined with the punishment prescribed by the rule "one who has been proven [guilty] shall pay."
The means of proof has been described through the distinction between human and divine;
now the partition of inheritance is described by Yogamūrti.
In this context, by the term *dāya* (inheritance), that wealth is meant which becomes the property of another solely on the basis of its connection with the owner.
It is of two kinds: unobstructed (*apratibandha*) and obstructed (*sapratibandha*).

Among these, the fact that the wealth of a father and the wealth of a grandfather become the property of sons and grandsons respectively by virtue of being sons and grandsons constitutes unobstructed inheritance.

In the case of paternal uncles, brothers, and others, however, when there is an absence of sons and an absence of ownership [by the father], it becomes their own property; thus, this inheritance is subject to restrictions (*sapratibandha*).
This should be inferred accordingly for their sons and so forth as well.
What is called "partition" (*vibhāga*) is the formal allocation of the various owners who have rights over a collective mass of property to specific portions thereof.
Intending this very point, Nārada has said:
"Where the division of the paternal estate is determined by the sons,
that is declared by the wise to be the legal title of 'Inheritance' (dāyabhāga) within the heads of litigation."
Thus:
"Where the division of paternal property is determined by the sons,
that is declared by the wise to be the legal head of dispute known as *dāyabhāga* (partition of inheritance)."
The term "of the father" (*pitryasya*) is an indication of the relationship that serves as the cause of ownership;
the term "by the sons" (*tanayaiḥ*) is likewise an indication of those who are proximate [to the owner].
This is what must be examined here.
At what time, for whom, in what manner, and by whom should the partition be made?
Regarding that, as for the questions "at what time," "in what manner," and "by whom," these will be explained in the commentary on the respective verses.
Here, only this much is considered: "for whom" is the partition to be made.
Is ownership [produced] from partition, or is it the partition of that which already exists as one's own?
In this regard, ownership itself must first be defined:
is ownership cognizable solely through the scriptures, or is it cognizable through other means of valid knowledge?

In this regard, it is first logical that ownership is to be understood solely through the treatises (*śāstra*), because of the statement of Gautama: "Ownership arises from inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and discovery; for a Brāhmaṇa, what is additionally acquired is *labdha*; for a Kṣatriya, what is won is *vijita*; for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, it is *nirviṣṭa*.
If ownership were cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this statement would not be purposeful.

Likewise, Manu says regarding the extension of the rules for thieves: "A Brāhmaṇa who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—even by officiating at sacrifices or by teaching—is exactly like a thief."
Thus:
"A Brāhmaṇa who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—
even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching— is exactly like a thief."

If ownership were merely worldly (*laukika*), it would be illogical to prescribe punishment for those who acquire property— even by means such as officiating at sacrifices— from one who has taken what was not given, since [the property] would already belong to them.
Furthermore, if ownership were worldly, one could not say, "My own property has been stolen by him," because the property would indeed belong to the thief.
Otherwise, if one thing were the property of another and that [property] were taken away by someone, it would not be the property of the taker.

If that were the case, there would be no doubt as to whether gold, silver, and so forth belong to this person or to another, just as there is no doubt regarding their essential nature. Therefore, ownership (*svatva*) is to be understood solely through the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*).
To this it is replied: ownership is indeed worldly (laukika), because it serves as the means for worldly purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), like rice and other such things.
For sacrificial fires such as the *āhavanīya*, which are known through scripture (*śāstra*), do not possess the quality of being means for worldly actions.
But surely, even the Āhavanīya fire and others possess the status of being means for cooking and so forth?
This is not so;
for in those cases, they do not function as means for cooking and so forth by virtue of their specific form as the Āhavanīya and other such fires.
Rather, [the capacity to perform functions] exists in the form of fire and so forth as perceived through perception and other means;
however, in this case, gold and the like do not serve as the means for purchase and so forth by virtue of their material form, but rather solely by virtue of being one's own property (*svatva*).
For that which is not someone's own property does not accomplish for them any purposeful action, such as purchasing.
Moreover,
even among those living in border regions who have not seen the treatises on legal procedure, the practice of ownership is observed, as evidenced by the occurrence of buying, selling, and so forth.
Furthermore:

The experts in Nyāya maintain that ownership (*svatva*) established by fixed means is indeed well-known in the world. For instance, in the third section (*varṇaka*) of the *Lipsā-sūtra*, the teacher [Śabara]— anticipating the impossibility of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "if the restrictive rules regarding the acquisition of wealth were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), then ownership itself would not exist, because ownership is non-worldly (*alaukika*)"— established the prima facie position by asserting that the acquisition of wealth through acceptance of gifts and other such means as a cause for ownership is established in the world.

But surely, if the acquisition of wealth were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), ownership itself would not come into being, and thus the sacrifice could not even take place; this was merely the idle chatter of someone who said that acquisition does not produce ownership, which is a contradiction. Likewise, even in the Siddhānta, the purpose of the inquiry is stated precisely by accepting the worldly nature of ownership; therefore, it is said that "the transgression of the rule pertains to the person, not to the sacrifice.
And the meaning of this has been explained as follows:

When the rules regarding the acquisition of wealth have the purpose of serving the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*), then the accomplishment of the sacrifice occurs only through wealth acquired in accordance with those rules, and not through wealth acquired by transgressing the rules; thus, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no fault for the person in transgressing the rules.

In the final view (*rāddhānta*), however, since the rule regarding acquisition is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), the accomplishment of the sacrifice (*kratusiddhi*) occurs even with wealth acquired by transgressing that rule; the fault lies solely with the person for violating the rule. Thus, it should be understood that ownership (*svatva*) exists even for what is acquired through the transgression of a rule, because [otherwise] there would be an absence of established ownership in common worldly practice and a contradiction in legal transactions (*vyavahāra*).

Thus, while worldly ownership (*svatva*) is established as having means such as acceptance (*pratigraha*) and so forth, there are restrictive rules for unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*): acceptance and so forth are the means for a Brāhmaṇa; conquest and so forth for a Kṣatriya; agriculture and so forth for a Vaiśya; and service and so forth for a Śūdra.

However, inheritance (*riktha*) and the rest are common to all, as it has been stated: "One becomes an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and discovery. In this context, *riktha* refers to an unobstructed inheritance (*dāya*).
Purchase is well known. Partition is an inheritance accompanied by an obstacle [to ownership].
Appropriation is the taking possession of water, grass, wood, and so forth, which have not previously belonged to another.
Realization (*adhigama*) is the attainment (*prāpti*) of meditative absorption (*nidhyāna*) and so forth.
When these causal signs (*nimitta*) are present, one becomes the master (*svāmī*).
Once they are known, the master is known.

"Whatever is obtained by a Brāhmaṇa through acceptance of gifts and so forth is his 'additional' (adhika) property; that is, it is his exclusive possession. Regarding the phrase "whatever is won by a Kṣatriya," the word "additional" (adhika) is understood to carry over from the previous statement.
Whatever is obtained by a Kṣatriya through victory, punishment, and so forth, is his exclusive possession.
In the phrase "nirviṣṭaṃ vaiśyaśūdrayoḥ" (the earnings of the Vaiśya and Śūdra), the word "adhikaṃ" (excessive) is also understood to carry over.

That which is obtained by a Vaiśya through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth—termed *nirviṣṭa*—is his exclusive property. That which is obtained by a Śūdra in the form of wages through service to the twice-born and the like is his exclusive property.

Thus, regarding the causes of ownership well-known in the world for those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) and the inverse order (*pratiloma*), whatever specific [duty] has been stated—such as "the driving of horses for *sūtas*" and so forth—all that is expressed by the term *nirviṣṭa*, because all of it consists of wages (*bhṛti*); for the *Trikāṇḍī* Smṛti records: "*Nirveśa* refers to both wages and enjoyment.
That specific [duty] should be understood [as such].

As for the legal tradition (*smaraṇa*) beginning with "the wife and the daughters," even there, since many [relatives] might be considered entitled to a share of the inheritance by virtue of their connection to the owner, this tradition exists to remove confusion regarding ownership, even though that ownership is well-known in the world; thus, everything is beyond reproach.

As for the argument that if one does not say "my property has been taken away by him," then ownership must be worldly (*laukika*), that too is incorrect, because a doubt regarding ownership can indeed arise from a doubt concerning the purchase or other grounds that constitute ownership.
The purpose of this reflection is as follows: "When Brāhmaṇas acquire wealth through a censurable action, they become pure by relinquishing it, and by means of recitation and austerity alone."
Thus:
"Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable action,
they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity."

When ownership (*svatva*) is understood solely through the scriptures, that which is acquired by reprehensible means such as accepting gifts from the unworthy or trade does not possess the very nature of ownership; therefore, it is indivisible among one's sons.

However, when ownership is understood in its worldly (*laukika*) sense, then even what is acquired by accepting gifts from the unworthy and so forth possesses the nature of ownership, and thus it is indeed divisible among one's sons. Regarding the rule "they are purified by its renunciation," this refers to the penance for the acquirer alone; since the sons' ownership arises through inheritance (*dāya*), they have no connection with the fault. There are seven righteous sources of wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest, [finding lost property], [receiving a gift from a worthy person], and [earning through labor].
Application, the yoga of action, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous as well.
Thus it is from the recollection of Manu.
Now this is doubted: does ownership arise from partition, or is it partition of that which already belongs to one?
In this regard, it is first logical that ownership arises from partition, because the injunction for the *ādheya* (consecration) is prescribed for one whose son has been born.

If ownership were established by birth alone, then even for a son who has been born, that property would be common to him as well; consequently, the father would lack the authority to perform rites such as the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), which must be accomplished with material wealth.

Likewise, the prohibition against dividing property obtained through the father’s favor prior to partition would be untenable, because since it is given with the consent of all, there would be no possibility of its being subject to partition.
As it is said: "Both the wealth acquired through valor and that acquired through a wife, as well as whatever may be the wealth acquired through learning..."
These three are indivisible: [the king's] favor and that which was inherited from the father.
Thus [it is said].
Both the wealth acquired through valor and that obtained from a wife, as well as whatever may be the wealth of learning— these three are indivisible, as is any gift received from a father.
Likewise: "Whatever has been given by a gratified husband to his wife, even after he has died, she may enjoy it as she wishes or give it away, with the exception of immovable property."
Thus:
"What has been given by a gratified husband to his wife, even after he has died,
she may enjoy at her pleasure or give away, with the exception of immovable property."
Furthermore, the statement regarding "gifts out of affection" (*prītidāna*) would be untenable if ownership were established by birth alone.

Nor is it logical to construe the phrase "that which is eaten [is lost], except for immovable property" (*na ca sthāvarād ṛte yad attam*) as a connection [with the preceding], for that would entail an improper syntactical separation (*vyavahita-yojanā*).
As for the verse: "The father is the master of all gems, pearls, corals, and so forth... [this too would be inconsistent].
But for all immovable property, there is neither a father nor a grandfather [as a claimant].
Likewise: "By the favor of one's father, garments and ornaments are enjoyed;
yet immovable property is not enjoyed, even when paternal favor exists."
Thus it is said:
"By the favor of the father, garments and ornaments are enjoyed;
yet immovable property is not enjoyed, even when paternal favor exists."
The prohibition regarding the gift of immovable property refers specifically to immovable property acquired by the grandfather.
When the grandfather has passed away, although that wealth is common to both father and son, items such as gems and pearls belong to the father alone;
however, it is understood from this very statement that immovable property remains common to both.
Therefore, ownership does not arise from birth; rather, ownership arises from the death of the owner or from partition.

For this very reason, there is no room for the objection that "since the ownership over the property has already ceased prior to partition after the father's death, another person taking it should not be prevented.
Likewise, even for a man with only one son, the property becomes the son's own immediately upon the father's passing, so that it does not depend on partition.
To this it is replied:
it has already been stated that ownership is indeed what is well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddha*).
And in the world, the ownership of sons and others by virtue of their very birth is more widely established than anything else; it does not deserve to be denied.

Furthermore, the term "division" (*vibhāga*) is well-known in common usage as referring to property belonging to multiple owners, not to that belonging to another person nor to abandoned property; likewise, the teachers hold that one acquires ownership of wealth by birth itself, based on the statement of Gautama: "And [ownership arises] from birth.
Moreover, the statement beginning with "of gems, pearls, and corals" is consistent only with the position that ownership arises through birth.

Nor is it correct to claim that this refers specifically to immovable property acquired by a grandfather, because of the scriptural declaration: "Neither the father nor the grandfather [has power over it]."
Indeed, the statement that "even what was acquired by the grandfather himself must not be given away while the son and grandson exist" establishes that ownership arises through birth.

Just as, according to the opponent's view, ownership over gems, pearls, corals, garments, ornaments, and so forth—though inherited from the grandfather—belongs to the father alone by virtue of this scriptural injunction, so too in our own view, there is no difference: although these items were acquired by the father, his authority to give them away exists by virtue of the scriptural injunction.

As for the statement of Viṣṇu beginning with "yat tu bhartrā prītena" (NSm 1.24)—which is not even attributed to Viṣṇu in the *Dharmakośa*—the indication that immovable property may be given as a gift of affection (*prītidāna*) must be explained as applying only with the consent of the son and others, since the previously cited statements regarding gems, pearls, and so forth establish that only property other than immovable land is fit for such a gift of affection.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that there is no entitlement to perform Vedic rites accomplished through wealth, the entitlement is understood precisely from the force of the injunctions for those very rites.

Therefore, ownership over ancestral and grandparental property arises by birth alone; nevertheless, it is established that the father has independence regarding the expenditure of movable property for essential religious duties, matters prescribed by scripture, gifts out of favor, the maintenance of the family, and the relief of the family from distress.

However, with respect to immovable property—whether self-acquired or inherited from a father or others—the son’s dependence remains absolute: "Even if immovable property or bipeds have been acquired by oneself, there can be neither gift nor sale without having assembled all the sons."
Those who have been born, those yet unborn, and those situated within the womb—
all of them desire a livelihood, not through giving nor through selling.
This is because of such traditional authorities (*smṛti*).

An exception to this rule is stated: "Even a single [coparcener] may perform a gift, a mortgage, or a sale of immovable property in times of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*)."
Thus:
"Even a single person may perform giving, mortgaging,
or selling of immovable property in times of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of dharma."

The meaning of this is as follows: when sons or grandsons have not yet attained legal capacity (*aprāptavyavahāra*), or when brothers are incapable of giving permission and the like, or even when they are undivided (*avibhakta*) but in such a state, then in a calamity affecting the entire family, or when the maintenance [of the family] must necessarily be performed, or in rites for the ancestors such as *śrāddha* that must be undertaken, even a single person who is capable may perform the giving, mortgaging, or sale of immovable property.
As for the statement: "Whether undivided or divided, *sapiṇḍas* are equal regarding immovable property;
for one alone has no power over the giving, mortgaging, or sale anywhere."
Whether undivided or divided, all sapinda relatives have equal rights over immovable property;
for no single person has authority anywhere to give, mortgage, or sell it.

Thus, since the property remains common among those who have not divided it, and because no single individual has sovereign power over it, the consent of all must necessarily be obtained. However, once they have divided, the consent of all is required at a later time—not because of any lack of individual sovereignty, but for the sake of facilitating legal transactions by removing doubts as to whether they are divided or undivided.
Therefore, it should be explained that legal transactions are indeed established even in the absence of the consent of those who have divided.
As for the verse: "And with the consent of one's own village, kinsmen, neighbors, heirs, and [other] successors..."
By the gift of gold and water, one traverses the earth through six [rebirths].

Thus, even in that case, there is the requirement for the consent of the village; for it is stated in the Smṛti: "The acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property. Therefore, the consent of the village is required solely for the purpose of making the transaction public; it is not the case, however, that a legal transaction fails to be established without such consent.
As for the consent of the neighbors, it is intended to eliminate disputes regarding boundaries.

However, the purpose for obtaining the consent of kinsmen and heirs has already been stated as being through the giving of gold and water. This is because of the prohibition against the sale of immovable property: "There is no sale of immovable property; one may, however, create a mortgage with their permission."
He who receives land and he who bestows land—
both of them are performers of meritorious deeds and are certain to go to heaven.
He who accepts land and he who bestows land—
both of them are performers of meritorious deeds and are destined for the heavenly realm.
And because of this demonstration of the praise of giving:
even when a sale must be performed, the meaning is that one should effect the sale of immovable property in the form of a gift by giving water along with gold.
Although ownership in wealth inherited from a father or a grandfather exists by birth alone, we shall explain the specific rule regarding land acquired by a grandfather in verse 2.114.
Now, showing at what time, by whom, and in what manner the partition should be made, he says:
"If the father should make a partition, he may divide his sons according to his will;
either he may give the eldest a preferential share, or they may all be equal sharers."
When the father desires to make a partition, he may then divide his sons from himself according to his will—[giving] one son, two sons, or many sons [to each].
Since there would be no restriction due to the unrestrained nature of his will, he states the following for the purpose of establishing a rule: "Or the eldest with the best share.
This implies that he should divide the eldest with the best share, the middlemost with the middle share, and the youngest with the smallest share.

Furthermore, the division into categories such as "the eldest" and so forth was not stated by Manu: "The eldest shall have an extra portion (*uddhāra*) of one-twentieth [of the estate] and whatever is the best among all the goods;
half of that shall belong to the middle son, and a fourth to the youngest."
Thus:
"The eldest shall have a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the property;
half of that shall belong to the middlemost, and a fourth to the youngest."
The word "or" (*vā*) refers to the alternative view about to be stated: "or all [sons] shall be equal sharers.
That is, all sons, beginning with the eldest, should be made recipients of equal shares.
Furthermore, this unequal division pertains to property acquired by the individual himself.
Since it will be stated later that there is equal ownership over property inherited through the paternal line, an unequal division by choice is not proper.
Regarding the rule "if the father should make a division," one occasion for division is when the father has the desire to divide.

Another occasion is even while the father is alive, provided he is indifferent to wealth and has ceased from worldly activity, and the mother has ceased her menstrual flow; in such a case, even against the father's wish, a division occurs solely by the sons' desire.

As stated by Nārada: "Henceforth, after [the death of] the father, the sons shall divide the wealth equally. Having thus established that partition occurs after both parents have passed away, he continues: "When the mother’s menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given in marriage, and when sexual pleasure has ceased and the father’s desire has departed..."
Thus it has been shown.
Here, the phrase "the sons shall divide the wealth equally" is to be supplied.
Gautama also, having stated that "after the father's death, the sons shall divide the inheritance," indicated a second occasion by saying, "and also when [the mother's] menses have ceased."
"If he lives and desires [it]" constitutes the third time.

Likewise, even when the mother has reached her menses, if the father does not desire it, or if he is acting unrighteously, or is afflicted by a chronic disease, partition occurs by the will of the sons.
As Śaṅkha says: "If the father is unwilling, there is no partition of the inheritance when he is aged, mentally deranged, or diseased. (2.114)
The division [of the estate] by the father's wish is shown to be of two kinds: equal and unequal. Regarding that, he states the specific rule for equal division:
"If he should make the shares equal, the wives must be made sharers of equal portions."
To those women for whom no woman's property (strīdhana) has been given by either the husband or the father-in-law.

When the father, by his own will, makes all his sons equal sharers, then he must also make the wives entitled to shares equal to those of their sons—provided that those wives have not been given separate property (strīdhana) by the husband or the father-in-law; for where separate property has been given, he will state that "if [property] has been given, one should assign half a share" (YDh 2.143).

But when he divides the property among the eldest and the others by means of the "preferential share" (*śreṣṭhabhāga*) and so forth, then the wives do not receive those preferential shares; rather, they receive equal shares from the remainder after the deductions have been set aside, as well as their own specific deductions.
As Āpastamba has said: "The household utensils and the ornaments in the house belong to the wife. (2.115)

Regarding the two positions—that the eldest shall receive the best portion or that all shall be equal sharers—he states an exception to both: "If he is capable but makes no effort, a separation may be made by giving him something. Even if he is himself capable of acquiring wealth but makes no effort regarding the paternal estate—meaning he has no desire for it—a separation (partition) must be made by the father by giving him something, however insignificant; this is so that his sons and others might not have a desire to seize the inheritance.
By the phrase "or the eldest with the best portion," a division that is unequal—either deficient or excessive—is indicated.
In this regard, he says [the following] to prohibit any other kind of unequal division apart from the unequal divisions such as the *uddhāra* (preferential share) prescribed by the scriptures:
"For those who have divided [the estate] unequally, whether deficiently or excessively, the division made by the father is declared to be lawful (*dharmya*)."

Regarding sons who have been divided by unequal shares, if that inequality of division is righteous—that is, if it is prescribed by the scriptures—then that division made by the father is indeed final and cannot be revoked; this is what was recorded by Manu and others.
Otherwise, however, even a division made by the father may be set aside; such is the intention.
As Nārada has said: "One who is diseased, one who is angry, and one whose mind is attached to sensual objects..."
Furthermore, a father who acts contrary to the scriptures has no authority over the partition of inheritance.
Thus [ends verse] 2.116.
A father who is diseased, angry, whose mind is attached to sensual objects,
or who acts contrary to the scriptures, is not the master with respect to the partition [of the estate].
Now he states the time, the other agent, and the rule regarding the manner of partition:
"The sons shall divide the estate and the debt equally after the parents.
By "after the parents," meaning after the departure of both the mother and the father, the time is indicated.
The term "sons" indicates those who are the agents;
"equally" specifies the rule regarding the manner [of division];
and "equally indeed" means they shall divide both the inheritance and the debt.
Now, having begun with the words, "After both the father and the mother," [it is said]: "The eldest alone, however, shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father."
Having said this, he further stated: "The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as an additional share, and whatever is the best among all the property;
half of that shall belong to the middle son, and a fourth to the youngest."
Thus:
"The eldest shall have a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the property;
half of that shall belong to the middlemost, and a fourth to the youngest."

A twentieth part from the entire collection of property, as well as whatever is the best among all the items, shall be given to the eldest. Half of that—a fortieth part—and the middling item shall be given to the middlemost. A quarter of that—an eightieth part—and the inferior item shall be given to the youngest. Thus has the distribution of the preferential share (*uddhāra*) been shown by the Sage for those dividing after the death of the mother and father.
Likewise: "But if their shares have not been set aside, this distribution of portions shall apply:
the eldest son shall take one share in excess, and the next younger brother shall take one and a half."
"Each younger brother shall receive a share [equal to his senior's]—thus the law is established."
Thus it is said:
"But if no preferential share has been set aside for them, this distribution of portions shall take place:
the eldest son shall take one share in excess; the next younger brother shall take one and a half."
"Each younger brother shall receive a share according to his seniority; such is the established law."

It has been shown that even apart from the *uddhāra* (preferential share), an unequal division exists for those dividing after the death of the parents: the eldest receives two shares, the one born immediately after him receives one and a half shares, and each of the younger brothers receives one share.
Furthermore, regarding division during the lifetime of the parents, an unequal division was explicitly shown by the rule: "or [one may give] the eldest the best share.
Therefore, since an unequal division exists in every instance, how can it be prescribed that they must divide only equally?
To this it is replied: True;

although this unequal distribution is seen in the scriptures, nevertheless, because it is loathed by the world, it should not be practiced, according to the prohibition: "One should not practice even that which is dharma if it leads away from heaven and is loathed by the world."

For example, even though there is an injunction stating that "one should provide a large bull or a large goat for a Vedic scholar," it is not practiced because it is loathed by the world. Or likewise, even though there is an injunction stating that "one should sacrifice a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa as the *anubandhyā* animal," it is not practiced because it is loathed by the world.
And as it has been said: "Neither the duty of *niyoga* nor the slaughter of the *anubandhyā* cow [is to be performed]."
Likewise, even the division of the inheritance no longer takes place at present.
Thus,
the duty of the sacrificial injunction does not exist for us, nor even the immolation of the Anubandhyā cow;
likewise, the division of the special share (uddhāra) no longer prevails at present.

Āpastamba also, having stated the principle of equality by saying "one should divide the inheritance among the sons while [the father] is alive," and having introduced the taking of the entire estate by the eldest as the opinion of some—stating that "in certain regions, gold, black cows, black soil, a chariot for the eldest, the father’s personal effects, ornaments in the house, the wife’s property, and the wealth of her kinsmen belong [to the eldest]"—then rejected this preferential partition (uddhāra-vibhāga) on the grounds that it is contradicted by the scriptures.
And Manu himself pointed out this contradiction with the scriptures: "One should divide the inheritance among one's sons"—thus it is heard without qualification.

Therefore, although an unequal division is seen in the scriptures, because it contradicts worldly custom and contradicts the revealed texts (śruti), it is not to be practiced; rather, it is ordained that "they should divide it equally."

It has been stated that sons shall divide the wealth of their mother and father. Regarding that, he states an exception concerning the mother's property: "The daughters [shall take] the remainder after the debt. The daughters shall divide the mother's wealth after deducting her debts.

"Remaining after the debt" refers to that portion of the mother's property which remains after the discharge of debts incurred by her; therefore, this is the scope of the rule that daughters shall divide the mother's wealth if it is equal to or less than the debt.
This is what is meant: debts contracted by the mother must be discharged by the sons alone, not by the daughters;
however, the wealth remaining after the debt should be taken by the daughters.
And this is logical: "A male is born when the semen of the man is in excess, and a female when that of the woman is in excess.
Thus, because the female constituents are more prevalent in daughters, the woman's property goes to the daughters;
and because the paternal constituents are more prevalent in sons, the father's property goes to the sons.

And in that regard, Gautama has shown a distinction: "The property of a woman belongs to the daughters who are unmarried and those who are unsettled. The meaning of this is: when there is a combination of married and unmarried daughters, the woman's property belongs to the unmarried ones alone; and among the married ones, when there is a combination of those who are unsettled and those who are settled, it belongs to the unsettled ones alone.
They are non-abiding and devoid of wealth.
Since there is no daughter, who shall take the mother's property remaining after the debts? To this he says:
"In her absence, the lineage [inherits]."
In the absence of those daughters—that is, in the absence of daughters—the lineage, consisting of sons and others, shall take [the inheritance].
This point, already established by the rule "sons shall divide the estate of their parents after [their death]," is stated here for the sake of clarity. (2.117)
He states what is not subject to partition:
"Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate,
as well as what is obtained through friendship or received at marriage, shall not belong to the heirs."
If one recovers property that was taken away but had been acquired through successive inheritance, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to property obtained through learning.

That which was acquired by oneself without depleting the property of one’s parents; that which was obtained from a friend through friendship (*maitra*); that which was received as a wedding gift (*audvāhika*) at marriage and the like; and that which does not belong to the paternal heirs (*dāyāda*), such as brothers—[these are exempt].

Furthermore, whatever property has come down through the paternal line and was seized by others, but was not recovered by the father or others due to incapacity or similar reasons, if a son recovers it with the consent of the others, he need not give it to the paternal heirs, such as his brothers; the recoverer alone shall take it.
In that case, the recoverer receives a fourth part of the estate, while the remainder is to be divided equally among all.
As Śaṅkha says:
"If one person recovers land that was previously lost,
others shall receive their shares in due order after he has given them a fourth part."
Thus:
"If one person recovers land that was previously lost,
the others shall receive their shares in due order after he has given them a fourth part."
The phrase "attained in due order" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Likewise, that which is acquired through learning—whether by the study of the Vedas, by teaching them, or by explaining their meaning—one should not give that to the heirs; the acquirer alone shall take it.
And in this context, the phrase "whatever has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate" applies as a supplement to everything mentioned.

And therefore, each of the following is to be connected [with the phrase] "without detriment to the paternal estate": that which is acquired through friendship, that which is obtained as a wedding gift, that which is drawn from [the estate] by succession, and that which is gained through learning—all without detriment to the paternal estate.

And likewise, that which is acquired through friendship by means of a service rendered without detriment to the paternal estate; that which is obtained in marriages such as the Āsura and others; that which has been extracted and inherited in due course by means of the expenditure of the paternal estate; and that which is obtained through learning acquired at the expense of the paternal estate—all of this must be divided by all the brothers and the father.

Furthermore, because the phrase "without detriment to the paternal estate" applies to all [the preceding categories], even what is obtained through a gift (pratigraha) must be divided without detriment to the paternal estate.

Furthermore, if this [rule] were not applicable to all remaining cases, then statements such as "that which is obtained through friendship" (*maitra*) or "that which is obtained through marriage" (*audvāhika*) would not need to be commenced.

If it is argued that the mention of "friendship" and so forth is meaningful because it serves to establish the non-divisibility of what is obtained through friendship and the like, even when it conflicts with paternal property, then there would be a contradiction with established practice (*samācāra*), as well as a contradiction with the statement of Nārada regarding what is obtained through learning (*vidyā*): "He who supports the family of a brother who is pursuing learning..."
Therefore, even if he has not studied, he shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning.
Thus:
"He who maintains the household for a brother who is acquiring learning shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself has not studied."
Likewise, Kātyāyana has stated the definition of the wealth of learning (*vidyādhanam*) which is not subject to partition:
"Whatever wealth is acquired through that learning which was obtained from another by means of subsisting on another's food— that is called 'wealth acquired through learning'."
Thus:
"But that wealth which is obtained through knowledge acquired from another by means of utilizing the food of another,
that is called 'wealth acquired through knowledge'."

Likewise, if the phrase "without detriment to the paternal estate" were a separate sentence, it would result in the conclusion that property obtained through acceptance of gifts is non-partible, which would contradict established custom.

This very point has been clarified by Manu: "That which is acquired by one's own labor without detriment to the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained through learning, one need not give to the co-heirs."
Thus, that which has been acquired by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
as well as what has been obtained through learning, one need not give to the co-heirs.
"By labor" means through service, warfare, and so forth.

Now, one might object: it need not be stated that "wealth acquired through friendship and other such means, provided it does not conflict with the paternal estate, is indivisible," because there is no possibility of its being divided.
It is more well-known that whatever is acquired by someone belongs to him alone and not to anyone else.
And this prohibition presupposes a prior possibility of occurrence.

Regarding this, someone states the following possibility: "When the father has died, whatever wealth the eldest son acquires, a share therein belongs to the younger brothers, provided they are devoted to learning."

Thus, by the explanation that "whether the eldest, the youngest, or the middlemost—whether the father has died or not, and whether [the sons] are younger or older"—it is established that the property of Maitra and others is subject to partition both while the father is alive and when he is dead; this [interpretation] is refuted.
That is incorrect.
For here there is no prohibition of what has been obtained; rather, this is merely a restatement of what is already established.
Generally, the statements in this section are restatements of what is already established in the world.
Or else: "But whatever is obtained by those who have come together, all of them shall have equal shares therein."
"However, that which is obtained by those who have come together, in that case all are equal sharers"—
let your honor be satisfied that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously established.

Therefore, the notion that there is a general application (*prāpti*) in the statement "whatever [is acquired] when the father has died," without intending the mention of the terms "eldest" and so forth, is mere delusion.

Therefore, this must be explained as an exception to the rule stating that "whatever [is given] when the father has died" is subject to partition, which was previously stated regarding the father's property through expressions such as "friendliness" (*maitrī*) and so forth.

Likewise, Manu has declared other things to be non-partible: "Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security and welfare (*yogakṣema*), and pasture grounds—they declare these to be non-partible."
Thus it is said:
"Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security of possession (*yogakṣema*), and pasture-land are declared to be indivisible."
Clothes that have been worn are indeed indivisible; whatever was worn by whom belongs to him alone.
However, the clothes worn by the father, when they are being divided after his death, must be given to the one who partakes in the *śrāddha*.
As Bṛhaspati has said:
Having honored with perfumes and garlands whatever belongs to the father— such as clothing, ornaments, bedding, or vehicles— one should present these to the recipient of the śrāddha meal.
Thus:
"Having honored with perfumes and garlands whatever garments, ornaments, beds, vehicles, and so forth belong to the father, one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha feast."
But new garments must indeed be divided.
As for vehicles—such as horses, palanquins, and so forth—that which was mounted by whom belongs to him alone. However, ancestral property is treated exactly like the garments.
However, when there is a large number of horses and so forth, they must indeed be divided among those who subsist by selling them.
Regarding unequal division, for the eldest: "One should never divide goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals unequally;
goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals are ordained for the eldest alone."

Thus it is from the recollection of Manu. Furthermore, an ornament worn by someone belongs to that person alone; one not worn is common property and must be divided. As it is said: "The ornaments which may have been worn by women while their husbands were living..."
The heirs shall not divide that property; those who do divide it fall from their status.
Thus:
"Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall."
Because of the specific mention that "ornaments shall be worn," it is understood that those not worn are subject to partition.
Cooked food—such as rice, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and so forth—is also not to be divided; rather, it should be consumed according to availability.
Water refers to a water-reservoir such as a well and the like; since that is indivisible by way of monetary value, it should be used in turn.
Female slaves, even if they are of unequal value, are not to be divided by means of their price; rather, they should be made to perform work in turn.

However, concubines and the like, even if acquired by the father, are not to be divided by the sons, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "There is no division among women who are united [in marriage].
Yoga and kṣema constitute *yogakṣema*.

By the word *yoga*, there is indicated the *iṣṭa* (sacrificial) rite, which is the cause for obtaining what has not yet been obtained and is accomplished through the fires prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

By the word *kṣema*, there is indicated the *pūrta* (charitable) rite, which is the cause for preserving what has already been obtained and consists of acts such as giving outside the sacrificial altar, constructing tanks, gardens, and so forth.
Both of these, even if ancestral—that is, even if acquired in opposition to the paternal estate—are indivisible.

As Laugākṣi said: "Those who perceive reality declare that security, purity, yoga, and what is desired are indivisible; and they have declared that these, as well as sleeping and sitting, are likewise indivisible."
Thus say those who perceive reality: "Security, purity, yoga, and the desired"— these,
as well as the bed and the seat, are declared by them to be indivisible.
Some say that by the term *yogakṣema* (security and prosperity) are meant those who provide security and prosperity, such as the king, ministers, and domestic priests;
others say it refers to items such as the royal parasol, fly-whisks, weapons, and sandals.
*Pracāra* (the common way) refers to the paths for entering and exiting houses, gardens, and so forth; that too is indivisible.
As for that which was stated by Uśanas regarding the indivisibility of a field:
"The field of a sacrificer, a document, cooked food, water, and women are indivisible among those of the same lineage, even up to a thousand generations."
Thus, this refers to the case of sons born to a Brāhmaṇa from wives of the Kṣatriya and other castes; [it means]: "Land received as a gift must not be given to a son of the Kṣatriya or other castes.
Even if their father should give it, when he is dead, the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take it."
Land received as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if their father should give it, when he is dead, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take it.
Thus it is from the traditional law (smṛti).
"Yājyam" refers to that which is obtained through the act of officiating at sacrifices.
It will be stated later that what is obtained through the favor of a father is not subject to partition.

The indivisibility of property acquired in violation of restrictive rules was refuted immediately [in the preceding verse]. It is established that what is acquired in opposition to paternal property is subject to partition; in that case, the acquirer receives two shares according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "He by whom among them something has been acquired by himself shall receive two shares. (2.118–2.119)
He states an exception to this:
"But when there is a joint undertaking for a common purpose, the division is ordained to be equal.

When brothers who are undivided engage in a joint undertaking—meaning the proper cultivation and increase of their common property through agriculture, trade, and so forth—if it is accomplished by someone [among them], the division is indeed equal; the acquirer does not receive two shares.
