The division of the paternal estate among sons has been shown. Now he states the specific rule regarding the division of the grandfather’s estate among grandsons:
"But for those who have different fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the fathers."

Although the grandsons possess ownership over ancestral property by virtue of birth, no less than that of their sons, nevertheless, the allotment of the ancestral property for them is determined solely through the mediation of their fathers, and not with regard to their own individual status.
This is what is meant.

When undivided brothers, having fathered sons, have passed away, and there is a disparity among the sons—such that one has two sons, another three, and another four—in that case, the two obtain one paternal share each, the other three also obtain one paternal share, and the four also obtain only one paternal share.

Likewise, even when some sons are living while others have perished after having been born, this same principle applies: the established rule based on scriptural authority is that those who are living receive their own shares, and the sons of those who have perished also receive the paternal shares. 2.120.

Now, in the case where the father has already divided [the estate] or has no brothers, there is no division for the grandson in the grandfather’s property; for it has been stated that "while the father is not deceased, the allotment of shares is according to the father.
Or, one might suspect that—as with property acquired by oneself—it should be according to the father's wish; to this, he says:
"Land acquired by the grandfather, or a fixed endowment (nibandha), or even wealth..."
In that regard, indeed, the ownership of the father and the son would be equal.
Land refers to rice fields and the like.
*Nibandha* is defined as follows: for one bundle of leaves there are this many leaves, or for one bundle of betel nuts there are this many betel nuts, and so forth.

As for *dravya*, such as gold, silver, and the like—which was acquired by the grandfather through gifts, victory in battle, or other means—there is a division of it because the ownership of both father and son therein is well-known in the world.
For because that [share] is similar—that is, equal—therefore the partition is not by the father’s will alone, nor is there a double share for the father.
Consequently, the rule "the allotment of shares is according to the father" is based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), even though ownership is equal.
And the statement "if the father should make a partition" refers to property acquired by himself (*svārjita*).
Likewise, the statement, "A father dividing his property may take two shares for himself," refers also to property acquired by him personally. [As it is said:
"While his parents are alive, he shall be dependent, even if he has reached old age."
This dependence [of the son] also pertains to property acquired by the parents; likewise, the statement "for they have no authority while [the parents] are living" refers to this as well.

Similarly, when the mother is still menstruating and the father is desirous [of her], even if he does not wish for the partition, a division of the grandfather's property occurs by the will of the son.
Likewise, when the father, though undivided, gives away or sells the grandfather's property, the grandson has the right to object.
However, there is no authority to prohibit [the use] of what was acquired by the father, because [the son] is dependent upon him;
nevertheless, his consent must be obtained.

For instance, although ownership over property inherited from the father or the grandfather arises by birth alone, nevertheless, in the case of the father's property, because the son is dependent on the father and because the father holds primacy as the original acquirer, the son must give his consent when the father intends to dispose of wealth acquired by himself.

However, in the case of ancestral property (*paitāmaha*), since ownership for both [the father and son] is indistinguishable, the distinction is that there exists a right to prohibit [its alienation]. Manu also says:
"But as for paternal wealth not yet acquired, whatever the father may acquire..."
One who is without desire should not share with his sons that which was acquired by himself.
Thus:
"But as for paternal property that the father has not yet acquired, if he should acquire it,
he need not share it with his sons, provided it was earned by himself without their desire."

By stating that "if something acquired by a grandfather has been seized by someone and not recovered by the grandfather, and the father recovers it, he should not divide it with his sons of his own accord as if it were his own acquisition," [the author] shows that property acquired by a grandfather may be divided with the sons even against the father's will, provided there is the sons' desire. (2.121)
To the question of how the partition is to be determined for a son born after the time of partition, he says:
"A son born after the [co-sharers] have been divided, from a wife of equal caste, is a partaker of the partition.
That is, a son born subsequently from a wife of equal caste when the sons have already been divided is a partaker of the partition.
"Vibhāga" means that which is divided (*vibhajyate*). One who partakes in the division of the parents is "an heir to the partition" (*vibhāgabhāk*).
The meaning is that after the death of the parents, he receives their share.

And the mother’s share goes to her daughter in the absence of [a son], because it has been stated that "the remainder belongs to the mother's daughters. However, one born of a woman of a different caste receives only his own paternal share,
whereas the entire maternal portion belongs to the mother.
This very point was stated by Manu:
"But one who is born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone."
But one born after the partition shall take only the paternal wealth;
"paternal" (*pitrya*) here should be explained as "belonging to the parents.
Prior-born [sons] have no authority over the share of their brother born after the partition of the parents.
"An elder brother born before the partition of his parents has no authority over the share of a brother born after the partition," according to the traditional legal text (*smṛti*).

The meaning is that one born before the division of the estate of the divided mother and father is not the owner [of that share], and one born after the partition is not the owner of the share of the brother.

Likewise, whatever has been acquired by the father after the time of partition belongs exclusively to the son born after partition—namely, that which was acquired by the father himself while living separately from his sons.
It is declared that the elder brothers have no right to all of that which belongs to the son born after partition.

Whatever has been acquired by the father himself after he has divided his property with his sons, all that belongs to the son born after the partition; the elder brothers are declared to have no right to it.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
Furthermore, those who were previously divided but have reunited with their father, with them the son born after partition (vibhaktaja) shall divide the inheritance after the father's death.
As Manu has said:

"Or, those who may have been associated with him, he shall divide [the property] together with them. "Or, those who may have been associated with him, he shall divide [the property] together with them."
Regarding how the distribution is to be determined for one born after his father has passed away and the sons have already divided the property, he says:
"Or that distribution shall be made from what is visible, after it has been cleared of income and expenditure."

When his father has died and at the time of the partition among the brothers, even for one born after the partition of the brothers while the mother is still pregnant with an unmanifested fetus, there is a partition.
From where does that partition arise? To this he says:
from the visible wealth already taken by the brothers.
From what kind of [income] purified by expenses?
Income is that which arises daily, monthly, or annually;
expense is the clearing of debts incurred by one's father.
Whatever has been cleared by those two [accounts of] income and expenditure should be extracted from that [total], and a share of it must be given.
This is what is meant:

having included the income arising therefrom within their respective individual shares, and having deducted the debt incurred by the father, one should extract a small portion from each of their own remaining shares and make the share of the son born after partition equal to his own share.

This should also be understood to apply to a son born after partition to a brother who was childless at the time of partition, provided his wife was not yet clearly pregnant; however, if she was clearly pregnant, the partition must be performed after waiting for her delivery. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Now, regarding the partition of inheritance among brothers: those women who are childless [shall remain with their husbands] until the birth of a son."
It should be understood that for those who have conceived, there is a waiting until delivery. || 2.122 ||
It has been stated that the son born after partition (vibhaktaja) takes all the paternal and maternal wealth.

In that regard, if the father or mother, being themselves divided, gives ornaments or other items to a divided son out of affection, then the son born after partition must neither prohibit that gift nor reclaim what has been given; thus he says:
"Whatever has been given by the parents to anyone shall belong to that person alone."

Whatever ornaments or other gifts were given by the parents to a son who was already divided from them before their own division belong to that son alone; they do not become the property of one born after the division (*vibhaktaja*).
By parity of reasoning, even prior to the division, whatever was given to whom belongs to him alone.
Likewise, in the absence of a *vibhaktaja*, it should be understood that when the two parents divide their shares after death, whatever was given to whom belongs to him alone and not to another.

In the section concerning partition during the father's lifetime, it was stated that wives are entitled to shares equal to those of their own sons by means of the rule beginning with "if he should make the shares equal.
Now, in order to demonstrate that even in a partition after the father’s death, wives are entitled to shares equal to those of their own sons, [the author] says:
"When they divide after the father’s death, the mother also shall take an equal share."

After the father—that is, after the father’s departure—when they are dividing [the estate], the mother shall also take a share equal to that of her own sons, provided that her woman’s property (*strīdhana*) has not been given to her;
however, it will be stated later that if it has been given, she is entitled to half a share. (2.123)
If the father has died and there are brothers who have not yet been consecrated, then who is authorized to perform their consecration? To this he says:
"But those who are unconsecrated are to be consecrated by the brothers who have already been consecrated.
When the brothers are dividing the estate after the father's death, those brothers who are unconsecrated must be consecrated by the brothers using the collective property.
Regarding the unmarried sisters, he states a specific rule:
"And the sisters, having given a fourth part from their own shares..."
The meaning of this is as follows:
sisters who have not been consecrated must be consecrated by their brothers.
Having done what?

"Having given a fourth part from his own share"—by this it is understood that daughters also become sharers of a portion after their father's death. In this regard, the meaning is not that a fourth part should be extracted and given from each individually allotted share; rather, whatever the caste of the daughter, she is to be made a recipient of a fourth part of the share belonging to a son of that same caste.
This is what is meant:
if that girl is a Brāhmaṇī, then she receives a fourth part of whatever share belongs to the son of a Brāhmaṇī. For example:

If a certain Brāhmaṇa has one wife, one son, and one daughter, then all the paternal property shall be divided into two parts; one of these parts shall be divided into four, and having given a fourth part to the daughter, the son shall take the remainder. But when there are two sons and one daughter, then the entire paternal wealth shall be divided into three parts; one of these parts shall be divided into four, and having given a fourth part to the daughter, the remaining portion shall be divided between the two sons, who shall take it.

Now, if there is one son and two daughters, then the paternal wealth should be divided into three parts; having divided one part into four, he should give two shares from that to the two daughters and take all the remainder for himself. This same principle is to be applied among brothers and sisters of the same caste, whether they are equal or unequal in number.

But when there is one son of a Brāhmaṇī woman and one daughter of a Kṣatriyā woman, the paternal wealth is divided into seven parts; the portion of the Kṣatriyā’s son is divided into four, and having given a fourth part to the Kṣatriyā daughter, the Brāhmaṇī’s son takes the remainder.

But where there are two sons of Brāhmaṇa women and one daughter of a Kṣatriya woman, the paternal wealth is divided into eleven parts; three of those shares are divided into four for the portion of the Kṣatriya son, and having given one-fourth of that share to the Kṣatriya daughter, the two sons of the Brāhmaṇa women shall divide and take all the remainder.
In this manner, it should be inferred in all cases regarding the inequality of birth among brothers and sisters, whether their number be equal or unequal.

Nor is it appropriate to explain the phrase "having given a fourth part from his own share" as meaning that one should give only such wealth as is necessary for the sacraments (saṃskāra), while disregarding the literal sense of a fourth part; for such an interpretation contradicts the statement of Manu:
"The brothers shall each separately give to the maidens portions from their own shares."
If they refuse to give, they shall fall from their own respective shares by one-fourth.
Thus it is said: "The brothers shall give to their unmarried sisters portions from their own respective shares;
each shall give a fourth part of his own share, for those who refuse to give shall become outcasts."
The meaning of this is as follows:

brothers who are Brāhmaṇas and the like should give to their sisters, beginning with the Brāhmaṇī, from their respective shares—those portions prescribed for their own castes—as will be stated later in the passage beginning "the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares," a fourth part each from their own individual allotments.

It is not stated here that a fourth part should be given by extracting from one's own share; rather, a fourth part is to be given to each individual daughter separately from each of the shares prescribed for her respective caste. Thus, the rule for the distribution of shares has already been explained in cases of disparity of caste and disparity of number. Since it is heard as a scriptural injunction that "those who do not wish to give would become outcasts," the necessity of giving is clearly understood.

If it is argued that even here the mention of "one-fourth share" is not intended, and what is intended is merely the giving of a substance sufficient for the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), we say no. This is because there is no evidence in either of the two *smṛtis* that the giving of one-fourth is not intended, and furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in failing to give it.

As for what some say—that if the intention were to give a share, a woman with many brothers would end up with great wealth while a man with many sisters would be left destitute—that has already been refuted by the reasoning stated above.

For it is not stated here that a gift of a fourth part is to be made by setting aside [a portion] from one's own share, which would imply such a thing; therefore, the interpretation of Medhātithi and others—who hold that [the daughter has no share]—is alone correct, and not that of Bhāruci. Consequently, after the father’s death, the daughter is entitled to a share, whereas if she dies before him, she receives only whatever her father gives her, since there is no specific statement to the contrary; thus, everything is faultless. (2.124)

By the continuous passage beginning with "If the father should make such a division" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.114), the rule for the distribution of shares among brothers of the same caste, both among themselves and with the father, has been stated.
Now, he describes the division for those of different castes:
"The sons of a Brāhmaṇa shall have four, three, two, and one shares respectively according to their caste."
Those born of the Kṣatriya [father] receive three, two, or one shares respectively; those born of the Vaiśya [father], however, receive two or one share.
"Three [wives] in the order of the castes"—thus are the wives shown: four for a Brāhmaṇa, three for a Kṣatriya, two for a Vaiśya, and one for a Śūdra.
In this context, "born of a Brāhmaṇa" means born from a Brāhmaṇa; by the word *varṇa*, the women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes are denoted.

Furthermore, because of the rule "after a numeral and a singular word, when there is repetition (*vīpsā*)," the suffix *śas* is applied to the singular case-ending expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa-kāraka*) to indicate repetition. Thus, *varṇaśaḥ* means "caste by caste."
And therefore, those born as Brahmins among each of the castes shall receive four, three, two, and one shares respectively.
This is what is meant:
those born from a Brahmin father and a Brahmin mother each receive four shares.
From that same [Kṣatriya] father, those born of a Kṣatriya woman each receive three shares; those born of a Vaiśya woman two each; and those born of a Śūdra woman one each.
"Born of a Kṣatriya" (kṣatrajāḥ) means those produced by a Kṣatriya; the phrase "according to the classes" (varṇaśaḥ) carries over, meaning they receive three, two, and one shares respectively.
Those born of a Kṣatriya man and a Kṣatriya woman each receive three shares; those born of a Vaiśya woman two each; and those born of a Śūdra woman one each.

The *viḍjas* are those born from a Vaiśya [father]. Here too, the phrase "according to their respective castes" (*varṇaśaḥ*) is understood to carry over; they are entitled to two and one shares respectively.
Those born from a Vaiśya father and a Vaiśya mother each receive two shares.
In the case of a Śūdra wife, there is one share each.
Since a Śūdra has only one wife, there is no possibility of sons from different castes; therefore, the division for his sons is exactly as previously stated.

Although it was stated without qualification that "the shares are four, three, two, and one," this should nevertheless be understood as referring to cases other than land acquired through inheritance (pratigraha).
For they remember:
"Land received as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if the father should give it, when he is dead, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take it."
Thus:
"Land received as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if the father should give it, when he is dead, the son of the Brāhmaṇa shall take it."
Land obtained through acceptance of a gift, purchase, or other such means certainly belongs even to the sons of Kṣatriyas and others;
for there is a specific prohibition regarding the son of a Śūdra: "One born of a Śūdra woman by twice-born men does not deserve a share of land."

One born of a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of land. If land were not already acquired through purchase or other means, then the specific prohibition against the son of a Śūdra woman would be untenable. Furthermore, it is stated: "The son of a Śūdra woman by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas does not inherit."
Whatever his father might give him, that alone shall be his wealth.
Thus, even that [rule] refers to a case where something might have been given by the father while he was still living to the son of a Śūdra wife;
however, when there is no such gift of favor, it is not contradictory for him to be entitled to one share. (2.125)
Now, something remaining after all divisions is stated:
whatever property is seen to have been taken from one another after the partition, that they shall divide again with equal shares; such is the settled rule.

The established rule and the limit of the scriptures is this: property belonging to the collective which was mutually misappropriated, or which was unknown at the time of partition, should be divided into equal shares when it is discovered after the paternal estate has been partitioned.
By stating "in equal shares" (*samair aṃśaiḥ*), the preferential allotment (*uddhāra*) is prohibited.
By stating "they should divide" (*vibhajeran*), it is shown that the item should not be retained by the very person who found it.

Thus, because the statement possesses meaning, it does not intend to convey that there is no fault in the misappropriation of collective property. Now, one might object: Manu has shown the fault for the eldest alone in the misappropriation of collective property, and not for the younger brothers: "The eldest who, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers—such a one shall lose his status as the eldest, shall be deprived of his share, and shall be restrained by the kings."
This is not so,

because by pointing out the fault even of an eldest brother who stands in the place of a father and possesses presumed independence, the fault of younger brothers who stand in the place of sons and are dependent on that elder is all the more clearly demonstrated by the logic of the "stick and the cake" maxim (*daṇḍāpūpika-nīti*). (For this maxim, see Jacob, *A Handful of Popular Maxims*).

And thus, a fault is heard of in an unrestricted sense: "He who deprives an heir of his share, him the [deprived] one destroys—whether he does not destroy him himself, he destroys his son, or else his grandson.

He who deprives an heir—one worthy of a share—of his share, i.e., excludes him from his portion and does not grant him a share; that [heir], being deprived of his share, destroys—that is, ruins and makes guilty—the one who excluded him.

If he does not destroy that [property], then he destroys his son or grandson; thus, the fault of one who misappropriates common property is declared in scripture even without a distinction based on seniority.
Now, if it is held that because common property is also one's own, its appropriation under the notion that "it is mine" does not entail fault—that is incorrect.

Even when one’s own property is being taken, because another’s property is inevitably taken along with it, the act necessarily incurs the fault [of theft] due to the application of the prohibition. This is illustrated by the following: When the *mudga* beans in a sacrificial porridge have spoiled and *māṣa* beans are substituted for them because of their similarity, the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) argues that the prohibition—"Indeed, *māṣa* beans are unfit for sacrifice"—does not apply, because they are being taken with the cognition that they are parts of *mudga* beans. To this, the proponent (*siddhāntin*) replies that even when the parts of the *mudga* are being taken, the *māṣa* grains are inevitably taken along with them; therefore, the prohibition certainly applies.
Therefore, it is established that there is indeed a fault in the misappropriation of common property, both according to scriptural authority and through logical reasoning. || 2.126 ||
Showing the specific share of the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (son of two fathers), he describes his essential nature:
"A son begotten through *niyoga* by one who is childless upon the field of another is,
according to the law, the heir to the property and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both."

"By one who has no son, with the permission of the guru," and so forth—according to this prescribed rule, a son begotten in the field of another (i.e., upon the wife of another) by a brother-in-law or similar relative through the appointment of the guru, belongs to both the progenitor (*bījī*) and the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*); he is the heir to their inheritance, the taker of their property, and the giver of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*), according to the law.

The meaning of this is as follows: when that appointed brother-in-law or similar relative, being himself sonless, engages in procreation in the field of one who is sonless for the sake of obtaining sons for both himself and the other, the son whom he begets is "twice-born" (*dvipitṛka*) and "belonging to two lineages" (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*); he is the heir to the property and the giver of the funeral oblation to both fathers.

But when a man who already has sons is commissioned and strives solely for the sake of a son for the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), then the son born from that union belongs to the owner of the field alone, not to the owner of the seed (*bījin*).
Furthermore, he does not necessarily inherit the estate of the owner of the seed, nor is he his giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍada*).
As stated by Manu: "When a field is given for the sake of seed through an agreement for the performance of the rite..."
In this matter, two parties are seen to be sharers of the fruit: the owner of the seed and the owner of the field.
Thus it is said:
"Because the labor is undertaken, the field that is given for the sake of seed—of that, two are seen to be sharers here: the owner of the seed and the owner of the field."

Regarding the phrase "because of the agreement regarding the act": because of the mutual consent that "let the offspring born [of this union] belong to both of us," when a field is given by the owner of the field to the owner of the seed for the purpose of sowing the seed, the great seers have observed that the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are both sharers and owners of the offspring produced in that field.

Thus: "But when no specific fruit is intended by the owner of the field or the owner of the seed, the benefit is clearly seen to belong to the owners of the field; the womb is stronger than the seed."
Thus:
"But when the fruit is not intended [by the owner], it belongs to both the owner of the field and the sower;
yet, in visible experience, the benefit accrues to the owners of the field, for the womb is more powerful than the seed."

"But without intending [it for oneself] as the fruit": here, when offspring is produced in another's field without the intention that "let the child belong to both of us," that offspring belongs to the owner of the field alone, because the womb is stronger than the seed, as is seen in the case of cattle, horses, and so forth.
In this context as well, the *niyoga* (authorization) applies only to one who has been verbally betrothed (*vāgdattā*), since *niyoga* in any other sense has been forbidden by Manu:
"By a brother-in-law or by a *sapiṇḍa*, a woman, being duly authorized..."
The desired goal is to be attained upon the complete exhaustion of the mental continuum.
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent,
shall procreate only one son at night, and never a second under any circumstances.
Having thus proposed this injunction, Manu himself prohibits it: "A widow must not be appointed to another [man] by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma."
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for the wedding ceremony.
For this practice of animal sacrifice was condemned by learned brahmins,
yet it was declared [as permissible] even for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom.
In former times, while ruling the entire earth, that foremost of royal sages,
his mind overwhelmed by lust, brought about the intermixture of the social orders.
From that time forward, virtuous men indeed censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring.
Thus it is said.
A widow must not be appointed to another man by members of the twice-born classes;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma.
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for the wedding ceremony.
For this practice, condemned as bestial by learned brahmins,
was declared [to have occurred] even among human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom.
In former times, while enjoying the entire earth, that foremost of royal sages,
his mind struck down by lust, brought about the intermixture of the social orders.
From that time forward, virtuous men indeed censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring.

Nor should it be thought that there is an option (vikalpa) because of the existence of both injunctions and prohibitions; for no censure is heard regarding those who would enjoin [such conduct], whereas in the duties of women, much fault is heard regarding transgression, and self-restraint is praised.
As Manu himself has said: "She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but when her husband is deceased, she must not even utter the name of another man."

Having thus forbidden seeking refuge with another man for the sake of livelihood, [the text continues]: "She should remain patient, self-controlled, and chaste until death, longing for that unsurpassed dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband."
Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without having established a lineage for their family.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates.
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.
Thus, he prohibits resorting to another man even for the sake of obtaining a son.
Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that there is an option (vikalpa) because [the practice] is both prescribed and prohibited.

Since the practice of *niyoga* with women consecrated by the marriage sacrament has thus been prohibited, one might ask: what then is the lawful *niyoga*? To this he says: "If the husband of a maiden dies after the verbal betrothal has been made, her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this rule."
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she who is clad in white garments and pure in her vows—
he shall consort with her in private once at each menstrual period until she gives birth.
Thus:
"If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this rule."
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she who is clad in white garments and observes pure vows—
he shall unite with her in private once during each fertile period until she gives birth.

From this very statement, it is understood that he to whom a girl has been verbally betrothed is her husband even without formal acceptance (*pratigraha*). When he has died, his brother—whether the elder or the younger, being his own uterine sibling—should take her as his wife;

having approached her according to rule and according to scripture, and having married her, he should approach her in private once every season until conception, following this procedure involving anointing with clarified butter, verbal restraints, and so forth, while she wears white garments, maintains pure vows, and is restrained in mind, speech, and body.

And this marriage, being scripturally ordained and involving rules such as the anointing with ghee, is an ancillary part of the authorized approach [to the brother-in-law]; it does not, therefore, establish the status of wife for the brother-in-law.
Consequently, the offspring born from that belongs only to the owner of the field (the husband), not to the brother-in-law.
However, by mutual agreement, it belongs to both. (2.127)
The method for the partition of property among sons of both similar and dissimilar classes has been stated.
Now, intending to demonstrate the rules for the inheritance of the primary and secondary sons, [the author] first describes their essential natures:
"The legitimate son (aurasa) is born of the lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta)."
But the *kṣetraja* son is one born of the wife by a man of the same lineage or by another.

A son born from the chest (*uraḥ*) is an *aurasa* son; he is one born of a lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). A wife of equal caste (*savarṇā*), wedded according to the lawful rite (*dharma-vivāha*), is a "lawful wife" (*dharmapatnī*); the son born of her is the primary *aurasa* son. Equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*). Equal to him means equal to the *aurasa* son. He is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*), and for that very reason, he is equal to the *aurasa* son.
As Vasiṣṭha said:
"I shall give you this daughter, who has no brother, adorned with ornaments;
whatever son is born of her shall be my son."
Thus [he said]:
"I shall give you this sisterless maiden, adorned with ornaments;
whatever son is born of her shall be my son."

Alternatively, the *putrikāsuta* (the son of an appointed daughter) is indeed a *putrika*; he is equal to a biological son (*aurasa*) because of the paucity of the father's constituent elements and the abundance of the mother's constituent elements.
As Vasiṣṭha says: "The third [son] is the *putrika* itself.
The meaning of "the third" is that the *putrikā* herself is the son.
But the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* is inferior to the biological son (*aurasa*) of the progenitor because he was born in the field of another.

As for the *kṣetraja*: "The *kṣetraja* is one born in the wife's field by a man of the same lineage or by another; a son begotten by another who is a *sapiṇḍa*, or by the husband’s brother (*devara*), is the *kṣetraja*. (2.128)
A son born secretly in the house is known as a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born);
one born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather.

The *gūḍhaja* son is one born in secret in the husband’s house; he is to be understood as such provided there is certainty that he was born of a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*), even if there is no certainty regarding the specific identity of the father, so long as the possibility of him being born of a man of a lower or higher caste is excluded. The *kānīna*, however, is one born of an unmarried girl (*kanyakā*); as before, if she remains in her father’s house while still unmarried, he is the son of his maternal grandfather among women of the same caste.
Furthermore, the son born then belongs to the husband alone;
as Manu says:
"But the son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father's house..."
One should call that son born of a maiden by the name of the husband "kānīna."

Thus: "A maiden, however, who bears a son in secret within her father's house, one should call him by the name 'Kānīna' (maiden-born), though he is produced from the maiden by a man other than her husband. (2.129)
A son born of a woman who has been previously married, whether she was still a virgin or not, is called a *paunarbhava*.
A son whom either the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* (given) son.

A *paunarbhava* son, however, is one born from a man of the same caste (*savarṇa*) to a *punarbhū* woman—whether she be unwidowed or widowed—who has been given by her mother with the husband’s permission, or by her father, or by both, to that man when the husband has gone abroad or is deceased. He is his *dattaka* (given) son.
As Manu says:
If the mother or the father should give a son who is similar [to themselves] and full of affection by means of water during a time of distress, he is to be known as a "given" (dattima) son.
Thus:
"If a mother or a father should give a son with water in times of distress—
one who is similar [in status] and given with affection— he is to be known as a 'given' (dattrima) son."
Because of the mention of "in times of distress," it should not be given when there is no distress;
this is a prohibition for the giver.
Likewise, an only son should not be given away.
However, one must never give away or receive in adoption an only son, according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha:
"By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes possessed of a son. Thus, even when there are many sons, the eldest is not to be given away.

Thus, because he alone is primary in performing the duties of a son, the method for adopting a son has been stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One intending to adopt a son shall summon his kinsmen, announce it to the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras in the middle of the house, he should adopt one who is not distant in kinship—that is, one closely related by blood. The phrase "not distant in kinship" is a prohibition against one who is extremely remote in terms of locality or language.
The same should be applied to those who are purchased, self-given, and artificially created, because the principle is identical. || 2.130 ||
One who is purchased by both [parents] is a "purchased" son; one who is sold is a "sold" son; one who is made so by himself is a "self-made" son;
one who gives himself is a "self-given" son; and one conceived in the womb and born with the bride is a "maiden-born" (sahoḍhaja) son.

But the *krīta* (bought) son is one who has been sold by those two, the mother and father, or by the mother or the father; as before, this applies provided he is of the same caste (*savarṇa*), with the exception of the case of distress and excluding an only son or an eldest son. As for that which was stated by Manu: "He whom one may purchase from his mother and father for the sake of offspring—whether he be similar or dissimilar—he is his *krītaka* (bought) son."

Thus, whether he is similar or dissimilar to him in qualities should be explained, and not by birth (*jāti*), because of the concluding statement: "This [classification] is declared among sons of the same caste. The *kṛtrima* (artificial) son is one who has been made a son by himself, seeking a son, through inducements such as the offering of wealth or land; he is one who is destitute of parents, for if they exist, he remains dependent upon them. The *dattātmā* (self-given) son is one who, being destitute of parents or abandoned by them, has approached of his own accord, saying, "I shall be your son," thus surrendering himself.

But the son born of a woman already pregnant at the time of marriage is the *sahoḍha*; he who is begotten by the husband upon a married woman is the son of the one who wed her (*voḍhuḥ putraḥ*). (2.131)
He who is taken up after having been abandoned is an *apaviddha* son.
One who is abandoned by both mother and father and is taken up becomes the son of the one who takes him; in all cases, he must be of the same caste (*savarṇa*).
Having thus enumerated the primary and secondary sons, he states the order of their succession in taking the inheritance:
"Among these, the one who offers the funeral cake (piṇḍada) shall take the share; in the absence of each preceding one, the next succeeding one does so."

Among these twelve sons mentioned previously, it should be understood that in the absence of each preceding one, each succeeding one is the performer of the *śrāddha*, the receiver of the share, and the taker of the wealth.

When there is a coexistence of the legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the appointed daughter’s son (*pautrika*), although the legitimate son alone would normally be entitled to take the wealth, Manu states this exception:
"But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born..."
In that case, the division shall be equal, for there is no seniority for a woman.

Thus (MDh 9.134): "But if, after a daughter has been appointed as a *putrikā*, a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman."
Likewise, Vasiṣṭha has stated that even when there are other sons, each preceding one being present, the subsequent sons share in a fourth part of the inheritance:
"If a legitimate son (aurasa) should be born after the adopted son (dattaka) has been received, the adopted son shall be entitled to a fourth part.
The mention of the "adopted son" is intended to illustrate those who are bought, those who are made (kṛtrima), and others, since there is no difference in the act of adopting them as sons.

And so Kātyāyana says: "But when a legitimate son (aurasa) has been born, the sons [of other kinds] who are of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a fourth part; those who are of a different caste (asavarṇa), however, shall be provided with food and clothing."
Thus it is said:
"But when a legitimate son of the body has been born, the other sons—whether of equal or unequal caste—are entitled to a fourth part;
those of unequal caste, however, are entitled only to food and clothing."
Those sons of the same caste, such as the adopted (*dattaka*) and the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) exists, are entitled to a fourth part of the inheritance.

However, those of a different caste—the maiden-born (*kānīna*), the secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), the one born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), and the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*)—do not receive a fourth part when a legitimate son exists; rather, they are entitled only to food and clothing.
As for the statement of Viṣṇu: "But the maiden-born, the secretly born, and the one born of a pregnant bride are unworthy."
And these [sons] who are subject to rebirth do not at all share in the funeral cakes or the inheritance.
Thus, that [text] also merely intends to prohibit the fourth share when a legitimate son (aurasa) exists;

however, in the absence of a legitimate son and the others, even the sons born of an appointed daughter (kānīna) and so forth certainly have the right to take the entire paternal estate, according to the statement: "In the absence of the former, each subsequent one [succeeds]."
As for the statement of Manu: "The legitimate son alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood."
Thus, that [rule] also should be understood to apply when the *dattaka* and other such sons are opposed to the *aurasa* son and lack good qualities.
In that regard, a specific rule for the *kṣetraja* son has been shown by him (Yājñavalkya) as follows:
"But one should give a sixth share of the paternal wealth to the *kṣetraja* son."
The legitimate son, when dividing the paternal inheritance, shall receive exactly one-fifth.
Thus it is said:
"But when dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth."

One should distinguish that the sixth part [of the inheritance] applies when both "contrariety" (*pratikūlatva*) and "lack of virtue" (*nirguṇatva*) are present, whereas the fifth part applies when only one of these two exists. Furthermore, although Manu, having presented two groups of six sons, stated that the first group possesses both inheritance rights and kinship (*dāyādabāndhavatva*), while the second group lacks inheritance rights but possesses kinship (*adāyādabāndhavatva*): "The legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*), the son begotten on the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*datta*), the son made (*kṛtrima*), the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), and the son cast off (*apaviddha*)—these six are heirs and kinsmen."
The son of an unmarried woman, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman,
the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.

Thus, even in that case, it should be explained that—provided there is no other nearer heir to the estate—the first group of six [relatives] inherits the estate of one's own father’s *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*, whereas for the second group of six, that inheritance does not exist.
Furthermore, their status as kinsmen (*bāndhava*)—consisting in performing duties such as the offering of water due to shared lineage (*gotra*) and being *sapiṇḍas*—is equal for both groups.
"An adopted son shall not share in the lineage or the estate of his biological progenitor."
The funeral cake follows the lineage and the inheritance; the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives [the property] away.
In this context, the mention of the *dattrima* (given son) is intended to illustrate the category of substitutes for a son;

however, the right to inherit the father's property belongs to all of them equally in the absence of each preceding one, because the text— "Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs to the father's estate"—
is devoted to establishing that all substitutes for a son other than the *aurasa* (legitimate son) possess the right to inherit the inheritance.

As for the legitimate son (*aurasa*), since the right to inherit has already been stated by the very text, "The legitimate son alone is the master of the paternal wealth," and because the word *dāyāda* is well known— e.g., in the phrase "he shall cause even the *dāyādas* to pay"— to refer to heirs other than the son who share in the inheritance; furthermore,
any variation in the order of the two groups found in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* and others should be understood as referring to those who possess qualities and those who do not.
In the Gautama-smṛti, however, the mention of the son of the appointed daughter (*pautrika*) as the tenth [in the list] refers to a case involving a different caste (*vijātīya*).
Therefore, it is established that in the absence of each preceding one, each succeeding one is the sharer of the inheritance.
But as for that which was said: "If among brothers born of the same father one should have a son, Manu declared that they are all possessed of a son by means of that son."

Thus, even that [statement] is intended to prohibit the adoption of others when the adoption of a brother’s son is possible; it is not, however, for the purpose of establishing [the brother's son] as a son, because that would contradict the rule: "His sons are kinsmen belonging to the same lineage. (2.132)
Now, under the guise of a concluding summary, he states the restrictive rule regarding that very matter:
"This rule has been declared by me for sons of the same class;
this rule—namely, 'in the absence of the preceding, the succeeding one'—is prescribed only for sons of identical caste, not for those of different castes."

And in that regard, the status of being of the same caste (*savarṇatva*) for the son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), the son taken with the bride (*sahoḍha*), and the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*) is by way of their progenitor, not by their own nature;
for it has been stated that they lack the defining characteristics of caste and birth (*varṇajāti*).

Likewise, since those born in the direct order (*anulomaja*), such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others, are included among the legitimate sons (*aurasa*), it should be understood that in their absence, the sons born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and the rest are the heirs to the estate.
However, even if he is the legitimate son (*aurasa*) of a *śūdra* woman, he does not receive the full share even in the absence of other [wives].
As Manu says:
"Whether there be a virtuous son or whether there be no son at all..."
According to the law, one should not give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman.
Thus it is said:
"Whether he has a virtuous son or even if he be sonless,
one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman."

Whether there be a legitimate son (*satputra*)—meaning a son of a twice-born woman—or whether there be no son (*aputra*)—meaning no son of a twice-born woman—if such a person has died, then a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) or any other *sapiṇḍa* shall not give more than a tenth part of that wealth to the son of a Śūdra woman; from this very rule, it is understood that in the absence of a son of the same caste (*savarṇāputra*), the sons of Kṣatriya and Vaiśya wives may take the entire estate.
Now he states the specific rule regarding the division of a Śūdra's wealth:
"Even one born of a Śūdra's slave-woman shall, if born of desire, be a sharer of the inheritance."
When the father has died, the brothers shall make him (the son of a remarried woman) a recipient of half a share;
one who has no brothers shall take the whole, except for the sons of the daughters.
A son begotten by a Śūdra on a female slave through lust receives a share at his father's wish.
However, after the father’s death, if there are sons born of wedded wives, then those brothers shall make that son of a female slave a recipient of half a share;
the meaning is that they shall give him half of their own respective shares.

Now, if there are no sons born of a wedded wife, then the son of a female slave shall take the entire estate, provided there are no daughters born of a wedded wife nor their sons. However, if such [daughters or their sons] exist, the son of a female slave is entitled to only a half-share.

And in this context, because of the mention of the Śūdra, a son begotten by a twice-born man on a female slave does not receive a share even by the father’s wish, nor a half-share; much less the whole.
But if he is favorable, he receives merely his livelihood. || 2.133 || 2.134 ||
It has been established that the primary and secondary sons inherit the estate;
in their absence, the order of succession for all heirs is now declared:
first the wife, then the daughters, then the parents, and likewise the brothers.
His son, a kinsman of the same lineage, a relative, a pupil, or a fellow student [should perform the rites].
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them becomes the heir to the wealth of the deceased who left no son; for this rule applies to all castes.

He who does not possess the twelve kinds of sons previously mentioned is "sonless. When such a sonless man has departed this world and gone to the next, the one among these enumerated heirs—beginning with the wife—who takes the wealth is the "receiver of the property. The connection is that in the absence of each preceding person, each succeeding one becomes the receiver of the wealth. This rule for the taking of inheritance and the sequence of succession should be understood to apply to all cases, including those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others, those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), and among the social classes (*varṇas*) beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. In that regard, first of all, the wife is the receiver of the wealth.
For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The wife, consecrated by the marriage sacrament, [participates] with her husband in the performance of sacrifice.
Furthermore, the singular number is used with reference to the class [of wives].
And if there are many such wives—whether of the same caste or of different castes—they take the wealth after dividing it according to their respective shares.

Vṛddha-Manu also states that the wife has a connection to the entire estate: "The sonless widow, preserving the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows, shall herself offer his funeral cake and receive the whole share."
Thus: "A wife who is childless, guarding her husband's bed and remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall indeed offer his funeral cake and receive his entire share."
Vṛddha-Viṣṇu also states: "The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to the wife;
in her absence, it goes to the daughter;
in her absence, it goes to the father."
"In the absence of those, it goes to the mother. Kātyāyana also says:
"The wife who has been unfaithful shall not be the taker of her husband's wealth; [only she who is] chaste [shall take it]."
But in his absence, if there should be a daughter who is unmarried, then [she shall take it].
Thus:
"The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall be the taker of his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall be the daughter, provided she be unmarried."
Likewise: For one who has no son, the wife born of a noble family, or even daughters, are [the heirs];
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [to be so].
Thus it is said:
For one who has no son, the wife born of a noble family, or even the daughters, are [the heirs];
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [to be so].
Bṛhaspati also says:
"When paternal uncles and uterine brothers exist,
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share."
When paternal kinsmen— fathers, brothers, or those related by blood— are present,
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share.
Indeed, statements that appear to be contradictory to this are observed:
"If among brothers one should die childless or should renounce the world,
the remaining brothers shall divide his property, excluding the woman's property."
And they should provide for his maintenance until the end of the women's livelihood;
if they preserve the bed of their husband, [he shall receive the inheritance], but in other cases, they shall forfeit it.

Thus, even when wives exist, Nārada has stated that the brothers take the wealth while the wives receive only maintenance. Manu, however, has shown that the wealth of one who dies without a son belongs either to the father or to the brothers, stating: "The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers alone."
Likewise, the mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
Thus, the connection to the property of the mother and the paternal grandmother has been shown.
Śaṅkha also states: "The property of one who has gone to heaven (died) without a son goes to his brothers;
in their absence, the parents shall take it, or the eldest wife. Thus, the connection to the property of the brothers, the parents, and the eldest wife is shown in this sequence.
Kātyāyana also says:
"When [the father] has died after partition, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the mother of that [father], in due order."

Regarding such statements of contradictory meaning, Dhāreśvara has shown the following systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*): the collection of texts beginning with "the wife shall take" refers to the wife of a brother who has been partitioned. And she [is entitled to take] only if she is desirous of *niyoga*.
Why is this? Because the taking of wealth by a wife is contingent upon *niyoga*, not by her own independent will.

Because of such statements as "the father shall take [the estate] of one who has no son," a basis for the legal arrangement must be stated there. Furthermore, because of the statement of Gautama—"Those connected by the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa), by the lineage (gotra), or by the seers (ṛṣi) shall divide the inheritance; or the wife of one who has no offspring may seek [another's] seed"—the meaning of this is as follows: those connected by the offering of the funeral cake, by the lineage, or by the seers shall divide the inheritance of one who has no offspring, or the wife shall take the inheritance provided she seeks [to obtain] seed.
Manu also says: "He who takes charge of the wealth and the wife of his deceased brother shall procreate offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to him."

By this, he shows the following: even when a brother has died after the property has been divided, the wife’s connection to the wealth occurs only through the medium of offspring, and not otherwise—even in the case where the property was divided. For example:
"If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder brother..."
In that case, the division shall be equal; such is the established law.
Thus it is said:
"If a younger brother should beget a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of the estate shall be equal; such is the established law."

Likewise, Vasiṣṭha also, by prohibiting *niyoga* on account of greed for inheritance with the words "there is no *niyoga*," demonstrates that the wife’s connection to the property occurs only through *niyoga* and not otherwise. Even in the absence of *niyoga*, the wife is entitled to mere maintenance according to the statement of Nārada: "And they shall provide maintenance for her until the end of her life."
And they should provide maintenance for their women until the end of their livelihood;
indeed, it is said by the Lord of Yogins:
"The wives of these [ascetics], provided they are of virtuous conduct, must be supported even if they are childless."
They shall be expelled if they are unfaithful or likewise if they are hostile.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore,
because the wealth of the twice-born belongs to them in accordance with reality, and because women lack authority in the sacrifice, their taking of wealth is improper.
And so it has been remembered by someone:
"Whatever wealth has arisen for the sake of a sacrifice, those who are not authorized therein shall all be recipients only of food and clothing, and not sharers of the inheritance."
Wealth is ordained for the purpose of sacrifice; therefore, one should employ it in ways consistent with dharma, and not among women, fools, or those who act contrary to dharma.
Thus:
"But those who are not entitled to the property produced for the sake of sacrifice, none of them shall be sharers of the inheritance;
they are entitled only to food and clothing."
Wealth is ordained for the purpose of sacrifice; therefore, one should employ it in matters consistent with dharma, and not among women, fools, or those who act contrary to dharma.
That is untenable;
for in the passage "the wife, the daughters," there is no perception of *niyoga*, nor is it the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, this must also be addressed here:
In the matter of a wife's acquisition of property, either *niyoga* (authorization for procreation) is the cause, or the offspring born thereof is the cause.

In that case, if *niyoga* alone were the cause, the connection to the property would accrue even to one who has not produced a son; conversely, the connection to the property would not accrue to the son once he is born.
Now, if it is held that the offspring alone is the cause [of the inheritance],
then, since the son alone would have a connection to the wealth, the section concerning the wife (*patnī*) need not have been commenced.
Alternatively, if the view is that for women, the connection to wealth occurs either through the husband or through the son, and not otherwise—

That too is incorrect, for it is traditionally taught that a woman’s property is of six kinds: what is given before the nuptial fire, what is received from the bridegroom, what is given as a token of affection, and what is obtained from her brother, mother, or father.

Because of contradictions such as these, and furthermore, because the text begins with "In the total absence of a son, the wife, the daughters," etc., the author, by stating that the wife appointed [for levirate] has a connection to the property, effectively asserts that the *kṣetraja* son alone possesses the right to the inheritance.

Since that has already been stated previously, there is no need to begin the section on the sonless widow with the word "wife" (*patnī*). Furthermore, as for the claim that the widow is entitled to a share of the wealth based on the statement of Gautama— "The sons of the same *piṇḍa*, *gotra*, and *ṛṣi* shall divide the inheritance, or the wife of one who has no offspring, provided she seeks to obtain seed"— that too is incorrect.
For the meaning "if she should desire to obtain an offspring, then the wife of one who has no son shall take the wealth" is not what is understood from this [text].

Rather, the meaning is that the kinsmen (piṇḍa), those of the same lineage (gotra), or those descended from the same seer (ṛṣi) shall divide the wealth of one who has no son; or else, the wife—provided that she desires to obtain an offspring or remains self-restrained (saṃyatā)—[shall take it]. This is an instruction regarding another duty for her, since the word "or" (vā) expresses an alternative position and does not convey the sense of "if.
Furthermore, it is logical that the taking of the wealth belongs only to the self-restrained woman, and not to the appointed woman (niyuktā), who is censured by both the Smṛtis and the world.
A wife who is childless, guarding her husband’s bed and remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall herself offer that funeral cake (piṇḍa) and receive his entire share.
Thus, it is stated that the taking of wealth applies only to one who is self-restrained.
Likewise, such a formal appointment (niyoga) has been condemned by Manu: "A widow must not be appointed to another [man] by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma."
By such statements as these;

and as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "There is no *niyoga* out of greed for inheritance," that should be explained to mean that when the husband has died—whether he was undivided or reunited—she has no connection to his wealth, and therefore *niyoga* should not be performed for the sake of establishing a connection to wealth for her offspring. Furthermore, as for the statement of Nārada: "And they should provide maintenance for her until the end of her livelihood."

Thus, that [text] as well— because the "those who are reunited" (*saṃsṛṣṭāḥ*) are under discussion in the statement, "But whatever share belongs to those who are reunited"— is intended solely to establish the mere maintenance of women who are childless. Furthermore, one should not suspect a redundancy between the rule, "If a brother should die childless," which pertains to the subject of reunion, and the rule, "But whatever share belongs to those who are reunited."
For, by the explanation of what was stated previously, the non-divisibility of a woman’s property is established, and she is ordained to receive only maintenance.
Furthermore, as for the statement beginning with "and the childless wives of these," that will be explained as referring to women such as those who are impotent (*klība*) and so forth.

As for the argument that it is improper for women to take wealth because the wealth of the twice-born is intended for sacrifice and women have no entitlement to sacrifice—that is incorrect; for if every kind of property were intended solely for sacrifice, then acts such as giving gifts (*dāna*) and burnt offerings (*homa*) would be impossible.

Now, if it is thought that because the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is an indicator of *dharma*, acts such as giving (*dāna*) and oblation (*homa*) are also *dharma* and therefore their purposefulness is not contradictory—

then in that case, wealth and pleasure, which are accomplished through wealth, would simply not be established at all. This being so, [the injunction] "one should not neglect *dharma*, wealth, and pleasure according to one's ability" [would be contradicted].

Likewise, there would be a contradiction with the statements of Yājñavalkya, Gautama, and Manu, such as: "One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly, but should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability," and "These [ends] cannot be properly regulated without practice," and so forth. Furthermore, if wealth were intended solely for the purpose of sacrifice, then the statement that "gold must be worn" would be contradicted; for by refuting the view that gold is common to both [sacrificial and personal use], its status as being for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha) was established, and that would be overturned.

Furthermore, if the word *yajña* (sacrifice) is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *dharma* (duty) in general, then since women also possess the entitlement to perform *pūrta-dharma* (works of public utility), their taking of wealth is even more appropriate.
As for the statements regarding dependence, such as "a woman does not deserve independence," let that dependence remain; however, what contradiction is there in her accepting wealth?
How then are we to understand such statements as "the property has been produced for the sake of sacrifice"?
It is said:

that wealth which has been acquired solely for the sake of sacrifice must be employed in sacrifice even by one's sons and others; such is the intent of that [scriptural passage]. For the hearing of the fault—"one who does not give what was obtained for the sake of sacrifice may become a vulture or even a crow"—applies without distinction to sons and others as well.

Furthermore, as it was stated by Kātyāyana: "An estate without an heir goes to the king, as do the wife's property, the servants' wages, and the funeral expenses, with the exception of the property of a Śrotriya;
that [property] one should bestow upon other Śrotriyas."

Thus, wealth that is "without an heir" (*adāyika*), meaning devoid of any claimant, goes to the king; this is the connection: setting aside what belongs to women, servants, and funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*), that which is used for the food and clothing of women, the funeral wealth of the deceased owner, and what is used for the *śrāddha* and other rites of another—all this, having been excluded from others, goes to the king.
The exception to this is stated in the second half [of the verse]:

"And the property of a *śrotriya*, setting aside what belongs to women, servants, and funeral rites, one should bestow it upon a *śrotriya*. This also refers to the case of a woman who is confined [to the household], because of the mention of the word "women" (*yoṣit*).
And the words of Nārada: "But other than a Brāhmaṇa, the king devoted to dharma shall provide for the livelihood of his [deceased] wives;
this is declared to be the rule of inheritance."
This [rule] refers exclusively to women who have not been married, because of the use of the word *strī* (woman).

Here, however, because of the word *patnī* (wife), it is not contradictory for a wedded and lawfully restrained wife to take the property. Therefore, the established meaning is this: when a man has died separated from his brothers and not reunited with them, leaving no son, the wife takes the property first; for partition has already been discussed, whereas the case of those who are reunited will be explained later.
By this, it should be understood that the claim made by Śrīkara and others—that [the rule] pertains only to those of small means—is refuted.

For indeed, even when legitimate sons (aurasa) exist, whether during the lifetime of the father or after his death, it has been stated that the wife is entitled to a share equal to that of a son: "If he should divide [the estate], the wives must be made sharers of equal portions."
Likewise: "When dividing after the father's death, the mother shall also take an equal share.
This being so, the notion that a wife does not receive anything beyond her maintenance from the estate of a deceased sonless man is mere delusion.

Regarding the statements, "Then the wives shall be made sharers of equal portions," and "The mother also shall take an equal share," the view that a woman takes only so much wealth as is necessary for her maintenance is incorrect; for this would result in the words "share" (*aṃśa*) and "equal" (*sama*) becoming meaningless.
It might be argued: "In the case of great wealth she takes what is necessary for her maintenance, but when the wealth is small, she takes a share equal to that of the sons.
That too is not tenable, because it would entail an inconsistency in the injunctions (*vidhi-vaiṣamya*).

For instance, the statements "wives should be made sharers of equal portions" and "the mother also shall take an equal share" establish that, in the case of abundant wealth, another scriptural injunction is required to provide for their mere subsistence; however, in the case of limited wealth, they establish that the wife's share is equal to that of a son.

For example, in the context of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices regarding the statement "they carry forward [the fire] at two [of the rites]," the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) first demonstrates that the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*—"they do not scatter the *uttaravedi* at the Vaiśvadeva, nor at the Śunāsīrīya"—is based on the extension (*atideśa*) of the *saumika-praṇayana*. Then, a partial follower of the final conclusion (rāddhāntaikadeśin) objects, stating that this prohibition of the *uttaravedi* does not apply to the *uttaravedi* obtained through the extension of the *saumika-praṇayana*, but rather to the *uttaravedi* obtained by the contextual injunction "they scatter [the earth] here" (*upātra vapanti*). To this, the proponent replies that the injunction "they scatter here" actually establishes the *uttaravedi* as an optional alternative for the first and last rites, since it depends upon the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* in those two rites.

However, it has been shown that in the case of the two middle [parvans], the text brings about the *uttaravedi* as if it were mandatory (*nityavat*), independent of anything else; thus, a disparity in the injunctions (*vidhi-vaiṣamya*) is demonstrated.

Even in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), out of fear of such a disparity in injunctions, the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* for the first and last parvans is shown to be a mandatory restatement (*nityānuvāda*). This is established by considering the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "they carry the fire in two," which indicates that the rule "they place the offering there" enjoins the *uttaravedi* specifically for the two middle parvans, namely the Varuṇapraghāsa and Sākamedha.
Furthermore, as for the opinion: "The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Manu, and likewise because of the teaching of Śaṅkha—"For the property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers;

in their absence, the parents shall take it, or the eldest wife"—it follows that the wealth of one without a son goes to his brothers. Furthermore, from such statements as "They should provide maintenance for the women until the end of their lives," it is established that the wife receives the portion of wealth necessary for her maintenance.
This being the case, when a wealthy man dies without a son, the wife takes what is necessary for her maintenance and the brothers take the remainder.

However, when there is only enough wealth—or even less—than what is required for the wife’s maintenance, then does the wife alone take it, or do the brothers as well? To resolve this conflict and demonstrate that the preceding rule is stronger, the text begins with the words "The wife, the daughters...
The venerable Teacher does not tolerate even this [interpretation].

For it has been explained that because of the traditional legal memory (*smṛti*) stating, "The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, or the brothers themselves," this statement is not intended to prescribe a specific order of succession; rather, it merely demonstrates eligibility for the acquisition of wealth. And since that [eligibility] applies even in the absence of the group beginning with the wife, [the author] has so interpreted it.
The statement of Śaṅkha also refers to the case of brothers who have reunited.
Furthermore, neither from this statement nor from the context is it understood that its scope is limited.

As for the rule "each subsequent one is the heir to the wealth," its status as referring to small amounts of wealth—dependent on another sentence regarding the two subjects of "the wife and the daughters"—and its status as referring to mere wealth in the case of the father and others, remains exactly as previously stated; thus, this [objection] is trivial.
As for the statement of Hārīta, "If a widow who has reached youth becomes harsh [in conduct],
then a livelihood must be provided for the sake of preserving her life," that too is intended to prohibit the taking of the entire estate by one whose potential for misconduct is suspected.

From this very statement, it is understood that the entire property is to be taken by her whose deviation [from virtue] is not suspected. With this very intent, Śaṅkha stated: "Or the eldest wife. The "eldest" is the one who is senior in virtue and whose deviation is not suspected; she, having taken all the wealth, protects the other—even if she be harsh—like a mother. Thus, everything is beyond reproach.

Therefore, it is established that when a man has died without a son—having been divided from his co-heirs and not reunited with them—his widow, being chaste, inherits the entire estate. In her absence, the daughters inherit.
The use of the plural "daughters" is intended to ensure that daughters of the same caste and those of different castes receive equal or proportional shares, respectively.
And so says Kātyāyana:
"The wife who is free from infidelity shall take the husband's wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall be the daughter, provided she be unmarried."
Thus:
"The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall be the taker of his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall be the daughter, provided she be unmarried."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"The wife is the heir to the husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is so considered.
From limb after limb she is produced from men, just like a son."
Therefore, how could another man take the paternal wealth?
Thus it is said:
"The wife is the one who inherits her husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is so considered.
From every limb of men, the daughter is born just like a son."
Therefore, how could another man take the paternal wealth?
In that regard, when there is a conflict between a married and an unmarried [daughter], only the unmarried one receives;
however, in her absence, it is the daughter who receives provided she be unmarried—
since such is the specific traditional teaching (smṛti).

Likewise, in the case of the conjunction of those who are both established and unestablished, that which is unestablished alone remains; in its absence, it becomes established. This is because Gautama’s statement—"the property of a woman belongs to her daughters, whether unmarried or unestablished"—is equally applicable to paternal wealth as well. Nor should it be thought that this refers only to the *putrikā* (appointed daughter), for the *putrikā* and her son are declared in the section on sons to be equal to the *aurasa* (legitimate) son, in the words "the son of an appointed daughter is equal to him.
By the force of the word "and" (*ca*), in the absence of a daughter, the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) is the heir to the wealth.
As Viṣṇu has said:
"In the absence of sons or grandsons, daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth;
for in the ancestral offering (svadhākāra) to the ancestors, grandsons are considered equal to daughters' sons."
Thus:
"In the absence of sons and grandsons, daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth;
for in the ancestral offerings (svadhākāra) to the ancestors, grandsons are considered equal to daughters' sons."
Manu also says:
"Whether she be appointed or unappointed, the maternal grandfather who obtains a son from a suitable man shall,
through that grandson, offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth."
Thus [it is said].

Whether she has been formally appointed or not, if she bears a son who resembles [the maternal grandfather], by that grandson the maternal grandfather becomes a "grandson's father" (pautrī); he shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and inherit the wealth.
In their absence, both parents—the mother and father—are the sharers of the wealth.

Although, because the rule for *dvandva* compounds prescribes that they denote things with simultaneous substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), and since the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation is an exception to that, the sequence of the parents is not perceived when the term "wealth" (*dhana*) is employed; nevertheless, because the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) is placed first in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), and because in the case where there is no *ekaśeṣa*—as in the form *mātāpitarau*—the word "mother" is heard first, the sequence of meaning is understood from the very sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). Thus, when there is a requirement for a sequence regarding the connection to wealth, it is understood that the mother is the first to receive the wealth, and in her absence, the father.

Furthermore, since a father is common to other sons as well, whereas a mother is not common, she possesses a superior degree of proximity; therefore, according to the statement, "The wealth of each person shall belong to that [heir] who is the nearest among the sapindas and others," it is logical that the mother alone should first take the property.

Nor is proximity restricted solely to the sapindas; rather, it is understood from this very statement that when the right to take the property would otherwise apply without distinction even to the samānodakas and others, it is proximity itself that serves as the restrictive factor.
Because of the mother’s superior proximity [to the child], it is more appropriate that she alone receive the inheritance;
in her absence, the father is the heir;
and in the father’s absence, the brothers are the heirs.
And so Manu says:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or else the brothers themselves."
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, or the brothers themselves.
Furthermore, as stated by Dhāreśvara: "The mother shall obtain the estate of a son who is childless;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth."
Based on this statement of Manu, even while the father is living, if the mother has passed away, the father’s mother—the paternal grandmother—shall take the wealth, not the father.

This is because wealth taken by the father passes to sons even of different castes (*vijātīya*), whereas wealth taken by the paternal grandmother passes only to those of the same caste (*sajātīya*); thus, the paternal grandmother alone takes it.
However, the Teacher does not approve of that view either.
