Since it has been stated that even sons of a different caste are entitled to receive wealth— according to such rules as "they shall have four, three, two, or one shares"— the Smṛti of Manu, which states, "The property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be taken by the king; this is the settled rule," refers to the intention of the king and not to the intention regarding the sons.

Among brothers as well, uterine brothers (sodara) shall take first, because non-uterine brothers (bhinnodara) are more remote due to their mother; for there is a traditional legal text (smṛti) stating that "the wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda. In the absence of uterine brothers, the non-uterine brothers are the heirs to the property.

In the absence of brothers as well, their sons are the heirs to the wealth according to the order of their fathers. When there is a coexistence of both brothers and nephews (brothers' sons), the nephews have no right [to inherit], because the texts declare the right of nephews only upon the absence of brothers. However, when a brother has died childless and the connection to the wealth has arisen among his brothers without distinction, if one of those brothers should die prior to the division of the brothers' wealth, then since the right of his sons arises through their father, it is logical that when they and the other brothers take the wealth by partition, the allotment of shares should be determined according to the fathers.
In the absence even of brothers' sons, the kinsmen of the paternal line (gotrajas) are the heirs to the property;
these kinsmen consist of the paternal grandmother, the sapindas, and the samānodakas.

In this regard, the grandmother is the first to inherit the wealth; and since it follows that "when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take [the estate]," the grandmother's acquisition of the wealth would thus follow immediately after the mother. However, because the succession of those beginning with the father and ending with the brother’s son is fixed, there can be no insertion of anyone in between. Furthermore, the statement "the father’s mother shall take the wealth" merely intends to establish her eligibility for inheritance. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that she takes the property after their sons (the brothers) when they have been passed over.

In the absence of the paternal grandmother, the paternal grandfather and other *sapiṇḍas* belonging to the same *gotra* are the heirs to the wealth; for those *sapiṇḍas* who belong to different *gotras* are included under the term "kinsmen" (*bandhu*).
In that regard, in the absence of the father’s lineage, the paternal grandmother, the paternal grandfather, the paternal uncles, and their sons are the heirs in succession.

In the absence of the paternal grandfather’s lineage, the great-grandmother, the great-grandfather, his sons, and their sons—in this manner, it should be understood that the inheritance belongs to the *sapiṇḍas* of the same *gotra* up to the seventh degree.
In their absence, the inheritance belongs to those who are *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen). They are to be understood as seven generations beyond the *sapiṇḍas*,
or until the limit where birth and name are no longer known.
As Bṛhan-Manu has said: "The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the state of being a samānodaka ceases with the fourteenth."
Some say that the lineage (gotra) is that which follows immediately after the recollection of one's birth and name.
Thus it is said: "Sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the state of being Samānodaka ceases with the fourteenth."
Some say that the lineage (gotra) subsequent to those is defined by the recollection of one's birth and name.
In the absence of agnates (*gotraja*), kinsmen (*bandhu*) are the heirs to the wealth.
Kinsmen are of three kinds: paternal kinsmen, maternal kinsmen, and maternal-affinal kinsmen (*mātṛbandhu*).
As it has been said:
The sons of one's father’s sister, the sons of one’s mother’s sister,
and the sons of one’s maternal uncle are to be known as one’s own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbandhu).
The sons of one's mother’s paternal aunt, the sons of one’s mother’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one’s mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as maternal kinsmen (mātṛbandhu).
Thus [it is said].
The sons of one's father's sister, the sons of one's mother's sister,
and the sons of one's maternal uncle are to be known as one's own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as the paternal relatives (pitṛbāndhava).
The sons of one's mother’s father’s sister, the sons of one’s mother’s mother’s sister,
and the sons of one’s mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as maternal relatives (mātṛbāndhava).

In that regard, because of their proximity, it should be understood that the order is as follows: first, the paternal relatives (ātmabandhu) are the heirs of the wealth; in their absence, the paternal relatives on the father's side (pitṛbandhu); and in their absence, the maternal relatives (mātṛbandhu).

In the absence of relatives, the teacher (ācārya) [is the heir]; in his absence, the pupil (śiṣya). In the absence of a son, whoever is the nearest *sapiṇḍa* [is the heir], and in his absence, the teacher.
Because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "In the absence of the teacher, the pupil [is the authority]."

In the absence of a student, a fellow religious student (*sabrahmacārī*) shall be the heir to the property. A fellow religious student is one who, together with another, has received initiation (*upanayana*), studied the Veda, and acquired knowledge of its meaning from the same teacher. In his absence, any learned *śrotriya* may take the property of a Brāhmaṇa; for the Smṛti of Gautama states: "Learned *śrotriyas* shall divide the inheritance of a childless Brāhmaṇa."
In the absence of those, any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever [shall inherit].
As Manu has said:
"But in the absence of all [others], Brāhmaṇas are the sharers of the inheritance."
Those who possess the threefold knowledge, who are pure and self-controlled—in such a way, the Dharma does not decline.
Thus it is said: "But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs; in this way, Dharma is not lost."

"A king shall never take the property of a Brāhmaṇa; the property of a Brāhmaṇa is eternally inviolable by the king—this is the established rule," according to the statement of Manu. Nārada has also said:
If there is no heir whatsoever for the property of a Brāhmaṇa, it must be given to another Brāhmaṇa; otherwise, the king would be a sinner.
Thus it is said.
If there is no heir whatsoever for the property of a Brāhmaṇa and that property is lost, it must be given to another Brāhmaṇa; otherwise, the king would be a sinner.
In the absence of anyone from the kṣatriya down to the fellow student (sabrahmacārin), the king shall take the property of a kṣatriya and others, but not a brāhmaṇa.
As Manu has said:
"But in the case of the other castes, in the absence of all [heirs], the king shall take [the property]."
Thus [ends verses] 2.135 and 2.136.
But for the other castes, in the absence of all [heirs], the king shall take [the property].
It has been stated that sons and grandsons take the inheritance, and in their absence, the wife and others.
Now, he states the exception to both of those rules.
The heirs of forest-dwellers, renunciants, and students are, in order: the preceptor, a virtuous disciple, a spiritual brother, and one who shares the same sacred site.

The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), the ascetic (*yati*), and the lifelong student (*brahmacārin*)—in their respective order, whether in direct or reverse sequence—are heirs to the inheritance of wealth, along with the teacher (*ācārya*), the virtuous pupil (*sacchiṣya*), and the co-student (*ekatīrthī*). Regarding the lifelong student (*naiṣṭika*): while the property of a temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*) is taken by the mother and others, it is stated that the teacher takes the property of the lifelong student as an exception to that rule.
The wealth of a *yati*, however, is taken by a good disciple (*sacchiṣya*);
a good disciple, moreover, is one capable of hearing, retaining, and practicing the meaning of the *adhyātma-śāstra*, for even a teacher of evil conduct is unworthy of a share.
The wealth of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is taken by a religious brother (*dharmabhrātṛ*) who belongs to the same *tīrtha*.

A "dharma-brother" is one who has entered the path together; a "co-religionist" (*ekatīrthin*) is one who shares the same stage of life (*ekāśramin*). A "dharma-brother who is also a co-religionist" is thus one who is both a dharma-brother and a co-religionist.

In the absence of these—beginning with the teacher and so forth—even if sons and others are present, he takes [the inheritance] from the co-religionist alone. But is it not the case that, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) of Vasiṣṭha—"those who have entered another stage of life are entitled to no share"—there is no connection to the inheritance at all for those who have entered another stage of life? How then could there be a division of it?
Furthermore, it is not appropriate for a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) to have a connection with wealth acquired by himself, because of the prohibition against accepting gifts and the like;
for Gautama records in his Smṛti that "a mendicant (bhikṣu) should be without accumulation.
Even for a mendicant, there is no possibility of a connection with wealth acquired by himself.
It is said:

For the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he should make a collection of wealth for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been prepared, he should discard it in the month of Āśvayuja.
Because of this statement, there is indeed a connection with wealth even for the ascetic:
"He may wear even a garment for the sake of covering his loins;
likewise, he may take up sandals and various requisites for yoga."

Based on such statements, there is indeed a connection with clothing and books; since even for one who has taken the vow of lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika) there is a connection with clothing and so forth for the sake of maintaining the body, the description of their distribution is entirely appropriate. || 2.137 ||
Now he states an exception to the rule that the wife and others of a son who has gone abroad (svar-yāta) are the heirs to his wealth:

"But the reunited coparcener (saṃsṛṣṭin) [inherits from] the reunited coparcener. One who has reunited property—that is, property which was previously divided and then mixed together again—is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*. Furthermore, this state of being reunited does not occur with just anyone, but only with a father, a brother, or a paternal uncle.
As Bṛhaspati has said: "One who, though previously divided, again lives together with his father, brother,
or paternal uncle out of affection, is called *saṃsṛṣṭa* (reunited)."
Thus it is said: "Furthermore, one who, though previously divided, has come to live together again with his father, brother,
or paternal uncle out of affection, is called *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one reunited)."
The co-sharer shall give the share—that is, the portion—of that deceased co-sharer to the son born later from a wife whose pregnancy was unknown at the time of partition;
in the absence of such a son, the co-sharer alone shall take it, and not the wife or others.
He states an exception to the rule "an associate shall [inherit] from an associate":
"But a uterine brother [shall inherit] from a uterine brother;
he shall give and take the share of one who is born and of one who has died."
The phrase "the reunited coparcener shall [give]" carries over from the previous rule.
Consequently, upon the death of a reunited uterine brother, that reunited uterine brother shall give the deceased's share to the son born after the reunion;
in his absence, he shall take it—this connection is to be understood as before.

Thus, in the case of an association between uterine and non-uterine brothers, the wealth of one who has associated with a uterine brother is taken by that very uterine brother who is the associate, and not by a non-uterine brother even if he is an associate; this is an exception to what was stated previously. (2.138)

Now, when a man who has entered into a partnership (saṃsṛṣṭin) has died without a son, and there exists both a uterine brother who is not a partner and a non-uterine brother who is a partner, the author states the reason for the division between these two regarding the acquisition of the property:
"But a non-uterine brother who is a partner shall take the wealth;
even one who is not a partner may take it, but one born of another mother who is not a partner shall not."
A half-brother born of a different womb who is a coparcener (saṃsṛṣṭin) shall take the wealth; however, a half-brother born of a different womb who is not a coparcener shall not take the wealth.

By this [statement], through the method of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka), it is stated that the status of being a coparcener is the cause for a half-brother born of a different womb to receive the property.
The term "not a coparcener" (asaṃsṛṣṭī) is also connected with what follows.
Therefore, even one who is not reunited may take the wealth of a reunited kinsman.
To the question "Who is that?", he says: "The reunited" means one who is reunited by being born from the same womb.
"Brother" (sodara) means a uterine brother.

By this, it is stated that even for a brother who is not reunited (asaṃsṛṣṭa), the fact of being a uterine brother is the cause for his taking the property; the term "reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭa) also connects with what follows.
In that context, "reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭa) means one who is a reunited co-heir (saṃsṛṣṭin).
"Not born of another mother.

Here, the explanation should be made by supplying the word "eva" (only): even one who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (a reunited coparcener) shall not take the wealth of a *saṃsṛṣṭin* if he is born of another mother.

And thus, because of the hearing of the word "api" (also)—implying that even one who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin* might take it—and because of the negation of the restriction that "the *saṃsṛṣṭin* [takes it] only if not born of another mother," it is stated that the division and taking of the property must be performed by both the uterine brother who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin* and the brother of a different womb who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*.
Because the grounds for each of the two to take the property exist equally.
This very point has been clarified by Manu:
"If those who were divided should live together again and divide once more..."

Thus, having introduced the division of mixed inheritances: "If among them the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution, or if either one should die, his share is not lost."
The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally;
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.

By saying this [the author means]: among those brothers who are *saṃsṛṣṭins* (those who have reunited their estates), whether the eldest, the youngest, or the middle one— regarding the distribution of shares (*aṃśapradāne*)— the suffix *-tasi* is used here in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).
"At the time of partition" means until that point.

"He would be deprived" means he would fall away from his own share; whether by entering another stage of life (*āśrama*), by committing a crime such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), or by dying, his share is not lost.
Therefore, it must be set aside separately; the meaning is that the reunited heirs (*saṃsṛṣṭin*) alone shall not take it.
He states the application of that extracted portion: "The uterine brothers shall divide it.

They—the uterine brothers (*sodarya*), meaning those born of the same mother—even if they are not reunited (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*), even if they have gone to different countries—having come together and assembled, including the sisters, shall divide it.
Having divided it equally, they shall take it; such is the clear meaning. (2.139)
He states an exception to what was said regarding the inheritance by those related through marriage, such as sons and wives: "The impotent, the outcast, his offspring, the lame, the insane,
the idiotic, the blind, and those afflicted with incurable diseases and the like, should be maintained but are entitled to no share."
A eunuch is one of the third gender;
an outcaste is one who has committed such acts as killing a Brahmin; "born of that" means born from an outcaste.
A cripple (*paṅgu*) is one deficient in feet.

A madman (*unmattaka*) is one overcome by forms of insanity characterized by wind (*vātika*), bile (*paittika*), phlegm (*ślaiṣmika*), a combination of the three humors (*sāṃnipātika*), or possession by a spirit (*grahāveśa*).
An idiot (*jaḍa*) is one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is impaired.
That is to say, one who is incapable of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful; "blind" means one whose faculty of sight is impaired;
"one afflicted by an incurable disease" means one seized by diseases such as consumption (yakṣmā) that cannot be remedied.

By the word "first" (ādya), there is the inclusion of those who have entered another stage of life (āśrama), those who hate their father, those guilty of minor offenses (upapātakin), the deaf, the mute, and those deprived of their senses.
As Vasiṣṭha said: "Those who have entered another stage of life are not entitled to a share. And likewise by Nārada:
One who hates his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these, though legitimate sons, shall not receive a share; how much less so a son born of the wife?
Thus:

"One who hates his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these, though legitimate sons (aurasa), shall not receive a share; how much less so a son born of the wife (kṣetraja)?"
Manu also says: "Eunuchs and outcasts, those born blind or deaf,
as well as the insane, the idiotic, the dumb, and those who are deficient in any organ, do not receive a share."
Thus: "The impotent and the outcast, those born blind or deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs— these have no share [in the inheritance]."
"Nirindriya" means one from whom the sense-faculties have departed due to disease or other causes; such a person is "nirindriya.
These individuals, beginning with the impotent (klība), are "without share" (anaṃśa); they do not become heirs to the inheritance.
They should merely be maintained by providing food and clothing.

However, there is the fault of being an outcast (*patita*) regarding non-provision; for a wise man should give to all according to his ability what is right, namely food and clothing to the utmost extent, for he who does not give becomes an outcast.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu,
the meaning is "absolutely," that is, for as long as one lives.

Since the state of being without a share (*anaṃśatva*) is established by the fact that the fault arises even before the division of these [properties], it does not apply, however, to one who has already been divided.

Even after the time of partition, if the defects [of the estate] are removed by means of medicine and the like, there is indeed a right to a share; for this is based on the same legal principle as the rule: "A son born after partition from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share.
However, in the case of those who have fallen from their caste (patita) and so forth, the masculine gender is not intended to be restrictive.
And for this reason, it should be understood that wives, daughters, mothers, and others who are tainted by the aforementioned defects are likewise excluded from inheritance. (2.140)

Since eunuchs and others are excluded from inheritance, it might follow that their sons are also excluded; to this [objection], he says: "But their legitimate (aurasa) or soil-born (kṣetraja) sons, being free from defects, are entitled to shares.

This means that the legitimate or soil-born sons of these [eunuchs and others]—provided they are "free from defects," meaning devoid of such flaws as impotence which would otherwise bar them from receiving a share—are "entitled to shares," that is, they shall receive a portion of the inheritance.

In that regard, for a eunuch, a son born of the wife (kṣetraja) is possible, whereas for others, even sons born of their own bodies (aurasa) are possible. The mention of both the aurasa and the kṣetraja is for the purpose of excluding other types of sons.
He states the specific rule regarding the daughters of eunuchs and others:
"And their daughters must be maintained until they have been given away to a husband."

The sons and daughters of these [categories], such as the impotent and others, must be maintained until they have undergone the sacrament of marriage; by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that they must also be initiated with the sacred rites. (2.141)
He states the specific rule regarding the wives of eunuchs and others:
"The childless wives of these men should be maintained if they are of virtuous conduct;
likewise, those who are unchaste or hostile should be expelled."

The wives of these [categories], such as the impotent and others, if they are childless, virtuous in conduct, and of good character, must be maintained—that is, provided for. However, those who are unchaste are to be expelled;
likewise, those who are hostile are both to be expelled and [nevertheless] maintained.
If they are not unfaithful, one must not fail to provide maintenance for them merely because they are disagreeable. 2.142.

Having briefly stated the division of the property of both women and men in the verse beginning with "the sons shall divide the property of the parents," the division of the man's property was explained in detail.
Now, intending to explain the division of a woman's property in detail, he first states its nature:
"Gifted by the father, the mother, the husband, or the brother; that which has come [to her] at the nuptial fire;..."
And that which is received upon taking a second wife and so forth is declared to be a woman's property (strīdhana).

That which is given by the father, mother, husband, or brother; that which is given at the time of marriage by maternal uncles and others with reference to the sacred fire (*agni*); and *ādhivedanika*—meaning that which is given on account of supersession, as will be stated later in the rule "one should give to a superseded wife"—this is what is called *strīdhana* (woman’s property) by Manu and others, acquired through inheritance, purchase, partition, acceptance of gifts, or finding. Furthermore, the term *strīdhana* is etymological (*yaugika*) and not technical (*pāribhāṣika*), for when an etymological derivation is possible, it is improper to resort to a technical definition.

Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu: "What is received from the teacher, what is obtained at the wedding, what is given as a token of affection, and what is received from brothers, mother, or father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman."
Thus, the sixfold nature of a woman’s property is stated for the purpose of excluding a smaller number, not for the purpose of excluding a larger number.
The nature of *adhyagni* and the other types has been declared by Kātyāyana:
"That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagnikṛta* woman's property (*strīdhana*)."
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives when being led away from her father’s house is declared to be that female property known as *adhyāvahanika*.
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
as well as that which is given for the purpose of saluting their feet, is called "given out of affection" (*prītidattam*).
This applies whether it is given by a married woman or an unmarried girl, even in the house of her husband's father.
That which is obtained from a brother or from one's parents is known as saudāyika (a woman’s separate property).
Thus [ends verse] 2.143.
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried maiden, what is obtained from the husband, from the father’s house,
or from a brother or from the parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a woman’s separate property).
Furthermore:
"The gift from kinsmen," as well as the *śulka* and the *anvādheya*.
That which is given by the kinsmen of the maiden—namely, by her maternal relatives and her paternal relatives.
*Śulka* is that which is given after taking a fee;
*anvādheyaka* is that which is placed or given subsequently after the marriage ceremony.
And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
Whatever property is acquired by a woman from her husband's family after marriage,
as well as that which is received from her father's family, is known as anvādheya.
Thus:
"Whatever is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after marriage,
as well as that which is obtained from her father's family, is known as anvādheya property."
The phrase "is declared to be a woman’s property" is to be connected with what has preceded.
Thus has the property of a woman been described;
he now states its distribution:
"If she dies without offspring, her kinsmen shall obtain it."

That aforementioned property of a woman, when she has died childless—meaning devoid of daughter, daughter’s daughter, daughter’s son, son, or grandson—is taken by her kinsmen, such as the husband and others who will be mentioned hereafter. (2.144)
The general heirs entitled to take the property have been shown. Now he states the distinction of heirs according to the difference in marriage forms:
"The wealth of a childless woman [belongs] to the husband in all four [marriages], beginning with the Brāhma."
If she has borne daughters, that [property] goes to the father among the remaining [heirs].

In the case of the aforementioned childless woman who has obtained the status of wife through one of the four marriages previously mentioned—the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, or Prājāpatya—her aforementioned property goes first to her husband upon her death. In his absence, it goes to his nearest *sapiṇḍa* relatives.
In the remaining marriages—the Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca—that property of the childless woman goes to her father.
Both mother and father are "parents" (*pitarau*); that which goes to them is "inheritable by the parents" (*pitṛgāmi*).

Although the mother is indicated by the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one term), it has already been stated that she takes the wealth first. In her absence, those closely related to her take the wealth.
In all forms of marriage, if she has given birth to offspring, that wealth belongs to her daughters;
here, by the word "daughters," the daughters of the daughter are meant.

This is because it was stated [in the previous rule] that for direct daughters, "the remainder belongs to the mother's daughters. Therefore, when the mother has passed away, the daughters take the mother’s wealth first.
In that regard, when there is a conflict between one who is unmarried and one who is married, only the unmarried woman receives [the inheritance]. In her absence, it goes to the married woman.
Even in that case, when there is a conflict between one who is established [in her husband's family] and one who is not established, the one who is not established receives it.
In the absence of that [daughter], it belongs to those who are established.
As Gautama says: "The property of a woman belongs to her daughters, both those who are unmarried and those who are unestablished.
And there, by the word "and" (ca), it is meant that it also belongs to those who are established.
[The woman] is without a husband, childless, or destitute;
and this applies apart from the *śulka* (bride-price).
As for the *śulka*, it belongs exclusively to the uterine brothers, because of the statement of Gautama: "The *śulka* of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers after the death of the mother."

In the absence of all daughters, the daughters' daughters take [the inheritance], based on the scriptural statement: "if the daughters have produced offspring. When there is an assembly of those [daughters' daughters] born of different mothers and in unequal numbers, the allotment of shares is determined by way of their mothers; or, according to the Smṛti of Gautama: "or, according to each mother, there shall be a specific division of shares within her own group."
In the case of a conflict between daughters and granddaughters, something small should be given to the granddaughters.
As Manu says:
"Whatever daughters they may have, for them also [a share] should be given according to their merit."
Something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth with affection.
Thus [it is said].
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection.
In the absence of even the daughters' daughters, the daughters' sons are the heirs to the wealth;
as Nārada has said:
"In the absence of the mother's daughters, [the inheritance goes to] the daughters' offspring."
Thus:
"In the absence of the mother, [the inheritance goes to] the daughters; in the absence of the daughters, their offspring.
Because the word "their" (tat) refers back to the daughters mentioned in close proximity, in the absence of the daughters' sons (dauhitrāḥ), the sons take [the inheritance].
For it has been stated that "the lineage [continues] through them.

Manu also demonstrates the connection of daughters and sons with the mother's property: "When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the mother's inheritance equally."
Thus:
"But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the mother's inheritance equally."

The construction is as follows: "All uterine brothers shall divide the maternal inheritance equally, and the uterine sisters shall also divide it equally. It is not, however, the construction that "the uterine brothers shall divide it equally and the uterine sisters shall also divide it equally," nor that "the uterine brothers and the sisters together shall divide it," because a mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga) is not perceived due to the absence of a copulative compound (dvandva) or a singular remainder (ekaśeṣa); furthermore, the use of the word "ca" (and) is justified by its connection with the act of dividing.
For example: "Devadatta should perform agriculture, and Yajñadatta [should do so as well].

The inclusion of the term *samagra* (all/together) is for the purpose of excluding the division of preferential shares (*uddhāra*). The inclusion of the term *sodara* (uterine) is for the purpose of excluding those born of different wombs.

However, the property of a childless woman of inferior caste is taken by the daughter of a co-wife of superior caste, even if she belongs to a different womb; in her absence, it is taken by that daughter’s offspring. As Manu has said:
Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to her offspring.
Thus:
whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to the offspring of that daughter.
The mention of the "Brahmin woman" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for women of the highest caste.

Consequently, in the absence of offspring, a daughter of the Kṣatriya caste inherits the wealth of a Vaiśya woman. This is because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "In the absence of sons, grandsons are the heirs to the grandmother's property; as those who inherit the estate, they shall discharge the debt," since grandsons likewise have the authority to liquidate their grandmother's debt according to the rule that "debt must be paid by sons and grandsons."
In the absence of even grandsons, the previously mentioned kinsmen, beginning with the husband, are the heirs to the property. (2.145)
In connection with the topic of a woman’s property, he says something regarding the case of a girl betrothed by word alone:
"Having given away a maiden, one who takes her back shall be fined and shall also pay the expenses along with interest.
Having verbally given a maiden, one who takes her back shall be punished by the king in accordance with the nature of the wealth involved and other relevant circumstances.

And this applies when there is no cause for the abduction; however, if there is such a cause, one may take back even a girl who has been given, as it is permitted to do so in the case where a more excellent groom renounces her—thus, he is not to be punished. Furthermore, whatever wealth was expended by the groom, or by his own relatives or the girl's relatives, for the sake of hospitality on account of the verbal betrothal, all of that the giver of the girl shall return to the groom with interest and profit.
Now, if she who has been verbally betrothed dies before the formal rite of disposal (saṃskāra), what should be done? To this he says:
"If she has died, one should take back what was given, after deducting the expenses incurred by both parties."
If a girl who has been verbally betrothed dies, the groom shall take back the ring and other items previously given as a bride-price (*śulka*).
Having settled both sets of expenses—
that is, having calculated and deducted the expenditures incurred by both himself and the giver of the girl— he shall take what remains.

However, as for that which was given to the maiden by her maternal grandfather and others—such as head-ornaments and the like—or that which has descended through inheritance, the uterine brothers shall take it; for according to the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana: "The uterine brothers shall take the estate of a deceased maiden; in their absence, [her] mother; in her absence, [her] father. (2.146)

It has been stated that the property of a woman whose children have died goes to her husband. Now, he declares in certain circumstances the husband’s permission to take the property even of a woman who is alive and has children:
"In times of famine, for religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction [to livelihood]."
A husband is not entitled to give back to his wife the woman's property that he has taken.

In times of famine, for the sake of maintaining the family, for a religious duty that must necessarily be performed, or during illness; and in cases of confinement such as capture by bandits or imprisonment—if a husband takes his wife’s property when he lacks other means, he need not restore it. However, if he misappropriates it in any other manner, he must give it back. No heir whatsoever shall seize the wealth of a woman while she is still living; for those who would take her property while she is alive are her own kinsmen.
A righteous lord of the earth should punish those disciples with the punishment prescribed for thieves.

Thus it is because of the prescription of punishment. Likewise: "The ornaments which may have been worn by women while their husband is alive, the heirs shall not divide; those who do divide them fall."
And because of the hearing of these faults [in the scriptures]. 2.1.47.

The woman’s property known as *ādhivedanika* (given upon supersession) has been mentioned; he now explains it: "One should give an equal amount as *ādhivedanika* to a wife who has been superseded. To her for whom no woman’s property has been given, one should assign half [of what was given to the superseded wife]."

She upon whom another marriage has been performed is called *adhivinnā*; she who is such a woman is an *adhivinna-strī*. To that *adhivinna-strī*, one shall give *ādhivedanika* wealth—that is, wealth caused by the supersession—equally; that is, as much as was spent for the purpose of the supersession, so much shall be given. If no separate property (*strīdhana*) has been given to her by the husband or the father-in-law, then when separate property has been given, one shall give half of the *ādhivedanika* substance.
And here, the word "half" (ardha) does not signify an equal division.
Therefore, the meaning is that as much as is necessary to make what was previously given equal to the compensation for supersession (ādhivedanika) should be paid. (2.148)

Having thus stated the division [of property], he now states the means of determination when there is doubt regarding it: "In the case of a denial of partition, the proof of partition is to be known through cognizant relatives, kinsmen, witnesses, written documents,
and separate houses and fields."

In the case of a denial or concealment of partition, the determination of partition—that is, the ascertainment of partition—must be understood through kinsmen (paternal relatives, maternal relatives, and maternal uncles and so forth), witnesses possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, and a written document in the form of a deed of partition (*vibhāgapatra*).
Likewise, it is established by separate houses and fields that have been individually assigned as *yautaka* (separate property).

Nārada has stated that the signs of partition include the commencement of separate activities such as agriculture and the performance of separate religious duties such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*).
In cases of doubt regarding the law of partition among heirs,
a decision shall be reached by kinsmen based on a written document of division, due to the commencement of separate activities.
For brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties also become separate for each.
Thus,
when there is doubt regarding the law of partition among heirs,
a decision is reached by kinsmen through a deed of partition, based on the commencement of separate activities.
For brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties also become separate for each.
Likewise, other signs of partition have been stated by him:
"Witnessing, acting as a surety, giving, and receiving—these brothers who are divided may perform; those who are undivided may never do so under any circumstances."
Thus [ends verse] 2.149.
Witnessing, acting as a guarantor, giving, and receiving—these brothers who have divided their inheritance may perform; those who have not divided it may never do so under any circumstances.
Now, the determination of boundary disputes is stated:
"In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders and others, cowherds, those who cultivate the borderlands, and all those who frequent the forests [shall decide]."
They should establish the boundary, marked by landmarks such as mounds, charcoal, husks, trees,
embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, and shrines.

In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field belonging to two villages, as well as in a dispute regarding the limits of a field situated within a single village, the neighbors and others shall determine—having been identified by previously established boundary markers such as mounds, charcoal, and so forth—the boundary that has been marked with signs.
"Boundary" (*sīmā*) refers to the limit of a field and the like;
it is of four kinds.
These are the boundary of a country, the boundary of a village, the boundary of a field, and the boundary of a house.
And that [boundary] possesses five characteristics as far as possible.
Thus it was stated by Nārada:
The boundary is declared to be of five kinds: that marked by a banner, that containing fish, the Naidhānī, that free from fear, and that established by royal decree.
Thus it is said:
"The boundary is recorded as being of five kinds: that marked by a banner, that marked by fish, that established by fire-altars, that free from fear, and that established by royal decree."
*Dhvajinī* is characterized by trees and the like, because trees and such are similar to banners (*dhvaja*) in that they serve as indicators.

*Matsyinī* is possessed of water, since the word "fish" (*matsya*) indicates its own substratum, namely water. *Naidhānī* contains buried husks, charcoal, and so forth, because these items, being buried, are similar to a treasure-trove (*nidhāna*).
Free from fear, it is brought about by the mutual agreement of the plaintiff and the defendant;
it is governed by the king’s decree, and in the absence of known marks [of ownership], it is established by the king’s will.
In such a case, a sixfold dispute may arise.
As Kātyāyana has said: "Excess, deficiency, [discrepancy] regarding the share, existence and non-existence,
possession without enjoyment, and boundaries— these six are the grounds for a dispute over land."
Thus [it is said].
Excess, deficiency, and even the existence or non-existence of a portion;
non-enjoyment, possession, and boundary—these six are the grounds for a dispute over land.
For instance:
when someone says, "I have more land than this five-nivartana plot," there is a dispute regarding excess, [the other party] claiming that it is exactly five nivartanas and not more.
When it is said, "This five-nivartana plot is my land," there is a dispute regarding deficiency, [the other party] claiming that it is actually less than that.

When it is said, "This is my share consisting of five nivartanas," a dispute over existence and non-existence may arise, such as [the claim] that there is no share at all. When it is said, "My land is being enjoyed even though its enjoyment was previously non-existent," a dispute arises regarding non-enjoyment versus enjoyment, such as [the claim] that my enjoyment has been continuous and long-standing. And when it is said, "Is this the boundary or that one? a dispute over boundaries arises. Thus, only six types of disputes are possible.

Since even in the sixfold dispute concerning land, the boundary is determined through both scriptural authority and actual facts, it is included within this section on the determination of boundaries.

Those who exist all around (*samantāt*) are the neighbors (*sāmantāḥ*); these are the villages and others immediately adjacent in the four directions, established according to each respective boundary: "A village is declared the neighbor of a village; a field, the neighbor of a field."
For it is stated by Kātyāyana: "A house is indeed designated as such because it encompasses [its contents] on all sides.
By words such as "village" (*grāma*), the persons residing therein are indicated, just as one says, "the village has fled."
And the mention of "neighbors" (sāmanta) is for the purpose of indicating those who are closely connected to them and so forth.
And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"The neighbors are the *saṃsaktakas*; likewise, those connected to them are the *uttaras*."
Those that are joined, attached, and closely joined are proclaimed to be of the lotus type.
Thus [it is said].
The immediate neighbors, their neighbors in turn, and those beyond them— these,
along with the neighbors of the neighbors' neighbors, are proclaimed to be arranged in the shape of a lotus.
"Sthaviras" means the elders. By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *maula* (original) and *uddhṛta* (extracted) [elders] is intended.

And the definition of an elder and so forth has been stated by him [the author] as follows: "Those who, endowed with those [required] qualities, have seen that task being performed while it was still in progress [are to be considered elders]."
Whether they be old or not old, they are proclaimed as "the elders."
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country are proclaimed by the seers as "original" (maula) because they are rooted in that very place.
Because they rescue [beings] who are characterized by eavesdropping, sensual enjoyment, and the performance of actions,
and because they have themselves been rescued [from those states], they are therefore known as "Uddhṛtas" (the Rescuers).
Thus [it is said].
Because they rescue [beings] by means of eavesdropping, enjoyment, performing tasks, and giving instruction,
and because they have been rescued [from saṃsāra], they are therefore known as "the Rescuers" (Uddhṛta).

The cowherds are those who tend cattle; the boundary-farmers are those who cultivate fields situated near the boundaries; and all those whose domain is the forest are forest-dwellers, such as hunters and others.
And these were declared by Manu:
hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
Thus [it is said].
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
"Sthalam" means a raised portion of ground;
"aṅgāraḥ" means the residue of fire;
"tuṣāḥ" means the husks of grain.
Trees such as the *nyagrodha* and others;
a *setu* is a dam that binds the flow of water;
a *caitya* is a structure built of stone and other materials.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), bamboo, sand, and so forth are included.
These are of two kinds, distinguished by whether they are visible or invisible.
As Manu says: "One should plant boundary trees such as the *nyagrodha*, the *aśvattha*, and the *kiṃśuka*."
And [he saw] śālmalī, śāla, and tāla trees, as well as milky sap-bearing trees.
By means of shrubs, various bamboos, śamī trees, creepers,
and level ground, as well as reeds, thickets, and bushes, the boundary is not lost.
Tanks, wells, ponds, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
Thus are the boundary markers of manifest form;
he should also cause other concealed boundary markers to be made,
having observed that in this world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung,
bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand;
And whatever objects of this kind the earth should not swallow due to the influence of time,
those he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at junctions and boundaries.
By these signs, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties.
Thus end the concealed marks.

By means of these marks, both manifest and unmanifest, as pointed out by the neighbors and others, the king shall effect the determination of the boundary between two parties disputing over a boundary. (2.150–2.151)

But when there are no marks, or when existing marks are doubtful because they lack definitive characteristics, he states the means for a decision: "Or four, eight, or even ten neighboring landholders,
wearing red garlands and garments, shall lead [the boundary] along the border."
The neighbors are those possessing the characteristics previously described.
Those from the neighboring villages— four, eight, or even ten, thus being equal in number—
should lead and point out the boundary, wearing red garlands and red garments, with clods of earth placed upon their heads.
The phrase "or neighbors" is a statement of an alternative option intended to refer to witnesses mentioned in other Smṛtis.
As Manu says: "The determination of a boundary dispute shall depend solely upon witnesses."
The determination of a boundary dispute must be based solely on the testimony of witnesses;
and in that regard, the authority to decide rests primarily with the witnesses. In their absence, it belongs to the neighboring landowners.
Thus it has been said: "In the absence of witnesses, however, four villagers residing near the boundary,
being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king."
Thus it is said: "In the absence of witnesses, however, four village residents living near the boundary shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king."
In their absence, those who are attached to them and so forth have the authority to decide.
As Kātyāyana has said:
"When the neighboring kings are corrupted in achieving their own ends, [the decision rests with others] due to the gravity of the matter."
But those who are associated with them must perform the extraction; there is no doubt in this matter.
Those who are attached to those who are themselves attached to faults are declared to be "associated with them";
however, a king who understands the Dharma should not punish those who are not actually corrupt.
Thus:
"When neighboring vassals have become corrupt in the pursuit of their own interests, one should effect a rescue through those closely associated with them, owing to the gravity of the matter;
there is no doubt in this."
Those who are attached to the faults of those who are themselves attached are declared to be "associated with them";
however, a king who understands the Dharma should not punish those who are not actually corrupt.

In the absence of neighbors and others, the primary (maula) and other [witnesses] should be accepted; in their absence, neighbors, primary, increased (vṛddha), and recovered (uddhṛta) witnesses, and so forth.
This applies even in the case of the six types of immovable property; there should be no hesitation in this matter.
Thus, because the sequence has been prescribed by Kātyāyana:

"These neighbors and others are possible through an excess of number and qualities; the neighbors are the primary means of proof, provided they are faultless and endowed with qualities. Those following them should be known as twice as many, and those beyond them are considered three times as many."
Thus it is from the Smṛti.
And those witnesses—the neighbors and others—having been sworn by their respective oaths, shall lead the boundary, "bearing the earth upon their heads, wearing garlands and red garments;
having been sworn by their own good deeds, they shall lead it correctly."
Thus it is from the Smṛti.

The plural number in the word "they should lead" (*nayeyuḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding two [persons], not one; for if one person should mark the boundary, he should mark it while fasting, wearing red garlands and garments, and holding earth upon his head.
Thus, because Nārada has authorized this for a single person.
"No single man, even if he be trustworthy, shall determine the boundary;
because of the gravity of this matter, the procedure for it rests with many."
Thus, the prohibition applies to one person alone; since that refers to a case other than one where both parties agree upon a knower of the law (dharmavid), there is no contradiction.
Even in the absence of marks such as mounds and the like, Nārada has stated a specific means for witnesses, neighbors, and others to determine the boundary:
"In cases where the marks have been washed away by river waters, removed, or destroyed..."
And because of the inference of that [object] from its location, and because of the perception of experience through valid cognition.
Thus:
"In cases where the land has been swept away by river waters, its boundaries lost and its marks destroyed,
[ownership is determined] by inference from the location of that place, by measurement, and by the observation of possession."

In those boundary lands where boundary markers have been swept away by a river, carried off, abandoned, displaced from their original location, or destroyed, one should determine [the boundary] either by inferring the ancient site from that region—such as by measuring a field of one thousand *daṇḍas* starting from a village, concluding "this belongs to the western part of this village"—or by means of possession characterized by a period beyond the reach of memory (*asmārta-kāla*), provided there is no contradiction in the presence of the opposing party. Bṛhaspati has also shown a specific rule regarding this matter: "Where boundary markers have been washed away by water, carried off, or destroyed, the king himself shall establish the boundary between the two villages by means of inference. Bṛhaspati further states: "When boundary markers are lost, the king himself shall determine the boundary between the two villages by means of inference. And: "When boundary markers are lost, the king himself shall determine the boundary
Those who know the title deed, the means of proof, the duration of possession, the name [of the owner],
and the characteristics of the plot of land are the witnesses in this matter.
Thus:
"Those who know the tradition, the evidence, the period of possession, the name,
and the characteristics of the portion of land— they are the witnesses in this matter."
And these witnesses, neighbors, and others, having been made to hear the oaths, should be questioned by the king in the presence of the family and other relevant parties.
As Manu says:
"The witnesses at the boundary should be questioned in the presence of the villagers and the families."
The boundary markers of those two disputants must be questioned.
Thus it is said:
"The witnesses regarding the boundary marks must be questioned in the presence of the village communities and of the two litigants themselves."
And those witnesses and others, when questioned, shall declare their decision regarding the boundary unanimously as a collective body.

The king should record in writing the boundary thus determined by them—along with all the marks they have pointed out and the names of the witnesses and others—for the purpose of preventing forgetfulness.
And it has been said by Manu:
Once they have been questioned, he should record the boundary decision exactly as all of them declare it, as well as the names of all those [witnesses].
Thus,
having been questioned, whatever decision they all declare regarding the boundary,
he shall record that boundary accordingly, as well as the names of all those [witnesses].

For these witnesses, neighbors, and others, starting from the day of the boundary-tour, if no misfortune caused by the king or by fate occurs within three fortnights, then the determination of the boundary is made through their testimony.
And this limit for royal or divine calamity has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"In the case of a boundary-tour, in the treasury, and likewise when the foot touches [the ground]," etc.
A period of three fortnights, one fortnight, or seven days is prescribed for calamities caused by the gods or the king.
Thus [it is said].
In the case of crossing a boundary, [theft from] a treasury, and likewise touching with the foot,
a period of three fortnights, one fortnight, and seven days is prescribed for offenses against gods and kings.

But when, within three fortnights, these witnesses who have given their testimony are seen to suffer from disease or the like, or if their statements are contradicted by other witnesses of superior number and quality designated by the defendant, then they are to be punished for speaking falsely; as it is said:
"In the case of falsehood, however, all [the neighbors] are to be punished separately by the king with the middle amercement.
When falsehood—that is, speaking untruth—is the cause, all the neighbors are each to be punished with the middle amercement, which consists of five hundred *paṇas* plus forty.
That this [fine] applies to witnesses, sureties, and others is understood from the prescription of different punishments for them in another Smṛti.
As Manu says:
"Those who proceed according to what has been stated are purified as truthful witnesses."
But those who lead them astray shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
Thus.
Those witnesses of truth who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
Nārada also says: "If, however, the neighbors should speak falsely in a boundary dispute, they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement."

Having thus prescribed the middle amercement as a fine for the neighboring landowners, [the text continues]: "If the others, being appointed to the work of the land, should speak falsely, each of them, being of the lowest rank, shall be punished with the first amercement."
If the remaining witnesses, when appointed for the examination of the land, should speak falsely,
each of those lowest-ranking ones shall be punished with the first amercement.
Thus he has stated the first degree of violence regarding those who are associated with him and so forth;
he now declares that very same punishment for the *maula* (hereditary) officers and others as well:
"But the *maula*, the *vṛddha* (elders), and the others are each separately liable according to their respective status in the administration of punishment."
Those to be disciplined are established in falsehood by the very first act of violence.
Thus it is said:
"But others, such as the *maula*, the *vṛddha*, and so forth,
who persist in falsehood, should each be punished individually with the first *sāhasa* according to the progression of the penalty."
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and forest-dwellers.

Although for fowlers and the like—who are devoted to sinful occupations—their utility lies solely in the observation of signs and not directly in the determination of boundaries, nevertheless, since the possibility of speaking falsely exists precisely upon the observation of such signs, the prescription of punishment is indeed appropriate.
However, the rule of punishment stating that "those who speak falsely shall be punished separately" refers to cases of ignorance.
But if those who have been appointed as witnesses, being many in number,
do not reach a verdict out of fear or greed, they shall be punished with the highest fine.

Thus, because Kātyāyana has prescribed a different punishment for witnesses and others in cases concerning the subject matter of knowledge (*jñānaviṣaya*), this same punishment applies even when there is a discrepancy in the testimony of witnesses; as stated by him: "If a discrepancy should arise after [the facts] have been proclaimed, they shall be punished with the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*)."
Thus it is said:
"If a discrepancy should arise after [the boundary] has been proclaimed, those [witnesses] should be punished with the highest fine.
In this manner, having punished the witnesses and others for speaking falsely due to ignorance or other causes, the investigation of the boundary should be undertaken once again.
Having punished those who speak out of ignorance, one should again determine the boundary.

Having said this, and having set aside the corrupt neighbors, one should have the boundary established by mixing them with others such as the original inhabitants (maula); thus do those who know the law understand it.
Thus, the method of determination has been stated by him.
But when there are no witnesses such as neighbors and no boundary marks, how is the decision reached? To this he says:
"In the absence of witnesses and boundary marks, the king is the establisher of the boundary."

In the absence of witnesses—such as neighbors and the like—as well as boundary markers—such as trees and the like—the King himself is the one who establishes (*pravartitā*) or causes to be established the boundary.
Here, the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is implied.

Having divided equally the land situated between two villages that has become the subject of dispute, and having assigned it to both parties by declaring, "This land belongs to this one; this land belongs to that one," he should establish boundary markers in the middle of it.
When an extraordinary benefit from one [party] is observed on that land, then the entire land of that very village should be surrendered to him.
As Manu said:
"When the boundary is difficult to determine, the king himself, who knows the Dharma, [should decide]."
One should assign land to some on account of their services; this is the established rule.
Thus [ends verse] 2.153.
When a boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, knowing the law, shall assign land to some [parties] on account of their benefit; such is the settled rule.
Even though there is no suspicion that this [object] might not be of that nature, he states an extended application (*atideśa*) to demonstrate that this legal tradition (*smṛti*) is rooted in logic:
"In the case of groves, temples, villages, water-reservoirs, gardens, and houses,
this very same rule is to be known as applying to rainwater, flowing streams, and the like."
An *ārāma* is a plot of land that serves as the cause for the cultivation of flowers and fruits.
An *āyatana* is a dwelling, a portion of land demarcated for purposes such as a stack of straw.
A *grāma* is well known.

The mention of "village" (*grāma*) is intended to include cities and the like by implication. A "watering place" (*nipāna*) refers to a reservoir for drinking water, such as a pond, well, and so forth.
An "orchard" (*udyāna*) is a pleasure grove.
"Veśma" means a house.
In these cases, such as gardens and the like, this very same rule—characterized by the testimony of neighbors and so forth—is to be understood.

Likewise, in disputes of the nature that "a flood of water arising from heavy rain flows between these two houses" or "it flows through these two," and by virtue of the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it should be understood that the aforementioned rule applies even to palaces and similar structures.
And so says Kātyāyana: "In the case of fields, wells, and tanks; likewise for rice-fields and groves;
and in the case of houses, palaces, dwellings, royal residences, and temples."
Thus [it is said].
Of fields, wells, and tanks, as well as of rice-paddies and groves,
and of houses, palaces, dwellings, royal residences, and temples of the gods.
Having stated the determination of boundaries, he now prescribes the punishment for the violation of boundaries and related offenses as a corollary:
"For the breaking of a boundary-mark, for the transgression of a boundary,
and likewise for the seizure of a field, there are punishments of the lowest, highest, and middle degrees."

The "common ground" (*sādhāraṇā bhūḥ*) refers to the boundary that demarcates many fields. For its excessive breach—that is, for crossing the boundary or plowing beyond it—and for seizing a field by instilling fear and so forth, the fines of the lowest, highest, and middle *sāhasa* are to be understood respectively.
Furthermore, the mention of "field" here is intended to include houses, gardens, and the like as well.
However, when one seizes a field or similar property through a mistake regarding ownership, the fine of two hundred *paṇas* is to be understood.
As Manu has said:
"One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine is two hundred."
Thus:
"One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine is two hundred."
Considering the great extent of the fields and other properties being stolen, sometimes even the highest punishment must be applied.
For this very reason, it is said:
"Death, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, and branding."
In that case, the punishment prescribed is the cutting off of the limb, which constitutes the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
Thus [it is said].
Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding,
and the amputation of limbs— this is declared to be the punishment of the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa).

Furthermore, regarding one who desires to construct a bridge, a well, or similar works on another's field—having obtained permission through solicitation or by the gift of wealth—the punishment falls upon the owner of the field himself for obstructing that work; thus [the author] says:
"A bridge that causes little harm but brings about welfare should not be obstructed.
A well that takes up little of another's land but provides abundant water [should likewise not be obstructed]."

Even if one seizes or destroys another's land, a water-channel (*setu*)—which is a dam for the flow of water—is not to be prohibited by the owner of the field, provided that it causes only slight harm and is of great benefit. And as for a well (*kūpa*), since it occupies little space, it causes little obstruction; and since it is beneficial by providing abundant water, if it yields much water, it must certainly not be stopped.
The mention of "well" is intended to include tanks (*vāpī*), lotus-pools (*puṣkariṇī*), and so forth by way of illustration.

Furthermore, when that [watercourse] is a source of great harm because it exists across all fields, or provides little benefit because it exists in fields near rivers and the like, then it is to be prohibited; this is what is meant by implication.
And the two-fold nature of a watercourse (setu) has been stated by Nārada:
"A watercourse is to be known as being of two kinds: one to be dug out (kheya) and likewise one to be bound (bandhya)."
By setting the water in motion, the excavation becomes fruitful; by stopping it, it becomes barren.
Thus it is said:
"The dam should be known to be of two kinds: the excavatable and likewise the blockable.
It is excavatable by causing water to flow through, and it is blockable by stopping that flow."

However, when one personally repairs a bridge constructed by another that has been destroyed by breaking or other means, one should repair it only after having consulted the former owner, his descendant, or the king.
As Nārada says:
"He who [repairs] what was previously begun but has fallen into ruin, without having asked the owner..."
If someone should cause a bridge to be built, he would not be a partaker of its fruit.
But when the master has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is no longer among the living,
one should then inform the king and proceed with the construction of the embankment.
Thus:
"But whoever should undertake the construction of a dam without first consulting the owner regarding a work that was previously begun but has fallen into ruin, he shall not partake in its fruit."
But when the master has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is no longer a human being,
one should then, after consulting the king, carry out the construction of the embankment.
This was taught with respect to the owner of the field.
Now, he speaks with respect to the one who initiates the irrigation channel:
"He who should construct an irrigation channel on a field without having informed the owner..."
When [the property] has been produced, it belongs to the owner; in his absence, it belongs to the king.

He who constructs a watercourse on another's field without having obtained the consent of the field-owner—or, in his absence, the king—does not partake of the fruit; rather, the enjoyment of the produce arising therefrom belongs to the field-owner, or, in his absence, to the king.

Therefore, the essential meaning is that a watercourse must only be constructed on another's field after having obtained permission from the field-owner through entreaty or by the payment of wealth, or, in his absence, from the king. (2.157)
It has been stated that the owner of the field must not prohibit the construction of an embankment.
Now, following this topic by way of incidental discussion, he states another rule regarding it in certain cases:
"He who would neither cultivate nor cause to be cultivated a field even when it has been struck by the plough [should be compelled to do so]."
He shall be compelled to pay the value of the ploughed crop and have the field cultivated by another.

Furthermore, if one who has promised before the landowner, "I shall cultivate this field," subsequently abandons it and does not have it cultivated by another—even if that field has been struck by the plow and slightly torn up by the share, yet is not fully fit for sowing seed—nevertheless, that cultivator must be made to pay as much of the fruit of that uncultivated land as is appropriate for its production, as determined by the neighbors and others;
and that field, having been taken away from the previous cultivator, should be caused to be worked by someone else. (2.158)

Since the titles of legal procedure stand in a relationship of mutual cause and effect, the sequential order of their enumeration—beginning with "Recovery of Debts" (ṛṇādāna)—is not intended to be significant; thus, the dispute between owner and herdsman is stated out of sequence:
"A buffalo that causes damage to crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that; and a goat or sheep, half of that."
A female buffalo that destroys another's standing crop shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that, four māṣas;
and goats or sheep shall each be fined two māṣas.
Since the queens and others have no personal ownership over wealth, the term refers to the man who is their master.
Furthermore, in this context, a *māṣa* is the twentieth part of a copper *paṇa*, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada: "A *māṣa* is declared to be the twentieth part of a *paṇa*."
And this refers to cases of unintentional [destruction].
But when it is preceded by intentional knowledge, [the rule is]: "For a goat, two quarters of a *paṇa*; for a cow, double that;
likewise for a buffalo; and for goats, sheep, and calves, a fine of two quarters is proclaimed."
For two quarters of a paṇa, one should pay a cow; for a buffalo, double that amount;
likewise, for goats, sheep, and calves, the fine is declared to be two quarters of a paṇa.
This should be understood as stated in another Smṛti.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Nārada: "One should cause a cow to pay a fine of one māṣa, and likewise a buffalo two māṣas;
for goats, sheep, and calves, the fine shall be half a māṣa."
Thus, that [prohibition] again refers to the consumption of roots that remain capable of sprouting. (2.159)
He states that in certain cases, due to the gravity of the offense, the fine is doubled:
"For those who remain after having eaten [the crop], the punishment is double that which was prescribed.
If animals, having eaten the grain in another's field, lie down right there without being restrained, then it should be understood that the punishment is double the one previously mentioned.

Furthermore, for those who have eaten and are sitting [with the meat] along with their calves, it should be understood that the fine is four times the aforementioned penalty; for it is stated in the legal texts: "For those who dwell [upon it], double is declared; for those with their calves, fourfold."
He states the extension [of the rule] to other fields and other animals:
"The same [penalty] applies to them even in a pasture; for a donkey or a camel, it is equal to that for a buffalo."
A *vivīta* is a protected and enclosed area of land abounding in grass and wood.
One should know that for damage to such a place, the punishment for these animals—buffaloes and the like—is equal to the penalty for other fields.
"Donkeys and camels" (*kharoṣṭram*) refers to donkeys and camels; they are treated the same as buffaloes.
Wherever a buffalo is punished with a certain fine, a donkey and a camel are each to be punished with that same fine.

Since the donkey and the camel are each equal to a buffalo insofar as they obstruct the crops, and since the punishment must correspond to the offense, the collective compound "donkey-and-camel" (*kharoṣṭram*) is not intended here. (2.160)
The punishment for the owner of the cow that destroys another's standing crop has been stated;
now he says that this person must also be made to pay the value of the crop to the owner of the field:
"To the extent that the crop is destroyed, to that extent shall there be loss of fruit for the owner of the field."
The cowherds shall be beaten, but the owner of the cattle deserves the previously mentioned fine.
The mention of "crops" (*sasya*) is intended as an illustration for the increase of the field.

Whatever amount of straw, grain, and so forth has been destroyed by cattle and other animals in a particular field, the owner of that field must be made to pay the value of the crop—calculated by the neighbors according to what would have been produced in that extent of land—as determined by the assessment: "In this much of a field, this much [result] occurs.
However, the cowherd is merely to be beaten; he is not to be made to pay the value of the crop.

The beating of the cowherd, together with the previously mentioned fine for the loss of grain, should be understood to apply when the destruction of the crop occurs through the fault of the herdsman: "But if a cow, due to the fault of the herdsman, should destroy the crops, there is no fine for the owner of the cattle; the herdsman deserves that fine."
Because of this statement.
Furthermore, when a crop is destroyed by the cowherd’s own negligence, he deserves only the previously mentioned fine and not corporal punishment.

However, the compensation for the loss shall always belong to the owner of the cattle; this is because the owner benefits from the produce of that field through the use of the milk of cows, buffaloes, and other animals nourished by its fruits.
The straw and other remains left over after the cattle have eaten must be taken by the owner of the cattle themselves, as they are effectively purchased by paying the price fixed by a mediator.
For this very reason, Nārada says:
"If a man demands compensation for grain eaten by cows,
that grain which was sown there should be given with the consent of the neighbors."
Straw should be given to the owner of the cattle, while the grain belongs indeed to the farmer.
Thus [it is said].
If a man demands compensation for grain that has been eaten by cattle,
the grain that was sown there should be given to him with the consent of the neighbors.
Straw should be given to the owner of the cattle, but the grain indeed belongs to the cultivator.
He states an exception regarding a specific type of field:
"On a path or at the edge of a village pasture, no fault is found in [trespassing] a field;
however, if it is done intentionally rather than unintentionally, one deserves punishment like that of a thief."

If cattle have grazed unintentionally on a field situated along a path near a village, or on a field adjacent to a village pasture (*vivīta*), there is no fault for either the herdsman or the owner of the cattle.
This demonstration of the absence of fault is intended to preclude punishment and to prohibit the payment of compensation for the value of the destroyed crop.

However, in the case of intentional grazing—that is, when they graze deliberately—he deserves the same punishment as a thief; whatever punishment is prescribed for a thief, such is the punishment he merits.
And this refers to the case of an uncultivated field; if cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the cattle.
Thus, because Manu has stated that the absence of punishment applies to uncultivated fields,
there is indeed still a fault even in the case of cultivated fields such as those used for roads;
furthermore, the construction of a boundary wall has been prescribed by him alone.
And one should construct a fence there such that even a camel cannot look over it;
one must eliminate every opening through which the snouts of dogs or pigs might pass.
Thus [ends verse] 2.162.
And one should construct a fence there such that even a camel cannot look over it;
one must eliminate every opening through which the snouts of dogs or pigs might pass.

He states that there is no punishment even for specific types of animals: "Bulls set at liberty, sacrificial animals, those recently calved, newcomers, and the like— for which there is no keeper— must not be held liable when they have been overwhelmed by divine forces or the king."
A "great bull" (*mahokṣa*) is a large bull, a male ox, or a stud bull.

"Released animals" (*utsṛṣṭapaśavaḥ*) are those abandoned according to the ritual procedures for the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) or dedicated to a deity. A "woman who has recently given birth" (*sūtikā*) is one who has delivered a child and is within the ten-day period of impurity.

A stray animal that has wandered away from its own herd and come from another region—these are to be released even when they eat another's crops; they are not to be punished. Furthermore, those for whom no keeper exists, and who have been overwhelmed or struck down by fate or the king, causing the destruction of the crops, are also not to be punished.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), elephants, horses, and others are understood; and these have been declared by Uśanas:
"Indeed, elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are traditionally held to be the protectors of the subjects."
Those who are permanently marked by such signs—the one-eyed and the humpbacked—are not to be punished.
A cow that is about to give birth, one that has recently calved, or one that is in heat shall not be punished;
likewise, cows are exempt from punishment during festivals and at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Thus:
"For elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are recorded as the protectors of the people;
likewise, those who are one-eyed or humpbacked, and those who bear permanent marks, are exempt from punishment."
A cow that is about to give birth, one that has recently calved, or one that is in heat shall not be punished;
likewise, cows are exempt from punishment during festivals and at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony.
In this context, animals that have been set free are cited by way of illustration because, being ownerless, it is impossible to punish them;
just as animals set free are not to be punished, so too are bulls and the like. (2.163)
The Gosvāmin has said:
now it is taught with reference to the cowherd;
just as the cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening, so [should one act].
And having caused those who perished through negligence to pay [the debt], he shall be made to pay the wages already received.
In the evening, the cowherd, having counted the cattle, shall return them to the owner exactly as they were counted and handed over by the owner in the morning.
A cowherd who has received wages—whether fixed or stipulated—must make good to the owner any cattle that have died or been lost through negligence or his own fault.
Regarding the determination of wages, it has been stated by Nārada: "For every hundred cows, a heifer shall be the fee; for two hundred, a milch cow."
Every year, O Gopa, let there be a milking of the herd on the eighth day.
Thus:
"From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the cowherd's fee; from two hundred, a milch-cow;
and every year, on the eighth day, the entire milk-gathering [shall be his]."
And the destruction [of the animal] through negligence has been clarified by Manu:
"The keeper alone shall restore what is lost, eaten by worms, killed by dogs, or dead from a mishap,
provided it was lacking in human effort."
Thus it is said.
