The keeper alone shall restore what is lost, eaten by worms, killed by dogs, or dead from a dangerous place,
provided it was deficient in human effort.
One who has been forcibly robbed by thieves should not be made to pay restitution.
As Manu says:
"But when cattle have been carried off by thieves after an act of violence, the keeper is not liable to make them good."
If, at the proper place and time, he reports [the matter] to his own master;
Thus it is said:
"But if cattle have been stolen by thieves after they were driven away, the keeper is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his master at the proper place and time."
Furthermore, for those who have died by natural causes, the ears and so forth must be shown.
One should present the ears, skin, hair, bladder, sinew,
and bile to the owners of the animals, showing these limbs when they have died.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu (2.164).
Furthermore:
"In the case of destruction caused by the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper,
consisting of twelve and a half paṇas, as well as the value of the property itself for the owner."
If the animal is destroyed solely through the fault of the keeper, the keeper shall be made to pay a fine of thirteen and a half *paṇas*.
The owner, moreover, shall receive the value of the lost animal as determined by arbitrators.
This verse is intended to specify the amount of the fine; everything else has already been stated previously. (2.165)
In connection with the cow, he describes the pasture for cattle:
"The pasture for cattle shall be according to the will of the villagers, or by the authority of the king;
a twice-born man may take grass, fuel, and flowers from everywhere at all times."

The pasture for cattle should be established according to the desire of the villagers—that is, the desire of the local people—or according to the king’s will, depending on whether the land is small or large.
The meaning is that a certain portion of uncultivated land should be set aside for the grazing of cows and other animals.

Furthermore, in the absence of grass, fuel, and so forth, a twice-born man may, like a bird, gather grass, wood, and flowers from everywhere for the sake of his cows, the sacred fire, and the deities, without being restrained.
However, one may take fruits only from that which is not enclosed.

For it is recorded in the Smṛti of Gautama: "One may take grass for the sake of cattle or fire, as well as the flowers of shrubs and trees and the fruits of those that are not enclosed, as if they were one's own.

And this refers to the case of what has been appropriated; for in the case of what is not appropriated, ownership is established for anyone other than a twice-born person simply through the act of appropriation itself.
Likewise, it was stated by that very same [author]: "The owner [is established] in the cases of inheritance, purchase, partition, acquisition, and finding.
Furthermore, it has been said: "Whether it be grass or wood, a flower or a fruit—one who takes these without asking permission deserves the amputation of the hand."
Whether it be grass or wood, or a flower or a fruit—
one who takes these without asking permission deserves the severing of his hand.
Thus, this [rule] refers either to persons other than the twice-born, or to times of non-distress, or to animals other than cows and the like. (2.166)
This further [rule] is stated for the sake of providing ease regarding the standing and sitting of cattle and other animals:
"The distance between fields around a village should be one hundred bows;
it should be two hundred for a *kharvaṭa*, and four hundred for a city."

The distance between a village and its field shall be one hundred *dhanus* in circumference; it must be made such that no crops are sown in any direction within that space. For a *kharvaṭa*—a village abounding in thorny shrubs—the circumference shall be two hundred *dhanus*.
A space measuring four hundred bow-lengths should be made for a city crowded with many people. || 2.167 ||
Now he begins the legal title known as "Sale Without Ownership. Its definition has been stated by Nārada:
"Having found, or having recovered, property belonging to another that was deposited, lost, or stolen..."
That which is sold in the presence [of the owner] should be known as "sale by one who is not the owner."
When property belonging to another that has been deposited, lost,
found, or stolen is sold in the presence [of the owner], that should be known as sale without ownership (*asvāmivikraya*).
Regarding this, what is the rule for a Pāṇḍeya? To this he says:
One may recover one's own property if it was sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if the defect was not disclosed;
[the seller becomes] a thief if the sale was made in secret to an inferior person for an inferior price at an improper time.

If one sees one's own property—meaning property related to oneself—that has been sold by another without the owner’s consent (*asvāmivikrīta*), then he may take it; for a sale by one who is not the owner lacks the capacity to produce ownership.
The mention of "sold" is intended to include what has been given or pledged, since they are equal in being sales by one who is not the owner.
For this very reason, it has been said:
He shall annul a sale by one who is not the owner, as well as a gift and a pledge.
Thus:
he shall annul a sale by one who is not the owner, a gift, and a pledge.
Furthermore, for the purchaser, a fault arises if the purchase is not made public but kept concealed.

Likewise, if from one who is "inferior"—meaning one lacking the proper means of acquiring such goods—and in secret, in private, even from a source where the substance is expected, he purchases it at an inferior price, that is, at a very low price; and if the purchase is "deficient in time" (*velāhīna*), meaning the purchase is made at an improper time, such as at night and so forth, then the purchaser becomes a thief. The meaning is that he becomes subject to punishment and other penalties like a thief.
As it has been said:
"Having obtained property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall recover it;
the buyer is cleared of guilt if the purchase was made openly, but there is theft if the purchase was made in secret."
Thus [it is said].
Having acquired property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall recover it;
the buyer is cleared of guilt if the purchase was made publicly, whereas it constitutes theft if the purchase was made in secret.
Pāṇḍeya says: [The word] *yukta* [is used]. To the question "What should be done by the purchaser? he replies:
"Having recovered what was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
and in case of delay regarding place or time, having seized [the property], one should surrender it oneself."

Having recovered another's lost or stolen property through purchase or other means, he should cause the thief or the seller to be apprehended by means of the *cauroddharaṇaka* (thief-catcher) and others, for the sake of his own purification and to avoid the king’s punishment.

However, if the person has gone to another land where he is unknown, or if he has died after some time, then, being unable to recover the original source, he should himself hand over that wealth to the owner (*nāṣṭika*) even without producing the seller.

The venerable Śrīkarācārya has explained that "by that much alone he becomes pure," but this is untenable because it would result in redundancy with the rule, "Purification occurs upon seeing the seller.
Therefore, it is explained otherwise:
the phrase "lost or stolen" is an instruction addressed to the original owner (*nāṣṭika*).
Having discovered his own lost or stolen property while it is in the hands of a purchaser, he should cause the thief—the purchaser—to be seized by the local guardians and others.

However, if there is a lapse of time or place—that is, if the proper time and location have passed, or if the local guardians and others are not present—and there is a fear that the thief might flee before the matter can be reported to them, he should seize him himself and hand him over to those authorities. (2.169)
When the purchaser has been caught, what should be done? To this he says:
"Purification [from the charge] comes from producing the seller; the owner recovers the property, and the king receives a fine.
The purchaser recovers the price from him who was the seller of that [property]."
If that purchaser, having been apprehended, declares, "This was not stolen by me; it was bought from another," then his purification occurs merely by the production of the seller.
He is not to be prosecuted further;
rather, the dispute between the claimant and the original owner shall proceed with the seller pointed out by him.
As Bṛhaspati has said:
"Once the original price has been recovered, the purchaser is not to be prosecuted in any way;
rather, a dispute regarding the original price is ordained for the claimant."
Thus it is said.
Once the original price has been recovered, the purchaser can by no means be prosecuted;
rather, a legal dispute concerning the original price is ordained for the owner who lost the property.

In that dispute, if it is determined to be a sale by one who is not the owner, then the owner—the claimant of the lost property—recovers his own goods from the seller, the one who sold the cattle or other property; and the king imposes a fine upon the seller according to the nature of the offense, while the buyer recovers the purchase price.

However, if the seller has gone to another country, then time must be granted for his recovery in proportion to the number of *yojanas* [the distance]; or he may effect a public sale, or produce the original source [the first seller].
In that case, the time for producing the original source must be granted in accordance with the number of stages on the road.
Because of this traditional teaching (smṛti).

If, however, one is unable to produce the root source because its location is unknown, then one becomes pure only by purifying the purchase; for there is this statement: "But one whose root source cannot be recovered must indeed purify the purchase alone."

But when he does not clear the purchase through witnesses and the like, or by means of an ordeal, and does not produce the original source [of the goods], then he alone becomes liable for the punishment.
Thus:
"Failing to produce the source, or failing to clear the purchase..."
He shall be made to pay the wealth to the creditor according to the claim, as well as a fine.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu (2.170).

It has been stated that one may recover property sold by another. To address what must be done by one who desires to obtain such property, he says: "Lost [property] must be recovered through title or through possession; otherwise, [it is not recovered]."
His self-restraint was bound fivefold; it was not perceived by that king.

The owner must establish—that is, prove—his claim by means of title (such as inheritance, purchase, and so forth), by possession, and by stating, "This property is mine; it was lost or stolen in this manner.
Otherwise, if that owner fails to prove his case, a fine of one-fifth of the lost property shall be paid to the king by the claimant.
And the procedure here is as follows:
The former owner shall recover his lost property.
Then, the purchaser must produce the seller for the purpose of clearing himself of the charge of theft and to recover the purchase price.
If he is unable to produce him, then, in order to clear himself of personal guilt, he must prove the legality of the purchase and restore the property to the original owner. (2.171)
Regarding one who conceals a thief, he says:
"He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost,
without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas."

If one seizes property—whether stolen, lost, or held in the hands of thieves and others—merely on the basis of a report to the king that "this person has taken my property," out of pride or similar motives, he shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*, because he is wicked for acting as a protector of thieves. (2.172)
To those brought by the king’s officers, he replied:
"If property that was lost or stolen has been recovered by customs officials or local guardians, its owner may reclaim it within one year; after that, the king shall take it."

When, however, lost or stolen property has been recovered from the side of the king by customs officials or guards of the precincts, the owner shall recover that property if he presents himself within one year;
but after a year, the king may take it for himself.
Furthermore, property brought by the king's own men must be proclaimed among the crowds of people and guarded by the king for the duration of one year.
As Gautama has stated: "Having found property whose owner has disappeared, they should announce it to the king;
it should be guarded by the king for a proclaimed period of one year.
Furthermore, another rule was stated by Manu: "The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in custody for three years."
Within three years, the owner may reclaim it; after that, the king shall take it.
Thus:
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that time the king shall take it.
This refers to Brahmins who are endowed with learning and good conduct.
And the taking of a sixth part and so forth on account of protection has been stated by that very same [author]:
"Then the king may take a sixth part of goods lost and found."
Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one should observe either the tenth or the twelfth [day].
Thus [it is said].
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king may take a sixth part, or even a tenth or a twelfth, of property lost and then found.
In the third, second, and first years, respectively, the sixth and subsequent portions are to be understood; this has been explained in detail previously. (2.173)
For killing a single-hoofed animal, one should pay five *paṇas*; for a human, four;
for buffaloes, camels, and cows, two each; and for goats and sheep, one-quarter *paṇa* each.
In the case of single-hoofed animals such as horses and the like that have been lost and recovered, their owner shall pay four *paṇas* to the king for the purpose of maintenance.
For human beings—that is, property consisting of persons—he shall pay five *paṇas*.
For buffaloes, camels, and cows, he shall pay two *paṇas* each for the purpose of maintenance; furthermore, for goats and sheep, he shall pay one-quarter *paṇa* each.
The phrase "he should give" is to be supplied everywhere.
Although there is a compound designation as "goats and sheep," the connection is understood to apply to each individually by virtue of the distributive repetition "foot by foot. (2.174)

Now, the legal title known as *dāna* (giving), which has received the two designations *dattānapakarma* (non-withdrawal of what was given) and *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what was promised), is being discussed. This is so because it relies upon two paths: that which is prescribed and that which is prohibited. Its essential nature was stated by Nārada:
"He who, having given wealth improperly, desires to take it back again..."
For that is indeed the legal title of dispute known as "Non-delivery of what has been given."
Thus it is said:
"When one who has given property improperly desires to take it back,
that is indeed the legal head of dispute known as *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what was given)."

When, by resorting to an improper and unestablished path, one gives property with the desire to take it back again, that subject of dispute is called *dattāpradānika*—the non-giving of what has been given, or the taking back of what was given. This refers to the legal title (*vyavahārapada*) known as *dattāpradānika*. By implication, its opposite, which resorts to an established path, is the legal title known as *dattānapakarma*;
the meaning is that where there is the non-withdrawal of what has been given—that is, the refusal to take it back—in a dispute concerning a gift, that is *dattānapakarma*.
And that [gift] is of four kinds, distinguished by what may be given, what may not be given, and so forth.
As Nārada said:
"Now, that which is to be given and that which is not to be given, as well as what has been given and what has not been given..."
In legal proceedings, the fourfold path of giving should be understood.
Thus (NSm 4.2):
Now, that which is to be given and that which is not to be given, as well as what has been given and what has not been given—
this fourfold path of giving should be understood in legal proceedings.
In this context, "that which is to be given" (*deyam*) refers to what is suitable for the act of giving, provided it is not prohibited.
"That which is not to be given" (*adeyam*) is that which is unfit for giving because it is not one's own property or because it is prohibited.
Furthermore, that which has been given by one who is in their natural state and is non-retractable is called "given" (*dattam*).
Now, that which is to be recovered—namely, what was taken without permission—is being discussed. To explain this briefly, he says:
"One's own property may be given without detriment to one's family. "One's own" means property belonging to oneself; "without detriment to one's family" means without causing hardship to the family.
That is to say, what remains after supporting the family;
he should give that, because supporting them is obligatory.
As Manu said:
Manu has declared that an aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be supported even by performing a hundred improper acts.
Thus [it is said]:
"Manu has declared that an aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be supported even after they have committed a hundred improper acts."
By the phrase "one's own property, provided it does not conflict with one's family," he shows one type of property that must not be given away.

Furthermore, by the statement "one should give one's own," he demonstrates by way of contrast (*vyatirekataḥ*) the non-giftability of five types of things that do not belong to oneself: what has been deposited for another (*anvāhita*), what has been borrowed (*yācitaka*), a pledge (*ādhi*), common property (*sādhāraṇa*), and a sealed deposit (*nikṣepa*).
As for the eightfold classification of non-givable items mentioned by Nārada: "What has been deposited for another, what has been borrowed, a pledge, and what is common... [and so forth].

Teachers declare that a deposit, one's sons and wife, and one's entire estate— provided there is a lineage to whom it may pass— must not be given away even by an embodied being enduring the most grievous calamities; nor should anything that has been promised to another be given.

Thus, this [statement] is intended merely to indicate that these things are not to be given away, and not because they lack the nature of property (*svatva*), since property does indeed exist in the case of sons, wives, and one's entire estate when they have been promised;
the nature of items such as those deposited with another (*anvāhita*) has already been explained in detail previously.

By the statement "one should give one's own," since there is no distinction in ownership regarding one's wife, sons, and so forth, the possibility that these too might be given arises; therefore, he states a prohibition:
"Except for his wife and sons; nor [should he give] his entire estate while a lineage remains, nor that which has been promised to another."
The meaning is that one should give away one's own property excluding wife and son—that is, apart from wife and son—one should not give away the wife and son.

Likewise, when there exists a lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth, one should not give away all the wealth; for the Smṛti states: "Having procreated sons and performed their sacraments, one should provide for their livelihood."
Likewise, gold and other such items promised to one person must not be given to another. (2.175)

Having thus described the objects to be given as distinct from wife, sons, and so forth, he states—by way of incidental discussion—that the acceptance of even prohibited property must be done openly by the recipient: "The acceptance of immovable property, especially, should be public. Acceptance means the act of receiving; that [act] must be performed publicly for the purpose of precluding disputes.
And in the case of the stationary [self], its apprehension must specifically be through manifestation alone;
for it is impossible to demonstrate that [self], which resides within oneself, in the same way as gold or other such objects.
Having thus spoken as a digression, he says, returning to the subject at hand:
"What is to be given, and what has been promised, one must not take back after having given it."

That which is to be given and that which has been promised must indeed be given to him for whom it was promised for the sake of *dharma*, provided that he has not fallen away from *dharma*. However, it should not be given again if he has fallen away from *dharma*;
for according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) of Gautama, "Even after promising, one should not give to one who is associated with unrighteousness (*adharma*)."
"Having given, one should not take it back again.
Whatever has been given according to the path of justice—even if it is of seven kinds—must never be taken back; rather, it must be accepted as it is.
On the other hand, that which is given unjustly is "not given," even if it is of sixteen kinds, and must indeed be returned; this is the meaning implied.
And by Nārada, having established that "the given is said to be of seven kinds, while the ungiven is sixteenfold," the nature of the given and the ungiven is explained:
"The price for goods, wages, [given] out of satisfaction, out of affection, and as a return favor..."

Those who know the law of gifts understand that what is given for the purpose of favoring a bride-price (*strīśulka*) is not a true gift. Likewise, they recognize as non-gifts those made by persons overcome by fear, anger, grief, or the force of disease, as well as those given through bribery, jest, exchange, or fraud.
Furthermore, that which is performed by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane,
as well as that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking "I am the doer of this action."
If one says "this is a worthy recipient" regarding an unworthy person, or speaks of a task connected with righteousness,
whatever is given out of ignorance is declared in the Smṛti to be as if not given at all.
Thus:

"Those who know the law of giving recognize as a gift that which is given for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return for a favor, or for the sake of a woman's dowry or as a mark of grace."
But what is taken without it being given may occur when one is overcome by fear, anger, or the force of grief,
as well as through bribery, jesting, a mistake, or by means of deception.
Furthermore, that which is done by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane;
and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking "I am the doer of this action."
If one says "this is a worthy recipient" regarding an unworthy recipient, or speaks thus regarding a task connected with dharma,
whatever is given out of ignorance is declared to be as if not given at all.

This is the meaning: whatever price has been paid for merchandise or purchased goods; wages or salary given for work performed; that which is given out of satisfaction to bards, wandering minstrels, and the like; that which is given out of affection to daughters, sons, and others; that which is given as a return favor to one who has rendered assistance in the form of a reciprocal gift; the bride-price (*strīśulka*) given to the kinsmen of a maiden for the purpose of marriage; and that which is given for the sake of favor or for the sake of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*); all these seven kinds of gifts, once given, are not to be reclaimed.

That which is given out of fear to kidnappers and the like; that which is given out of anger to one's own son or others for the sake of revenge; that which is given under the influence of grief caused by the separation from a child or similar misfortune; that which is given as a bribe to officials in order to remove obstacles to a task; that which is given in jest or derision.
"Exchange of giving" (*dānavyatyāsa*) refers to one person giving his own wealth to another, while the other also gives [wealth] to him.
"Through the application of deception" means intending to give a hundred, but after stipulating "a thousand," one gives it.
By a child who has not reached sixteen years of age;
by one who is deluded and ignorant of worldly conventions;
by one who is not independent, such as a son, a slave, or the like.

That which is given by one who is distressed, overcome by disease, intoxicated by liquor, or insane—seized by a wind-disorder (vātika) or similar affliction; that which is given with the desire to entice someone, thinking, "By this gift, he will perform this service for me"; or that which is given to one who does not know the four Vedas but claims, "I am a knower of the four Vedas," or to one who, having obtained wealth for the purpose of performing a sacrifice, squanders it on gambling and such activities—all such gifts, though of sixteen kinds, are said to be "not given" (*adatta*), because they must be recovered.

The fact that what is given by one in distress is not considered a valid gift applies only to matters other than those pertaining to religious duty (*dharmakārya*). "Whatever has been given, whether by one who is healthy or one in distress, for the sake of a religious purpose, and has been formally declared [as such]—if the giver dies without having completed the act, the son shall be made to pay it; there is no doubt in this matter."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana.
Likewise, this is another statement of concise meaning applicable to all disputes: "Whatever is mortgaged, sold, or purchased through fraud; whatever gift or acceptance is fraudulent;
or wherever one perceives deceit—that entire matter one shall annul."
Thus.
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given, or received through fraud,
or wherein one perceives deceit— that entire transaction he shall annul.
The term *yoga* refers to a condition (*upādhi*).

The meaning is that if a purchase, sale, gift, or acceptance has been made under a specific future condition, those transactions—such as the sale and so forth—should be rescinded upon the cessation of that condition.
Furthermore, the punishment for one who takes what has not been given in any of its sixteen forms, and for one who gives what should not be given, has been stated by Nārada.
He who, out of greed, takes what is not given, and he who gives what should not be given—
the giver of what is not to be given, as well as the receiver of what has been so given, are both to be punished.
Thus [it is said].
He who, out of greed, takes what is not given, and he who gives what should not be given—
the giver of what is not to be given, as well as the receiver of what has been given, are both to be punished.
Now, the rescission of a purchase is discussed.
Its nature was stated by Nārada:
"When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, does not hold it in high regard..."
The legal dispute known as "repentance after purchase" is now being discussed.
Thus:
"When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, does not value it highly,
this is called the legal dispute known as 'regret over what has been purchased'."

And regarding that, he stated: "On the very day the merchandise is purchased, it must be returned in its unaltered state. "When a buyer, having purchased merchandise for a price, considers it a bad purchase, it should be returned to the seller on that same day, provided it is undamaged."
Thus:
"If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is undamaged."
Regarding the specific rule for returning [the object] on the second day or subsequent days, it has been stated by that same authority:
"If the buyer returns it on the second day, he should pay a thirtieth part of the price;
on the third day, however, he must pay double; after that, it belongs to the buyer alone."
Thus [it is said].
On the second day, the buyer, while returning it, shall pay a thirtieth part of the price;
on the third day, however, he shall pay double that amount; beyond that, the loss falls upon the buyer alone.
The meaning is that one must not harbor a latent resentment (*anuśaya*) toward others.
Furthermore, this refers to perishable objects such as the enjoyment [of goods] that are distinct from the seed;
however, regarding the purchase of seeds and the like, there is a different procedure for their restitution, as he says:
The examination of seeds, iron, vehicles, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten, one, five, seven, one month, three days, and half a month respectively.
Seed refers to seeds such as rice and the like;
iron refers to metal;
and the external [factor] refers to oxen and the like.
Jewels refer to pearls, coral, and so forth;
"woman" refers to a female slave;
"that which is to be milked" refers to buffaloes and the like.
The man is a slave.
The period for examination of these items, beginning with seeds, should be understood as ten days and so forth, respectively.

Furthermore, if during the examination of the seeds and other items a lingering doubt arises regarding their being defective, then the rescission of the purchase must occur within that same period of ten days or more; it cannot take place after that time. This is the purpose of the instruction.
As for the statement of Manu: "If, after having bought or sold anything, one should have regret in this matter, he may give back that object or take it back within ten days."
Thus, this refers to objects such as houses, fields, vehicles, beds, and seats—which are perishable and distinct from the aforementioned metals and other items.
Furthermore, all of this concerns what has been purchased without prior inspection.
However, that which is purchased after having made an agreement that it shall not be returned once inspected must not be returned to the seller.
Thus it has been said:
"The buyer should personally examine the merchandise beforehand for its qualities and defects;
once it has been examined and purchased as desired, it shall not be returned to the seller."
Thus [it is said].
A buyer should personally examine a commodity beforehand for its qualities and defects;
once it has been examined and purchased as desired, it shall not be returned to the seller.
In connection with the examination of milk and other substances, he describes the examination of gold and the like:
"Gold is not diminished when heated in fire; silver [loses] two palas per hundred;
tin and lead [lose] eight; copper [loses] five; and iron [loses] ten."
Gold heated in fire does not diminish;
therefore, as much gold as has been placed in the hands of the goldsmith for the purpose of fashioning bracelets and other ornaments must be returned by them weighed exactly as it was.
Otherwise, they shall be made to pay for the loss and shall be punished.
When a hundred *pala*s of silver are being melted, two *pala*s are lost;
eight [are lost] in the case of tin and lead.
The word "in a hundred" (*śate*) is understood to carry over.
When one hundred *pala* of tin and lead are melted, eight *pala* are lost;
in the case of copper and iron, five *pala* are lost from one hundred *pala* of copper,
and ten *pala* are lost from [one hundred *pala*] of iron.

In this case as well, the fine shall be exactly one hundred [paṇas]. However, since bell-metal originates from tin and copper, the loss should be calculated accordingly. Artisans who cause a greater loss than that shall be punished. (2.178)
In some cases, such as with blankets and the like, he states the interest:
"On woolen cloth, cotton, and silk, the interest is ten palas per hundred;
on medium quality, the interest is five palas; but on fine quality, it is considered to be three palas."
In the case of a woolen blanket or similar item made from coarse woolen thread, an increase of ten palas should be understood for every hundred palas [of base weight].
The same should be understood for cloth and other items made from cotton thread.
In the case of cloth and other items made from medium thread that is not overly fine, the increase is five palas.
In a hundred [pieces] woven with very fine thread, an increase of three palas is to be understood; and this refers to unwashed cloth. (2.179)

He states a specific rule regarding other substances: "In the case of woven silk (*kārmika*) and that which is sewn with wool (*romabaddha*), a loss of one-thirtieth is recognized. There is neither loss nor increase in the case of silk (*kauśeya*) and garments made of bark-fiber (*vālkala*)."

*Kārmika* is that which is fashioned by various types of work. When a cloth has been completed, the decorative patterns such as wheels (*cakra*) or svastikas are executed with threads; that is called *kārmika*.
Where wool fibers are woven into garments such as upper robes (*prāvāra*), that is *romabaddha*; in that case, the thirtieth part should be understood as the loss (*kṣaya*).

In the case of silken garments produced from cocoons or in the case of bark-cloths made from tree-bark, there is neither increase nor decrease; rather, only as much as was given to the weavers and others for the purpose of weaving must be returned. (2.180)
Because it is impossible to demonstrate the loss and increase for each individual substance due to their infinite variety, he states the means for knowing decrease and increase in general:

"Having ascertained the place, the time, and the use, as well as the strength and weakness regarding lost items, those who are skilled shall declare what that substance must be made to pay; of this there is no doubt."

When goods such as hemp or linen have been lost or depreciated, those experts who are knowledgeable regarding the increase and decrease of commodities—having examined the place, the time, the usage, as well as the strength or weakness and the quality or worthlessness of the lost goods—whatever they determine, that must undoubtedly be made good by the artisans. (2.181)
Now he begins to describe another head of dispute called "non-performance of service" (*aśuśrūṣā*).
Its nature has been stated by Nārada:
"But he who, having undertaken service, does not perform it..."
This title of law, following upon a failure to fulfill one's obligations after having entered into them, is now described.
Thus it is said:
"But he who, having undertaken service, does not perform it—
this ground for dispute is called 'failure to perform service after undertaking it'."

Service consists in carrying out orders; when one has accepted such service but subsequently fails to perform it, that subject of dispute is called "non-performance after agreement" (*abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*). Furthermore, the servant is of five kinds:
the student (*śiṣya*), the resident pupil (*antevāsī*), the hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*), the overseer (*adhikarmakṛt*), and the slave (*dāsa*).

Among them, the first four are called laborers (*karmakara*), and they perform virtuous deeds. Slaves (*dāsa*), on the other hand, are of fifteen types, beginning with those born in the household and so forth.
They perform inauspicious tasks such as cleaning the house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps;
this has been made clear by Nārada:
"In the treatises, the wise have observed that there are five kinds of attendants."
There are four kinds of laborers, and their servants number thirty-five.
Students, resident pupils, and hired servants—the fourth being the laborer for extra tasks—these are to be known as laborers; slaves, however, are those born in the house and so forth.
The wise have declared that their common characteristic is dependence;
however, the distinction [between them] and their very mode of subsistence is said to be determined by genus and action.
Action also should be known as being of two kinds: indeed, the unwholesome and the wholesome.
The unwholesome is said to be the work of a slave; the wholesome is remembered as the work of those who perform actions [with mastery].
Cleaning the house, doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; touching private parts, limbs, or food remnants; and the taking up and discarding of feces and urine.
Furthermore, serving the master with one's own limbs when he so desires should be understood as impure action; other than that, it is pure.
Thus.
In the treatise, the wise have observed five kinds of attendants:
four types of laborers, and fifteen types of slaves among them.
Pupils, resident students, and hired servants—the fourth being the laborer for extra work—these are to be known as laborers; slaves, however, are those born in the house and so forth.

The wise have declared that their lack of independence is their common characteristic; however, the distinction based on genus and action, as well as their specific function, has already been described.
Action, too, should be known as twofold: indeed, the unwholesome and the wholesome.
The unwholesome is said to be the work of a slave; the wholesome is remembered as the work of those who perform actions.
The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; the touching of private parts, and the taking up and discarding of food remnants, feces, and urine.
Furthermore, serving the master with one's own limbs when he so desires should be understood as inauspicious action; that which is other than this is auspicious.
In this context, a *śiṣya* is one who seeks the knowledge of the Vedas;
an *antevāsī* is one who seeks training in a craft;
and one who performs work for wages is a *bhṛtaka*.

The *adhikarmakṛt* is the supervisor of those performing the work. An *aśucisthāna* is a pit or similar place for the disposal of leftovers. An *avaskara* is a place where the dust and other debris swept from the house are piled up.
Abandonment means relinquishing.
Furthermore, the laborer here is of three kinds.
As it has been said: "In this context, the warrior is the best, while the farmer is the middling."
The lowest shall be a carrier of loads; thus is the hired servant of three kinds.
Thus:
"In this regard, the highest [type of] hired laborer is the warrior, the middle is the farmer, and the lowest should be the porter; thus the hired laborer is of three kinds."

Furthermore, the [eight kinds of] slaves are: one born in the house, one purchased, one obtained as a captive, one received through inheritance, one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who has been pledged by his master.
I have been released from great bondage, won as a prize in battle,
approached you saying "I am yours," and have been made one who has completed his period of wandering life.
One who becomes a slave through food, one brought as a prize for a mare,
and one who sells himself— these are declared in the scripture to be the fifteen kinds of slaves.
One born in the house of a female slave is "born in the house" (gṛhaja).
One obtained for a price is "bought" (krīta). One who has come through inheritance is "received from an heir," such as a slave belonging to one's father or other relatives.

One who was maintained during a famine at an improper time and saved from death by becoming a slave; one who was pledged by his master through the receipt of wealth and reduced to the state of a pledge;
and one who entered into slavery through the discharge of a debt—these are known as slaves for debt.
One captured after being defeated in battle;
one won at a stake after having made a formal agreement in this dispute, saying, "If I am defeated, then I shall become your slave";
and one who has approached of his own accord, having personally agreed, saying, "I am yours" or "I am your slave."
One who has fallen from the religious life is one who has lapsed from the state of renunciation.
A "slave by agreement" is one who has consented, saying, "I am your slave for this much time.
A "slave for food" is one who has entered [into servitude] having agreed to remain in slavery solely for the sake of food at all times.

"Seized by a *vaḍavā*": he was seized by a female slave (*gṛhadāsī*) out of greed for her; having married her, he entered into servitude. He who sells himself is an "seller of self. Thus, there are fifteen types [of slaves].

As for that which was stated by Manu: "One captured under a banner, one who serves for food, one born in the house, one bought, one given, one inherited from an ancestor, and one enslaved as a penalty—these seven are the origins of slavery."
Thus, the sevenfold nature has been stated; this is for the purpose of demonstrating their status as slaves (*dāsa*), and not for the purpose of an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*).

Among these—namely, the student (*śiṣya*), the resident pupil (*antevāsin*), the hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*), the assistant (*adhikarmakṛt*), and the slave—the conduct of the student has already been explained previously by such passages as: "He should study when summoned, and he should report whatever he has acquired to him," and so forth.

As for the supervisor of laborers (*adhikarmakṛt*), his wages shall be explained in the section concerning the non-payment of wages, beginning with the verse: "He who performs as much work as he does, to that extent is his wage," and so forth.
He states a specific rule regarding slaves and apprentices:
"One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves, or even one who has been sold,
is released by saving his master's life, by abandoning his food, or by the payment of his ransom."

One who has been made a slave by force—that is, by means of physical compulsion—and one who has been abducted and sold by thieves; by the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that one who has been pledged or given is also included—such a person is released.
If the master does not release him, then he must be set free by the king.
And so it was said by Nārada:
Those who have been abducted by thieves, sold, or forcibly made into slaves must be released by the king; for servitude is not permitted in their case.
Thus:
Those who have been stolen by thieves, sold, or forcibly made into slaves must be released by the king; for servitude is not permitted among them.

He who gives his life or protects the life of a master who is besieged by thieves, tigers, and the like, must also be set free. This is a common cause for the cessation of servitude for all types of slaves: "Whosoever shall deliver them from a danger to their lives, he is released from slavery and shall receive a share equal to that of a son."
Whosoever among them should liberate their master from a life-threatening danger,
he is released from slavery and shall receive a share equal to that of a son.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Nārada.
The means of liberation for each of the categories beginning with the *bhaktadāsa* (servant for food) is now stated.

The *anākālabhṛta* (servant taken in times of distress) and the *bhaktadāsa* (servant for food) are liberated by returning everything they have consumed, starting from their status as a servant, up to the master’s property; that is, by giving back whatever was used. However, the *āhitadāsa* (servant pledged as security) and the *ṛṇadāsa* (debtor-slave) are liberated by the repayment of the price for which they were pledged; that is, by returning with interest the sum for which the master took them as security, or the amount for which he was released by the creditor after paying it.
Nārada has also stated a specific rule:
"One who was maintained during a time of famine is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle;
however, that which was consumed during a famine cannot be purified by such an act."
By the lifting up of his food, a slave for food is immediately released;
even one who was pledged [as a slave] is freed by giving back the wealth, provided that the master rescues him.
But by paying back the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from slavery.
Thus [it is said].
But by paying back the debt along with the interest, the debtor is released from slavery.
Likewise, he himself has stated the specific reasons for the release of those who have come saying "I am yours," those captured in battle, those won at a wager, and those brought by force as slaves.
As it is said:
"One who has come saying 'I am yours,' one captured in battle, and one won at a wager..."
By the gift of a head for each [head taken], they shall be liberated through an equal act.
Even one who has acted [wrongly] is liberated when the appointed time has passed;
likewise, one seized by a *vaḍavā* is released through the restraint of that *vaḍavā*.
Thus,
by the restraint of the mare, one who has been seized by a mare is released.
The meaning is that [liberation] occurs through the cessation of enjoyment together with the master.

Thus, for those who are born in the house, purchased, obtained as a gift, acquired by inheritance, or who have sold themselves, there is no liberation apart from the common causes consisting of the surrender of one's life to the master and the resulting favor;
this is because no specific causes [for their liberation] have been stated.

And the emancipation of a slave should be performed by him in this sequence: he who, with a joyful mind, desires to make his own slave a non-slave, should take from the slave's shoulder a jar full of water and break it.
One should sprinkle water, together with raw rice grains and flowers, upon his head;
then, having said "Thou art no slave," one should release him three times while facing eastward.
Thus it was said by him. 2.182.

But he says that for one who has fallen from renunciation, there is no liberation: "One who has fallen from renunciation is the king's slave until the end of life. Renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is the same as *saṃnyāsa*; one who has fallen from it is one who has been deprived of it.
If he does not accept the prescribed penance, he becomes the slave of the king alone; death is the only end to that state of slavery, for there is no release at any other time.
He states the regulation regarding servitude with respect to the social classes:
"Servitude exists among the classes according to the natural order, not in the inverse order."
The state of servitude for the social classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, occurs according to the natural order (*ānulomyena*):

for a Brāhmaṇa, [servitude may be performed by] Kṣatriyas and others; for a Kṣatriya, Vaiśyas and Śūdras; and for a Vaiśya, a Śūdra. Thus, the condition of being a slave exists according to the natural order and not in the inverse order (*prātilomyena*). However, in the case of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) who has abandoned his own duty (*svadharma*), servitude is indeed accepted even in the inverse order.
As Nārada said:
"Servitude by means of the inverse order of castes is not ordained;
except for those who have abandoned their own duty, servitude is considered to be like [the taking of] a wife."
Thus [it is said].
Servitude is not ordained through the inverse order of the castes;
elsewhere, however, servitude is considered to be like marriage for one who has abandoned his own duty.
He stated the duties of a resident pupil: "Even when he has mastered the craft, the resident pupil should remain in the teacher's house for the prescribed period;
having received his food from the teacher, he shall give the fruits thereof to him."

A pupil, having agreed that he would reside in the house of his teacher for a fixed period of four years for the purpose of learning the arts such as Āyurveda, should dwell there for that duration, even if he has acquired the required knowledge of the art before the end of the four years. How should he live?
He is one who receives his food from the teacher; that is, he is one by whom food is obtained from the presence of the teacher.
"Bestowing the fruit thereof" means that he gives the fruit of that craft to the teacher;
such a person should reside [there].
A specific detail regarding this has also been shown by Nārada.
Desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his relatives,
he should live in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time.
The teachers should instruct him in their own home while providing him with food;
they should not make him perform other work, but should treat him like a son.
If one who is being instructed by an uncorrupted teacher should abandon that teacher, he should be made to dwell [with him] by force; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment.
Even if he has been trained, the pupil shall receive his fee when the time appointed has arrived;
furthermore, whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs solely to the teacher.
Having mastered the craft at the proper time and having circumambulated his teacher from left to right,
the pupil, once instructed, takes leave of him and departs.
Thus:
"Desiring to acquire his own craft, he should live with a teacher after obtaining the permission of his relatives, having fixed a well-determined period of time."
The teachers, having provided him with food in their own home, should instruct him;
they should not make him perform other work, and they should treat him like a son.
If one who is being instructed by a teacher should abandon that teacher without having been corrupted, he should be forced to stay; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment.
Even if he has been trained, the pupil shall receive the fee once the time [of training] is completed;
whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs to the teacher alone.
Having mastered the craft at the proper time and having circumambulated his teacher from left to right,
the pupil, once instructed, takes leave of him and departs.
In this context, the word "vadha" (killing) has the meaning of "beating," because the fault is minor. || 2.184 ||
Now, the violation of a compact (saṃvid-vyatikrama) is discussed.
Its definition has been shown by Nārada through a negative formulation:
"The established practice of heretics, merchants, and others is called a compact (samaya)."
The non-performance of a compact is recorded as that title of dispute.

Thus, "convention" (samaya) is the establishment by means of a technical definition; its non-abandonment is non-transgression, which is its preservation. The meaning is that when this [convention] is transgressed, it becomes a ground for dispute.
To introduce that subject, he says something:
Having established a residence in the city and appointed Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide for those learned in the three Vedas and say to them, "Let your own duty be protected."

The king, having constructed a residence such as a white palace within his own city, fortress, or other location, and having stationed and settled the Brāhmaṇas there, should provide that class of Brāhmaṇas with the threefold knowledge—that is, being endowed with the three Vedas—and with a livelihood consisting of land, gold, and so forth; he should then say to those Brāhmaṇas: "Let your own duty, which arises from your caste and stage of life and is ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti, be performed by you. (2.185) He now states what action must be performed by them when thus appointed:
"But he who, without contradicting his own duty, should be a member of a convention..."
Even that dharma established by the king must be protected with great effort.

That dharma which is established by convention (*samaya*) without contradicting the *śrauta* and *smārta* duties—such as the grazing of cattle, the protection of water sources, and the maintenance of temples—that too must be protected with effort.

Likewise, the king must also preserve that conventional dharma (*sāmayiko dharmaḥ*) which has been established without conflict with his own duty, such as "food must be given to every traveler" or "horses and other animals must not be sent into our enemy's territory. (2.186)
Having stated that the rules of the community (*samayadharma*) must be observed in this manner, he declares the punishment for their transgression and so forth:
"But whoever should seize the property of the community or whoever should violate the agreement,
having confiscated all his possessions, the king shall banish him from the realm."

Furthermore, whoever steals property belonging to a *gaṇa*—that is, common property belonging to a collective group such as a village community—or whoever violates a *saṃvit*, that is, an agreement made by the assembly or by the king, [the king] shall confiscate all of that person's wealth and banish him from his own kingdom.
And this punishment is to be understood as applying when there is an excess in the persistence [of the offense] and so forth.

But when the consequences are minor: "A man who, having made a formal agreement with truth regarding villages, districts, or assemblies, should violate it out of greed—he the king shall banish from the realm."
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the agreement to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one śatamāna of silver.

Thus, among the four punishments prescribed by Manu—banishment, four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and a śatamāna—one or another should be determined in accordance with considerations such as caste and capability. (2.187)
And he says that this must be done by them:
"The word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be followed by all.
Among the members of a group, the speech of those whose habit is to speak for the welfare of the community should be followed by others who belong within that group."
Otherwise, he says there is punishment:
"Whoever therein should act contrary [to the rule] shall be made to pay the first fine."
But he who, in the midst of an assembly, obstructs the speech of those speaking for the welfare of the group, shall be punished by the king with the first amercement. (2.188)

The king should conduct himself toward the members of the assembly in this manner, as it is said: "The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the community with gifts, respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business has been accomplished."

Having gratified with gifts, honor, and respectful treatment those heads of monastic communities who have come to his side to accomplish the affairs of the collective and have completed their own purposes, that king should dismiss them. (2.189)
Regarding one who misappropriates what was given for a collective purpose, he says:
"One sent on business for a group shall deliver whatever he obtains;
if he does not deliver it himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value."

Whatever gold, clothing, or other items a person, dispatched by a group of people for the sake of the collective business, receives from the king's presence, he shall report that to the group even without being asked;
otherwise, he should be made to pay a fine eleven times the amount received. (2.190)
And he says that those who contemplate affairs should be of such a kind:
"Those who contemplate affairs should be knowers of the Dharma, pure, and free from greed;
the word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out."

Those who know the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, who are endowed with external and internal purity, who are free from greed regarding material interests, and who deliberate upon what ought to be done, should be appointed [as assessors]. Their word must be acted upon by others; this repetition is for the sake of showing respect. (2.191)
Now, extending the dharma prescribed for those learned in the three Vedas to guilds and other groups, he says:
"This same rule applies to guilds, merchant corporations, heretical sects, and assemblies;
the king shall protect their internal divisions and preserve their traditional livelihood."
Guilds (*śreṇi*) are those who subsist through a single trade or craft.
*Naigamas* are those such as the Pāśupatas and others who accept the authority of the Veda on the grounds that it was composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*).
Heretics (*pākhaṇḍin*) are those such as the naked ones (*nagna*) and the Buddhists (*saugata*) who do not accept the authority of the Veda at all.
A *gaṇa* is a group of those who live by a single occupation, such as armed soldiers and the like.
For these four types [of groups], this very rule has been established by the statement beginning with "provided it does not conflict with their own dharma.
Furthermore, the king shall protect the internal divisions and the settled rules of dharma among these guilds and other such associations.
And he should maintain the livelihood previously acquired. || 2.192 ||
Now the legal head of dispute known as *vetanasyānapākarma* (non-payment of wages) is introduced.
Its nature has been stated by Nārada:
"The procedure for the giving and non-giving of wages to servants has been declared."
The non-payment of wages is recorded in the legal treatises as that title of dispute.
Thus has been stated the sequence of rules for the giving and receiving of wages for servants. Non-payment of wages is recorded as a title of dispute.

The meaning of this is as follows: that subject of dispute (*vivādapada*) wherein the procedure for giving and taking wages for servants—as described in the forthcoming verses—is termed "non-payment of wages" (*vetanasyānapākarma*). Regarding that, he states the legal decision: "One who, having received wages, abandons his work, shall pay double."
If it has not been taken away, the master shall cause the implements to be returned equally; meanwhile, the servants must guard them.
He who has received wages but abandons the work he has undertaken shall pay double the wage to his master.
However, when he abandons the agreed-upon work before wages have been received, then he shall be made to pay an amount equal to the wages agreed upon, but not double.

Alternatively, having paid the agreed wage, he should be forced to perform the work; "having promised [to work], if he does not do so, he should be compelled to do it by force after the wage has been paid."
Thus, from the words of Nārada;
the matter of wages has also been stated by him:
"The master of the work shall give remuneration to the servant in due order."
Whatever is firmly resolved regarding an action—whether at its beginning, middle, or end.
Thus:
"The master of the work shall give wages to the servant in due order—
at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of the work— as has been determined."

And those servants must protect the equipment—the tools for ploughs and so forth, such as reins and yokes—to the best of their ability; otherwise, the accomplishment of agriculture and other tasks would be impossible. (2.193)
Regarding one who causes labor to be performed without having determined the wages, the author says:
"But he who causes work to be done without having fixed the wages must be made by the king to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle, or crops."

But if a master—a merchant, a cattle-owner, or a landowner—causes a servant to perform work for which no fixed wage has been determined, the king, the ruler of the earth, must compel him to give to that servant the tenth part of whatever profit is obtained from that work consisting of trade, cattle, or crops. (2.194)
Regarding one who does not act as instructed, he says:
"He who exceeds the place and the time, and he who effects a gain otherwise—therein the master's will shall prevail; if more has been done, more should be given."

However, if a servant, out of pride or other such motives, fails to perform the sale of goods at the appropriate place and time, or if he performs the sale in that very same place and time but realizes a profit that is inferior due to excessive expenditure and so forth, then regarding the payment of wages for that servant, the master’s *chanda*—that is, his will or desire—shall prevail; the meaning is that he may give as much as he wishes, but not necessarily the full amount of the wages.
But when, through knowledge of the place and time, an additional gain has been achieved, then the master must give even more wealth to the servant than the previously agreed-upon wage. (2.195)
He states the method for giving wages regarding work that must be accomplished by many servants:
"Whatever amount of work one performs, that much shall be his wage;
however, if the task is impossible for both, they should perform it according to what was heard [in the agreement] once it becomes possible."

Furthermore, when a single task with a fixed wage is performed by two people, and it remains unaccomplished by both—due to being overcome by illness or other causes—and if it is not completed by either one (as implied by the word "both," nor even by many), then the wage for that servant shall be given according to the amount of work he has actually performed, as determined by a neutral arbitrator; it is not, however, to be equal [to the full wage].
Nor should it be thought that no wage is to be paid because the wage was not previously stipulated for each individual component of the work.

But when the work is completed by both together, they should each give what has been prescribed or stipulated according to the agreement; however, neither should each pay the full wage individually, nor should it be given after calculating a portion according to the specific share of work performed. 2.196.
He says to the soldier and the carrier of the load:
"The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or providence;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the journey shall be made to pay double wages."
That merchandise for which no loss caused by the king or by fate exists is described as such.
If that [merchandise] has been destroyed by the carrier through lack of care, then he must be made to pay that merchandise in accordance with the extent of the loss.
Regarding this, Nārada says:
If the goods should meet with loss due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever is destroyed therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
Thus:
"If the goods should meet with loss due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever is destroyed therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king."

Furthermore, if one who has previously agreed to perform the rites necessary for the departure of someone setting out on an auspicious day for the purpose of marriage or similar occasions, then fails to do so and creates an obstacle to that departure by saying, "I will not do it," he shall be made to pay double wages, because of his obstruction of work caused by extreme negligence. (2.197)
Furthermore:

If he abandons the hireling on the way after he has set out, he must pay him a seventh part of the wage; if he abandons him halfway, he must pay the full wage, and the one who abandons him shall also be made to pay it.
If one abandons the work he has undertaken once the journey has commenced and been resolved upon, he shall be made to pay a seventh part of his wages.

Now, an objection may be raised: "In this very context, it was previously stated that for obstructing the departure, double the wages must be paid; how then is there no contradiction with the present rule regarding a seventh part? It is replied: [The two rules apply to different circumstances].

If a person abandons the work he has undertaken when an opportunity arises to take on another servant, he shall be made to pay a seventh part [of the wages]. However, there is no contradiction in the rule that if one abandons the work at the very moment of departure, double the wages shall be paid.
Furthermore, if one abandons the work while the journey has already begun and is in progress, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of the wages.
Furthermore, on the half-way point, the employer must cause the entire wages to be paid.

However, if the employer causes a worker who does not wish to quit to quit by force within the aforementioned locations, he too must be made to pay the aforementioned seventh part and so forth to the servant.
This applies to cases where the servant is not ill and so forth; for: "A servant who, being unafflicted, out of pride does not perform his work as it is required..."
He shall be fined eight kṛṣṇalas, and his wages shall not be paid.
Thus, according to the statement of Manu:

"When, however, the illness has passed and he completes the work by counting the intervening days, he certainly receives his wages; but one who was ill should perform the work as originally agreed once he is healthy.
He shall receive his own wages even after a long period of time."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu.

However, for one who is free from illness and healthy, yet does not perform the work he himself began even slightly due to laziness or the like, or does not complete it with another, wages should not be paid to him.
As Manu has said: "Whether afflicted or healthy, he who does not cause that work to be done..."
No wages shall be paid for that work, even if it is only slightly incomplete.
Thus [ends verse] 2.198.
As it has been said: "Whether he be afflicted or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be performed, his wages must not be paid, even for work that is only slightly incomplete."
Now the title of law known as gambling and betting is taken up.
Its nature has been described by Nārada:
"Gambling with dice, sticks, slips, and so forth, conducted in a deceitful manner."
And gambling with dice, playing with birds, and betting on animal fights constitute the category of "gambling and challenging."
Thus:
"Gambling with dice, sticks, and so forth, conducted with deceit;
and playing for stakes with birds—this is the stage of gambling and betting."
The *akṣas* are dice;
the *vadhra* is a leather strap;
the *śalākās* are long, square pieces made of ivory or similar materials.

And by the inclusion of the word "first" (ādi), the means for playing with horses and so forth—such as elephants, horses, chariots, and the like—are understood. That gambling or play involving those inanimate objects which is conducted with a stake is one [type]; likewise, that play involving birds such as cocks and pigeons, and [the word] "and" (ca) indicates [play] involving living beings such as wrestlers, rams, buffaloes, and so forth, which is conducted with a stake—that both together, in their respective order, constitute the legal subject matter known as *dyūta-samāhvaya*. *Dyūta* and *samāhvaya* together form the compound *dyūta-samāhvaya*.
Thus it has been said by Manu:
"In this world, that which is performed with inanimate objects is called *dyūta* (gambling);
but that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as *samāhvaya* (betting)."
Thus [it is said].
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world;
however, that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "betting" (samāhvaya).
Regarding that, he states the livelihood of the superintendent of the gambling hall:
"The keeper of the hall shall take five percent from a gambler who stakes a hundred,
and ten percent from any other [gambler]."
A stake (*glaha*) is that which is established as a wager by gamblers through mutual agreement.

In that context, a *śatikavṛddhi* is one whose interest is a hundred or more than a hundred, based upon that stake; from such a fraudulent gambler, the keeper of the gaming house (*sabhika*) shall take five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*) for his own livelihood.
That is to say, a "five-percent" stake is a hundred in which the profit consists of five *paṇas*.

In this context, the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule beginning with "vṛddhyāyalābha-," meaning that one should take a twentieth part of the stakes won. A *sabhā* is a place for gamblers to reside; one who possesses such a place is a *sabhika*.
The master of the gaming hall is one who provides all the implements for play, such as fabricated dice and other equipment, and subsists on the wealth accumulated therefrom.
Furthermore, from the other [player], the gambler, he should take ten percent—that is, a tenth part—of the wealth won, calculated at a full hundredfold interest. || 2.199 ||
Regarding what must be done by the keeper of the gambling house who has thus established his conduct, he says:
"Being properly protected, he shall give the king the share as determined;
he shall cause the winner to recover what was won and shall give the truthful word to the victor, remaining patient."
The superintendent of gambling who has established such regulations, being protected by the king from rogue gamblers, shall pay the king his agreed-upon share.
Likewise, he shall cause the won wealth to be recovered—by means of seizing pledges, through legal restraint (*āsedha*), and so forth—from the one defeated;
and having recovered that money, the keeper of the gaming house (*sabhika*) shall give it to the victorious winner.
Having thus become patient, he should give truthful testimony for the sake of establishing trust among the gamblers.
As it was said by the King of Men: "The master of the gaming house shall conduct the gambling, and he shall pay what is won therein. (2.200)
"The keeper of the gaming house shall cause the gambling to take place and shall pay what was won therein.
Furthermore, when the keeper is unable to make [the debtor] pay, then the king shall make him pay; so it is said:
"When the king's share has been obtained and the circle of gamblers is well-known..."
One should cause the winner to pay the stake in a place where there is an assembly; otherwise, one should not.

In a well-known, open gambling hall attended by royal officials and presided over by a *sabhika* (the master of the game), once the *sabhika* has received his share for the king, the king shall compel the rogue gambler who does not contest the decision to pay the won stake.
Otherwise, in a secret gambling match held without a *sabhika* and where no share for the king has been paid, he shall not compel the winner to give up the won stake to the victor. M 2.201.
He states the means of decision in the event of conflicting claims regarding victory and defeat:
"For they alone are the observers and witnesses of the legal proceedings.
Indeed, those very gamblers themselves must be appointed by the king as the assessors who observe the gambling disputes.
In that case, there is no restrictive rule such as "those perfected in learning and study [must serve as witnesses]";
furthermore, in a gambling dispute, gamblers themselves must be made the witnesses.
In that context, there is no prohibition against women, children, the elderly, gamblers, and so forth.
In some cases, he prescribes punishment to prohibit gambling: "The king shall banish those who play with fraudulent dice or through deceit, marking them with a sign."

The king shall brand those who gamble with fraudulent dice and the like, or by means of deception intended to mislead the mind—such as through gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth—with the mark of a dog's foot or similar insignia, and banish them from his own kingdom.
However, Nārada has stated a specific rule regarding banishment:
"The king shall banish from the kingdom those wicked gamblers who use fraudulent dice."
Placing a rosary around his neck—this indeed is recorded as their discipline.
Thus:
"The king should banish from the kingdom those wicked men who play with false dice;
having placed a rosary around their necks, for that is declared to be their punishment."

And as for those words of Manu which are intent on prohibiting gambling: "The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in or cause others to engage in gambling or betting, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born."
These and other such passages are also to be applied to the context of gambling with false dice, as well as to gambling conducted without a king, a supervisor, or an official arbiter. (2.202)
Furthermore:
Gambling should be conducted with a single opening for the purpose of identifying thieves.
That gambling which was mentioned previously should be performed "with a single opening," meaning that gambling of which one opening—the primary means—is the principal feature; it is thus described.
The meaning is that [the gambling hall] should be caused to be built by the king under the supervision of a royal official, for the purpose of identifying thieves.

Having considered the objective—which consists of identifying thieves—it is because gamblers are generally those who have acquired wealth through theft that the hall must be conducted under a single authority for the sake of recognizing thieves.
Extending the rules for gambling to betting on animal contests, he says:
"This same rule should be understood to apply to betting on animal contests and to betting on personal combats."

The law of gambling that has been declared by the rule beginning with "in a stake of a hundredfold interest" and so forth, that same law is to be understood as applying to *prāṇidyūta* (gambling with living beings), which is known by the name *samāhvaya* and is carried out with wrestlers, rams, buffaloes, and the like. (2.203)
Now, verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) is introduced. Its definition has been stated by Nārada:
"An insult directed at [another's] country, caste, family, and so forth, accompanied by a disparaging reference to their physical defects..."
"Speech whose meaning is contrary [to another] is called verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*).
Thus it is said: "Insulting one's country, caste, family, and so forth, accompanied by disparagement..."
Speech that has a contrary meaning is called harsh speech (*vākpāruṣya*).
It consists of reviling [another] regarding their country and so forth, accompanied by insults (*nyaṅga*).

Reviling (*ākrośa*) is speaking loudly; an insult (*nyaṅga*) is a blemish (*avadya*). That speech which is associated with both of these, having a contrary meaning for the purpose of producing agitation, is termed harsh speech.

In this regard, "The people of Gauḍa are indeed fond of quarreling" is an insult to the country (*deśākrośa*). "The Brahmins are indeed excessively greedy" is an insult to the caste (*jātyākrośa*). "The descendants of Viśvāmitra are indeed of cruel conduct" is an insult to the family (*kulākṣepa*).

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the harsh verbal insult directed at a learned person’s knowledge, craft, and so forth—by way of disparaging their own [knowledge, craft, etc.]—is included.

And regarding that [insult], having stated its threefold division into *niṣṭhura* (harsh), *aślīla* (obscene), and *tīvra* (severe) for the purpose of determining the gradations of punishment, its definition was stated by that same author:
"It is traditionally held to be of three kinds according to its being harsh, obscene, or severe."
According to the sequence of their relative importance, the punishment for each shall likewise be progressively more severe.

The wise declare that speech accompanied by reproach and harshness is "indecorous" (aślīla), while that joined with the mention of physical defects and severe accusations involving grounds for expulsion is called "fierce" (tīvra).
Thus it is said:
"That [abuse] is also remembered as being threefold, according to whether it is harsh, vulgar, or extreme;
and the punishment for it shall likewise be increasingly severe, following the order of their gravity."

The wise declare that speech which is accompanied by reproach and is harsh is "indecorous" (aślīla); that which is joined with the mention of physical defects and consists of accusations involving acts leading to loss of caste is called "fierce" (tīvra).
Among these, "Fie on you, fool! and "wretch! are examples of the reproachful (*sākṣepa*).

Here, "defective" (*nyaṅga*) refers to the indecorous (*asabhya*). "Blameworthy" (*avadya*) refers to sexual intercourse with a sister and so forth; that which is associated with such acts is the obscene (*aślīla*).
Harsh speech is that which is joined with insults such as "You are a drinker of liquor," referring to the great sins (mahāpātakas) and so forth.
Regarding that, he states the punishment for harsh abuse directed toward those of the same caste:
"If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, sense organs, or afflicted by disease by means of praise— whether true, false, or otherwise— he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas."
Those with deficient limbs are those lacking hands, feet, or other parts; those with deficient sense organs are those deprived of eyes, ears, and so forth;
and the diseased are those suffering from skin diseases and the like.
For them, by means of truth, untruth, and praise that is otherwise—namely, praise intended as censure:
where one who lacks a pair of eyes is called "blind," that is truth;
but where one who possesses eyes is called "blind," that is untruth.
Where one who is indeed deformed in appearance is told, "You are handsome," that is a "contrary praise" (*anyathāstotra*).
He who performs such an insult or derision shall be fined thirteen and a half *paṇas*. This applies whether [the person insulted] is one-eyed, or lame, or otherwise of such a [deformed] nature.
Even when speaking the truth, he shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa.
Thus, that statement of Manu refers to those of extremely wicked character;
however, when sons and others swear at their mothers and others, it has been stated by that same author that they are to be fined one hundred [paṇas]:
"The mother, the father, the wife, the brother, the father-in-law, and the teacher..."
One who reviles [another] shall be made to pay a hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher.
Thus:
"One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, father-in-law,
or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher."
And this should be understood to apply to teachers such as one's mother when they have committed an offense, and to one's wife when she is without offense. (2.204)
Regarding the punishment for offensive insults, he says:
"If one swears, 'I shall violate your sister or your mother,' the king should cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]."

If a man swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," or if he swears, "I shall violate another wife of yours," the king shall cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five *paṇas*—that is, a punishment consisting of twenty plus five *paṇas*. (2.205)
Having thus stated the punishment for Brahmins of equal merit, he speaks in order to establish the punishment for those of unequal merit:
"Half [the fine] for those of inferior [merit], double for women belonging to others, and for those of superior [merit].
For those of inferior [merit], meaning those whose conduct and other qualities are less than that of the accuser, the fine is half."
