Since twenty-five [paṇas] were the subject of the preceding statement, the "half" in relation to that should be understood as consisting of twelve and a half paṇas.
Furthermore, in the case of the wives of others, the fine is uniformly double—that is, fifty paṇas—with reference to those same twenty-five.
Likewise, in the case of superior men—those whose learning and conduct exceed one's own—the fine is indeed fifty paṇas.
Regarding the mutual insults among the castes, such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others, he states the determination of punishment:
"The infliction of punishment must be carried out according to the higher or lower status of the caste and birth."
The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth;
the *jātis* are the Mūrdhāvasikta and so forth.
Both the *varṇas* and the *jātis* are collectively termed *varṇajātis*.

"Higher and lower" means those who are superior and inferior; "castes and classes" refers to those same higher and lower groups, hence "castes and classes, higher and lower. When mutual insults are made by these castes and classes, higher and lower, the "infliction of punishment"—meaning its application, administration, or determination—is to be understood [as follows].

Furthermore, because the specific qualification "by the higher and lower" is employed, it is understood that this calculation of punishment must be carried out specifically with regard to the relationship of superiority and inferiority.

Just as a Brahmin, having reviled a Mūrdhāvasikta who is inferior to a Brāhmaṇa and superior to a Kṣatriya, deserves a fine of seventy-five paṇas—slightly more than the fifty paṇas prescribed for insulting a Kṣatriya; and a Kṣatriya, having likewise reviled him, also deserves that same fine of seventy-five [paṇas], which is less than the hundred paṇas prescribed for insulting a Brāhmaṇa;
and even a Mūrdhāvasikta, having reviled those two, deserves that very same fine.
When a Mūrdhāvasikta and an Ambaṣṭha mutually insult each other, the fines prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya for mutual verbal abuse should be understood to apply to them respectively.
In this same manner, it should be inferred in other cases as well. (2.206)
Having thus declared the punishment regarding those of the same caste, he now states the punishment for insulting members of the castes themselves, whether in the reverse or the natural order:
"In cases of insult involving the reverse order of castes, the fines shall be double and triple;
in the natural order, they decrease by half and half again from that [maximum]."

*Apavāda* refers to insults. *Prātilomyāpavāda* means insults directed in the reverse order [of the social classes]. In the case of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa, the fines should be understood as follows: compared to the fifty *paṇas* mentioned in the preceding statement, they are doubled to one hundred *paṇas*, and tripled to one hundred and fifty *paṇas*, respectively.
In the case of a Śūdra reviling a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment shall be either flogging or the cutting off of the tongue.
As Manu has said:
"A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment."
Thus:
"A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment."

By the same logic, for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra who are respectively immediate and one degree removed from a Kṣatriya, it should be understood that when they revile a Kṣatriya, the fine is one hundred and one hundred and fifty respectively.
And for a Śūdra who reviles a Vaiśya, the fine is one hundred.

But in the case of the *varṇas* following the order of precedence—when a Brāhmaṇa utters abuse against a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra—he should be fined fifty, twenty-five, and twelve and a half *paṇas* respectively; that is, having reduced by one-half each of the fines prescribed for abusing a Brāhmaṇa (which total one hundred *paṇas*), the remaining amounts are the fines to be imposed on the Brāhmaṇa according to the respective order.
This has been stated by Manu:
"A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty *paṇas* for insulting a Kṣatriya."
"For a Vaiśya it shall be forty-five [paṇas], and for a Śūdra the fine is twelve.
Thus [it is said].
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
in the case of a Vaiśya, the fine should be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
When a Kṣatriya is defamed by a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the fines are fifty and twenty-five respectively.

And in the case of a Vaiśya reviling a Śūdra, the fine should be understood to be fifty [paṇas], because of the traditional teaching of Gautama that "the rule for a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya applies likewise to a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya," and because of the traditional teaching of Manu that "for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, it is exactly thus toward their own respective castes. (2.207)
Furthermore, concerning harsh verbal abuse, he says:
"For verbal threats of injury to the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred [paṇas];
for those involving the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that."

When the destruction of each [limb], such as the arms and so forth, is verbally declared—that is, expressed by speech in a form such as "I shall cut off your arms"—a fine of one hundred [paṇas] is to be understood.

In the case of verbal declarations regarding the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth—the inclusion of "and so forth" referring to the buttocks and other parts—the fine is half of that; that which possesses half of that hundred is "half-of-that," meaning a fine of fifty paṇas is to be understood. (2.208)
Furthermore: But one who is incapable, if he speaks thus, should be fined ten paṇas;
likewise, one who is capable should be made to provide a surety for his security.
Furthermore, he who, being weakened in strength by fever or other ailments, swears an oath saying, "I shall break your arm or some other limb," is to be fined ten *paṇas*.

On the other hand, he who, though capable, insults one who is weakened in strength as before, shall, after the aforementioned fine of one hundred *paṇas* or more, be compelled to provide a surety for the safety of that incapacitated person. (2.209)
He states the punishment for harsh verbal abuse:
"For an insult involving a crime causing loss of caste, the punishment is the middle amercement;
but for one involving a minor offense (upapātaka), he shall be made to pay the first amercement."
When an accusation is made against members of the [first three] castes using grounds for loss of caste, such as the killing of a Brahmin, the punishment is the middle amercement.
However, when an accusation is made involving a minor offense, such as "you are a cow-killer" and the like, he is to be punished with the first amercement. (2.210)
Furthermore:
For the insult of those learned in the three Vedas, of kings, or of gods, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for castes and guilds, it is the middle amercement; and for villages or districts, it is the first amercement.

For the insult of those kings who are "Traividyas"—that is, those perfected in the three Vedas—as well as of the gods, the punishment is the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa). Furthermore, for the insult of corporations or assemblies (*pūga*) consisting of Brāhmaṇas, Mūrdhāvasikta, and other such castes, the punishment is the middle fine (madhyama-sāhasa).
It should be understood that for the insult of a village or a district individually, the first fine (prathama-sāhasa) is to be applied. (2.211)
Now, assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) is introduced. Its nature has been described by Nārada:
"Assault consists of violence against the limbs of another person by means of hands, feet, weapons, and so forth."
And injury by means of ashes and so forth is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault).
Thus:
"Assault against the bodies of others by means of hands, feet, weapons, and so forth,
as well as injury by means of ashes and the like, is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (corporal assault)."

Assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) consists of both: (1) injury (*abhidroha*), which is the infliction of harm or the production of pain by means of hands, feet, weapons, or—as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—stones and other such objects, directed toward the limbs of others, that is, toward substances consisting of both the stationary (*sthāvara*) and the moving (*jaṅgama*); and (2) insult (*upaghāta*), which is the production of mental distress through the act of touching with ashes, or—as indicated by the word "and so forth"—with dust, mud, excrement, and the like.

It is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* because it is a form of harshness (*pāruṣya*) committed against a substance such as a living being by means of a "staff" (*daṇḍa*), so called because one is punished (*daṇḍyate*) by it; that is, the hostile treatment meted out to such a thing.

Having described its threefold nature according to the distinctions in causes such as threatening and so forth, it is further stated that there is another threefold division based on the three types of objects—inferior, middling, and superior—which constitute the form of the act.
Regarding that [act], the observed threefoldness is likewise [distinguished] by way of the sequence of inferior, middling, and superior:
namely, by threatening, causing a free fall, and showing a wound.
Because of the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior objects, they say there are exactly three types of *sāhasa* (crimes of violence); therein lies the purification of thorns.
Thus it is said:
"The visible [result] of that [action] is also threefold— low, middling, and superior—
in accordance with the sequence of threatening, causing a fall without attachment, and witnessing an injury."

Because of the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior objects, they say there are exactly three types of *sāhasa* (crimes of violence); therein lies the purification of the thorns [of society].
Causing someone to fall without hesitation and striking without fear—
these are the three types of *sāhasa* (acts of violence).
The meaning is that these are acts of physical assault committed impulsively.
Likewise, when both have engaged in verbal or physical assault and a quarrel has ensued, he who remains patient incurs not only the absence of punishment but is indeed worthy of honor.
Conversely, for one who first initiated the quarrel, the punishment is severe;
and in a quarrel, only the one who harbors a persistent grudge is subject to punishment.
Likewise, when the specific nature of the offense of those two is not known, the punishment is equal.

Similarly, when an offense is committed against noble persons by outcastes (*śvapaca*) and others, only virtuous people are authorized to bring about the infliction of punishment; if they are unable to do so, the king must simply have them executed and must not take their property. Thus, five types of procedures have been stated by him. Indeed, this fivefold procedure has been declared for both of these cases as well.
When harshness arises from agitation between two people who have become angry.
He thinks: "He who forgives passes over his share of punishment;
but he who first utters an accusation will certainly be the one to bear the guilt."
Even he who is the first of the five is one who lacks respect; however, discipline is paramount.
Furthermore, when two have fallen into equal offense, he who continues to adhere to the other [is at fault].
He who is the first, or if it be the other, incurs the punishment for those two when they have simultaneously engaged in mutual abuse, both being shrouded by the fault of harshness.
If no distinction is perceived, there should be discipline toward both [the teacher and the student],
even toward those who are outcastes, eunuchs, caṇḍālas, the deformed, or those who live by killing.
In the case of transgressing established rules regarding elephant-drivers, outcasts, slaves, teachers, preceptors, and kings,
immediate corporal punishment is the prescribed discipline.
For indeed, that very king among men who would correct these people while they are still virtuous will surely be one who possesses true discipline.
For these are indeed the stains of men, and their wealth is of the nature of stain;
therefore, the king should have them executed, rather than punishing them with a fine of money.
Thus [it is said].
The procedure for both of these cases when verbal abuse has occurred due to the outburst of anger between two enraged parties is said to be fivefold.
He thinks: "The one who forgives passes over his share of punishment;
but he who first utters an accusation will certainly be the one to bear the guilt."
Even he who is the first among the five is one who acts improperly; for discipline is weighty even in the past.
Furthermore, he who continues to bind together two people who have fallen into equal transgression [is likewise at fault].
He incurs the punishment for both of them, whether it be the first or the other,
if they have simultaneously engaged in mutual abuse while being shrouded by the fault of harshness.
If no distinction is perceived, there would be discipline toward both [the high and the low],
even toward dog-cookers, eunuchs, Caṇḍālas, the deformed, and those who live by killing.
In the case of elephants, outcasts, slaves, as well as teachers, preceptors, and kings,
the only punishment for transgressing established boundaries is immediate execution.
For that very man among men whom these [vices] might overcome while he is still virtuous—he alone must surely impose discipline; indeed, such a king is a possessor of true discipline.
For these are indeed the stains of men, and their wealth is of the nature of stain;
therefore, the king should have them executed, rather than punishing them with a fine of money.
Since the infliction of punishment is preceded by a determination regarding such physical violence, he states the grounds for determination when there is doubt about its nature:
"In a case of killing where there are no witnesses, the legal proceeding must be examined through marks, circumstantial reasoning, and tradition,
for [false accusations] may arise from the fear of forged evidence."

When someone reports in secret to the king, "I have been killed by this person," then an investigation must be conducted through marks—such as those pertaining to the physical appearance of the complexion and so forth—through reasoning—which consists of a deliberation on causes and motives—and through tradition and public rumor; and by the word "or" (*ca*), it may also be done through divine means, out of fear that the suspicion of having fabricated false marks might arise. (2.212)
When the specific nature of the offense has been thus determined, he states the specific punishment for each means of contact:
"For contact with ash, mud, or dust, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
for contact with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, the fine is double that."
In the case of women equal [in status] to those of the same class, the punishment is the same; for women of higher classes, it is double;
for women of lower classes, it is half; however, there is no punishment if [the offense is committed] through delusion, intoxication, and so forth.
He who causes another to touch him with ashes, mud, or dust shall be made to pay a fine of ten *paṇas*.
By "impure substance" (*amedhya*) is meant tears, phlegm, nails, hair, earwax, excrement, rheum of the eyes, food remnants, and so forth.
The "heel" (*pārṣṇi*) is the rear part of the foot.
*Niṣṭhyūtam* refers to water expelled from the mouth.
Upon being touched by these, a fine of twenty *paṇas*—double the previous amount of ten *paṇas*—is to be understood as the penalty.
Furthermore, regarding contact with feces and so forth, a specific rule has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"If one becomes defiled by vomit, urine, feces, or the like, that [penance] shall be fourfold;
it shall be sixfold if on the middle part of the body, but is traditionally held to be eightfold if on the head."
Thus it is said:
"That [pollution] is considered fourfold when caused by vomit, urine, feces, and so forth;
it is sixfold within the body, but eightfold on the head."
By the inclusion of the word "first," fat, semen, blood, and marrow are understood.
Such a previously mentioned fine is to be applied in the case of women of the same caste (*savarṇa*), as well as without distinction in the case of the wives of others.
Likewise, in the case of superior women—those whose learning and conduct exceed one's own—the fine should be understood as double the previously mentioned ten *paṇas* or twenty *paṇas*.

In the case of those who are inferior—meaning those whose conduct, learning, and so forth are less than one's own—the previously mentioned half-fine should be understood as five *paṇas* or ten *paṇas*.
"Delusion" (*moha*) is a derangement of the mind.
"Intoxication" (*mada*) is a particular state produced by the drinking of liquor.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," possession by spirits and similar conditions are meant.
When one is afflicted by these, even if he touches ashes or other such things, no punishment shall be imposed. || 2.213 || 2.214 ||
He states the punishment for an offense committed in the reverse order [of castes]:
"But in the case of a non-Brāhmaṇa who causes pain to a Brāhmaṇa, the offending limb shall be cut off;
if he merely raised his hand, the first amercement is the penalty, but if there was physical contact, half of that."
The limb—such as a hand or a foot—of a non-Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or others, which causes pain to Brāhmaṇas, shall be cut off.
Even for a Śūdra who inflicts pain upon a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, there must likewise be the amputation of a limb.
Indeed, if a low-born person (antyaja) should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that limb shall be severed.
That very thing which is to be cut away belongs to him; such is the instruction for that mind.
Thus it is said:
"If a low-born man should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu."

Since the cutting off of limbs is prescribed for a Śūdra as punishment for an offense against any member of the twice-born (dvija), this same penalty applies to a Vaiśya who harms a Kṣatriya as well, because the principle is the same.
When a weapon or similar object is raised—that is, prepared for the purpose of killing—the first amercement (prathamasāhasa) is to be understood as the punishment.

However, for a Śūdra, even when [the weapon] is merely raised, there shall be the cutting off of the hand or other limb; for it is said: "Having raised his hand or a staff, he deserves the cutting off of his hand."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Manu.
But for touching weapons and the like for the purpose of brandishing them, it should be understood that the punishment is half of the first *sāhasa*, namely, half of that [first] fine.

Furthermore, in cases of contact with ashes and the like, or in insults involving the reverse order of castes (*prātilomya*) among Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, one should determine the fines as double or triple according to the principle stated under verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*).
Even in those cases, for a Śūdra, there shall be the amputation of the hand alone: "If out of arrogance he spits upon [a superior], the king shall have both his lips cut off;
if he urinates upon him, his penis; if he passes wind against him, his anus."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Manu. (2.214)
Having thus declared the punishment for offenses committed in the reverse order of castes, he speaks again concerning those of the same caste:
"If one merely raises his hand or foot against another, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively; but if they strike one another with a weapon, the middle amercement applies to all."

When the hand or foot is raised for the purpose of striking, a fine of ten paṇas and twenty paṇas respectively should be understood as the punishment. When the hand is raised for the purpose of mutual killing, the middle amercement is the punishment for all social classes (varṇas). (2.216)
Furthermore: For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, or for seizing them by the hand, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
for causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a cloth, or placing the foot [upon another], the punishment shall be one hundred [paṇas].
Having seized any one of the feet, hair, clothes, or hands, he who pulls or suddenly drags [the person] shall be fined ten paṇas.
"Torture" (pīḍā), "dragging" (karṣa), "wrapping with a cloth" (aṃśukāveṣṭa), and "placing the foot upon" (pādādhyāsa)—when these are combined, he shall be fined one hundred [paṇas].
This is what is meant: [he is liable for all four].
"He who, having tightly wrapped [the garment] with a cloth, pressed it down, pulled it, and struck it with his foot, shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred paṇas. (2.217)
Furthermore:
A man who inflicts pain with wood or other such objects without shedding blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine is double.
Furthermore, he who strikes with wood, clods of earth, or other objects in such a way that blood is not visible shall be fined thirty-two paṇas.
Furthermore, when blood is seen due to severe beating, then one should be punished with sixty-four paṇas, which is double the thirty-two.
Moreover, a specific distinction regarding the piercing of skin, flesh, and bone has been shown by Manu:
"One who pierces the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to appear."
But one who cuts flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
Thus [ends the verse]. 2.218.
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
Furthermore:
In the case of breaking a hand, foot, or tooth, or cutting off the ear or nose, the middle fine shall be imposed;
likewise for causing a wound or striking someone who is as good as dead.

In the case of breaking each of the hands, feet, or teeth, or cutting off each of the ears or nose, or reopening a healed wound, when one is struck or beaten so that he becomes as if dead, it should be understood that the middle *sāhasa* (fine) applies; here, equality of the offense must be established by considering the consequences (*anubandha*) and other factors. (2.219)
Furthermore:
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [sensitive parts];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
In the case of obstructing the movement, eating, or speaking of the eyes—and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," also of the tongue;
and in the case of breaking the neck (the throat), the arm (well-known), or the thigh (the leg)—for each of these, the middle amercement is the punishment. (2.220)
Furthermore: "For many who strike one person, the punishment is double that which has been prescribed.

When, moreover, many people acting together inflict a fracture of a limb or the like upon a single individual, then for whichever specific offense whatever specific punishment has been declared, it should be understood that the punishment for each of them is double that amount.

Because of their extreme cruelty, one should determine the reduction or increase of this very same class of punishment prescribed for offenses involving those of equal caste—whether committed in the inverse or natural order—according to the sequence stated for verbal abuse: "Whatever punishment has been declared for verbal abuse according to the inverse or natural order, that same punishment shall be imposed by the king in cases of physical assault, respectively."
Thus it is from the traditional Smṛti.
Furthermore: that which was taken away during a quarrel must be restored, and a fine twice that amount shall be imposed.
When a quarrel is occurring, whatever has been seized by someone must be returned by that person;
furthermore, a fine equal to twice the value of the seized property, on account of the seizure, shall be paid. (2.221)
Furthermore:
"He who causes pain shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for its removal,
as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel."
He who causes pain to another by beating him shall pay for whatever expenses are incurred for the purpose of healing his wound and providing suitable diet;
"samutthāna" means the healing of the wound.
Furthermore, he must pay the fine imposed for the quarrel itself, and not merely the expenses for recovery. (2.222)
Having stated the punishment for injuring the limbs of another, he next declares the punishment for the destruction of external property:
"In cases of striking, cutting, breaking, or the causing of a wall to fall,
one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of repair."
When a wall is struck with a mallet or similar object, torn open, or split in two, the fines shall be understood to be five *paṇas*, ten *paṇas*, and twenty *paṇas* respectively.
Furthermore, if the wall is brought down, these three fines are to be taken cumulatively;
additionally, one must pay the owner the cost of rebuilding the wall. (2.223)
Moreover:
He who throws into a house property that causes pain or likewise property that is life-threatening shall be made to pay sixteen *paṇas* for the first offense and the middle fine for the second.
One who throws into another's house objects such as thorns that cause pain shall be fined sixteen paṇas;
however, one who throws life-threatening things such as poison or serpents shall be fined the middle amercement. (2.224)
He states the punishment for injuring livestock:
"In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise cutting off a limb or a member [of the body],
the fine for small animals shall start from two paṇas and increase in sequence."

Regarding small animals—those consisting primarily of goats, sheep, and deer—if one causes them pain by beating them, draws their blood, or cuts their branches and limbs: here, by the word "branches" (*śākhā*), hornless parts such as horns and the like (which are devoid of the movement of vital breath) are indicated; "limbs" (*aṅga*) refers to the hands, feet, and so forth; "branches and limbs" (*śākhāṅga*) is a compound of branch and limb; for cutting such [parts], the fine is two *paṇas* and upwards. A fine of two *paṇas* is called "two-*paṇa*" (*dvipaṇa*); that group of fines which has two *paṇas* as its starting point is "two-*paṇa*-and-upwards" (*dvipaṇaprabhṛti*).
And that group of fines consists of two *paṇas*, four *paṇas*, six *paṇas*, and eight *paṇas*—of such a form; it does not consist of two *paṇas*, three *paṇas*, four *paṇas*, and five *paṇas*.
If one asks why, it is said:
because of the gravity of the offense, the three subsequent fines are understood to be progressively heavier than the first fine.

In this regard, it is faultless to conclude that it is better to establish weightiness by relying on the repetition of the two-fold number explicitly stated in scripture, rather than resorting to the three-fold number and other such figures which are not heard in the text. 2.224.
Furthermore:
"In the case of cutting off the male organ or killing [the animal], the middle amercement shall be paid, as well as its value;
for these great animals, the fine in these circumstances is double."
For the mutilation of the genitals or the killing of these small animals, the punishment is the middle amercement;
and one shall pay the value [of the animal] to the owner.

Furthermore, in the case of large animals—such as cows, elephants, horses, and so forth—for these same acts, namely beating, causing the flow of blood, and the like, it should be understood that the punishment is double that which was previously stated. (2.226)
He states the punishment for injuring stationary beings:
"For the cutting of branches, trunks, or the entire [body] of trees that bear shoots,
as well as for trees that provide livelihood, the fine is double twenty [paṇas]."

*Prarohas* are sprouts; *prarohiṇyaḥ śākhāḥ* are branches possessing such sprouts—those branches which, when cut and replanted, grow again from each cutting. Those trees, such as the banyan (*vaṭa*) and others, which possess such branches are called *prarohiśākhins*. Regarding the cutting of their branches: the *skandha* is that from which the root-branches emerge; regarding its cutting and the cutting of the entire tree along with its roots, starting from a fine of twenty *paṇas*, each subsequent fine is double the preceding one, respectively. This is what is meant: [the fines increase progressively for these acts].

Fines of twenty paṇas, forty paṇas, and eighty paṇas—these three penalties apply respectively to offenses such as cutting branches and so forth. Even for trees that do not regrow but are useful, such as mango trees and others, these same aforementioned fines apply when they stand in the previously mentioned locations; however, for trees that neither regrow nor provide utility, the fines should be determined accordingly. (2.227)
Regarding specific types of trees, he says: "In the case of trees grown at a shrine, a cemetery, a boundary, a sacred site, or a temple,
as well as for a tree of renown, the fine is double."
For the cutting of branches and so forth from trees growing near shrines (caityas) and the like, the fine is double that previously mentioned.
For well-known trees such as the Pippala and Palāśa, the fine is likewise double. (2.228)
Regarding shrubs and the like, he says: "For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines,
the fine shall be half of that previously mentioned for the places already specified."
*Gulmas* are thickets of not very tall, dense creepers such as *mālatī* and others.
*Gucchās* are those that are not of the form of long creepers and are mostly non-erect, such as *kuraṇṭaka* and others.
*Kṣupas* are mostly erect, such as *karavīra* and others.
Climbers (*latā*) are those that extend for great distances, such as grapes (*drākṣā*) and the *atimukta* creeper;
creepers (*pratāna*) are those that grow straight without aerial roots (*kāṇḍapraroha*), such as the *sārivā* plant;
and medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit, such as rice (*śāli*).
Climbing plants (*vīrudhaḥ*) are those such as *guḍūcī* and others which grow back in various ways even when cut.
For cutting or lopping these in the aforementioned locations, it should be understood that the fine is half of the previously mentioned penalty. (2.229)
Now, desiring to explain the legal head of dispute known as *sāhasa* (violence), he first states its definition:
"Sāhasa is declared to be the forcible seizure of common property.

The forcible seizure (*apaharaṇa*) of common (*sāmānya*)—that is, shared—property, or of another's property, because there is no distinction in the fact that it is unfit for disposal according to one's own will, constitutes *sāhasa*.
Why? Because of "forcible seizure," that is, because of seizing by force;
in other words, because of seizing through the application of physical power.
This is what is meant:

when any act such as killing, theft, or the violation of another's wife is committed in the presence of royal officials and other people, having transgressed both royal punishment and public censure, all that is *sāhasa* (violence); this is the definition of *sāhasa*.
Therefore, even the taking away of common property or the property of another constitutes *sāhasa*, because it is performed by relying upon force.
Nārada also has explained the nature of *sāhasa*:
"Whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is called *sāhasa*; here, *saha* is said to mean strength."
Thus:
whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant with strength is called *sāhasa* (rashness); here, *saha* is said to mean strength.

This *sāhasa* (violence), although included within the categories of theft, verbal and physical assault, and adultery with women, is distinguished by the factor of relying on the arrogance of one's own strength; thus, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of imposing a higher punishment.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the variety of its punishments, [the author] has explained its threefold nature—first and so forth—and its definition has been elucidated by him through that very same [classification].
Moreover, that [violence] should be known as threefold: first, middling, and likewise [highest].
And its characteristic as the supreme is stated separately in the scriptures.
The first degree of *sāhasa* (violence) is declared to consist of the breaking, seizing, or crushing of fruits, roots, water, and other such items used for the cultivation of fields.
Regarding clothing, cattle, food and drink, and household utensils—
the theft of these by this very same method is recorded as the middle amercement.
Malice, the use of poison, weapons, and the like, the violation of another's wife, and whatever else obstructs life— these are declared to be the highest form of violence (uttamasāhasa).
For the first of these, the punishment depends on the specific act and shall not be less than one hundred;
for the middle one, however, it is seen by those learned in the scriptures as being not less than five hundred.

In the case of the highest violence (uttama-sāhasa), the fine is prescribed as starting from one thousand [paṇas] upwards; furthermore, the punishments include execution, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding,
or the amputation of that specific limb— this is declared to be the punishment for the highest violence.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, that [discipline] is to be known as threefold— namely, the initial, the intermediate, and the superior— and its specific characteristics have been stated separately in the treatises.
The first degree of *sāhasa* (violence) is declared to consist of the breaking, seizing, or crushing of fruits, roots, water, and other such items, as well as the implements of agriculture.
Regarding clothing, cattle, food, drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.
Malice, the use of poison, weapons, and the like; the violation of another's wife; and whatever else obstructs life—these are declared to be the highest form of violence (uttama-sāhasa).
For that first [offense], punishment dependent on the action shall be at least one hundred;
for the middle [offense], however, it is seen by those learned in the scriptures to be at least five hundred.
In the case of the highest violence (*uttama-sāhasa*), a fine of at least one thousand [paṇas] is prescribed; furthermore, execution, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding,
and the amputation of that specific limb are declared to be the punishments for the highest violence.
And acts such as killing, according to the gradation of the offense, should be applied either collectively or individually in cases of the highest violence.
In that regard, he states the punishment for violence consisting of the seizure of another's property:
"The fine shall be double the value of that [property], but if there is denial, it shall be fourfold."
The fine for one who has stolen property is double its value.
Furthermore, he who, having committed a violent act (*sāhasa*), denies it by saying "I did not do it," shall be fined four times the value of the object.
From this very prescription of a specific fine, it is understood that the general prescriptions of fines—such as the first *sāhasa* and so forth—apply to cases other than theft. (2.230)
Regarding the instigator of a violent act, he says: "He who causes a violent act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
and he who, having said 'I will give,' causes it to be done, shall pay four times [the fine]."
But he who, having said "Do this act of violence," causes it to be done, shall be made to pay double the fine for the violent act.

Furthermore, he who, having said "I will give you wealth; you do it," causes a violent act to be committed, shall be made to pay a fourfold fine because of the excessive gravity of the consequence. (2.231)
Regarding specific types of perpetrators of violence, he says: one who throws away or violates the guest-offering (*arghya*), one who strikes his brother's wife,
one who fails to give what has been promised, and one who breaks through a house situated by the sea.
For those who cause harm to neighboring householders and others,
the settled rule is that their fine shall be fifty paṇas.

He who insults or disobeys the commands of those worthy of the *arghya* offering, such as his preceptor (*ācārya*) and others; he who beats his brother’s wife; he who fails to give what has been promised or agreed upon; he who breaks open a sealed house; and he who does harm to the *kulikas*—those born of his own family who are owners of houses, fields, and so forth attached to his own home—as well as (by the inclusion of "and so forth") those belonging to his own village or district—all these are to be punished with a fine of fifty *paṇas*. (2.232–233)
Furthermore:

one who approaches a widow of his own accord, one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help, one who cries out falsely, and a Caṇḍāla who touches those of the highest caste; [these shall be punished].
One who feeds those among Śūdras who have renounced the world at rites for the gods or the ancestors;
one who takes an improper oath; and one who performs the duties of an unfit person—these are unworthy.
One who destroys the virility of bulls or small animals,
one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant’s fetus;
Father, son, sister, brother, husband and wife, teacher, and pupil— among these,
one who abandons another without the latter having fallen from caste shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas].

He who approaches a widow of his own will without her husband’s authorization; he who, though capable, does not run to the rescue when others are crying out in fear of thieves and the like; he who utters groundless abuse; he who, being a Caṇḍāla, touches Brāhmaṇas and others; he who feeds Śūdras, renunciants, Digambaras, and others at rites for the gods or ancestors; he who makes an improper oath such as "I shall violate my mother"; likewise, he who, though unfit, performs the duties and studies appropriate for a Śūdra or others; he who destroys the virility—the procreative power—of bulls or small animals such as goats and the like (in the reading *vṛkṣakṣudrapaśūnām*, one who causes the falling of fruits and flowers from trees by the application of medicinal herbs like *hiṅgu*); he who denies a common property or deceives those entitled to it; he who causes the miscarriage of a maidservant’s fetus; and those fathers and others who, while not themselves outcastes, abandon one another—all these are individually liable to a fine of one hundred *paṇas*. (2.234–237)
In connection with acts of violence, he states the punishment for washermen and others in cases of similar offenses:
"A washerman who wears another's garment is to be fined three *paṇas*;
but in cases of selling, mortgaging, pledging, or borrowing [another's garment], he is to be fined ten *paṇas*."
A washerman who, having been entrusted with garments for the purpose of cleaning, wears them himself, shall be fined three *paṇas*.

Furthermore, he who sells them, or gives them on hire—meaning one who provides the garment for a period of time in exchange for a fee, stipulating "so much money must be paid to me"—or who pledges them as collateral, or gives them to his own friends upon request, shall be fined ten *paṇas* for each such offense.

And those garments are to be washed on a smooth board of *śālmalī* wood, not on a stone; they must not be rubbed against one another, nor should they be kept in the washerman’s own house—otherwise he shall be punished. On a smooth *śālmalī* board the washerman shall wash the clothes; he shall not rub clothes together with clothes, nor shall he let them stay [in his house].
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu.
Furthermore, when one destroys them through negligence, then that which was spoken by Nārada should be observed:
"One-eighth of the value is lost for a garment washed once;
for a second time, a half [is lost]; for a third time, a third part; and for a fourth washing, exactly half."
But beyond the point when half has been exhausted, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter at each stage until it reaches the state of being worn out;
for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its exhaustion.
Thus:
"One-eighth of the value is lost for a garment washed once;
for one washed twice, one-quarter; for one washed thrice, one-third; and for one washed four times, exactly half."
But beyond the point where half has been exhausted, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter at each stage until it reaches the state of being worn out;
for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its exhaustion.
For a garment purchased for eight *paṇas* that has been washed once and is ruined, its value shall be paid minus one-eighth of a *paṇa*.
For one washed twice, it shall be two *paṇas* minus one-quarter; for one washed three times, it shall be less by one-third;
and for one washed four times, half the price, namely four *paṇas*, shall be paid.
After that, the remaining value for the cleansing must be paid, decreasing by one-quarter for each quarter [of the cloth's life].
As long as the worn-out garment has not been destroyed, the determination of the payment of its value shall be according to one's wish. (2.238)
In a dispute between father and son, the fine for witnesses is three paṇas;
but for anyone who stands between them, the fine shall be eightfold.
He who accepts the role of witness in a quarrel between father and son but does not prevent the quarrel shall be fined three *paṇas*.

Furthermore, he who acts as a surety for the payment of the wager in their contested dispute—and by the word "and" (*ca*), he who aggravates their quarrel—shall be punished with twenty-four *paṇas*, which is eight times the amount of the three *paṇas*.
This same punishment is to be applied in cases involving husband and wife, and so forth. (2.239)
One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins,
as well as anyone who deals with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
*Tulā* is a balance-beam;
*śāsana* is as previously described;
*māna* refers to measures such as the *prastha* and *droṇa*.
"Coin" refers to [currency] such as the *dramma* or *niṣka*, marked with seals and other signs.

Of these, he who is a forger—who makes the *dramma* and so forth otherwise than their standard measure established by the country, either by reducing or increasing it, or by making them non-standard coins or filled with copper and other base metals—and he who, knowing them to be forged, nevertheless uses them in trade: both of these are to be punished individually with the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). (2.240)
He says with regard to the examiner of coins:
"He who calls a genuine coin counterfeit, or a counterfeit coin genuine—
he, as an examiner of coins, shall be made to pay the highest fine."

Furthermore, whoever who examines coins, declaring that a dramma or similar coin containing copper or other base metals is genuine, or conversely, declaring a genuine coin to be counterfeit, shall be punished with the highest amercement. (2.241)
He says to the physician:
"A physician who practices falsely shall be punished with the first amercement for treating animals,
the middle amercement for humans, and the highest amercement for royal officers."

Furthermore, any physician who, being ignorant of Āyurveda and yet practicing medicine falsely for the sake of livelihood by claiming "I am a knower of medical treatment," performs medical treatment upon animals, humans, or royal servants, shall be punished with the first, middle, or highest fines respectively.

Even in those cases involving animals and the like, the relative severity or lightness of the punishment must be determined according to the specific value [of the patient], the specific caste, and the specific degree of proximity to the king. 2.242.
He who binds one who should not be bound, he who releases one who has been bound,
and he who obstructs legal proceedings, shall be made to pay the highest fine.

Furthermore, he who imprisons one who does not deserve imprisonment and is innocent, except by the king’s command; and he who releases one who has been imprisoned, summoned for a legal proceeding, and whose case has not yet been concluded—he shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.243)
Whoever should take even an eighth part [of the value] by means of a measure or a scale,
he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred, as determined for cases of increase or decrease.
Furthermore, a merchant who, by means of false measures or false weights, otherwise embezzles an eighth part of merchandise such as rice, cotton, and so forth, shall be fined two hundred *paṇas*.
Moreover, in accordance with the increase or decrease of the value of the stolen goods, an increase or decrease of the fine shall be determined. (2.244)
If one adulterates medicinal herbs, oils, salts, perfumes, grains, molasses, and other such commodities with inferior substances, he shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen paṇas.
Medicine refers to medicinal substances; unctuous substances refer to ghee and the like;
salt is well known.
Fragrant substances include *uśīra* and so forth; *dhānya* (grain) and *guḍa* (molasses) are well known; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *hiṅgu*, *marīca*, and others are included.
For one who mixes worthless substances with these for the purpose of sale, the fine is sixteen paṇas. (2.245)
Furthermore:
For making a false designation of genus for clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark, or cloth when they do not possess that genus, the fine shall be eightfold the value of the saleable item.

That in which no high-value species exists—such as clay, leather, and so forth—is *ajāti*. Regarding such a thing, for the purpose of sale, one brings about the appearance of a high-value species by introducing different scents, colors, and tastes; that is, by producing a resemblance to a high-value species.
For example, by infusing the scent of jasmine, one calls clay "fragrant myrobalan";
by imparting an excellence of color to cat-skin, one calls it "tiger-skin"; and by changing the color of a crystal gem, one calls it a "ruby."
Just as cotton thread becomes "silk thread" by being endowed with an excellence of quality;
or iron becomes "silver" by being endowed with an excellence of color;
or wood from the *bilva* tree becomes "sandalwood" through the infusion of the fragrance of sandalwood.
Regarding *kaṅkola*, it is called "bark" (*tvākhyam*) or "cloves" (*lavaṅgam*). Regarding cotton cloth, because of its excellence in quality, it is called "silk" (*kauśeyam*).

An eightfold fine should be understood as the penalty for merchandise such as clay or leather that has been made to resemble something else for the purpose of sale. (2.246) Furthermore, [the same applies to] exchanging a small box for a valuable commodity or to artificial goods.
For one who mortgages or sells [the image], a punishment shall be prescribed.
For damage of one paṇa, the fine is fifty; for one of five paṇas, it is said to be one hundred;
for two paṇas, the fine is two hundred; and as the value increases, the fine increases accordingly.
A *samudga* is a casket (*karaṇḍaka*) that contains a covering (*mudga*) together with its contents; *parivartana* means exchange or substitution.

The prescribed punishment for one who, having shown a casket filled with one thing such as pearls, hands over another casket filled with something else such as crystals through sleight of hand, or who sells or mortgages counterfeit precious goods such as artificial musk, should be understood as follows:
it applies when the *paṇa*—the monetary value of the artificial musk and so forth—is either broken or deficient.
That is to say, "for a value of less than one paṇa. When such a counterfeit item is sold, the fine is fifty paṇas; however, if its value is one paṇa, the fine is one hundred.
If the value is two paṇas, the fine is two hundred; in this manner, the increase of the fine should be inferred from the increase in value. (2.247–248)
He says in reply to the merchants:
"For those who act in concert to cause distress to artisans and craftsmen by manipulating the price—
whether they knowingly cause a decrease or an increase in the price— the punishment is the highest amercement."

Even though they know the decrease or increase in the price fixed by the king, merchants who, having banded together, establish a different price that is oppressive and harmful to artisans such as washermen and craftsmen such as painters out of greed for profit, shall be fined ten thousand paṇas. (2.249)
Furthermore: For merchants who, acting in concert, withhold merchandise by fixing an improper price,
or who sell it [at such a price], the prescribed fine is the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa).

Furthermore, those merchants who, having assembled together, obstruct goods brought from another country by demanding a low price when it is worth more, or sell them at a high price when it is worth less—for them, the highest fine (uttamasāhasa) has been prescribed by Manu and others. (2.250)
But by what price should it be bartered? To this he says: "The price that is established for the king, by that daily sale or purchase [is made];
from that, the outflow is known as the profit of the merchants."

When the king is present, whatever price is established or determined by him, trade—whether purchase or sale—must be conducted daily according to that price. Any surplus (*niḥsrava*) derived from that royal-determined price is what benefits the merchants, and not that which is arbitrarily devised by themselves. Furthermore, Manu has shown a specific rule regarding the determination of prices: [Manu 8.159–160] "The king shall establish the price of commodities after considering their origin, their destination, the duration of storage, the distance of transport, and the profit and loss. [Manu 8.397] "He who sells for a price lower than that fixed by the king, or buys at a price higher than that, shall be fined one suvarṇa. [Manu 8.401] "If he sells for less than the fixed price, he shall pay a fine of six hundred paṇas; likewise, if he buys for more, he shall be punished in the same manner. [Manu 8.402] "But if he sells for less because of the goods' deterioration, or buys for more because of their improvement, he commits no offense, provided he informs the king. [Manu 8.403] "The king shall fix the price of commodities on the first day of the fortnight, taking into account the place, the time, and the quality of the goods. [Manu 8.404] "He must never sell commodities himself, nor cause them to be sold by others; nor should he, being greedy, obstruct the sale of merchandise. [Manu 8.405] "He shall cause the price of all commodities to be proclaimed publicly every morning and evening. [Manu 8.406] "In the marketplace, he shall have a balance, weights, and measures tested every five days. [Manu 8.408] "He shall cause the price of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven cloths, perfumes, and medicinal herbs to be determined by experts. Every five nights, at the end of a fortnight, and likewise at the end of a month,
the king should perform the formal offering of the guest-water (argha) in their presence.
Thus [ends verse 2.251].
Every five nights, at the end of a fortnight, and likewise at the end of a month,
the king should perform the formal offering of water (argha) in their presence.
Furthermore:
A merchant who buys and sells immediately shall take five percent on goods from his own country, but ten percent on those from a foreign land.

One who sells merchandise obtained in his own country shall take a profit of five per cent— that is, five *paṇas* for every hundred *paṇas*. However, in the case of merchandise obtained from a foreign country, he shall take a profit of ten *paṇas* for every hundred *paṇas* of value,
provided that the sale is completed on the very day the purchase was made.
Furthermore, for one who sells after a lapse of time, an increase in profit should be calculated based on the lengthening of that period.
And thus, once the price has been determined, the king should fix the price for goods produced in his own country in such a way that a profit of five *paṇas* accrues on every hundred *paṇas*. (2.252)
He states the method for determining the price of foreign merchandise:
"Having added to the value of the merchandise the expenses incurred in its production,
a price that provides favor to both the buyer and the seller should be established."

When merchandise has arrived from another country, the king should calculate the total amount of wealth expended at the various stages—such as the journey to and from the foreign land and the collection of duties on the goods—and, having added that sum to the cost price of the merchandise, he should fix the market price (*argha*) so as to provide favor to both the buyer and the seller, ensuring that a profit of ten per cent is realized on every hundred coins. (2.253)
Having concluded the incidental discussion, the non-delivery after sale (*vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*) is now introduced. Its nature has been described by Nārada:
"When, having sold a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer..."
The non-delivery after having sold is called that title of dispute.
Thus:
"When, after selling a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer—
that is called the legal head of dispute known as 'non-delivery after sale'."
In that regard, having stated that merchandise for sale is of two kinds—distinguished as mobile and immobile—the same author further established its sixfold nature:
"In this world, merchandise is of two kinds, namely mobile and immobile;
however, the rules for the giving and taking thereof are recorded by the wise as being sixfold."
It was calculated, weighed, measured, and assessed by its action, form, and splendor.
Thus it is said:
"In this world, merchandise is of two kinds: moving and stationary;
however, the wise have prescribed a sixfold rule for its giving and receiving."
It has been calculated, weighed, measured, and examined by its action, its form, and its splendor.
That which is counted includes betel nuts and the like; that which is weighed includes gold, musk, saffron, and so forth;
and that which is measured includes rice and the like.
Horses, buffaloes, and the like are characterized by their activity, such as carrying or milking;
courtesans and the like by their form;
and emeralds, rubies, and the like by their splendor or luster.
He states the penalty for one who sells these six kinds of merchandise but does not deliver them:
"If a person has received the price but does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be made to pay it with interest;
or, if the goods were brought from another region, he shall pay the profit derived from that region."

If the seller does not deliver to the purchaser—a merchant from his own country who has requested it—the commodity for which the price was already received, and if that commodity, having been high-priced at the time of purchase, can subsequently be obtained for a low price, then the seller must cause the purchaser to receive the commodity together with the profit (*udaya*) arising from the decrease in its value, whether the commodity be immovable or movable.

When there is no increase in the value of the commodity caused by a decrease in its market price, but rather at the time of purchase it was agreed that "for this much price, this much commodity is obtained," then the seller, taking that commodity and selling it in that region, shall be made to pay the buyer the profit derived from that sale, combined with the interest (vṛddhi) specified as two-fold, three-fold, and so forth; or he may be made to pay the profit combined with the interest as determined by the buyer's desire.
As Nārada says:
"If the market price should fall, the seller shall deliver the commodity together with the interest."
This rule applies to those who remain stationary; for those who travel through various directions, it concerns the acquisition of their respective regions.
Thus:
"If the profit (argha) should fall short, one shall bring back the merchandise with interest.
This rule applies to those staying in place; for those traveling in various directions, it concerns the profits of their respective regions."

But when, due to the high value of the price, the commodity becomes deficient [in utility], then the seller must be made to deliver that commodity—such as clothing, a house, or the like—along with whatever enjoyment it provides, such as the pleasure of wearing it or the comfort of dwelling in it.
As Nārada says:
"He who, having sold a commodity for its price, does not deliver it to the buyer..."
One shall be made to pay the loss of immovable property, and the fruit of the labor for movable property.
Thus:
"He who, having sold a commodity for its price, does not deliver it to the buyer,
shall be made to pay the loss of the immovable property, and the fruit of the labor for the movable property."

The "consumption" (*upabhoga*) of the seller is said to be its depletion, because it is being depleted through its connection with the buyer; it does not, however, refer to forms such as the collapse of a wall or the destruction of crops. For that [seller], however: "If the commodity should be damaged, burnt, or stolen, that loss belongs solely to the seller who, having sold it, does not deliver it."
This is because it has been stated thus.

However, when the buyer has come from another country for the purpose of acquiring merchandise, then the seller must cause the merchandise—along with whatever profit he may have made by selling it in another country—to be delivered to the buyer. And this rule regarding the delivery of the purchased merchandise is to be understood as applying in the absence of a rescission of the sale.
But when a latent tendency remains, one should understand that what was stated by Manu—"having bought or sold something," and so forth—applies. 2.254.
Furthermore: Even if a commodity has been sold, it may be resold if the original buyer does not take delivery;
for if the loss occurs due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall indeed belong to the buyer alone.

Furthermore, when the purchaser, having developed a latent aversion (*anuśaya*), does not wish to take possession of the commodity, then even though it has been sold, the commodity may be sold elsewhere.

However, when the purchaser does not accept the commodity being offered by the seller, and that commodity is subsequently destroyed by the king or by an act of God (*daiva*), then this loss shall belong to the purchaser alone, because it was ruined by the purchaser's own fault in the form of his refusal to accept the commodity. (2.255)
Moreover:
"If a defect arises in the merchandise due to injury caused by the king or fate,
the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked for it, does not deliver it."

But when the seller does not deliver the commodity even though it is requested by the buyer, and although he has no subsequent regret, the commodity is nevertheless destroyed by the king or by fate, then that loss falls upon the seller alone.
Therefore, he must give to the buyer another non-defective commodity that is equivalent to the one lost. (2.256)
Furthermore:
If one has sold [an item] into the hand of another, or if one sells what is defective as if it were non-defective,
the fine in that case shall be double the value.

Furthermore, if one sells what has already been sold into another's hand without the prior owner's consent, or sells a defective commodity while concealing its defects, then a fine double the value of that commodity should be understood to be imposed.
Nārada also shows a specific rule in this regard:
"He who, having sold it into one person's hand, delivers it to another..."
He shall be made to pay double the value of the object, and the fine for his correction shall be exactly that same amount.
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double the price and an equal amount as a fine.
Thus [it is said].
He who, having sold an item into the hand of one person, delivers it to another, shall be made to pay double the value of that property; the fine for his misconduct shall be exactly the same amount.
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double the price and an equal amount as a fine.
This entire rule is to be understood as applying when the price for the commodity has been paid.

However, regarding a commodity for which the price has not been paid, if there is a mere verbal agreement of purchase, there is no fault whatsoever—whether in proceeding with or withdrawing from the transaction—for either the buyer or the seller, provided they have not entered into a formal contractual obligation (*samaya*). As Nārada says:
"This rule has been proclaimed for a commodity whose price has been paid."
Except in accordance with an agreement, there is no non-delivery by the seller once the price has been received.
Thus [it is said].
This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
when it has not been paid, except by prior agreement, there is no non-delivery on the part of the seller.
The rescission of sale has been explained;
the nature of the rescission of purchase, however, was already detailed previously.
Now, he states the rule common to both of them.
A merchant who, being ignorant of the depreciation or appreciation of his wares, has no right to rescind a purchase; if he does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth.

Regarding goods purchased after inspection, once the purchase has been finalized, the buyer shall not exercise a right of rescission (*anuśaya*) if he fails to perceive the increase in value resulting from the price fluctuations between the time of purchase and the later period. Likewise, the seller shall not seek rescission if he fails to perceive the loss of value of the commodity resulting from high prices at the time of sale.
By implication, it is stated that rescission is permissible for both buyer and seller only when there is a failure to ascertain such increases or decreases in value.
Regarding the time limit for the period of the latent defect (anuśaya), Nārada has stated: "If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is still unspoiled."
If the purchaser delivers it on the second day, he shall pay a thirtieth part of the price as a fine;
if on the third day, double that amount; after that, the loss falls solely upon the purchaser.
Thus:
If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is undamaged.
If the purchaser delivers [the item] on the second day, he shall pay a thirtieth part of the price;
but on the third day, double that amount; after that, it belongs to the purchaser alone.

Furthermore, regarding sales and purchases made without due inspection, the limit for rescission based on defects in the merchandise has already been shown by such statements as "ten days, one day, five days, seven days," and so forth.
By this line of reasoning, it is understood that the thorough knowledge of increase and decrease is the cause for rescission.

Just as the determination of the merits and defects of merchandise through the rules of examination is a cause for rescission, therefore, in the absence of these three factors—the defect in the merchandise, its increase, or its decrease—if one effects a rescission even within the period allowed for rescission, he shall be fined one-sixth of the value of the merchandise.
Even when the grounds for a latent claim (*anuśaya*) exist, this same penalty applies to one who allows the period for such a claim to lapse.
Regarding durable goods of stable value that do not perish through use, the penalty prescribed by Manu should be understood to apply to one who lets the period for a latent claim expire.
However, after ten days have passed, one shall neither deliver the item nor cause it to be delivered.
One who takes [the property] or one who gives it away shall be fined six hundred by the king.
Thus it is said.
But after ten days, one should neither give nor cause [the object] to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
The legal topic known as "Joint Undertaking" is now being expounded.
When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a collective association,
their gains and losses shall be according to their respective contributions or as determined by their agreement.

The consensus that "we all, having gathered together, shall perform this work" constitutes a *samavāya* (partnership). By virtue of this, for those such as merchants, actors, and dancers who, desiring profit, perform their respective individual tasks, their gains and losses—that is, their increases and decreases—must be determined according to the goods, in accordance with the amount of wealth each contributed for the purpose of purchasing merchandise and so forth.

Alternatively, they are to be understood as having been agreed upon by a convention (*saṃvita*) consisting of a mutual understanding that "this is one part" and "this is the other part," based on a consideration of their primary and secondary status. || 2.259 ||
Furthermore:

"Whatever has been forbidden, whatever was not specifically assigned, and whatever has been lost through negligence—he shall restore that; and from what is recovered after a disaster, he shall receive a tenth part."

Among those who are trading together, if one acts contrary to what has been prohibited—thinking "this merchandise must not be dealt with in this way"—and thereby causes loss; or if, while acting without instruction or permission, he causes loss through negligence or lack of intelligence, he shall give that lost merchandise back to the merchants.
Furthermore, whoever among them protects the merchandise from calamities such as thieves or kings shall receive a tenth part of that protected merchandise. (2.260)
The king shall take a twentieth part as duty from the offering of the *argha*;
however, that which is established by experts (*vyāsiddha*), what is fit for the king, and what has been sold [as such], belongs to the king.

The *argha* (market price) is the value assigned to such a quantity of merchandise; because of its presentation—that is, its appraisal by the king—he shall take the twentieth part of that value for the purpose of tax (*śulka*).

Furthermore, regarding that which is "prohibited" (*vyāsiddha*)—meaning forbidden by the king from being sold elsewhere—and that which is "fit for the king" (*rājayogya*), such as jewels, rubies, and the like, even if not explicitly forbidden: if these are sold without informing the king out of greed for profit, then all such merchandise shall be confiscated by the king, regardless of whether the seller has paid its value. This is the meaning of verse 2.261.

One who speaks falsely regarding the quantity [of goods] while departing from a customs station shall be made to pay eight times [the value]; the same applies to one who practices fraudulent buying and selling.

Furthermore, any merchant who conceals the quantity of his merchandise for the purpose of defrauding the customs duty, or who evades the place where duties are collected, or who buys or sells merchandise that has become the subject of a dispute—saying "this belongs to him" or "that belongs to him"—all such persons shall be fined eight times the value of the merchandise. (2.262)
Moreover:
A ferryman taking toll for goods transported by land shall be fined ten *paṇas*;
this same fine applies to Brahmins and neighbors for failing to invite one another [to a meal].
For toll is of two kinds: land-based and water-based.
Regarding the land-based, it has been stated here that "the king shall take a twentieth part as toll from the setting of the price.
As for the water-based, however, it has been declared by Manu.
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
an animal and a woman, a quarter paṇa; and an empty-handed man, half of a quarter paṇa.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without luggage, shall pay whatever little they can.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering ascetic,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks— these persons shall not be made to pay ferry tolls.
Thus [it is said].
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
a beast and a woman, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half a quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they possess.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a renunciant,
a sage, Brahmins, and those bearing religious marks— these persons shall not be made to pay ferry tolls.
Regarding both types of tolls, there is this further distinction:
there is no toll on a broken kārṣāpaṇa coin, nor on the proceeds of a craft, nor on an infant, nor on a messenger;
nor on what is obtained as alms, nor on the remnants of a plundered haul, nor on a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), nor on one who has renounced the world, nor at a sacrifice.
Thus.
There is no customs duty on a broken kārṣāpaṇa coin, nor on artisan’s wares, nor on an infant, nor on a messenger;
nor on what is obtained as alms, nor on the remnants of a plundered spoil, nor on a learned Vedic scholar, nor on one who has renounced the world, nor at a sacrifice.
That by which one crosses is a "crossing" (*tari*), such as a boat; one who is authorized over the toll (*śulka*) arising from that is a "toll-collector" (*tarikah*).
When he collects a toll levied on land, he is to be fined ten *paṇas*.
A "dwelling" (*veśa*) is a house; a "neighboring dwelling" (*prativeśa*) refers to that which is situated facing one's own house or adjacent to it.
In this context, "neighboring Brahmins" refers to those who are both residents and Brahmins;

for them—provided they are endowed with learning and good conduct—if they are not invited to śrāddha ceremonies and the like despite having the means, this same fine consisting of ten paṇas is to be understood as the penalty. (2.263)
Regarding the inheritance of a merchant who has died in a foreign land, he says:
"When one has died while traveling in a foreign land, his heirs, kinsmen, or relatives shall take the property upon their arrival; in their absence, the king shall take it."

When, among those who have engaged in a joint enterprise, anyone has gone to another country or died, then his share shall be taken by the heirs—consisting of the group of offspring such as sons and so forth; or by the kinsmen from the mother’s side, such as maternal uncles and others; or by the cognates, that is, the *sapiṇḍas* other than the group of offspring; or by those who have come from another country and are partners in the business.
In the absence of these heirs and others, the king shall take it.
By the word "or" (*vā*), he indicates that the entitlement of the heirs and the rest is optional.
The rule regarding priority (*paurvāparya-niyama*)—established previously by the passage beginning with "the wife, the daughters," and so forth—is to be understood here as well.
The purpose of the statement is to exclude the student (*śiṣya*), the fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*), and the *brāhmaṇa*, while including the merchant (*vaṇik*).
Even among merchants, he who is capable of offering the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and discharging debts and so forth should take [the inheritance].
If there is no difference in their respective capacities, however, all the merchants shall divide and take the property as co-sharers (*saṃsṛṣṭinaḥ*).
In the absence of even them, the king should wait for ten years for the arrival of the heirs; if they do not arrive, the king himself may take it.
This has been made clear by Nārada.
If there should be death of one [member], his heir shall receive that;
or, if there is no heir, all of them together shall receive it, provided they are capable.
In the absence of such a person, however, he should cause it to be kept in secret for ten years;
thereafter, that which has remained for ten years shall be ownerless and without an heir.
The king should indeed appropriate that for himself; in this way, the Dharma is not lost.
Thus [ends verse] 2.264.
Then, after ten years have passed, it becomes ownerless and without an heir.
The king should indeed make that his own; in this way, the Dharma is not lost.
Furthermore:
"They should abandon the dishonest one who yields no profit; if unable [to do so], they should have another perform it.
"Dishonest" (*jihma*) means deceitful. They should abandon—that is, expel from the group—the one who yields no profit, having stripped him of his gain.

And whoever among those acting in partnership is unable to perform tasks such as the inspection of merchandise should have his own work—namely, the carrying of the load of goods and the examination of income, expenditure, and so forth—performed by another.
He extends the duty of merchants previously taught to the officiating priests and others:
"By this rule, the procedure for officiating priests, cultivators, and laborers has been declared."

By this discourse on the duties of merchants, beginning with "gain and loss according to the goods," the rule—that is, the mode of livelihood—has been declared for the officiating priests such as the *hotṛ* and others, for farmers, and for those who subsist by their craft, such as actors, dancers, and wrestlers.
And regarding the division of wealth among the officiating priests, a specific rule has been shown by Manu:
"The principal [priests] receive half of everything; the others receive half of that [half]."
Those entitled to a third share receive one-third, and those entitled to a quarter receive one-fourth.
Thus [it is said].
Among all [the priests], the chief ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third part, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part.
This is the meaning:

by the statement, "They consecrate him with the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice using a hundred [cows]," a hundred cows are assigned to the function of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the form of the propitiation of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
And the officiating priests are sixteen, beginning with the Hotṛ.
In this regard, when the question arises as to who receives what portion, the following is stated:

Among all sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), beginning with the *hotṛ*, those four who are primary—the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, *brahman*, and *udgātṛ*—are entitled to half of the hundred cows. This is because they receive a share consisting of forty-eight forms, which serves to complete the distribution for all.
The others—the *maitrāvaruṇa*, *pratiprasthātṛ*, *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, and *prastotṛ*—receive half of that, namely twenty-four forms, which constitutes half of the primary share.
Furthermore, those who receive a third share—the Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Āgnīdhra, and Pratihartṛ—are entitled to a third share of the principal portion in the form of a sixteenth cow.
Those who receive a fourth share—the Grāvastut, Unnetṛ, Potṛ, and Subrahmaṇya—are entitled to that which is the fourth share of the principal portion, consisting of a twelfth cow.

Now, how is this restriction of shares possible? For there is neither a convention here, nor an inherence in a substance, nor a scriptural statement by virtue of which such a restriction of portions could exist. Therefore, according to the maxim "it should be equal because it is not heard otherwise," it is logical that all [heirs] should receive equal shares, or that they should receive shares in proportion to their labor.
To this it is replied:

In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which has the Jyotiṣṭoma as its archetype, the descriptive reference—“the half-sharers, the third-part sharers, the quarter-sharers”—as an established fact would not be possible if the Maitrāvaruṇa and others did not possess the status of receiving a half, a third, and a fourth part in that archetype, the Jyotiṣṭoma. Therefore, by the force of the Vedic designations such as *ṛddhi* and so forth, the previously mentioned rule regarding the portions is justified; thus, [the position] is faultless. 2.2.65.
Now theft is introduced. Its definition has been stated by Manu:
"Sāhasa (violent crime) is that act which is committed with force, provided there is evidence of the perpetrator."
"Theft is that which is committed without connection [to witnesses] and what one denies having done;
whereas *sāhasa* (violence) is an act committed by force with connection [to witnesses]."
Theft (*steya*) is that which occurs without witnesses (*niranvaya*), as well as when one commits an act and then denies it.
An act accompanied by witnesses (*anvayavat*) is that which is done in the presence of the guardian of the property, the king, or officials;
whereas *sāhasa* (violence) is the seizing of another's wealth and so forth, performed through forceful coercion (*prasabham*).

Theft, however, is defined as the taking of another's property by deceiving them, in their absence, and without the presence of the owner of the goods or others; it is distinct from that [other form of taking].
Moreover, even when an act is committed in the presence of others, if one denies it out of fear, saying "I did not do this," that too is theft.
Nārada also said: "The wise declare that theft consists of the removal of these [goods] after having deceived them by various means, [taking from those who are] asleep, intoxicated, or heedless."
Thus [it is said].
The wise declare that theft consists of the removal of these [goods] after deceiving them by various means, while they are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless.
In this regard, since punishment is preceded by the apprehension of the thief, and apprehension is preceded by knowledge, he first states the means of gaining that knowledge:
"The thief is apprehended by the pursuers either through the stolen property or through his tracks;
likewise, one who has committed a prior offense, as well as one who resides in an impure place."
He who is proclaimed by the people as "this is a thief" is to be seized by the apprehenders— the king’s officers, local guardians, and so forth—
