One whose two years are deficient—that is, less than two years old—one should bury that deceased child; having made a pit in the ground, one should place him there, but one must not cremate him—this is the meaning.

Nor should one perform the funeral rites for the deceased, such as the offering of water and so forth, which are prescribed with reference to the dead, according to the rule "they do not pour water once" and other such injunctions.
Furthermore, having adorned the child with perfumes, garlands, ointments, and the like, he should be buried outside the village in clean ground—other than a cemetery and free from heaps of bones.
As Manu has said:
"Relatives should place a deceased child who is less than two years old outside,
having adorned it on pure ground, except for the collection of bones."
For him, no funeral rite with fire should be performed, nor should the water-libation be offered;
having abandoned him like a log in the forest, they should simply cast him away after three days.
Thus:
"Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside [the village],
having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones."
For him, no consecration with fire should be performed, nor should the water-rite be performed;
having abandoned him in the forest like a log of wood, they should simply cast him away after three days.
The meaning of the phrase "having abandoned [the child] like a piece of wood in the forest" is as follows:

just as people become indifferent toward a piece of wood abandoned in the forest, so too, having cast away a child less than two years old in the ground, one should remain indifferent regarding funeral rites (*śrāddha*) and other post-mortem ceremonies for that child. By this illustration, the absence of *śrāddha* and other rites—though otherwise required by custom—is indicated.

Furthermore, such a child should be buried after being anointed with ghee while those reciting the verses of Yama perform the rite: "One should bury a deceased child less than two years old in the earth, anointed with ghee."
Singing the Yamagāthā while recollecting the Yamasūkta.
Thus, according to the recollection of Yama.

Therefore, other than that child less than two years old, one who has died at full two years of age is to be followed as far as the cremation ground by the kinsmen—the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*—preceded by the eldest. From this very statement, it is understood that following a child less than two years old is not mandatory.

And having followed [the deceased], while reciting the *Yamasūkta* beginning with "pareyivāṃsam" and the verses dedicated to Yama, he should be cremated by means of a worldly (*laukika*) fire that has not been consecrated (*asaṃskṛta*), provided that a fire-drill (*araṇi*) has not been produced.

However, if such a fire-drill exists, he should be cremated by fire produced by churning it, and not by a worldly fire; for the worldly fire arises solely for the purpose of performing tasks accomplished by fire.

Furthermore, the worldly fire to be used must be one distinct from that of a *caṇḍāla* and others, for it is said: "The fire of a *caṇḍāla*, the fire of impurity (*amedhya*), and the fire of a woman who has recently given birth—these should never [be used]."
The fallen fire and the funeral pyre fire are not fit to be accepted by the learned.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Devala. And Laugākṣi has stated a specific rule regarding this:
"One should perform the water-libation silently, and likewise the funeral rite (saṃskāra) silently."
For all those who have had their tonsure ceremony performed, both [options] apply even in other cases, according to one's wish.
Thus:
"One should perform the water libation silently, and likewise the funeral rite silently;
for all those who have undergone the tonsure ceremony, both may be performed even otherwise according to one's wish."
The meaning is this: immediately after the *caula* ceremony, the offering of fire and water must invariably be performed.

Furthermore, even in other cases after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), even for one whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has not yet been performed, the two rites consisting of the offering of fire and water may be performed silently at will out of a desire for the deceased's spiritual welfare; however, this is not mandatory, and thus there is an option.
Manu also has shown a specific rule regarding this matter.
The water-rite (udakakriyā) should not be performed for one who has not reached three years of age by his relatives;
however, they may perform it once teeth have appeared, or even when the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa) has been completed.
Thus:
"The water-rite (udakakriyā) should not be performed for one under three years of age by his relatives;
however, they may perform it for one whose teeth have emerged, or once the naming ceremony has been completed."

The mention of "water" (*udaka*) is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the fire-rite (*agni-saṃskāra*) as well, due to their association; this is because of the statement, "not for one under three years of age. Furthermore, even when the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) is postponed out of regard for family custom, it is understood that the rule regarding the offering of water, fire, and so forth applies after the third year.
However, based on the statement of Laugākṣi, it must be discerned that for one who has already undergone the tonsure ceremony, the rule for those two [rites] applies even before the third year.

If he is "endowed," that is, if he has been initiated (*upanīta*), then he should be cremated with the procedure for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), according to the method well-known in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and so forth, using only the ordinary fire (*laukikāgni*).
This is "purposeful" (*arthavat*), meaning it serves a specific purpose.

The meaning is this: if there exists for him a prescribed means of cremation that serves a functional purpose—such as the selection of the ground, its sprinkling, and so forth—that [procedure] should be adopted.
Furthermore, those [rites] such as the preparation of the sacrificial vessels whose purpose has ceased are discontinued.

Likewise, because their purpose has been superseded by the injunction for cremation with the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*)—as opposed to the injunction for cremation with the worldly fire (*laukikāgni*) for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)—the *āhavanīya* and other such fires are also discontinued.
And the rule regarding other fires has been stated by Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya:
"A person who has maintained the sacred fires (Āhitāgni) should be cremated according to the rule with the three fires;
one who has not maintained the sacred fires (Anāhitāgni) with a single worldly fire; and any other person with [a single] worldly fire."
Thus: One who has maintained the sacred fires should be cremated according to rule with the three fires;
another person who has not maintained the sacred fires [should be cremated] with one common fire.

Furthermore, a Śūdra must not perform the task of bringing firewood, fuel, and so forth to the cremation ground; for he whose Śūdra brings the fire, the grass, the wood, and the sacrificial oblations remains forever in the state of a ghost, and he is defiled by unrighteousness.
Thus, according to the recollection of Yama.

Likewise, the cremation must be performed immediately after the ritual bathing, because of the traditional injunction: "One should cremate the deceased after he has been bathed with auspicious perfumes and adorned with garlands.
This has also been stated by Pracetas.
The sons and other relatives should perform the bathing of the deceased and likewise offer worship with garments and other articles;
one must never cremate a naked body, and one should give up nothing [that is required].
Thus it is said: "The sons and others should perform the bathing of the deceased and likewise the honoring with garments and other offerings;
one must never burn a naked body, nor should one abandon anything that ought to be given."
The meaning is that one should give away—that is, relinquish—a portion of the shroud of the corpse as something to be given, for the purpose of clothing those who dwell in the cremation ground.
Likewise, Manu has also shown a specific rule regarding the removal of a corpse:
"One should not have a deceased Brāhmaṇa carried away by a Śūdra while his own kinsmen are present;
for that offering, defiled by contact with a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven."
And here, the phrase "while their own [elders] are present" is not intended to be emphasized, because of the scriptural mention of defects such as the failure to attain heaven.
One should carry out a deceased Śūdra by way of the southern gate;
but the twice-born [castes] should be carried out by the western, northern, and eastern gates, respectively.
Likewise, Hārīta also states: "They should not carry a deceased person facing toward a village.

However, when the body of one who has died while away from home cannot be found, then one should fashion a substitute using bones; or, if even those are unavailable, one should fashion a substitute using leaf-veins (*parṇaśara*) according to the procedure taught in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* of Śaunaka and others, and the funeral rite (*saṃskāra*) must be performed.

In this case, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for ten days and so forth, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "If one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) dies while traveling abroad, having performed the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), the period of impurity is the same as for a corpse."

But one who has not maintained the sacred fires shall be cremated with well-ground [grains] mixed with water by his kinsmen after three nights have passed, while they say: "To that man for the sake of the heavenly world, svāhā!"
Having thus burned a leaf-quiver, one shall remain impure for three nights.
Because of this statement, the meaning is as follows: prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), there is only burial and no offering of water or other rites;
thereafter, until the end of the third year, the offering of fire and water is optional.
Thereafter, until the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the offering of fire and water is invariably performed silently;
this applies even for one who has undergone the tonsure (*cūḍā*) prior to the age of three.

After the initiation, however, having performed the cremation according to the ritual procedure for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), all the post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadehika*) must be carried out.

But this is the distinction: for one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), cremation must be performed with a common fire (*laukikāgni*); for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), cremation must be performed with the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), and the joining of the ritual vessels (*pātrayojana*) should be performed as far as possible. 3.1–3.2.
Regarding what should be done after the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*), he says:

"From the seventh or even the tenth day, the kinsmen approach the water facing the direction of the ancestors, [reciting]: *May the evil burn away from us with this [water]*. (*apa naḥ śośucad agham*).

Within seven days, or up until the tenth day, the kinsmen—those of the same lineage (*samānagotra*), those who share the funeral cake (*sapiṇḍa*), and those connected by water (*samānodaka*)—approach the water while facing south, reciting the mantra: *apa naḥ śośucad agham*. By the term "approaching" (*abhyupagamana*), what is indicated is the specific act of offering water for that purpose; this is because an extension (*atideśa*) of the water-offering is seen immediately thereafter in the rule regarding maternal grandfathers and teachers: "In the same way [it is done] for maternal grandfathers and teachers. Furthermore, this should be performed on odd lunar days, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "The water-rite is performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth [days]."

And this [rite] is to be performed immediately after the bath, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śātātapa: "Having cast the body into the fire, they enter the water without looking back.

Likewise, a specific rule has been shown here by Pracetas: "The kinsmen of the deceased, descending into the water according to their seniority, should not splash [the water]; at the edge of the water, they should pour it out while wearing their sacred threads and garments over the right shoulder (apassavya), facing south for a Brāhmaṇa, facing north for a Kṣatriya, and facing west for a Vaiśya."
In another Smṛti, however, it is stated that the offering of water should be repeated for as many days as the period of impurity lasts.
As Viṣṇu says: "They should offer water and rice-balls (piṇḍas) for the deceased for as long as the period of impurity continues."
And likewise it has been said by Pracetas:
"Day after day, one should offer full handfuls of water for the sake of the deceased;
the increase [of offerings] should be continued until the final rice-ball (piṇḍa) is completed."
Thus:
"Day by day, one should offer full handfuls of water for the sake of the deceased;
the increase should be continued until the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is completed."
The meaning is that one must increase the number of *añjali*s every day until the tenth *piṇḍa* is completed.

Although the purpose of the scripture is accomplished by performing either one of these two procedures—the heavy or the light—nevertheless, because it is impossible for one to engage in the heavier procedure due to its bringing about much affliction, it must be assumed that it will result in a superior benefit for the deceased; otherwise, there would be the consequence of the uselessness of the tradition of the heavier procedure.
Vasiṣṭha has also stated a specific rule: "They should perform the water-rite with both hands, the left over the right. (3.3)

He states an extension [of the rule] for the offering of water to maternal grandfathers and others who do not belong to the same *gotra*, which is distinguished by the qualities of name, lineage, and so forth, as well as by the "single pouring" (*sakṛtpraseka*) that will be described hereafter:
"In this manner, the water-rite is performed for deceased maternal grandfathers and teachers;
voluntary water-offerings are made for friends, married daughters, sisters' sons, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests."

Just as water is offered for deceased persons who are of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or are *sapinda* relatives, so too must the perpetual water-rite (*udakakriyā*) be performed for deceased maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*), teachers (*ācārya*), friends (*sakhi*), married daughters and sisters (*pratta*), nephews (*svastrīya*), fathers-in-law (*śvaśura*), and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). For these deceased individuals beginning with friends, the "water of affection" (*kāmodaka*) should be offered;
"affection" (*kāma*) here means desire.

The meaning is that "water-offering out of desire" (*kāmodaka*) refers to the giving of water when there is a desire for the prosperity of the deceased; if such a desire is absent, water need not be given, and there is no fault (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance. (3.4)
He states the rule for the merit of giving water:
"Restraining their speech, they should sprinkle water once, [pronouncing] the name and clan [of the deceased]. And that giving of water should be performed in this manner."

The *sapindas* and *samānodakas*, having become silent, should pronounce the name and lineage of the deceased and pour water only once, saying, "May the deceased named so-and-so of such-and-such a lineage be satisfied," or they may do so three times; for it is recorded in the *Smṛti* of Pracetas: "They should perform the pouring three times, saying, 'May the deceased be satisfied. Furthermore, the daily increase of the number of *añjalis* has already been established.
Likewise, this specific detail was stated by that same author:
Then, having gone to the riverbank and performed purification according to the rules,
one should first thoroughly clean one's garment and thereafter perform the ritual bath.
Then, having bathed with his clothes on, being pure and with a restrained mind,
he should take a stone and offer ten handfuls of water to the brahmins.
One should give twelve [strokes] for a Kṣatriya; fifteen are prescribed for a Vaiśya;
thirty should be given for a Śūdra. Then one should enter the house; thereafter, bathing must be performed again, and the purification of the house should be carried out.
Thus [it is said].
Then, having gone to the riverbank and performed purification according to the rules,
one should first wash one's clothes and thereafter perform the ritual bath.
Then, having bathed with his clothes on, being pure and with a restrained mind,
he should take a stone and offer ten handfuls of water to the brahmins.
One should give twelve [strokes] for a Kṣatriya; fifteen are prescribed for a Vaiśya;
thirty are to be given for a Śūdra; thereafter one should enter the house. Then a bath must be performed again, and one should cause the purification of the house to be carried out.
Among the sapindas, he states the prohibition of the offering of water for certain individuals:
"Students and likewise those who are outcasts shall not perform the water-offering."

Even though they are kinsmen, those who are celibate students (*brahmacārin*) until their return home (*samāvartana*), as well as those who have fallen (*patita*)—having lost their entitlement to the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*)—should not perform the offering of water and other rites.
However, after the period of celibacy has passed, one must certainly perform the offering of water and observe the impurity (*aśauca*) for one's *sapiṇḍa* relatives and others who died previously.
As Manu said:
One who has been initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of the vow;
but once it is completed, having offered the water libation, he shall remain impure for three nights.
Thus it is said:
"One who has been initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
but once the vow is completed, having offered the water libation, he shall remain impure for three nights."

"Ādiṣṭī brahmacārī" (the student who has received instructions). The NSP edition reads: "kasya brahmacārī. He is called a *brahmacārī* because of his engagement in the assignment of vows (*vratādeśa*), such as: "Drink this water, perform your duties, do not sleep during the day," and so forth. And he will state that this [designation] is distinct from the father and others, in the passage: "The teacher, the father, and the sub-teacher. Furthermore, the Teacher (Bhartṛyajña) considers it thus: "Ādiṣṭī" refers to one who has commenced a penance; this prohibition regarding the offering of water and so forth applies to him alone. After the completion of the vow consisting of penance, there is the rule for the offering of water and the period of impurity.

Likewise, the offering of water libations is prohibited for eunuchs and others: "Eunuchs and the like, thieves, those who have not undergone initiation, those who act contrary to the law, those who destroy the fetus or their master, and women who drink liquor—these shall not offer water."
Thus, because of the traditional recollection of Vṛddha-Manu. 3.5.

Having thus stated the prohibition regarding specific types of donors in the offering of water, he now states the prohibition based on specific types of recipients: "Heretics, those who have not taken refuge [in the Triple Gem], thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who commit adultery, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide— these are not entitled to the impurity rites or the offering of water."

"Pākhaṇḍa" refers to the wearing of sectarian marks outside of what is prescribed by the Śruti, such as human skulls and the like; those who possess these are "pākhaṇḍins. "Anāśritas" are those who, despite being eligible for religious duties, have not undertaken any specific stage of life (āśrama).
"Stenas" are those who steal superior goods such as gold and the like.
Those who kill their husbands are "pratighātinyaḥ"; those who go according to their lust are "kulaṭāḥ.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), those who kill their own fetuses or Brahmins are included.
"Drinking women" (*surāpyaḥ*) are those addicted to drinking that liquor which is prohibited for them.
"Suicides" (*ātmatyāginyaḥ*) are those who take their own lives by means of poison, fire, water, hanging, and so forth.

These—including heretics (*pākhaṇḍins*) and others—are not entitled to the three-night or ten-night period of impurity (*āśauca*) to be described hereafter, nor to the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) such as the offering of water (*udakadāna*).
"Those who share [the funeral cake] are *bhājana*s"; thus, they do not become the cause for impurity (*āśauca*) and so forth for their *sapiṇḍas* and others.
Therefore, this statement is intended to establish that upon their death, the offering of water and other rites need not be performed by the *sapiṇḍas*.

Furthermore, in this context, the gender (*liṅga*) in expressions such as "those who drink *surā*" is not intended to be significant; for it is said: "Gender, number, place, time, and the fruit of the action [are not always intended]."
Those skilled in Mīmāṃsā declare that there are five things not to be accepted.
This is because [these acts] fall under the category of what is not to be undertaken (*anupādeya*).
And this refers to cases where there is prior intention (*buddhipūrva*).
As Gautama said: "By means of fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice], for those who desire [death]."
"Mahāprasthāna" is generally the great departure; "anāśaka" is fasting unto death;
"avapāta" from a mountain peak is leaping down.

In this context, because of the inclusion of the qualification "if they so wish," it should be understood that there is no fault in an act committed through negligence; for instance: "If someone should die through negligence by fire, water, or the like, impurity must be observed for him and the water-libation rite must be performed."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Aṅgiras.
Likewise, there is a prohibition of impurity and other rites even due to specific modes of death:
"Death from a *caṇḍāla*, from water, from a snake, from a Brāhmaṇa, from lightning,
or from fanged beasts, belongs to those who have committed sinful deeds."
Whatever water and offerings of rice balls are given to the departed spirits, none of that remains; it perishes in mid-air.
Thus, this [text] also concerns suicide preceded by intention, because Gautama’s statement explicitly prohibits impurity and other rites for one killed by water when it is done intentionally;
furthermore, here too, the determination that it refers to intentional acts follows from the observation of its association with "from a Caṇḍāla, from water, or from a serpent."

Therefore, for one who, out of pride or similar motives, goes to kill Caṇḍālas and others and is killed by them, this prohibition of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth—based on the transgression of the injunction that "one should protect oneself from all [harm]"—applies. Likewise, it should be understood that this prohibition also applies to the death of one who, out of pride, goes directly toward dangerous fanged animals and the like.

Furthermore, this prohibition of impurity (*aśauca*) pertains to that which is delimited by periods such as ten days, because immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) will be prescribed for those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, as well as for suicides, according to the rule: "For those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and for suicides, [purity is] immediate."
Likewise, cremation and other such rites are not to be performed for them; nor should there be impurity, nor water libations, nor tears, nor funeral rites such as cremation.
For those slain by the rod of a Brahmin, one should not even carry the bier.
Thus, according to the recollection of Yama:
"Slain by the staff of Brahman" means slain by the staff of a Brāhmaṇa. The word *kaṭa* refers to items such as a cot (*khaṭvā*) used as a means for carrying the deceased.

One should not suspect that this Smṛti prohibition against cremation and so forth does not apply to an *āhitāgni* (one who maintains the sacred fires) killed by a *vipra* or similar [high-caste person], on the grounds that it would result in the violation of the scripturally ordained disposal (*pratipatti*) of the fires and sacrificial vessels.
For, in another Smṛti, a different method of disposal is prescribed for the fires and sacrificial vessels belonging to an *āhitāgni* killed by a *caṇḍāla* or others:
"One should cast the *vaitāna* (sacrificial) fire into water, and the *āvasathya* fire at a crossroads."
But one should burn the vessels in the fire if the sacrificer has died in vain.
Thus:
one should cast the *vaitāna* fire into the waters and the *āvasathya* fire at a crossroads; however, if the sacrificer dies prematurely, one should burn the sacrificial vessels in the fire.
Likewise, another method for the disposal of their bodies has been stated: "For those who have abandoned their lives or for those who have fallen from their caste, no [ordinary] ritual act exists;
for them as well, immersion in the waters of the Gaṅgā is beneficial."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
Therefore, there is a prohibition against burning and so forth for all [categories of persons] without distinction.

Consequently, when the prohibition is transgressed out of affection or similar motives, a penance must be performed: "Having performed [the funeral rites], one should perform fire-rites, water-libations, bathing, touching [the body], carrying [the corpse], and speaking [of the deceased]."
And for cutting a rope or shedding tears, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.

Thus it is from the Smṛti. And this should be understood to apply when each act is performed intentionally; however, regarding an unintentional act, [it is said]: "Whoever should carry or cremate any one of these Pretas..."
Having performed the water-libation rite with [the deceased's] clothes, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Saṃvarta:
"Furthermore, if one merely touches that corpse or sheds a tear for it,
and has not performed the previously mentioned rites, there shall be a fast of one night."

Thus, fasting has been prescribed for touching [a corpse] or shedding tears. Furthermore, regarding the cutting of bonds or burning [a corpse], Sumantu has stated that for one unable to perform the *kṛcchra* penances, one should subsist on alms for a month and bathe three times a day; this subsistence on alms is likewise intended only for one who is incapable.
In this manner, other Smṛti passages concerning the same subject should also be properly interpreted according to their specific scope.

Furthermore, this prohibition against cremation and other rites refers to persons other than aged forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others who are incapable of performing obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), for such cases are seen to be permitted: "An old man whose memory of purity has failed, who has rejected medical treatment, may destroy himself by means of Bhṛgu, fire, fasting, or water."
For him, the period of impurity lasts three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones takes place;
on the third day, having offered water, one should perform the Śrāddha on the fourth day.

Thus, because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), when self-slaughter is permitted by the scriptures through various specific conditions, and the performance of *śrāddha* and other post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadehika*) is forbidden for those who have taken their own lives by any path other than those [specifically] authorized, there arises the expectation: "What, then, should be done for them? In response to this, Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya and Chāgaleya have stated:
"Out of fear of public censure, men should perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali."
Yama has declared that their purification shall be achieved in this manner and not otherwise;
therefore, food accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given even to them.
Thus, out of fear of public reproach, men should perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali;
Yama has declared that their purification occurs only in this way, and not otherwise.
Therefore, food itself, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given even to them.
Vyāsa has also said:
"Whatever is offered dedicated to Nārāyaṇa or Śiva, that act shall be the purifier of it; this is not otherwise."
Thus:
"Whatever is offered with Nārāyaṇa or Śiva in view, that act shall be purifying; it cannot be otherwise."

Thus, the Nārāyaṇabali, by means of effecting purification for the deceased, generates the fitness for being the recipient of *śrāddha* and other rites; therefore, all post-mortem (*aurdhvadehika*) ceremonies must indeed be performed.
For this very reason, the permission for post-mortem rites is seen even in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"And for those killed by cows or Brahmins, as well as for the fallen (*patita*)."
After one year has passed, he should perform the entire set of rites for the deceased.
Thus it is said:
"In the case of those killed by cows or Brahmins, as well as for those who have become outcasts (patita),
one should perform all the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) after the lapse of one year."
Thus, after one year has passed, having performed the Nārāyaṇabali, the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) should be carried out.
The Nārāyaṇabali is to be performed in this manner:

on any eleventh day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight, having duly worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, one should offer ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) mixed with sesame seeds and soaked in honey and clarified butter near them. Recalling the deceased as being in the form of Viṣṇu and pronouncing his name and lineage, one should face south and place them upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing south. Having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings and completed the rites up to the dismissal of the cakes (piṇḍapravāhaṇa), one should cast them into a river; they should not be given to the wife or others.

Then, on that very night, having invited an odd number of Brahmins and observed a fast, on the following day at midday, he should perform the worship of Viṣṇu. Having performed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite according to the prescribed rule—from the washing of the Brahmins' feet up to the question regarding their satisfaction—he should silently perform the sequence from the drawing of lines for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* up to the *avanejana* (sprinkling of water). Then, having offered four *piṇḍas* to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva, and Yama along with their retinues, and having recollected the deceased by mentioning his name and lineage while chanting the name of Viṣṇu, he should offer the fifth *piṇḍa*.

Then, having gratified the Brāhmaṇas who have sipped water with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and remembering one among them who is most excellent in virtue as being the deceased (preta), he should especially satisfy him with cows, land, gold, and other gifts. Thereafter, having had the Brāhmaṇas—whose hands hold purifiers (pavitra)—cause water mixed with sesame seeds and other items to be offered for the deceased, he should eat together with his kinsmen.
However, in the case of one killed by a snake, there is this distinction:

For one year, having performed the worship of the Naga on the fifth lunar day according to the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas, and when the year is complete, having performed the Nārāyaṇabali sacrifice, he should give a golden Naga and a living cow.
Thereafter, he should perform all the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika).
And the nature of the Nārāyaṇa-bali is described in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa] as follows:
"Having reached the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight,
one should worship the god Viṣṇu as well as Yama, the son of Vivasvat."
Restrained and facing south, one should indeed offer ten balls of rice anointed with ghee, mixed with sesame seeds, accompanied by the *manus*, upon blades of *darbha* grass.
Having invoked Viṣṇu in one's intellect, one should then cast [the image] into the river water;
there, one should perform worship with flowers while pronouncing the name and lineage.
One should offer incense, lamps, and various kinds of food, both solid and soft; one should indeed invite five, seven, or even nine Brahmins.
When another day had arrived, having fasted and being concentrated in mind, [he approached] those who were rich in knowledge and austerity, born of noble lineage.
Having performed the worship of Viṣṇu, he should seat those Brahmins facing north, according to seniority, while recollecting them as having the form of the ancestors.
Having fixed the mind upon Viṣṇu, one should indeed perform everything without sloth;
whatever has been prescribed beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, that one should perform preceded by the deity.
Then, having recognized that the Brahmins were satisfied and having asked them about their satisfaction according to the prescribed rule,
[he should offer] only sacrificial food (haviṣya) with its side-dishes, accompanied by sesame seeds and other ingredients.
One should offer five morsels of food while recollecting the forms of the gods;
first, one should give to Viṣṇu, and then to Brahmā and Śiva.
One should offer the fourth ball of rice to Yama along with his attendants;
thereafter, one should mentally mention the deceased by name, preceded by their *gotra*.
Having thus uttered the name of Viṣṇu for the fifth time as before, he should cast [the water];
then, having caused the Brahmins to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule, he should honor them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should honor a most venerable Brahmin with gold,
a cow, clothing, and land, while mentally recollecting that deceased person.
Then the Brahmins, with *darbha* grass held in their hands, should scatter sesame-water while mentally reciting the name preceded by the *gotra*.
With a concentrated mind, they should offer him oblations of fragrant sesame seeds and water;
afterwards, he should eat while maintaining silence, together with his friends and servants.
Thus, abiding by the doctrine of Viṣṇu, whoever gives [liberation] to one who has committed suicide quickly rescues that person; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Regarding the occasion of being bitten by a snake, the gift of a golden *nāga* in the form of a representation was prescribed by Sumantu in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"Having fashioned a *nāga* out of a *bhāra* of gold, and likewise a cow,
and having given them to Vyāsa according to the prescribed rite, one shall attain freedom from debt to one's father."
Thus [ends the section]. 3.6.
Having fashioned an image of Nāga out of a bhāra of gold and likewise a cow,
and having given them to Vyāsa according to the prescribed rite, one shall attain freedom from debt to one's father.
Having thus stated the water-offering along with its prohibitions, he next states what should be done thereafter:
"When they have finished the water-offerings, have emerged from the water, and are standing upon soft grassy ground after having bathed,
one should address them with ancient historical narratives."

To those sons and others who have performed the water-libation (*udakadāna*), who have bathed, and who have properly emerged from the water and are standing firmly upon a soft grassy plot of ground covered with newly sprouted tufts of grass, the family elders should console them—meaning they should awaken them—with ancient historical narratives (*itihāsa*) to be related hereafter, using words capable of dispelling their grief. || 7 ||
He states the nature of history (itihāsa), which is capable of dispelling sorrow:
"He who seeks the essence in human existence— which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on water— is utterly deluded."

By the word "human" (manuṣya), the fourfold collection of living beings—those born from a womb, from an egg, and so forth—is indicated; the state of being such is "humanity. In this saṃsāra, which by its very nature is like the trunk of a plantain tree—lacking any internal core—and like a bubble on the water—perishing before long—one who seeks or searches for a stable essence is utterly deluded, his mind completely ruined.
Therefore, you who know the true nature of saṃsāra should not act in this manner. (3.8)
Moreover:
If this body, which was composed of the five elements, has returned to the state of the five elements,
what cause for lamentation is there in that, since it arose from one's own actions?

The body, which was produced and fashioned in five ways from the five elements—earth and the rest—as a composite of the seeds of karma generated by one’s own bodies in previous births for the sake of experiencing their respective fruits, has, upon the cessation of that experience of fruit, returned to the state of the five elements and attained the nature of earth and the others. In this regard, what purpose does lamentation serve for you? Since it is devoid of utility, you should not grieve, because such is the nature of reality; indeed, no one is able to transcend the established order of things. (3.9)
Moreover:
The earth, the ocean, and the gods all go to destruction;
how then will the world of mortals, which resembles foam, not go to destruction?
Death is not a cause for wonder, since even the great elements such as earth and the rest go to destruction.

Likewise, even the oceans—which are free from old age and death—and even the immortals come to an end at the time of universal dissolution; how then could this aggregate of beings, which is subject to death and resembles foam in its instability, not go to ruin?
For departure is indeed appropriate for one whose nature is subject to death;
therefore, an immersion in grief is purposeless. 3.10
He says that lamentation should not be performed because it leads to undesirable consequences:
"Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should therefore not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability."

Since the deceased, being powerless and even against his will, must consume the phlegm and tears shed from the mouths and eyes of mourning kinsmen, therefore one should not weep; rather, those who desire the welfare of the deceased should perform the śrāddha and other rites according to their own capacity. (3.11)
Having heard this, they should go home preceded by children;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of the house.

Having sipped water and touched fire and other elements, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds, they should enter while touching these; then, having placed their feet slowly upon a stone, they should proceed.
Having thus properly heard the words of the family elders, they should cast off their grief and go home, placing the children in front of them.

Having gone and stood at the door of the house, remaining self-controlled with restrained minds, they should bite neem leaves (*nimba-patra*) with their teeth, tearing them into pieces and eating them; then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and having touched fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds—and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," as stated by Śaṅkha, also touching sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and a bull, as well as a stone—they should place their foot upon the stone and enter the house slowly and without stumbling. (3.12–3.13)
He states the extended application:
"Even for those who have touched a corpse, the rites beginning with entry [into the village] are performed;
for those who so desire, purification occurs instantly, while for others it comes through bathing and self-restraint."

This aforementioned ritual, beginning with the biting of neem leaves and ending with the entry into the house, applies not only to kinsmen but also to others who perform the decoration and removal of the corpse for the sake of dharma.
Regarding the phrase "entry and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) is intended here to follow a reverse order due to its inauspicious nature.

For those non-sapiṇḍas who, having engaged in the removal and other rites for the sake of dharma, desire purification at that very moment, their purification occurs through bathing and breath-control alone.
As Parāśara has said:
"Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in successive order."
For those of virtuous deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin;
for them, purification is ordained immediately by immersion in water.
Thus it is said.
Those twice-born who carry a deceased brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in successive order.
For those of virtuous deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin;
for them, immediate purification is ordained by immersion in water.
Regarding the removal [of the corpse] by means of oil and other such substances, however, there is a specific rule stated by Manu:
"A Brahmin who, like a kinsman, carries out the corpse of a deceased twice-born person who is not a *sapiṇḍa*,
or the maternal relatives of his mother, becomes pure after three nights."
If one eats their food, one is purified in ten days;
if one does not eat their food, one is purified in a single day, provided one does not dwell in that house.
Thus:
Having carried out a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the maternal relatives of his mother.
If one eats their food, however, one is purified in ten days;
but if one does not eat their food and does not dwell in that house, one is purified in a single day.

In this regard, the established rule is as follows: he who, having performed the removal of the corpse by means of unctuous substances (*sneha*) and so forth, eats that person's food and dwells in his house, attains purification after ten days alone.
He who merely dwells in that house but does not eat that person's food attains purification after three nights.
Furthermore, he who performs only the removal of the corpse, neither dwelling in the house nor eating the food, attains purification after one day.
This refers to cases involving those of the same caste (*sajātīya*).
However, regarding those of a different caste (*vijātīya*), one must observe the period of impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for the specific caste of the deceased whom one carries out.

As Gautama has stated: "If a lower caste person touches a higher caste person, or a higher caste person touches a lower caste person, in that case the impurity is that which is declared for the corpse."
"Upasparśana" means carrying out [the corpse].

When a Brāhmaṇa carries out a Śūdra, the period of impurity lasts for one month; but when a Śūdra carries out a Brāhmaṇa, it lasts for ten nights. The meaning is that the impurity should be observed in this manner, according to the status of the corpse. (3.14)
He says in response to the religious student (brahmacārin):
"Even after carrying out the funeral rites for his teacher, father, or preceptor, the one observing the vow remains a vow-keeper;
he should not eat food from a source of distress, nor should he dwell together with them."

The teacher (*ācārya*) is one whose characteristics have been described; "parents" (*pitarau*) refers to the mother and father; and the "sub-teacher" (*upādhyāya*) is as previously mentioned. Even after carrying out the funeral rites for these, the religious student (*brahmacārī*) remains indeed a student (*vratī*); there is no lapse of his vow (*vratabhraṃśa*). By the word *kaṭa*, impurity (*aśauca*) is indicated; food associated with that is "food from a *kaṭa*" (*sakaṭānna*), which the religious student must not eat. Nor should he dwell together with those who are impure.

By stating this, it is implied that for a student (*brahmacārin*), there is a violation of his vow (*vratalopa*) when carrying out the removal of a corpse other than that of a teacher (*ācārya*) or similar superior;
for this very reason, Vasiṣṭha has stated: "For a student performing the rites for a corpse, there is a cessation of his vows, except in the case of [the death of] his mother or father. (3.15)
He states the specific rules for those in a state of impurity: "They should eat food that is purchased or obtained [unasked], and sleep separately on the ground;
food should be offered to the deceased for three days according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍayajña."

"Those for whom food is obtained either by purchase or by request" means those whose food is acquired through buying or solicitation; "they should be [such]" is the ellipsis. Because of the rule regarding obtaining food through purchase or acquisition, it follows by implication that in the absence of such food, fasting occurs.

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "Having gone to their homes, they should remain for three days without food on a layer of grass spread on the ground; they should subsist on what has been purchased or produced [for them].

A "layer of grass" (*adhaḥprastara*) is a mat made of straw intended for the sleeping and sitting of those in a state of impurity. Furthermore, those *sapiṇḍa* relatives should sleep separately on the bare ground, not on beds or similar furniture.
Manu has also shown a specific rule in this regard:
"They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, they should immerse themselves in water for three days,
they should not consume meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground."
Thus:
they should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days;
they should not eat meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground.
Likewise, Gautama has also stated a specific rule: "Those who sleep on the ground, remain celibate, and perform the funeral rites [must observe these].

Furthermore, according to the procedure of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña—characterized by wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin) and so forth—food in the form of rice-balls (piṇḍa) should be offered silently to the deceased upon the ground for three days.
As Marīci says:
Having bathed and with a restrained mind, one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) in the northeast and offer the piṇḍa for the pretas outside, devoid of darbha grass and mantras.
Thus [it is said].

The exclusion of *darbha* grass and mantras pertains to those who have not been initiated (*anupanīta*), according to the traditional teaching of Pracetas: "One should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) on the ground for those who are unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*), and on *kuśa* grass for those who are refined (*saṃskṛta*)."
Likewise, the restriction regarding the performer should be understood from the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:

"Having bathed and being pure in mind, one should offer the *piṇḍa* for the deceased outside [the sacrificial ground], devoid of *darbha* grass and mantras; having prepared the *caru* in the north-eastern direction."
Whether of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man,
whoever offers the first day's [funeral] water must complete it for ten days.
Thus:
whether of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man,
whoever offers [the water] on the first day shall complete it for ten days.
Likewise, the restriction regarding the materials has been shown by Śunaḥpuccha:
"One should offer with rice, or with barley-meal, or even with vegetables;
whatever material is used on the first day, that same material shall be used for the ten-day period."
Silently, one should offer the water libation, as well as flowers, a lamp, and incense.
Thus:
"One should offer [the oblation] with rice, or with groats, or even with vegetables;
whatever substance was used on the first day, that same substance shall be used for the ten-day period."
Silently, one should offer the water libation, flowers, a lamp, and likewise incense.
The funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) should be offered on a stone; for Śaṅkha records that "they should offer the garland, the ball, and the water either on the ground or on a stone.
Nor should one suspect from the plural verb "they should offer" (*dadyuḥ*)—as in the case of the offering of water—that the offering of the ball must be performed by all [the sons];
rather, it must be performed by the son alone.

In the absence of a son, the sapindas, the mother’s sapindas, and the disciples should perform [the rite]; in their absence, the officiating priest (ṛtvij) and the preceptor (ācārya), according to the traditional teaching of Gautama. Furthermore, when there are many sons, the eldest alone should perform it, for: "Whatever has been performed by the eldest alone, after obtaining the consent of all, or with undivided property, is considered as performed by all."
Thus, according to the recollection of Marīci:
"The rule regarding the number of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is that there are ten for a Brāhmaṇa and twelve indeed for a Kṣatriya.

Likewise, Viṣṇu has declared this according to the number of days of impurity (*āśauca*): "As long as the period of impurity lasts, they should offer water and one funeral cake for the deceased. Also in another Smṛti: "With a concentrated mind, one should offer nine funeral cakes over nine days."
Having offered the tenth ball of rice, one shall remain pure for the remainder of the night.
This statement regarding purity is intended for the purpose of inviting Brahmins for the *śrāddha* to be performed on the following day.
However, the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*) has prescribed the offering of three *piṇḍas*.
Regarding these two procedures—the more elaborate and the simpler—the established rule concerning the offering of water should be understood as applicable.
In this regard, there is another specific rule from Śātātapa:
"Even when the period of impurity is shortened, one should nevertheless offer exactly ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas)."
Even when the period of impurity is shortened, one should nevertheless offer ten *piṇḍas*.
Furthermore, Pāraskara has shown a specific rule for those whose impurity lasts three nights:
"On the first day, three *piṇḍas* should be offered by those who are composed."
On the second day, one should offer four [oblations] as well as the collection of the bones.
But on the third day, one should give three [gifts] such as clothing and so forth, and likewise wash them.
Thus [ends verse] 3.16.
On the first day, three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered by those composed in mind;
on the second day, one should offer four, as well as the collection of the bones.
On the third day, however, one should give three [gifts] such as clothing and so forth, and likewise wash them.
Furthermore:
water and milk should be placed in earthen vessels for one day in the open air.
Water and milk should each be placed separately in two distinct earthen vessels and set out in the open air, such as on a swing-stand or similar support, for one full day.

Since no specific distinction is mentioned here, the rite should be performed on the first day; likewise, according to the statement of Pāraskara: "Having set out water with the words, 'O deceased one, bathe here,' and milk with the words, 'Drink this.
Furthermore, the collection of bones (asthisaṃcayana) should be performed on the first day and subsequent days.
Thus says Saṃvarta.
On the first day, or the third, the seventh, or likewise the ninth,
the collection of bones should be performed by the members of that lineage together on that day.
Thus:
On the first day, or the third, the seventh, or likewise the ninth,
the collection of the bones should be performed by those of his lineage together with him.

In some places, however, it is stated that the collection of bones occurs on the second day; in the *Vaiṣṇava* tradition, one should perform the collection of bones on the fourth day and cast them into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Therefore, on whichever day [is chosen], the collection of bones must be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
And regarding this, Aṅgiras has shown a specific distinction:
"The sacrifice for the gods is prescribed for the collection of the bones;
if one who is pure does not perform it on behalf of that deceased person, [there is a fault]."
But when one performs sacrifices for the deities, the deities then curse him.
And the deities residing here in the cremation ground are those previously mentioned; therein, the gods dwelling in the cremation ground are proclaimed to be the attendants of corpses.
Thus it was said by him.

Therefore, it is stated that one should perform worship there for those gods and for the deceased who has recently passed away, by means of incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as with food in the form of ritual balls (piṇḍa).
Likewise, the shaving of the hair should be performed on the tenth day; when the tenth day has arrived, the bath shall take place outside the village.
There, the clothes, as well as the hair of the head, the beard, and the nails, are to be discarded.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Devala.
Likewise, in another Smṛti:
"On the second day, the rite of shaving (kṣurakarma) should be performed with diligence;
or on the third, the fifth, or even the seventh day from the offering."
Thus it is said:
"On the second day, the rite of shaving (kṣurakarma) should be performed with great care;
or on the third, the fifth, or even the seventh day from the time of the offering."
The phrase "there is no fixed rule prior to the offering of the *śrāddha*" means that [the shaving] is not mandatory until then.
Regarding the question of who must undergo the shaving (*vapana*), Āpastamba has stated: "And there is the shaving for those who follow [the deceased].

The meaning is as follows: "those who experience" (*anubhāvinaḥ*) refers to the *sapiṇḍas*, because they experience the suffering of death; when the question arises whether this shaving applies to them all without distinction or only to those of younger age, this very rule—"and there is the shaving for those who follow"—is applicable.
"Anubhāvinaḥ" refers to those who come after, namely the younger ones; their shaving [of the head] is what is intended.

Some consider "anubhāvinaḥ" to mean sons. It is traditionally taught that shaving is prescribed in seven instances: at the Gaṅgā, in the field of Bhāskara, upon the death of one's mother, father, or guru, at the time of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), and during the *soma* sacrifice.
Because such a restrictive rule is observed.
Since it might follow that all eligibility for rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti ceases due to impurity, he says the following in order to permit certain [rites]:
"The Vaitāna and Aupāsana rites and other actions must be performed, because of the injunctions of the Śruti."

The term *vaitānāḥ* refers to those rites pertaining to the *vitāna*, which is the expansion of the sacred fires; these are the rituals accomplished by the three fires, such as the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and others.

The term *aupāsanāḥ* refers to those rites pertaining to the *aupāsana*, which is the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) that is worshipped daily; these are the ritual acts of the evening and morning oblations (*sāyaṃprātar-homa*).
These *vaitāna* and *aupāsana* rites are the Vedic actions that ought to be performed.
If it is asked how these possess Vedic authority, it is because they are enjoined by Śruti.
For instance, the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites are quite explicit in such Śruti passages as "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives.
Likewise, the domestic fire sacrifice (aupāsana-homa) is also enjoined by the Śruti: "Day after day one should offer the Svāhā-call; in the absence of food, [one may do so] with anything up to wood."
And here, by the inclusion of the qualification "being based on Śruti," it is understood that there is no performance of Smārta rites such as giving gifts and the like.
For this very reason, it was stated by Vaiyāghrapāda: "In the case of impurity due to birth or death, except for [the eclipse of] Rāhu, there is an abandonment of Smārta rituals;
however, regarding Śrauta rituals, one attains purity by bathing at that specific time."

Thus, the statement that Śrauta rites are to be performed is intended with reference to obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. As Paiṭhīnasi says: "Obligatory rites may be suspended; some say [they may be suspended] except for those pertaining to the *vaitāna* [fires] and those in the domestic (*śālāgni*) fire. Regarding the phrase "obligatory rites may be suspended," since there is no qualification, the suspension of all necessary rites—both obligatory and occasional—would follow as a consequence; therefore, the phrase "except for those pertaining to the *vaitāna* fires" serves as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of those necessary rites that are accomplished by means of the three sacred fires.
Regarding the statement "some [say] in the hall-fire," this indicates that even for those rites performed in the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) that are mandatory, there is an optional exclusion;
therefore, in those cases, there is indeed no impurity (*āśauca*).
As for optional rites (*kāmya*), however, they are not to be performed due to the absence of purity.
Manu also has stated with this very intention: "One should not interrupt the rites in the fires.

By the phrase "one should not interrupt the rites in the fires," there is the suspension of those rites such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) which are not accomplished by means of the fires.
For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
One should perform the Homa there with dry food or fruit;
however, one should not perform the ritual of the five great sacrifices during death or birth.

Thus, although the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is normally accomplished by means of fire, it is excluded here by a specific scriptural injunction, for it has been stated by that same [author]: "A Brahmin shall remain for ten days devoid of the Vaiśvadeva. In that case, one should perform the oblation with dry food or with fruit.
One should not perform the ritual of the five sacrifices during death or birth.
"During *sūtaka* (impurity), the suspension of rituals such as the *saṃdhyā* is prescribed.
Although thus the cessation of the *saṃdhyā* is heard [in the scriptures], nevertheless one should perform the throwing of the *añjali* and so forth.

For there is a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Paiṭhīnasi: "During *sūtaka*, having thrown an *añjali* with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, having circumambulated [the sun] while meditating upon the Sun, one should offer salutation."

Although it has been stated in general that "the domestic (aupāsana) rites should be performed [by oneself]," nevertheless, they must be caused to be performed by another, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Paiṭhīnasi: "Others should perform these.
Bṛhaspati also said: "In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), or indeed incapacity regarding the eating at a *śrāddha* feast..."
On account of causes such as travel abroad and the like, one should cause the sacrifice to be performed, but one must not let it lapse.
Thus:
"In cases of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka), when unable to eat at a śrāddha,
or due to causes such as being on a journey, one should cause [the sacrifice] to be offered, but one must not let it lapse."

Likewise, even though they belong to the Smṛti tradition, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the Śravaṇākarma, the Āśvayujī sacrifice, and so forth, as well as the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), must certainly be performed. However, when impurity (sūtaka) has arisen, how can the Smārta rite be carried out?
One should have the Piṇḍayajña and the Caru-homa performed by someone who does not belong to one's own gotra.
Thus it is from the *Jātūkarṇya-smṛti*.

Even though there may be another as the performer in the case of auxiliary rites (*saṅga-karma*), nevertheless, one should personally perform the primary rite consisting of the renunciation of one's own property (*svadravyatyāga*), because that cannot be accomplished by anyone else.
For this very reason it has been said: "In a Śrauta rite, one who has bathed at that time shall attain purity."

Thus it is said: "In the case of a Vedic rite (*śrauta-karman*), one who has bathed at that time shall attain purity. Furthermore, regarding the prohibition of the *homa* in the statement, "giving, receiving, *homa*, and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) are suspended," this prohibition of *homa* must be established as referring either to optional rites (*kāmya*) or to the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice.

Likewise, one must not eat food from a house where a birth-impurity (sūtaka) has occurred; for Yama’s legal tradition states: "In both cases, the food of the family is not to be eaten for ten days. Here, "in both cases" refers to birth and death. The phrase "for ten days" is an indicative mark for the entire period of ritual impurity (āśauca).
The food belonging to a family affected by birth-impurity must not be consumed by those who are not members of that kin-group (asakulya).

Furthermore, there is no fault regarding the *sakulyas* (agnates). For Manu has stated: "In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the food of the family is declared by him to be without fault. And this prohibition is to be understood as applying when either the giver or the eater becomes aware of a birth or death; if it is not known by both parties, the birth-impurity does not constitute a fault.
Even if it is understood by only one person, it may bring harm to the eater.
Thus, according to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:

"Likewise, in marriages and other ceremonies, food prepared separately for Brahmins must indeed be eaten even before the onset of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). However, during marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interim, no fault is proclaimed regarding items previously intended for the purpose."
In the case of marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interim,
no fault is proclaimed regarding matters previously intended.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati. Furthermore, another specific rule is shown in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"But if a death-impurity (*mṛta-sūtaka*) occurs during the interval between a wedding, a festival, or a sacrifice..."
Others should provide the food, and it should be eaten by the best of the twice-born.
But while the Brahmins are eating, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interval,
they are all considered pure provided they rinse with water from another house.
Thus it is said:
"But during marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interval,
food should be offered by others and may be eaten by the best of the twice-born."
But while the Brahmins are eating, if a death or birth occurs in the interim,
they are all considered pure once they have rinsed their mouths with water from another house.
Likewise, even when impurity (āśauca) has taken hold, there is no fault regarding certain substances.
As Marīci says:
"In the case of salt, honey, meat, and flowers, roots, and fruits..."
In vegetables, wood, grass, water, curd, clarified butter, and milk;
In the case of sesame, medicinal herbs, and skins— whether cooked or uncooked— as well as in all articles of trade, there is no impurity regarding birth or death when one takes them oneself.
Thus it is said: "Regarding salt, honey, meat, flowers, roots, and fruits;
regarding vegetables, wood, grass, water, curd, clarified butter, and milk."
In the case of sesame, medicinal herbs, and skins— whether cooked or uncooked— as well as in all articles of trade, there is no impurity regarding birth or death when one takes them for oneself.
"Prepared food" refers to items such as *modakas* (sweetmeats) and the like, while "unprepared" refers to rice and the like.

"Taking by oneself" means that one should take it only after having been permitted by the owner. The permission regarding both prepared and unprepared food pertains specifically to those engaged in a food-distribution festival (*annasatra*); for those engaged in a food-distribution festival, raw food is not censurable.
Having eaten their cooked food, one should drink only milk for three nights.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Aṅgiras,
the word "cooked" (pakva) refers here to boiled rice and the like, excluding food intended for eating.
Regarding impurity caused by contact with a corpse, a specific rule has been stated by Aṅgiras:
"If impurity should fall upon a householder through such contact, his ritual acts are not suspended, nor does that impurity affect his domestic rites."
Thus:
"If impurity should fall upon a householder through contact with someone else, his domestic rites are not suspended, nor does that impurity affect his household duties."
The meaning is that this impurity (āśauca) pertains solely to the householder himself, and not to his wife and others living in his household, nor to the property belonging to him.
This same principle is shown in another Smṛti even regarding an impurity that has already passed:
"If, after the ten-day period has elapsed, the householder subsequently becomes aware [of the death]..."
For him, the impurity lasts for three nights, but never for the substance itself.
Thus [ends verse] 3.17.
But if, after ten days have passed, the householder later becomes aware [of the birth], his impurity lasts for three nights; it never pertains to that object.
Having thus stated the duties consisting of injunctions and prohibitions for those in a state of impurity (āśauca), he now declares the cause of impurity and the regulation of time:
"Impurity on account of death (śāva) is prescribed as either three nights or ten nights;
however, in the case of a child less than two years old, it applies to both [parents], while birth-impurity (sūtaka) belongs to the mother alone."
"Śāva" means caused by a corpse (*śava*).
By the word "sūtaka," which denotes birth, the impurity (*āśauca*) caused thereby is indicated.
By stating this, it is shown that both birth and death are the causes of impurity.

And that birth or death is indeed a cause [of impurity] only when it has actually occurred and been known; for we see such indicative marks as: "having heard of the death of a relative within ten days, and the birth of a son," and so forth. Likewise: "But he who hears of one who has gone abroad and died within ten days shall remain impure only for whatever portion remains of those ten nights."
This is also because of the force of the commencement of such statements as these.

For if impurity depended solely on the occurrence [of birth or death], then since the rules regarding the duration of impurity—such as ten days and so forth—would begin precisely from those respective points, it would follow by implication that upon hearing of the death of a relative who has not yet reached ten days, the remaining portion of the ten-day period itself constitutes the impurity. Consequently, the rule "that which remains of the ten nights" would be unnecessary to state.
Therefore, it is only when birth and death have been known that they constitute the cause [of impurity].
And this impurity (āśauca), though caused by both [the birth of a son and the death of a relative], is intended by Manu and others to last for three nights and ten nights respectively.
In this section on impurity, the mention of "days" (ahaḥ) and "nights" (rātri) is for the purpose of indicating a full day and night (ahorātra).

The statement "is intended by Manu and others" is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between the objects [of the rules] as described by them, namely the categories of *sapiṇḍa* and *samānodaka*.
For it is thus stated:
"Impurity on account of death is ordained for ten days among the sapindas;
the same applies to birth for those who desire complete purification."
"Regarding those who share the same water [in funeral rites] for a single birth, purification is prescribed after three nights;
those who touch a corpse are purified after three days, as are those who offer water.
By these statements, a distinction is established between the periods of three nights and ten nights, pertaining respectively to the *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen) and the *sapiṇḍa* (near kinsmen).
Therefore, for *sapiṇḍas* up to the seventh generation, the period of impurity is ten nights without distinction;
for *samānodakas*, it is three nights.
Furthermore, as for the statement in another *smṛti*: "In the fourth [generation] it should be ten nights, and six nights for a male in the fifth."
In the sixth [case], purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, it is on the very day itself.
Thus, because it is contradicted [by other authorities], it is not to be respected.

Even that which is not contradicted, nevertheless, like the slaughter of an animal as a subsidiary part of the *madhuparka* rite, must not be practiced because it is loathed by the world; for Manu has recorded: "One should not practice even a duty that leads away from heaven if it is loathed by the world."

Nor is it logical that there should be one day of impurity for a *sapiṇḍa* who is close, such as one within the seventh degree, while there is three days for *samānodakas* who are distant, beginning from the eighth degree.
Thus, when the impurity of *sapiṇḍas* has been established without distinction, he states a restriction for certain cases:
"When a child less than two years old dies, the ten-day period of impurity applies only to both parents, not to all *sapiṇḍas*."
But regarding them, he will state later that for those from birth until the end of the first year, the impurity is immediate (*sadyas*).

Likewise, Paiṅgya says: "If one dies while in the womb, the impurity lasts ten days for the mother; if born, for both; and once the naming ceremony has been performed, for the uterine brothers as well.
Alternatively, this is the meaning: when one under two years of age passes away, the impurity characterized by untouchability belongs only to both parents, while for the *sapiṇḍas* it is different.

Likewise, in another Smṛti: "When one dies before reaching two years of age, [impurity] belongs only to the mother and father, and not to others"—this is intended as the definition of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*).

However, regarding the other [type of impurity], characterized by disqualification from religious rites (*karmānadhikāra*), since it has been ordained even for *sapiṇḍas* by such rules as "until the eruption of teeth, [impurity is] immediate" (*sadyaḥ*), there is no contradiction.
In this regard, the illustrative example is: "Indeed, birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs only to the mother."

Just as the impurity (*āśauca*) characterized by untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) caused by birth pertains solely to the mother, so too, in the case of a child under two years of age who dies, untouchability belongs only to the mother and father.
By prohibiting the untouchability of *sapiṇḍas* regarding a child under two years of age, untouchability in other cases is thereby permitted.
And thus says Devala:
The time for touching [the corpse] should be understood as one-third of the period of one's own impurity,
as prescribed according to the scriptures for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas.
Thus it is said:
"The time for touching [another] should be understood as one-third of one's own period of impurity,
as prescribed according to the scriptures for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas."

And this should be understood to apply to cases where death occurs before initiation (*anupanīta*), as well as to impurity (*aśauca*) that has already elapsed, such as the three-night period and so forth.
Regarding the case of one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), it has been stated by that same author:
"When the collection of bones (*saṃcayana*) has been performed in the sequence of one-tenth and so forth of the ten-day period."
Those who perceive the truth desire the touching of the limbs of the social classes.
The castes are to be touched by three, four, five, and ten [limbs] respectively;
a Brahmin’s food may be eaten by those with ten [limbs], while the remaining castes are purified by two, three, and six more [respectively].
Thus,
when the collection of the bones has been performed by dividing the ten-day period and so forth into three parts in succession,
those who perceive the truth desire the touching of the limbs of the social classes [in that order].
The social classes (varṇas) are to be touched by three, four, five, and ten [limbs] respectively;
a Brahmin may eat the food of others with ten [limbs], while the remaining [classes] do so with two, three, and six more [respectively].
It should be understood as [increased] by twelve, thirteen, and fifteen days respectively.
He now describes the impurity (*āśauca*) characterized by untouchability caused by birth:
"But for the parents there is *sūtaka*; for the mother it is certain because of the appearance of that blood."
On that day, one should not be defiled, because it was the cause of the birth of the ancestors.
*Sūtaka*—the impurity characterized by untouchability caused by birth—belongs only to the parents, that is, the mother and father, and not to all *sapiṇḍas*.
Furthermore, that untouchability of the mother is "certain" (*dhruvam*), meaning it remains fixed for ten days. Why?
"Because of seeing her blood"—that is, because of seeing the blood belonging to her.
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"No impurity exists for a man, provided he does not enter into physical contact."
In that context, *rajas* should be understood as impure, and it does not exist in the male.
Thus it is said:
"Impurity does not exist for a man if he does not undergo contact;
in that context, it is the *rajas* (menstrual flow) that should be known as impure, and that does not exist in a man."
However, in the case of a father, untouchability does not certainly cease by mere bathing alone.
As Saṃvarta says:
"Upon the birth of a son, bathing with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father."
The mother becomes pure after ten days, but the father may be touched upon bathing.
Thus it is said:
"Upon the birth of a son, a bath with one's clothes on (sacaila) is prescribed for the father;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, but the father may touch her immediately after bathing."
The statement that "a mother is purified after ten days" refers merely to fitness for ordinary social intercourse (*saṃvyavahāra*).

Regarding rites intended for transcendental purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*), however, Paiṭhīnasi has stated a specific rule: "One should have a woman who has given birth to a son perform ritual acts after twenty nights;
one who has given birth to a daughter, after a month."
Furthermore, it is made clear that among those related by sapinda-connection, there is no state of untouchability during the period of impurity (*sūtaka*):
"During *sūtaka*, contact with anyone except the woman who has given birth is not forbidden;
however, in the case of contact with the woman who has given birth, bathing alone is prescribed."
Thus it is said:
during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), contact with anyone except the woman who has given birth is not prohibited;
however, regarding contact with the woman who has given birth, bathing alone is prescribed.
The day on which the birth of the prince occurs shall not be defiled;
the meaning is that it does not cause the loss of the entitlement to perform rites such as giving gifts for that occasion.
Because on that day there is the birth—meaning the manifestation—in the form of a son of the ancestors, beginning with the father, therefore that day shall not be defiled.
And so it has been stated by Vṛddhayājñavalkya: "On the day of a son's birth, Brahmins should accept gifts of gold, land, cows, horses, goats, clothing, beds, seats, and so forth."
In that case, one may accept all kinds of prepared food, but one must not eat it;
if, however, a twice-born man eats it out of delusion, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus [it is said].
On the day of a son's birth, Brahmins should accept gifts of gold,
land, cattle, horses, goats, clothing, beds, seats, and so forth.
In that case, one may accept all kinds of prepared food but must not eat them;
however, if a twice-born man should eat them out of delusion, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Vyāsa has also stated a specific rule in this regard:
"The deities named Janmadās reside in the lying-in chamber;
for the purpose of sacrificing to them, one is declared pure at the time of birth."
On the first day, the sixth, and the tenth— on these three days at all times— one should never observe impurity (sūtaka) upon the birth of a son.
It was also stated by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"Likewise, the sixth night must be protected with special care;
one should perform the vigil at night during the period of birth-impurity on the tenth day as well."
Thus [ends the section]. 3.19.
Likewise, the sixth night must be guarded with special care;
they should perform a vigil at night on the tenth day, even during a period of birth-impurity.

When another birth or death occurs during a period of impurity (*āśauca*), the rule that "the occasional rite repeats for every occasion" would imply that the ten-day period of impurity and so forth must begin again. To provide an exception to this, he says:
"In the event of a birth or death occurring in the interval, one becomes pure by the remaining days.

In consideration of caste or age, whatever the duration of the period of impurity may be for a particular person, if a birth or death—whether of equal or lesser duration—occurs as a cause for impurity within that interval, one becomes pure by means of the very days remaining from the previous period of impurity.
Furthermore, one should not perform separate periods of impurity (*āśauca*) for each subsequent cause, such as birth and so forth.
However, when a long-term period of impurity falls within a shorter current period of impurity, purification does not occur by means of the remainder of the former.
As Uśanas has said:

If a long period of impurity should occur during the midst of a short period of impurity, purification does not come through the former; one becomes pure only by the time of one's own [longer] period.
Thus:

"But if, in the midst of a short period of impurity, a long period of impurity should occur, purification does not come through the former; one becomes pure only by the time of one's own [longer] period."
Yama also said: "One should conclude the period of impurity, which involves an increase in sin, with the latter [rite]."
One should conclude a period of impurity characterized by an increase in sin with the subsequent [period].
