And although it has been stated here without distinction that "in the interval between birth and death," nevertheless, there is no purification of a *śāva* (impurity due to death) occurring within a *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) by means of the remainder of the preceding impurity.
As Aṅgiras said:
If a death-impurity should occur during a birth-impurity, or a birth-impurity during a death-impurity,
one should perform the purification by taking the death-impurity as the governing factor, and not the birth-impurity.
Thus:
"If a death-impurity should occur during a birth-impurity, or if a birth-impurity should occur during a death-impurity,
one should perform purification with respect to the death-impurity, and not the birth-impurity."

Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "When birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs while death-impurity (*śāva*) has already arisen, the birth-impurity is purified by the death-impurity; the birth-impurity does not purify the death-impurity."
Thus it is said:
"When birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs while death-impurity (śāva) has already arisen, the birth is purified by the death;
but the birth does not purify the death."

Therefore, impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) that falls within the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is not purified by the remainder of the former; rather, it is the birth-impurity falling within the period of death-impurity that is so purified. Likewise, even though the death-impurity falls within a period of the same kind (*sajātīya*), an exception to purification by the remainder of the former is shown in another *smṛti*: "If the father dies while the mother has already died and remains unpurified..."
There shall be purification through the remainder of the father's period; however, for the mother, one should observe a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night).

Thus it is said: "If the father dies while the mother has already passed away and the period of impurity has not yet ended, his purification shall occur at the conclusion of the father's period; however, he should observe a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) for the mother."

The meaning is as follows: if, after the mother has died first, the father should pass away during the period of impurity caused by her death, then purification does not occur through the remainder of the previous period; rather, purification must be performed according to the duration of the period of impurity caused by the father’s passing.

Likewise, if the mother should die while the period of impurity caused by the father’s passing is still in progress, purification does not occur merely through the remainder of the previous period; instead, having completed the prior period of impurity, one should add a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with an intervening night).

Likewise, an exception based on the specific time of the concurrence of impurities (*āśauca*) has been stated by Gautama: "If [another impurity] occurs when only one night remains, [purification is] by two nights; if it occurs at dawn, by three nights. The meaning is this: if another impurity, such as birth, should occur while the previous impurity has only one night remaining, then after completing the previous impurity, purification is achieved in two subsequent nights. However, if another impurity occurs during the last watch (*yāma*) of that night—that is, at dawn—then purification is by three nights, and not merely by the remainder of the first.
Śātātapa has also stated: "If [the impurity] remains for the rest of the night, purification occurs after two days; if it remains for the rest of a watch (yāma), one is pure after three days.
Furthermore, he stated that the funeral rites for the deceased do not cease even upon the occurrence of birth-impurity (sūtaka):
"If death should occur within the ten-day period after a birth..."
The offering of rice balls (piṇḍadāna) should be performed by one's own kinsmen on behalf of the deceased.
If a birth should occur during the performance of the *pretapiṇḍa* offerings,
one should likewise offer the remaining *āśauca-piṇḍas* according to the prescribed rule.
Thus:
"If death should occur within ten days after a birth,
the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) must be performed by one's own kinsmen for the sake of the deceased."
If a birth should occur during the performance of the *pretapiṇḍa* offerings,
one should likewise offer the remaining *āśauca-piṇḍas* according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise, even when there is a coincidence of impurity due to death with another period of impurity, the funeral rites must be performed, because the same principle applies.
Similarly, rites such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*), which are occasioned by the birth of a son, must certainly be performed even when another period of impurity coincides with it.
Thus says Prajāpati:
But when the birth of a son occurs while a period of impurity has already arisen, the performer attains immediate purification;
he is purified by the preceding impurity alone.
Thus [it is said].
But when the birth of a son occurs while a period of impurity has already arisen, the performer attains immediate purification;
he is purified by the preceding period of impurity itself.
Having described the impurity resulting from birth at the time of full term, he now states the impurity caused by the discharge of a fetus that has not reached its time:
"In the case of a miscarriage, nights equal in number to the months [of gestation] are the cause of purification."
Although in common usage the term *sravati* is employed for the flowing of liquid substances, here it refers to falling downward—a state common to both liquid and non-liquid substances.

Why? Because [if it referred to the flow of a liquid], the first month itself would be impossible; and since there are nights equal in number to that month, the use of the plural (*niśāḥ*) would be untenable.
In the case of a miscarriage (*garbhasrāva*), as many nights as there were months of gestation constitute the cause of purification.

And this [period of impurity] applies to the woman alone, because of the traditional teaching of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha: "In the case of a miscarriage, the nights are equal to the number of months for women; for a man, there is merely a bath.

As for the three-day period mentioned by Gautama, it should be understood as applying before three months have passed: "In the case of a miscarriage, according to the month, but if it is recent, for the highest caste (Brāhmaṇa) there are three days;
for a Kṣatriya, four nights; and for a Vaiśya, five days."
But for a Śūdra, this purification is proclaimed to take eight days.
Thus, according to the recollection of Marīci:
"In the case of a miscarriage occurring within three months, for one born of the highest Brāhmaṇa caste, the period is three nights"—this is the meaning.
And this should be understood to apply up until the end of the sixth month.

Furthermore, in the case of the seventh month and onwards, the full period of impurity due to childbirth must be observed; for there, one sees the emergence of a living fetus with all its limbs complete, and because the word "birth" (*prasava*) is used in common parlance for that event. However, as long as a miscarriage occurs within six months, their purification is held to be achieved by days equal in number to the months of pregnancy.
From this point forward, the impurity prescribed for their own respective classes is ordained for them;
however, when there is a miscarriage, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is required for the sapinda relatives.
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa).
And this rule prescribing immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for *sapiṇḍas* should be understood to apply to the miscarriage of a fetus that has become liquid.

As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha—"In the case of a child under two years of age having died, and in the case of a miscarriage, there is a three-night period for the *sapiṇḍas*"—that refers to the context of a solid miscarriage occurring in the fifth or sixth month; for "up to the fourth month it is a flow (*srāva*), in the fifth and sixth it is a fall (*pāta*);
beyond that it is a birth (*prasūti*), and there shall be ten days of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*)."
In the case of a miscarriage, there shall be a three-night period of impurity for the mother, excluding the impurity of the sapinda relatives;
in the case of a full-term birth, the mother's impurity lasts according to the number of months of pregnancy, while that of the father and others lasts for three days.
Thus, according to the recollection of Marīci.

From the seventh month onwards, if a birth occurs that results in the child's death, or if the child dies after being born, the full period of impurity (*āśauca*) occasioned by birth applies to the *sapiṇḍas*. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Hārīta: "Whether the child dies after being born (*jātamṛta*) or is born after having died (*mṛtajāta*), for the *sapiṇḍas* there is a ten-day period. Furthermore, this follows from the statement of Pāraskara: "In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), if [the child] dies, the impurity lasts until the rising [from the confinement], just like [ordinary] birth-impurity. "Until the rising" means until the mother who has given birth rises; that is, for ten days. "Like birth-impurity" means that it is devoid of the offering of water (*udakadāna*) which is occasioned by the death of a child.
Bṛhanmanu also says:
"If a child dies within ten days, its relatives shall not observe the impurity of death (śāvāśauca); rather, the impurity of birth (sūtyāśauca) is prescribed."
Thus it is said:
"If a child dies within ten days, its kinsmen shall not observe the impurity of death (śāvāśauca); rather, the impurity of birth (sūtyāśauca) is prescribed."
And likewise, another Smṛti text also states: "For one who dies within ten days, the impurity lasts for the same number of days as the birth-impurity.
By reflecting on this collection of such statements, it is understood that there is no curtailment of the birth-based impurity for Sapiṇḍas.

As for the statement of Bṛhad-Viṣṇu, "If a child is born and then dies, or if it dies at birth, there is immediate purification for the family," that is intended to establish purification from the impurity caused by the death of an infant through bathing, not from the impurity caused by birth.

And likewise Pāraskara states: "If a miscarriage should occur in the womb, the period of impurity (sūtaka) shall last ten days, because the cause for the impurity of the sapinda relatives—the birth—is present.
The statement, "If one born alive should die, one is purified immediately," refers to the impurity regarding the deceased (pretāśauca).
And so it has been stated by Śaṅkha: "Before the naming ceremony, there is immediate purification."

Furthermore, as for the statement of Kātyāyana: "But if one should pass away before the ten-day period has elapsed, there shall be purification immediately; there is neither the status of a deceased person nor the performance of water-libations."
Thus, that [text] also has the same meaning as the Vaiṣṇava [text].

However, when the reading is "na pretaṃ naiva sūtakam" (neither death-impurity nor birth-impurity), then the meaning is that there is no impurity (*sūtaka*)—that is, no state of untouchability—for the father and others. Alternatively, this is the meaning: if a child dies within ten days, then there is no impurity due to death (*pretāśauca*).

If a birth occurs among the sapinda relatives at that time, then even the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) need not be observed; rather, purification is attained through the preceding period of impurity alone.
As for the statement of Bṛhan-Manu: "If one born while [the parents] are alive then dies, there is indeed *sūtaka*;
the *sūtaka* lasts for the full duration for the mother, but for the father and others, it is three nights."
Thus, as for the statement of Bṛhatpracetā:
"If an infant dies within a muhūrta of birth, the mother is purified after ten days, but the agnates (gotriṇaḥ) are purified immediately."

Thus, the established rule in this regard is as follows: if death occurs after birth but before the naming ceremony (*nābhivardhana*), the impurity (*āśauca*) of the father and other relatives caused by the birth lasts for three days.

However, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for the purpose of performing the *agnihotra* and other rites, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "For the sake of the *agnihotra*, purification is attained immediately through bathing and touching water. But after the time of the naming ceremony, even upon the passing of the infant, the full impurity caused by birth applies to the *sapiṇḍa* relatives: "As long as the umbilical cord is not severed, so long does one not incur the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*)."
After the stalk has been severed, the birth-impurity (sūtaka) is then prescribed.
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Jaimini. This same point has also been shown by Manu:
"In the case of a miscarriage, one is purified after nights equal in number to the months [of gestation]."
When her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who was menstruating becomes pure through bathing.
Thus:
"In the case of a miscarriage, she is purified by nights equal in number to the months [of gestation];
when her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who is menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath."
The first half has been explained. This, however, is the meaning of the latter half:
when the menstrual flow has ceased—that is, when it has stopped—the woman who was menstruating becomes pure through bathing and thus fit for rites dedicated to the gods and other such purposes.
Furthermore, regarding the object of contact and so forth, even if the impurity has not ceased, she becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day.
Thus it was said by Vṛddha-Manu:
"On the fourth day she becomes completely purified for worldly transactions."
Thus,
on the fourth day she becomes pure for worldly affairs.
Likewise, another Smṛti states:
A woman who has reached her menses becomes pure for her husband on the fourth day by bathing;
however, she becomes pure for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors on the fifth day.
The phrase "on the fifth day" is intended as an indicator for the time when the menstrual flow has ceased.
When there is a recurrence of menstruation within seventeen days from the onset of the initial flow, there is no impurity at all;
however, on the eighteenth day, purification occurs after one day.
In the nineteenth [day], purification occurs after two days;
thereafter, for the subsequent [days], purification occurs after three days.
As Atri has said:
If a woman who has become menstruating becomes menstruating again after having already bathed,
there is no impurity as long as it is within eighteen days.
For a period of less than nineteen days, it shall be one day; beyond that, two days;
from twenty days onwards, one shall remain impure for three nights.
Thus:
"If a woman who has become menstruating becomes menstruating again after having already bathed,
there is no impurity before the eighteenth day."
For a period of less than nineteen days, the impurity lasts for one day; from that point until twenty days, it lasts for two days; and for periods beyond that, one remains impure for three nights.

Another Smṛti text states that impurity does not exist before fourteen days; in this context, what is intended is the commencement of purification through bathing and other rites. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, this prohibition of impurity applies to the case of one whose menses generally appear only after twenty days.
However, for one who has reached puberty and whose discharge of menses occurs frequently even before eighteen days, the period of impurity is only three nights.

And she must remain for three nights without bathing or other such purification; for it is said in the *Smṛti* of Vasiṣṭha: "A woman in her courses remains impure for three nights. She should not apply collyrium, nor anoint herself, nor bathe in water, nor sleep on the ground, nor sleep during the day, nor look at the planets, nor touch fire, nor eat, nor spin thread, nor clean her teeth, nor laugh, nor perform any action whatsoever. It is known from tradition that she should drink from a vessel that is not broken, or with her cupped hands, or from a vessel of red iron. There is also a specific rule in the *Āṅgirasa*:
The eater of sacrificial oblations (Havirbhuk) should eat from his hand or from an earthen vessel and sleep on the ground;
a woman in her courses, having bathed on the fourth day, shall attain purity.
Thus it is said:
"The consumer of sacrificial offerings (havirbhuk) should eat from the hand or from an earthen vessel, and sleep upon the ground;
a woman in her courses, having bathed on the fourth day, shall attain purity."

In the *Pārāśara* [Smṛti] as well, there is this specific rule: "If a woman becomes menstruating when an occasional bath (naimittika-snāna) is required, she should perform the bath by means of water filtered through another vessel and then observe her vow."
She should somehow have her limbs, including the major and minor parts, sprinkled with water;
she should not wring out her garment, nor should she put on another one.
Thus it is said:
"If a woman becomes menstruating when an occasional bath (naimittika-snāna) is required,
she should perform the bath using water transferred through another vessel and then observe her vow."
Her limbs, including her major and minor members, should somehow be sprinkled with water;
she should not wring out her garment, nor should she wear another cloth.
Uśanas has also shown a specific rule in this regard:
"If a woman is overcome by fever and drenched with menstrual flow, how may she attain purification? By what ritual act may she become pure?"
When the fourth day has arrived, another woman should touch her;
having plunged into the water with her clothes on and bathed again and again,
she should touch herself ten or twelve times, and sip water repeatedly.
And after the discarding of the garments, she shall then become pure;
thereafter, she should give gifts according to her capacity, and through a *puṇyāha* ceremony, she becomes completely purified.
Thus it is asked:
"If a woman is overcome by fever and simultaneously overwhelmed by her menses, how may she attain purification? By what ritual act may she become pure?"
When the fourth day has arrived, another woman should touch her;
she, having immersed herself in water with her clothes on, should bathe again and again and touch [the other] repeatedly,
and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) ten or twelve times over.
And after the discarding of the garments, she shall then become pure;
thereafter, she should give a gift according to her ability, and through a *puṇyāha* ceremony, she is purified.

This method of bathing for one who is ill should be followed: when the need for bathing arises for the sick person, ten times a healthy person should bathe and touch him; then that sick person shall become pure.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Parāśara:

"But when the death of a woman in her courses or of a woman who has recently given birth occurs, this is the method for bathing: 'When a woman who has recently given birth has died, how do the performers of sacrifice act?
Having taken water in a jar, and likewise the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)..."
Then, having consecrated water with meritorious verses, one should obtain purification through speech;
having bathed [the deceased] with that very water, one should perform the cremation according to the prescribed rule.

But regarding a menstruating woman who has died: having bathed her with the five products of the cow, and having covered her with another garment, one should cremate her according to the prescribed rule.
Thus, having bathed the deceased woman in her menses with the five products of the cow,
and having covered her with another garment, one should cremate her according to the prescribed rule.

Regarding this matter of the appearance of menses, the birth of a son, and so forth: if these occur after sunrise, then the calculation of the days and nights of impurity (*āśauca*) must be made starting from that very day.

However, when the appearance of menses, the birth of a son, or similar events occur during the night, there are two views: one view holds that if the birth or other event occurs before midnight, then even though the impurity spans only a portion of the preceding day, the calculation must begin from that preceding day itself.
The second view holds that the night should be divided into three parts; if the birth or other event occurs within the first two parts, the preceding day is to be taken [as the start].
Another [teacher] says it is before sunrise;
as Kaśyapa has said:
"When the menses appear in women after the sun has risen..."
For whom there is birth, for him there is death; for whom there is prosperity, for him there is adversity. For whom there is day, for him there is night.
The time limit for impurity (sūtaka) and similar conditions is prescribed as ending at midnight;
one should divide the night into three parts, and the first two parts are considered part of the preceding day.
In the case of the birth-impurity (*ṛtusūtaka*), the latter half of the night is joined with the dawn;
however, when death occurs or when the impurity of menstruation (*rajas*) arises during the night itself, [the full period applies].
The preceding day alone should be taken, as long as the sun has not yet risen.
Thus it is said:
"But when the menses of women are seen after the sun has risen,
whether it be birth or death, the night belongs to that very day."
The period of time beginning from midnight is prescribed for impurity (sūtaka) and similar occasions;
one should divide the night into three parts, and the first two parts are considered part of the preceding day.
In the case of birth or death resulting from the menstrual flow, the latter part of the night is joined with the dawn;
however, if it occurs at night, the birth or death impurity lasts until the following morning.
The preceding day alone should be taken, as long as the sun has not yet risen.

The determination of these ritual periods (kalpas) should be understood according to local custom. Furthermore, this period of impurity (āśauca) must be observed for one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni), beginning from the day of the cremation rite (saṃskāra). For one who does not maintain the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), however, it begins from the day of death; yet, since the collection of the bones (saṃcayana) applies to both, it should be discerned that [the period] begins from the day of the cremation rite.

As Aṅgiras said: "For one without the sacred fire, purification occurs at the time of departure; for one with the sacred fire, it occurs after the funeral rites, including the collection of the bones and the cremation. However, the day of death is determined according to the prescribed rule."
Thus:

for one who maintains no sacred fire, purification occurs upon the departure [of the soul]; for one who maintains a fire, it occurs after the funeral rites. There is the collection of bones, the cremation, and the day of death according to the prescribed rule.

Because of the scriptural statement, "of the purificatory rite for one who maintains the sacred fires," it should be understood that when a father who has maintained the sacred fires dies in another country, there is no lapse of duties such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) for his sons and others until the purificatory rite is performed.
And so says Paiṭhīnasi:
"For among the twice-born, impurity lasts until the departure [of the body] from the fireless [state]."
One should know that [the victim] possessed fire due to burning, provided he died while staying in a foreign land.
Thus [ends the section]. 3.20.
For among the twice-born, impurity lasts until the cremation for one who maintains no sacred fire;
however, for one who maintains a sacred fire, one should know that it lasts from the cremation when he has died in a foreign land.
Regarding the application of the ten-day period and so forth due to sapinda-relationship and other factors, he states an exception in certain specific cases of death:
"In the case of those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and immediately for those who commit suicide;
[here] 'king' refers to an anointed Kshatriya or similar."
The mention of "cows" is intended as an illustration for animals such as horned and tusked creatures;
the mention of "Brahmins" is an illustration for those of the lowest castes (*antyaja*).
This refers to the *sapiṇḍas* who are related to those killed by these [beings].
Those who intentionally take their own lives by means of poison, hanging, and so forth, are "suicides" (ātmaghātinaḥ).

The mention of "suicides" is intended to indicate, as a secondary implication, those who have fallen [from their status] (patita) as included in the same rule as "heretics and those who do not rely [on the Vedas]" (pākhaṇḍyanāśritāḥ).
Regarding their relatives, "immediate" (anvakṣa)—meaning following immediately after the eye (akṣa), that is, instantly—there is purification; this is the meaning.

And for those related to such [deceased persons], impurity lasts as long as they remain within sight, not for ten days or the like. Thus says Gautama: "For those killed by cows or Brahmins, and for those killed by the king's wrath in non-battle, there is immediate [impurity]; likewise for those who die by suicide through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling, provided they did so intentionally.
The inclusion of the term "wrath" (krodha) is for the purpose of excluding those killed through negligence.

The mention of "non-battle" is for the purpose of indicating that there is one day of impurity for one killed in battle: "For women who have perished for the sake of Brahmins, and also for those killed while seizing cattle, and for those killed in combat, there is one night of impurity."
Thus it is remembered [in the Smṛti].
And this [impurity] applies only to one who dies after some time due to a wound sustained during battle;
however, for one slain at the front of the fray, there is immediate purification.
As Manu has said: "For one slain in battle with raised weapons in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is completed immediately; such is the established rule regarding impurity."
Thus.
For one slain in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya by weapons raised in battle, the sacrifice is immediately completed and so too is the period of impurity; such is the settled rule.

Since birth and the like become causes for impurity (āśauca) only when they are known, [the author] states an exception regarding the case where [the event] is known at a time subsequent to the day of birth, even though a period of ten days or more would otherwise apply:
"In the case of one who has gone abroad, the remainder of the period [shall apply]; once the full period has elapsed, one becomes pure by offering water."

When a *sapiṇḍa* has gone abroad or resides in another country, and the birth of a *sapiṇḍa* or similar event is not known by the person [at home] on the very first day, the remaining period of time—that portion of the ten-day period of impurity which has elapsed—is itself the cause of purification.
However, when the full period of impurity, such as the ten days, has expired, purification occurs after offering water to the deceased.
Since the offering of water is preceded by bathing, one becomes pure by bathing and then offering the water.
Thus it was said by Manu:
"Upon hearing of the death of a relative or the birth of a son after ten days have passed,
a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes."
Thus:
Having heard of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed,
a man becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes.

Because it is ordained that "having given water for the full [period], one becomes pure," which establishes that the period of impurity associated with the offering of water for the deceased (*pretodakadāna*) is the cause of purification, it is understood that for *sapiṇḍas*, there is no impurity for births that have passed.
However, for the father, there is indeed bathing even after ten days have elapsed following a birth, because of the statement: "and having heard of the birth of a son.
And this mention of the "son" is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that for *sapiṇḍas* generally, there is no impurity for births that have passed.
Otherwise, having heard of the death of a relative after the ten-day period has passed, as well as a birth during that same period, he would have stated exactly that;
yet he did not say so.
And thus Devala says:
"There is no impurity once the period of birth-impurity has passed, even if days [of the period] have elapsed.
Therefore, it is established that the lapse of the period of impurity occurs only in the event of a calamity.
Some read this verse differently: "There is no impurity during the birth-impurity even when the days have passed;
if [the father] has gone abroad, there shall be a remainder of the time; but if none remains, it is only three days.
For all [cases], when a year has been completed and [the deceased] has died, one becomes pure after offering water."
Thus it is said:
"If [the relative] has gone abroad, the period of impurity shall last for the remainder of the time; if no time remains, it shall be exactly three days.
When a year has been completed, all become pure after offering water for one who has died."
When one has gone abroad or has died, for all classes—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others alike—the remaining period of time is the cause of purification.
However, if that period, such as ten days, has passed without remainder, then for everyone the impurity lasts for only three days.
If the departure of the one who had gone abroad becomes known only after a full year has elapsed, then every person, beginning with the Brahmin, shall become pure by bathing and offering water.
And so Manu says:
"But when a year has passed, one becomes pure simply by touching water."
When a year has elapsed, however, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
This three-day period is to be understood as applying after ten days have passed but before three months have elapsed.
The previously mentioned immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca), on the other hand, is to be understood as applying from the ninth month onwards until the end of the year.

Furthermore, as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha that "having heard [of a death] after ten days, [the impurity lasts] one night," that refers to the period from beyond six months up until the ninth month. As for the statement of Gautama that "and having heard it after the tenth day, [it lasts] two nights (pakṣiṇī)," that refers to the period from beyond three months up until before the sixth month.
And so says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:

For a period of three months, there shall be a fast of three nights; likewise, for six months, a fast of one day and two nights (pakṣiṇī); but for less than nine months, it is one day; beyond that, one becomes pure by bathing.
Thus:

for a period of three months, there shall be a fast of three nights; likewise, for six months, a pakṣiṇī fast; but for a period prior to nine months, it is one day; beyond that, one is purified by a ritual bath.
And this refers to cases other than one's mother and father; for even if a son is far away, if his parents should die, from the moment he hears of it, he shall remain impure for ten days.

Thus it is from the Smṛti of Paiṭhīnasi. Likewise, in another Smṛti it is said: "But upon the death of a great guru, one wearing wet clothes and fasting must perform the funeral rites according to rule, even if a year has passed."
Thus it is said:
"But upon the death of a great guru, one wearing wet clothes must perform the funeral rites according to the rule, even if a year has passed."

The meaning is that even after a year has passed, the funeral rites—such as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) and the offering of water (*udakadāna*)—must still be performed; purification does not occur merely by bathing.
Regarding the wife of one's father who is other than one's own mother, a specific rule is shown in another *Smṛti*:
"When the wife of one's father has passed away, the best of the twice-born [should observe the rites], excluding his own mother."
Even when a year has passed, one remains impure for three nights.
Thus:
"When the wife of one's father has passed away, the best of the twice-born shall remain impure for three nights, even if a full year has elapsed, with the exception of his own mother."

However, if someone dies in another country separated by a river or other obstacles, for their *sapiṇḍas*, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) after ten days have passed, even if it is within three months: "Upon hearing that one has died in another country, or that a eunuch, a forest hermit, or an ascetic has died, or in the case of a miscarriage, the members of the lineage are purified by bathing."
Thus it is said:
"Upon hearing that a kinsman has died in another country, or that a eunuch, a forest hermit,
or an ascetic has died, or in the case of a miscarriage, the members of the lineage are purified by bathing."
And the definition of "another country" (deśāntara) was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"Where there is the interval of a great river, or where a mountain acts as a barrier,
or where speech is divided— that is called another country."
Some say the other country is sixty yojanas in length;
others say forty, and others likewise thirty.
Thus it is said:
"Where there is the interval of a great river, or where a mountain acts as an obstruction,
or where languages differ— that is called a different country."
Some say that another land extends sixty yojanas in length;
others say forty, and others likewise thirty.
And this "excessive impurity" (*atikrāntāśauca*) refers to the death of one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), and not to the impurity pertaining to specific stages of life (*vayovasthā*).
Thus it has been stated by Vyāghrapāda:
"For all [classes], it is the same during [the period of] youth, and likewise when [that period] has passed."
But when that [time] has passed, it becomes dangerous, arising from excessive delay.
Thus it is said:
"Among all [the sons], the [penalty for] age is the same when it has passed;
but when [the initiation] has been performed, it is different, even though the time has likewise lapsed."

The meaning is as follows: regarding age—such as the period beginning from three years—the impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed by such statements as "until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate" (*sadyaḥ*) and so forth, is equal and undifferentiated for all castes, including Brāhmaṇas and others.
Furthermore, when the [initial period] of ten days and so forth has elapsed, the impurity consisting of three days and so forth is likewise undifferentiated for all.
However, when one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) dies, the impurity for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes is unequal, being respectively ten, twelve, fifteen, and thirty days.

In that very case of the death of one who has been initiated, there occurs an impurity arising after the [prescribed] time has elapsed, but not an exceeding of the impurity based on age-status. (3.21)
He states an exception to the ten-night period of impurity for sapinda relatives among Kṣatriyas and others:
"For a Kṣatriya it is twelve days; for a Vaiśya, fifteen;
for a Śūdra, thirty days; but for one who lives according to the law, half of that."
Upon the birth of a *sapiṇḍa* relative or upon their death, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras is, respectively, twelve, fifteen, and thirty days.

However, for a Śūdra who lives righteously and is devoted to the *pākayajña* sacrifices and service to the twice-born, that period is halved; thus his impurity lasts for half a month, which is fifteen nights.
In this way, since the options of three nights or ten nights remain, this ten-night period of impurity is established as applying specifically to the Brāhmaṇa.
In other Smṛtis, however, rules for impurity (āśauca) lasting ten days and so forth are also shown for Kṣatriyas and others.
As Parāśara says:
"But a Kṣatriya who is devoted to his own duties becomes pure after ten days."
In the same way, a Vaiśya shall attain purification in twelve days.
And so says Śātātapa:
"A Kṣatriya is purified after eleven days, a Vaiśya likewise after twelve,
and a Śūdra after twenty nights, in the case of death or birth impurity."
Vasiṣṭha, however, says: "A Kṣatriya [is purified] in fifteen nights, and a Vaiśya in twenty nights. Aṅgiras, on the other hand, says:
"For all castes alike, in the case of birth or death [impurity],..."
"Śātātapa has declared that their purification occurs after ten days."
Thus, various high and low rules regarding impurity have been shown.
Since there is no common practice among people in the world regarding them, demonstrating a fixed system would not be particularly useful; therefore, no such system is presented here.
However, when Kṣatriyas and others are the *sapiṇḍas* of Brāhmaṇas and the like, then the rules for impurity stated by Hārīta and others should be followed.
A Brahmin is purified after ten days following a birth among those of his own caste;
however, he is purified in six, three, or one day respectively when it occurs among those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes.
Thus:
"A Brahmin is purified in ten days from birth or death occurring among those of his own caste;
[he is purified] in six, three, or one day [respectively] among those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes."

Viṣṇu also says: "For a Kṣatriya, purification occurs after six nights among Vaiśyas and Śūdras who are *sapiṇḍa* relatives; for a Vaiśya, purification occurs after three nights among Śūdras who are *sapiṇḍa* relatives; and for Śūdras, purification occurs after six nights. However, when births or deaths occur among *sapiṇḍa* relatives of a higher caste, purification for those of lower castes occurs upon the lapse of that [higher caste's] period of impurity. But Baudhāyana has stated, without distinction, that it is ten days: "Those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes who may be the kinsmen (*bāndhava*) of a Brāhmaṇa..."
Regarding their period of impurity, the purification of a Brāhmaṇa is held to occur after ten days.
Thus:
"If there are relatives of a Brāhmaṇa who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes,
it is prescribed that the Brāhmaṇa's purification from their impurity occurs after ten days."
The determination between these two positions is based on whether the situation involves a time of distress or not.
However, for female slaves and others, touchability according to the purity of their master applies, while their lack of entitlement to perform religious rites lasts only until the end of one month.
Thus said Aṅgiras:
Whatever the caste of a female or male slave may be, their purification shall be according to that same caste; however, the period of birth-impurity for a female slave lasts one month.
Thus:

"Whatever the caste of the master may be, the male and female slaves shall follow the purification rules of that same caste; however, for a female slave, the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) lasts for one month."

However, for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), there is indeed an absence of ritual impurity (āśauca), because of the traditional teaching of Manu that "those born in the inverse order are devoid of dharma.
Nevertheless, upon death or birth, there is certainly a purification for the purpose of removing physical filth, just like after the voiding of urine or feces. (3.22)
He states an exception to the ten-day period of impurity based on specific stages of age:
"Until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it is declared to last one night;
until the initiation into vows (vratādeśa), it lasts three nights; and beyond that, ten nights."

For as long as it takes for the teeth to erupt, during that period, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) for the relatives of a deceased child. For one who dies before the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the impurity for the relatives lasts for a night—that is, it extends throughout the day and night. For one who dies after the tonsure but before the initiation (*vratādeśa*, i.e., *upanayana*), the impurity lasts for three days.

And here, although the expression "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) is stated without distinction as "until the eruption of teeth," it should nevertheless be understood to apply to cases where there is no consecration by fire (*agni-saṃskāra*). For the *Vaiṣṇava* [Smṛti] ordains immediate purification for one who has died before the eruption of teeth, stating: "When a child dies before the eruption of teeth, purification occurs immediately; there is neither consecration by fire nor the rite of libation (*udaka-kriyā*)"—thus prescribing immediate purity for one devoid of fire-consecration. However, when fire-consecration does take place, the period is one day, as will be stated later: "But in the case of unmarried girls and children, [the impurity lasts] one day. And so says Yama:
In the case of a son whose teeth have not yet emerged, or a young child, or likewise in the case of a miscarriage,
there is a period of impurity lasting one day and night for all the sapinda relatives.
Thus:
"In the case of a son who has not yet cut his teeth, a child, or likewise one miscarried from the womb,
the period of impurity for all sapinda relatives is one day and night."

Prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is indeed mandatory, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "Before the naming ceremony, there is immediate purity. Furthermore, the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) is prescribed for the first or the third year: "The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to dharma in the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Vedas."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
Consequently, from the eruption of teeth until the first annual *cūḍā* ceremony, the period of impurity lasts for one day.
In that regard, even if the teeth have erupted, for one whose *cūḍā* has not yet been performed, the period lasts for only one day until the completion of the third year.
And so Viṣṇu says: "Even when teeth have appeared, if the tonsure (cūḍā) has not been performed, purification occurs after one day and night.
Beyond that, prior to initiation (upanayana), it is three days.
As for the statement of Manu: "For men whose tonsure has not been performed, impurity is declared to last for one night."
But for those whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, purification is held to occur after three nights.
Thus, this very same subject applies to him as well.

However, regarding a child less than two years old, it has been stated by that same [author]: "Having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, they should throw him away after only three days."
Having abandoned [the body] like a log in the forest, they should discard it after only three days.

And as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "When a child less than two years old has died, or in the case of a miscarriage, the impurity for the sapindas lasts three nights," that refers to the intention that the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has been performed within the first year. As for the statement of Aṅgiras, "Even if he has not had the tonsure ceremony, but has teethed and has passed away..."
Nevertheless, having cremated him, one should observe the period of impurity for three days.

Thus, this [period] should be understood to apply when the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) is postponed beyond three years due to considerations of family custom; for it has been stated by that same author: "But if a Brahmin dies before three years have passed, purification occurs after one night. Nor should it be suspected that this single day applies in the absence of the eruption of teeth.
For it is not possible for teeth not to have emerged in one less than three years of age;

were that the case, there would be an unavoidable contradiction with the statement of Viṣṇu, who prescribes a single day of impurity even when teeth have appeared, provided the tonsure (cūḍā) has not been performed.
Therefore, the ancient interpretation alone is superior.

As for the statement of Kaśyapa that there is purification in three nights for children who have not yet cut their teeth, that refers to the case of parents; however, having emitted semen, a man becomes pure by touching water, though he should observe the impurity for three days due to his connection with the seed.
Thus, because it is remembered as lasting for three nights due to its being conditioned by the relationship between the produced and the producer.

And thus the meaning is as follows: prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*); after that and before the eruption of teeth, in the case of a cremation rite (*agnisaṃskārakriyā*), there is impurity for one day, otherwise there is immediate purification; for one whose teeth have erupted, before the first-annual tonsure (*caula*), there is one day; from the first year onwards until the age of three, for one who has had the tonsure performed, there are three days, while for another there is one day; after three years, even for one who has not had the tonsure performed, there are three days; and after the initiation (*upanayana*), for all [classes] such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, there is the period of ten nights and so forth. (3.23)

Now he states an exception regarding women according to their specific stage of life: "But in the case of unmarried girls and young boys, purification lasts for one day. Unmarried means those who have not been wedded; in the case of such girls, even if they have had the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), prior to the formal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), one day and night is specifically the cause of purification.

The sapinda relationship among sapindas and for unmarried girls extends only to three generations, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "For unmarried women, the sapinda relationship is understood to extend to three generations. Furthermore, in the case of infants who have not yet cut their teeth, if the cremation rite has been performed, purification takes one day;

however, in the case of an unmarried girl who has not undergone the tonsure ceremony, immediate purification is prescribed: "In the case of an unmarried girl who has not had her tonsure, immediate purification is ordained."

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: after the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) but before the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), the period of impurity lasts for exactly three days on both the husband’s side and the father’s side. As Manu has said:
But for female relatives who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, those who share the same ancestry (sanābhayaḥ) become pure according to the rule already stated.
Thus:
"But for female relatives who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) become pure according to the very rule already stated."
Relatives on the husband’s side are purified in three nights;

however, uterine relatives on the father’s side who are *sapiṇḍas* are purified by the very same rule already stated—namely, by the three-night period mentioned in the passage beginning with "for those whose tonsure has been performed," and not by the ten-night period, because that is inappropriate prior to marriage.
For this very reason, Marīci says:

That [gift] which was previously promised with water but not actually delivered is to be known as "unconsecrated" (asaṃskṛtā); for both parties, it is traditionally held that [the period of impurity] lasts three nights.
Thus it is said:
"A girl who has been given with water but not formally bestowed [in marriage] is to be known as unrefined (asaṃskṛtā); for both [parties], a period of three nights is prescribed."

Regarding both sides—the husband's and the father's—Viṣṇu has specified a distinction for the period after marriage: "In the case of women who have been consecrated [by marriage], there is no impurity on the father's side; however, if their birth or death occurs in the father's house, then there is one night or three nights [of impurity].
In that regard, the settled rule is: one day for a birth, and three nights for a journey [to the husband's home].

Furthermore, this impurity based on age is common to all social classes (*varṇa*), because the rule "twelve days for a Kṣatriya" is stated by specifying that particular class. For this very reason, although Manu’s injunction regarding impurity does not specify a particular class and thus establishes a general rule for the entire fourfold order (*cāturvarṇya*), he states again: "For all four classes, duly and in their proper sequence."
Likewise, it has been stated by Aṅgiras:

"For all castes without distinction, purification occurs after three nights until the performance of the sacramental rites; however, for girls, it is ordained that purification takes place in one day."
Thus:
"For all castes without distinction, purification occurs after three nights following the performance of the purificatory rites; however, for girls, it is ordained to take place in a single day."
Furthermore, the statement of Vyāghrapāda—that [the rite] is equal for all regardless of age—has been demonstrated previously.
Therefore, just as the rule for the offering of rice-balls and water, beginning with "it should be given according to the procedure of the Piṇḍayajña," is common to all social classes (varṇas).

Just as the rule for impurity due to a common water-relationship (*samānodaka*), the rule for impurity arising from the coincidence of births and deaths (*saṃnipātāśauca*), the rule for impurity due to miscarriage—stating "in the case of a miscarriage, the nights are equal to the months"—and the rule for impurity when one has gone abroad—stating "if the time [of the period] remains, it shall be the remainder; if none remains, it is only three days"—as well as the rules for impurity concerning teachers and others which are common to all castes (*sarvavarṇasādhāraṇa*), so too impurity caused by age and stage of life ought to be common to all castes.
For this very reason, it is said: "When the *cūḍā* ceremony is performed for a Kṣatriya at six years, and for a Vaiśya at nine."
But for a Śūdra who has passed three years [of age], a twelve-day period is prescribed.
Likewise: "Where a three-night period of impurity is observed for Brahmins, there it is twelve days for a Śūdra, and six or nine days for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas."

Teachers such as Dhāreśvara, Viśvarūpa, Medhātithi, and others—who do not disregard the statements of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and others due to a perception of their being contradictory—have accepted this very common position.
And those [other] non-contradictory statements are to be explained as referring to Kṣatriyas and others who are distressed or undistressed.
He states an extension [of the rules] to the teacher and others:
"And in the case of the teacher's resident pupil, the Vedic scholar, and the maternal uncle.

Here, "teacher" (*guru*) refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); "resident pupil" (*antevāsī*) refers to the student (*śiṣya*); "Vedic scholar" (*anūcāna*) refers to one who expounds the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*); and by the mention of the "maternal uncle," those related by birth—namely, one's own kinsmen, the mother's kinsmen, and the father's kinsmen—are indicated.
And these [categories] have been shown in the passage beginning with "wives and daughters.

A *śrotriya* is one who studies a single branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda; for Baudhāyana records that "one who has studied a single branch is a *śrotriya*. When these persons have died, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts for a day and a night.
However, in the case of the primary guru, the father, upon his death, the period is ten days because of the *sapiṇḍa* relationship.

But in the case of a father who, having procreated sons, performed their sacraments, taught them the Vedas, caused them to grasp the meaning of the Vedas, and provided for their livelihood—that father being a "great guru" (*mahāguru*)—upon his death, the period is twelve nights.
In this regard, one should observe what was stated by Āśvalāyana: "In the event of the death of great gurus, they should abstain from giving gifts and Vedic study."
But upon the death of the teacher, it lasts for three nights.
As Manu said:
"They declare that the period of impurity is three nights when the teacher has passed away."
This rule applies day and night to his son and his wife.
Thus it is said:
"When a teacher has passed away, they declare that the period of impurity lasts for three nights;
for his son and for his wife, the rule is one day and night."

But when one performs the funeral rites for a teacher or the like, there is impurity for ten nights; however, a disciple should perform the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rites) for his deceased guru, and in that case, he becomes pure after ten days along with those who carry the corpse.
Because this was stated by him [Āpastamba]:

"But for a Śrotriya living in the same village, this impurity applies," according to the Smṛti of Āśvalāyana: "One day [of impurity] for a fellow student (sabrahmacārin) and for a Śrotriya living in the same village.
One initiated by the same teacher is a fellow student (sabrahmacārin).
And this should be understood to apply when [the person] is not present;
but when a disciple or similar person is present, it lasts for three nights and so forth, as Manu said:
"If a learned scholar (śrotriya) has died, one shall remain impure for three nights."
One should observe a fast for a night with its two preceding days on account of a maternal uncle, a disciple, an officiating priest, or a kinsman.
Thus it is said:
"Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has arrived as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights;
for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one shall remain impure for a night with its two flanks (a pakṣiṇī rātriḥ)."

"Upasaṃpanna" refers to one who is connected through being a neighbor of loving-kindness (*maitrī-prātiveśya*) and so forth, or one endowed with virtuous conduct (*śīla*). The mention of "maternal uncle" (*mātula*) is intended as an illustration for maternal aunts and others.
"Relatives" (*bāndhava*) refers to one's own kin, maternal relatives, and paternal relatives.
And so Bṛhaspati says:
"One shall be impure for three days in the case of the maternal grandfather, the teacher, and a Śrotriya."
One remains impure for three days in the case of the maternal grandfather, the teacher, and a Śrotriya; likewise Pracetas says:
"Upon the death of an officiating priest or a patron, one becomes pure after three nights."
Thus it is said: "If the officiating priest (ṛtvij) or the patron (yājya) has died, one becomes pure after three nights. And so says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
When a daughter's son has died, the impurity lasts for three nights;
however, if he has been consecrated [with initiation], it shall last for three days and nights—thus the law is established.
"But what should be the case for married women when their parents have passed away?
Purification occurs in exactly three nights," so said the venerable Yama.
One should spend the night as a bird (in silence) with one's father-in-law, mother-in-law, sister, maternal aunt, maternal uncle, and likewise with one's father’s or mother’s sister.

Likewise: "In the case of a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a friend, a teacher, or the wives of one's teachers, there is impurity for a *pakṣiṇī* night; and also if the maternal grandmother has died."
And so says Gautama: "For three nights [one observes impurity] for one who is not a sapinda, for a kinsman by birth, and for a fellow student.
Kinsmen by birth include the maternal uncle, the daughter of the mother’s sister, the daughter of the father’s sister, and others.
Likewise, Jābāla says:
For those who share the same water (i.e., distant relatives), the impurity lasts for three days; for those born of the same lineage, it is remembered as one day.
The same applies to a maternal relative, a teacher, a friend, and likewise a local ruler.
Thus it is said:
"For those who share the same water (ekodaka), the impurity lasts for three days; for those born of the same lineage (gotraja), it is remembered as one day.
Likewise, for a maternal relative, a guru, a friend, and a regional ruler."
Viṣṇu: "If one dies in one's own house who is not a sapinda, [the impurity lasts] for one night. Likewise, Vṛddha [Yājñavalkya]:
"But when a sister has been consecrated [by marriage], and also when a brother has been consecrated..."
Upon the death of a friend, a son-in-law, a daughter’s son, a sister’s son,
a maternal uncle, or his son, one becomes pure immediately by bathing.
When the lord of a village, the head of a family, a learned Vedic scholar, an ascetic,
or a pupil has met his death, one remains pure until the appearance of the stars.
As long as the corpse of anyone remains within the center of a village, that village remains impure;
once it has been removed, it attains purity.
Such Smṛti statements that establish specific rules regarding impurity (āśauca) should be sought out;
they are not written here for fear of making this work too voluminous.

Furthermore, since these texts establish heavy and light periods of impurity concerning the same subject matter, their application must be determined according to the circumstances of proximity or distance when they appear to be mutually contradictory. 3.24.
Furthermore: "In the case of non-legitimate sons, wives who have gone to others,
and when the resident king has died, that very day is the cause for purification."
The word "day" (ahar) is understood to carry over.
Non-aurasa sons include the kṣetraja, dattaka, and others.
When such sons are born or have died, the period of impurity lasts for one day and night.

Likewise, when one's own wives have gone to others—meaning they have resorted to someone other than their husband, provided that person is not of a lower caste (pratiloma)—or when they have passed away, the impurity lasts for only a day and night; it does not last for ten days even though *sāpiṇḍya* exists. Furthermore, there is no impurity at all in the case of women who have resorted to those of a lower caste (*pratiloma*), because of the prohibition stated in the verse beginning, "Heretics, thieves... and so forth.
And because the words "wife" and "son" are relative terms, this period of impurity applies only to that which is their counter-correlative—namely, wifehood and sonship.
For the *sapiṇḍas*, however, there is indeed an absence of impurity.
For this very reason, Prajāpati says:
In the case of wives dependent on others, and the sons of another's wife,
the kinsmen become pure by bathing, while the father becomes pure after three nights alone.
Thus it is said:

"In the case of wives dependent on others, and in the case of the sons of another's wife, those of the same lineage (gotra) become pure by bathing; however, their father becomes pure after three nights alone."
But for one who has taken as his dependents women such as unchaste women and the like, the impurity lasts for exactly three nights.
As Viṣṇu says:
"In the case of non-legitimate sons (anaurasa), whether they have been born or have died..."
When wives who have had previous husbands have given birth or have died.
Thus:
when non-legitimate sons have been born or have died,
and when wives who previously had another husband have given birth or have died.
In this context, a period of three nights is the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, the application of these two periods—the three-night and the one-night—is determined by whether the relatives are in proximity or living in a distant location.
When the father’s impurity lasts for three nights, then that of the sapindas lasts for one night.
As Marīci said:
"In the case of birth or death, for those whose [former] wives were others, there is a three-night period;
but for sapindas, it is one day, whereas for the father, it is indeed three nights."
Thus:
"In the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), for those whose previous husbands are others, the impurity lasts three nights;
however, for sapinda relatives, it is one day, whereas for the father, it is indeed three nights."
The father.
Furthermore: that in which one dwells is called a "residence" (*nivāsa*), meaning one's own country.
The king who is its master, the lord of the realm (*viṣayādhipati*), on whichever day he passes away, that very day constitutes the cause for purification.
If [the king] has passed away during the night, then [the impurity lasts] for the duration of that night alone.
For this very reason, Manu says:
"When a king has died, whoever resides within his realm remains impure as long as the light [of the sun or stars] persists."

Thus [it is said]: "When a king has died, for one who resides within his domain, the impurity lasts as long as the light [endures]. "Sajyotis" means that which exists together with the light; this refers to the period of impurity.
The meaning is: if during the day, for as long as the sun is visible; if at night, for as long as the stars are visible. || 3.25 ||
He states the impurity resulting from following [a corpse]:
"A Śūdra must never be followed by a Brāhmaṇa, nor a twice-born man by anyone.
Having followed [the corpse], one becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter."
A twice-born person, such as a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, or a Śūdra, who is not a *sapiṇḍa* relative, must not follow a deceased person.
If, out of affection or other reasons, he does follow them, he becomes pure by bathing in water from a pond or similar source, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Since there is no authority for interpreting this consumption of clarified butter as a substitute for a meal, it does not imply a prohibition against eating.
This refers to the case of those of equal or superior caste.
As Manu says:
"If one follows out of desire a deceased kinsman or even a non-kinsman..."
Having bathed with one's clothes on and touched fire, one becomes pure by consuming clarified butter.
Thus:
"Having followed a deceased kinsman or even a non-kinsman out of a desire to accompany them,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter."
"Relatives" refers to those who share the funeral oblation (*mātṛ-sapiṇḍas*).
However, there is no fault in the case of others, because it has been prescribed for them.
Regarding, however, following after someone of a lower caste, one should look to what is stated in other *smṛtis*.
In that regard, concerning following a Śūdra: "But a Brāhmaṇa who, being weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse as it is being carried away, becomes pure after three nights."

If, however, he has survived for three nights, he should go to a river that flows into the ocean, perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and consume clarified butter; thus he becomes purified.
Thus it was stated by Parāśara.
Regarding following a Kṣatriya [in death], however, it is for one day and night.

Having touched a human bone that is oily, there is impurity for three nights; if it is not oily, it is for one day and night; and likewise for following a corpse, it is for one [day and night]—thus it was stated by Vasiṣṭha.
Furthermore, upon following a Vaiśya, the impurity lasts for a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night).

Similarly, when a Kṣatriya follows an immediate Vaiśya, it is one day and night (*ahorātra*); when he follows a Śūdra separated by one caste, it is a *pakṣiṇī*; and when a Vaiśya follows a Śūdra, it is one day (*ekāha*)—this is to be inferred accordingly.
This is just as Pāraskara has stated regarding weeping as well.
Having performed lamentation together with the relatives of the deceased,
one should avoid giving gifts, performing śrāddha rites, and other such ceremonies for that day and night.
Thus:
Having performed lamentation together with the relatives of the deceased,
one should avoid giving gifts, performing *śrāddha* rites, and other such ceremonies for that day and night.
Likewise, one should not perform the decoration [of the corpse]; if the decoration of a non-sapiṇḍa deceased is performed, there is a penance of one quarter-kṛcchra.
If done through ignorance, there should be a fast; if one is unable, a bath is prescribed.
Thus, because a penance has been prescribed by Śaṅkha. (3.26)
Regarding the impurity of sapinda relations, he states an exception in certain cases:
"There is no impurity for kings when they are slain by lightning,
nor for those killed in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, nor for one whom the king desires [to be pure]."

Although the word *mahī* (earth) denotes the entire terrestrial globe, nevertheless, because it is impossible for the whole earth to have a single lord, and in accordance with the plural form *mahīpatīnām* (of the lords of the earth), it here indicates the political circles (*maṇḭalas*) that constitute parts of it.
For those Kṣatriyas and others who are consecrated and authorized to protect those [circles], there is no impurity (*āśauca*). The meaning is that they should not observe impurity.
Likewise, those who are *sapiṇḍa* relatives of persons struck by lightning or of those who have perished while protecting cows or Brahmins shall not observe impurity (*āśauca*).

Furthermore, a king who desires the absence of impurity for a minister, domestic priest, or similar official—on account of the successful performance of rites such as secret counsel or magical incantations (*abhicāra*) that cannot be accomplished by anyone else—shall likewise not observe it.

And in this context, regarding that protection of subjects which is prescribed as the unique duty of kings, there is an absence of impurity (*āśauca*) only in those activities—such as the distribution of gifts, honors, and hospitality, and the administration of justice—without which such protection would not be possible; it does not apply, however, even to the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and the like.
Thus says Manu:
"Immediate purity is ordained for a king in his high office."
The seat is also for the purpose of protecting the subjects; this is the reason here.
Thus it is said:
"Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high office;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting the subjects."
Gautama also stated: "And for the sake of the non-obstruction of royal business," whereby even the king's servants and others do not undergo impurity (*āśauca*).
As Pracetas said:
"Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves..."
Kings and the royal servants are declared to be immediately pure.
Thus: artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves,
kings, and royal servants are declared to be immediately pure.
Artisans (*kāravaḥ*) are those such as cooks and the like;
craftsmen (*śilpinaḥ*) are those such as painters, washermen, and so forth.

Regarding the question of what the scope of this absence of impurity (*aśaucābhāva*) is, since the specific occupations of each are brought to mind by words denoting the causes of their respective actions, this [absence of impurity] should be understood to apply specifically to those [occupations].

For this very reason, Viṣṇu demonstrates that the absence of impurity applies only to specific domains: "not for kings in their royal duties, not for those under a vow during the vow, not for those performing a Sattra sacrifice during the Sattra, and not for artisans in their artisanal work.
It is also stated in the Śātātapa-smṛti:
"Śūdras who perform labor for wages, as well as female and male slaves..."
They are not defiled during bathing, personal grooming, or household chores.
Thus:
Śūdras who work for wages, as well as male and female slaves,
are not defiled in matters of bathing, personal grooming, or household chores.
And it should be understood that this purification of slaves and others is applicable to those who have attained contact [with the impurity] because it cannot be avoided.
For this very reason, another Smṛti states:
"A slave born in the house (garbhadāsa) becomes touchable immediately; a slave for food (bhaktadāsa) is pure after three days."
Likewise: "Whatever a physician does cannot be done by another;
therefore, a physician is always pure in touch."
Thus [ends verse] 3.27.
What a physician does cannot be performed by another;
therefore, a physician is always pure in his touch.

Furthermore: [There is no fault] for officiating priests, for those who have been initiated, for those performing sacrificial rites, as well as for those observing the *sattra* vow, for celibate students, for donors, and for those who know Brahman.
In matters of giving, marriage, sacrifice, battle, or national calamity,
as well as in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained.

The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are those specifically qualified to perform the *vaitāna* (sacrificial) and *aupāsana* (domestic) rites, who have been selected for their appointment and consecrated by initiation (*dīkṣā*). For them, while performing sacrificial acts (*yajñiya*) pertaining to the sacrifice, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained; this phrase is to be supplied everywhere [in the following rules].

Although the entitlement [to perform these rites] is already established by the rule that "the initiated one must perform the *vaitāna* and *aupāsana* rites," the repetition here is for the purpose of prescribing that the sacrificer himself must act as the performer and for the sake of purification through immediate bathing.

By the mention of *sattrins*, those engaged in an *anna-sattra* (food-distribution rite) are indicated by virtue of its similarity to the continuous performance [of a sacrifice]; for as for the primary *sattrins*, they are already established by the mention of *dīkṣitas*.
By the word *vratis*, those engaged in penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, as well as those engaged in the vows of a *snātaka* or in expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), are meant.
Likewise, by the mention of *brahmacārins*, there is the inclusion of both the performer and the eater of the *śrāddha*, as they are joined with vows such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"Even for one who regularly gives food, when the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances have been completed,
and after the performance of the Kṛcchra-homa and other rites, [the feeding of] Brāhmaṇas and others [should be performed]."
Even for one who has taken a vow, it shall not apply to anyone else when the Brahmins have been invited and the Śrāddha rite has commenced.
For a Brahmin who has been invited and is devoted to the study of his own Veda,
there is never any impurity as long as the ancestors remain within his body.
Likewise, for those engaged in performing expiatory rites, as well as for donors and knowers of Brahman.
Thus,
even for one who constantly provides food, [the following applies] regarding the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances,
once the Kṛcchra-homa and other rites have been completed, and when Brahmins and others are fed.
Even for one who has undertaken a religious vow, it shall not be [permissible] for anyone else when the Brahmins have been invited and the Śrāddha rite has commenced.
For a Brahmin who has been invited and is devoted to the study of his own Veda,
there is never any impurity (āśauca) as long as the ancestors remain within his body.
Likewise, for those engaged in performing penance, as well as for donors and knowers of Brahman.

For those engaged in a sacrificial session (*satrin*) or those observing a vow (*vratī*), purification occurs in relation to the session or the vow, not merely in respect of an action or ordinary social interaction.
Thus says Viṣṇu: "Not for those under a vow during the vow, nor for those engaged in a session during the session.
The student (*brahmacārin*) is of two kinds: the temporary student (*upakurvāṇaka*) and the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).
But he who is always only a giver and never a receiver is called a *vaikhānasa* by the term "giver";
he is a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) and an ascetic (*yati*).
Regarding these three stages of life (*āśrama*), there is purity in all cases, as there is no evidence for any specific restriction.
Furthermore, there is no impurity regarding a substance previously intended for a gift; a substance previously intended does not become defiled when being given away.
This is because of the *Kratu-smṛti*.
Moreover, a specific rule on this point is stated in another *Smṛti*:

If an impurity due to death or birth occurs during a wedding, festival, sacrifice, or similar occasion, the remaining food should be served by others; it shall not touch either the givers or the eaters.
Thus:

"If an impurity due to death or birth occurs during a wedding, a festival, a sacrifice, or the like, the remaining food should be provided by others; it shall not touch either the givers or the eaters."
In a sacrifice, such as the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), and in a marriage where the preliminary materials have been gathered;
likewise, another Smṛti states:
"In a sacrifice when the materials have been gathered, in a marriage, and in the performance of a Śrāddha."
Thus:
in the case of a sacrifice where the materials have been gathered, a marriage, or a śrāddha rite,
immediate purity (sadyaḥśauca) is prescribed here.

The mention of "marriage" (*vivāha*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for previously commenced sacramental rites (*saṃskārakarma*) such as the tonsure (*caula*) and initiation (*upanayana*).

And the mention of "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is an elliptical expression for previously commenced festivals (*utsava*) such as the consecration of a deity (*devapratiṣṭhā*) or the planting of a grove (*rāma*), because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "There is no impurity (*āśauca*) during the consecration of a deity, the performance of a *utsarga*, or a marriage; nor during a disturbance of the country, nor even in times of dire distress. [It is also mentioned] "in battle," meaning in combat.

In the case of the rule for donning armor as stated by Āśvalāyana and others—namely, "one should arm the king when battle is joined"—as well as in the *prāsthānika* propitiatory oblations (*śāntihoma*) and similar rites, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśuddhi*).

When a region is afflicted by an epidemic such as smallpox or by a calamity due to fear of the king, there is immediate purity for the sake of performing propitiatory rites (*śāntikarma*) to pacify those disturbances.
Even in the absence of such a calamity, Paiṭhīnasi has prescribed purification for certain specific regions.

In the case of a marriage, a difficult situation, a sacrifice, a journey, or a pilgrimage to a sacred site, there is no impurity (sūtaka) therein; likewise, one may perform rituals such as sacrifices and the like.
Thus it is said:

"In the case of marriage, a difficult situation, a sacrifice, a journey, or a pilgrimage, there is no impurity (sūtaka) therein; likewise, one should cause the performance of rites such as sacrifices."

Likewise, even in a dire calamity such as the state of being on the verge of death due to the onset of disease and so forth, there is purity regarding a gift made for the purpose of pacifying misfortune.

Similarly, for one whose means of livelihood have contracted and who has a large family including parents exhausted by hunger, there is immediate purification regarding the acceptance of gifts necessary for their maintenance.
And this purification applies to one who lives from day to day (*aśvastanika*) and for whom the alleviation of distress does not occur without immediate purity.

For one who has accumulated wealth sufficient for a single day, the period of impurity lasts one day; for one who accumulates enough for three days, it lasts three days; and for one who has procured goods for four days—namely, one who possesses grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānyaka*)—it lasts four days. For one who possesses grain in a granary (*kusūladhānyaka*), it lasts ten days. Thus, for whomever there is an absence of distress for a certain duration, for that person the impurity lasts for that duration, since the contraction of the period of impurity is conditioned by the presence of adversity. Therefore, Manu says: "Or he may be one who possesses grain in a granary, or one who possesses grain in a jar; or he may be one who has enough for three days, or even one who does not store for the morrow (*aśvastanika*)."
In this regard, with reference to the four types of householders established here, impurity on account of death (śāva-āśauca) is prescribed for ten days among the sapindas;
or [it may be] three days or even one day prior to the collection of the bones.

Thus, the fourfold scheme [of impurity] has been set forth. Furthermore, the restricted rules for impurity concerning *samānodaka* relations—consisting of the "two-day" (*pakṣin*), "one-day," and "immediate" (*sadyas*) purifications—which are observed in other *smṛtis*, should be applied only on the condition of a restriction in one's livelihood (*vṛtti-saṃkoca*).
Moreover, it must be understood that this contraction of impurity applies only to those cases where there is no distress (*ārti*) without receiving gifts and so forth, and not in all instances.

Is it not so? Although all editions read *manuḥ* here, the cited text is attributed to another *smṛti*. Furthermore, the *Mitākṣarā* never introduces a verse using the nominative *manuḥ* alone; it always uses *āha manuḥ*. I believe the word here should be *nanu*, introducing the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument), to which a response is given several lines below with *ucyate*.
*Manu*: "A Brāhmaṇa who is possessed of the sacred fires and the Vedas becomes pure after one day."
One who possesses only the Vedas is deprived of them after three days, but one who lacks all ten is deprived after ten days.

Why is it not accepted that, based on a consideration of such statements from other Smṛtis, those who are devoted to study, knowledge, and ritual performance attain complete purification in one, three days, and so forth? [As it is said: "A Brāhmaṇa who possesses the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day; but one who possesses only the Vedas, being devoid of the fires, is purified in three days; and one who is destitute of both is purified in ten days."

It is said: "Impurity (āśauca) due to death (śāva) is ordained for ten days among sapinda relatives. This [statement], "A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after one day," is indeed an injunction that functions by setting aside the ten-day period obtained through general application.
