other than during the rains, one should dwell for four months during the rainy season."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Kāṇva (3.58).
Regarding how one should go about begging for alms, he says:
"One should wander for alms with vigilance in the evening, unobserved,
in a village free from other mendicants, seeking only enough for sustenance and free from greed."
Being vigilant and free from the fickleness of speech, eyes, and so forth, he should wander for alms.
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha has shown a specific rule: "He should go for alms to seven houses without prior intention.
This is in the evening, during the fifth part of the day.

And so Manu says: "A mendicant should always go for alms when the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed."
Thus it is said: "When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal,
and when the removal of the dishes has been completed, the ascetic should always go for alms."
Likewise, he should go for alms at a single time and not engage in excessive wandering;
for an ascetic who is overly attached to begging becomes attached even to sense-objects.
Thus:
"One should go for alms at a single time, but one should not be attached to abundance;
for an ascetic who is attached to alms becomes attached even to sense-objects."
He should not be conspicuous, being unmarked by the teaching of astrology and the like, nor by portents or omens, nor by the science of the limbs of the stars;
he should never seek alms through instruction or discourse.
Because it has been stated by him thus.

Furthermore, as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha— "In a village free from mendicants who are habitually begging, such as heretics and the like, he should eat what he obtains in a Brāhmaṇa family, both morning and evening, excluding meat"— that refers to the case of one who is incapable [of fasting]. Regarding this, a specific rule has been stated by Manu:
One should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants.
Thus:
"He should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants."
One should go for alms only as much as is required for the maintenance of life. And so says Saṃvarta:
"A sage, having collected eight, seven, or five alms..."
Having washed them all with water, he should then eat while maintaining silence.
Thus,
having collected eight, seven, or five morsels of alms-food,
the sage should wash them all with water and then eat while remaining silent.
Not greedy, he is unattached to sweet foods, condiments, and the like.
He speaks of the alms-bowl for the purpose of wandering for alms:
"The vessels of an ascetic are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
water is their purification, as well as scrubbing with cow-hair."
The alms-bowls of ascetics should be made of materials such as clay;
for them, purification is achieved by washing with water and scrubbing with cow-hair.
This purification pertains to the implements used for activities such as wandering for alms, and does not concern objects defiled by impurities and the like.
In the event of its defilement, the rules for the purification of objects mentioned in the section on the purification of substances should be observed.
For this very reason, Manu stated:
"His vessels should be made of non-metallic materials and should be free from cracks."
Their purification is prescribed by means of water, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.
Thus:
his vessels should be non-metallic and free from flaws;
their purification with water is prescribed, as in the case of the *camasa* cups during a sacrifice.
By taking up the illustration of the *camasa* (wooden sacrificial vessel), the purity resulting from preparatory effort (*prāyogikī śuddhi*) is shown.

Even when another vessel is unavailable, the eating must be done in that very [vessel], for Devala’s traditional teaching states: "Having taken that alms-food, one should eat only as much as is necessary for life, silently, in a secluded place, using either that vessel or another. (3.60)
Regarding such an ascetic, he states the subject of the observances (niyama) as a limb of the meditation on the Self:
"Having fully restrained the collection of senses, having abandoned passion and hatred,
and having cast off fear toward all beings, the twice-born becomes immortal."

Having properly restrained and withdrawn the collection of senses, such as the eyes, from objects such as forms; having abandoned and cast off passion and hatred toward pleasant and unpleasant objects—and by the use of the word "and," likewise envy and other such states—while not causing fear through harm to living beings, he, being one whose internal organ is purified, becomes immortal through the direct realization of non-duality; that is, he becomes liberated. || 3.61 ||
Moreover:
A mendicant, in particular, must purify his intention for action,
because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence.
The purification of the internal organ—the seat of intention—which is defiled by the faults born of desire for sense objects and aversion, must be accomplished through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
This is because such purification serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge in the form of the direct realization of the non-duality of the Self (*ātmādvaita-sākṣātkāra*).

This being so, when the obstacles consisting of attachment to sense objects and the faults produced thereby have been destroyed, one becomes independent in the practice of meditation on the Self (*ātma-dhyāna*) and its sustained concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth.

Therefore, this purification must be especially practiced by the mendicant (*bhikṣuka*), because his primary aim is liberation, and because liberation is difficult to attain without a purified internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
As Manu has said:
"Just as the impurities of ores are burned away when they are being smelted..."
In the same way, the defects of the senses are burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath.
Thus [ends verse] 3.62.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
He speaks of the investigation into the true nature of saṃsāra as a means for the cessation of the sense faculties:
"One should contemplate dwelling in the womb, as well as the destinies born of karma,
mental afflictions, diseases, the defilements, old age, and the transformation of physical form."
Throughout thousands of births, there is the reversal of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
For the sake of achieving detachment (*vairāgya*), one must contemplate and reflect upon dwelling in various kinds of wombs filled with urine, feces, and so forth;
by the word "and" (*ca*), the cessation of birth is also included.
Likewise, there are destinies consisting of falling into hells such as Mahāraurava, produced by actions such as the performance of prohibited deeds;

likewise, mental afflictions (*ādhi*), physical ailments (*vyādhi*) such as fever and dysentery, the five *kleśas*—namely ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live—old age (*jarā*), which is the overcoming by wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth, the transformation of form (*rūpaviparyaya*), which is the alteration of one's previous appearance through being lame, humpbacked, and the like, and birth (*bhava*) among various species such as dogs, pigs, donkeys, and serpents.

Having reflected upon the nature of saṃsāra—which brings about manifold afflictions such as the non-attainment of the desired and the attainment of the undesired—one should strive for the conquest of the senses, which is the means to self-knowledge, for the sake of its cessation. (3.63)
Having thus reflected, he says what should be done immediately thereafter:
"By means of the yoga of meditation, one should perceive the subtle Self abiding within the self."

Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; meditation (*dhyāna*) is one-pointedness of the self, which is the withdrawal of that very [mind] from external objects. Through the yoga of meditation—also known by the synonym *nididhyāsana*—one should correctly perceive and realize for oneself the non-difference between the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, namely that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Self, which is distinct from the subtle body, the vital breaths, and so forth, is established in the Self, which is Brahman. Thus, one should see the identity of these two and make it directly manifest.

For this very reason, in the Śruti, having referred to vision in the form of direct realization in the words "The Self, my dear, is to be seen," hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption are prescribed as its means in the passage: "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon. (3.64)
Furthermore:
"Lifestyle stage (āśrama) is not the cause of dharma, for dharma exists when it is being practiced. Therefore, one should not do to others that which is harmful to oneself."

Regarding the dharma known as the meditation on the Self mentioned in the preceding verse, the specific stage of life (*āśrama*)—such as the carrying of the staff and water-pot—is not the cause; for if practiced, that [meditation] would indeed not be excessively difficult.

Therefore, one should not practice toward others that which is unwholesome to oneself, such as causing agitation or harsh speech. By this, because the abandonment of passion and hatred is internal (being the means to achieve purity of the inner organ, which is the cause for the arising of knowledge), it is praised as the primary factor; thus, the rejection of the stages of life is for the sake of praise, and not for the purpose of abandoning them altogether, since those too are prescribed by rule.
Thus it was said by Manu:
"Even one who has fallen into fault should practice dharma, regardless of which stage of life he is devoted to;
being equal toward all beings, outward appearance is not the cause of dharma."
Thus [it is said].
Even if he has fallen into fault, one should practice dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life (āśrama) he may be in;
being equal toward all beings, the external mark (liṅga) is not the cause of dharma.
Furthermore: truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint,
control of the senses, and knowledge— all this is declared to be dharma.
Truthfulness is speech that is factual and pleasant.
Non-stealing is the non-appropriation of another's property. Freedom from anger is the non-arising of anger even toward one who causes harm.
Hrī is modesty;
śauca is purity regarding food and so forth;
dhī is the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful.

Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the restoration of the agitated mind to its former state upon the loss of what is desired or the acquisition of what is undesired. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the abandonment of intoxication; it is the control of the senses and the absence of excessive attachment even toward objects that are not forbidden.
"Knowledge" (*vidyā*) is the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*).
When these [qualities], beginning with truthfulness (*satya*), are practiced, every duty (*dharma*) becomes practiced.
By this, he demonstrates that the internal qualities of the Self, such as truthfulness and the rest, are more essential than external characteristics such as carrying a staff or a water-pot.

Now, one might object that it is illogical to say "one should see the Self situated within the self through the yoga of meditation," because there is no distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme Self (paramātman). To this, he says: "Just as sparks fly forth from a heated mass of iron, even so do individual selves indeed emerge from the [supreme] Self."

Although there is no ultimate difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), nevertheless, because individual souls arise from the Self as differentiated by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), the designation of a distinction between the individual soul and the Supreme Self is indeed appropriate.

For just as sparks, which are particles of fire, issue forth from a heated iron ball or globe and, once issued, receive the designation of "sparks," so it is here. Therefore, it is established that the Self is to be seen abiding within the self.

Or rather, this is the meaning: [one might object] that since at the time of deep sleep and during cosmic dissolution all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are merged into Brahman, for whom is this injunction to meditate upon the Self intended? To this, he says: "issuing forth," and so on.

Even though they are dissolved in a subtle form at the time of dissolution, the individual souls (jīvātman) nevertheless emerge from the Self as differentiated by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of ignorance; furthermore, under the influence of karma, they are born again as those who identify with a gross body. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the injunctions for meditation; the illustration of the iron ball is given because of the similarity in the state of being distinct within the fiery [element]. 3.67.

Now, one might object: since the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*) possesses no body and is devoid of movement, how can there be the assumption of the four types of bodies—womb-born, egg-born, and so forth—which are dependent upon that [movement]? To this, he says:
"In that regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, some by its own nature, and some, consisting of both merit and demerit, through habituation."

Even though in that state there is an absence of action consisting of physical movement (*parispanda*), nevertheless, mental action (*karma*) consisting of the determination of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) certainly exists.

And it indeed possesses the quality of being the cause for assuming a specific body, according to the traditional teaching of Manu: "By verbal [actions] one attains the state of birds or wild animals; by mental [actions], the state of those born of the lowest castes."

Thus, having assumed a body, independent of [present] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), when the drinking of breast-milk and so forth is performed, satisfaction arises; when it is not performed, it does not. Being independent of such positive and negative concomitances, the cognition of the effect—arisen from the power of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) cultivated by experiences in a previous birth—performs some acts like drinking breast-milk; some it performs by its own nature through chance, without regard for a purpose, such as the eating of ants and the like; and some, by the force of practice in another life, it performs in the form of both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
And so another Smṛti says: "Whatever—be it generosity, study, or austerity—has been practiced throughout successive births, by the very force of that practice, one practices that same thing again."
Thus [it is said].
Whatever— be it generosity, study, or austerity— one has practiced throughout successive births,
by the very force of that habituation, one practices that same thing again.
Thus, the diversity of karma among living beings and the resulting diversity of bodies—such as those born from a womb and so forth—is indeed logical. 3.68

Now, one might object: "If this is so, since the Brahmin himself is somehow designated as the 'living being' (jīva) and possesses attributes such as eternity, how can there be the common usage that 'Viṣṇumitra was born'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Imperishable (akṣara) is the efficient cause (nimitta), the agent, the knower, Brahman, the possessor of qualities, and the controller; though unborn, he is proclaimed to have been 'born' due to the assumption of a body."

It is true that the Self, by virtue of the influence of the penetration of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the manifestation of the entire phenomenal world (*jagat-prapañca*), is itself the threefold cause—namely, the material cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), the non-material cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*)—and is not, moreover, included within the category of effects.
This is because it is imperishable and indestructible.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the modifications of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest—which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion—are observed in the phenomenal world that is an effect, it is appropriate that the agency of the world belongs only to *Prakṛti*, which possesses those qualities, and not to the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman.
Do not think thus:
the self alone is the agent;
for it is the knower of that which causes the pleasure and pain experienced by the individual soul, such as the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth.

For it is not possible for the insentient *prakṛti* to fashion the manifold expansion of the world—including the differentiation of names and forms, the various classes of enjoyers, and the objects of enjoyment and the bodies of enjoyment suitable for their experience.
Therefore, the Self alone is the agent;
likewise, He alone is *brahman*, the expander and the one who causes growth.
Nor is it devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*),

because it possesses the power of the three qualities (*triguṇa-śakti*), which is known by such synonyms as *avidyā*, *prakṛti*, and *pradhāna*. Therefore, although it is inherently devoid of qualities, it is said to be endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and so forth by way of its power.

Nor does this much establish that *prakṛti* is the cause; for it is the Self alone that is the controller and independent, whereas what is called *prakṛti* is not an independent principle, as there is a lack of evidence for its existence as such. Nor should it be said that she herself, in the form of power (*śakti*), is the agent; because the causal factor is the possessor of power, not the power itself. Therefore, the Self alone is the threefold cause of the world.

Likewise, he is "unborn" (aja), meaning devoid of origination. Therefore, although direct birth is not possible for him, he is nevertheless said to be "born" merely by taking on a body; this is because he undergoes a change of state, just as one says, "the householder is born. (3.69)
He describes the manner of assuming a body:
"Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, air, light, water, and earth,
each possessing one additional quality, so too does he take them up when coming into existence."

At the time of creation, that Supreme Self creates space and the other elements with their qualities increasing by one at each stage: the sky has the single quality of sound; the wind has the qualities of sound and touch; fire has the qualities of sound, touch, and form; water has the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste; and the earth has the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Likewise, the Self, having attained the state of a living being (jīva) and coming into existence, also assumes [the body] as the constituent cause of its own physical frame. 3.70
How do earth and the other elements initiate the body? To this he says:
"The sun is nourished by the oblation; from the sun comes rain, and from that, plants.
That food, in the form of sap, attains the state of semen."
The sun is nourished by the essence of the sacrificial cakes and other offerings cast into it by the sacrificers.
From the sun, through the power of time, rain arises from the ripened essence of the oblations such as clarified butter.
From that, food in the form of grains and other plants comes forth.
And that food, when consumed, undergoes the process of chyle, blood, and so forth, until it reaches the state of semen and ovum. (3.71)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"But when there is union of a woman and a man, and the semen and blood are pure,
the Lord himself, as the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements."

At the time of the season (*ṛtu*), during the union of man and woman, there is semen and blood—this is "semen-blood" (*śukra-śoṇita*). When these two are joined together and purified—being free from the defects mentioned in another Smṛti, such as being corrupted by wind, bile, or phlegm; being afflicted with nodules, pus, or emaciation; or having the odor of urine or feces, which makes them non-seeds (*abīja*)—the Lord, the Self (*ātman*), who is the sixth element consisting of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*), remaining therein, being capable through its connection with the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa-karma*) that initiates the body, simultaneously takes up and appropriates as the locus of yoga the five elements—the five great principles beginning with earth—which serve as the originators of the body.

And so it is stated in the Śārīraka: "Upon the union of a woman and a man, the semen, mixed with the menstrual blood in the womb, remains in the uterus at that very moment, impelled by the vital air (vāyu) together with the elemental self (bhūtātman) and the qualities (guṇas) of sattva, rajas, and tamas. (3.72)
Furthermore: the sense organs, the mind, the vital breath, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude,
retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense.
Effort, form, color, likes and dislikes, existence and non-existence—
all this is born from his self, as he desires a beginning for that which is without beginning.
The faculties are the organs of cognition and action which will be described hereafter,
as well as the mind, which is common to both.

The bodily air (*śārīro vāyuḥ*)—distinguished by its fivefold functions as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*—is called *prāṇa*. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is comprehension (*avagama*). Life-span (*āyuḥ*) is living delimited by a specific period of time. Happiness (*sukha*) is contentment (*nirvṛti*). Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is steadiness of mind (*cittasthairya*). Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*) and intelligence (*medhā*). Impulsion (*preraṇa*) is the presiding authority over the organs of knowledge and action. Suffering (*duḥkha*) is agitation (*udvega*). Desire (*icchā*) is longing (*spṛhā*). Egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the sense of "I" (*ahaṃkṛti*). Effort (*prayatna*) is exertion (*udyama*). Form (*ākṛti*) is shape (*ākāra*). Color (*varṇa*) is whiteness and so forth. Tone (*svara*) is the scale notes such as *ṣaḍja* and *gāndhāra*. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is enmity (*vaira*). Existence (*bhava*) is the possession of children, cattle, and so forth; non-existence (*abhava*) is the opposite of that. The meaning is that for this beginningless and eternal Self, which desires a beginning—that is, one wishing to assume a body—all these things, beginning with the senses, are produced by the Self and generated from the seeds of actions belonging to a previous life. (3.74)
He describes the sequence of the transformation of the combined semen and blood into the form of the body:
"In the first month, it becomes a mass of moisture, a coagulation of the elements;
in the second month, it is an *arbuda*; but in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs."
This conscious sixth element is "coagulated in the elements," meaning it has become merged within the elements such as earth and so forth;
that is to say, it has become unified like milk and water.
During the first month of gestation, it remains in a state of moisture, having attained a liquid form, and does not yet transform into solidity.
In the second month, the *arbuda* occurs, which is a slightly hardened mass of flesh.
This is the intended meaning:

the collection of elements, which has attained a state of liquidity through contact with semen and is being dried up little by little every day by the abdominal wind and digestive fire, reaches a state of hardness after thirty days.
And so it is stated in the Suśruta [Saṃhitā]: "In the second month, the mass of elements, being cooked by cold, heat, and wind, becomes solid.
But in the third month, it becomes endowed with limbs and sense organs. (3.75)
Furthermore: from space [come] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, strength, and so forth;
and from wind, the sense of touch, movement, expansion, and even dryness.
From bile (pitta), however, come vision, digestion, heat, form, and luminosity;
from phlegm (rasa), however, come taste, coolness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness.
The unborn Self perceives the smell of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and form; thereafter, it vibrates in the third stage.
The phrase "the self grasps" is to be connected with every [instance].

From space (*ākāśa*), it grasps lightness—which is useful for the act of leaping—subtlety, which is the capacity for minute vision, sound as its object, the ear, which is the organ of hearing, and strength, which is firmness.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," one should understand porosity and distinctness; for the *Garbhopaniṣad* shows that from space [one grasps] sound, the ear, distinctness, and the collection of all apertures.

From *pavana* (wind) arise the sense of touch, movement such as coming and going, the various expansion of the limbs (*vyūhana*), and roughness (*raukṣya*)—and by the word "ca" (and), touch as well; from *pitta* (bile), which is fire, arise vision—the faculty of sight—the digestion (*pakti*) of consumed food, heat (*auṣṇya*) as the hot touch of the limbs, color (*rūpa*) such as darkening, and luminosity (*prakāśitā*) as brilliance.

Likewise, heat, indignation, and so forth; for the *Garbhopaniṣad* teaches that "the faculties of heroism, indignation, sharpness, digestion, heat, brilliance, color, form, and the senses are of the nature of fire (*taijasa*). Similarly, from the water-element (*rasa*) comes the sense of taste, coldness, the unctuousness of the limbs along with softness, and moisture—that is, wetness. Likewise, from the earth-element come smell, the sense of smell, heaviness, and material form.
All this the Self, though in reality birthless, assumes during the third month.
Then, in the fourth month, it throbbs and moves.
Thus, in the *Śārīraka*, it is said: "Therefore, in the fourth month, it forms an intention regarding movement and so forth. (3.76, 3.77, 3.78)
Furthermore:
By failing to grant her pregnancy-longings, the fetus may incur defects, deformity, or even death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman.

The fetus has one heart and the pregnant woman another; thus, she is "two-hearted" (*dvihṛdayā*). Whatever is desired by that woman is called *dauhṛda*. By not granting that desire, the fetus incurs a defect such as deformity or even death. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding that defect and for the nourishment of the fetus, whatever is dear and desired by the pregnant woman must be fulfilled.

And so it is stated in the *Suśruta*: "They call a woman who possesses two hearts 'one with *dauhṛda*'; one should grant her what she desires, for she gives birth to a son who is vigorous and long-lived."

And likewise, physical exercise and the like must also be avoided by her from the time of conception onwards; for it is stated in that very same [text]: "From that time forward, she should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, over-satiation, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, grief, fear, riding in vehicles, suppressing natural urges, sitting in the *kukkuṭāsana* posture, and bloodletting.
Furthermore, the onset of pregnancy is to be understood through signs such as fatigue and so forth.

For one who has just conceived, there is fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, weakness in the thighs, the retention of semen and blood, and throbbing in the vagina; these and other symptoms are described in that very same [text]. (3.79)
Furthermore:
in the fourth [week] there is the stabilization of the limbs; in the fifth, the emergence of blood;
and in the sixth, the production of strength, complexion, nails, and body hair.
In the fourth month, the mass of limbs that appeared in the third month attains stability and firmness.
In the fifth month, there is the emergence and production of blood.
Likewise, in the sixth month, there is the development of strength, complexion, and the nails and body hair.
Furthermore:
endowed with mind and consciousness, joined with channels, sinews, and arteries,
he possesses skin, flesh, and memory in the seventh and eighth [weeks] as well.

That aforementioned embryo, in the seventh month, becomes endowed with mind, consciousness, and volition; it is joined with channels that carry the vital breath, with sinews that bind the bones, and with vessels that carry wind, bile, and phlegm.
Likewise, in the eighth month, it becomes endowed with skin, flesh, and memory.
Moreover:
his vital energy (ojas) flows again toward the nurse and again toward the womb;
therefore, the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of life.
In the eighth month, a certain vital energy (*ojas*)—a specific quality—moves with extreme instability and great speed back and forth between the nurse and the fetus.
Consequently, the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of life. By this, he demonstrates that the very stability of the *ojas* is the cause of life.
The nature of *ojas* is also shown in another Smṛti:
"That which resides in the heart, pure, slightly warm, and yellowish—this is reckoned as *ojas* in the body; through its destruction, one meets with destruction."
Thus [ends verse] 3.82.
That which resides in the heart—pure, slightly warm, and yellowish—is reckoned as the vital essence (*ojas*) in the body; through its destruction, one meets with destruction.
Furthermore:
In the ninth or even the tenth month, he is expelled by powerful winds of birth,
like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish distress.

Thus, with his limbs and sense organs—hands, feet, eyes, and so forth—fully developed, in the ninth or tenth month—or even earlier, as indicated by the word "api" (even), in the seventh or eighth month—the body-machine, constructed of sinews, bones, skin, and other parts, is impelled by the powerful winds that cause birth and are characterized by defects such as excessive exertion; through its narrow opening, he is expelled while afflicted by fever and overwhelmed by unbearable suffering, like an arrow shot from a bow by a skilled archer. Immediately upon emerging and touched by the external air, his former memory perishes. As stated in the eighteenth chapter of the *Nirukta*: "Once born and touched by the wind, he does not remember his previous birth, death, or his auspicious and inauspicious actions. (3.83)
Explaining the true nature of the body, he says:
"Its bodies are sixfold, and it possesses six layers of skin;
likewise, its limbs are six, and its bones number three hundred and sixty."

Of that self, those bodies which are born from a womb or from an egg are each of six kinds, by virtue of being associated with six locations of fire that serve as the causes for the maturation of the six elements beginning with blood.
For instance, the essence of food, being cooked by the digestive fire, attains the state of blood;
and the blood, being cooked by the fire residing in its own sheath, attains the state of flesh.
And the flesh, ripened by the fire within its own sheath, becomes fat;
the fat also, cooked by the fire of its own sheath, becomes bone;
and the bone too, fully ripened by the flame within its own sheath, becomes marrow.
The marrow also, being cooked by the fire within its own sheath, transforms as the final element;
however, since there is no further transformation of the final element, that itself constitutes the first sheath of the self.
Thus, because of their connection with the fire of the six sheaths, bodies are of six kinds.
However, because the first constituent (*dhātu*), which consists of the essence of food (*annarasa*), is indeterminate, it does not constitute a distinct category [from the other constituents].

Moreover, those bodies maintain six layers of skin (*tvac*); the six constituents known as blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen exist in the form of outer and inner layers like the bark of a plantain trunk. Because they act as a covering, like a skin, these are called "skins," and the body maintains those six skins.
This is well-known in the *Āyurveda*.
Likewise, the limbs are exactly six: the pair of hands, the pair of feet, the head, and the trunk.
As for the bones, their number is three hundred and sixty, which should be understood from the six verses that follow. (3.84)
Furthermore:
there are sixty-four teeth together with their sockets, twenty nails, and the digits of the hands and feet; these constitute four groups of locations.
The sockets are the bones located at the roots of the teeth; together with the thirty-two teeth, they total sixty-four.
The nails are the twenty [bones] growing on the hands and feet—specifically, the pin-like bones situated at the bases of the fingers and toes above the wrists and ankles.
Thus, including the four locations for those nails and pin-like bones—the two feet and the two hands—there are one hundred and four bones in total. (3.85)
Furthermore: there are sixty bones in the fingers; two in the heels and four in the ankles;
four bones in the forearms, and likewise as many in the shanks.

There are twenty fingers; since there are three bones for each of them, there are thus sixty bones connected to the fingers. Regarding the feet, the two rear parts are the heels (*pārṣṇī*); there are two bones for those, one in each foot. There are two ankle-bones (*gulpha*) in each foot, so there are four bones in the four ankles. In the forearms there are four bones measuring one cubit (*aratni*), and likewise in the shanks there are four; thus, there are seventy-four [bones]. (3.86)
Furthermore:
one should designate two each arising from the knees, the cheeks, the thighs, the shoulder-blades,
the eye-sockets, the palate, and the hip-blades.

The knee is the joint of the shank and the thigh; the cheek is the *galla*; the thigh is the *sakthi*, and its flat surface is the *tatphalaka*; the shoulder is the head of the arm (*bhujaśiras*); the *akṣa* is the region below the temple between the ear and the eye; the palate is the *kākuda*; the hip is the *kakudmatī*, and its flat surface is the *tatphalaka*. One should point out that there are two bones for each of these; thus, there are fourteen bones in total. (3.87)
Furthermore: there is one bone in the pubic region, forty-five in the back,
fifteen bones in the neck, one in each clavicle, and likewise one in the jaw.
There is one bone in the secret region; on the back, in the posterior part, there are forty-five bones.

The neck, the cervical vertebrae, consists of fifteen bones. The junction between the chest and the shoulders is the clavicle (*jatru*), and there is one for each side. The jaw is the chin (*cibuka*).
In that case as well, there is one [remaining] bone; thus, there are sixty-four.
Furthermore:
At its base are the two [bones] of the forehead, the eyes, and the cheeks; the nose consists of solid bone;
and there are seventy-two ribs together with their sockets (*sthālaka*) and tubercles (*arbuda*).

At the root of that jaw are two bones. The forehead (*lalāṭa*) is the brow; the eye (*akṣi*) is the vision; the cheek (*gaṇṭa*) is the region between the temple and the eye. The compound *lalāṭākṣigaṇḍa* refers to the collection of these, and in each of these locations there is a pair of bones. The nose consists of the bone known as the *ghana*.

The *pārśvakas* are the bones connected to the region below the armpits; the *sthālakas* are the bones that serve as their supports. Together with those *sthālakas* and the *arbudas*, which are specific types of bones, there are seventy-two *pārśvakas*.
When added to the nine previously mentioned, they total eighty-one. (3.89)
Furthermore:
"There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise seventeen bones in the chest; such is the collection of bones in a person."
The two specific bones in the region between the eyebrows and the ears are the *śaṅkhakas*.
There are four skull-bones (*kapālas*) connected to the head.
The chest (*uraḥ*, *vakṣas*) consists of seventeen bones; thus, there are twenty-three [bones] in total.
Together with those previously mentioned, there are three hundred and sixty; thus has the collection of bones of a person been described. (3.90)
He speaks of the sense organs together with their objects:
"Smell, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects;
the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ear are the sense organs."
These objects, beginning with smell, are the causes of bondage for the person (*puruṣa*), because the word *viṣaya* is derived from the verbal root *ṣiñ*, meaning "to bind.

And by means of these objects—smell and the rest—which are established as things to be cognized, the five sense organs, such as the nose and so forth, become inferable through their function as the instruments for the cognition of their respective domains. (3.91)
To demonstrate the organs of action, he says:
"The two hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the two feet—these indeed one should know as the five organs of action; and the mind is of the nature of both."

The hands are well known; the anus is the rectum; the organ of generation is the means for producing the pleasure resulting from sexual union; the tongue is well known; and the feet as well—one should know these five, beginning with the hands, to be the organs of action (karmendriyas), which are the instruments for the actions of grasping, excretion, procreation, speaking, and locomotion.

The mind (manas) is the internal organ, to be inferred from the fact that cognitions do not arise simultaneously; and it is of a dual nature, acting as an auxiliary to both the organs of cognition and the organs of action. 3.92.
To demonstrate the seats of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
he says: "The navel, the *ojas*, the anus, the semen, the blood, the two temples,
as well as the head, the shoulders, the throat, and the heart— these are indeed the seats of the *prāṇa*."
The navel and so forth are the ten locations of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Although the wind named *samāna* moves through all the limbs of the body, the specific mention of locations such as the navel is intended to indicate its predominance there. (3.93)
In order to elaborate upon the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇāyatana*), he says: "The omentum, the diaphragm, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine,
the two kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces."
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine,
the anus, the abdomen, and the two internal rectums— this is declared to be the extent [of the trunk].

The *vapā* is well known; the *vasā* is the fat of the flesh; the *avahanana* is the lungs; the *nābhi* is well known; and the *plīhā* is well known in Āyurveda, and these two are shaped like masses of flesh located in the left side of the abdomen.

The liver (*yakṛt*) is blackish; the gall-bladder (*kloma*) is a mass of flesh, and these two are located in the right side of the abdomen. The small intestine (*kṣudrāntra*) is the intestine situated at the heart. The kidneys (*vṛkkau*) are two masses of flesh situated near the heart. The bladder (*basti*) is the receptacle for urine. The receptacle for feces (*purīṣādhāna*) is the receptacle for excrement. The stomach (*āmāśaya*) is the place where undigested food resides. The heart (*hṛdaya*) is the lotus of the heart. The large intestine, anus, and abdomen are well known. From the outer ring of the anus, there are two inner rings of the anus; these two are the anal canals (*gudau*), which are abdominal (*kauṣṭhya*), existing in the region below the navel within the trunk. This is the detailed description of the abode of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
In the preceding verse, however, there was a summary;
for this very reason, some of the points mentioned in the previous verse are recited here [in verses 3.94 and 3.95].
Furthermore, for the sake of elaborating upon the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇāyatana*),
he says: "The two pupils, the two eye-sockets,
the two ear-cavities, the two ear-flaps, the two ears, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins."
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, and the breasts are produced from the accumulation of phlegm;
likewise are the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, and the calves and thighs.
The palm of the hand, the abdomen, the head of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, and the nape of the neck—
these are the locations in this body.
The two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the anus,
and the genitals— these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).

The *kanīnike* are the pupils of the eyes; the *akṣikūṭe* are the junctions between the eyes and the nose; the *śaṣkulī* is the auditory meatus; the *karṇapatrakau* are the earlobes; the *karṇau* are the well-known ears; the *dantaveṣṭau* are the gums; the *oṣṭhau* are the well-known lips; the *kukundare* are the hollows of the loins; the *vaṅkṣaṇau* are the junctions of the thighs and the groin; the *vṛkkau* have been mentioned previously; the *stanau* (breasts) are produced from a massification of phlegm (*śleṣman*); the *upajihvā* is the uvula; the *sphijau* are the buttocks; the *bāhū* are the well-known arms; the *piṇḍikā* in the calves and thighs refers to the fleshy parts of the calves and thighs; the *galaśuṇḍike* are the junctions at the base of the jaw and the cheeks; the *śīrṣam* is the head; and the *avaṭaḥ* is any depressed region on the body, such as the base of the throat, the armpits, and so forth.
In the reading *avaṭu*, it refers to the nape of the neck (*kṛkāṭikā*).
Likewise, there are four colors: the two white sides of each of the pupils of the eyes;
or alternatively, the four sockets of the eyes.
The rest is well known.
Thus, these are the locations within this contemptible body:
likewise, the pair of eyes and the pair of ears.
The two nostril apertures, the mouth, the anus, and the generative organ—these aforementioned nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa). 3.96–99.
Furthermore: there are exactly seven hundred veins, nine hundred sinews,
two hundred arteries, and five hundred muscles.

The vessels (*sirā*) are forty-four in number, connected to the navel; they carry wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), pervade the entire body, and branching out in various ways, they become seven hundred in number.
Likewise, the sinews (*snāyu*), which bind the joints of the limbs and their subdivisions, are nine hundred.
The channels called *dhamanī*, originating from the navel, are twenty-four in number; carrying the vital airs (*prāṇa* and so forth), they become two hundred through their various branches.
Furthermore, the muscles (peśyaḥ), which are fleshy in form and connect the major and minor limbs such as the masses of the thighs and so forth, number five hundred. || 3.100 ||
Furthermore, he states another number for these very vessels and so forth, due to the abundance of their branches:
"Know that there are twenty-nine hundred thousand, as well as nine hundred and fifty-six, vessels designated as *sirās* and *dhamanīs*."

O Sāmaśravas and other sages, know that the veins and arteries, when combined according to their divisions of branches and sub-branches, amount to twenty-nine lakhs, nine hundred, and fifty-six. 3.101.
Furthermore: It should be known that embodied beings possess three hundred thousand hairs on their beard and head;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas) and two hundred joints.
The body hairs and facial hair of embodied beings, when combined, should be known to number three hundred thousand.
The vital points (*marmāṇi*), which are locations that cause death and affliction, should be known as one hundred and seven.
Of the bones, however, there are two hundred joints; the joints of the tendons, veins, and so forth, moreover, are infinite. (3.102)
He states the number of the pores and other cavities of the entire body:
"There are fifty-four crores and sixty-seven and a half lakhs of hair-pores, together with the openings for sweat."
The atoms are enumerated and distinguished by those belonging to the wind-element; even though a single atom may perceive their nature and their arrangement.

The atoms of the body hairs, together with the previously mentioned head-hairs and so forth— parts that are extremely subtle in form, along with the pores for the flow of sweat— are reckoned at fifty-four crores, sixty-seven lakhs, and fifty-five thousand, having been divided and separated by the atoms of wind (pavana-paramāṇu). This and this have been stated according to the perspective of the scriptures,
because this subject matter does not fall within the range of the sensory organs such as the eyes.
O sages, whoever among you understands this extremely profound subject concerning the nature and configuration of the bodily constituents is indeed great and foremost among the wise;
therefore, the wise should strive diligently to comprehend the arrangement of these constituents.
He states the quantities of the bodily fluids and so forth:
"Nine añjalis of rasa are to be known; ten of water;
seven indeed of feces; and eight of blood are proclaimed."
Phlegm is six [parts], bile five, urine four, fat three, and adipose tissue two; marrow is one, while the brain is above it.
"Of phlegm, of vital essence (*ojas*), and likewise of semen—this body is thus unstable; he who acts for the sake of liberation [should renounce it]."
The essence of food that has been properly digested is the nutrient fluid (*rasa*); its measure is nine handfuls (*añjali*).
It should be understood that there are ten handfuls of water, which serves as the cause for the cohesion of the earth-atoms;
and of feces (*purīṣa*, *varcas*), there are exactly seven.
Eight *añjali*s of the essence of food (*annarasa*)—which has acquired its redness through digestion by the digestive fire (*jāṭharānala*)—are proclaimed;
six *añjali*s of phlegm (*śleṣman*);
and five [of] bile (*pitta*), which is of the nature of fire (*tejas*).
There are four handfuls of urine and feces;
three of muscle-fat (vasā), which is the grease of the flesh;
and two handfuls of fat (medas), which is the essence of the flesh.

The marrow contained within the cavities of his bones amounts to one handful; furthermore, there is half a handful in the head. This marrow belongs to the essence of phlegm (*śleṣma*), the quintessence of phlegm.
Likewise, of the semen, the final constituent element, there is likewise only half a handful.
And this has been stated with reference to a person whose constituent elements (dhātu) are in equilibrium;
however, for one whose elements are imbalanced, there is no fixed rule, because bodies are dissimilar, unstable, and likewise [variable],
and because no definite measure exists for the humors (doṣa), elements, and waste products (mala).
Thus, according to the *Āyurveda*:

"He who possesses the understanding that this body—composed of bones, sinews, and so forth—is an unstable receptacle of impurities, is a man of action, a wise person, and capable of liberation; for detachment (*vairāgya*) and the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānitya-viveka*) are the means to liberation, and the knowledge of the abundance of bone, urine, feces, and the like is the cause of detachment.
For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
For the sake of even this tiny body— a storehouse of all impurities, ungrateful, and perishable— fools commit sinful deeds.
If indeed that which is inside this body were to be outside,
people would take up sticks to ward off dogs and crows.
Thus it is said: "For the sake of even this tiny body— a mere repository of all impurities, ungrateful, and perishable— fools commit sinful deeds."
If indeed that which is inside this body were to be outside,
people would take up sticks to ward off dogs and crows.
Therefore, for the sake of the absolute cessation of such a contemptible body, one should strive in the meditation upon the Self. 3.105–107.
He describes the nature of the Self which is to be worshipped:
"Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā and Ahitā have issued forth from the heart; in their midst [is that which] has the luster of the moon."
The mandala is centered upon him, and his self is as immovable as a lamp;
that is what should be known, for by knowing it here, one is not born again.

Emerging from the region of the heart like the filaments of a *kadamba* flower, seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍīs*) extend in all directions; they are designated as "beneficial" (*hitā*) and "non-beneficial" (*ahitā*) according to whether they produce benefit or harm.

There are three other channels among them: two, known as *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, are situated on the left and right sides of the heart respectively, are inverted, connected to the nostrils, and serve as the seats of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths.
The third, called *suṣumnā*, stands like a staff in the center and extends upward to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

In the midst of those channels is a lunar-mansion (*maṇḍala*) with the luster of the moon; within that, the Self remains motionless and radiant, like a lamp in a windless place. One should know it to be thus, because by the direct realization of that, one does not wander again in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), but attains immortality. 3.108–3.109.
Furthermore:
"The Āraṇyaka which I obtained from the Sun,
as well as the Yoga-śāstra proclaimed by me, must be known by one who desires yoga."

Yoga is the steadiness of the mental faculty within the Self by means of setting aside interest in other objects; for the sake of attaining that, you must understand what has been received by me from the Sun known as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, and likewise, you must also understand the Yoga-śāstra which has been taught by me. 3.110

But how is this Self to be meditated upon? To this he says: Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses free from other objects, that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp—that Self is to be meditated upon.

Having withdrawn the mind, intellect, memory, and senses from objects external to the Self and having made them have the Self as their sole object, the Self is to be meditated upon—that Lord who dwells unshakable in the heart, shining like a lamp placed in a windless spot. This alone constitutes His state of being an object of meditation: that the mental fluctuations, by setting aside the appearance of external objects, possess a tendency toward the Self; it is like a lamp whose spreading rays of light are confined within a pair of joined bowls, resulting in a single-pointed concentration. 3.111.

However, for one whose mental fluctuations do not find delight in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) because they lack a formless object of focus, it is said that he should practice the worship of the *Śabdabrahman* (the Brahman of Sound):
"By reciting the *Sāma-veda* chant without error according to the prescribed rule,
one who is attentive attains the Supreme Brahman through that practice."

Singing the *sāman* means singing the *sāman* without transgressing the path understood through one's own study (*svādhyāya*). Although the *sāman* consists essentially of singing, the specific term "singing" (*gāyam*) is used for the purpose of excluding non-chanted mantras. Singing it "unwaveringly" (*avicyutam*) means without stumbling and with full attention; that is, reciting while the mental fluctuations are focused one-pointedly upon the self as permeated by the sound of the *sāman*. Through the power of such practice, one who is proficient therein attains the Supreme Brahman by means of meditation in which the form of the word is transcended.
Thus it has been said: "One who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman attains the Supreme Brahman. (3.112)
"One who is proficient in the *śabdabrahman* attains the supreme *brahman*.
However, for one whose mind does not find delight in Vedic song, he says that the practice of self-worship should be performed by means of recollecting worldly songs:
the *aparāntaka*, the *ullopya*, the *madraka*, and likewise the *prakarī*."
The *auveṇaka*, the *sarobindu*, the *uttara*, and the *gītakas*.
The Vedic verses, the Pāṇika songs, those composed by Dakṣa, and the hymns of Brahmā—this is what is called "chanting" (geya); through the practice of that, it is designated as "liberation."
The *aparāntaka*, *kollūpya*, *madraka*, *prakarya*, *auveṇaka*, along with the *sāravinda*, and the *uttara*—these seven songs are known as the *prakara*.

By the word "and" (*ca*), the great songs such as the *āsārita* and *vardhamānaka* are included. These four types of songs, beginning with the *ṛggāthā*, constitute the collection of songs starting with the *aparāntaka*. This entire collection of songs should be understood as being designated by the term "liberation" (*mokṣa*) because they superimpose the nature of the Self and serve as a means to liberation; for, by means of producing one-pointedness through their practice, they cause the attainment of one-pointedness of the Self. (3.113–3.114)
Furthermore:
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, who is proficient in the musical scales and modes,
and who understands rhythm, attains the path of liberation without effort.
One who knows the truth of playing the lute as expounded by the sage Bharata and others;
that which is heard is "śruti," which is of twenty-two kinds within the seven notes (*svaras*). For instance:

The notes ṣaḍja, madhyama, and pañcama each have four *śrutis*; ṛṣabha and dhaivata each have three *śrutis*; and gāndhāra and niṣāda each have two *śrutis*. As for the *jātis*, there are seven pure ones beginning with ṣaḍja, and eleven mixed *jātis*, making eighteen types in total; one who is skilled (*viśārada*) in these is proficient. *Tāla* is said to be the measure of song.

And one who knows its true nature, by means of meditating on Brahman as permeated by that [sound], reaches and attains the path of liberation with very little effort, because the one-pointedness of the mind upon the Self is easily achieved through the fear of breaking the rhythm and so forth. 3.115.
He states another result for one who knows song but is struck by obstacles such as mental distraction:
"If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through yoga,
having become an attendant of Rudra, he rejoices together with him."
If one who knows song does not somehow attain the supreme state through yoga, then, having become an attendant of Rudra, he rejoices and plays together with him. || 3.116 ||
He summarizes what was stated previously:
"The self is said to be beginningless, but its beginning is the body;
the entire world originates from the self, and the self originates from the world."

According to the manner previously stated, the self (*ātman*) is beginningless; its "origin" (*udbhava*), namely the assumption of a body, has been described in the passage: "The unborn [self] [arises] from the assumption of a body" (YDh 3.69). Furthermore, the origin of the entire world, beginning with the earth, from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) has been described by the verse beginning: "At the beginning of creation, as space... (3.117), as well as the emergence of individual souls (*jīva*) into their gross bodies from the aggregate of elements such as earth, which have themselves arisen from that [Supreme Self].
He explains this very point by means of a question:
"How is it that we, along with the gods, asuras, and humans, are utterly bewildered?
Tell us how the world arose and how the Self exists within it."

We are bewildered regarding this matter: how this entire world, together with all its gods, asuras, humans, and so forth, has arisen from the Self, and how the Self comes to assume the bodies of animals, humans, reptiles, and the like within that world.
Therefore, for the sake of dispelling our delusion, please explain this to us in detail. (3.118)
Thus questioned by the sages, he gave this reply: "Indeed,
that person who is seen here after casting off the net of delusion has a thousand arms,
a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, and the splendor of the sun."
He is indeed the Self, the sacrifice, the omniform Prajāpati;
as Virāj, he attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food.

In this world, having cast aside that web of delusion which consists of the conceit of self (*ātman*) regarding what is not-self—such as the gross body—one perceives the Person (*puruṣa*) who is distinct from that [body]: one who possesses many hands, feet, and eyes; who has the luster of the sun; who is of infinite radiance; who is thousandfold; and who has many heads.
This [description] is stated by way of his being the substratum of the powers within their respective domains, since he lacks any connection with direct perception and the like.
He alone is the Self (*ātman*), the Sacrifice (*yajña*), and the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*).
For he is the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), whose very nature is everything.
If one asks how his universal form consists precisely of this, it is because he, as the *virāj*, attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
And from sacrifice, through the mediation of rain and so forth, comes the creation of living beings; thus is his universal form. (2.119–2.120)
He elaborates on this very point:
"That supreme essence which arises from the renunciation of substance and deity,
having fully satisfied the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit."
Having been joined with the wind, the Soma is then led by its rays;
it is brought to the solar abode as ordained by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
From that solar orb, this sun emits the supreme nectar,
from which arises the birth of all beings, whether their nature be characterized by eating or not eating.
From that food, again comes sacrifice; from sacrifice, again food; and from food, again the ritual.
Thus this wheel, without beginning or end, revolves perpetually.

From the substance—such as the *caru* or the *puroḍāśa*—which is offered with the deity in mind, there arises a supreme essence (*rasa*) that is of the nature of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), a further transformation of the self, and most excellent by virtue of being the seed for the birth of the entire world. Having thoroughly gratified the deities who constitute the recipient (*sampradāna-kāraka*), and having united the sacrificer with his desired fruit, this essence, impelled by the wind, is led toward the lunar orb. Thence, by means of its rays, it proceeds from the lunar orb to the solar orb.
Because of the statement of non-difference, "This very triple knowledge shines," he is presented as consisting of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman.

And from his own orb, that Sun emits the supreme nectar-essence in the form of rain, which is the cause of birth for all beings—both moving and stationary, whether they subsist on food or do not eat—which consists of the totality of living things.

Therefore, from that food consisting of herbs produced by rain—which is the cause of the birth of living beings—sacrifice arises again; from sacrifice, food arises again in the manner previously described; and from food, sacrifice arises again. In this way, this entire wheel of saṃsāra revolves perfectly in the form of a continuous flow, devoid of beginning or end. By this sequence, the origin of the entire universe proceeds from the Self, and therein, the Self assumes a body in accordance with its own karma. (3.121–124)
Now, if the transmigratory wandering of the self is indeed without beginning and end, does it not follow that liberation is impossible? To this, he says:
"The self is beginningless; no origination exists for the inner self;
rather, the person (puruṣa) is a composite [entity] born of delusion, desire, aversion, and karma."

Although no origination exists for the inner self (*antarātman*), which is pervasive throughout the body and beginningless, nevertheless, the person (*puruṣa*) stands in an inherent relation (*samavāyin*) with the body; he experiences the collection of objects of experience consisting of pleasure and pain within that abode of enjoyment. Thus, through such a connection, he indeed becomes related [to the body]. And that inherent relation is produced by karma generated from delusion, desire, and aversion, but it is not innate. Since its destruction is possible due to its being an effect, there is no lack of liberation. (3.125)
It has been stated that the world is born from the Self; to elaborate upon that, he says:
"The primordial deity who was described by me as having a thousandfold self—from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the social classes (varṇas) were produced in their respective order."
From his feet the earth was born, and from his head the sky;
from his nose the vital breaths, from his ears the directions, from his touch the wind, and from his mouth the fire.
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun;
from his loins came the intermediate space and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings.

That one who has been described by me as the primordial deity (ādideva)—who possesses a thousandfold self and manifold forms because he is the essence of all individual souls and the essence of the phenomenal world, and likewise because he is the cause of the entire universe—from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet were born, respectively, the four castes beginning with the Brahmins.

Thus, from his feet came the earth; from his head, the abode of the gods; from his nose, the vital breath; from his ears, the quarters of space; from his touch, the wind; from his mouth, the fire; from his mind, the moon; from his eyes, the sun; and from his loins, the sky and the entire world consisting of both the moving and the unmoving. || 3.126-128 ||
Regarding this, they raise an objection: "If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born in evil wombs?
How can he, who is the Lord, be joined with undesirable states of being?"
O Brahmin, Lord of Yogins, if the Self alone assumes the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, then how can it be born in evil wombs such as those of beasts, birds, and the like?
If it is argued that birth there occurs because of being defiled by faults such as delusion, attachment, and aversion, that is not so.
Since the Lord is independent, how could he be joined with undesirable states such as delusion, passion, and the like? (3.129)
Furthermore: Even though it was previously endowed with the instruments [of perception], how is it that there was no cognition?
And why does the all-pervading [self], although itself all-pervading, not perceive the sensation [of another]?
Likewise, this is also a refutation here:
why does that self, even when accompanied by the means of cognition such as the mind and so forth, not produce a prior cognition whose object was experienced in another birth?
Similarly, although it is omnipresent and resides within all bodies, why does it not itself perceive the sensations—consisting of pleasure, pain, and so on—that belong to all living beings?
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the Self alone, as the Lord, assumes the state of the individual soul and so forth. 3.130
Regarding this, he states the answer to the previous objection:

"By means of the defects born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, this living being goes to existence among the final classes of birds and stationary beings, as well as through hundreds of wombs."

Although the Lord is by nature characterized by truth, knowledge, and bliss, nevertheless, under the influence of the entry of ignorance (avidyā), being overwhelmed by states such as delusion and passion, he performs a threefold accumulation of karma—mental and so forth—which is the means for birth in various inferior wombs.

By that [karma], he falls into the state of inferior wombs beginning with the outcastes (antyaja). Outcastes are those such as the Caṇḍālas; birds are those such as crows; and immovable things are those such as trees. This individual soul (jīva) attains, in due order over thousands of births, that state of being an outcaste, bird, or immovable thing through the defects of actions initiated by mind, speech, and body. (3.131)
Moreover: Just as the states of embodied beings within their bodies are infinite,
so too are the forms of those embodied beings here in all wombs.

Just as the dispositions—the specific intentions—of embodied living beings within their bodies are infinite due to the varying degrees of the predominance of *sattva* and the other qualities (*guṇas*), so too do their effects, such as physical forms like being hunchbacked or dwarfed, occur for those possessing bodies across all species of birth. 3.132.

Now, one might object: "If conditions such as being humpbacked are produced by karma, then they ought to occur immediately after that karma. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The ripening of some karmas occurs after death; for some, it arises in this life;
and for others, it occurs both here and in the next. In that regard, the state [of the individual] is the determining factor."

The ripening—the fruit—of certain actions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma occurs after death in another body; that of certain others such as the Kārīrī sacrifice results in rain and so forth in this very life;
and for some, such as the Citrā sacrifice, the fruit, such as cattle and the like, is indefinite, occurring either in this life or in another body.
For it is not the meaning of the treatise that the fruit of action must necessarily follow immediately;

rather, in this context, the state of being *sattva* and so forth is the actual determinant in the production of the auspicious or inauspicious fruits of actions, because the gradation of those fruits is dependent upon them. (3.133)

It has been stated that one attains the lowest and other types of births through actions born of mind, speech, and body; to elaborate upon that, he says: "Coveting the property of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable, and being intent on what is false, one is born into the lowest wombs."

One who meditates with direct intent on how one might steal the wealth of others, or who contemplates committing undesirable, violent acts such as the killing of a Brahmin—possessing such an obsession (*abhiniveśa*) and repeated mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) toward unreal and false objects—is born in the lowest wombs, such as those of dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and other outcastes. (3.134)
Furthermore:
A person who speaks untruth, who is slanderous, harsh,
and a speaker of idle gossip, is born among animals and birds.

But that man who is habitually a liar, a slanderer, a whisperer into the ear, one whose speech causes distress to others, a babble of incoherent talk, and a speaker of irrelevant matters—due to the gradations of whether such acts were intentional or unintentional—he is born among inferior or superior beasts and birds. (3.135)
Moreover: One who is devoted to taking what is not given, one who consorts with the wives of others,
and one who is a violent aggressor against stationary beings contrary to the rules, is reborn among them.

One who delights in taking what is not given, being addicted to seizing the wealth of others that has not been bestowed, who is intent on another's wife, and who kills living beings by unrighteous means, is born among stationary beings such as trees, creepers, and spreading vines, according to the relative degree of the gravity or lightness of their faults. (3.136)
He speaks of the ripening of qualities such as *sattva*:
"One who knows the self, who is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered the senses,
performs righteous deeds, and is learned in the Vedas and sciences— such a person of *sattva* attains the state of divine birth."

One who knows the Self, free from pride regarding learning, wealth, lineage, and so forth; pure, endowed with both external and internal purity; self-controlled, possessed of tranquility; ascetic, engaged in penances such as the *kṛcchra*; likewise unattached to the objects of the senses; devoted to the performance of obligatory and occasional duties; and a knower of the meaning of the Vedas—such a person is *sāttvika*. And by virtue of the varying degrees of the predominance of *sattva*, he attains births among the gods that are progressively more and more excellent. (3.137)
Furthermore:
"The man among humans who delights in the non-existence of the effect [in the cause], who is undisciplined, enterprising, and sensual— he, being of rajasic nature, attains birth after death."

But he who is devoted to non-productive activities such as instrumental music, dancing, and the like; who is thus undisciplined, with a distracted mind, always restless in his undertakings, and excessively attached to sense objects—he is endowed with the quality of rajas. Due to the varying degrees of that quality, after death he attains birth among the inferior or superior classes of human beings. (3.138)
And likewise, Seltur omits *ca*:
"One who is sleepy, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar,
as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct, becomes a tamasic being among the animals."

Furthermore, one who is habitually sleepy, who causes pain to living beings, who is possessed by greed, as well as an atheist, a reviler of dharma and other virtues, one who is prone to begging, negligent, devoid of discrimination between what should and should not be done, and one of contrary conduct—such a person is endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas); according to the degree of that quality, he is born in inferior, more inferior, or animal wombs. || 3.139 ||
He summarizes what was stated previously:
"Thus, possessed by both rajas and tamas, wandering here,
and joined with undesirable states, one enters into saṃsāra."

Thus, this self, pierced by ignorance and thoroughly possessed by *rajas* and *tamas*, wandering here in *saṃsāra*, overwhelmed by various states that produce manifold sufferings, repeatedly undergoes *saṃsāra*, which is the assumption of a body.
Therefore, there is no room for the objection: "How can that Lord be joined with undesirable states? (3.140)

Regarding the second objection— that [the self] is not capable [of knowing] even when endowed with the instruments— he states the reply: "Just as a mirror that is tarnished is incapable of reflecting forms,
so too the self whose instruments are unripened is incapable of self-knowledge."

Even though the self is endowed with the means of knowledge such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, it is nevertheless incapable of cognizing objects experienced in other births, because its faculties are unripe and its mind is overwhelmed by impurities such as passion;
just as a mirror covered with grime is not capable of producing the cognition of forms. 3.141

Now, one might object: "Since even the knowledge belonging to a previous birth is manifested by the self, and since that [self] is established by itself (*svataḥsiddha*), non-perception [of that knowledge] is not logical. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as in an unripe *kaṭvervāru* fruit, its sweet taste is not perceived even though it exists, so too, when the instruments [of perception] are unripened, cognition is not found within the self."

Just as the sweet taste present in an unripe bitter cucumber or a bitter karkaṭikā fruit is not perceived, so too, although the capacity for knowing—the state of being a knower—exists within the self when the instruments [of perception] are unrefined, it does not attain its range of objects from previous births. 3.142.
Regarding the question, "Why does the all-pervading one not experience sensation, even though he is omnipresent? the following answer is given:
"The embodied soul experiences sensation that resides in all bases within its own body;
however, the yogin who is liberated does not undergo any sensation whatsoever."

Furthermore, that embodied being who is possessed of the conceit of being the body experiences only in his own body—acquired through his own karma—the sensation that rests upon everything in the form of internal and other types; he does not experience that which belongs to another body, precisely because the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) that initiates the formation of a locus of experience differs [in each case].

However, the liberated yogi, from whom the ego-sense and so forth have been released, becomes the knower of all cognitions of pleasure, pain, and so on occurring in all fields, because his faculties have reached full maturity.

Now, one might object: "If the Self is one, then the perception of difference among the bodies of gods, humans, and others would not be possible. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as the single ether appears distinct within jars and other vessels, so too the single Self appears manifold, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water."

Just as the single sky is experienced as manifold when divided by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as wells and jars, or just as the sun, though one, is experienced as manifold in various water-vessels such as water-pots, crystal bowls, and jasmine cups, so too the Self, though one, appears as many through the division of the limiting adjuncts of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The employment of the second example is for the purpose of illuminating that the plurality of the Self is not ultimately real. (3.144)
Having summarized the meaning of what was stated previously—that "the Lord, as the sixth himself, simultaneously takes up the five elements"—he says:
"The elements are Brahma, space, wind, fire, water, and earth;
these are the worlds, and this is the Self; from that [arises] all that is moving and unmoving."

Brahman is the Self; space is the sky; wind is the air; fire is *tejas*; water is well known; and earth—these elements (*dhātavaḥ*), beginning with wind, are so called because they pervade and sustain the body. Among them, the five elements beginning with space are "worlds" (*lokāḥ*) because they are perceived or seen;
that is to say, they are insentient.
This Self is the element of consciousness; from this aggregate of the insentient and the sentient, the world consisting of the stationary and the moving is produced. || 3.145 ||
He explains how this Self creates the world:
"Just as a potter makes a jar through the conjunction of clay, a staff, and a wheel,
or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, clay, and wood."
Just as a goldsmith [fashions] a form by taking up mere gold,
or a silkworm [produces] a cocoon through the union with its own saliva;
Having thus taken up the causal factors, the Self, having come together with the instruments, creates itself within those various wombs here.
For just as a potter, depending upon a collection of causes such as clay, a wheel, and a cloth, fashions various kinds of effects such as water-jars and bowls;
or just as a carpenter produces a single effect called a "house" by means of grass, mud, and wood which are mutually dependent;
or just as a goldsmith, taking only gold as his material, produces effects that follow from that very gold, such as bracelets, crowns, and earrings.

Or just as a particular kind of insect called a silkworm begins to construct a cocoon—known as a "sheath"—which is its own prison and which it has started with its own saliva, so too the Self, having taken up the elements such as earth and other means that are mutually dependent, as well as the instruments such as the ears and so forth, creates itself by its own power in this cycle of existence within various wombs such as those of gods, bound by the fetters of its own karma, in the form of a body. (3.146–148)
Anticipating the objection, "What, then, is the proof for the existence of a self distinct from the sensory organs that perceive objects? he says:
"The great elements are real; indeed, the self is exactly the same.
Otherwise, how could one see with one eye what was seen by the other?"
Or who indeed recognizes speech after hearing it again and again?
For just as the great elements, such as earth and the rest, are real because they are accessible through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too the self (*ātman*) is real.

Otherwise, if there were no permanent knower distinct from the intellect and the sense organs, then who would recognize with another sense organ, such as the sense of touch, an object previously seen by the visual sense organ, thinking, "I am touching that very thing which I saw"?
Likewise, having previously heard the speech of a certain person, who could recognize as "this is that person's speech" the speech being heard again?
Therefore, it is established that the knower is permanent and distinct from the organs of cognition.
Furthermore: Whose is the recollection of past objects, or who is the agent of a dream?
Proud of one's birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth,
one exerts oneself toward objects such as sound through action, mind, and speech.

If the self were not permanent, then whose would memory be—that memory which has as its object things previously experienced and is based on the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience? For it is not possible for one person to have a memory of an object seen by another.
Likewise, who is the agent of dream-cognition? Indeed, the sense organs cannot be its agents, as their operations have ceased.

Likewise, for whom does such a connecting cognition arise as "I alone am endowed with noble birth and so forth," if there were no stable self distinct from [the mind]? Similarly, who would exert effort through mind, speech, and body for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of objects such as sound and touch? Therefore, the self exists as distinct from the intellect and the sense organs. (3.150–3.151)
Explaining the nature of transmigratory existence for the purpose of prescribing specific forms of worship, he says:
"With a doubtful mind, [the seeker] wonders whether the fruit of action exists or not;
indeed, even though unaccomplished, he considers himself accomplished."

That aforementioned self, which is ruined and corrupted by egoism, becomes one whose mind is filled with doubt as to whether or not there is a fruit in all actions. Likewise, though unaccomplished and having failed to achieve his purpose, he considers himself to be already accomplished and one who has achieved his goal. (3.152)
Moreover: "My wife, my son, my ministers—I am their master," such is the established view;
yet one's mind is always perverted regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful.

For me, whose mind is thus corrupted, there arises an extreme state of being agitated by possessiveness (*mamatā*), thinking, "I am theirs" and "they are mine," regarding wife, children, servants, and so forth.
Likewise, in matters concerning what is beneficial or harmful, that person of corrupted mind will always possess a perverted intellect. (3.153)
Moreover:
