he is indistinguishable toward the object of knowledge and the knower, as well as toward primordial nature and its transformations; he strives to end his life by fasting, fire, weapons, or by leaping from waterfalls.
One who behaves in this way— undisciplined in self, possessed of false attachments—
is bound by action through hatred, delusion, and desire.

One who knows the knowable is a "knower of the knowable. Regarding that Self, he becomes undiscriminating—that is, ignorant of the distinction—both with respect to Prakṛti, which is the state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), and with respect to its transformations, such as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth.
Likewise, under the influence of delusion, he may make efforts toward fasting, entering fire, drowning in water, consuming poison, and the like.

Thus, engaged in various kinds of improper actions, being one whose self is undisciplined and unrestrained, and being possessed by an attachment to what is not a true goal, he is bound by the collection of actions produced thereby, as well as by passion, hatred, and delusion. (3.154–155)
How, moreover, does confidence in that [Self] arise by means of the assumption of a body? To this he says:
"Service to the teacher, discrimination regarding the meaning of the Vedic scriptures, the performance of those duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech."
Abstention from looking at women and touching them, seeing the Self in all beings,
renouncing possessions, and wearing worn-out saffron robes.
Restraining the senses from their objects, abandoning drowsiness and laziness,
a thorough examination of the body, and seeing evil in worldly activities.

Through these means— purity of the *sattva* quality by being free from *rajas* and *tamas*, freedom from desire, and tranquility— one who is thoroughly purified becomes fit for *sattva* and attains immortality.

Service to the teacher for the sake of knowledge; discernment regarding the meanings of Vedānta and the Yoga-śāstras such as those of Patañjali; the practice of the meditations and rituals taught therein; association with virtuous persons; speaking words that are pleasant and beneficial; the renunciation of looking at women and of sexual desire; viewing all beings as oneself, which is the vision of equality; the abandonment of possessions such as children, fields, and wife; wearing worn-out ochre robes; likewise, the restraint of the activity of the senses, such as hearing, toward objects like sound and touch; the specific abandonment of drowsiness—which resembles sleep—and laziness, which is a lack of enthusiasm; the contemplation of the body through an enumeration of its defects, such as instability and impurity; likewise, reflecting upon the fault of the subtle killing of living beings in all activities such as walking; likewise, freedom from passion (*rajas*) and ignorance (*tamas*), and the purification of one's state of being through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other means; freedom from longing, which is the absence of desire for sense objects; and tranquility (*śama*), which is the restraint of the external and internal organs. One who is thoroughly purified by these means, such as service to the teacher, and who is endowed with pure *sattva*, shall become immortal—that is, liberated—through the worship of Brahman. (3.156–159)
To the question of how the attainment of immortality occurs, he says:
"Through the presence of the recollection of reality, through the application of being, through the complete destruction of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, yoga proceeds."

Through the remembrance of the reality called the Self, by its presence in the Self with unwavering steadiness, through the purification of the mind-stuff (*sattva*), through the connection with the quality of pure *sattva* alone, through the total exhaustion of the seeds of karma, and through association with virtuous persons, the yoga of the Self proceeds. (3.160)
Moreover: "Furthermore,
he whose mind, upon the dissolution of the body, is firmly established in the Lord with a steady intellect, shall attain the full recollection of his former births."

Furthermore, when a yogin of undisturbed intellect, at the time of the body's dissolution, directs his mind—endowed with *sattva*—toward the Lord with perfect one-pointedness, he may, if due to a lack of proficiency in the practice of worship he does not realize the Self, nevertheless, by the force of the intensity of his specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), come to remember the various sufferings arising from dwelling in wombs such as those of worms and insects experienced in other births. And through that recollection, becoming agitated, he turns toward liberation, which brings an end to those [sufferings]. (3.161)
As for the question of what becomes of one who, due to a lack of sharp mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), does not remember their previous birth, he says in response:
"Just as an actor paints his own body with colors,
assuming various forms, so too does the self [assume] bodies born of karma."

Just as an actor named Bharata, assuming various forms such as Rāma or Rāvaṇa, fashions and colors his own body with white, black, yellow, and other hues, even so the Self assumes various bodies—such as those of the hunchbacked or the dwarf—caused by karma, for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of those respective actions. (3.162)
Furthermore:
"The deformity of the embryo at birth— such as being deficient in limbs— is observed to result from defects in time, karma, the self, and the seed, as well as those of the mother."

Not only is karma alone the cause of conditions such as being hunchbacked or dwarfed; rather, in the case of karma related to time (*kāla-karman*), the defects of one's own parents' seeds and the defects of the mother are all auxiliary causes.

By means of this collection of causes, consisting of both visible and invisible factors, a deformity such as the deficiency of limbs in the embryo is observed from birth onwards, occurring at an indefinite time. (3.163)

Now, one might object: "At the time of the elemental dissolution (*prākṛtika-pralaya*), when all transformations beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) have perished, the *karma* is also destroyed; how then can the first assumption of a physical body, which is dependent upon that *karma*, occur? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This Self has never before been separated from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the mind (*manas*), the movement [of past actions], the fruit of *karma*, and the body in any way whatsoever."
The mind (*manas*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) are well known.
"Motion" (*gati*) refers to the mass of defects that serves as the cause for transmigration.
"Fruit of action" (*karmaphala*) consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
This self is never released from this body, which consists of the subtle linga composed of these elements beginning with egoism, until liberation is attained. (3.164)

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for individual living beings (*jīva*) with their specific karmas, cessation [of life] is only logical at a specific time, and not rather a simultaneous destruction of life at an improper time in battle and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the wick, the support, and the oil, and its modification is likewise observed, so too is the destruction of life at an improper time."

For just as there is a simultaneous existence of many flames from numerous wicks soaked in oil, and once they have stood thus, there occurs a simultaneous cessation due to the simultaneous onset of causes for their destruction—namely, the impact of a violently blowing wind—even so, the simultaneous exhaustion of the life-force of living beings such as charioteers, drivers, horses, and elephants, due to the simultaneity of the causes for cessation known as battle, is not impossible even at an untimely hour.
This is what is meant.

The obstruction of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), which is the cause of misfortune at a specific time, occurs through the encounter with a perceived cause that produces an effect contrary to it. || 3.165 ||
He describes the path to liberation:
"Infinite are his rays, like those of a lamp situated in the heart;
they are white, black, variegated in form, tawny, blue, and red."
One among them stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [path] one goes to the supreme goal.

That *jīva* which resides in the heart like a lamp has infinite rays—namely, the channels (*nāḍīs*)—which are the causes of pleasure and pain, described as being seventy-two thousand in number and so forth, and which exist everywhere in forms such as white, black, and variegated. Among them, one ray is situated upwards; it pierces the orb of the sun and passes beyond the abode of Hiraṇyagarbha. By means of that [ray], the *jīva* attains the supreme goal, characterized by non-return. 3.167.
That other hundred of its rays which are established directed upwards, by means of them he reaches the bodies of the gods together with their abodes.

From that ray of this self which constitutes the path to liberation, there exists another hundred rays established in an upward direction; by means of them, he attains the celestial bodies of the gods—luminous, the exclusive locus for the experience of happiness, together with their abodes and the divine cities fashioned from gold, silver, and jewels. || 3.168 ||
He describes the path of transmigration:
"Those various rays of his that shine below with gentle light—
by means of them, he transmigrates here helplessly for the sake of experiencing karma."

Furthermore, those rays beneath it which are of gentle luster—by means of them, one wanders helplessly in saṃsāra for the sake of experiencing the fruits [of karma], dependent upon one's own performed actions. (3.169)
Desiring to refute the position of those who maintain that consciousness is inherent in the elements (bhūtacaitanyavāda), he says:
"By means of the Vedas, the scriptures, and specific cognitions; by birth and by death;
by affliction, by going, and likewise by coming; and indeed by truth and by falsehood."
Through higher states, through pleasure and pain, through auspicious and inauspicious actions,
and through the fruits arising from omens, the knowledge of birds, and the conjunctions of planets.
Through the movements of the stars and constellations, through waking states and those born of dreams,
and likewise through space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness.
Through the periods of the Manvantaras, through the attainment of the Yugas, and even by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, and fruits,
one perceives the Self as wealth and likewise as the cause of the world.

This very Self is known through the Vedas by such passages as "Not this, not this," "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," and "without hands or feet"; through the scriptures such as Mīmāṃsā and Ānvīkṣikī; through cognitions such as the experience of a Self distinct from the body in the form "this is my body"; likewise, through birth and death—which are governed by the merit and demerit performed in previous lives—there is an inference of a Self distinct from the body; through suffering, which is governed by the performer of actions in a previous life; and similarly, through coming and going, which are governed by the substratum of knowledge, desire, and effort, there is an inference of a Self distinct from the material body.
For consciousness and the like cannot possibly belong to the body;
because, according to the established principle that the qualities of the cause produce corresponding specific qualities in the effect-substance, we observe that such qualities arise in the product.

However, the inherence of consciousness and the like is not possible in the earthly atoms and so forth which constitute its causes, since it is not perceived in the physical objects such as pillars and jars composed of those [atoms].
Nor should it be said that [consciousness] arises from contact with another substance, such as water, in the manner of the power of intoxication; for power is a common property [of substances].
Therefore, one must accept a substratum of consciousness and so forth that is distinct from the material body.
Truth and falsehood are well-established [in experience].
The attainment of the beneficial is the highest good;
pleasure and pain pertain to the next world.
Likewise, there is the performance of virtuous actions and the abandonment of non-virtuous actions.
And by means of these [types of] knowledge that are restricted to specific objects, there is the inference of a self distinct from the body.
"Omens" refers to earthquakes and the like.
"Knowledge of omens" (*śākunajñāna*) is knowledge characterized by the signs of the movements of birds such as the *piṅgalā* and others.
The planets, beginning with the Sun, [are known] by the fruits born of their conjunctions.

O sages, know—that is, understand—that which is experienced through the movements of *tārās* (the stars), namely the constellations (*nakṣatras*) such as Aśvinī and others, which manifest auspicious and inauspicious results; through "waking states" (*jāgaras*), namely the visions of the sun with a hole or other such phenomena arising from the waking condition; likewise through dreams, such as the knowledge of mounting a chariot yoked with donkeys or boars; likewise through space and so forth, which are created for the sake of the soul's experience; likewise through the attainment of different *manvantaras* and *yugas*, which cannot logically apply to the body; and likewise through the powers of mantras and medicinal herbs, including minor rites performed with foresight, whether directly or indirectly, none of which can logically apply to the body. Know this! 3.170–173.
Furthermore: ego-consciousness, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude,
the transition between the various sense organs, desire, retention, and life-force.
Heaven, dreaming, the impelling of entities, the movement of the mind,
the winking of an eye, consciousness, effort, and the grasping of the five elemental constituents [are his].
Since these marks of the Supreme Self are perceived,
therefore there exists a Self beyond the body, the all-pervading Lord.

Self-conception (*ahaṃkṛti*) is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Memory (*smṛti*) is that which is based on the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) formed by experiences in a previous birth, and has as its object the drinking of breast milk and so forth. Pleasure (*sukha*) is worldly. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is steadfastness. The "movement among the senses" (*indriyāntarasaṃcāra*) is the process of synthesis consisting of the thought, "I who saw this am now touching it," which occurs when an object seen by one sense is apprehended by another sense.
In this context, desire, effort, and consciousness (*caitanya*) function as logical marks (*liṅga*) by their very nature.
However, in the preceding verse, they function as logical marks in an implied sense (*ārthika*) as the causes for movement, truthful speech, and so forth; thus there is no redundancy.

Likewise, the maintenance of the body; life, which is the sustenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); heaven, which is a particular kind of happiness to be experienced in another fixed body; and dream, which is well known.

However, while in the previous verse the dream was mentioned as a sign for indicating auspicious results, here it is mentioned in its own nature; thus there is no redundancy. Similarly, the impelling of the states of the senses and so forth; the movement of the mind, which is pervaded by the presiding conscious principle; blinking, which is well known; and likewise, the taking up of the five elements.

Since these marks, whether directly or through a traditional lineage, are seen to be impossible among the material elements and instead manifest the Supreme Self, it is established that there exists a Self distinct from the body, the all-pervading Lord. 3.174–176.
He states the nature of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña): "The sense organs together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action,
as well as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the elements beginning with earth."
The Unmanifest is called the Self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of this Field;
it is the Lord dwelling within all beings, who is both being and non-being, and that which is both existent and non-existent.

The sense organs, beginning with hearing, together with their objects such as sound; the mind; the organs of action, beginning with speech; likewise the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the intellect (buddhi), which consists of determination; the five elements beginning with earth; and the unmanifest (avyakta), which is primordial nature (prakṛti)—this is the field (kṣetra). That which is its Lord (īśvara), all-pervading, and for that very reason of the nature of existence (sat-rūpa), because it cannot be grasped by other means of valid cognition; yet non-existent (asat), because it is not perceived clearly—this Self (ātman), being of the nature of both existent and non-existent, is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). || 3.177 || 3.178 ||
He states the origin of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest:
"The origin of the intellect is from the Unmanifest; from that, the emergence of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);
and from the ego-sense, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth, possessing one additional quality each."
The equilibrium of the qualities such as *sattva* and the others is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

From that, the intellect (*buddhi*) arises, consisting of the three types—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. And from that [intellect], the threefold ego (*ahaṃkāra*) arises, namely: the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*.

Among these, from the *tāmasa* ego known as *bhūtādi*, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the gross elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*) are also included, and these arise with each successive quality added.
By virtue of the word "and" (ca), the sense organs of cognition and action arise from the Vaikārika and Taijasa [forms of ego]. (3.179)
He states the nature of their qualities:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever among these has emerged from which [element], that dissolves back into that very one."
It should be understood that the five qualities, beginning with sound, increase by one for each of those five elements, beginning with space.

Furthermore, among these transformations such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, whatever arises from a particular source, such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), that very thing dissolves back into that same source in its subtle form at the time of dissolution. (3.180)
Concluding the meaning of the treatise, he says:
"I have explained to you how the Self creates itself,
even though it is the Lord, through the maturation of the three kinds of karma."
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are proclaimed to be its very qualities;
indeed, when possessed by rajas and tamas, it revolves like a wheel.
He alone is the supreme Puruṣa, both beginningless and possessing a beginning;
he is described as having a form perceivable by the subtle body and the senses, and as being subject to transformation.
It has been explained to you how the Self, although being the Lord, creates itself according to the ripening of the three types of karma— mental and so forth—
and how the qualities such as *sattva* belong to that very Self when it is characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Likewise, it has also been stated that the same Self, when possessed by *rajas* and *tamas*, wanders here in this cycle of existence like a wheel.

That very same beginningless Supreme Person, by assuming a body, becomes possessed of a beginning; endowed with transformations such as being hunchbacked or dwarfed, and transformed into a gross form, he is described as having a nature perceivable through the marks of the senses. (3.181–183)
He describes the path to heaven: "The space between the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), the path of the sun's chariot (ajavīthī), and the star Agastya—
by that path those who maintain the *agnihotra* sacrifice and desire heaven go toward the celestial realm."

The path of the Aja-vīthī is the path of the immortals; that which lies between it and Agastya is the Pitṛyāna (the path of the ancestors), by which those who maintain the sacred fire and desire heaven go to the sky—that is, they attain heaven. || 3.184 ||
Moreover: Those who are devoted to generosity and endowed with the eight qualities correctly,
they too, being dedicated to the vow of truth, follow that very same path.

And those who are devoted to the traditional rites such as giving, being perfectly free from hypocrisy, and likewise endowed with the eight personal qualities—compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of weariness, auspiciousness, generosity, and lack of longing—as set forth by Gautama and others;
and those who are intent on speaking the truth—they too reach the abode of the gods by that very same path of the ancestors. (3.185)

Now, one might object: "In the dissolution following the Pratisaṃcara of the Naimittika type, since all teachers have perished, how will the people above them—who have not learned the Vedas—perform rituals such as the Agnihotra? And how much less, being devoid of performed rites, will they ascend the path to heaven? To this, he says:
"In that [dissolution], eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders shall return again; they are the seeds, the promoters of Dharma."

In that regard, on the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), there are eighty-eight thousand sages who, while remaining householders, are subject to the law of return; at the beginning of creation, by virtue of being the instructors of the Veda, they serve as the seeds for the manifestation of the tree of dharma and are the initiators of religious duties such as the agnihotra. Therefore, the aforementioned defects do not apply here. 3.186.
Moreover: Between the Seven Sages and the Nāgavīthī, there dwell those who have taken refuge in the world of the gods;
they are sages equal in number, entirely free from all worldly undertakings.
By means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom,
they go there and remain until the dissolution of all beings.

The seven sages (saptarṣayaḥ) are well known. The Nāgavīthi is the path of Airāvata; in the space between them dwell exactly as many sages, numbering eighty-eight thousand, who are free from all undertakings, established in absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), endowed with austerity and celibacy, and having abandoned all attachments, they have taken refuge in the world of the gods (devaloka) and remain there until the dissolution of the elements (prākṛtapralaya), that is, until the end of the cosmic absorption (ābhūtasaṃplava). Abiding there, at the beginning of creation, they are the initiators of spiritual duties (ādhyātmikadharma). 3.187–3.188.
What are those sages like? To this he says:
"From whom [proceed] the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, as well as the verses, the aphorisms, the commentaries, and whatever else consists of speech."

Since from both types of assemblies of sages the four Vedas, the Purāṇas, the auxiliary sciences, and the Upaniṣads—which are eternal and have come down through a lineage of students—have proceeded; and likewise the verses consisting of Itihāsas, the Sūtras pertaining to grammar and Mīmāṃsā, the commentaries (*bhāṣya*) which take the form of explanations of those Sūtras, and whatever other body of literature exists such as the science of medicine (*āyurveda*), has proceeded from them—those sages are thus the promulgators of Dharma.
This being so, there is no consequence of the fault of non-eternality even for the Veda. (3.189)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The study of the Vedas, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-control,
faith, fasting, and independence are the causes of knowledge of the Self."

Since the Veda is eternal, by virtue of its authority, the recitation of the Veda and other such acts become logically established as causes for the knowledge of the Self, by means of bringing about the purification of the mind. (3.190)
Moreover:
He is indeed to be sought after by all the stages of life in this very manner;
furthermore, he is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born.
Those twice-born ones who know it thus, and those forest-dwellers who, endowed with supreme faith, worship the Truth; |||

Since the Veda, being eternal, is the authoritative means of knowledge regarding the Self, it must be investigated in the various ways described by all those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) according to the path already stated. He demonstrates that very method: "It is to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*), meaning it is to be directly realized (*aparokṣīkartavyaḥ*) by the twice-born.
He shows the means for this: "It is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) and "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*).
First, it must be determined through the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the Vedānta;
immediately thereafter, it must be reflected upon (*mantavya*), that is, investigated by means of reasoning.
Thereafter, it becomes directly perceived (*aparokṣībhavati*) through meditation (*dhyāna*).

Those twice-born ones who, being endowed with extraordinary faith, have retired to a solitary place and worship this Self—which is Truth and the ultimate reality—in the manner described, they know the Self; that is, they find and attain it. 3.191–3.192.
He describes the path of attainment as the way of the gods: "In due order, they proceed to the light, the day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice,
the world of the gods, the sun, and the lightning."
Then a person born of the mind approaches them and makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahmā;
for them, there is no return here again.

Having realized their true nature, they rest successively in the abodes of the presiding deities of fire and the other elements, which constitute the path to liberation; being escorted by them, they reach the supreme state.

Arcis is fire, ahas is the day, śuklapakṣa is the bright fortnight, likewise uttarāyaṇa is the northern solstice, surasadma is the world of the gods, savitā is the sun, and vaidyutaṃ tejaḥ is the lightning-splendor. A mental person (mānasaḥ puruṣaḥ) leads those who have thus reached the stations beginning with arcis to the world of Brahmā.

For them, there is no returning again to this cycle of existence; rather, at the time of the dissolution of primordial nature (prakṛti-pratisaṃcara), having cast off their subtle bodies (liṅga-śarīra), they become one with the Supreme Self. 3.193–3.194.
He describes the path of the ancestors mentioned previously:
"Those men who have conquered heaven by means of sacrifice, austerity, and gifts,
[travel] through smoke, the night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice."
The world of the ancestors, the moon, the wind, rain, water, and the earth—
they arise here in this sequence, and they return once again.
The self-possessed person who does not understand these two paths shall become either a venomous serpent, a moth, an insect, or a worm.

Furthermore, those who enjoy the fruit of heaven through prescribed paths—namely, sacrifice, charity, and austerity—reach, in due order, the deities presiding over the stages beginning with smoke and ending with the moon; then, having reached air, rain, water, and earth, and having attained the state of semen in the form of food such as rice and the like, they enter the womb as transmigrating beings.

He who, being heedless, does not understand these two paths and does not perform the practice of dharma which serves as the means for both paths, shall become a biting serpent, a moth, a locust, or a worm. (3.195–197)
He describes the method of worship:
"With the feet turned upward and placed upon the thighs, having laid the right hand upon the left,
and slightly lifting the face while supporting it with the chest."
With eyes closed, established in sattva, not touching the teeth with the teeth,
the tongue placed motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly steady.
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses, sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) either twice or thrice.
Then the wise one, maintaining concentration, should hold the self there— in that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp— and meditate upon Him.
One whose two feet are placed upon the thighs with the soles upward is thus described as being in the *baddhapadmāsana* (bound lotus posture).

Likewise, having placed the right hand, palm upward, upon the left hand which is also turned upward, slightly raising the face and supporting it by pressing against the chest, steadying [the body], and likewise closing the eyes, remaining in *sattva*—that is, free from desire, anger, and the like—not touching the teeth with the teeth, and likewise having the tongue fixed motionlessly against the palate; such a person is thus described.

Likewise, with the mouth closed and the face covered, remaining perfectly still and unwavering, and having properly withdrawn the entire collection of sense-faculties from their objects, he should sit neither on a seat that is too low nor one that is too high—so that no distraction of the mind occurs—and then begin the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) two or three times.
Then, by the yogi who has brought the vital air under control, that Lord who dwells in the heart, motionless like a lamp, should be meditated upon;
and there in the heart, one should hold the Self as an object of the mind.
Focusing on the dhāraṇā and its essential nature: the time taken for a snap of the fingers while rotating the knees forward constitutes one *mātrā*.
With those fifteen mātrās, the breath control (prāṇāyāma) is inferior;
with thirty, it is middling;
with forty-five, it is superior.
Thus, one *dhāraṇā* consists of three *prāṇāyāmas*. Three of these are denoted by the term "yoga," and one should maintain them.
As it is said elsewhere: "Having whirled [the breath], one should snap the fingers, with the tips of the hands upon the kneecaps."
Prāṇāyāma consisting of fifteen mātrās is declared to be the lowest.
The middling [concentration] is twofold, and the best is threefold;
likewise, each dhāraṇā is said to consist of three [dhāraṇās], and yoga is composed of those in the same way.
Thus [ends the section] 3.198–201.
Having stirred [the mind], one should snap the fingers with the tip of the hand upon the knee-circle;
with fifteen measures (mātrās), this is known as the lowest breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The middling [concentration] is twofold, and the superior is threefold; likewise for dhāraṇā.
Each one is said to consist of three [dhāraṇās], and yoga is likewise composed of them.
He states the purpose for practicing the yoga consisting of concentration (dhāraṇā):
invisibility, memory, luster, vision, as well as knowledge through hearing,
and the ability to enter another's body after casting off one's own.
The creation of objects at will is indeed the characteristic mark of perfection in yoga;
for one who has attained yoga, by casting off the body, he becomes fit for immortality.
Antardhāna is invisibility to others through the attainment of the power of atomization (aṇimā).
Smṛti is the recollection of objects beyond the senses, like that of Manu and others.
Kānti is loveliness.
Vision [extends] even to objects past and future;
likewise, auditory knowledge is the capacity to know sounds that have not yet reached the path of hearing because they are manifested in an extremely distant location;
and the entry into another's body by means of relinquishing one's own body.
The creation of objects by the power of one's own will, independent of external causes, is the defining characteristic and sign of the perfection of yoga.
Moreover, this is not its sole purpose; rather, once yoga is perfected, one who casts off the body becomes fit for immortality and is capable of attaining the state of Brahman. (3.202–3.203)
He states another means for purifying the mind when sacrifices, gifts, and so forth are impossible: "Alternatively,
even by practicing the Veda while living in the forest, having renounced ritual actions,
eating only what is unasked for and in moderation, one may attain supreme perfection."

Alternatively, one who has abandoned both optional and prohibited actions, who studies one of the Vedas, who is devoted to solitude, and whose purity of being is brought about by eating only what is unasked for and measured, attains through the meditation on the Self the supreme perfection characterized by liberation. || 3.204 ||
Furthermore:
"One who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites,
and who speaks the truth— even such a householder is indeed liberated."

Since even a householder—who has acquired wealth through righteous means such as receiving gifts, who is intent on honoring guests, who is devoted to the performance of obligatory and occasional *śrāddhas*, who is habituated to speaking the truth, and who is absorbed in meditation on the reality of the Self—attains liberation, it follows that the adoption of the wandering life (*parivrājya*) alone in this world is not the sole means to liberation. (3.205)

"Tell us, without omission, the duties of those belonging to the castes (*varṇa*), the stages of life (*āśrama*), and others. Having thus stated five types of duty among the sixfold duties promised as the subject matter to be explained, and now desiring to commence the remaining category of occasional duties (*naimittika*) designated by the term "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*), [the author] first states the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*) in the form of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), for the purpose of generating interest in that subject and for the purpose of demonstrating the specific qualified person (*adhikārin*).

"Having experienced the terrible and dreadful hells born of great sins (*mahāpātaka*), those who have committed great sins are reborn here in this world upon the exhaustion of their [karmic] effects."

The designation "great sins" (*mahāpātaka*) for the group of five beginning with the killing of a Brāhmaṇa will be explained in the passage, "the killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinker of intoxicants," and so forth. Those who are joined with such [acts] are great sinners; having reached the hells such as *Tāmisra* produced by those great sins—which are terrible because they cause exceedingly intense pain, most fearsome due to their extreme severity, and harsh as abodes of exclusively suffering—and having reached them until the exhaustion of karma—that is, until the exhaustion of the experience of hellish suffering born of karma—due to the remainder of that karma, they are born again and again in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) with great frequency among animal wombs such as dogs and jackals, which abound in suffering.
The mention of "those who have committed great sins" (mahāpātakins) is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of others as well, such as those who have committed minor sins (upapātakin) and so forth;
for it will be stated later that they attain births among animals and other such states. (3.206)
Having stated that those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter the cycle of rebirth, he speaks in order to describe their specific destinies:
"The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a deer, a dog, a pig, or a camel;
the drinker of spirituous liquor [enters the womb] of an ass, a Pulkasa, or a Venā; of this there is no doubt."
A stealer of gold shall attain the state of worms, insects, and moths;
and one who violates the preceptor’s bed shall gradually become a blade of grass, a shrub, or a creeper.
A killer of a Brāhmaṇa attains, by the remainder of his own karma, the womb of wild animals such as deer, as well as dogs, pigs, and camels, which are well known.

A donkey is a *rāsabha*; a *pulkasa* is one born from a Niṣāda of the inverse order (*pratiloma*) with a Śūdra woman; a *veṇa* is one born from a Vaidehaka with an Ambaṣṭhī woman—a drunkard attains their wombs.

Worms are those produced from meat, excrement, cow-dung, and so forth, which are independent of conspecific mating; slightly larger than them are insects such as ants, which lack wings and bones; and moths are locusts—a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold shall attain their wombs.
"Grass" refers to *kāśa* and the like; "shrubs and creepers" are as previously described. One who has violated the Guru’s bed attains the state of those [beings] in succession.
And this applies to cases where the act was committed unintentionally;
however, in the case of intentional acts, they transmigrate through other wombs as well that abound in suffering.
As Manu has said:
"The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; of a cow, a horse, a goat, a deer, or a bird; or of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa."
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures.
A Brahmin who is a thief [incurs the fate] of spiders, snakes, lizards, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, and Piśācas, for thousands of births.
The spider,
the lizard,
the chameleon, and [the creatures] of grass, shrubs, and creepers, as well as those that are carnivorous and fanged.
And even those who have committed hundreds of cruel deeds, as well as those who have violated the teacher's bed.
Thus [ends the section]. 3.207–8.
The violator of the Guru’s bed [is reborn] hundreds of times as grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as carnivorous beasts, as fanged creatures, and as those who perform cruel deeds.

Furthermore: [In the NSP and Pāṇḍeya editions, there is an introductory statement: "And thus, for those who have emerged from the state of animals, there arise in their human existence characteristics such as disease; with this in mind, he says: and *kiṃ ca* is given as part of the commentary. Since this is unusual, I believe Seltur is correct in taking this as the introduction. He notes that the longer sentence is found only in a single manuscript. A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; a drinker of liquor shall have black teeth.
One who steals gold becomes one with deformed nails; one who violates the teacher's bed becomes one with a skin disease.
Whosoever dwells with these [sinners] is born bearing their very characteristics.

Thus, after experiencing terrible suffering in the hells such as Raurava and in births as dogs, pigs, donkeys, and so forth, they subsequently—due to the remainder of their evil deeds—wander through abundant human bodies at the very moment of birth, afflicted by symptoms such as consumption and other diseases.
A killer of a Brahmin shall become one who suffers from consumption and pulmonary tuberculosis (rājayakṣman).
One who habitually drinks forbidden liquor becomes black-toothed;
a stealer of a Brahmin’s gold acquires deformed nails;
and one who violates the teacher’s wife suffers from skin diseases and leprosy.
Among these, such as the slayer of a Brahmin and the rest, whichever fallen person a man associates with, he is born bearing that same mark.
Furthermore:
"The stealer of food shall be afflicted with chronic illness; the stealer of speech shall be mute."
One who steals grain shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a foul-smelling nose;
one who steals oil, shall be a drinker of oil; and a backbiter, a foul-smelling mouth.
The stealer of food becomes afflicted with disease and suffers from indigestion.

The stealer of speech—whether by reciting without permission or by stealing books—becomes mute or defective in the organ of speech. One who adulterates grain becomes possessed of redundant limbs, such as having six fingers and so forth. A slanderer, being habitually disposed to proclaim the existing faults of others, [becomes deformed].
One who steals oil becomes a *tailapāyin*, a specific kind of insect with a putrid nose and a foul-smelling snout.
A slanderer who proclaims false faults is born with a foul-smelling mouth.
This should be understood as occurring upon attaining a human body after having first attained the state of an animal; for whatever another's property a man has forcibly seized—
Having consumed an oblation that was not offered in sacrifice, one inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu: 3.210 || 3.211 ||
Furthermore:
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin,
one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest.

In place of the actual commentary, the NSP edition has mistakenly placed here a portion of the commentary on verse 3.213: "One who steals the jewels and so forth of others is born into a low caste called the goldsmith caste among the species of birds. One who steals the property of a Brahmin—other than gold—is born in a waterless region as a *brahmarākṣasa*, a specific kind of spirit. He who abducts another's wife and steals the property of a Brahmin, other than gold, is born in a forest, in a waterless region, as a *brahmarākṣasa*, a specific kind of spirit. (3.212)
Moreover: One who steals the jewels of others will be born into a low caste;
by killing a peacock one becomes a leaf-eating bird, and by stealing auspicious perfumes one becomes a muskrat.
In a low-born species known as the goldsmith caste, one who steals the jewels and other treasures of others is born;
and so too says Manu:
"A man who, out of greed, steals gems, pearls, and corals..."
And various kinds of jewels are produced from goldsmiths.
Thus: "A man who, out of greed, steals gems, pearls, corals,
and various other jewels, is born among the goldsmiths."
Having stolen leafy vegetables, one becomes a peacock;
having stolen auspicious perfumes, one is born as a musk-rat called a "princess-mouse. (3.213)
Furthermore:
a mouse shall be the stealer of grain, a camel his vehicle, a monkey his fruit,
a water-fowl his water, a crow his milk, and a house-builder (the white-ant) his household utensils.

A honey-thief becomes a gadfly; a thief of meat, a vulture; a cow-thief, an iguana; likewise, a fire-thief, a crane; a thief of cloth, one with white leprosy; a thief of liquids, a dog; and a thief of salt, a cricket.

Having stolen grain, one becomes a rat; having stolen a vehicle, a camel; having stolen fruit, a monkey; having stolen water, a water-fowl known as a *śakaṭavila*; having stolen milk, a crow (*dhvāṅkṣa*); having stolen household utensils such as a pestle, a house-builder, a specific kind of insect known as a *caṭaka*; having stolen honey, an insect known as a *dāṃśa*; having stolen meat (*pala*), a bird known as a vulture; having stolen a cow, a specific creature known as a *godhā*; having stolen fire, a bird known as a crane (*baka*); having stolen cloth, one becomes a leper; having stolen the juice of sugarcane and the like, a dog; and a stealer of salt becomes a high-pitched-sounding insect known as a *cīrī*. (3.214–3.215)

Having spoken thus for the sake of illustration, since it is impossible to speak of every single substance by means of exhaustive questioning, he says the following to demonstrate the ripening of karma through a single limiting condition (*upādhi*):
"This which I have stated regarding the act of theft is merely for the sake of illustration; for just as there are various kinds of objects, so too are the classes of living beings."
The species of living beings that become perpetrators of the act of theft correspond exactly to the types of objects being stolen;
for example, a swan is the thief of bell-metal.
Alternatively, one who steals an object that serves as a means to achieve a particular result becomes deprived of that very means, such as a horse-thief becoming lame.
In some instances, a specific distinction has been shown by Śaṅkha.

A killer of a Brahmin becomes a leper; a stealer of gold becomes afflicted with circular skin spots (*maṇḍalī*); one who reviles gods or Brahmins becomes bald (*khalati*); a poisoner and an arsonist become insane (*unmatta*); an assailant of his teacher suffers from epilepsy (*apasmārī*); a cow-killer becomes blind; one who abandons his lawful wife and engages with another becomes a *śabdavedhin*, a species of animal; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* (the son of an adulteress) becomes a consumer of female organs (*bhagabhakṣa*); a stealer of the property of gods or Brahmins suffers from jaundice (*pāṇḍurogin*); a stealer of a deposit becomes one-eyed (*kāṇa*); one who lives by selling women becomes a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*); one who abandons his wife while she is still a virgin becomes unfortunate (*durbhaga*); one who eats only sweets suffers from wind-tumors (*vātagulmin*); a consumer of forbidden food suffers from goiter (*gaṇḍamālin*); one who has sexual intercourse with a Brahmin woman becomes seedless (*nirbījin*); one of cruel deeds becomes a dwarf (*vāmana*); a stealer of clothes becomes a moth (*pataṅga*); a stealer of a bed becomes a mendicant (*kṣapaṇaka*); a stealer of conch-shells or mother-of-pearl becomes a skull-bearer (*kapālin*); a stealer of lamps becomes an owl (*kauśika*); a betrayer of friends suffers from consumption (*kṣayin*); and one who reviles his mother or father becomes lame (*khañjaka*).
Thus it is said.

A killer of a Brahmin becomes a leper; a stealer of gold becomes afflicted with circular skin spots; one who reviles gods or Brahmins becomes bald; a giver of poison or an arsonist becomes insane; one who strikes back at his teacher suffers from epilepsy; a cow-killer becomes blind; one who abandons his lawful wife and takes to another becomes a creature that pierces with sound; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* (the son of an adulteress) becomes a consumer of excrement; a stealer of the property of gods or Brahmins suffers from jaundice; a stealer of a deposit becomes one-eyed; one who lives off the sale of women becomes a eunuch; one who abandons his wife after marriage becomes ill-fated; one who eats sweets alone suffers from wind-tumors (*vātagulma*); a consumer of forbidden food suffers from goiter; one who has sexual intercourse with a Brahmin woman becomes seedless; a doer of cruel deeds becomes a dwarf; a stealer of clothing becomes a moth; a stealer of a bed becomes a mendicant beggar; a stealer of conch-shells or mother-of-pearl becomes a skull-bearer (*kapālin*); a stealer of lamps becomes an owl; a betrayer of friends suffers from consumption; and one who reviles his mother or father becomes lame.
Gautama also stated a distinction in certain instances.

One who speaks untruth becomes a water-snake; one whose speech is constantly faltering becomes a frog; one who abandons his wife becomes one with dropsy; a false witness becomes one with elephantiasis and severed shanks and feet; one who obstructs a marriage becomes one with a cleft lip; one who threatens another becomes one with severed hands; a matricide becomes blind; one who violates his daughter-in-law becomes one with testicles like those of a dog; one who voids excrement or urine at a crossroads suffers from dysuria; a defiler of virgins becomes a eunuch; an envious person becomes a mosquito; one who quarrels with his father becomes epileptic; one who misappropriates a deposit becomes childless; a stealer of jewels becomes extremely impoverished; one who sells knowledge becomes a "deer-man" (a beast-like human); a seller of the Vedas becomes a leopard; one who officiates for many patrons becomes a water-buffalo; one who officiates for those unfit to sacrifice becomes a boar; one who eats without being invited becomes a crow; one who eats only delicacies becomes a monkey; one who eats haphazardly here and there becomes a cat; one who burns a thicket becomes a firefly; a teacher of children becomes foul-mouthed; one who eats stale food becomes a worm; a thief becomes an ox; a jealous person becomes a bee; one who extinguishes a fire becomes afflicted with ringworm; a teacher of Śūdras becomes a dog-cooker; a stealer of cows becomes a serpent; a stealer of oil becomes consumptive; a stealer of food suffers from indigestion; a stealer of knowledge becomes mute; one who has sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī or a Pulkasī becomes a python; one who approaches a female ascetic becomes a desert-demon; one who approaches a Śūdra woman becomes a long-worm; one who approaches a woman of his own caste becomes poor; a carrier of water becomes a fish; a carrier of milk becomes a crane; a usurer becomes crippled in limb; a seller of forbidden goods becomes a vulture; one who approaches the queen of a king becomes a eunuch; one who reviles a king becomes a donkey; one who approaches a cow becomes a frog; one who studies on forbidden days becomes a jackal; a stealer of others' property becomes a servant to others; and one who kills a fish dwells in a womb. These are the ones who do not ascend upwards.
Thus [it is said].

A speaker of falsehood becomes a water-snake; one who repeatedly interrupts speech becomes a frog; a deserter of his wife becomes one with dropsy; a false witness becomes one with elephantiasis and severed shanks and feet; one who obstructs a marriage becomes one with a cleft lip; one who threatens with a raised hand becomes one with severed hands; a matricide becomes blind; one who violates his daughter-in-law becomes one with testicles like those of a dog; one who voids excrement or urine at a crossroads becomes afflicted with dysuria; a defiler of virgins becomes a eunuch; an envious person becomes a mosquito; one who quarrels with his father becomes epileptic; a stealer of deposits becomes childless; a stealer of gems becomes extremely impoverished; a seller of knowledge becomes a beast-like man; a seller of the Vedas becomes a leopard; an officiant for many patrons becomes a water-bird; an officiant for those unfit to sacrifice becomes a boar; one who eats without being invited becomes a crow; one who eats only delicacies becomes a monkey; one who eats indiscriminately here and there becomes a cat; one who burns a thicket becomes a firefly; a teacher of children becomes foul-mouthed; one who eats stale food becomes a worm; a taker of what is not given becomes an ox; an envious person becomes a bee; one who extinguishes a fire becomes afflicted with ringworm leprosy; a teacher of Śūdras becomes a dog-cooker; a stealer of cattle becomes a serpent; a stealer of oil becomes consumptive; a stealer of food becomes indigestible; a stealer of knowledge becomes mute; one who has sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī or a Pulkasī becomes a python; one who has intercourse with a female ascetic becomes a desert-demon; one who has intercourse with a Śūdra woman becomes a long-worm; one who approaches a woman of his own caste becomes poor; a carrier of water becomes a fish; a carrier of milk becomes a heron; a usurer becomes deficient in limbs; a seller of forbidden goods becomes a vulture; one who approaches the queen of a king becomes a eunuch; one who reviles a king becomes a donkey; one who approaches a cow becomes a frog; one who studies on forbidden days becomes a jackal; a stealer of another’s property becomes a servant of others; and one who kills a fish dwells in a womb—these are those who do not ascend upwards.
Women also, under these same circumstances, experience womanhood within those very same castes mentioned previously.
As Manu says:
"Women also, by taking [these things] according to this same rule, shall incur the same guilt."
They become the wives of these very same creatures.
Thus it is said: "Women also, by stealing according to this same rule, incur guilt;
they become wives of those very creatures."

Furthermore, this description of the characteristics such as perishability is intended to produce a sense of urgency in those who have become inclined toward penance—such as the slayer of a Brahmin—and not for the purpose of establishing twelve-year vows or the like for those already characterized by perishability, nor for the purpose of avoiding social contact.
For penance is for the sake of destroying sin;
and there is no purpose whatsoever in the destruction of the unseen force (*apūrva*) of a sin whose fruit has already begun through penance.

For an arrow released from a bow does not require any further existence of the archer or his action once it has struck the target. Nor is it necessary to seek the destruction of an *apūrva* (unseen potency) for the sake of destroying the fruit initiated by that [action];
for the destruction of an effect such as a water-jar initiated by its causes is not brought about by the destruction of the instrumental causes, such as the wheel or the potter's cloth.
Furthermore, innate defects such as deformed nails cannot be removed.
Moreover, for one who has experienced the succession of sufferings produced in the hells, the animal realm, and so forth, deformities such as deformed nails are the final fruit.
And by the mere arising of that [fruit], the destruction of its own cause—the *apūrva*—is produced, just as the destruction of the fire-drill wood is produced by the fire generated through friction.

Therefore, the observance of vows is neither for the purpose of destroying sin nor for the purpose of social intercourse. For the learned do not avoid association with those who have bad nails and so forth.
Since social acceptability is already established through the destruction of sin by the exhaustion of past karma, there is no need for the practice of vows.

As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"One with deformed nails or black teeth shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights"—that should be understood as merely occasional (naimittika), like the Kṣāmavatī offerings, and not for the purpose of destroying sin or for the sake of establishing fitness for social intercourse. 3.216.
Moreover:
Having obtained the fruit according to their karma, through the passage of time they are born as animals;
then, fallen from auspicious marks, they become impoverished and the lowest of men.

Having obtained, in accordance with their own committed good and evil deeds and without escaping them, corresponding fruits such as rebirth in hell or the state of an animal, they are eventually born among men as those with deformed characteristics, impoverished, and lowly, once their karma has been exhausted over the course of time. (3.217)
Moreover: Then, having become free from blemish, they are born into a great family as enjoyers of wealth,
endowed with knowledge, and possessed of riches and grain.

Then, immediately after that birth as a human being with inauspicious marks, having become free from stain and having exhausted their sins through the experience of hell and other realms, they are born into great families endowed with enjoyments, wealth, and grain, by virtue of the remainder of their merits from previous lives. (3.218)
Having thus described the ripening of karma for the purpose of encouraging people toward penances, he now speaks in order to define those who are eligible for them:
"By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the performance of what is censured,
and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes downfall."
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world become propitiated.

The term "vihitam" (enjoined) refers to both that which is mandatory—such as the daily twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and the fire sacrifice (*agnihotra*)—and that which is prescribed as occasional (*naimittika*), such as bathing following contact with impurities; by the non-performance of these, and by the performance of what is censured or forbidden, such as drinking liquor, and through the lack of restraint of the senses, a person undergoes a fall—that is to say, he becomes one who incurs sin (*pratyavāyin*).

[Objection: But surely, since it has been stated that "one should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire," and because attachment to the senses is already prohibited, its purpose is already covered by the mention of "blameworthy acts" (*nindita*). Why, then, is there a separate inclusion of the phrase "and from the non-restraint of the senses"? [Response: It is said in reply: The prohibition of attachment to the senses does not have the nature of an absolute negation (*pratiṣedha*), because it is recited among the *snātaka* vows. Furthermore, since the context there is governed by the word "vow" (*vrata*) in the injunction "one should maintain these vows," and because of the presence of the negative particle (*nañ*), what is enjoined is a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that serves to prohibit attachment to the senses.
And since that [non-performance] is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*), it is mentioned separately.
Now, how is it determined that one incurs sin from the non-performance of what is enjoined?
First of all, the injunction regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites—which consists in the impelling of a person toward action—does not imply that non-performance is a cause of sin.

For that [injunction] culminates merely in the understanding that the performance of the object [of the act] serves the human purpose (puruṣārtha), since activity is possible through that much alone; it does not, however, state that non-performance is a cause of sin (pratyavāya), because such a claim would lack validity as its capacity [to convey it] has been exhausted.

Furthermore, if another result were postulated for the sake of establishing activity by way of removing an inconsistency, then even though the human purposefulness of avoiding [the prohibited act] is established simply as the avoidance of the sin produced by the prohibited action, one would have to postulate yet another result [for that avoidance].
And this is not accepted by anyone.

[Objection: But why should it not be the case that, just as in the case of prohibited acts, their status as human goals (puruṣārthatva) consists precisely in the avoidance of the demerit (pratyavāya) understood from the explanatory passages (arthavāda), so too in the case of enjoined acts, their purpose might consist in the avoidance of the demerit produced by non-performance, as understood from the explanatory passages?
[Reply: Not so. For such explanatory passages do not exist in all cases, such as the Agnihotra and other rites.

Nor is it tenable to claim that the Smṛti rule, "A man does not incur downfall by the non-performance of what is enjoined," serves as a supplementary explanatory passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) for this [Vedic injunction].
For an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) cannot function in one sentence regarding an action already established by another sentence.

Or, even if it were somehow an explanatory passage through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), it still would not be capable of producing a distinct effect in the form of a non-existence upon the failure to perform what was enjoined.

One might object: "Since the Ayurvedic statement 'In fever and in diarrhea, fasting is the supreme medicine' leads us to understand that fasting—consisting of the absence of food—produces the cessation of fever, let it be the same here as well.
Do not say so; for even here, the cessation of fever does not result from fasting itself.

Rather, it should be understood that it occurs when, in the absence of food—which is an obstacle to the destruction of fever—there arises a balance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-sāmya*) produced by the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*).
Therefore, one must explain how the following traditional teaching (smṛti)—"By the non-performance of what is enjoined, a man incurs downfall"—is to be understood. It is said in reply:
there is no fault, for it is intended to refer to the demerit (pratyavāya) consisting in the failure to establish one's qualification (adhikāra) for rites such as the Agnihotra.
Is it not so that a Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Ulkāmukha, who eats vomit;
and a Kṣatriya becomes a Kaṭapūtana, who eats impure matter and corpses?
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Maitrākṣajyotika who feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.
Thus it is said:
"The Brāhmaṇa who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta named Ulkāmukha, who eats vomit;
and the Kṣatriya becomes a Kaṭapūtana, who eats impure matter and corpses."
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta named Maitrākṣajyotika who feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.
How are these statements of Manu, which concern the sin (*pratyavāya*) arising from the non-performance of what is enjoined, to be reconciled?

It is said: Just as there is suffering for one who eats vomit or for one whose mouth is being burned by a firebrand, so too for this person who does not perform what is enjoined, because his human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is not accomplished; thus, the censure of non-performance is for the sake of encouraging its performance, and so there is no contradiction.

Or rather, [the state of being] a *vāntāśyulkāmukha* ghost and so forth is produced by passion, laziness, and the like, which oppose the performance of prescribed duties and are projected by the practice of prohibited acts in a previous life; thus, one should not maintain that non-existence (*abhāva*) is ever a cause.
Now, it is argued:

from this very injunction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) intended for the destruction of sin, it is inferred that a latent impression of demerit (*pāpāpūrva*) produced by the practice of prohibited acts committed in another birth has been projected; therefore, it is postulated that the curse and such [misfortunes] were removed by this person through the performance of the expiation necessitated by that [demerit].
Because it is logically impossible for sin, which is of the nature of an effect, to arise independently of human effort;

nor does sin arise in one person through the effort of a harlot or the like, since merit and demerit are necessarily inherent in the agent. Therefore, the enumeration of three conditions as the occasion for penance (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed correct.
And so says Manu:
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and remains addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to penance.
Thus:
"A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, performs censured acts,
and is addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to expiation."

The mention of "men" (*narāḥ*) is intended to include even those born of inverse unions (*pratilomaja*), so that they may obtain the right to perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*); for it is possible even for them to transgress common duties such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).

Since one incurs sin through such acts as the performance of forbidden deeds, therefore, that person who has committed forbidden service and the like must perform expiation for the sake of purification in this world and the next.
Furthermore, this word *prāyaścitta* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) to denote a specific ritual act performed on a particular occasion (*nimittika*) for the purpose of destroying sin.
Thus, when the penance has been performed, his inner self becomes serene through purification, and the world also becomes inclined to engage with him in social intercourse.
By saying this, the following is shown:

this entitlement to perform penance is occasional (*naimittika*); and therein, even the destruction of evil (*durita*) mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is accepted as the objective to be accomplished (*sādhya*), according to the logic of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice.

Nor should one entertain the suspicion that this [penance] falls under the category of optional rites (kāma-adhikāra) merely because it is performed by one who desires to avoid evil; for it is said: "Therefore, penance must always be practiced for the sake of purification, since those whose sins are not expiated are born with censurable marks."
Thus,
for the sake of purification, one must always perform penance;
for those whose sins have not been expiated are born endowed with censurable physical marks.
Thus, because the hearing of the fault in non-performance leads to the understanding of its necessity. 3.219 || 3.220 ||
He states the fault in failing to perform expiation:
"Men who do not perform expiation, being devoted to sins and devoid of remorse,
go to terrible and agonizing hells."

Men who are addicted to sins produced by the transgression of the meaning of the scriptures, who feel no remorse—thinking "a wicked deed has been committed by me"—and who, being devoid of such agitation, do not perform expiation, attain unbearable hells. (3.221)
Explaining the nature of the hells, he says: Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka.
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃprapātana,
the great hell Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and Mahāpatha.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, likewise Asipatravana, and Tāpana— the twenty-first.
Accompanied by the terrible consequences born of major sins as well as minor sins,
these lowest of men go [to hell] without having performed expiation.

Those lowest of men who have not performed expiatory rites, being possessed by the terrifying misfortunes produced by great and minor sins, fall into the twenty-one hells beginning with Tāmisra and ending with Tapana, whose internal subdivisions are indicated by their descriptive names. (3.222–225)

It has been stated that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is for the purpose of destroying committed sins. Regarding this, he states a specific rule: "Sin that may have been committed through ignorance is removed by expiations."
However, one becomes subject to legal proceedings here on account of one's speech arising from desire.

The sin—that is, the evil committed through ignorance—is removed, meaning it departs, by means of the expiations whose characteristics will be described hereafter; however, this does not apply to what is done intentionally.
Rather, by the force of the scriptural injunctions prescribing expiation, one becomes fit for social intercourse in this world.

Furthermore, since the opening statement here is "the sin committed through ignorance is removed by expiations," when its opposite must be stated, one could have said "intentionally" (*jñānataḥ*); yet, the use of the word "intentionally" (*kāmataḥ*) is intended to demonstrate the equivalence between knowledge and desire.
For it is thus stated: "That which is prescribed for those acting unintentionally shall be doubled when done intentionally.

Likewise, in the case of an act committed without prior awareness, the penance is half; and similarly: "A Śūdra who has been approached by a Mleccha through ignorance should perform three *kṛcchra* penances, but if it was intentional, it shall be double."

From such statements as these, since an identical expiation is observed for both knowledge (*jñāna*) and desire (*kāmanā*), their fruits must indeed be equal. Furthermore, independent activity is invariably determined by both the knowledge of the object and the desire for it; since that activity is impossible if either one of these two is absent, the term "intentionally" (*kāmataḥ*) is used.
Even if one were to say "whether knowingly or unknowingly," intention would still follow by virtue of its inseparable connection.
Nor should it be argued that there is no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) because one who is being forced by thieves and the like lacks desire even though they possess knowledge of the object;
for in such a case, although knowledge exists, it is equivalent to non-existence since it lacks the capacity to cause activity.

Furthermore, as for the falling into mud through delusion by one who wishes to fall [into water] upon dry ground, even there, due to the absence of actual knowledge, there is likewise an absence of desire regarding that object.
In this way, there is likewise no deviation regarding ignorance and lack of intention as well.
Now, it might be argued that the statement "sin departs through expiations" is not tenable, because karma is to be destroyed only by its fruit.
This is not so; for just as the arising of sin is known through scripture, so too is its destruction, and thus no other means of knowledge applies here.
For this very reason, Gautama has demonstrated this matter through the method of presenting prima facie and conclusive arguments:
"In this regard, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or not.
They say: 'One should not perform it.'"
"For indeed, karma is not exhausted.
Others say, "One should perform [the rite] again," for it is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the *punaḥstoma*, they return to the *punaḥsavana*."
"Having sacrificed with the Vrātyastoma, one overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of an embryo who performs the Aśvamedha.
[The phrase] "they return to the *savana*s" means that one becomes fit for the duties of the twice-born, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, which are accomplished through the *savana* rites.
Nor is this merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*).

Since there is a requirement for a specific qualification of the person entitled to perform the act, it is logical—according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice—that the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) itself should be postulated; therefore, it is correct to say, "By means of penances, sin departs. Now, one might object: since there is no penance for an intentional act, how can there be eligibility for social intercourse? And as for the absence of such penance, it is because of the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "Penance is prescribed for an offense committed unintentionally. Furthermore: "This purification has been declared for having killed a twice-born man unintentionally; for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is ordained."
This is understood from the statement of Manu:
"If a man should ever commit a great sin intentionally... [this is not so].
No atonement for that is seen except by falling from a precipice or into fire.

Thus it is said; likewise, "that which is prescribed for those acting unintentionally shall be doubled for one acting intentionally. Furthermore, since penances are seen to be prescribed even for intentional acts, as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha, that too [applies] to an offense committed unintentionally, where penance brings about purification.
This is the intended meaning; it does not mean, however, that there is an absence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for intentional acts.

As for the statement of Manu beginning with "This purification has been declared," that too refers specifically to the performance of the twelve-year vow and so forth, as indicated by the pronoun "this" (*iyam*).

By the rule "No atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brahmin," there is a prohibition [of specific rites], but not of expiation in general, since expiations such as those ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) have already been shown.

Now, if there is indeed an expiation even for an act committed intentionally, why should there not also be a destruction of the sin, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]? And if there is no destruction of the sin, how can one become fit for social intercourse? It is said in reply: although the expiation is the same in both cases, a difference in the result is understood from the scriptures.
However, in all cases where an act is committed unintentionally, there is the destruction of sin.

But regarding those acts for which Gautama has prescribed loss of caste (*patana*), such as killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, violating the teacher’s bed, and so forth—including those related to one's mother, father, or kin, as well as theft, atheism, habitual performance of censured acts, and abandoning those who have fallen or those who abandon the fallen, as well as those who associate with such outcasts—in the case of performing such a *patanīya* (causing-fall) act intentionally, there is merely the restoration of social eligibility (*vyavahāryatva*), but not the destruction of sin.
Nor is it illogical that social eligibility should follow even in the absence of the destruction of sin.
For sin possesses two powers: that which produces rebirth in hell and that which obstructs social intercourse.

In this regard, even if the former power is not destroyed, the destruction of the power that obstructs social intercourse is not logically impossible; therefore, it is not unreasonable that one remains fit for social intercourse even though the sin has not [entirely] vanished.
As for the statement of Manu: "The wise know that when a sin is committed unintentionally, there is expiation."
Some say that even when an act is performed intentionally, [the same applies], based on the evidence of the Śruti.

Thus, that [statement] also is intended for the purpose of establishing the necessity of penance when an act is committed intentionally, and not for the purpose of demonstrating the destruction of sin [without it]. However, even in the case of a non-fatal sin (*apatanīya*) committed intentionally, the destruction of sin certainly occurs through penance; for "sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas, but that committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of penances."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Manu:

even in the case of an act leading to loss of caste (patanīya) committed intentionally, the destruction of the taint (kalmaṣa) certainly occurs through penances ending in death, because there is no other result [of such penance].
For the Smṛti of Āpastamba states: "In this world, his restoration to status does not exist; however, the taint is destroyed. (3.226)
It has been stated that the performance of prohibited acts and so forth constitutes the occasion for penance; in order to elaborate upon that, he says:

"The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), as is one who associates with them."
The term *hanti* is conventionally established in the sense of an action that causes the separation of life.
That action—whether immediately following the act or at a later time—is such that the separation of life occurs independently of any other cause;
one who has performed such an act is a *brahmahā*, meaning "one who has killed a Brāhmaṇa."
A drinker of intoxicants is one who drinks prohibited liquor.

A thief is a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba that "the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold is a mortal sin" (mahāpātaka). One who violates the Guru’s bed is one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of a Guru.
By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated through association (*sāhacarya*).
These are the perpetrators of great sins (*mahāpātakin*), such as the slayer of a Brahmin and others.
They are called *pātakas* because they cause one to fall; thus, the killing of a Brahmin and so forth are the *pātakas*.
By the word "great" (mahat), their gravity is made known, such that those associated with them are called "great sinners" (mahāpātakin).
This designation is made for the sake of brevity.

Furthermore, by the principle to be stated later—namely, "He who associates with each of these, beginning with the slayer of a Brahmin, for a year, he too is equal to them" (YDh 3.266)—he too is a great sinner.
The word *tathā* expresses a manner or type, intended to include various types of agents such as the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*) and the instigator (*prayojaka*).
A benefactor is defined as one who assists by obstructing an enemy who is fleeing, protecting him from an assailant, and thereby instilling confidence in the killer.
For this very reason, Manu has shown that the benefactor is connected to the fruit of the act of violence.
Regarding the term "those who commit great sins" (*mahāpātakinaḥ*):
this is a technical designation created for the sake of brevity.
And he who dwells together with each of those—such as the slayer of a Brahmin and others—whether they be many engaged in a single undertaking or all bearing weapons.
If one person should cause a killing there, all of them are considered killers.
Thus it is said: "When many people, all bearing weapons, have a single common purpose,
if one among them should strike, they are all traditionally considered killers."

Likewise, Āpastamba has stated the connection of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and others with the fruit [of the action]: "The instigator, the consenter, and the doer—among actions whose fruits are heaven or hell, the distinction in the fruit belongs to whichever of these initiates the greater effort. In this context, the instigator is one who prompts someone not yet engaged in an act. He is of three types: the commander, the requester, and the instructor.
Among these, the "commander" is one who, being himself of higher status, impels a subordinate such as a servant, saying, "Kill my enemy"; he is so called.
One who, being himself incapable, instigates another with great force through entreaties and the like, saying, "Kill my enemy," is designated as the *abhyarthayamāna*.
In both these cases, the agency consists solely in acting for the sake of achieving one's own purpose.
The *upadeṣṭṛ*, on the other hand, is described as one who incites another by first providing instruction—such as exposing their vulnerabilities—saying, "You should kill the enemy in this manner."
And in that case, their distinction lies in the fact that the fruit belongs only to the one who is prompted.
The "consenter" (anumantṛ), however, is one who incites someone who has already begun to act;
he is of two kinds: one who consents for the sake of achieving his own purpose, and another who does so for the sake of another's purpose.
Now, how can inference be a cause of killing? It cannot be by producing the separation of the vital breaths (*prāṇaviyoga*), because that [separation] is produced by the direct action of the agent.

Nor can it be like the instigator (*prayojaka*), because [inference] functions as an inciter only through the production of activity in the direct agent. And one should not suspect that it merely approves of an action already set in motion by saying, "Well done, you have resolved [to do this]."
For such consent is neither a cause for violence nor is it purposeful.
It is said in reply:

where, due to dependence on a king or others, one who has personally initiated the action with the mind nevertheless relies upon the king’s or another’s permission—either out of fear of interrupting the undertaking or fear of future punishment—there the consent, by strengthening the perpetrator's activity, becomes a cause for the result of violence.
Likewise, even one who provokes others to anger through reviling, beating, or the seizure of wealth, certainly becomes a cause of violence by way of generating the resentment that leads to death.
