For this very reason, Viṣṇu has stated:
"Whether reviled, beaten, or deprived of his wealth..."
He for whose sake one would give up one's life, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
Thus:
"Whether he has been reviled, beaten, or even deprived of his wealth,
he with reference to whom one gives up one's life— him they call a slayer of a Brahmin."
Likewise, he for whose sake one would give up one's life— whether for the sake of kinsmen, friends, or wife, or even for the sake of a friend’s field— is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
Thus it is said:
"He for whose sake one would sacrifice one's life— whether for the sake of kinsmen, friends, or wife, or even for the sake of a friend's field— is called a slayer of a Brahmin."

Nor should it be suspected that [abusive speech and the like] are not causes because anger is not seen to arise in everyone even when such acts have been committed; for this is due to the diversity of human nature.
Since those who become angry even at a very slight cause do exist, there is no lack of invariable concomitance, and thus they are indeed causes.

Furthermore, regarding these [accessories], such as the abettor (*anugrāhaka*) and the instigator (*prayojaka*), the gravity or lightness of the penance must be understood based on the gravity or lightness of the result, in consideration of proximity or remoteness and the relative weight of their respective functions, according to the statement: "In him who undertakes more [of the act], there is a specific distinction in the result."

For instance, in the case of the one who provides assistance (*anugrāhaka*), although he possesses independent agency (*svatantra-kartṛtva*) because he himself has engaged in the act of violence, his fruit is minor and his penance is light; this is because, lacking the connection with activities such as striking with a sword that directly results in the loss of life, he does not—as much as the direct perpetrator—initiate the violence to a great extent. As for the instigator (*prayojaka*), because he is mediated by being the generator of the activity of the independent agent, his fruit is even more minor than that. Among the various types of instigators, the fruit of the instructor (*upadeṣṭṛ*) is the most minor, because he acts for the sake of another.

Objection: Since the person being prompted (prayojya) stands in the position of one whose hand is held by the prompter (prayojaka), it is not logical for him to have a connection with the fruit [of the action].

If there were a connection even for one who acts under the prompting of another, then it would follow that architects, diggers of tanks, and others who work for wages would also attain fruits such as heaven. To this it is replied:

According to the principle that "the fruit declared by the scripture accrues to the performer," activities such as the construction of temples, wells, and tanks produce fruits for the person holding the entitlement (*adhikārin*).
Furthermore, architects, diggers of tanks, and the like are not entitled (*adhikārin*) to the act of constructing temples, wells, and tanks, because they do not desire heaven (*asvargakāmitva*).

In this case, however, even those who proceed to act only through the instigation of another possess entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding non-violence; therefore, the fault resulting from its transgression certainly occurs for them as well.

However, the one who consents (*anumantr*) has even less fruit than the instigator (*prayojaka*), because consent is external to the activity of the instigator and is [therefore] lighter. Furthermore, for the causal agent (*nimittakartṛ*)—such as the one who reviles—the connection to death is even more remote than that of the one who consents, because it is mediated by the production of anger which causes the [victim's] activity, and because [the reviler] acts without intending the death [of the victim].
[Objection: If even that which is remote can be a cause, then it would follow that even parents are killers by way of producing the person who becomes the killer.
It is said:
mere priority in time does not constitute causality, for it is possible for that which is a cause to likewise exist [subsequently].
Indeed, that which possesses an operation conducive to the production of an effect distinct from its own nature is a cause.

"If the Soma sacrifice should have the *rathantara* as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu"—thus, the possession of the *rathantara-sāman* is the cause for the precedence of the Indra-Vāyu cup in the ritual (*kratu*).

For in that case, the Soma sacrifice in its own form is not the cause, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Nor do parents possess such a characteristic of being a cause; thus, there is no over-extension of the principle.

By this very same principle and with this same underlying intention regarding the Dharma, there is no fault for the one who digs a well when a Brāhmaṇa or similar person falls into it through negligence and dies.
For the killing is not caused by the digging of the well in the way it is in cases such as verbal abuse—where one thinks, "This well was dug by him, therefore I shall kill myself.

Thus, even for the maker of the well, there is only the status of being a remote cause (*kāraṇakāraṇatva*), and not the status of being a direct cause of violence (*hiṃsāhetutva*); therefore, he is indeed equal to a mother or father.

Likewise, even when there is an association with the cause of violence, there is an absence of fault due to the scriptural injunction when one is engaged in an action for the sake of benefiting others.
As Saṃvarta says:
"In the case of tethering a cow for the purpose of medical treatment, or in the release of a fetus that is dead."
If misfortune occurs despite effort having been made, no expiation is required.
One who provides medicine, oil, or food to cows, Brahmins, and others,
is not tainted by sin even if misfortune should occur while it is being given.
For those who provide assistance through efforts such as cauterizing, cutting,
or lancing veins for the purpose of saving a life, no expiation is required.
Thus:
"If a mishap occurs despite efforts made for the purpose of treating a cow in captivity or for the extraction of a dead fetus, no expiation is required."
One who provides medicine, oil, or food to cows, Brahmins, and others,
is not tainted by sin even if misfortune should occur while it is being given.
For those who provide assistance through efforts such as cauterization, incision,
or bloodletting for the sake of achieving the preservation of life, no expiation is required.
This concerns the domain of a skilled physician regarding the cause of death.

However, in the case of another [physician], the fault has been shown in the rule that "a physician practicing falsely shall be made to pay. But where one kills oneself through madness or similar causes by uttering even the name [of another] without having engaged in verbal abuse or the like motivated by anger, there too there is no fault; for it is said: "If any twice-born man should abandon his life without cause..."
The fault would belong to that very person there, but not to the one whom he might proclaim.
Thus it is from the Smṛti.

Likewise, even in a case where one who has been provoked to anger by an abuser strikes himself with a sword or similar weapon, and before dying is appeased by the giver of the abuse through the payment of wealth or other means, and then proclaims aloud in the presence of people that "there is no fault here on the part of the abuser"—even there, because of the statement [of the law], there is no offense.
As Viṣṇu says:
"Having struck [himself] in anger while pointing [the abuser] out, if he is appeased, he may proclaim [his innocence] again."
If he dies after the proclamation has been made twice for both of them, there is no fault.
Thus,
having become angry at someone and having killed them, one should satisfy [the deity] and then cause [the victim] to hear the teaching again.
When that person has died, there is no fault, provided that the proclamation for both has been performed.
And we shall explain the specific penances for these [offenses] by considering the relative gravity or lightness of the fault according to the instigator and other factors. (3.227)
He states those equal to the killing of a Brahmin:
"Insulting one's teachers, reviling the Vedas, the murder of a friend,
and the destruction of what has been studied— these should be known as equal to the killing of a Brahmin."

Excessive reviling of gurus and false accusation against them—specifically, "false accusation against a guru"—are equal to the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), according to the traditional teaching of Gautama. Furthermore, this refers to the case of accusing someone of a fault unknown to the world, based on the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "Having learned of a fault, one should not be the first to proclaim it to others; rather, one should avoid such a person in social dealings."
Through the obsession with nihilism comes the reviling of the Vedas; for such a person who is no longer a Brahmin, even the killing of a friend or a well-wisher [is not a sin].
The destruction or forgetting of the studied Veda occurs through diversion by false treatises, or through laziness and the like.
Each of these is equal to the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).

As for the inclusion of "abandoning one's Vedic study, the sacred fire, or one's son" among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), that should be understood as referring to forgetting [the Veda] due to being preoccupied with supporting a family or distracted by listening to heterodox scriptures. (3.228)
He states those acts equal to drinking liquor:
eating forbidden food, crookedness, false speech for the sake of self-exaltation, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses— these indeed are equal to drinking liquor.
The intentional consumption of garlic and other such prohibited items is forbidden;
for this very reason, Manu says:
"Mushrooms, village pigs, garlic, and the village cock..."
Having intentionally eaten onions or garlic, a man shall fall [from his caste].
Thus:
"Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, onions, or leeks, a man shall fall [from his caste]."
But in the case of unintentional consumption, there is another expiation: "Having eaten these six things unintentionally, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* *kṛcchra*, or even the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*;
for the remaining [forbidden] items, one should fast for a day."
Thus, he declares these to be equal to the theft of gold:
"The seizure of a horse, a jewel, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow,
as well as that of a deposit— all these are indeed equated with the theft of gold."

The theft of horses and other such animals belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as the misappropriation of a deposit consisting of anything other than gold—all this should be understood as equal to the theft of gold. (3.230)
He states those acts equal to violating the Guru’s bed:
"Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, with virgins, with women of one's own uterine kin,
with women of the lowest castes, with women of the same lineage (sagotra), and with the wives of sons is recorded as equal to violating the Guru’s bed."

His friend is his companion, and his wife is a maiden of the highest caste; among them, if they are willing and of compatible status, there is no fault, but otherwise there is punishment. For defiling [a woman], however, the hand shall be cut off; likewise, for defiling a woman of the highest caste, there is death.
Thus, because a specific punishment is prescribed for that very case, it is appropriate that the penance be severe.

One's own kin (*svayoni*) means a sister; an *antyajā* means a Cāṇḍālī; one of the same lineage (*sagotrā*) means one of the same *gotra*; and the wife of a son (*sutastri*) means a daughter-in-law. Sexual intercourse with each of these is equal to violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*).
And this should be understood to apply after the emission of semen.

But in the case of returning before [the act is completed], it is not equal to violating the Guru's bed; rather, the penance is indeed slight: "They know that the emission of semen in women who are one's own sisters, in virgins, in women of the lowest castes, and in the wives of a friend or a son, is equal to violating the Guru's bed."
This is because of the inclusion of the specific qualification "emission of semen" in the verse from the *Mānava*.

Although the status of a woman as a *sagotrā* (of the same lineage) would already be established by the mention of "one's own [daughter]," the further mention of "the wife of a son" (*sutastrī*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the gravity of the penance.

Furthermore, the statement here regarding equality with the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth is intended to prescribe the specific penances required for those respective causes, such as the reviling of a guru.
An objection may be raised: "Since the fault in cases such as the reviling of the Vedas is slight, it would not be appropriate to prescribe a heavier penance like that for killing a Brahmin.
This is not so; for the gravity of the fault is understood precisely through the force of the instruction regarding the heavy penance.
Nor should one suspect that this statement is intended merely to extend the penance for killing a Brahmin by analogy, rather than being solely aimed at demonstrating the gravity of the fault itself.

For if they were intended merely to convey that much [i.e., equality], then the designation of "equality" through distinctions such as "this is equal to the killing of a Brahmin" or "equal to violating the Guru's bed" would be untenable.
Furthermore, that expiation, being taught by means of the word "equal," is taught as being slightly less than the expiations for the killing of a Brahmin and so forth;

this is because in worldly expressions such as "the minister is equal to the king," we observe the use of the word "equal" to denote something slightly inferior, and because it is illogical for a great sin and another [lesser] sin to be identical.

This being the case, although Yājñavalkya stated that forsaking the Veda (*brahmojjhatva*), reviling the Vedas (*vedanindā*), and killing a friend (*suhṛdvadha*) are equal to the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), Manu nevertheless equated them with the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*): "Forsaking the Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food or the food of those unworthy of offerings—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor. (MDh 11.56)
This has been stated for the purpose of providing an alternative penance.
In this same manner, contradictions in other statements must also be resolved.

As for the light penance mentioned by Vasiṣṭha—namely, that "in the case of falsely persisting against a guru, one becomes purified through the guru's grace after performing a twelve-night *kṛcchra* and bathing with one's clothes on"—that should be understood to apply when the act is committed once unintentionally. (3.231)
He states the instruction regarding those who have violated the Guru’s bed:
"The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, and even a daughter-in-law;
likewise, the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and the teacher’s daughter."
But one who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed;
having had his penis cut off, he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing.

The paternal aunts and others are well known; approaching them constitutes violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpaga*). Having cut off his male organ, he must be executed by the king as a punishment, and that same act serves as his penance (*prāyaścitta*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), queens, female ascetics (*pravrajitā*), and others are included.
As Nārada says:
A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife,
a paternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle, a female friend, a female disciple, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
One who approaches any one of these is said to be a violator of the Guru’s bed;
for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained.
Thus: mother, maternal aunt, mother-in-law, maternal uncle’s wife, paternal aunt,
the wife of a paternal uncle or a friend, a female disciple, sister, her female friend, and daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
One who approaches any one of these women is said to have violated the teacher’s bed;
for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained.
*Rājñī* is the wife of the ruler of a kingdom, not necessarily of a *kṣatriya* alone, because a different expiation is prescribed for approaching her.
*Dhātrī* is a nurse other than one's own mother, who nourishes one by giving breast milk and so forth.
*Sādhvī* is a woman observing a vow.
A Brāhmaṇī is the highest of castes; here, the mention of the "mother" is for the sake of illustration.

Furthermore, this punishment consisting of the cutting off of the male organ and execution applies to anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa, because his execution is prohibited by the rule: "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime. This is because execution itself constitutes the form of his expiation.
We shall explain its subject matter in detail in the section on penances for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*).
Here, the daughter-in-law and the sister, who were equated with the Guru’s bed in the preceding verse, are mentioned again for the purpose of providing alternative penances.
Furthermore, when these women, being desirous, bring these very men under their control and enjoy them, then for them too, the punishment is death just as for the men, and the penance is likewise.

These acts, beginning with the reviling of one's guru and ending with the study of the Tantras, constitute the scope for the extension of the rules regarding mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*); they are called *pātaka*s because they cause immediate downfall (*sadyaḥ-patana*).
As Yama has said:
"A mother’s sister, a mother’s female friend, a daughter, and a father’s sister..."
Having approached a maternal aunt, a sister, or a mother-in-law, a man shall fall from his caste immediately.
Thus: "Having approached a mother’s sister, a mother’s female friend, a daughter, a father’s sister,
a maternal aunt, a sister, or a mother-in-law, a man shall fall [from his caste] immediately."
Gautama, moreover, has stated that others also constitute offenses:

"Those related by birth to one's mother or father, a thief of [one's] limb, an atheist, one who habitually performs censurable acts, one who abandons those who have fallen from their status, and one who abandons those who have not fallen—these are outcasts (patita), as are those who associate with such outcasts.
Since these are listed between the major sins (mahāpātaka) and the minor sins (upapātaka), it is understood that they are less grave than the major sins and more serious than the minor sins.
Thus it has been said:
"Those sins which have been declared equal to the great transgressions (mahāpātaka) are designated as 'transgressions' (pātaka); that which is inferior to those is a minor transgression (upapātaka)."
Thus it is said:
"Those sins which have been described as equal to the great transgressions (mahāpātaka) are designated as 'pātaka'; that which is inferior to those is an 'upapātaka'."
And likewise Āṅgiras says: "For mortal sins (pātaka), there shall be a thousand years; for great sins (mahāpātaka), twice that;
for minor sins (upapātaka), a quarter; such is the number of years in hell."
Thus [ends verses] 3.232 and 3.233.
For minor sins, the stay in hell shall be for a thousand years; likewise, for major sins, it shall be double that;
and for secondary sins, it shall be a quarter of that, according to the number of years.

Having thus enumerated the great sins (mahāpātakas) and the sins equal to them, he speaks in order to enumerate the minor sins (upapātakas): "Killing a cow, being a Vratya, theft, non-payment of debts, not maintaining the sacred fires, selling forbidden goods, and complaining [of one's misfortunes]."
Receiving instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, causing a younger brother to marry before the elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt.
The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of censured wealth;
atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons.
Stealing grain, base metals, or livestock; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice;
abandoning one’s father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a grove.
Defiling a maiden, officiating at a sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother,
giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, crookedness, and the breaking of a vow.
Undertaking actions for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning one's Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's children, as well as abandoning one's kinsmen;
Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, living by the slaughter of women or by medicinal herbs, the construction of lethal machines, vices, and the sale of oneself— these are [prohibited].
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the base, consorting with those of low birth,
likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others.
Studying false scriptures, exercising authority over mines,
and the sale of one's wife— each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).

The killing of a cow is the destruction of a cow’s body; being uninitiated at the proper time constitutes *vrātyatā*; theft is the appropriation of another’s property other than a *brāhmaṇa*’s gold or its equivalent; the non-return of gold or similar items once received; the failure to repay debts; likewise, the failure to discharge debts owed to the gods, sages, and ancestors; and, while qualified for it, not maintaining the sacred fires (*anāhitāgnitva*).

Objection: Is it not well-established among the Mīmāṃsakas that the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites impel the performance of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) for the sake of producing the fires which constitute their own constituent parts? Consequently, for one who has a need for the fires, there is engagement in the consecration—which is the means to them—just as one who desires rice and the like engages in the acquisition of wealth; whereas for one who has no need for the fires, there is no such engagement. Thus, how can there be the fault of being one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)? It is replied:

Precisely because of this statement regarding the necessity of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), the intention of the authors of the *Smṛtis* is observed to be that even the obligatory scriptural injunctions (*nitya-śruti*) serve as motivators for the *ādhāna*, since there is no difference in their possessing the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*). Thus, there is no fault.

Likewise: the sale of forbidden goods such as salt; *parivedana*, which is the taking of a wife by a younger brother while his elder uterine brother remains unmarried; receiving instruction from a teacher who teaches for a fee; teaching for a fee; sexual intercourse with another man's wife—excluding the wives of one's guru or those equal to them; *pārivittya*, which is the elder brother’s failure to marry after the younger brother has already married; usury, which is living off prohibited interest; the manufacture of salt; the killing of a woman—even if she is not a Brāhmaṇī—provided she is not an *ātreyī*; the killing of a Śūdra; the killing of a Vaiśya or Kṣatriya who has not been initiated for a sacrifice; living off censured wealth, that is, wealth established by one other than a king; atheism (*nāstikya*), which is the dogmatic adherence to the view that there is no other world and so forth; the breach of a vow, such as a student’s (*brahmacārin*) sexual dalliance with a woman; the sale of children or descendants; and the theft of grain such as rice, base metals such as tin and lead, or cattle such as cows.

Since the offense of theft is already established by the mention of "theft" (*steya*) in the phrase "killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, or theft," the separate mention of the theft of grain, base metals, and so forth, is for the purpose of establishing that this is a mandatory penance.
Therefore, in the case of stealing substances other than grain and the like, this specific penance is not necessarily required; rather, a penance even less than this certainly applies.
By this, the separate mention of "abandoning one's father and others" is explained as being redundant, since it is already established by the mention of "abandoning kinsmen" (*bāndhavatyāga*).

Performing sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice—such as those defiled by birth or conduct, Śūdras, Vratyas, and the like; abandoning one's father, mother, or son who have not been outcasted, which means expelling them from the home; selling a tank, a grove, a garden, a park, or similar property;

defiling a maiden, which refers to piercing her vulva with a finger or the like (but not sexual intercourse), since the latter is stated to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed in the rule concerning "the wives of friends" and "maidens";
and officiating at the sacrifice of a younger brother who marries before his elder, as well as giving a daughter in marriage to such a man.
Deceit toward anyone other than one's teacher is prohibited; however, deceit directed toward one's teacher is said to be equal to the drinking of liquor.

Furthermore, the mention of "the violation of a vow" (*vratalopa*) is intended to include even those minor observances not explicitly forbidden by the learned—such as the resolve, "I shall not consume betel and the like before beholding the lotus feet of Śrī Hari"—and is not for the purpose of enjoining the specific *snātaka* vows.
In that regard, for the violation of a *snātaka* vow, the expiation is fasting.
This is because a light expiation has been prescribed by Manu for such an act;
likewise, the undertaking of the act characterized as cooking for one's own sake is prohibited by the very same authority: "He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin."
If, however, it were restricted solely to the act itself, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in postulating a prohibition.
"The enjoyment" refers to the frequenting of a woman who drinks liquor, even if she is one's own wife.
The abandonment of Vedic study has already been explained.

The abandonment of the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires; the abandonment of one's son, which means failing to perform his sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth; the abandonment of kinsmen such as paternal uncles and maternal uncles, meaning their failure to be protected when one has the means to do so; the cutting down of green trees for the sake of accomplishing visible purposes such as cooking, but not even for the sake of protecting the *āhavanīya* fire; and subsistence through women, violence, or medicine—this is "subsistence by women, violence, and medicine.
Among these, "subsistence by women" refers to either making one’s wife a commodity for profit and living off what is thereby obtained, or subsisting on a woman’s property.
"Living by violence" means making one's livelihood through the slaughter of living beings;
"living by medicine" means [making a living] through methods such as subjugation spells (*vaśīkaraṇa*);
and "operating a machine of violence" refers to the operation of a device that crushes sesame or sugarcane.
The eighteen vices include hunting and so forth.
Selling oneself means entering into servitude to another by accepting wealth.
Serving Shudras means forming friendships with those of lower status.
For one who has not married a wife of his own caste, it is the taking of a wife solely from a lower caste and sexual union with a common woman.

It is dwelling outside the stages of life (anāśramavāsa), that is, remaining without having entered an āśrama despite being qualified to do so. It is being nourished by the food of others, that is, taking delight in the cooking of others.
The study of false treatises, such as the works of the Cārvākas and others; holding office by royal command over all mines, which are the sources of gold and other minerals;
and the sale of one's wife.
By the word "and" (*ca*), the consumption of garlic and other such things mentioned by Manu and others—when performed with the intent to perform malevolent magic (*abhicāra*)—is included.
It should be understood that each of these acts, beginning with the killing of a cow, is designated as a minor offense (*upapātaka*).

Furthermore, Manu has enumerated other causes designated as causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), causing mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), causing unworthiness for receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), and causing impurity (*malinīkaraṇa*).

Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, performing sorcery, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats,
sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa).
Accepting wealth from those who are censurable, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa).
Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.
Thus [it is said].

Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, performing a magical rite (kṛtyā), smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, deceit, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants,
as well as goats and sheep, and likewise of fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa).
Accepting wealth from those who are censurable, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa).
Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.
Therefore, other miscellaneous causes [for penance] are now described.

Bṛhadviṣṇu has shown all the causes for penance in descending order of gravity, distinguished by their respective specific names: "Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing the gold of a Brahmin, and violating the teacher's bed—these are the mortal sins (mahāpātakas), as is association with such persons.
Sexual intercourse with one's mother, daughter, or daughter-in-law—these are the heinous sins (atipātakas)."

The killing of a Kṣatriya engaged in a sacrifice, as well as the killing of a Vaiśya, a woman in her menses, a pregnant woman, a woman of a different lineage, an embryo of unknown sex, or one who has sought refuge, are equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa.
Giving false testimony and the killing of a friend—these two are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The seizure of land from a Brāhmaṇa is equal to the theft of gold.

Sexual intercourse with a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, or the wife of a king is equal to violating the bed of one’s guru; so too is intercourse with a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, or the wives of a learned *śrotriya*, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a teacher (*upādhyāya*), or a friend.

Intercourse with one’s own sister, a female friend, a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), a woman of a higher caste, a woman in her menses, a woman seeking refuge, a female ascetic (*pravrajitā*), or a woman who has been entrusted to one’s care—these are minor offenses (*anupātaka*).

Also included are speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation, slander directed toward the king, persistent deception of one’s guru, reviling the Vedas, abandoning what has been studied, and deserting the sacred fires, one’s father, mother, son, or wife.

Eating food that should not be eaten, stealing the property of others, adultery with the wives of others, officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, being a *vrātya*, teaching for a fee, receiving instruction from a teacher who teaches for a fee, having authority over all mines, operating large-scale mechanical works, living by the destruction of trees, shrubs, creepers, and medicinal herbs, engaging in malevolent incantations (*abhicāra*) and root-magic (*mūlakarma*), undertaking actions solely for one's own sake, failing to maintain the sacred fires, failing to discharge one's debts to the gods, sages, and ancestors, studying heterodox scriptures, atheism, immoral conduct, and consorting with women who drink liquor—these are the minor offenses (*upapātaka*).

Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that are foul-smelling or intoxicants, crookedness toward cattle, and engaging in sexual intercourse with a male— these are acts that cause loss of caste (*jāti-bhraṃśakara*). Killing domestic or wild animals, performing rites for those who do not undergo sacramental ceremonies (*asaṃskārya*), accepting wealth from censurable persons, trade, living by usury, speaking untruths, and serving Śūdras— these are acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*).
The killing of birds, aquatic creatures, and water-born beings; the killing of worms and insects; and eating food accompanied by liquor—these are the acts that bring impurity.
Whatever has not been mentioned [elsewhere] is classified as miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka).
Thus it is said.
Kātyāyana, however, has shown that even those acts which Viṣṇu classified as minor offenses (upapātaka) are equal to mortal sins (mahāpātaka) and should be designated as "sins" (pātaka):
"Great sin, excessive sin, likewise sin itself,
incidental sin, and minor sin— such is the group of five."
Thus: "Great sin (mahāpāpa), extreme sin (atipāpa), as well as transgression (pātaka),
incidental sin (prāsaṅgika), and minor sin (upapāpa)— such is the group of five."
Now, one might object: how can minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and the like be considered *pātaka* (mortal sins), given that they lack the quality of being causes for falling [from caste]?

If they too are causes for falling, then the enumeration beginning with "those related by birth to mother or father" (*mātṛ-pitṛ-yoni-sambandha-aṅga*) would be purposeless. If this is what is being said:

Even though there is no cause for immediate loss of caste (*sadyaḥ-pātitya*) in these cases as there is in the case of the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and their equivalents, nevertheless, it is not contradictory that they can cause loss of caste depending on the degree of repetition.
[The opponent argues: "This is so because of the statement of Gautama: 'One who habitually performs censurable acts [falls from his caste] due to such habituation' (*abhyāsāt*). [The author replies:
"Not so, because the nature of 'habitual practice' (*abhyāsa*) is not precisely defined."

Regarding the phrase "twice or a hundred times," if no distinction were admitted therein, then one who sleeps during the day twice and another who commits the slaughter of a cow a hundred times would both incur loss of caste (*pātitya*) without distinction.
To this it is replied:

In a case where a specific transgression is heard of in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), or where a multiplicity of expiations is prescribed, then for that censurable act, the degree of repetition required to reach a level equal to a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) constitutes the cause of loss of caste. Thus, it is that specific amount of repetition which is the ground for *pātitya*.

However, in the case of sleeping during the day and similar acts, even if practiced a thousand times, they do not attain equality with a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*); thus, there is no loss of caste (*pātitya*) therein.
Therefore, it is logical that minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and the like become causes for falling [from caste] depending on their repetition. (3.234–242)
Having thus enumerated the occasions for penance along with their respective designations for the sake of conventional usage, he speaks in order to demonstrate the specific penances:
"Bearing a skull as his banner, subsisting on alms, proclaiming his deed,
and eating sparingly, the slayer of a Brahmin shall attain purification after twelve years."
One who possesses a skull from a head is called a *śiraḥkapālī*;
likewise, having made a banner consisting of a corpse's head, according to the Smṛti of Manu;
one should take another skull fixed to the top of a staff, which is denoted by the word "banner."

And that skull must be taken from the head of a Brāhmaṇa whom he himself has killed, because of the traditional teaching of Śātātapa: "A Brāhmaṇa, having caused another Brāhmaṇa to be slain, should take the very skull of that [victim] and wander to sacred fords. In the absence of such a skull, it may be taken from the head of any other Brāhmaṇa. Both of these must be held in the hand alone, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "With a skull-staff in his hand."

By the term *khaṭvāṅga*, a banner consisting of a skull fixed upon a staff is intended, and not merely a part of a bedstead, for that [specific object] is well-known in common usage such as "the great bull is the *khaṭvāṅga*" or "the axe is the *khaṭvāṅga*.

Furthermore, this carrying of the skull is for the sake of a mark, and not for the purpose of eating or for begging alms, because of the traditional rule of Gautama: "With an earthenware skull in hand, he should enter the village for alms.
Likewise, he must be a forest-dweller: "The slayer of a Brahmin, having constructed a hut, shall dwell in the forest for twelve years."
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu:
"Having shaved his head, he should dwell near a village, at the edge of a village, in a cow-pen, in a hermitage,
or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins."
Because it was stated by him thus:
"Or one who has shaved his head," since this expresses an option (*vikalpa*), it is understood that he may also have matted hair (*jaṭī*).
For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
"Brahmā, for twelve years, wearing the dress of a child, with matted hair and carrying a banner.
Thus it is said:
"Brahmā, for twelve years, wearing the dress of a child, with matted hair and carrying a banner."
Likewise, he should be one whose habit is eating alms-food (*bhikṣāśanaśīla*).
And the alms-food should be received in a red earthenware fragment-plate; for the *Smṛti* of Āpastamba states: "He should enter the village for alms with a red fragment-plate.

He should enter for the sake of alms seven houses that have not been pre-selected, thinking, "Food may or may not be obtained"; for the *Smṛti* of Vasiṣṭha states: "He should go about for alms at seven houses that have not been pre-selected."
Likewise, that [alms-gathering] should be performed at only one time, because it has been stated by that same [author]: "One whose food consists of a single meal.

Furthermore, this begging for alms must be done among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, according to the traditional teaching of Saṃvarta: "One who carries a skull-topped staff and has restrained his self should wander for alms among the four castes.

Likewise, proclaiming his own deed, saying "I am a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa," he should stand at the door and beg for alms, as it is said: "I stand at the door of the house seeking alms, a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Parāśara.

Furthermore, this rule regarding subsisting on alms is to be understood as applying when one is unable to live on forest-grown products, because of the traditional teaching of Saṃvarta: "One may enter the village for alms if one does not survive on forest-grown products."

Furthermore, he must be endowed with celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and other such qualities; carrying a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a begging bowl in his hand, he shall enter a village for alms for twelve years as a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), proclaiming his deed.

He may approach a noble person (*ārya*) upon seeing him. As it is recorded in the *Smṛti* of Gautama: "He shall pass his time standing or sitting; by bathing in water at the [three] libations, he shall be purified. (Note: The verse enclosed in parentheses is likely an interpolation into the *Gautama Dharma Sūtra* passage, yet it is provided by all three editions.)

The mention of the term *brahmacārī* (celibate student) is for the purpose of attaining those duties not contradicted [by other rules] that are declared in the section on the *brahmacārī*: "He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, exhilaration, dancing, singing, calumny, and fear.
For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
"Standing, seated in the *vīrāsana* posture, observing silence, wearing a girdle of muñja grass, and carrying a staff and water-pot..."
The practice of begging for alms, the fire-ritual, and the constant recitation of the Kūṣmāṇḍī mantras [are required].
Thus: "Abiding in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), observing silence, wearing a girdle of muñja grass, carrying a staff and a water-pot,
practicing the alms-round, performing the fire-ritual, and always reciting the Kūṣmāṇḍī mantras."
The word "for him" (*tasya*) is understood [to mean] "it shall be for him.

Here, because the rule that "one must perform ritual action with purity by touching water during the *savanas*" is common to all ritual acts, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) just like bathing, in order to achieve the purity that is an auxiliary part of the observance of vows (*vratacaryā*); for that too, by way of producing purity, is a subordinate element of all ritual acts. And so says Dakṣa:
One who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever deed he performs, he shall not partake of its fruit.
Thus it is said: "One who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever deed he performs, he shall not partake in its fruit."

Nor should it be suspected that because of the statement "falling [from caste] is the loss of the duties of the twice-born" (*dvijātikarmabhyo hāniḥ patanam*), the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*)—being itself a duty of the twice-born—is not applicable [to one who has fallen]. For since the observance of vows is taught specifically for one who has fallen, the performance of the twilight devotions and so forth is obtained precisely as an integral part of those vows.

Therefore, the "loss" refers only to those duties of the twice-born that are not constituent parts of the vow-observance, such as "study, sacrifice, and giving" for the twice-born in general, and "teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts" which are additional privileges for the Brāhmaṇa; it does not refer to all [duties], because the scriptural declaration of "loss" finds its fulfillment through the sublation of only that much.
And this practice of the twelve-year vow, as propounded by Manu, Yājñavalkya, Gautama, and others, is one and the same, not distinct; for they are mutually dependent and non-contradictory.
To illustrate: when [the text] enjoins that "one who subsists on alms, making his actions known," an expectancy naturally arises as to what the alms-bowl is, in whose houses, or how many.
In that regard, the fulfillment provided by Āpastamba’s statement, "with a reddish broken earthenware bowl," is entirely consistent.

Therefore, because all [these texts] teach a single course of action (*ekakalpopadeśa*), the claim made by some—that even though the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed by Manu, Gautama, and others are mutually dependent, there is nevertheless an option (*vikalpa*) between them—should be understood as having been stated without due consideration.

Having thus performed the practice of the vow for twelve years, the slayer of a Brahmin attains purification. And this refers to the case of intentionally killing a Brahmin; for it is said: "This purification has been declared for one who has killed a twice-born man unintentionally; no atonement is ordained for the intentional killing of a Brahmin."
Thus it is from the recollection of Manu.
Here, this must be considered:
in the case of the killing of two or three Brahmins, is there a single performance (*tantratva*) of the penance, or is there its repetition (*āvṛtti*)?

In this regard, some hold the view that since the word *brahman* in the rule "the slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*) [shall perform penance] for twelve years" is common to one, two, or many, the very same expiation prescribed for the killing of one Brahmin applies equally to a second or even a third.
Since the performance of a single expiation occasioned by the killing of one Brahmin has been carried out, it is impossible to say, "this was done, but that was not.

Because there is no perceived distinction among the place, time, and agent—which constitute the auxiliary factors of the ritual application—the accomplishment of the result, characterized by the destruction of sin, is logically achieved through a single, collective performance (*tantra*).

Just as, when performed according to a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), the *prayāja* and other rites produce multiple effects characterized by assistance within the *āgneya* and other sacrifices through that very same procedure;

nor should it be argued that—because the sin is greater in the case of killing two or three Brahmins—the performance of the expiation must necessarily be repeated, on the grounds of Gautama’s statement, "When the offense is heavy, the penances are heavy; when light, they are light," since it is impossible for distinct effects to be produced by a single procedure (*tantra*).
For this statement does not prescribe repetition; rather, its purpose is to establish the systematic application (*vyavasthā*) of the various heavy and light alternatives already taught.
Furthermore, there is no greater gravity of sin in the killing of a second Brāhmaṇa, as there is a lack of authoritative evidence.
As for that which was stated by Manu and Devala: "From this first injunction, in the case of a second [offense] it shall be double;
in the third it is declared to be triple; in the fourth, there is no atonement."

Thus, according to the maxim that "for every specific cause, the rule concerning that effect recurs," this [text] is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the recurrence of the rule for the occasion of killing two or three Brahmins; it is intended to enjoin the absence of [penance] in the fourth instance, but not to enjoin a doubling of the performance of penance for a second killing of a Brahmin, as that would entail the fault of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Therefore, even in the case of killing two or three Brahmins, it is proper to perform the twelve-year penance and so forth only once; just as, for instance, when the *kṣāmavatī* and other rites enjoined for occasions such as a house fire—such as "one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat"—are performed only once even when multiple occurrences of the house fire and other such causes happen simultaneously.
To this it is replied:
indeed, when there is a contradiction with a direct scriptural injunction (*vacana*), logical reasoning (*nyāya*) has no power.

And the statement beginning with "and from the first [performance] of the injunction" (vacanaṃ ca vidheḥ prāthamikād) refers to the rule regarding the repetition of the performance of penance in the case of killing two or three Brahmins.
This being so, by setting aside the single performance obtained through logic (*nyāya*), this statement would serve to produce a specific course of action in the injunction for repetition;
otherwise, it would be purposeless as a mere restatement of what is already established by scripture.

Nor does this result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because there is a single purpose: by means of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the fourth and subsequent Brahmin murders, it prescribes the performance of the penance elsewhere.

Furthermore, from the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "there is no atonement for the fourth," it is understood that as the number of Brahmins being killed increases, the gravity of the fault increases; this is likewise established by the words of Devala and others:
"Whatever sinful act may have been committed once unintentionally..."
The wise who know the Dharma have prescribed this atonement for it.
Thus:
"Whatever sinful deed may have been committed once unintentionally— for that,
this expiation has been prescribed by the wise who know the Dharma."
Furthermore, the destruction of two defects of dissimilar nature—one heavy and one light—is not accomplished by a single performance (*tantra*).

Therefore, in such cases, because the effects differ due to the relative gravity of the defects, it is logical that the remedial rite (*naimittika*) should be repeated for each respective cause (*nimitta*).

In the case of the *Kṣāmavatī* offerings and similar rites, however, since the effect is not different, the application of a single performance (*tantrabhāva*) is appropriate; enough of this elaboration.

As for the statement in the fourth [section] that "there is no atonement," that too refers to the category of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), because its purpose is to demonstrate the absence of expiation due to the extreme gravity of the offense.

Therefore, even when the consumption of food from a Śūdra and similar acts have been practiced many times, one must conceive of a repetition of the corresponding expiation rather than an absolute absence of expiation.
For this very reason, it was stated by Manu:
"But when a full cartload of boneless creatures has been killed, one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra.
Thus it is said.
"But when a full cartload of boneless creatures has been killed, one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra."
Furthermore, this twelve-year vow applies specifically to the actual slayer, as he alone is designated by the term "brahmahā" (slayer of a Brahmin).
However, for the instigator, the abettor, and others, a gradation of penance must be determined according to their respective degrees of fault.
In that regard, the abettor who assists a person liable to penance should perform that penance reduced by one-quarter.
Furthermore, the one who gave consent [shall observe] one and a half quarters, which is four and a half years; the one who provided the pretext [shall observe] one quarter, which is three years.
For this very reason, Sumantu says:
"When a Brahmin, having been insulted, kills himself and dies..."
One who is devoid of virtue [commits such acts] out of recklessness, anger, or for the sake of houses, fields, and the like.
One should observe a vow for three years, or one should go to the Pratiloma Sarasvatī for the sake of purification from that sin; this is certain.
Indeed, a Brahmin who is utterly devoid of virtue, having been rebuked without cause and dying out of anger over one who is likewise utterly devoid of virtue; [is reborn as a worm].
A person should perform the Kṛcchra penance for three years for the sake of purification.
Thus: when a Brahmin, being insulted, kills himself and dies—
whether devoid of merit, out of rashness, anger, or on account of a house, field, or the like.
One should observe a three-year vow or go to the Pratiloma Sarasvatī for the sake of purification from that sin; this is certain.
For a Brahmin who is utterly devoid of merit, yet excessively superior to those likewise devoid of merit,
shall indeed die from anger if he is reviled without cause.
A person should perform the Kṛcchra penance for three years for the sake of purification.

Furthermore, when the victim possesses extreme virtues while the self-slayer is utterly devoid of merit, he shall perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for exactly one year; having shaved his hair, beard, nails, and so forth in the forest, the Brāhmaṇa, practicing celibacy, becomes purified in one year.
Because it has been stated by him thus:
"In this very manner, one should also determine the penance for those who are the benefactors or instigators of the benefactor or instigator, and so forth.

And the basis for this determination is the statement of Āpastamba: "Regarding actions that result in the fruits of heaven or hell, the instigator, the consenter, and the doer are all partakers; however, a distinction in the fruit accrues to whichever of them initiates the greater effort."
In the same way, punishments and penances should be prescribed for the instigator and others as well.
As Paiṭhīnasi says:
"The killer, the instructor of the mantra, and likewise the one who provides the means..."
The encourager, the companion, and likewise the guide along the path.
The basis [of the crime], the provider of weapons, the provider of food for those who perform forbidden acts,
the one who looks on with indifference while being capable [to stop it], the one who points out the fault, and the one who approves [of the act].
But for those who commit forbidden acts, he shall prescribe an expiation;
and according to his ability and in accordance with the nature of the offense, he shall also impose a punishment upon them.
Thus: "The killer, the instructor of the mantra, the one who likewise provides the means,
the encourager, the assistant, and likewise the one who points out the path."
The basis [of the crime], the provider of weapons, the provider of food to those who perform forbidden acts,
the indifferent bystander if one is capable, the one who points out the fault, and the one who approves— all these are participants.
But for those who commit improper acts, he should prescribe an expiation;
and he should also prescribe for them a punishment appropriate to their capacity.

Likewise, even though children, the elderly, and others are capable of direct perception, they deserve only half [the penance]; for it is said: "One who is eighty years of age, or a child less than sixteen, as well as women and the sick, deserve only half the expiation."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Aṅgiras;
likewise, Sumantu says:
"But before the twelfth year, or indeed after eighty years..."
It would be half for men, and a fourth part for women therein.
Thus [it is said].
But for men, [the period] prior to twelve years or after eighty years shall be exactly half;
for women in that case, it shall be a quarter.
Likewise, even for an uninitiated boy, the expiation is only one quarter; half should be assigned to women, and likewise to the elderly and the sick;
a quarter should be assigned to children—this is the rule regarding all sins.

Thus it is from the *Viṣṇusmṛti*. And for this reason, Śaṅkha states: "For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five years, a brother, a father, or another kinsman shall perform the penance."
Having thus established the point, it was said: "Therefore, for this most childish person, there is neither offense nor sin;
he is subject to no royal punishment, nor is any expiation required."

Thus, that [text] also is intended to demonstrate the absence of a complete expiation, and not to demonstrate its total absence; for in such injunctions as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" and "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor," the qualification is established independently of any specific stage of life (*āśrama*), since no particular age is required.

Therefore, even his expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be performed by the father and others themselves; for it is the father alone who is authorized to act for the welfare of his son and others, according to the injunction: "Having procreated sons, having performed their sacraments, and having taught them the Veda, he should provide them with a livelihood. However, where there is a convergence of heavy and light expiations—such as when one person has become an instigator (*prayojaka*) in a certain killing of a Brahmin while another is the direct agent (*sākṣātkartṛ*)—there the accomplishment of the rite follows from the application (*prasaṅga*) of the lighter expiation related to the instigator, which is included within the scope of the heavier expiation, such as the twelve-year penance.
Nor should it be suspected that, this being the case, the accomplishment of even a great rite would follow from a minor procedure due to a lack of distinction;

for here, since no distinction is perceived when the performance is included within [the minor rite], the accomplishment of the task is understood to occur by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental application).
And since a "great ritual" (*mahākalpa*) is not included within a "minor one" (*laghu*), how can there be any suspicion of such *prasaṅga*?

Nor should it be argued: "How can the cessation of the sin produced by the killing of Viṣṇumitra be achieved by performing [a rite] for the purpose of exhausting the defilement generated by the killing of Caitra? For the specific reference to Caitra and so forth is not a determining factor (*atantratvāt*). Therefore, just as the fulfillment of the obligatory injunction (*nitya-niyoga*) occurs through the performance of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices—whether performed for the sake of completing a desired injunction (*kāmya-niyoga*) or for the sake of heaven (*svarga*)—in the same way, the accomplishment of the task is achieved even by a light expiation (*laghu-prāyaścitta*).
As for the statement of Madhyama-Aṅgiras: "One should duly bestow a thousand cows upon worthy recipients."
Even a slayer of a Brahmin shall be liberated from all sins indeed.

Thus, this refers to a Brāhmaṇa who is present at a *savana* (sacrificial session) and possesses virtuous qualities. Furthermore, this should be understood as applying to one who is incapable of performing the twelve-year vow prescribed by the statement, "One should prescribe a double vow for a Brāhmaṇa present at a *savana*," because of the extreme severity of such an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
However, this does not refer to the case of the twelve-year penance that has not been interrupted.
For in that case, if one calculates twelve days as equivalent to each *prājāpatya* penance, there would be three hundred and sixty *prājāpatyas*.

Even though at the conclusion of a *prājāpatya* there is an additional three-day fast (*upavāsa*), here—because it is conjoined with specific austerities such as dwelling in the forest, wearing matted hair, and subsisting on forest produce—the twelve-day period of each [penance] is equal to a *prājāpatya*, even in the absence of the formal fast.
And therefore, when one is unable to perform the *prājāpatya* rite, a wise person should give a cow;
in the absence of cows, its price should be given—of this there is no doubt.
According to this reasoning, when one cow is given for each Prajāpati, there are three hundred and sixty cows, and not a thousand;
therefore, the subject matter is correctly as previously stated.

As for the statement of Śaṅkha, which—as before—prescribes that "having unintentionally killed a Brāhmaṇa among the four castes, one should impose penances for twelve years, six, three, and one and a half years respectively; at the conclusion of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, half of that again, and half of that again, in order for all the castes," this should be understood as referring to the killing of an *ācārya* and others, because of their extreme gravity; it is intended to enjoin the combination (*samuccaya*) of the twelve-year penance and the gift of a thousand cows.
And likewise Dakṣa says: "A gift given to a non-Brāhmaṇa is equal [in merit]; it is twofold when given to one who calls himself a Brāhmaṇa;
it is a hundred-thousandfold when given to a teacher; and what is given to a Śrotriya is inexhaustible."
Having thus established this, he said: "The specific fruit of giving increases respectively by a factor of two, three, and a thousandfold, and likewise, the same applies to injury."
Thus:
"In giving, there shall be a distinction of fruit—equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite—respectively; for it is exactly the same in the case of injury."

Likewise, after prescribing a twelve-year penance, Āpastamba has stated regarding this very subject: "Having killed a Guru or a Śrotriya, one should perform this same vow until the final breath. In that case, when a threefold or fourfold repetition of the vow is possible throughout one's life, this combination of charity and austerity should be understood to apply to a capable person possessing great wealth.
As for the other penances prescribed by Sumantu, Parāśara, and others, which differ from the twelve-year penance, we shall explain their application later on.
Now, from what source is the restriction (*vyavasthā*) regarding the twelve-year penance and other such alternatives determined?
It is not reasonable to say that it is established by the scriptural injunctions prescribing the twelve-year penance and so forth, for such a restriction is not perceived therein.

Nor should it be argued that the restriction is postulated so that there might not result the sublation (*bādha*) of the heavy and light alternatives as understood through the means of valid cognition; for even by resorting to one of the other options—namely, optionality (*vikalpa*), combination (*samuccaya*), or the relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*)—the charge of sublation can be easily avoided.
To this it is replied:

First of all, an option (*vikalpa*) between the twelve-year penance, the visiting of the Setu, and so forth—which are of unequal status—is not tenable; for if one were to resort to such an option, there would be the consequence of futility (*ānarthakya*), since the performance of the more arduous penances would become impossible.
Nor should it be argued that an option between these two unequal alternatives is possible, as in the case of the taking or non-taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
Therefore, even in that case, it is logical to assume that the performance [of the rite] occurs only when [the additional element] is possible;

or else, one must assume that through the Atirātra sacrifice assisted by the Ṣoḍaśin cup, there is either the swift attainment of heaven and so forth, or an excellence of the heavenly reward itself—otherwise, the injunction for the cup would result in meaninglessness. Nor is there a combination [of both].

A combination [of two rites] is not possible without the attainment of both direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), because that would entail the sublation of the independence understood from the direct injunction.
Nor is there a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), due to the absence of the means of application such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest.
Direct statement, indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*) are the means of application.
Therefore, in order to avoid mutual contradiction, it is appropriate to postulate a fixed determination of their respective domains (*viṣayavyavasthā*).

And that [determination] should be postulated with reference to genus (*jāti*), capacity (*śakti*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth; for it is said: "Having understood the connection (*anubandha*) and other factors, one should prescribe the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) accordingly, based on genus, capacity, and quality, as established by a single cognition."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Devala (2.243).
He states the limit for the completion of the occasional expiation for killing a Brahmin and other such acts previously mentioned:
"By rescuing a Brahmin, or by [rescuing] twelve cows,
or likewise by bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice, one attains purification."

And he who, having placed even a single Brāhmaṇa—who is being slain by thieves, tigers, or the like—on a level with his own life, effects the preservation of that person's life, shall be purified even if the full twelve-year penance has not been completed, provided it was for a group of twelve cows.
Even if, though intent upon saving a life, he dies without having accomplished it, he is nevertheless purified.
For this very reason, it was stated by Manu:
One who immediately gives up his life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow,
and one who protects a cow or a Brahmin, is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus, the protection of a Brāhmaṇa and dying for that purpose are mentioned separately.

Likewise, at the time of the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) belonging to another’s horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), one may personally undergo the bath and thereby attain purification from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa;
and this bath should be performed after publicly proclaiming one’s own transgression.
And so Manu says: "Or, having informed the gods on earth (the Brahmins) at the arrival of the god of men (the king),
one is released from one's own sin by bathing in the *avabhṛtha* rite of the horse sacrifice."
Having thus instructed the gods of the earth upon the arrival of the god of men,
he is released from his own sin by bathing at the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*hayamedha*).

When there is an assembly of "earth-gods"—that is, Brahmins who are officiating priests—with a king acting as the sacrificer, one becomes purified by leaving behind one's own sin and proclaiming it, and then bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), provided that one has been permitted by them; for Śaṅkha records: "Having gone to the *avabhṛtha* of the horse sacrifice, one who bathes there with permission becomes instantly pure."

The mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) of the Aśvamedha is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other sacrifices such as the fifteen-night rite (*pañcadaśarātra*) and others that have the Agniṣṭut at their center, or those that conclude with the Agniṣṭut, such as the Sarvamedha; for Gautama records: "Or [the vow ends] at the *avabhṛtha* of the Aśvamedha, or even at another sacrifice if it concludes with the Agniṣṭut.
And this is stated to be the limit for the completion of the vow for one who has commenced the twelve-year penance and somehow effects the saving of a Brāhmaṇa's life or similar acts.

Just as in the Sārasvata Satra there is a rising (conclusion) upon reaching the Plākṣa spring—either with one hundred and one bulls or a thousand cows, or, in their absence, by the gift of all one's possessions—and also in the event of the death of the Gṛhapati; yet this is not an independent, separate expiation. Thus says Śaṅkha: "One attains purification in the twelfth year, or earlier by releasing a Brāhmaṇa from bondage, or by protecting twelve cows, or immediately by bathing in the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; thus one becomes pure."

For this very reason, after introducing the ancillary rule for the twelve-year penance—"or he may live with his hair shaven"—Manu states: "By immediately giving up his life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, one who protects a cow or a Brāhmaṇa is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa."

Having thus described, in the middle [of the passage], the protection of Brāhmaṇas and so forth, [it is said]: "In this way, one who is firm in his vows, constantly celibate, and composed, dispels the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa upon the completion of the twelfth year."
Thus, it is concluded that this [penance] lasts for twelve years.

Now, one might object: since it is understood from the statement "he shall attain purification from the killing of a Brahmin" that acts such as saving a Brahmin and so forth share the same result as the twelve-year penance, it is more appropriate that they be independent alternatives rather than auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
Furthermore, they cannot be auxiliaries because they would contradict the primary act.
For a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is that which assists the principal (*pradhāna*).
Moreover, this injunction does not apply to one who has already commenced a twelve-year penance, such that it could be understood as an injunction for the performance of that [twelve-year rite].

Just as in the case of the rule, "Having intended to undertake a *satra* sacrifice, one should perform the *Viśvajit*," which is an injunction for the *Viśvajit* for one who has set out on the performance of a *satra* but is unable to complete it—therefore, independence is indeed appropriate here, as in the cases of entering fire or becoming a target.
Nor should it be suspected that these [mantras] are subsidiary to those [rites], on the grounds that they are recited at the beginning, middle, and end of the twelve-year rite;

for even though they occur in the middle, since their purpose is already known, they lack the expectancy for a purpose (prayojanākāṅkṣā), and thus it is not logical for them to stand in a mutual relationship of principal and subsidiary.

This is just as, for example, the *nirvit* words occurring within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses—having the same function as the *sāmidhenīs* by virtue of illuminating the kindling of the fire—are not themselves subsidiaries to the *sāmidhenīs*.

Furthermore, acts such as entering the fire are not recited exclusively within the context of the twelve-year penance by Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and others, because these authorities recite them prior to the commencement of the twelve-year rite. It is precisely to demonstrate this independence that Manu, the upholder of the scriptures, has included the word "or" (*vā*) in every clause—such as "he may become a target for archers or throw himself into the fire"—and likewise concluded each specific expiation with the statement: "Therefore, having undertaken one of these rules, a Brahmin should remain composed."
It removes the sin committed by killing a Brahmin for the sake of self-purification.
Thus,
by adhering to one of these rules with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin removes the sin committed through the killing of a Brahmin for the sake of self-purification.
Therefore, it is logical that acts such as entering the fire possess independence.
Consequently, since even acts like saving a Brahmin from danger share a single fruit, they cannot be considered subordinate members [of a rite]. To this, it is replied:

This has already been resolved by the statement of Śaṅkha beginning with "having rescued a Brāhmaṇa in the interim," from which it is understood that [the rescue] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Since it exists as an auxiliary, its connection to the fruit occurs through the medium of the primary act (*pradhāna*).

Nor is there any contradiction with the primary act, because it is enjoined that the performance of the vow is a means to the fruit only when it is qualified by the rescue of a Brāhmaṇa; thus, there is no contradiction. (3.244)
Furthermore:
Having seen on the road a Brahmin or even a cow afflicted by a long-lasting and severe disease, the slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure by restoring them to health.

Having seen on the road a Brāhmaṇa or likewise a cow afflicted and tormented by a long-lasting, intense, and unbearable malady such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), one who restores them to a state free from fear and free from disease becomes pure, even if he is a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, one might ask: since the protection of a Brāhmaṇa was already mentioned in the rule "by rescuing a Brāhmaṇa," why is it stated again here as "a Brāhmaṇa or a cow"?
This is true.

However, the distinction is this: in the preceding statement, the protection of a Brahmin was described through the sacrifice of one's own life, whereas now it is described through the giving of medicine and so forth.
With this very intention, Manu stated:
"Or, upon the recovery of the Brahmin's life for that purpose, he is released [from the sin]."
Thus [ends verse] 3.245.
Or, if he recovers his life for the sake of that Brahmin, he is liberated. Furthermore: having brought away all the property of a Brahmin, or having seized it, or even having caused him to be killed—
One who has been wounded by weapons for that purpose is purified even while still alive.

He who brings back and protects the property—such as land, gold, and so forth—belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who is perishing because his entire wealth has been stolen, and who restores it in its entirety, is purified. Furthermore, if he is killed by thieves while engaged in bringing it back, or if he is wounded by weapons while fighting there for the sake of recovering the Brāhmaṇa’s entire property and is thus rendered near death (or even if he survives), he is purified.
The use of the plural "by weapons" (*śastraiḥ*) is intended to indicate a multiplicity of wounds.
For this very reason, Manu has employed the term "at least three" (*tryavaram*) in the verse: "Or one who obstructs [the thief], or having recovered all the property.

Since this set of five alternatives mentioned in the two verses is subsumed under the statement of Śaṅkha—"or having rescued a Brāhmaṇa in the interim"—by virtue of its nature as the protection of a Brāhmaṇa, it is not independent; rather, it is applied as the limit for the completion of the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika*). (3.246)
He states another expiation:
"With the mantra 'Svāhā to the body hairs,' one should indeed offer oblations, starting from the hair and ending with the marrow, using these mantras in their proper sequence."
One should offer the body, beginning with the hair and ending with the marrow, by means of the mantras beginning with "Svāhā to the hairs" (*lomabhyaḥ svāhā*).
The word *iti* is intended to indicate the instrumentality [of the mantras],
while the word *evam* is intended to indicate the manner [of the procedure].
The word *hi* serves to indicate that skin and the other substances, which are well-known from other Smṛtis, are implied by the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*).
Consequently, hair and the other substances intended for the oblation are designated by the dative case; one should offer them with those mantras after reciting the word *svāhā*.
Since the substances being offered—hair, skin, blood, flesh, fat, sinew, bone, and marrow—are eight in number, there are eight mantras.

And likewise Vasiṣṭha says: "The slayer of a Brahmin, having kindled the fire, shall offer oblations, [reciting]: 'I sacrifice the hairs to Death; by means of the hairs, I satiate Death'—this is the first [oblation].
(1) 'I sacrifice the skin to Death; by means of the skin, I satiate Death'—this is the second.
(2) 'I sacrifice the blood to Death; by means of the blood, I satiate Death'—this is the third. (3)"
"I offer the flesh to Death; satisfy Death with the flesh," he says for the fourth oblation.
(4) "I offer the fat to Death; satisfy Death with the fat," he says for the fifth.
(5) "I offer the sinews to Death; satisfy Death with the sinews," he says for the sixth. (6)
"I offer the bones to Death; with the bones, I cause Death to cry out"—with this he offers the seventh oblation.
"I offer the marrow to Death; with the marrow, I cause Death to cry out"—with this he offers the eighth oblation.
Thus [it is said].

And here, because the statement "one should offer the body beginning with the hair" (*lomaprabhṛti tanuṃ juhuyāt*) makes it known that the hair and other parts are the substances for the oblation (*homadravya*), the status of the hair and so forth as deities (*devatātva*) is not postulated—even though there is an indication by the dative case in "to the hair, svāhā" (*lomabhyaḥ svāhā*)—since the mantras can serve as means for the oblation simply by manifesting the substance.

Rather, by examining the Vasiṣṭha-mantra, "With the hairs, cause death to be appeased" (*lomabhir mṛtyuṃ vāśaya*), it is understood that death itself is connected to the oblation, and thus its status as the deity is postulated.
Therefore, having taken the hair and other parts with the razor by implication, and having performed eight oblations dedicated to Death (*mṛtyu*), he should finally cast the body [into the fire].

Consequently, that which has been stated by some—that because no specific substance is prescribed, these oblations have clarified butter as their offering material—is an assertion made without investigation and should be disregarded.

Since the act of "offering" (*juhuyāt*) already implies the fire, the repeated mention of "fire" in the phrase "the killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*) having established the fire" is for the purpose of indicating the common (*laukika*) fire.

And this is logical, because there are prescribed rites for the disposal of the fires of those who have fallen [from their caste]: "If a Brahmin who has maintained the sacred fires should become a partaker of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), he cannot be purified by penances; what then is the fate of his fires?"
The wise man should cast the sacrificial fire into water and extinguish the domestic fire of the hall.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Uśanas: "If one who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) should by fate happen to possess the sacred fires, a son or other relative shall maintain those fires, being diligent until the destruction of the fault."
If one does not perform penance, or if he dies while performing it,
he should extinguish the domestic fire and cast the Śrauta fires along with their implements into water.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana.
Furthermore, the casting of the body [into the water] should be performed three times, rising again and again, with the face turned downwards;
as Manu has said:
"Or he should throw himself into a kindled fire, three times with his head downward.
Thus:
"Or he should throw himself into a kindled fire, three times with his head downward."
Gautama also has shown a specific rule in this regard: "The expiation for a slayer of a Brahmin is attachment to the fire after having been shorn three times.
"Shorn" means one whose body has been emaciated by fasting.
And so says the Kāṭhaka Śruti: "Emaciated by fasting, he should ascend the fire."
And this penance ending in death applies to cases of intentional action.
As Madhyama-Aṅgiras said:
"The penance ending in death which has been proclaimed by the wise..."
That should be understood as pertaining to the domain of acting according to one's own will; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus,
