it should be understood without any doubt that the penance ending in death which has been proclaimed by the wise applies specifically to intentional acts.
Likewise: "If a man should ever commit a great sin intentionally, no purification for him is prescribed except by leaping from a precipice or entering fire."
Thus:
"If a man should ever commit a great sin intentionally,
no purification for him is prescribed except by leaping from a precipice or entering fire."
And this is indeed an expiation alone; it was stated previously that it is not included within the twelve-year penance like the protection of a Brāhmaṇa and other such acts. (3.247)
Moreover: Or, being made a target and slain in battle, he attains purification;
even while living, though afflicted by wounds and nearly dead, he is purified.

Alternatively, one who has become a target in battle on the battlefield—at the place where a shower of arrows is discharged by both armies—and dies there, shall attain purification. Even while living, one who is as if dead, being unconscious due to the intense pain caused by a deep wound to a vital organ, is purified.

Furthermore, this state of being a target for the sake of penance must be undertaken voluntarily in battle by those learned in archery who know the rules, and it must not be forced upon anyone by the king.
As Manu has said:
"The target may be those who bear arms, or it may be at the will of the learned man himself."
The target may be either those who bear arms or learned men, according to the wish of the individual.
And because this penance ends with death, it pertains to a Kṣatriya perpetrator who acts out of his own will.
By the use of the word "also," one is purified even by means of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and other rites.
As Manu said:
"Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, and the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt and Agniṣṭut."
Thus it is said:
"One should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, and the Gosava;
or else with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut."

The performance of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) belongs exclusively to a universal sovereign (*sārvabhauma*) Kṣatriya, according to the traditional teaching of Parāśara: "A Kṣatriya who is a lord of the earth may indeed sacrifice with the horse sacrifice"; and because we see a prohibition against those who are not universal sovereigns: "One who is not a universal sovereign shall not sacrifice. Furthermore, this performance of the horse sacrifice by a universal sovereign should be understood as a substitute for the penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) when committed intentionally; for it is said: "Those who commit the four great sins (*mahāpātaka*) intentionally..."
They become pure by entering the fire, or by participating in a great sacrifice.
Thus, because Yama has described the great horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) as being equivalent to entering the fire at the time of death;

furthermore, sacrifices such as the *svarjit* are optional alternatives to the twelve-year penance for a member of the three higher castes who has maintained the sacred fires and performed his first sacrifice.

Nor should one perform the consecration of the fires or the performance of the first sacrifice for the sake of the *svarjit* and other such rites, because one who has fallen [from caste] lacks the entitlement to the rituals of the twice-born.

Nor is it correct to argue that there is no contradiction [between these penances] as there is with the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), because the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) and other rites do not constitute subsidiary elements of subsequent sacrifices.

Furthermore, those penances are to be applied directly to killers and others who deserve twelve-year penances and the like, by resorting to a reduction or increase in the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). (3.248)
Moreover:
Having recited the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times in the forest with self-restraint, or by eating moderately while traveling upstream along the Sarasvatī, one shall indeed be purified.

"In a forest, in a secluded place, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should recite [the Veda]," according to the traditional teaching of Manu. Having recited the Veda—consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa—three times, one becomes purified.
The mention of the *saṃhitā* is for the purpose of excluding the *pada* and *krama* recensions.

Alternatively, having become one who eats measured food, by going along the Sarasvatī against the current from the Plakṣa-prasravaṇa until the western ocean, reaching stream after stream, one becomes purified;
for the Smṛti of Manu states: "And his meal should consist of sacrificial food (haviṣya); or, eating sacrificial food, he should follow the Sarasvatī against the current."

And this recitation of the Vedas (*vedajapa*) is to be understood as applying to a learned killer who is penniless and otherwise highly virtuous, when the killing of one devoid of merit was committed through negligence. However, going to the Sarasvatī river should be understood to apply to one lacking in learning within that same kind of situation. And regarding the instigator: "When a Brahmin devoid of merit, having been insulted, dies..."

Since the statement of Sumantu has thus been shown, as for the statement of Manu— "Having recited one of the Vedas, he should walk a hundred yojanas"— that too should be understood as referring to one who is unable [to perform the penance] within the very scope of the rule "having recited it while restrained in a forest. (3.249)
Furthermore:
Having given sufficient wealth to a worthy recipient, one may attain purification;
for the sake of the purifier’s own purification as well, the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice is prescribed by tradition.

By giving to a recipient characterized as described in the passage beginning "not by knowledge alone," such as cows, land, gold, and other capable wealth sufficient for a lifetime, one may attain purification.
For him who accepts that wealth, an *iṣṭi* sacrifice dedicated to Vaiśvānara must be performed for the sake of purification;
and this applies specifically to one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).

However, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is a sacrificial pap (*caru*) dedicated to those same deities; for the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* states: "Whatever is the rule for one who maintains the fires, that very same rule applies to one who maintains the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). Because of the word "or" (*vā*), he may also give his entire property along with its furnishings, or his house;
as Manu says:
Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas;
or wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings.
Thus it is said:
"Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas;
or wealth sufficient for a livelihood; or a house together with its furnishings."

Furthermore, this gift of wealth in a vessel is to be understood as applying to a wealthy man devoid of merit who has committed murder; in that very same case, the rule is that for one who lacks descendants, there shall be a gift of all one's possessions, whereas for one who has descendants, there shall be a gift of the house along with its furnishings. As for what was stated by Parāśara: "But for the slayer of a Brahmin who is endowed with the fourfold knowledge, according to the prescribed rule..."
One should prescribe the journey across the ocean bridge as the expiation.
On the path to Setubandha, he should collect alms from the four castes,
avoiding those engaged in forbidden occupations, and remaining without umbrella or shoes.
I am indeed one of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins;
as a slayer of a Brahmin, I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms.
In cow-pens and cattle-sheds, in villages and cities,
in forests of asceticism, at sacred fords, and by rivers and springs.
One should confess one's sin in these places after going to the ocean;
even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated by bathing in that great ocean.
Then, purified, having returned home and fed the Brāhmaṇas,
and having given garments and sacred threads, he, with his soul purified, should enter his house.
Or he may give a hundred cows as a sacrificial fee to one learned in the four Vedas;
thus, with the approval of the one learned in the four Vedas, he attains purification.
Thus, that [statement] also has the same scope as the phrase "wealth sufficient for a worthy recipient."

And as for the statement of Sumantu: "A slayer of a Brahmin shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, making his occupation known, subsisting on alms, and dwelling by the banks of celestial rivers, at confluences, hermitages, cow-pens, mountains, springs, and groves of ascetics; remaining standing or in the *vīrāsana* posture, when the year is complete, he becomes purified by giving gold, gems, cows, grain, sesame, land, and clarified butter to Brahmins"—that too should be understood to apply to the killing of a wealthy, foolish [Brahmin] who is such by birth alone.

Furthermore, as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "Having killed a eunuch who is a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra—either subsisting on water for twelve nights, fasting for twelve nights, performing a Cāndrāyaṇa, or indeed two Parāka penances."
This statement from the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* is to be understood as referring to the intentional killing of a man whose virility cannot be restored.
Regarding this very subject, Bṛhaspati speaks concerning unintentional killing:
"At the world-renowned confluence of the Aruṇā and the Sarasvatī..."
A twice-born man who bathes at the three periods of the day and fasts for three nights shall be purified.
Thus it is said: at the world-renowned confluence of the Aruṇā and the Sarasvatī,
a twice-born man who bathes three times a day and fasts for three nights shall be purified.
In this manner, having investigated other Smṛti statements as well, the determination of those that are inconsistent should be understood;
however, for those that are consistent, there is an option.
And these [penances], beginning with the twelve-year penance and ending with the gift of wealth, apply only to a Brāhmaṇa.
But for a Kṣatriya and others, it is double and so forth.
As Āṅgiras said:
"That which is the assembly for Brāhmaṇas is considered to be double for kings."
For Vaiśyas, it is declared that [the assembly] shall consist of three times as many members, and the penance is remembered to be the same as for the assembly.
Thus it is said: "The assembly for Brahmins is as described; for kings, it is considered to be double that;
for Vaiśyas, it is declared to be triple. And the penance is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly."

And thus, regarding Brahmins, whatever specific penance has been established according to the specific quality residing in the slayer or the slain, that very same penance should be understood as being double or triple when the slayer is a Kṣatriya or others distinguished by such qualities. Following this same direction, in the case of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or others, where a superior person is killed by an inferior, a doubling or other increase of the penance must be devised due to the gravity of the fault. And the gravity of the fault is understood from the gravity of the punishment.
As it has been said:
"In cases of defamation involving the inverse order of castes, the fine shall be double or triple;
for those in the direct order of castes, it shall be reduced by half and half again from that amount."
Thus:
"In cases of defamation involving the inverse order of castes, the fine shall be double or triple;
whereas in the direct order of castes, it shall be reduced by half and half again from that amount."

As for the statement from the Caturviṃśatimata: "Whatever expiation has been prescribed by the great seers for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya should perform three-quarters of it, and a Vaiśya should perform half."
A Śūdra shall perform one quarter of the penance even for all manner of sins without exception.
Thus, this refers to cases other than those involving the fourfold violence committed in the inverse order [of castes].
Likewise, for those born in the direct order, such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others, the penance should be inferred in accordance with their respective punishments.
The gradations of punishment have been shown; the infliction of punishment must be carried out according to the higher or lower status of the castes and classes.
Thus,
the infliction of punishment must be carried out according to the relative superiority or inferiority of the castes and classes.

Consequently, in the case of a Mūrdhāvasikta killing a Brāhmaṇa, the penalty is twelve years' imprisonment— more than that prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, yet less than that for a Kṣatriya, being one and a half times the latter.
In this very same manner, the increased gravity of the penance for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) should also be inferred.
Likewise, Aṅgiras has shown a specific rule even regarding those belonging to the [other] stages of life (āśrama):
"If those in the [other] stages of life commit the sins prescribed for householders..."
They should perform purification just as they do for cleanliness, until the vision of Brahman is attained.
Thus:
"If those belonging to other stages of life commit the sins prescribed for householders,
they should perform purification just as they do for ritual impurity, until the realization of Brahman."
Regarding "as in the case of purity": this purity is twofold for householders, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.

According to this statement, the meaning is that just as the purity (*śauca*) of students (*brahmacārin*) and others increases in a sequence of doubling and so forth, so too does the purification (*śodhana*), which is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). However, for a student, the doubling of the expiation occurs only after the age of sixteen; prior to that, on the contrary, it is stated that "a child, or one under sixteen, deserves half the expiation," because an expiation of half-measure is prescribed for those younger than sixteen.

Nor should it be suspected that the undertaking of the twelve-year penance—when performed with its fourfold repetition—is impossible because completion cannot be achieved due to the fear of death occurring in the interim;
for even if death occurs during the performance of an already commenced penance, the destruction of sin certainly takes place.
As Hārīta says:
If the performer dies after the penance has been resolved upon,
he becomes purified on that very day, both in this world and in the next.
Thus:
"If the performer dies once the penance has been determined,
he becomes purified on that very day, both in this world and in the next."
Vyāsa also said:
"If a man strives for the sake of dharma but is unable [to complete it], he nevertheless attains that merit; of this there is no doubt."
Thus [ends verse] 3.250.
If a man, striving for the sake of dharma, is unable [to complete it], he nevertheless attains that merit; of this there is no doubt.
Now, he states the extension (*atideśa*) of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa to other specific circumstances:

"One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; likewise one who destroys an embryo according to its caste, and one who kills an *Ātreyī* woman."

One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya while they are engaged in the performance of a Soma sacrifice, beginning from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and ending with the *udavasānīyā*, shall perform that twelve-year vow and the like which is prescribed for a person who has committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*).

Although the word "sacrifice" (*yāga*) is a general term, it refers here specifically to the Soma sacrifice; for Vasiṣṭha specifies the Soma sacrifice itself—which is accomplished through three pressings (*savana*)—in the rule: "A Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who have entered the *savana*."

And here, the application of the twelve-year penances and other observances for the killing of a Brahmin—ranging from heavy to light—should be understood as being determined according to caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth, as previously stated.
The same applies to the killing of an embryo and similar offenses.
However, the penance ending in death is not extended [to these cases], because the text specifically mentions the undertaking of a vow (*vrata*).
Therefore, for the intentional killing of a Kṣatriya or others engaged in a sacrifice, there is a doubling of the vow itself.
And this vow must be performed in its entirety;
for Āpastamba, having introduced the topic with "having killed a student of the Veda belonging to the two preceding castes," prescribes a twelve-year penance.

Having killed a fetus produced in a womb, one should perform that same penance which has been prescribed for the killing of a person of a particular caste, according to the caste of that fetus; this refers to a case where the gender-characteristics (liṅga) of female, male, or neuter have not yet developed, because a specific distinction is seen in the *Mānava* [text]: "having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown."

And here, although the obligation to perform the vow occasioned by the killing of that [fetus] arises for one who kills a Brāhmaṇa fetus precisely because of its being a Brāhmaṇa, nevertheless, since the possibility of it being female also exists, there would also arise the obligation to perform the penance for a minor offense (upapātaka), namely "the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya. Therefore, the statement of extended application (atideśa) is purposeful, meaning that even when the fetus is not known as male, female, or neuter, one should perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa based solely on its being a Brāhmaṇa fetus. Once the distinguishing characteristics of female, male, and so forth have appeared, the penance is to be performed exactly according to the case.
And he who is the slayer or the one who causes the death of an Ātreyī should likewise perform the vow;
the meaning is that he should perform a vow corresponding to the caste of the Ātreyī being killed.
By the word "Ātreyī," a woman in her menses is meant, for according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha: "They call her an Ātreyī who has bathed after her menses, since from her offspring [is born]."
And because of the Smṛti of Viṣṇu, which states: "a woman born of the Atri lineage, or a woman belonging to the Atri lineage.
This is what is meant:
for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa fetus and for the killing of an Ātreyī Brāhmaṇa woman, the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyāvrata*) applies.
In the case of killing a Kṣatriya fetus or killing a Kṣatriya Ātreyī woman, the vow for killing a Kṣatriya applies; the same holds true for other cases as well.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), this includes false testimony and similar offenses.
Thus says Manu:
Having given false testimony, having obstructed a teacher,
having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend;
Having spoken thus, and likewise having given false testimony, obstructed a teacher,
misappropriated a deposit, or committed the murder of a woman or a friend.
This refers to a legal proceeding in which the killing of living beings results from false speech, because the penance for such an act is exceedingly grave.
"Obstruction" means an outburst of anger;
and "deposit" refers to one belonging to a Brāhmaṇa.
And the woman is said to be one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), endowed with qualities such as devotion to her husband (*pativratā*), and being present at the *savana* rites;
as Aṅgiras has said:
"Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires..."
One who has killed an Ātreyī woman should likewise perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus:

"Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin; and the same applies to the killer of an Ātreyī."
Having killed a woman engaged in a Soma sacrifice, one should observe the vow for killing a Brahmin.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Parāśara.

And thus, because the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is extended by analogy to the killing of an Ātreyī woman who maintains the sacred fires and attends the Soma-pressing, the killing of women other than her is classified as a minor offense (upapātaka), since it is listed among the minor offenses in the passage beginning, "the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya."

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the prohibition "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," gender and number are not intended to be significant because they reside in a factor that is not to be enjoined (*anupādeya*), and since the Brāhmaṇa caste is common to both women and men, the rule prescribing the penance for its transgression—namely, "The slayer of a Brāhmaṇa [must perform] twelve years"—applies equally to both? Why, then, is there this extended application (*atideśa*) stating, "Likewise, the slayer of an Ātreyī"? [Reply: It is said in response: 1. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the killing occurs unintentionally (*abuddhipūrva*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to intentional killing—as in the case of the rule "one who intentionally kills a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be unnecessary. 2. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the killing is done by means other than weapons. For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to killing with a weapon—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa with a weapon shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be unnecessary. 3. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the killer is a woman. For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to a male—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 4. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not fallen from their caste—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who is not fallen from his caste shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 5. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a mortal sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a mortal sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 6. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a minor sin (*upapātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a minor sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a minor sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 7. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a secondary sin (*anupātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a secondary sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a secondary sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 8. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a slight sin (*kṣudrapātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a slight sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a slight sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 9. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a very slight sin (*svalpapātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a very slight sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a very slight sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 10. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a sin of intermediate degree (*madhyamapātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a sin of intermediate degree—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a sin of intermediate degree shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 11. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a grave sin (*gurupātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a grave sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a grave sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 12. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a very grave sin (*gurutara-pātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a very grave sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a very grave sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 13. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a most grave sin (*gurutama-pātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a most grave sin—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a most grave sin shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 14. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a sin of the highest degree (*parama-pātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a sin of the highest degree—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a sin of the highest degree shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 15. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a sin of the lowest degree (*adhama-pātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a sin of the lowest degree—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a sin of the lowest degree shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 16. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a sin of the middling degree (*madhyama-pātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a sin of the middling degree—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a sin of the middling degree shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 17. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a sin of the superior degree (*uttama-pātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" would apply only to those who have not committed a sin of the superior degree—as in the case of the rule "one who kills a Brāhmaṇa who has not committed a sin of the superior degree shall enter the forest"—this extended application would be necessary. 18. To indicate that the penance is to be performed even when the Brāhmaṇa killed is one who has committed a sin of the inferior degree (*adhamottama-pātakin*). For otherwise, since the rule "

Even though he possesses Brahminhood, this is for the purpose of excluding the penance for a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) in the case of killing an *Anātreyyā*; therefore, because she is listed among the minor sins (*upapātaka*), the penance is precisely that for a minor sin.
Furthermore, among the extended applications (*atideśika*), it is only the penance that is extended, not the loss of caste (*pātitya*).
Consequently, the ritual acts such as the abandonment of an outcaste do not apply here. (3.251)
Furthermore:
Even if he does not kill, one should observe the vow if he has come with the intent to kill;
however, if it is a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a sacrifice, one should prescribe a double vow.

The phrase "according to the caste" (*yathāvarṇam*) is understood to carry over here. If one has resolved upon the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or another [member of the higher castes] and, having approached them properly for the purpose of slaying them, strikes them with a weapon or other means, but they do not die due to some obstacle such as resistance, then even though he has not killed them, he should perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa or other [offenses] according to their respective castes.
Thus says Gautama: "If [the victim] has been struck in the case of Brāhmaṇa-killing, even if he does not die.
Now, one might object: it is not logical that there should be a single expiation both when the killing occurs and when it does not.
True.

For this very reason, because they are inferior to those prescribed by direct injunction (*aupadeśika*), the penances for killing a Brahmin and so forth, which apply by extension (*ātideśika*), consist of twelve-year vows and the like reduced by one quarter.
This has been explained in detail previously.
Furthermore, one should prescribe a twelve-year vow and so forth, doubled, for one who kills a Brāhmaṇa performing a Soma sacrifice accomplished through the *savana* (pressing) rites.

Regarding these vows, which vary in gravity, the specific application must be understood as before—depending on caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth—even though the fact of being engaged in a *savana* remains the same.

However, it has been stated that for acts equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, such as reviling a guru, the penance is half less than the twelve-year vow and so forth, because they are even lighter than those cases where the rule is extended (*atideśika*). (3.252)
Now begins the section on the expiation for drinking liquor, which follows in sequence: Having drunk any one of these— liquor, water, ghee, cow-urine, or milk— that is as hot as fire,
the drinker of liquor attains purification through death.

Among *surā* and the other [liquors], having made any one of them resemble fire—that is, possessing the power to cause a burning sensation upon contact with heat produced by boiling—one who drinks it attains purification through death.
Because of its association with cow’s urine, only products of the cow (*gavya*) are to be understood for the clarified butter and milk;
and because of their association with clarified butter and milk, the cow’s urine must likewise be that of a female cow.

And this must be performed while wearing wet clothes, because of the traditional teaching of Paiṭhīnasi: "The drinker of spirituous liquor, wearing wet clothes, shall drink spirituous liquor that is red-hot like fire"; and likewise because of the traditional teaching of Pracetas: "The drinker of spirituous liquor shall drink spirituous liquor red-hot like fire from a vessel made of iron, or from a vessel of black iron, or of copper.
And this applies to the mere act of drinking once: even having drunk spirituous liquor only once, one shall drink spirituous liquor red-hot like fire.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Aṅgiras.

As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "But in the case of repeated practice of liquor, a twice-born man should drink [liquor] that is fire-colored," that refers to the drinking of intoxicants other than *surā*.
And this refers to the case of intentional action; for drinking liquor intentionally, one should cast a blazing [metal] ball into his mouth.
Having been consumed by it, he attains purification upon death.

Thus it is from the Smṛti of Bṛhaspati. As for the fact that Manu included the mention of "delusion" (*moha*) in the verse, "Having drunk liquor through delusion, a twice-born man shall drink liquor the color of fire," that was intended to refer to a lack of understanding of the meaning of the scriptures.

In this regard, the following must be considered: Is the word *surā* conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for intoxicating liquor in general, or only for the three types—namely, that made from molasses (*gauḍī*), that made from honey (*mādhvī*), and that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*)? Or is it established for the flour-based liquor alone? On this point, some describe it as being conventionally established for intoxicating liquor in general. For they observe the use of the word *surā* for intoxicating liquor in general even outside the context of the three types beginning with the flour-based one, as in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*: "But [the penance] for the repeated drinking of *surā*... Nor should it be suspected that this is a figurative usage; for since its primary application is justified everywhere by the qualifying condition (*upādhi*) of possessing the power to produce intoxication, it is improper to assume a figurative sense.

That is incorrect; [for there are many kinds of intoxicants: that derived from the *pānasa* tree, that from the *dākṣa*, that from the *mādhūka*, that from the date palm (*khārjūra*), that from the *tāla* palm, that from sugarcane (*aikṣava*), that produced from honey (*madhūttha*), that from the *saira* plant, *āriṣṭa*, *maireya*, and that produced from the coconut.
One should know that there are exactly eleven types of intoxicants that are equal;
however, the twelfth is the liquor of *surā*, which is recorded as the lowest of all.

Thus, because Pulastya has specified *surā* as a particular type of intoxicant (*madyaviśeṣa*), the application of the word *surā* to intoxicants in general is therefore figurative (*gauṇa*). Others, however, maintain that the word *surā* is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) specifically for the three types beginning with that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*).

For instance, although the use of the word *surā* is observed in many instances, when there is doubt as to where its primary application lies, the statement of Manu—"Surā is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (*gauḍī*), that from honey (*mādhvī*), and that from flour (*paiṣṭī*)"—determines its primary application to the products of molasses, honey, and flour, since it is therein that its beginninglessness is established. Nor is there the fault of postulating multiple denotative powers (*śakti*), for this is easily avoided by relying on the power of intoxication (*mada-śakti*) as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Nor does this lead to an over-extension of the principle, because the adjunct (upādhi) is present even in the juices of the palmyra palm and so forth; for we rely on the principle that these terms function through both etymological derivation and conventional usage (*yogarūḍhi*), just like the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus"). Consequently, the statement, "Just as one [type of liquor] is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born," is intended to demonstrate that the three types of *surā* share an equal degree of fault, and it does not, however, establish the equality of the *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* with the *paiṣṭī* *surā*.

The mention of "the best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*) is intended as an indication for all twice-born castes (*dvijāti*). This too is incorrect, because in the statement of Pulastya— “But the twelfth [type], spirituous liquor made from grain (*surā-madya*), is recorded as the lowest for all”— it is observed that *surā-madya* exceeds even the *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* varieties.

Likewise, because of the designation of *surā* as a modification of food in the passage, "Wine (*surā*) is indeed the impurity of foods, and evil is called impurity," and because the word "food" (*anna*) is seen to be used exclusively for modifications of rice and other grains in such expressions as "seasoning with food" (*annena vyañjanam*), and because molasses and honey consist of liquid essence (*rasa*), and furthermore, because the word *surā* is heard in the context of the *sautrāmaṇī* libations as referring specifically to a modification of food, *surā* in its primary sense denotes only that which is made from flour (*paiṣṭī*).
In the case of the other two [types of *surā*], however, the term *surā* is used figuratively.
As for what was stated—that because of the Manu-smṛti verse "gauḍī mādhvī," the inherent nature [of the three] is determined even regarding the other three [liquors]—that too is incorrect.

For this [verse] does not aim to establish the beginninglessness of the relationship between words and their meanings, as is the case with grammatical treatises; rather, it aims to prescribe a specific action.
Therefore, the application of the word *surā* to *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* is figurative, based on their being causes for heavy penance.
And thus, there is no fault of postulating multiple potencies, nor has recourse to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) been made.
Furthermore, the mention of "the best of the twice-born" here is not intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore: "Wine is indeed the dregs of foods, and sin is said to be a dreg."
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*.
Thus, the prohibition applies specifically to liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) in relation to all three castes.

However, regarding liquors such as *gauḍī* and others, the prohibition applies only in relation to the Brāhmaṇa, and not to the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya. As it is said: "Liquor, meat, and fermented spirits (*surā-āsava*) are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas;
that must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who eats the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) of the gods."
Thus, because of the specific mention of "by a Brāhmaṇa" in the *Mānava* [Smṛti],
Bṛhad-Viṣṇu also demonstrates that the prohibition of liquor applies only to the Brāhmaṇa:
"The *mādhūka*, the sugarcane [juice], the *saira*, the *tāla*, the date-palm, and the *pānasa*..."
Likewise, that which is derived from honey (mādhvīka), maireya, and that produced from coconut;
These ten intoxicants are indeed impure for a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus.

The honey-wine from *mādhūka*, that from sugarcane (*aikṣava*), that from the *sīra* plant, that from the palm tree (*tāla*), that from the date palm (*khārjūra*) and the *pānasa* fruit; likewise, that produced from honey (*madhūttha*), *mādhvīka*, *maireya*, and that from the coconut.
These ten kinds of intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa.

Bṛhadyājñavalkya also demonstrated the absence of fault for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas: "For even if a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should drink liquor or *surā* out of desire under any circumstances whatsoever, he incurs no guilt."
Thus it is said:
"For even out of desire, if a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should somehow drink liquor or *surā*, he incurs no fault."

Vyāsa also permitted the drinking of honey-wine for those two: "Both Keśava and Arjuna were seen by me intoxicated with honey-liquor, both anointed with sandalwood paste, and both seated upon a single chariot-seat."
Thus:
"Both intoxicated by honey-wine, both anointed with sandalwood paste,
I saw Keśava and Arjuna seated together upon a single chariot with a single seat."

Thus, although there is a general prohibition against all types of intoxicants for those connected with the Brahmin caste, it is specified: "Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Paiṣṭī—liquor is to be known as threefold.
Just as one [type] is so, so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born."

Thus, the separate prohibition of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* [liquors] is intended to establish their equivalence to *surā* on account of the gravity of their faults. Furthermore, this prohibition of *surā* certainly applies even to one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) and to an unmarried girl (*kanyā*), because of the prohibition restricted solely by caste: "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*."

Therefore, in the prescriptive statement regarding expiation—"Having drunk *surā* through delusion, a twice-born man [shall perform penance]"—the mention of "twice-born" (*dvija*) by Manu is intended as an indicator for all social classes (*varṇa*). This is because the occasional rite (*naimittika-vidhi*) depends upon the prohibition that serves as its occasion, and in that prohibition, all classes without distinction are the limiting factor.

Just as in the causal statement, "If the moon rises before the sacrificial oblation has been set aside," the rising of the moon is understood to be the cause with respect to the oblation in general; therefore, even though the phrase "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts" is heard in the subsequent conditional injunction dependent upon that cause, the mention of "rice-grains" (taṇḍula) is merely an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for the oblation in its entirety, whether it consists of rice-grains or other materials.

However, there is this distinction: because of the statement, "A quarter [of the penance] should be assigned for children; this is the rule regarding all sins," even in the case of intentional (*kāmakāra*) action, the penance ending in death does not apply, but rather a six-year penance should be given by doubling the quarter-penance. For the Smṛti of Aṅgiras states: "Whatever has been prescribed for those acting unintentionally, one should perform that doubled for intentional acts. This should be applied similarly to cases involving the elderly, the sick, and so forth.

Likewise, because it is prohibited for a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) for the gods to consume that [meat], and because liquor (*madya*) is likewise prohibited by the mere restriction of caste, it must not be drunk even by one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*).

[Objection: But how can there be fault for one who is uninitiated? For Gautama states: "Prior to initiation, one may act as he pleases, speak as he pleases, and eat as he pleases. Likewise, [it is said]: "In the consumption of liquor, urine, and excrement, there is no [sin]."
But the fault [of not performing the rite] lasts until the fifth year; beyond that, it applies to the parents, friends, and teachers.
And because the absence of fault is understood from these words of the Prince,
it is said:
since the restrictive factor in the prohibitory statement regarding *surā* and *madya* is heard to be the mere genus (*jāti*), the operation of the prohibition remains entirely unimpeded.

For this very reason, there is a prohibitory statement in another Smṛti: "The established rule is that the prohibition against drinking liquor pertains to [all] castes. Thus ends the section on the prohibition of drinking liquor.
Therefore: "A quarter [of the penalty] should be given for offenses against children; this is the rule regarding all sins.
Thus:
"A quarter should be given for offenses against children; this is the rule regarding all sins."
Because of the statement, "even among all sins, such as the drinking of liquor," the penance for drinking liquor is indeed one quarter [of the standard penance].
Likewise, Jātūkarṇya has also prescribed a penance for the drinking of intoxicants (*madya*).
If an uninitiated fool should drink liquor out of delusion,
his mother, brother, and father must perform three *kṛcchra* penances for him.
Thus it is said:
"But if an uninitiated boy should drink liquor out of delusion,
his mother, brother, and likewise his father, must perform three *kṛcchra* penances for him."
Therefore, the statement of Gautama refers to substances such as fermented gruel (*śukta*) and stale food that are distinct from liquor (*surā*) and the like;
however, the statement of Kumāra is intended to indicate that the fault is slight.
For this very reason, Manu has stated that for a fault committed prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the initiation itself serves as the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Through the fire-oblations performed at conception, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle,
the sin derived from the seed and the womb is wiped away for the twice-born.
Thus:
"By means of the oblations pertaining to the womb, and by the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass,
the taint derived from seed and the taint derived from the womb are wiped away for the twice-born."
This is the meaning here:
for members of the three [upper] castes, there is a prohibition against liquor distilled from flour (*paiṣṭī*) from birth onwards;
however, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is a prohibition against all intoxicants (*madya*) indeed from birth onwards.
But for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, there is never a prohibition against liquor made from molasses (*gauḍī*) and other such intoxicants.
For the Śūdra, there is neither a prohibition against *surā* nor a prohibition against intoxicants (*madya*). (3.253)
He states another expiation:
"Clad in hair-cloth or even with matted locks, one should perform the vow for killing a Brahmin;
or one should eat oil-cakes or grain-particles at night for three years."
"Clad in hair-cloth" (*vālavāsas*) means covered with a garment made from the hair of cows, goats, and the like.

The mention of "hair-cloth" is intended as an illustration for rags (*cīra*) and bark (*valkala*) as well, because of the traditional teaching of Pracetas: "The violator of a cow and the violator of the Guru's bed shall perform the vow for killing a Brahmin while wearing rags and bark garments.
The mention of "having matted hair" (*jaṭin*) is for the purpose of excluding the state of being shaven-headed.

Since the rule "one should perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa" alone would have sufficed, the specific mention of wearing garments of hair and so forth is intended to exclude the carrying of the skull of the person killed by oneself, which might otherwise be applicable in other cases. This [penance] pertains to one who unintentionally drinks liquor under the impression that it is water; for this purification has been prescribed as an extension (*atideśa*) of the twelve-year penance specifically enjoined with the condition of being unintentional, according to the rule: "This purification is declared for having killed a twice-born man unintentionally."

And here, because drinking liquor is a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), even though it is extended [to other cases] by analogy, one should perform the full twelve-year penance and not one reduced by a quarter.
For this very reason, Vṛddha-Hārīta says: "Those who have committed mortal sins are purified in twelve years.
Alternatively, one may eat oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) in a lump for three equal years—that is, for a period of three years—during the night.
Or he may eat grains—that is, fragments of rice—as previously described;
and this should be done only once. For the Smṛti of Manu states: "Or he may eat grains for a year, or oil-cake once at night."

Since this consumption of oil-cake and the like is prescribed for the purpose of eating, there is a total renunciation of other food. This should be understood to apply to the drinking of *surā* under the impression that it was water, at a time subsequent to vomiting; "A drinker of intoxicants, having vomited, shall perform this very vow.
And the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are declared for him as a daily purification of the body."
This is because of the statement of Vyāsa.

Nor is it correct to claim that this [prohibition] refers to drinking water in which liquor has been slightly mixed such that its smell and taste are still perceptible; for even when mixed, the nature of being *surā* (liquor) does not depart from it, just as the nature of being *ājya* (clarified butter) does not depart from *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter).
For this very reason, those learned in logic have stated that the ritual invocations (*nigama*) should be made as "O drinkers of *ājya*," and not as "O drinkers of *pṛṣadājya*."

Furthermore, as for the statement of Āpastamba: "Having committed theft, drunk liquor, approached the wife of a guru, or committed the murder of a Brahmin, one who eats sparingly at the fourth mealtime, follows the ritual procedure of the *savana*s, and alternates between standing and sitting, removes the sin in three years"—and as for the statement of Aṅgiras: "Those joined with great sins (*mahāpātaka*) are purified in three years"—both of these refer to the same subject matter as the rule: "Or [eating] oil-cakes or grain-dust."

Furthermore, as for the two penances mentioned by Yama: "A Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor, having performed the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, shall again attain equality with Brāhmaṇas; such is the Vedic revelation."
If the best of the twice-born, having drunk liquor, should make a gift of land and never drink it again, he becomes purified once he has undergone the purificatory rite.
Thus, both of these, together with the former, share the same subject matter.
Alternatively, by resorting to a ritual procedure involving additional sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), they may be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpyate*) to the twelve-year penance.

In this case as well, one should apply the following calculation: for children, the elderly, and others, the penance lasts one and a half years; however, for those who have not received initiation (*anupanīta*), it lasts nine months.

As for the statement of Manu: "For the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor, one should eat either grains or oil-cake once at night for a year, wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks, and carrying a banner."
Thus, this [definition] should be understood as referring to the unintentional contact of liquor with the palate alone.
Now, it may be argued that "drinking" (pāna) is defined as the swallowing of a liquid substance;
and swallowing consists of leading the substance down from the throat, not merely the contact with the palate and so forth.
Therefore, how can there be an expiation for drinking in that case?
It is said:
that contact of the palate and other organs, without which the act of drinking cannot be accomplished, is also prohibited by the prohibition of the act of drinking itself.

Therefore, although there is no major offense (*mahāpātaka*) due to the absence of actual drinking, nevertheless, because the prohibition of that [act] also prohibits the contact with the palate and other parts—which are its inseparable constituent elements—the fault remains present; thus, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed required.

This is according to the rule: "One should perform the vow even without killing, if one has come together for the purpose of killing," just as the prescription of expiation occurs because the determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth that constitute the limbs of the act are prohibited by the prohibition of the killing itself.

As for that which is taught by Baudhāyana—that for unintentionally drinking *surā* one should perform a quarter of a year’s *kṛcchra* penance and undergo re-initiation—and that which is taught by Yama: "Having drunk *surā*, having killed a twice-born man, having stolen gold from a twice-born man, or having entered into association with outcasts, a twice-born man shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*."
Thus:
"Having drunk liquor, having killed a twice-born man, having stolen the gold of a twice-born man,
or having entered into association with outcasts, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

Furthermore, according to Bārhaspatya: "Having drunk *gauḍī*, *mādhvī*, *surā*, or *paiṣṭī* liquor, a Brahmin shall perform the *taptakṛcchra*, the *parāka*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances in that order."
Thus:
Having drunk liquor made from molasses, honey, or flour, a Brahmin shall perform the *taptakṛcchra*,
the *parāka*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances in that order.

All three of these [substances] are to be understood as being for consumption in order to alleviate a disease that cannot be cured by any other medicine, because the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is minor.
However, when one eats food that is mixed with *surā* and has become dry in taste, then there is a re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*).
As Manu says:
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything mixed with *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again.
Thus:
"Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or that which is mixed with *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again."

And when one drinks water from a dried liquor vessel, then one should perform what was stated by Śātātapa: "In the case of drinking water from a liquor vessel, there shall be vomiting, the consumption of clarified butter, and a fast for a day and night. As for that which is taught by Baudhāyana: "He who drinks water kept overnight in vessels used for drinking liquor should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* and clarified butter for three days."

Thus, that [penance] is greater because of the stale nature [of the substance]. Furthermore, regarding repeated unintentional consumption, Manu says: "Having drunk water kept in a vessel for *surā* or likewise water kept in a vessel for intoxicants, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights."
Thus:
"Having drunk water that has been in a vessel for *surā* or likewise in a vessel for intoxicants,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights."

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu—"Having drunk water situated in a vessel that held *surā*, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights"—that refers to drinking intentionally. However, regarding repeated intentional practice, Bṛhad-Yama says:
"If any twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held *surā*..."
For twelve days, he should drink Brāhmī and Suvarcalā with milk.
Thus:
"If any twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held liquor,
he must drink the *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* herbs with milk for twelve days."

But upon smelling the breath from the mouth of one who has drunk liquor, a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma becomes purified by performing the Prāṇāyāma three times in water and consuming clarified butter. As for a common man, he must perform the Mānava penance.
Thus, this applies only to one who has performed the Soma sacrifice unintentionally;
however, if it is intentional, the penance is double.
For one who has not drunk the Soma, the penance must be determined accordingly.

But smelling the actual odor of liquor constitutes the smelling of what is unfit to be smelled and of intoxicants; because it causes loss of caste—having intentionally performed an act that causes loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance, but if unintentionally, the *prājāpatya* penance.
Thus, that which was stated by Manu is to be understood. 3.254.
Having thus stated the penance for drinking the primary types of *surā*, he now states the penance for drinking *madya*:
"But having drunk *surā* through ignorance, as well as semen, feces, or urine,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again."

Furthermore, if a Brāhmaṇa drinks *surā* or *madya* liquor through ignorance, thinking it to be water, and those Brāhmaṇas and others who consume semen, feces, or urine—all three of these twice-born castes (*dvijāti-varṇa*) deserve the penance of re-initiation preceded by the *taptakṛcchra*. In this regard, this re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*) applies only to the Brāhmaṇa, since permission for it has been shown for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya.

In this context, the word *surā* refers to intoxicating liquor (*madya*), because the penance prescribed is exceedingly light, and because a twelve-year penance is ordained for intentionally drinking the principal *surā*.

For this very reason, Gautama employs the word *madya* here: "If one drinks intoxicating liquor unintentionally, he should drink hot milk, ghee, or water for three days; that is the *taptakṛcchra* penance. Thereafter, his initiation [into Vedic study] may take place. The same applies to consuming urine, feces, a corpse, semen, or [the aforementioned liquids when they are not hot]. Furthermore, regarding this very subject, Manu has stated: "Having drunk *vāruṇī* unintentionally, one becomes pure through the rite of initiation."
Thus, that [penance] also must be preceded by the *taptakṛcchra*, in accordance with the statement of Gautama.
Furthermore, "re-consecration" (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) means re-initiation (*punarupanayana*);
and that should be performed according to the procedure set forth by Āśvalāyana and others.

As it has been stated: "Now, for one who has previously undergone initiation, there is the shaving of the hair—whether performed or not—and the production of a cloud; the *anirukta* [mantra] is the *paridāna*, and the time is that of the *sāvitrī*: 'We choose that of Savitṛ'.

Regarding intentional drinking of intoxicants, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "For intentional drinking of *asurā* or *surā* when done unknowingly, there is the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*), and a re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
Or, the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed by Śaṅkha: "One who drinks *asurā* or intoxicants should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*."

Regarding the mere entrance of liquor into the mouth, Āpastamba prescribes a penance of six nights: "If one consumes things that are not to be eaten, drunk, or licked, what shall be the expiation for [the consumption of] semen, urine, and excrement?
[The penance involves consuming the leaves] of the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, the palāśa, and the kuśa."
Having drunk their water, one becomes purified in six nights.
Thus:
"If one consumes what is not to be eaten, what is not to be drunk, or what is not to be licked,
how should there be an expiation for [the consumption of] semen, urine, and feces?"
Having drunk the water of these— of the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, the palāśa, and the kuśa— one becomes purified in six nights.
And this refers to intoxicants such as *tāla* and the like.

Regarding the drinking of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors, however, as well as the drinking of *asurā* and *surā* liquors when done unintentionally, Vasiṣṭha has prescribed a re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) accompanied by the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśa*).
But for the intentional drinking of those two, the three-year penance consisting of "oil-cake or grain-particles" (*piṇyākaṃ vā kaṇān vā*) applies.

Regarding the habitual consumption of that [liquor] out of desire, Vasiṣṭha states: "But in the case of the habitual drinking of *surā*, one becomes purified by death from drinking *surā* as red-hot as fire"; this penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) should be understood [to apply here].

The word *surā* in this context does not refer to *paiṣṭī* (liquor made from flour), because it has been shown that a penance ending in death applies even for a single instance of drinking that [specific type]. Regarding the unintentional drinking of water contained in a dry vessel that has been scented with intoxicants, [the rule] spoken by Bṛhad-Yama is as follows:
If a twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held liquor,
he must subsist on milk for three days that has been boiled with the roots of kuśa grass.
Thus:
"If a twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held liquor,
he should subsist for three days on milk boiled with the roots of *kuśa* grass."

Regarding practice [of drinking] out of ignorance, Vasiṣṭha has stated: "If a twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held liquor, [he must fast for three days] upon lotus, udumbara, bilva, palāśa, and kuśa [leaves]."
Having drunk their water, one becomes purified after three nights.
If any twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held liquor,
he must [consume] the leaves of the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, the palāśa, and the kuśa grass.
Having drunk their water, one becomes purified after three nights.
Regarding drinking [liquor] unintentionally, Viṣṇu has stated: "Having drunk water kept in a vessel for liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Regarding intentional repetition, however, Śaṅkha has stated: "Having drunk water kept in a vessel for liquor, one should drink barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) mixed with cow's urine for seven nights."
Regarding the case of absolute appearance (atyantābhāsa), however, Hārīta has stated:
"If a twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel for liquor,
he should drink the *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* [plants] with milk for twelve days."
Thus:
"If a twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel for liquor,
he must drink the *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* plants with milk for twelve days."
In these statements, it has been shown previously that the mention of "twice-born" (dvija) refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas, because there is no prohibition for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
Furthermore, this rule concerns the drinking of water from vessels containing *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* liquor, due to the severity of the expiation;
however, in the case of drinking water from vessels containing *tāla* or other types of liquor, the penance must be determined accordingly. (3.255)
He said to the wife of a twice-born man:
"That Brāhmaṇī who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband;
in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, and a sow."

A wife of the twice-born who drinks liquor, even if she has performed meritorious deeds, does not go to the world of her husband; rather, in this very world, she successively enters the wombs of animals characterized by dogs, vultures, and swine.
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇī" here is an illustration for all wives of whichever twice-born man there may be, according to the principle that "the three [classes] follow the order of their castes.
For this very reason, Manu says:
Half of the body of that man falls [with him] whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no atonement is prescribed.
Half of the body of him whose wife drinks liquor falls away;
for one whose half-body has fallen away, no atonement is prescribed.

Because husband and wife share authority over dharma, artha, and kāma, they constitute a single body; therefore, when the wife of a twice-born man drinks liquor, that half of his body which is his wife falls.
And for that fallen half-body in the form of a wife, no expiation is prescribed.
Consequently, liquor must not be drunk by the wife of a twice-born man, whether she be a Brāhmaṇī or otherwise.

Therefore, since the prohibition "a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*"—in which the gender [of the subject] is not intended to be restrictive—the prohibition is established for the wives of all three castes as well. Nevertheless, the repetition [of the rule] is for the purpose of extending the prohibition against *surā* to the Śūdra wife of a twice-born man.
Consequently, when the wives of twice-born men drink *surā*, half of the prescribed penance must be performed.
But for a Śūdra woman who is the wife of a Śūdra, there is no prohibition at all, as she is exactly like a Śūdra.
However, regarding acts equal to drinking *surā*—such as eating forbidden food—it was stated previously that the penance is half of that for drinking *surā*. (3.256)
He now states the expiation for stealing gold, which follows in due order:
"But one who steals the gold of a Brahmin shall offer a mace to the king, proclaiming his own deed; whether slain by it or released, he is purified."

He who steals gold belonging to a Brahmin should present a wooden pestle to the king, declaring his own deed thus: "I have committed the theft of gold. Since the purpose of presenting the pestle is visible [as a means of execution], the king shall strike him with that pestle.
Whether killed by that king or released, he becomes purified.
By the word "seizing" (*apaharaṇa*), taking possession—whether in the presence or absence of the owner, by force or by theft, and without any cause for ownership such as purchase—is expressed.
Although it is stated generally that "one should hurl a club," nevertheless, because its purpose is to strike, one should take up an iron weapon or the like capable of inflicting a blow.
For this very reason, it was said by Manu:
Taking up a pestle, or a club made of khadira wood,
or a double-edged sword, or even an iron staff.
Thus [it is said].
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood,
or a double-edged sword, or even an iron mace.

Śaṅkha has also stated a specific rule in this regard: "A gold thief, with disheveled hair and wearing wet clothes, should take an iron mace and present himself before the king, saying: 'I have committed this sin; strike me with this mace.
Having been struck by the king, he becomes purified.
And since there is no injunction for repetition, the striking should be performed only once.
For this very reason, it has been stated by Manu:
"Then, taking up a pestle, he himself should strike him once."
Then, taking up a club, he himself should strike him once.
Thus, by being struck once by the king, he who was killed would be purified upon death; or, having been released from death, even while living, he would be purified—this is the meaning.
And so it has been stated by Saṃvarta:
Then, taking up a pestle, he himself should strike him once;
if that thief survives, he is purified from the theft.
Thus it is said.
Then, taking up a club, he himself shall strike him once;
if that thief survives, he is purified from the theft.
As it has been stated regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa: "One who is afflicted by a blow and rendered as if dead is purified even while living."
Now, one might ask: why is this meaning not accepted—that a thief would be purified even if he were released by the king without being struck?

It is said in reply: because in the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra*, it is stated that "the king becomes a sinner if he does not strike," thereby attributing fault to the king who fails to inflict corporal punishment.

If it is argued: "Granted that the king incurs fault; nevertheless, how could a thief not be purified when released by a king out of affection or other motives, despite having transgressed the prohibition? [The answer follows:]...
It is said: if this were so, it would follow that purity occurs without a cause.
Now, it might be argued:

The claim that [the state of being pure] is not without cause because one accepts purity through the performance of twelve-year penances and so forth after liberation is also unsatisfactory; for by stating "the liberated one is pure," it is liberation itself that is declared to be the cause of purity.
Therefore, the former explanation alone is superior.
That is to say, one may be purified even while living, or else by death.

Furthermore, this penance ending in death applies to any thief who steals gold, not exclusively to a Brāhmaṇa; for in the occasional injunction stating "the stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold," no specific distinction is made, and because there is no difference in their status as perpetrators of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*) among Kṣatriyas and others, and because no other expiation is prescribed for them.

Furthermore, as for the mention of the term "Brahmin" (*vipra*) in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] in the passage, "A Brahmin who commits the theft of gold," that is merely an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of any human being at all; for it is that very person who is the subject under discussion in the statement, "The man undergoes penance," and because no specific qualification is provided in the causal statement, "Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife. Therefore, even though the word "Brahmin" is heard in the conditional statement dependent upon that [causal basis], namely, "A Brahmin who commits the theft of gold," it is proper to regard it as an elliptical indication only, just as in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, the mention of "rice grains" (*taṇḍula*) in the sentence "Whose sacrificial offering (*havis*)" refers to the sacrificial material in general.

And this execution by the king applies to one other than a Brāhmaṇa, for it is forbidden to kill a Brāhmaṇa even if he is established in every kind of sin, according to the Mānava [Dharmaśāstra]. Even if, somehow, the prohibition is transgressed and he is executed by the king, he nevertheless becomes pure; "A thief is purified by death, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone."

(Manu Smṛti 11.101): "A thief is purified by execution, or a Brāhmaṇa by austerity alone. Since this passage explicitly states that even a Brāhmaṇa is purified by execution, the particle *eva* (alone) in the phrase "or by austerity alone" does not prohibit execution; rather, its purpose is to indicate that purification may occur through austerity by itself as well.

If killing is prohibited, then the statement of an alternative—that it may be performed "by austerity alone"—is untenable. Nor can this statement of an alternative be intended to refer to punishment (*daṇḍa*), because that has not been specified.

Furthermore, according to the maxim that "alternatives apply only to things serving the same purpose," an alternative is possible only for those things that serve a single purpose, as in the case of rice and barley.

Furthermore, there is no identity of purpose between punishment (*daṇḍa*) and austerity (*tapas*), because punishment has the purpose of subduing, whereas austerity is the cause for the destruction of evil.

Nor is it possible to establish an option (*vikalpa*) between the general rule, "A thief is purified by execution," and the specific rule, "A Brāhmaṇa [is purified] by austerity alone," on the grounds that execution applies to the general case while austerity applies to the specific case.
For there can be no option such as, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, or buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya"; therefore, both rules must indeed have the same scope.

Alternatively, there is no prohibition even for a Kṣatriya; for after Manu has stated, "A Brāhmaṇa who commits the theft of gold," he prescribes the act of killing by referring specifically to the aforementioned Brāhmaṇa through the use of the pronoun "him": "Having seized a club, the king himself shall strike him once. Thus, the injunction "one must never kill a Brāhmaṇa" is also logically consistent as referring to a form of punishment consisting of killing that is distinct from penance (*prāyaścitta*). Furthermore, this penance ending in death applies to the case of intentional theft of gold, for it has been declared by the wise: "That penance which ends in death..."
But that [expiation] is to be understood as applying to a sin committed intentionally; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Madhyama-Aṅgiras.

And here, the word *suvarṇa* refers to the substance gold as qualified by a specific measure, not merely to the genus [gold]. "The mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*; eight of those are a *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*."
Six of those *gauras* make one *yava*; three of those *yavas* make one *māṣa*;
five of those *māṣas* make one *kṛṣṇala*; and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.
Thus, since the word *suvarṇa* is technically defined as gold weighing sixteen *māṣas*,

it is appropriate that in usages such as "the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s *suvarṇa* is a mortal sin" (*mahāpātaka*), only gold of that established measure is intended; for the purpose of establishing a specific measure is for a visible (practical) end,
and there is no traditional rule (*smṛti*) regarding a measure intended for an invisible (transcendental) end.
Nor is it for the sake of worldly convention, because the activity of the authors of the *Smṛtis* is not directed toward that end.
For this very reason, it has been stated by those who know the *Nyāya*: "Technical names (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) present themselves at the time of performing the action.
Likewise, it has been stated regarding the passage "the *ājya* hymns are fifteen" that names are meaningful through their connection with qualities and results.

Nor is it correct to say that there is a traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) regarding the measurement of the staff merely for its application; for there is no evidence that its purpose is limited to that alone.
Therefore, since there is no distinction, it is logical that it serves as a supplement to everything.

Furthermore, since the staff is for the purpose of subduing (*damana*), and subduing is accomplished even without a specific measurement, the traditional rule concerning measurement is not of much use.
However, regarding matters such as being a "great sinner" (*mahāpātakin*), which can be understood solely through scriptural testimony (*śabda*), recollection is absolutely necessary.
Therefore, it is logical that the status of being a great sinner, as well as the prescription of penances such as those ending in death, applies only to the theft of gold weighing sixteen *māṣas*.
On the other hand, the theft of gold weighing two or three *māṣas* is merely a minor offense (*upapātaka*), just like the theft of gold belonging to a Kṣatriya or others.

Furthermore, since a different expiation is prescribed for stealing gold of a quantity less than a *suvarṇa*, it is logical that the expiations ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) and so forth apply only to the theft of gold of that specific measure.
Thus it has been stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
If even a hair-tip's worth [of gold] is stolen, one should perform a breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma);
likewise, for a louse-egg's worth, a wise man should perform three breath-restraints.
For a sin the size of a black mustard seed, one should perform four breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and recite the Gāyatrī mantra eight thousand times for the purification of that evil.
If [the theft] is the size of a white mustard seed, one should indeed recite the Sāvitrī mantra for one day;
if it is the size of a barley grain of gold, the expiation lasts for two days.
Having stolen even a single *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala* of gold, the best of the twice-born should perform the *sāntapana* penance for the removal of that sin.
Having stolen even a single *māṣa* of gold, the best of the twice-born is purified in three months by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel.
For the theft of gold, one must subsist on barley-gruel for a year; beyond that, the penance is known to be either ending with death or the vow prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin.

And this practice of subsisting on barley-gruel for one year pertains to the theft of slightly less than a *suvarṇa* of gold; for regarding the theft of a full *suvarṇa*, the Great Smṛtis such as those of Manu prescribe a twelve-year penance.
"Those lowest of men who seize their own property by force or through lust—for those plunderers, a punishment ending in death is declared here."
The intended meaning is that this applies even for amounts less than the measure of a *suvarṇa*.

Furthermore, this penance for theft must be performed only after the stolen wealth has been restored to its owner; for in the case of theft involving gold or other property belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, it is said:
"The stolen property must be returned to the owner by the thief, along with an additional eleventh part."
For it is so stated in the Smṛti; likewise, from the Smṛti of Manu: "He who has paid that [debt] should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of his own purification.
It is also stated in the section on punishments: "In the remaining cases, he should be made to pay eleven times that amount, and that wealth shall belong to him [the creditor]."
Thus it is said:
"In the remaining cases, he shall be made to pay eleven times [the value], and that property shall belong to him."
Alternatively, if the king is unable to kill him due to extreme weakness, then that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "A thief with disheveled hair should supplicate the king;
then the king should give him an udumbara weapon, with which he may take his own life.
It is known from scripture that by dying [in this way], he becomes purified."
The *audumbara* is made of copper.

As for that second penance which was stated by him—"One who is clean-shaven and anointed with cow's ghee should cause himself to perish by means of a fire of cow-dung, starting from his feet; it is known that he becomes purified through death"—that too refers to the theft of property belonging to a Guru, a learned *śrotriya*, or a Brahmin engaged in a sacrifice, or to a thief who is a Kṣatriya or of similar status.
In that context, "clean-shaven" (*niṣkālaka*) denotes one whose hair, beard, and body hair have been removed.
Or likewise, by the performance of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other rites.
Thus, after describing penance ending in death, Pracetas stated: "Or, having sacrificed with the horse sacrifice or the *gosava*, one shall be purified."
Or, having performed either the Aśvamedha or the Gosava sacrifice, he may be purified; and this refers to one who has stolen [the property] of a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or others. 3.257.
He states another expiation:
"Without having informed the king, one may become pure by performing the vow for a liquor-drinker;
or one may give gold equal to one's own weight, or do what pleases a Brāhmaṇa."
Having failed to report one's own theft to the king, one becomes purified by performing the twelve-year vow prescribed for a liquor-drinker (*surāpa*).

It is stated that this "vow of the liquor-drinker" is intended to exclude the carrying of a skull-bowl with a corpse-head as its banner. And this refers to the case of unintentional action: "This purification is declared for having killed a twice-born man unintentionally."
Thus, because there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the twelve-year penance itself even for an act committed unintentionally.
Now, an objection is raised: since theft is not possible at all when committed unintentionally, how can that [penance] have such a case as its object?
It is said in reply:
