When one steals gold or similar items that are sewn into the hem of a garment out of ignorance, or steals them with the notion that they are some other substance such as silver, and having so stolen them, either gives them away to another or destroys them immediately without returning them to the owner, then an unintentional theft (*akāmataḥ apahāraḥ*) certainly occurs.

However, this expiation does not apply to the theft of copper or other metals that have been transformed into the appearance of gold through processes such as *rasavedha* (mercury transmutation), because the primary species (*mukhyajāti*) is absent.
Furthermore, the properties of the primary do not apply to the secondary merely on the basis of similarity to the primary.

Even if one steals such a thing that is not gold under the mistaken impression that it is gold, nevertheless this expiation does not apply, precisely because it is the theft of what is not gold. Nor should it be argued that a fault exists here on the grounds of the analogy: "If he has been commissioned for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, even if he does not kill him. For that [analogy] refers to a case where one has set out against someone who is not a Brāhmaṇa; it is not the scope of the rule regarding one who has been commissioned.
And regarding that mental sin which one has contemplated, one should mentally recite the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the *praṇava*;
one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with each *vyāhṛti*.

In the case of such an offense being committed, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights. As it was stated by Vyāsa: "A thief should perform this very vow reduced by one quarter," this nine-year period should be understood [to apply].

But when one steals for the sake of protecting a family emaciated by hunger in such a manner, then that twice-born man should perform a six-year sacrifice such as the Svarjit prescribed by Atri, or undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords; or he should practice the Kṛcchra penance for six years, or perform a sacrifice, or wander to sacred fords—the wise man is thus liberated from the theft.
Thus:
"A twice-born man shall either perform the Kṛcchra penance for six years, or sacrifice with a ritual, or wander to sacred fords; by these means, the wise man is liberated from theft."

But when, immediately after the theft, one feels remorse, thinking "Alas, what a tragedy! I have done this," and then returns the object or abandons it, then the rule of Āpastamba regarding subsisting on food taken at every fourth mealtime for three years, or the three-year penance of Aṅgiras called the *vajra*, should be observed. Now, an objection: since the meaning of the verbal root *apahṛ* (to steal) is already accomplished through the returning or abandoning, how can there be such a small penance?
On the other hand, if it were not accomplished, then there would simply be an absence of penance, rather than a reduction in the penance.
Not so.

Since theft extends until its fruit—namely, enjoyment—is reached, if it ceases before enjoyment, the full purpose of the theft is absent; thus, a lesser penance is indeed appropriate, just as in the case of one who has drunk and then vomited an undrinkable substance.

But if this were the case, then even when an object is forcibly seized from the hand of a thief, since there is no fruit characterized by enjoyment, the consequence would follow that the penance must be light.
Not so; for there is no spontaneous inclination toward abandoning that [gold], whereas there is a spontaneous inclination toward its removal when it culminates in the acquisition of a fruit.

However, in the case of one who steals gold mixed with silver, copper, or the like, this light penance does not apply; because even in a mixture, the nature of gold (suvarṇatva) does not depart, just as the nature of clarified butter (ājyatva) does not depart from *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter).
Therefore, in that case, it is proper that only the twelve-year penance applies.
Now, it is argued that since the light penance (*laghuprāyaścitta*) and so forth constitute a different substance altogether, the light penance is prescribed [here].
If that were the case, then the three-year penance and others would not apply there simply because the object is not gold; rather, only the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) would apply.
Furthermore, another rule stated by Āpastamba is: "Having committed theft or having drunk liquor, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year."
Thus, this refers to a substance exceeding the measure of a *māṣa* but less than a *suvarṇa*.
As for that which was stated by Sumantu—"A thief of gold should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Sāvitrī mantra for one month;

fasting three nights each day, he becomes purified through the *taptakṛcchra* penance"—that is to be treated as an alternative (*vikalpyate*) to the previously mentioned expiation for the theft of gold weighing a *māṣa*.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by that same author—that "one who steals gold becomes purified by subsisting on air for twelve nights"—this should be understood to apply to one who has engaged in mental theft but has spontaneously desisted from the desire to take it.
In this case as well, it should be understood that the penance is only half for women, children, the elderly, and so forth.

And regarding those acts which were established as equal to the theft of gold—such as "the stealing of horses, gems, humans, women, land, and milch-cows"—for these too, only half [of the prescribed penance] should be performed.

Furthermore, as for the statement in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "A twice-born man who, out of delusion, steals silver weighing ten *gadyāṇas* or more, up to a hundred, shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* vow, doubling it for every subsequent ten."
But for gold exceeding one thousand [units], the procedure prescribed above is remembered as triple;
however, for all other metals and ores, one should perform the Parāka penance.
For the theft of grain, a Kṛcchra penance is prescribed; for sesame seeds, an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa) is traditionally taught.
For stealing gems, a Brahmin should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Thus:
Having stolen silver through delusion, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
for an amount exceeding ten gadyāṇas up to one hundred, he shall perform double that penance.
But for gold exceeding one thousand [units], the procedure prescribed above is remembered as triple;
however, for all other metals and ores, one should perform the Parāka penance.
For stealing grains, a Kṛcchra penance is prescribed; for stealing sesame seeds, an Aindava is traditionally taught.
Upon stealing gems, a Brahmin shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

Furthermore, that [penance] is intended to establish a penance equal to that for stealing gold even when stealing silver exceeding one thousand *gadyāṇas*, but not for the purpose of precluding it [in cases of lesser value].
Moreover, the *cāndrāyaṇa* prescribed for the theft of gems should be understood to apply to the theft of gems valued at less than one thousand *gadyāṇas*;
however, for those of higher value, it is equal to the theft of gold. (3.258)
He states the expiation for one who violates the Guru’s bed, which follows in the sequence of the topical outline:
"Having seized his testicles and having cut them off, he should lie upon a heated iron bed together with an iron woman; then, in the southwest, he should cast off his body."
The term *gurutalpagah* (one who violates the teacher’s bed), which occurs in the verse to be cited as "equal [is] the violator of the teacher’s bed," is connected here.

On a heated iron bed made of black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*) that has been rendered red-hot like fire—prepared in such a way that it is capable of causing death—the violator of the teacher’s bed shall lie down together with a heated female effigy made of iron.
Having thus slept, he shall cast off his body.
"Should die" means:

he should perform the act after proclaiming his own deed, saying, "I have committed incest with the teacher's wife," according to the Smṛti of Manu: "The violator of the Guru’s bed, having confessed his sin...

Likewise, he should do so while embracing a woman, according to the Smṛti of Vṛddha-Hārīta: "The violator of the Guru’s bed, having made an image of a woman out of clay or iron and heated to the color of fire, becomes purified by embracing it upon a bed of black iron."

Likewise, it should be performed by one who has shaved his hair and beard and is anointed with clarified butter; for the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha states: "It is known that one who is naked and anointed with clarified butter becomes purified through death after embracing that heated iron image (sūrmī) or one made of clay. Nor does this contradict the rule: "One who has violated the Guru’s bed, having confessed his sin, should lie down upon a red-hot iron bed; he is purified by death after embracing a blazing iron image."

Based on this statement of Manu, one should not suspect that the heated iron bed and the embrace of the heated iron woman are two independent penances. Since the expectation arises as to "where" one should lie with an iron woman, and because the phrase "on a heated iron bed" satisfies that expectation, they are understood to be mutually dependent; therefore, it is proper to regard them as a single ritual procedure (*ekakalpa*).

Alternatively, having himself cut off and severed his two testicles along with the penis, and holding them in his joined palms, he should go in a straight path toward the south-western direction—between the southern and western quarters—until his body falls, and there cast off his frame.
As Manu has said:
"Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms..."
One should proceed toward the southwestern direction in a straight line until one falls down.
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms,
he should walk straight toward the region of Nirṛti until he collapses.
One must proceed without looking back; for the Smṛti of Śaṅkha and Likhita states: "Having cut off the penis and testicles with a razor, one should go without looking behind.

Walking in this manner, wherever he is obstructed by a wall or the like, he should remain there until death; for the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha states: "Having cut off the penis along with the testicles and holding them in his joined palms, he should go facing south; wherever he is stopped, there he should remain until the dissolution [of his body]. This same penalty applies here as well.
As Nārada said:
"He who approaches any one of these women is called a violator of the Guru's bed;
in that case, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained."
Thus, even the cutting off of the penis and other organs for the purpose of punishment also serves the purpose of destroying sin.
It was with reference to this very punishment ending in death that Manu said:
"But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings..."
Being stainless, they go to heaven, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
Thus:
"But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds."

Furthermore, there is indeed expiation through a monetary fine; for all castes performing the prescribed expiation, they shall not be branded on the forehead by the king, but shall instead be made to pay the highest amercement.
Because it has been stated by him thus:
"By the performance of either one of these two [penances] ending in death, the violator of the Guru's bed is purified.
And here, the word *guru* refers primarily to the father, as [it is said]: "He who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the rule..."
And that brahmin who honors him with food is called his guru.

Thus, because in this statement by Manu—which is intended to establish the status of a *guru*—the status of being a *guru* is attributed specifically to the biological father (*janaka*) who performs the *niṣeka* (conception) and other rites;
and because the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*) has stated with reference to the rites beginning with *niṣeka*: "He is a *guru* who, having performed the [initiatory] rite, imparts the Veda to him.

Now, one might object that the word *guru* is seen to be used elsewhere as well, such as in the passage: "Having initiated the pupil, the *guru*... and so on, [referring to the *ācārya*]; and: "He who benefits another with what he has heard, whether little or much..."
"One should know him also as a *guru* here"—this refers to the *upādhyāya*.

Vyāsa has also shown the application [of this term] here: "The *gurus* are the mother, the father, the husband, the noble one (*ārya*), the giver of knowledge, the elder brother, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the protector from fear, and the giver of food.

Nor is there the fault of postulating multiple meanings, because the quality of being worthy of honor—which constitutes the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *guru*—is continuous throughout all these cases.

And its status as the *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for application) has been demonstrated by the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*) himself, who, beginning with the words "These are to be honored according to seniority" and concluding with "The mother is weightier than these," establishes that she is the one to be honored. Nor should it be argued that the father alone is primary because of the statement, "An *ācārya* is ten times more venerable than a *upādhyāya*, and a father is a hundred times more venerable than an *ācārya*," which expresses the father's superiority over the *ācārya* who is superior to the *upādhyāya*; for such superiority is no less evident in the case of the *ācārya* as well, since it is said: "Between the biological progenitor and the giver of the *brahman*, the father who gives the *brahman* is weightier."
Thus it is said:
"Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable.
And it has also been stated by Gautama: "The teacher is the most excellent among gurus."
Furthermore, if preeminence were asserted merely on the basis of being superior, then by the statement "a thousand," the mother alone would possess the status of a guru.
Therefore, it is logical that all [ancestors] are gurus, and thus approaching their wives constitutes "approaching the wife of a guru" (*gurvaṅganāgamana*). To this, it is replied:
The statement of Manu, "the [rites] beginning with impregnation" (*niṣekādīni*), is intended to establish the status of the biological father as a teacher (*guru*) because it has no other purpose.
On the other hand, the statements of Vyāsa and Gautama are intended for another purpose, serving as praise by way of being supplementary to the rules concerning service and worship.

Therefore, since the statement of Manu—"the [rites] beginning with impregnation"—is devoted to establishing the status of the teacher, it is settled that the primary status of the teacher belongs to the father alone.

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha stated that the penance for violating the Guru’s bed applies by extension to the wives of the teacher, saying: "And likewise in the case of the teacher's son, pupil, and wife.
Similarly, Jātūkarṇya and others have also stated: "One should perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed in the case of the wives of the teacher and so forth," and so on.
If the teacher and others were indeed the primary gurus, then since the vow would be obtained through their instruction alone, the extended application (*atideśa*) would be entirely purposeless.
Furthermore, Saṃvarta has explicitly mentioned the taking of the father’s wife:
"Having ascended to his father’s wives, excluding his mother, that lowest of men..."
Thus [it is said].
Having ascended to the wives of his father, excluding his mother,
the lowest of men [is so described] in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* as well.
"But he who, having recognized her as his father's wife, approaches a woman of the same caste...
[repeated].
"But he who, having recognized her as his father's wife, approaches a woman of the same caste..."
For this reason as well, the father alone—who performs the rites of impregnation (*niṣeka*) and so forth—is the primary *guru*.
And that status of being a *guru* is not distinguished among the four castes, because the role of performing the rites of impregnation and so forth is common to all.
Therefore, in the statement "that Brahmin is called the *guru*," the mention of the "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, sexual intercourse with the wife of one's father alone constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). And "intercourse" is defined as lasting until the emission of the final element;
consequently, if one desists before that point, one does not incur the status of a mortal sinner.
In this regard, two penances ending in death have been stated, beginning with "there, on a bed of heated iron, together with one made of iron," and so forth.

These should be understood to apply when [the act] is committed unintentionally toward one's own mother, but when committed intentionally toward her co-wife who is of the same caste or of a higher caste; for: "He who, having recognized his father’s wife as being of the same caste, approaches her, or even approaches his own mother without recognizing her—unless he dies, he shall not attain purification."
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.

However, in the case of intentionally committing [the act] with one's mother, the rule of Vasiṣṭha should be observed: "Having been cleansed of all hair and anointed with ghee, he should burn himself with a fire of cow-dung, starting from his feet.
This same penance applies even to repeated unintentional practice.
But surely, one who approaches the co-wife of his mother, a sister, the daughter of his teacher,
the wife of his teacher, or his own daughter, is a violator of the Guru's bed.

Since this is stated as an extended application (*atideśa*), it would be improper for the penance prescribed by direct injunction (*aupadeśika*) to apply to the case of approaching the wife of one’s mother’s co-wife.

It is replied: because of the very statement, “the father’s wife of the same class” (*pitṛbhāryāṃ savarṇām*), and due to the inclusion of the term “of the same class,” this extended application refers specifically to a co-wife of a lower caste; thus, there is no contradiction.
And this [designation] applies only to the primary son;
as for the others, however, they possess merely the function of a son, but not the status of being a son. As Manu said:

The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, who are appropriate according to their respective orders, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.
Thus:
"The wise declare these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, who are appropriate as they are, to be substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites."
In that regard, if the engagement occurs by mutual desire, the first penance is lying on a heated iron bed.

However, if he incites her himself, the second penance is "having seized and cut off his testicles," because it has been stated that the severity of the penance increases with the intensity of the motive.
But for one who is incited by her, the penance prescribed by Manu—either lying on a heated iron bed or embracing a glowing iron image (sūrmī)—should be understood as applicable.

As for that twelve-year penance which was stated by Śaṅkha: "Sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, he should eat only once a day; then, when twelve years have passed..."
The stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow.
Thus, sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, and subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits, he should eat only once a day; and when twelve years have passed, [he attains his goal].
The stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow.
This should be understood as applying to the unintentional act of approaching a father’s wife who is of the same caste or of a superior caste.
In that very case, for one who has intentionally engaged but desists before the emission of semen, the penance is six years;

however, if it was unintentional, it is three years. But in the case of the mother, for one who has intentionally engaged but desists before the emission of semen, twelve years should be prescribed; if unintentional, six years. Thus it should be determined.
As for that which was stated by Saṃvarta—"Having ascended to the wife of his father, excluding his mother, the lowest of men...

and so forth, prescribing a *taptakṛcchra* for the mere act of mounting—this should be understood to apply to cases involving the wives of a guru of a lower caste, provided that ejaculation has not occurred. (3.259)
He states another expiation:
"One who has violated the Guru's bed should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year,
or he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, or he should study the Vedic Saṃhitā for three months."
Alternatively, one should perform for three years (*samāḥ*)—that is, for three years—the *prājāpatya* penance, whose characteristics will be described later.
This should be understood to apply to the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who intentionally approaches the wife of his Guru when she belongs to the Śūdra caste.

However, when he unintentionally approaches the wife of his Guru who is of the same caste (*savarṇā*) and is already unchaste, then he should perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances accompanied by the recitation of the Veda.

Regarding intentional engagement in that very act, the *Auśanasa* [Smṛti] states: "One who has sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru shall perform the vow of a Brahmin-slayer for one year, or the *taptakṛcchra* penance for six months.

However, in the case of approaching a Kṣatriya woman intentionally, the rule of Yājñavalkya applies; because of the extension of the vow for violating the guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) to the cases of "the mother's co-wife, a sister, or likewise the teacher’s daughter," the penance lasts for nine years.

And this extended application (*atideśika*) does not concern the case of approaching the wife of a teacher who is of the same caste (*savarṇa*), because in that case, a penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) is prescribed for intentional acts, while a twelve-year penance is prescribed for unintentional acts.

Therefore, it is logical that this refers only to the case of a Kṣatriya woman and others. In that very context, a penance ending in death applies to repeated intentional practice: "Having intentionally gone again to the wife of his teacher, a twice-born man [who is] the daughter of a Kṣatriya..."
Having cut off the penis together with the testicles, he becomes pure upon death.

Thus, according to the *Kaṇvasmaraṇa*. Regarding this very subject, when one does not wish to perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), then the corporal punishment prescribed by Yājñavalkya—"Having cut off his organ, he shall be executed; the same applies to the woman who acted with desire"—is to be understood as taking the place of the expiation.
However, for intentional sexual intercourse with the wife of one's guru who is a Vaiśya woman, the penance is six years.

For this very reason, another Smṛti states that if the son of a Brāhmaṇa has intercourse with his mother who is a Kṣatriya woman, the penance is twelve years reduced by one quarter (pādahāni). The same applies to women of other castes as well.
This is the meaning:

for the son of a Brāhmaṇa who approaches a Kṣatriya woman who is his mother’s co-wife, the penance lasts for twelve years minus one quarter (nine years); for that same person approaching such a Vaiśya woman, it is six years; but for approaching a Śūdra woman, the penance is three years. Likewise, for the son of a Kṣatriya approaching a Vaiśya woman who is his mother, it is nine years; but for approaching a Śūdra woman, it is six years.

The same applies to the son of a Vaiśya woman as well. However, in the case of intentional repetition with a Vaiśya woman, the penance ends only in death: "But he who intentionally approaches the wife of his guru, a Vaiśya woman, again and again, shall be purified from that sin only after having the tip of his penis cut off."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Laugākṣi:

"But in the case of intentional repeated practice with a Śūdra woman, the penance is twelve years: 'Having intentionally gone again to a Guru’s Śūdra wife, a composed Brāhmaṇa of uncorrupted soul shall observe the vow of celibacy for twelve years.'"
Thus, according to the *Upamanyu-smaraṇa*,

in the case of unintentionally approaching the wife of one's guru who is of the Kṣatriya caste, the penance prescribed by Yama— consisting of eating at the eighth meal-time for three years— should be observed: "Eating only at the eighth meal-time, always remaining celibate and observant of his vow,
moving between standing and sitting postures, and approaching water three times a day."
Sleeping on the ground for three years, he may dispel that sin.
Thus: eating at the eighth meal-time, always remaining a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) and observant of his vow,
passing his time by alternating between standing and sitting, and approaching water for ritual sipping three times a day.
Sleeping on the ground for three years, he may dispel that sin.

Regarding this very practice, Jātūkarṇya has stated: "If one unintentionally approaches the wife of a guru who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya, he shall be purified by cutting off only his testicles, whether he remains alive or dies."
Thus:
"If one has approached the wife of a guru who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya again, even unintentionally,
he shall be purified by cutting off his testicles, whether he remains alive or dies."
Regarding unintentional intercourse with a Vaiśya woman, one should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra; this is precisely the rule of Yājñavalkya.
And likewise, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"In the case of approaching the wife of a Guru, and likewise in approaching the wife of a father..."
But for three years, if done unintentionally, one should constantly perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Thus:
"In the case of approaching the wife of a guru, and likewise upon approaching the wife of one's father,
one should constantly perform the *kṛcchra* penance for three years if it was done unintentionally."
Regarding that same case of repeated practice, Hārīta has stated the penance ending in death for celibacy:
"If a Brahmin, deluded by ignorance, practices [sexual intercourse] with a Vaiśya woman belonging to his teacher,
he shall observe the six-limbed vow of celibacy for the remainder of his life."
Thus, a Brahmin who, deluded by ignorance, has practiced [sexual intercourse] with a Vaiśya woman against the will of his guru,
shall observe the six-limbed vow of celibacy for the remainder of his life.
If one unintentionally approaches the wife of a guru who is a Śūdra woman,
he should, with a concentrated mind, wear a staff made from a bedstead, dress in rags, let his beard grow, and perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year in a secluded forest.
Thus it is said:
"Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard grown, in a solitary forest,
one should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind."

Alternatively, one who has approached the wife of a guru becomes purified by embracing a thorny branch for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing at the three periods of the day, and subsisting on alms; thus one should perform what was stated by Sumantu.
In the case of repeated practice of that same act, the penance prescribed by Manu applies:
"Or, with senses restrained, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months."
Thus:
"Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months.
This refers to the case stated by Vyāghra regarding one who has intentionally engaged with a Kṣatriya woman and desists before the emission of semen.
A Brahmin who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of his preceptor (guru) shall perform the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and likewise the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances for three months.
Thus:
"A Brahmin who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of his preceptor (guru) shall perform the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and likewise the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances for three months."
In this matter, the established rule is as follows:
for one who has been incited by her, the performance of the Prājāpatya penance for three months is prescribed;
likewise, for one who proceeded out of mutual desire, the performance of the Atikṛcchra penance for that same duration is required.
Furthermore, if she has been incited by him, the performance of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances is likewise for that same duration.
In that very case, for one who proceeds intentionally, prior to the emission of semen, that which was stated by Kaṇva should be observed:
"The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra."
If a twice-born man, out of ignorance, approaches the wife of his guru—who is a Kṣatriya—only once;
Thus: "A twice-born man who, through ignorance, has once approached the wife of his guru or a Kṣatriya woman, [must perform] the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra."
For one incited by her, it is an *atikṛcchra*;
for one who engages out of mutual desire, it is a *taptakṛcchra*;
but when she has been incited by him, it is a *cāndrāyaṇa*.

Regarding one who has engaged with a Vaiśya woman out of lust but desists before the emission of semen, Kaṇva has stated: "Having intentionally approached his teacher’s Vaiśya wife once, a twice-born man should perform the Taptakṛcchra, the Parāka, and likewise the Sāntapana penances for one month."
Thus, having intentionally approached the wife of his guru who is a Vaiśya only once, a twice-born man shall perform the Taptakṛcchra, the Parāka, and likewise the Sāntapana penances for one month.
In this case, if both engage in the act by mutual desire, it is a *taptakṛcchra*.
If she was incited by him, it is a *parāka*. If he was incited by her, it is a *sāntapana*.
Regarding that very case, Prajāpati said for one who has acted unintentionally:
"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, has once approached his teacher's Vaiśya wife, shall not eat for five nights, or likewise for seven or eight."
Thus it is said:
"A twice-born man who, through ignorance, has once approached his teacher’s Vaiśya wife, shall likewise not eat for five, seven, or eight nights."
If she incites him, it is five nights;
if they both engage out of mutual desire, it is seven nights;
if he incites her, it is eight nights.

Regarding one who has intentionally engaged with a Śūdra woman but desists before the emission of semen, Jābāli says: "A Brahmin who, having intentionally approached his teacher’s Śūdra wife once, shall perform either an Atikṛcchra, a Taptakṛcchra, or likewise a Parāka penance."
Thus:
"Having intentionally approached the Śūdra wife of his guru even once, a Brāhmaṇa should perform either an Atikṛcchra, a Taptakṛcchra, or likewise a Parāka penance."
For one incited by her, it is an *atikṛcchra*.
If the act proceeds from the desire of both, it is a *taptakṛcchra*.
If she was incited by him, it is a *parāka*.
In that very case, for one who has engaged [with the teacher's wife] unintentionally, a Brahmin, being composed, should perform the Dairghatamas,
the Prājāpatya, the Sāntapana, or a seven-night fast,
having approached the Guru’s Śūdra wife even once.
Thus:
Having approached the Śūdra wife of his guru even once, a composed Brāhmaṇa shall perform the Prājāpatya penance, the Sāntapana penance, and a fast for seven nights.
For one who is incited by her, the penance is a *prājāpatya*;
if the act proceeds from the desire of both, it is a *sāntapana*;
and if she was incited by him, it is a fast for seven nights.
In this very manner, the determination of the scope of other Smṛti statements should also be inferred.
And just as for men, so too for women, the status of being a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin) is here without distinction.
For instance, Kātyāyana says:
Thus have the offenses and the purification for those who have fallen been declared;
this same rule is prescribed for women as well when they are similarly involved.
Thus, the fault and the purification for those who have fallen have been declared;
this same rule is recorded as applicable even to women who have committed such acts.

If she too should proceed out of lust, her punishment is no different from that ending in death. For this very reason, having stated that the punishment for a man ends in death, the Lord of Yogis has likewise shown that for a woman who acts with desire, the punishment is the cutting off of the organ and death.
Thus [it is said].
But regarding unintentional [offenses], it has been stated by Manu:
"This very same vow must be performed even for women who have fallen."
Thus it is said:
"This very same vow must be performed even for women who have fallen [from their status]. The twelve-year penance itself must be performed by applying the principle of reduction by one half."

Furthermore, those acts which are equal to violating the Guru’s bed are traditionally recorded as follows: [intercourse] with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own uterine kin, women of the lowest castes, women of the same lineage (sagotra), and the wives of sons is considered equal to violating the Guru’s bed.
Thus these have been explained, as well as those who are the subjects of the extended application (atideśa): the father’s sister, the mother’s maternal uncle’s wife, and even the daughter-in-law;
likewise the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and the teacher’s daughter.
But he who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is one who has violated the bed of his guru.
Thus they have been explained; regarding these, when practiced intentionally for more than one night, the penance should be understood to be six years and nine years respectively.
In this very same case, if there is excessive practice done intentionally, the penance ends with death.
And so says Bṛhadyama:
Having emitted semen into virgins, women of one's own kin, women of the lowest castes, female sapindas, or the wives of one's offspring, the abandonment of life is prescribed as the penance.
Thus:
"Having emitted semen into virgins, into women of one's own kin, into women of the lowest castes,
or into the wives of sapinda-relations, the abandonment of life is prescribed."
And among these, the outcastes (antyajas) are the Caṇḍāla, the Śvapaca, the Kṣattṛ, the Sūta, the Vaidehika, as well as the Māgadha and the Āyogava; these seven are the Antyāvasāyins.
Thus, those shown by Madhyamāṅgiras are to be understood;
however, those described as "washermen, leather-workers," and so forth, are not included, because light penances have been prescribed for them.

Likewise, by approaching women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, or by eating their food, or by accepting gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal to them.

Thus, by Manu himself, who establishes the equality [of the offender] with Caṇḍālas and others, it is shown that for excessive repetition committed intentionally, the penance ending in death (*maraṇāntika*) is prescribed.
For it is said: "By excessively repeating intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman out of ignorance, one falls; therefore, one should perform the twelve-year penance for a fallen person (*patita*).
And by excessively repeating it intentionally, one attains equality with Caṇḍālas."

Therefore, one should perform the penance ending in death for more than twelve years; this refers to the case of long-term practice. However, in the case of practice for only one night, the penance lasts for three years.
As Manu has said:
"Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by constantly subsisting on alms and reciting [sacred texts] for three years."
Thus:
"Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [the Veda] for three years."

In this context, by the word *vṛṣalī*, the Caṇḍālī is denoted; for it is said: "The Caṇḍālī, the unchaste woman, the prostitute, the girl who has reached puberty, and she who is married to a man of the same lineage—these five are proclaimed as *vṛṣalīs*."
Thus, because the term *vṛṣalī* is seen used for a *caṇḍālī* in another Smṛti text,
[it follows that] *bandhakī* means a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*).
But how, then, is repetition understood here?
It is said:

because we observe the use of the instrumental case in the phrase "that which one performs in a single night" (*ekarātreṇa*), which expresses both an uninterrupted connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) and a completion (*apavarga*).
Since an uninterrupted connection with "a single night" is impossible for the act of going without repetition, the repetition of the going is understood.

Therefore, the previously mentioned penances—ranging from a single night up to the twelve-year vow prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed, as well as the penance ending in death—apply to cases of repeated practice over a long period.

However, when one approaches a Caṇḍālī or similar women even once, whether intentionally or unintentionally, then: "Having eaten the food of, or having gone to the women of, Caṇḍālas and Pulkasas, one should perform a Kṛcchra for one year if intentional; if unintentional, two Aindavas."
Thus, what was stated by Yama regarding the performance of the *kṛcchra* penance for one year and two *cāndrāyaṇa*s should be understood as applying respectively [to the cases mentioned].

Because of the syntactic connection within this single sentence—"among those born of her own womb and among the lowest-born (*antyaja*) women"—this same rule must be understood to apply even to [the case of] one's sister and others.
And in this context, the penance ending in death consists of entering the fire; as it is said: "In the case of one's mother, a sister, and likewise one's own daughter..."
And approaching one's daughter-in-law should be known as an extreme transgression (atipātaka).
But those who have committed heinous crimes should enter the fire.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana.

It should be understood that entering the fire [is the penance] for approaching one's mother once, or for approaching a sister or others repeatedly; for it is impossible for the act of approaching one's mother—which is a mortal sin (mahāpātaka)—to be equal to the act of approaching a sister or others, which falls under the category of a secondary mortal sin (atipātaka) by extension from that rule.
As for what was stated by Bṛhadyama: "In the case of a mother, a sister, and likewise a daughter..."
And approaching one's daughter-in-law should be understood as a most heinous sin.
But those who have committed heinous crimes should enter the fire.
A Caṇḍālī, a Pulkasī, a Mlecchī, a daughter-in-law, a sister, a female friend,
the sister of one’s mother or father, a woman entrusted to one’s care, and a woman who has sought refuge.
Having approached his maternal uncle's wife, a female ascetic, a woman of his own lineage, a king's wife, a disciple's wife, or a teacher's wife, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Thus, as for the statement of Aṅgiras: "Having approached women who are outcasts or of the lowest castes, having eaten [their food], or having accepted gifts from them, one should perform a month-long fast or else the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

Thus, both of these [penances] are to be understood as applying to one who has intentionally engaged in acts that are subject to the extension of the rule regarding the Guru’s bed, provided he desists before the emission of semen. Furthermore, there is the statement of Saṃvarta: "Having approached out of delusion these women—a sister, a maternal relative, a sister born of another mother—one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance."
Thus, this should be understood as applying to one who has engaged unintentionally with the very subject just mentioned and desists before the emission of semen.

When, however, he approaches these same women who are excessively unchaste, then this same pair of penances—consisting of the Cāndrāyaṇa and the Taptakṛcchra—should be understood to apply respectively to intentional and unintentional engagement.

But in the case of women who are common to all (sādhāraṇastrī), even if they have been enjoyed by a Guru, there is no fault of violating the Guru’s bed (gurutalpa); likewise, there is no adultery as defined by caste, nor is there the defilement of a maiden.
And with a common woman, there is no offense of violating the Guru’s bed.
Thus, according to the recollection of Vyāghra.

In this manner, other Smṛti statements as well—intended for the determination of various high and low penances—should be sought out and their application to specific cases inferred; they are not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. (3.260)

Having thus described the penances for those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātaka), such as the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, the author now states the penance for associating with them, as the occasion has arisen:
"He who indeed associates with these for a year becomes equal to them.
He who dwells together with or conducts himself in the company of these aforementioned persons—the slayers of Brāhmaṇas and so forth—for one full year, he too becomes equal to them.

The mention of "association with them" (*tatsama*) is for the purpose of extending the specific penance of that person to whoever associates with him, meaning that such a person should perform the very same penance as the one he associates with; it is not, however, for the purpose of extending the status of being a *pātakin* (an outcaste), since that is already established by the direct injunction: "and whoever should dwell together with them.
And in this case, even though there is an extension [of the rule], the full twelve-year penance must be performed, because the associate is a *mahāpātakin* (a great sinner) by direct designation.

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is shown that not only is one who associates with a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*) equal to him, but furthermore, among those who commit heinous sins (*atipātakin*), sins (*pātakin*), or secondary sins (*upapātakin*), whoever enters into association with another, he too becomes equal to him and must perform that very person's penance.
For this very reason, after Manu has set forth the entire range of penances, he states:
"Whichever of these men a person enters into association with, [he becomes equal to him]."
"He should perform that very same vow for the sake of purification from contact with him.
Thus,
"Whatever man enters into association with any one of these outcasts..."
He should perform that very same vow for the sake of purification from contact with him;

for Viṣṇu has also shown in general that one who comes into contact with anyone guilty of a minor sin (upapātaka) must undergo the penance prescribed for that person: "Whosoever associates with one who is evil-minded, he should perform that very person's vow.
For this very reason, Manu has issued a general prohibition against associating with any sinner whatsoever.
"One should not engage in any business with those who have committed offenses and have not been purified.
Thus it is said:
"One should not engage in any business with those who have committed offenses and have not been purified."

Likewise: "Once the penance has been performed, one should not associate with the virtuous. And: "A man who, knowing [the other to be fallen], lives together with a fallen person for one year... This penance for the fallen, such as that lasting twelve years and so forth, pertains to the case of intentional association; for it is said: "A man who, knowing [the other to be fallen], lives together with a fallen person for one year..."
Because of that mixture, at the end of the year, he himself shall fall.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Devala. Furthermore, regarding contact through ignorance, Vasiṣṭha has stated: "In the case of association with outcasts—whether by means of Vedic study, marriage, or sacrificial rites—whatever wealth has been acquired from them must be abandoned. One should not dwell with them; having gone toward the northern direction, fasting and reciting the Saṃhitā, one becomes purified; so it is known. Likewise: "The killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed..."
These are the perpetrators of mortal sins, as well as whoever dwells together with them.
Thus: "The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru's bed—
these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), as is he who dwells together with them."

By the use of the instrumental case in the word *taiḥ* (by them), the text declares that only one who associates with the four types of persons previously mentioned—beginning with the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa—is a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). Therefore, one who merely associates with such a person is not himself a perpetrator of a mortal sin.

Now, it might be argued: "The mere association with a perpetrator of a mortal sin is the cause for becoming a perpetrator of a mortal sin, not specifically the association with the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa and the others, because the latter would involve an over-extension (*vyabhicāra*).

Consequently, since even the associate of an associate of a Brāhmaṇa-slayer possesses association with a perpetrator of a mortal sin, he too should be considered a perpetrator of a mortal sin; yet there is no prohibition against this."
It is replied:
This might be so if being a perpetrator of a great sin (*mahāpātakitva*) were cognizable through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

But since that status is to be understood solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*), it must apply to those very persons [specified by the scripture]. For, by the use of the pronoun "by them" (*taiḥ*), which refers back to the specific subjects under discussion, it is understood that the connection with specific individuals such as the slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*) alone is the cause of being a perpetrator of a great sin.
This being the case, even the absence of a prohibition is not a reason [for the lack of penance], precisely because there is no contact.

Therefore, for those who have come into contact with those who have had contact, there is no loss of their status as members of the twice-born; however, penance certainly does apply. Nor should it be argued: "If there is no loss of status for one who has come into contact with those who have had contact, how can there be penance? For it is said: "One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins until they have been purified."

Thus, since by this general prohibition against contact with anyone who is merely an offender (*enasvin*), contact even with one who associates with a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*) is also prohibited, the penance is indeed appropriate even in the absence of actual loss of caste (*pātitya*). And that [penance] is reduced by one quarter. "Whoever associates with another for a year shall attain equality with him."
That twice-born man shall perform the penance for each of those offenses, reduced by one quarter.
Thus, what was stated by Vyāsa is to be understood.

In this manner, for those who associate with [an outcast] through desire in the fourth and fifth degrees as well, it should be understood that the penance is reduced by half and reduced by three-quarters respectively.

Therefore, it is established that the entitlement to perform the specific penance belongs only to one who associates directly with a slayer of a Brahmin or others, and not to one who associates with such a person.

And here, although for those such as the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa death at the end [of life] is prescribed when the act is intentional, nevertheless that [penance] is not extended to one who has associated [with such a person]. This is because only the vow (*vrata*) is extended by the rule "he shall perform the very same vow as he," and because death cannot be designated by the word "vow.
Therefore, in this case, even if the association was intentional, the penance is twelve years; but if unintentional, it is half of that.
Furthermore, association is divided into many types according to the differences in the specific actions that constitute its basis.
As the elder Bṛhaspati said:
"Sharing a bed or a seat, sitting in the same row, mixing of vessels, rows of food, officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching, sexual union, and likewise eating together."
Ninefold confusion has been declared; one should not engage in it with the base.
Thus: sharing a bed or a seat, sitting in the same row, mixing of vessels, mixing of food,
officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching, kinship, and likewise eating together.
Ninefold confusion has been declared; one should not engage in it with the base.
Devala also says: "Through conversation, touch, breathing together, traveling together, sitting together, eating together,
officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching one another, and through marriage, the sin of men is transmitted."
Thus: "Through conversation, touch, breathing together, traveling together, sitting together, eating together,
officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching one another, and through marriage, the sin of men is transmitted."
Sharing a bed and seat means lying on the same couch; eating in the same row; cooking in the same vessel; mixing with food—meaning, contact consisting of eating his food;
officiating at sacrifices for an outcaste or for oneself by him; and teaching him or being taught by him.
Sexual intercourse consists of giving a maiden to him or receiving a maiden from him;
eating together means eating from the same vessel;
and conversation means talking with one another.
Touching is the physical contact of limbs;
breathing is the contact with the breath exhaled from the mouth;
traveling together is mounting the same horse or other vehicle.

In response to the inquiry as to which of these acts causes loss of caste (*pātitya*) and after what duration of time, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu states: "One becomes an outcast by associating for one year with an outcast through sharing a vehicle, food, a seat, or a bed; however, through primary connections such as sexual intercourse or officiating at sacrifices, one becomes an outcast immediately.
Here, "sharing food" means eating in the same row (*ekapaṅkti*);
but in the case of eating from the same vessel (*ekāmatra*), loss of caste occurs immediately.

"By performing a sacrifice for [an outcast], by forming a matrimonial alliance, by studying [the Veda] together, or by eating together—by doing these, one falls immediately with the fallen; of this there is no doubt. Thus says the traditional teaching of Devala.

The word *srauva* denotes officiating at a sacrifice (*yājana*), while the word *mukhya* denotes teaching (*adhyāpana*) because it originates from the mouth (*mukha*). Although there is a dual compound in the expression "by means of the *yauna*, *srauva*, and *mukhya* [connections]," each of them individually constitutes a cause for immediate loss of caste (*patana*). This is because of the traditional teaching of Sumantu: "If one should enter into any one of these connections—whether matrimonial (*yauna*), teaching (*mukhya*), or sacrificial (*srauva*)—with those who have fallen from their caste, for him also this very same penance applies."

However, the fourfold set beginning with the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) constitutes a cause for downfall only when taken collectively, because they are specified as being mutually connected: "by means of the single vehicle, eating, sitting, and lying down. Although there is no cause for downfall in the performance of each individually, there certainly remains the cause of a fault: "From sitting, from lying down, from the vehicle, from conversation, and from eating together—sins indeed spread like a drop of oil upon water."
Thus, because of the statement of Parāśara, it is understood that even these acts are causes of sin when performed independently.

However, regarding conversation, touch, and breath, their status as causes of falling applies only when they are combined with the fourfold set beginning with travel as incidental occurrences, not when they exist separately, due to their minor nature.
Nevertheless, their quality of being causes of sin certainly remains, as has been shown by the statement of Devala: "Conversation, touch, and breath..."
Therefore, when the four acts—such as traveling together and so forth—are performed without conversation and the like, one should perform the twelve-year penance reduced by one-fifth;
however, if they are accompanied by those [other acts], the full penance is required.

This being the case, it is logical that the statement of the Lord of Yogis (Yājñavalkya), "He who indeed lives with these for a year becomes equal to them," refers specifically to the set of four acts beginning with traveling together.
Since conversation and the like do not individually constitute a cause for loss of caste (*pātitya*),
for this very reason Manu stated: "One falls from caste by associating with an outcaste for a year through officiating at sacrifices,
teaching, or marriage, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food."
Thus, it has been stated that the fourfold set beginning with vehicles alone constitutes the cause for loss of caste (*pātitya*) within one year.

Here, the mention of "seating" (*āsana*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of "lying down" (*śayana*) as well. Furthermore, the connection here is with the term "vehicles, food, and seating" (*yānāśanāsanāt*), which is separated [from the verb], as in: "By associating with an outcaste for a year, one falls [from caste] through [partaking in] vehicles, food, and seating. This is in accordance with the previously cited statement of Viṣṇu; likewise: "By associating with an outcaste for a year, one falls [from caste], provided one constantly engages in eating, sitting, lying down, and so forth."
And this is also because of the statement of Devala.

Nor is there the fault of non-connection (*ananvaya-doṣa*), for the relationship is established by the intention to express a distinction, as in "practicing [and] performing conduct" (*ācāram ācaran kurvan*) on account of [proper] vehicles, seats, food, and so forth; just as in the case of "having sacrificed with this sacrifice equal to the re-establishment of the fires" (*etayā punarādheyasaṃmitayeṣṭyā iṣṭvā*).

Alternatively, because the sense of causality is conveyed by the suffix *śatṛ* in the word *ācaran*, the ablative case in *yānāśanāsanāt* functions in the sense of the accusative. One does not fall [from caste] through officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), or matrimonial alliance (*yauna*), but rather immediately; this is solely in accordance with the collection of statements from the Easterners.

Therefore, one falls immediately through the fourfold [contact] beginning with sexual union (*yauṇa*), whereas through the fourfold beginning with riding in the same vehicle (*yāna*), one falls after a year of uninterrupted practice; this is logical because of the use of the accusative case in the phrase "for a year he too becomes equal to him," which expresses continuous duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Thus, the counting of intervening days must be performed.

For instance, if the association extends over three hundred and sixty days, then [the full penance applies]; but if it is less than that, there is no penance for an outcaste (*patita*), but rather something else.
As Parāśara says:
If a Brahmin unintentionally associates with those who have fallen (patita) and others,
he shall observe penance for five days, ten days, or even twelve days;
or for half a month, one month, or even three months.
It may last for half a year or one full year; beyond that, it is equal to those [previous durations].
In the first fortnight, one should observe a three-night fast; in the second, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance;
in the third fortnight, however, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra;
in the fourth, it should be ten nights; and thereafter, in the fifth, it is the Parāka.
In the sixth [case], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; but in the seventh, two Aindavas.
And likewise, during the eighth fortnight, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six months.
Thus:
"If a Brahmin unintentionally associates with those who have fallen [from their caste] and so forth,
he shall observe [penance] for five days, ten days, or even twelve days."
Whether for half a month, one month, three months,
or even half a year, one year, or more than that, he shall remain equal to them.
In the first fortnight, one should observe the three-night fast; in the second, one should perform the *kṛcchra*;
in the third fortnight, however, one should perform the *sāntapana* *kṛcchra*.
In the fourth, it should be ten nights, and then in the fifth, the *parāka*.
In the sixth [case], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; but in the seventh, two Aindavas.
And likewise, during the eighth fortnight, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six months.
Furthermore, regarding contact through desire, a specific rule is stated in another Smṛti.
Sumantu says: "In the case of five days, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; in ten days, the Taptakṛcchra;
in half a month, the Parāka; and in a full month, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa."
Thus:
"For a five-day period one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for ten days, the Taptakṛcchra;
for half a month, the Parāka; and for a full month, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa."
For a period of three months, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa;
however, in the case of contact lasting six months, one should perform the Kṛcchra for half a year.
But if the contact lasts for a full year, a man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one year.
Thus: "In the case of three months, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa;
but in the case of six months' contact, one should perform the Kṛcchra for half a year."
But if the contact lasts for a year, a man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one year.
In this context, regarding "contact" (*saṃsarga*) for a year, it should be understood as being somewhat less than full; for when the year is complete, Manu and others prescribe a twelve-year penance.

As for the statement of Bṛhaspati: "But in the case of contact lasting six months through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and so forth, or by sharing a seat or bed, one should perform half of the penance."
Thus it is said:
"In the case of association for six months through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and so forth,
or by sharing a seat and a bed, one should perform half of the prescribed penance."

The statement regarding loss of caste (*pātitya*) after six months for officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), teaching (*adhyāpana*), traveling together (*yāna*), and eating from the same vessel (*ekapātrabhojana*) should be understood as applying to cases where these acts are performed unintentionally during extreme distress, specifically when the officiating involves the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and similar rites, or when the teaching is merely of auxiliary (*aṅga*) subjects, and when the sexual relationship involves a kinswoman other than one's own daughter or sister. This is because immediate loss of caste has been declared for superior forms of officiating and the like. Following this very principle, for those who associate with committers of heinous sins (*atipātakin*)—such as those who violate their own daughters, sisters, or daughters-in-law—the penance should be determined as nine years if intentional, and four and a half years if unintentional.

For those who intentionally associate with sinners who have sexual relations with a female friend, a paternal uncle’s wife, and so forth, the penance lasts six years; for unintentional association, it lasts three years.

Furthermore, it should be inferred that for those who associate with upapātakin (minor sinners) and others, if intentional, the penance is exactly the same as theirs—three months—and if unintentional, it is half of that.
Just as in the case of men, women also incur loss of caste (*pātitya*) equally through association with those guilty of great sins (*mahāpātakin*) and the like.
As Śaunaka has said: "Whatever causes for downfall apply to a man, those same apply to women as well;
however, a Brāhmaṇī woman falls even more severely by serving a man of lower caste.

Therefore, among those [women] who have committed great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth, the penance belonging to whichever person they associate with should be applied to them after reducing it by one half.

Likewise, for children, the elderly, and the sick, the penalty is half if intentional and a quarter if unintentional; similarly, for a child who has not yet been initiated, the penalty is a quarter if intentional and half of that (an eighth) if unintentional—this is the general principle.
Regarding the prohibition of matrimonial alliance that was forbidden by the interdiction against associating with outcasts, he states an exception in certain cases:
"One may marry a maiden from among these [outcasts] who is fasting and possesses nothing."

One should marry the daughter of these fallen men, born while they were in a state of fall, who has observed a fast, performed the penance appropriate for the time of her association [with the fallen], and is destitute—meaning she has not received any paternal wealth such as clothing or ornaments.
By stating "one should marry the girl," he shows that one should marry the girl herself once she has abandoned her association with the fallen, and not receive her from the hand of the fallen man.
This being the case, the contradiction regarding the prohibition of sexual association with the fallen is also resolved.

And this point has been clarified by Bṛhaddhārīta: "One should marry the daughter of one who has fallen [from his caste], having fasted for a day and night, dressed in a clean, unwashed garment at dawn, and making her declare three times in a loud voice, 'I am not theirs, nor are they mine,' either at a sacred bathing place or in her own home.

Likewise, from the statement, "one should marry their daughter," he demonstrates that the offspring of such persons, excluding the female, is unfit for social intercourse (*saṃsarga*). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha [states]:
One who is born from one fallen [from caste] becomes fallen, except in the case of a woman; for she belongs to another, and he may marry her as one who does not inherit property. || 3.261 ||
Because there is the possibility of contact with those whose association is forbidden, he states the penance for killing those born from forbidden unions, such as those of the *pratiloma* class:
"One should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* after killing all those of inferior birth.
Those of inferior birth are the *sūta*, *māgadha*, and others born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*); for the killing of each of them individually, the *cāndrāyaṇa* is required.

And likewise Śaṅkha says: "For the killing of each of all those who are of lower status, there is a Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Or as stated by Aṅgiras: "In the case of approaching, eating with, or causing the death of any of the lowest-born (antyaja), purification occurs through a Parāka penance; such is the teaching of Aṅgiras."
Thus one should perform the Parāka penance.
In that regard, for the intentional killing of a Sūta or similar castes, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed;
however, for the unintentional killing of a Sūta, the Parāka penance is required.
For killing a Vaidehaka, it is three-quarters [of the penance];
for killing a Caṇḍāla, two quarters;
and for killing a Māgadha, a Parāka minus one quarter.
For a Kṣattṛ, two quarters;
and for an Āyogava, two quarters.
In this same manner, the relative gradations for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance should also be determined.
As for the statement of Brahmagarbha: "For women born in the inverse order (pratiloma), the period is remembered as one month;
for those of intermediate origin and for Sūtas and the like, it is four, two, and six [months respectively]."
Thus, that [penance] refers to the subject of repetition.
In that regard, the application according to suitability is as follows: six months for killing a Sūta, four months for killing a Vaidehaka, and two months for killing a Caṇḍāla.
Likewise, the settled rule is four months for killing a Māgadha, two months for a Kṣattṛ, and two months for an Ayogava.

Since the observances (*vrata*) based on specific signs are to be accomplished through recitation (*japa*) and other such means, and since these are impossible for those devoid of sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), such as *śūdras* and others, one might suspect they lack the qualification—just as the blind lack qualification for rites to be accomplished by gazing at clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even a *śūdra*, though lacking qualification, becomes purified by this [period of] time."

Although a Śūdra is devoid of the entitlement to recite prayers (*japa*) and so forth, he nevertheless becomes purified by this vow (*vrata*) which is to be accomplished over a period of twelve years and the like.
The mention of the Śūdra is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) for women and those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*).
Although for him the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* and other such mantras is impossible, there is nonetheless the recitation of mantras consisting of salutations (*namaskāra*).
For this very reason, it is stated in another Smṛti: "His food shall be the leavings [of others], and his mantra shall be the word of salutation (namaskāra), as permitted.

Alternatively, by the force of that statement, one may perform the vow entirely devoid of recitation (japa) and other such rites; therefore: "Having approached a Śūdra who always stands upon the path of dharma, penance should be prescribed for him, excluding recitation and fire-offerings (homa)."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Aṅgiras;
likewise, another [rule] was stated by that same author:
"A Śūdra devoted to the welfare of cows and Brāhmaṇas shall become pure in the course of time."
Whether by gifts, or by fasts, or likewise by service to the twice-born.
Thus:
"A Śūdra devoted to the welfare of cows and Brāhmaṇas shall be purified in time,
either by gifts, or by fasts, or likewise by service to the twice-born."

As for the statement from the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], "One should not teach him the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow for him," which is intended to prohibit the instruction of vows for a Śūdra, that refers to a Śūdra who has not approached [a teacher]. Furthermore, as for the statement from another Smṛti: "These penances (kṛcchra) are always to be performed by the three castes..."
In these hardships, no entitlement for a Śūdra is prescribed.
Thus, that [statement] refers to the *kṛcchra* penances performed for specific desires.

Therefore, it is established that women, Śūdras, and those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*) possess the entitlement to perform vows (*vrata*) just like the three higher castes. As for the statement of Gautama, "Those born of inverse unions are devoid of dharma," that refers to specific dharmas such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). 3.262.

Having explained the penances for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), the secondary sins (*atipātaka*), and the minor sins (*anupātaka*) among the five categories beginning with the great sins, he now, while expounding the penances for the minor sins (*upapātaka*), first states the penance for killing a cow as it occurs in the sequence of the text: "The killer of a cow shall drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month, remaining self-controlled, sleeping in a cow-pen, and following the cows; he is purified by the gift of a cow."
Or, being composed in mind, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, one should give eleven cows along with a bull.
"One who kills a cow is a cow-killer (goghna); the suffix *ka* is applied here because the word belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*.
This person should remain concentrated for a month."
Doing what?

Drinking those five products of the cow—cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter—mixed according to the prescribed rule, having abandoned all other food, since that is ordained for him as his meal;
likewise, sleeping in a cow-pen.
Since the cow-pen is prescribed by way of reference to the already established practice of sleeping, and since sleeping during the day is prohibited, he sleeps in the cow-shed at night.
He follows the cows; this is his vow (*vrata*), thus he is an *anugāmī* (one who follows the cows). The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of a vow (*vrata*).
And for this reason, he should follow those very cows that lie in the cow-pen due to their proximity, as they roam the forest in the morning.
From the expression "he should follow," it is understood that he himself should follow them at the very moment they depart;
however, when they stand or sit, since it would be impossible to follow behind them, it follows that he too should stand or sit.
Since following [the cows] is specifically prescribed, it follows by implication that he must enter the cow-pen along with them as they go there in the evening.

Performing this for a month, having given one cow as a gift at the end of the month, he is purified from the sin of killing a cow because the purpose of the scripture is thereby fulfilled; this is one vow.
The phrase "lying in the cow-pen for a month, following the cows" continues to apply.
The cessation of consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), however, follows precisely from the prescription of the *kṛcchra* penance itself.
Consequently, there is another rule stating that one should perform the *kṛcchra* continuously for a month with a concentrated mind.
For this very reason, Jābāla has stated that the monthly *prājāpatya* constitutes a distinct expiation.
If one has killed a cow unintentionally, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for a month;
being intent on the welfare of cows, he should follow after them, and he becomes pure by the gift of a cow.
Thus:
"If one who has killed a cow does so unintentionally, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for a month;
he should follow the cows for their benefit and is purified by the gift of a cow."
Or likewise, one may perform the *atikṛcchra* penance; this is another option.
The characteristics of the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* will be explained later.
Alternatively, having fasted for three nights, one should give away cows of which a bull is the eleventh; these constitute the fourfold set of vows (*vrata*).

In that regard, for the unintentional killing of a mere cow belonging to a *brāhmaṇa* by birth alone, one should observe a three-night fast accompanied by the gift of ten cows and a bull; this is because heavier penances will be prescribed for the killing of a cow belonging to a distinguished owner or possessing distinguished qualities. However, for the killing of a cow related to a *kṣatriya* under such circumstances, the first penance is consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month.
Here, because the consumption of *pañcagavya* for one month is extremely slight, it is equivalent to a month-long fast.

Furthermore, by calculating six *upavāsa* fasts for each of the six [days] as equivalent to one *prājāpatya* penance, there are five *kṛcchra* penances; through their substitution (*pratyāmnāya*), there are five cows, and at the end of the month, the single cow that is given makes six cows in total. Thus, this is lighter than the three-night vow accompanied by the gift of eleven cows including a bull. But how is it that the cows belonging to Brahmins carry such gravity?
For it is known: "The property of Vedas, Brahmins, and kings should be understood as the highest [in value]."

This is because Nārada has declared that such property is of the highest quality, and because a greater severity of punishment is observed in the case of "cows belonging to Brāhmaṇas. However, for the killing of a cow belonging to a Vaiśya under similar circumstances, one should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance for one month.
Regarding the *atikṛcchra*, it is stated that during the first three sets of three nights, one should eat only as much food as fills the palm of the hand.
In the final three nights, there is fasting. Thus, when the month-long vow is performed according to the rules of the *atikṛcchra*, there is fasting for six nights,
and for twenty-four days, one eats only as much food as fills the palm of the hand.

Consequently, by calculating the substitution for the difficult penance (*kṛcchra*), it amounts to slightly less than five cows; thus, being the lightest of the two preceding vows, it is rightly applicable to the case of killing a cow owned by a Vaiśya.
In that same category of cases, for the killing of a cow owned by a Śūdra, there is a second vow consisting of the *prājāpatya* for one month.

Since the substitute for that consists of two and a half *prājāpatyas*, which amounts to slightly more than two cows, its applicability to the case of a Śūdra is appropriate due to its being the lightest of all the previous ones.

Now, this fourfold set of expiations should be applied to the very same subject matter previously mentioned, taking into account the relative degree of gravity among the direct perpetrator, the abettor, the instigator, and the consenter.

As for the three Vaiṣṇava vows: "For a cow-killer, there shall be daily consumption of three *pala*s of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month; or else the *parāka* penance, or even the *cāndrāyaṇa*."

Thus, that which is stated by Kāśyapa—"having killed a cow, one should remain clothed in its hide, sleeping in a cow-pen for a month, bathing at the three sessions of the day, and constantly subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)"—and that which is stated by Śātātapa—"subsisting on the five products of the cow for a month"—this pentad of rules also has the same scope as the rule of Yājñavalkya regarding subsistence on the five products of the cow.

And as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Pracetas—"A cow-killer, subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), shall fast for twenty-five nights; having shaved his head including the top-knot, covered with a cow-hide, following the cows, sleeping in a cow-pen, he shall give a cow as a gift"—this should be understood to apply to the same case as the month-long *atikṛcchra* vow prescribed by Yājñavalkya, or else to the case of "having fasted for three nights, he shall give [a cow]," provided the killer is one possessed of extreme virtues.

Regarding this very subject, for one who is unable to consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), it is established that there is a second method according to Kāśyapa: for one month, one should subsist on *pañcagavya*; furthermore, one should eat only at the sixth meal-time, follow the cows as they walk and sit down beside them when they are comfortably seated; one should not walk too fast nor cause them to descend onto very uneven ground; one should not make them drink water where it is scarce; and at the conclusion, having fed the Brahmins, one should give a sesame-cow (*tiladhenu*) as a gift—this is how it should be understood.

In this regard also, it should be understood that for one who is incapable [of the aforementioned penances], Paiṭhīnasi has stated: "The cow-killer is purified by eating for a month a *yavāgū* (gruel) cooked with a handful (*prasṛti*) of rice, while doing what is pleasing to cows.

As for that which was stated by Saumanta—"For the cow-killer, the gift of a cow, sleeping in a cow-pen for twelve nights, consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and following after the cows"—and that which was stated by Saṃvarta: "Eating barley-meal (*saktu*), barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), and alms-food; milk, curd, and clarified butter once [a day];
he should consume these in sequence for half a month, being well-composed."
Having fed the Brahmins, one should give a cow for the sake of one's own purification.

Thus, the twelve-night penance of Bṛhaspati involving the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), as well as that [other penance]—these three together—should be understood as having the same scope as the month-long *Prājāpatya* of Yājñavalkya, or as referring to the killing of a cow that is almost dead, or to a death resulting from disease induced by terror in an uneven place.
All of this previously mentioned applies to cases where the act was unintentional (*akāma*).

Furthermore, when one intentionally causes the death of such an ordinary cow belonging to an ordinary Brahmin, Manu has prescribed a triad of penances: drinking barley-gruel for one month; eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) at every fourth mealtime for two months; and subsisting on vegetables and the like for three months while performing the gift of eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh.
As he says:
"A cow-killer who is guilty of a minor offense (upapātaka) shall drink barley-gruel for one month."
Having shaved his hair, he should dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a wet hide.
One should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with senses restrained, one should perform ablutions using cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
One should stand when they stand, follow when they walk,
and likewise sit when they sit— self-controlled, free from envy.
One should liberate by every possible means a woman who is ill, or one who is being accused, or one threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one who has fallen, or one stuck in the mud.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking.
