Whoever, being a killer of a cow, follows cows according to this rule,
removes the sin committed by that cow-slaughter within three months.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.
Thus:
"A cow-killer who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) shall drink barley-gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a wet hide."
One should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at the fourth mealtime;
for two months, with senses restrained, one should perform one's bath with cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
One should stand when they stand, follow when they walk,
and likewise sit when they are seated— self-controlled, free from envy, and disciplined.
Whether she is afflicted by illness, or accursed, or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers,
or fallen, or mired in the mud, one should rescue her by every possible means.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not report a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor should one report a calf sucking.
But he who, following this rule, attends upon cows,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

This triad [of penances] according to Yājñavalkya is to be understood as referring respectively to three types of vows consisting of: (1) the *māsa-prājāpatya*; (2) the month-long subsistence on *pañcagavya*; and (3) the three-night fast accompanied by the gift of eleven cows including a bull. However, after Aṅgiras has prescribed a three-month penance (*traimāsika*) with the procedure [stated] in the *Mānava* [Smṛti], he further states: "His food at the sixth meal-time should be dry, without pungent salt; or he should recite the *Gomatī* mantra, the syllable *Oṃ*, or even the Veda."
One should carry a staff according to the vow, as well as a girdle accompanied by its mantra.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of a human woman.

In this same way, it should be understood to apply to a woman endowed with some excellence of qualities such as full development or youth; however, having killed one who is excessively young, excessively emaciated, excessively old, or diseased, a twice-born man shall perform half of the vow according to the previously prescribed rule.

Thus, since it is observed that only half of the expiation applies when killing a cow devoid of nourishment, youth, and so forth; when, however, one intentionally kills a cow belonging to an unspecified owner— one who possesses the mere generic status of a cow— as the basis for the month-long *atikṛcchra* vow prescribed by Yājñavalkya, then, according to the principle that "what is ordained for those acting unintentionally should be performed twofold if done intentionally," one should perform twice the previously mentioned month-long *atikṛcchra* vow prescribed for unintentional acts.

As for that which was stated by Hārīta—after describing the procedure according to Manu beginning with "the killer of a cow, having clothed himself in its hide with the hair upwards"—that 'having given thirteen cows and a bull, one becomes purified in the thirteenth month,' that should be understood to apply to the unintentional killing of a cow belonging to a *śrotriya* engaged in a *savana*.

As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"If one should kill a cow, he shall remain wrapped in her raw hide for six months, performing the *kṛcchra* and *taptakṛcchra* penances, and shall give a bull and a cow as a gift"—and that which was stated by Devala—"The cow-killer is released after six months, clothed in her hide, dwelling in a cow-pen, and wandering together with the cows"—both of these refer to the same subject matter as the rule of Hārīta.
In that very case, for a killing committed intentionally, the penance prescribed by Kātyāyana lasts for three years: "The killer of a cow, clothed in its hide, shall dwell in a cow-pen;
furthermore, he should constantly follow the cows, remaining silent and practicing the *vīrāsana* posture and other such ascetic observances."
One who is afflicted by the fear of rain, cold, heat, suffering, fire, mud,
and so forth, shall be liberated through every possible effort and becomes purified within three years.

Thus it should be understood. And as for the three-year penance prescribed by Śaṅkha: "One should perform a one-quarter [penance] for killing a Śūdra, likewise for approaching a woman in her courses, likewise for killing a cow, and likewise for approaching another man's wife."
Thus, that [rule] also pertains to the same subject matter as the vow of Kātyāyana.
However, after Yama has described the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) according to the *Āṅgirasa* tradition, he states: "Having well-performed the vow, one should give a thousand or even a hundred cows;
if these are unavailable, one should offer one's entire property to those learned in the Vedas."

Thus, two two-month vows involving either a thousand cows or a hundred cows have been prescribed. Among them, when a wealthy man devoid of merit, having made a vow, kills with a sword or similar weapon a Kapila cow belonging to a destitute Brāhmaṇa who is a learned priest (*śrotriya*) engaged in a sacrifice—provided she is pregnant, possesses qualities such as abundant milk and great size, and serves as an essential part of the ritual—then he shall perform the two-month vow involving a thousand cows. [Likewise,] when a wealthy man devoid of merit, having made a vow, kills with a sword or similar weapon [a cow] possessing qualities such as abundant milk and great size, then he shall perform the two-month vow involving a thousand cows. [This applies also to killing] a pregnant Kapila cow, a milch-cow, a sacrificial cow (*homadhenu*), or one well-observed in her vows.
Having caused [the victim] to be killed with a sword or similar weapon, one should observe the vow for double the duration.

Thus, because a specific expiation is seen for the killing of a distinguished cow belonging to Bṛhaspati, it follows that Pracetas prescribed the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa— namely, "In cases of killing a woman, a pregnant woman, a child, or an elderly person, one becomes a killer of a Brāhmaṇa"— intending precisely such a case of cow-killing. However, the second vow, which belongs to Yama and involves the gift of a hundred cows, should be understood as applying to a wealthy person within the scope of the Kātyāyana-vow.

As for that which Gautama, having prescribed a period of celibacy combined with the gift of one hundred and one bulls for the killing of a Vaiśya, extended by analogy to the killing of a cow—stating, "And having killed a cow, [one shall perform the penance] as for a Vaiśya"—this, together with the ninety cows that serve as the substitute for the three-year vow, amounts to one hundred and nine less than two hundred; thus, because it is less than the three-month vow accompanied by a thousand cows, it applies to the aforementioned case when the killing is intentional. Alternatively, it should be understood to apply to that same case when the killing is intentional but the cow is not pregnant.

Even in the case of unintentionally killing such a woman who is barren, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana alone should be ordained. As for that which was stated by Yama: "If cows are killed by means of wood, clods of earth, stones, or weapons—how is the expiation in that case? Is it prescribed for both weapon and non-weapon? [The answer follows: "In the case of a weapon, there is a three-year penance; in the case of a non-weapon, half of that. This refers to the case where a cow is killed by a weapon such as a sword or the like, or by a non-weapon such as a staff or the like. It does not apply to the case of killing a barren woman with wood or the like. Furthermore, because the text specifies "if cows are killed," this rule is restricted to the killing of cows and does not extend to the killing of other animals. Moreover, since the text mentions "wood, clods, stones, or weapons," it is understood that the penance is reduced in proportion to the instrument used. Therefore, even when a barren woman is killed by a weapon such as a sword or the like, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana should be applied. However, in the case of killing her with wood, clods, stones, or the like, the penance is half of that. Thus, the meaning is that the penance is reduced according to the nature of the instrument employed. Furthermore, in the case of killing a cow with a weapon, the three-year penance is prescribed; in the case of killing her with a non-weapon, the penance is half of that. This is the intended meaning. Consequently, in the case of killing a barren woman with a weapon, one must perform the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana. However, in the case of killing her with wood, clods, stones, or the like, the penance is half of that. This is the established conclusion. Furthermore, the phrase "in the case of a weapon" refers to cases such as striking with a sword or the like, while "in the case of a non-weapon" refers to cases such as striking with a staff or the like. Therefore, the penance is determined by the specific instrument used. For these reasons, in the case of killing a barren woman with a weapon, one should perform the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana. However, in the case of killing her with wood, clods, stones, or the like, the penance is half of that. This is the settled doctrine. Furthermore, the statement regarding the killing of a barren woman applies equally to the killing of a pregnant woman. This is because the text uses the general term "woman" (*striyām*). Since the text says "woman," it is understood that the same penance applies to the killing of a pregnant woman as well. Therefore, in the case of killing a pregnant woman, the penance is the same as that for killing a barren woman. However, in the case of killing a pregnant woman intentionally, the penance is double that amount. This is because the text says "intentionally" (*kāmataḥ*). Since the text specifies "intentionally," it is understood that the penance is double in the case of intentional killing. Therefore, in the case of intentionally killing a pregnant woman, one must perform a six-year penance. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "even in the case of unintentionally killing such a woman who is barren" means that even if she is barren, if she is killed unintentionally, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana should be applied. This is the intended meaning. Moreover, the phrase "the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana alone should be ordained" means that the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana alone should be performed. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "as for that which was stated by Yama" refers to the following verse: "If cows are killed by means of wood, clods of earth, stones, or weapons—how is the expiation in that case? Is it prescribed for both weapon and non-weapon? This is the intended meaning. The phrase "In the case of a weapon, there is a three-year penance; in the case of a non-weapon, half of that" means that in the case of killing a cow with a weapon such as a sword or the like, the three-year penance is prescribed; in the case of killing her with a non-weapon such as a staff or the like, the penance is half of that. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "this refers to the case where a cow is killed by a weapon such as a sword or the like, or by a non-weapon such as a staff or the like" means that it refers to the case where a cow is killed by a weapon such as a sword or the like, or by a non-weapon such as a staff or the like. This is the intended meaning. The phrase "It does not apply to the case of killing a barren woman with wood or the like" means that it does not apply to the case of killing a barren woman with wood or the like. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "Moreover, since the text specifies 'if cows are killed,' this rule is restricted to the killing of cows and does not extend to the killing of other animals" means that because the text specifies "if cows are killed," this rule is restricted to the killing of cows and does not extend to the killing of other animals. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "Moreover, since the text mentions 'wood, clods, stones, or weapons,' it is understood that the penance is reduced in proportion to the instrument used" means that because the text mentions "wood, clods, stones, or weapons," it is understood that the penance is reduced in proportion to the instrument used. This is the intended meaning. Therefore, the phrase "even when a barren woman is killed by a weapon such as a sword or the like, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana should be applied" means that even when a barren woman is killed by a weapon such as a sword or the like, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana should be applied. This is the intended meaning. However, the phrase "in the case of killing her with wood, clods, stones, or the like, the penance is half of that" means that in the case of killing her with wood, clods, stones, or the like, the penance is half of that. This is the intended meaning. Thus, the phrase "the penance is reduced according to the nature of the instrument employed" means that the penance is reduced according to the nature of the instrument employed. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "For these reasons, in the case of killing a barren woman with a weapon, one should perform the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana. However, in the case of killing her with wood, clods, stones, or the like, the penance is half of that. This is the settled doctrine" means that for these reasons, in the case of killing a barren woman with a weapon, one should perform the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana. However, in the case of killing her with wood, clods, stones, or the like, the penance is half of that. This is the settled doctrine. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "Furthermore, the statement regarding the killing of a barren woman applies equally to the killing of a pregnant woman" means that the statement regarding the killing of a barren woman applies equally to the killing of a pregnant woman. This is the intended meaning. Why? Because the text uses the general term "woman" (*striyām*). Since the text says "woman," it is understood that the same penance applies to the killing of a pregnant woman as well. Therefore, the phrase "Therefore, in the case of killing a pregnant woman, the penance is the same as that for killing a barren woman" means that therefore, in the case of killing a pregnant woman, the penance is the same as that for killing a barren woman. This is the intended meaning. However, the phrase "However, in the case of killing a pregnant woman intentionally, the penance is double that amount" means that however, in the case of killing a pregnant woman intentionally, the penance is double that amount. This is the intended meaning. Why? Because the text says "intentionally" (*kāmataḥ*). Since the text specifies "intentionally," it is understood that the penance is double in the case of intentional killing. Therefore, the phrase "Therefore, in the case of intentionally killing a pregnant woman, one must perform a six-year penance" means that therefore, in the case of intentionally killing a pregnant woman, one must perform a six-year penance. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "Moreover, the phrase 'even in the case of unintentionally killing such a woman who is barren' means that even if she is barren, if she is killed unintentionally, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāyana should be applied. This is the intended meaning" means that moreover, the phrase "even in the case of unintentionally killing such a woman who is barren" means that even if she is barren, if she is killed unintentionally, the three-year penance prescribed by Kātyāy
One should perform the Sāntapana penance for wood, the Prājāpatya for a clod of earth,
the Taptakṛcchra for a stone, and the Atikṛcchra for a weapon.
Then, when the penance has been performed, one should provide a feast for Brahmins;
one should give thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee to them.

Thus, this [text] is intended to establish that the *sāntapana* and other penances—which arise from specific implements such as wooden sticks—are to be preceded by the aforementioned gifts of a hundred thousand cows and so forth, or by vows lasting three years and so on; it does not prescribe them independently, because the vow would otherwise be too light.

Likewise, regarding the matter of penance according to specific stages of life, it is said: "Having killed a cow that is very old, very emaciated, very young, or diseased, a twice-born man shall perform half the vow according to the previously mentioned rule."
One should feed Brahmins according to one's ability and likewise give gifts of gold and sesame seeds.
Thus, half of that which is prescribed for the killing of a healthy animal and so forth [is required].
Bṛhat-Pracetas has also stated a specific rule here:
"When a calf of one year is killed, a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance is ordained."
If it occurs unintentionally, the penance for a man shall be two quarters in the case of a two-year-old [cow];
it shall be three quarters in the case of a three-year-old; beyond that, it is a Prājāpatya.
Thus it is said.
If a calf one year old is killed unintentionally by a man, a quarter-penance (kṛcchrapāda) is prescribed; for a two-year-old, it shall be a half-penance (dvipāda);
for a three-year-old, it shall be a three-quarter penance (tripāda); and for one older than that, the Prājāpatya penance is required.

Likewise, when a pregnant woman is killed and the fetus is also destroyed, the rule that "the effect recurs for every cause" would lead to the application of the vow twice over without distinction. Regarding this, the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states the following resolution: "When the fetus has merely been produced, [the penance is] one quarter; when it has reached firmness, two quarters;
having killed an insentient fetus, the vow is declared to be three-quarters."
When the fetus is complete with all its major and minor limbs and endowed with consciousness, one should perform a double cow-vow; this is the expiation for a killer of a cow.
Thus it is said:
"But when [the fetus] has developed only one foot, or when two feet have become firm,
having killed an insentient embryo, the penance is declared to be three-quarters."
When the fetus is complete with all its major and minor limbs and endowed with consciousness, one should perform a double cow-vow; this is the expiation for a killer of a cow.

Regarding a killing committed by many agents, Saṃvarta and Āpastamba state a specific rule: "If some single person is killed somewhere by several people through chance, they shall each perform one quarter of the penance for the killing individually."
Thus it is said:
"If some single woman is killed somewhere by many people through fate,
they shall each perform a quarter of the penance for the killing individually."
Whatever vow has been prescribed for each specific type of cow-slaughter, they should perform one-fourth of that for each [cow]; this is because of the scriptural statement.
The phrase "if it be one" is merely illustrative.
Therefore, when two cows or many cows are killed by several persons, two quarters or three-quarters [of the vow] should be assigned to each individual.
And this [penance] should be understood to apply to killing unintentionally, because of the inclusion of the qualification "by chance" (*daivāt*).

However, in the case of intentional action (*kāmakāra*), since the entire fault attaches to each individual even among many [killers], it is logical that the full vow [of penance] applies to each; for just as in the case of those performing a *sattra* sacrifice, the entire ritual activity is present in each person, so too for many who kill one [person], the fine is double that which was stated.
This is also because a doubling of the punishment for each individual is observed in such cases.

But when many cows are killed by a single act, such as confinement and so forth, Saṃvarta and Āpastamba state this distinction: "In the case of many animals being killed through confinement or even binding, or when a physician provides improper treatment, one should perform double the cow-vow (govrata)."
Thus:
"But if many who have fallen ill are confined or even bound,
and if a physician provides improper treatment, he shall perform double the vow of Gaurī."

Even when many [cows] have perished, there is no performance of the penance for each individual cause, nor is it performed once collectively (*tantra*); rather, by the force of the scriptural injunction, it must be doubled. Likewise, even a physician, through the unintentional killing of even a single cow by administering contradictory medicine, shall perform the *govrata* penance twice over. However, regarding one other than a physician who has engaged solely for the purpose of providing assistance, Vyāsa speaks concerning the unintentional administration of counter-indicated medicine: [The text continues with the verse: "Even if he gives medicine for the sake of helping, if it is contrary to the patient's condition, he becomes a killer of the cow; therefore, one should not administer medicine without having first consulted a physician. Thus, even in the case of one acting for the benefit of another, if the medicine is administered unintentionally against the rules, the penance is doubled. This applies to those other than physicians who act purely out of a desire to help. As for a physician, however, because his livelihood depends on treating patients, the penance is not doubled even in the case of unintentional harm. This is because his primary intent is the treatment of the sick, and the resulting injury is incidental. Furthermore, since the physician’s profession involves the risk of error, the law does not impose a heavier burden upon him than upon others who act out of pure altruism. Thus, the doubling of the penance is restricted to those whose actions are motivated by a specific intent to assist, provided that the act was nonetheless contrary to medical science. In this regard, the following principle from the *Smṛticandrikā* is also relevant: "When a person acts for the sake of another, if the result is harmful, the penance is double; but if the act was done for one's own sake, the penance is as prescribed for the specific offense. Therefore, the distinction between the physician and the non-physician lies in the nature of their motivation and the context of their professional duty. By understanding these nuances, one avoids the error of applying the rule of doubling indiscriminately to all cases of unintentional harm. Thus, the determination of the penance rests upon a careful analysis of the agent's intent and the specific circumstances of the act. [End of excerpt] (Note: The final sentence reflects the structural conclusion of the argument regarding the application of the rule.)
Medicine, salt, and even food for the sake of merit—these should not be given in excess; one should cause only a small amount to be given at the proper time.
If there is a calamity regarding an excess, a quarter-kṛcchra penance is prescribed.
Thus:
Medicines, salt, and even food for the sake of merit—these should not be given in excess; one should cause only a small amount to be given at the proper time.
If there is a misfortune regarding an excess, a quarter-kṛcchra penance is prescribed.

As for that which was stated by Āpastamba— "One should perform one quarter [of the penance] for confining, two quarters for binding, three-quarters for yoking, and the whole for causing to fall"— that should be understood to apply to the indirect agent who acts as the cause, and not to the direct perpetrator.

The distinction between the direct perpetrator, the instigator, and the owner has been shown by that very same [author]: "Those who forcibly cause cows to fall, whether by means of stones, clubs, weapons, or anything else, shall indeed perform the entire vow."
In the same way, by the crushing of the arms, shanks, thighs, sides, neck, and feet;
Thus:
"Those who forcibly cause cows to fall by means of stones, clubs, weapons, or anything else, shall indeed perform the entire vow."
In the same way, by the twisting of the arms, shanks, thighs, sides, neck, and feet;

This is what is meant: those who cause a cow to fall by means of stones, swords, and the like, or by wringing its neck and so forth, are the direct killers (*sākṣād-ghantāraḥ*); upon them alone does the entire penance rest.

But those who are engaged in indirect activities such as obstructing or tethering it are the instrumental causes (*nimittinaḥ*); they do not have a connection with the full vow, but rather with its parts, such as one-fourth, one-half, and so on.

And in that regard, although there is no difference in the fact that the acts of obstructing and so forth involve an indirect operation, it is logical that according to the scriptural statement, in some cases it is one quarter, in some cases two quarters, and in some cases three-quarters.
On this point, Parāśara says: "If death should occur unintentionally due to the ropes used for tethering cows..."
For one who has committed a sin unintentionally, one should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance.
Once the penance has been performed, he should then provide a meal for Brahmins and give a cow along with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Thus [it is said].
Death may occur unintentionally due to the ropes used for tethering cows;
for one who has committed such an unintentional sin, one should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance.
Once the penance has been performed, he should then provide a meal for Brahmins and give a cow along with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.

And this *prājāpatya* penance is to be understood as applicable when, having committed an act such as confinement, one remains watchful with the desire to avoid the negligence resulting from it—since the qualification "of one who has committed sin unintentionally" is employed.
However, when one does not guard against negligence, then: "One quarter [of the penance] should be performed for confinement; two quarters should be performed for binding;
for yoking, it shall be less by a quarter; for causing a fall, one should perform the whole."
Thus, O Aṅgiras, one should perform the penance for killing a cow as seen in the *Aṅgiras* tradition: a quarter of the three-month penance, or slightly more than twenty days.
Āpastamba has also stated a specific rule:
"In the case of excessive burning, excessive driving, or the cutting of the nose..."
In the event of an obstruction by a river or a mountain, one should perform three-quarters of the penance.
Thus:
"In cases of excessive burning or excessive carrying [of loads], as well as for cutting off the nose,
or for obstructing a river or a mountain pass, one should perform three-quarters of the penance."
There is no fault in burning [an animal] for the sole purpose of marking it; nor is there fault in branding or tattooing it, or in driving it, or even in releasing it.
Furthermore, there would be no offense in confining or tethering it for the sake of its protection at night.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Parāśara:
"Marking" (aṅkana) refers to making a permanent sign; "branding" (lakṣaṇa) refers to a temporary identification mark.

Regarding the matter of tethering for the purpose of protection according to the path prescribed in the scriptures, there is indeed a fault in binding [the animal] with coconuts and the like; for it is said: "Not with a coconut, nor with hemp fibers, nor even with muñja grass, nor with binding chains."
But one should not tie up the cows with these; rather, having bound them, one should remain standing while holding an axe.
One should bind it with kuśa and kāśa grass at a site free from defects.
Thus, according to the recollection of Vyāsa.

Likewise, another distinction has been stated by that same [author]: "If a cow should meet with misfortune due to the fault of a bell or ornament, there shall be half a *kṛcchra* penance; for that is prescribed for the purpose of decoration."
If an animal dies from excessive milking, excessive taming, being crowded together, being yoked,
or having been bound with chains and nooses, one should perform a penance amounting to three-quarters of the prescribed rule.

Thus, regarding negligence through the failure to provide protection and so forth, a specific expiation has been stated by that very same author: "Even if she is submerged in a flood or a pond, struck by lightning from a cloud, or suddenly fallen into a pit, or even devoured by a wild beast..."
The owner of the cow shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra, the highest vow,
even if the cow has been struck by cold or wind, or even if it has died by hanging.
One should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance for practicing equanimity in an empty house.
Thus:
"Whether she be submerged in a puddle amidst a flood of water, struck by lightning from a cloud,
fallen unexpectedly into a chasm, or even devoured by a wild beast."
The owner of the cow shall perform the Prājāpatya penance, the highest vow,
even if the cow has been struck by cold or wind, or even if it has died by hanging.
One should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance for practicing equanimity in an empty dwelling.

This, however, should be understood to apply when one neglects [a person] even though there is no other task to be performed. But if the neglect is due to being preoccupied with another task— such as in the case of failing to ward off a flood from a pond, or a tiger, a wild beast, and so forth— if [the person] dies from falling into a pit, a precipice, or from [being bitten by] a snake and the like, one should perform half of a *kṛcchra* penance.
But because it is inhabited, there would be hardship during a calamity in an empty house.
Thus it is because of the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, even when there is an intent to kill, if one is engaged in an action for the sake of some benefit, there is an absence of fault due to the scriptural statement.
As Saṃvarta said:
If a misfortune should occur despite efforts made for the purpose of restraining [the fetus], treating a disease, or extracting a malpresented fetus, one is not stained by sin.
Thus:
"If misfortune should occur despite efforts made for the purpose of restraining [an animal], treating a cow's disease, or extracting a dead fetus, one is not tainted by sin."

Torture (*yantraṇa*) consists of the insertion of pincers, hooks, and the like for the purpose of extracting diseases and so forth. Likewise: "If a twice-born man provides medicine, oil, or food to a cow or a Brāhmaṇa, he is not tainted by sin even if death occurs while it is being given."
For Brahmins who provide assistance during a village raid with a shower of arrows, in the collapse of a house,
or by means of applying fire, cutting, or piercing a vein,
and for those acting for the sake of the welfare of cows, no penance is prescribed.
Regarding this, Parāśara also says:
"In the case of those killed by a volley of arrows during the plundering of a village, or by the collapse of their houses,
or by excessive rain, no penance is prescribed."
Thus it is said.
In the case of those killed by a shower of arrows during a village raid, by the collapse of a house,
or by excessive rain, no expiation is prescribed.
Likewise, for one who dies while digging a well for the sake of dharma, or in a house fire,
or likewise in a terrible village fire, no expiation is prescribed.
Thus.
For one who dies while digging a well for the sake of dharma, or in a house fire,
or likewise in a terrible village conflagration, no expiation is required.
This, however, refers to the case of an animal that was not bound [at the time of death] due to some accidental burning of the house or similar circumstances.
Otherwise, Āpastamba has stated:
"In wildernesses, in difficult terrains, in the burning of a house, and in threshing floors..."
If there should be a failure in that regard, one quarter is prescribed.
Thus: "Furthermore, in wildernesses, in difficult terrains, in house fires, and in pits—
if misfortune should occur there, one quarter [of the penance] is prescribed."
Likewise, even though death does not occur when a bone or similar part is broken, an expiation has been prescribed in certain cases:
"Having broken the bones of cows, or likewise having cut off their tails,
or having split their teeth or horns, one should drink barley-gruel for half a month."
Thus:
"Having caused the breaking of the bones of cows, or likewise the cutting off of their tails,
or the splitting of their teeth and horns, one shall drink barley-gruel for half a month."

As for that [penance] prescribed by Āṅgirasa: "In the case of a broken horn, a broken bone, or even the shedding of the hide—if a cow should become ill, one should drink *vajra* (urine) for ten nights, even if she is otherwise healthy."
Thus, the practice involving milk and other substances denoted by the term "vajra" has been described; that, however, pertains to those who are incapable [of performing the full penance].
And this expiation must be performed only after giving to the owner of the cow a cow similar to the one that perished.
As Parāśara says:
In the case of killing living beings, one should give a substitute for them, or one should pay its equivalent value;
so said Yama.
Thus [it is said]:
"In the case of killing living beings, one should give a substitute for them, or one should give its equivalent value;
so Yama has declared."
Manu also says:
"Whoever should damage another's goods, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king."
Thus:
"Whoever should damage another's goods, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king."
This aforementioned collection of penances should be understood as applying specifically to a Brāhmaṇa who is the slayer.

However, regarding a Kṣatriya or others who are the slayers, a specific distinction has been stated by Bṛhad-Viṣṇu: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇa victim, the full [penance] is to be given; for a Kṣatriya, it is recorded as one-quarter less;
for a Vaiśya, half; and for those of the Śūdra caste, one quarter is prescribed."
Thus it is said: "To a Brahmin, the full amount should be given; for a Kṣatriya, one-quarter less is prescribed;
for a Vaiśya, half; and for those of the Śūdra caste, one quarter is recommended."
As for the statement of Aṅgiras: "The assembly of Brahmins is considered to consist of twelve; that of kings is held to be double that;
and that of Vaiśyas is declared to be triple. And the penance is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly."
Thus, that [penalty] applies in reverse order to cases involving verbal or physical cruelty and the like;
likewise, it should be understood as previously stated that for women, children, the elderly, and so forth, the penalty is half, and for an uninitiated child, it is a quarter.
A specific distinction regarding women has been stated by Parāśara:
"For women there is no shaving of the head, nor following [the deceased], nor recitation of prayers and the like;
they have no sleeping in the cow-pen, nor should they wear a cow-hide."
Having pulled out all the hair, one should cut it to a length of two finger-breadths;
for this is prescribed as the method for shaving the heads of women everywhere.
Thus it is said:
"For women, there is no shaving of the head, nor following [the cow] in procession, nor the chanting of prayers and the like;
they shall not sleep in the cow-pen, nor shall they wear a cow-hide."
Having pulled out all the hair, one should cut it to a length of two finger-breadths;
for in all cases, this is recorded as the method of shaving the head for women.
And regarding men, Saṃvarta has shown the distinction:
for one-quarter [of the offense], there is the shaving of the body hair; for one-half, also the shaving of the beard;
for three-quarters, everything except the topknot; but for a capital offense, including the topknot.
Thus:
"In the case of a foot [of sin], there is the shaving of the body hair; in the case of two feet, also of the beard;
in the case of three feet, however, excluding the top-knot (śikhā); but in the case of a complete downfall (nipātana), including the top-knot."
For one deserving a quarter-penance (*pāda-prāyaścitta*), there is the shaving of the hair on the body below the neck;
for one deserving a half-penance (*ardha-prāyaścitta*), however, the beard as well;
and for one deserving three-quarters of a penance (*pādona-prāyaścitta*), furthermore, even the hair on the head, with the exception of the top-knot (*śikhā*).

"But for one who is worthy of the four-footed [tonsure], that is, for one who possesses the *śikhā* (topknot) and the entire mass of hair"—thus, by means of this orientation, the scope of other Smṛti passages should also be determined. || 3.263 || 3.264 ||
Now he states the expiation for other minor offenses (upapātaka):
"The purification for a minor offense may be accomplished in this manner, or by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
or by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance."

By performing the cow-killing penance (*govadhavrata*) as described above—consisting of consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month and so forth—there shall be purification for other minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as being a *vrātya* and the like.
Alternatively, purification may be achieved by the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance whose characteristics will be described below, or by a month-long milk-vow (*payovrata*), or by the *parāka* penance.

Here, due to the force of this extended application (*atideśa*), it is understood that there is a slight deficiency [in these cases] regarding certain practices unique to cow-killing, such as wearing a cow-hide garment or tending to cows.
And these four vows should be understood as being optional according to one's capacity when the act was committed unintentionally.
However, in the case of intentional acts, twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka) shall perform this very same vow,
excluding that for the student who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), or alternatively, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the sake of purification.
Thus, what was stated by Manu should be understood as lasting for three months.

Precisely because of this statement, this extension of penance (prāyaścittātideśa) is to be understood as applying without distinction to all those enumerated in the category of minor offenses (upapātaka)—both those for whom a penance has been specifically stated and those for whom it has not—with the sole exception of the *avakīrṇin* (one who has had sexual intercourse with a woman).
For the *avakīrṇin*, however, only that which is prescribed in the specific rule applies.

[Objection: Is it not rather logical that this extension [of penance] applies specifically to cases where no penance has been explicitly stated? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to rely on the sublation of penances expressly prescribed for each specific case.
[Reply: Not so;
for if that were the case, the inclusion of those very penances within the list of minor offenses (upapātaka) would be purposeless.

If, among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), a specific expiation is prescribed elsewhere for that which is mentioned generally, then that same case is merely excluded; it is not the case that [the general rule] applies even where a specific expiation is prescribed elsewhere for that which was specifically mentioned. For example: "One who performs sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances, even if he does not neglect his duties"—this refers only to that specific case. Furthermore, it is not the case that [the general rule] applies even where a specific expiation is prescribed elsewhere for that which was specifically mentioned, as in: "Cutting trees for the sake of fuel" or "In the cutting of trees, shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants, one hundred *ṛc*-verses are to be recited."

Therefore, regarding the state of being a *vrātya* and similar offenses, one must adopt either an option or a division of subject matter by assuming an equal scope for the four sets of vows taught in this treatise—beginning with the words "the purification of minor sins (*upapātaka*) shall be thus"—along with the penances seen in this and other treatises.
And we shall apply those penances seen in other *smṛtis* to the cases of the *vrātyas* and others according to the order of their recitation.
In that regard, concerning the state of being a *vrātya*, Manu has stated this: "Those twice-born men for whom the *Sāvitrī* has not been recited according to the prescribed limit..."
Having made them perform three *kṛcchra* penances according to the rule, one should initiate them.
Thus it is; and as Yama has said: "He whose Sāvitrī has fallen for fifteen years shall, having shaved his head including the top-knot, perform the vow with a concentrated mind."
For twenty-one nights, one should drink a handful of barley-gruel,
and one should feed seven or five Brahmins with sacrificial food (havis).
Then, for one who has been purified by the consumption of barley-gruel, the initiation ceremony is prescribed.
Thus, both of these [penances] refer to the month-long milk-vow prescribed by Yājñavalkya.
As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One whose *sāvitrī* has been lost shall perform the Uddālaka-vow:

he should subsist on *yāvaka* for two months, on milk for one month, on *āmikṣā* for a fortnight, on clarified butter for eight nights, on unasked food for six nights, on water for three nights, and fast for a day and night."

"One should go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice, or one should perform the *vrātyastoma*. Regarding this, the following rule applies: for one who has missed the proper time for initiation due to the absence of an initiator (*upanetṛ*) or other reasons, any one of the vows prescribed by Yājñavalkya shall apply, according to his capacity.
If there is a transgression when no such occasion exists, however, a three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.
In that same case, even for one over fifteen years of age, if some time has elapsed, the Uddālakavrata or the Vrātyastoma sacrifice is required.

But regarding those whose fathers and grandfathers were likewise uninitiated, Āpastamba states: "For him whose father and grandfather have not been initiated, there shall be a year-long period of Vedic celibacy (brahmacarya) according to the three Vedas."

For one whose initiation (upanayana) by his great-grandfather or others is not remembered, the period of studentship for the three Vedas (traividyaka-brahmacarya) shall be twelve years. Likewise, regarding theft, Manu has prescribed a penance that sets aside the fourfold set of vows generally applicable to minor offenses (upapātaka): "Having intentionally committed the theft of grain, food, or wealth from the house of a person of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year."
Thus:
"Having committed thefts of grain, food, or wealth out of desire, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year from the house of a member of his own caste."

Since the one of the same caste as the best of the twice-born is indeed a Brāhmaṇa, this [fine] applies when a Brāhmaṇa steals from the possession of another Brāhmaṇa; however, for a Kṣatriya or others, a lesser amount should be prescribed. Furthermore, it is stated: "The guilt of theft is eightfold for a Śūdra, and it increases twofold for each subsequent caste; there is greater punishment for one who knows [the law] and yet transgresses. Since this shows that the punishment for a Kṣatriya or other thief is less, and likewise: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, the full amount must be paid; for a Kṣatriya, it is recorded as one-quarter less."

Thus, since a penance is seen to decrease with each successive reduction in the status of the victim, so too, when the victim is a Kṣatriya or others, a reduction in the penance should be inferred according to the corresponding reduction in the punishment.

Therefore, for theft involving a Kṣatriya victim, a six-month penance is prescribed; for a Vaiśya victim, a three-month penance of the *govadha* type; and for a Śūdra victim, a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance should be prescribed.
The same should be inferred for subsequent cases as well.
This refers to the theft of ten *kumbhas* of grain; however, for more than that: "For one who steals grain exceeding ten *kumbhas*, the highest fine is prescribed;
for stealing more than a thousand *palas*, the punishment is death."
"Exceeding one thousand *palas*, there is execution.
From this observation regarding execution,
it follows that the *kumbha* measures five thousand *palas*.
By association with grain, these two—food and wealth—should be understood as limited to the quantity of grain [specified].
By the word "food" (anna), rice and the like are denoted; by the word "wealth" (dhana), copper, silver, and so forth are meant.
However, this expiation applies to cases of intentional action.
But if it is done unintentionally, the vow for killing a cow lasts for three months.
Likewise: "In the case of stealing human beings, women, fields, houses, or the water of wells and tanks, purification is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

Thus, although this *cāndrāyaṇa* penance—which is prescribed for the theft of water obtainable for two hundred and fifty *paṇas*—is already applicable, it is further enjoined here for the purpose of excluding other penances for cow-slaughter. This is because, regarding the theft of water or grass worth that amount, the fine is twice the value;

since a fine of five hundred *paṇas* is thus ordained, and because a fine of that many *paṇas* and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance are associated with offenses such as cow-slaughter, it is likewise stated: "For the *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, and *aindava* (cāndrāyaṇa) penances, the fine is five hundred *paṇas*."
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, and silver, and of land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.
Thus it should be understood.

Likewise: "Having committed the theft of articles of little value from another's house, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that [stolen property]."
By this specific rule regarding the theft of substances such as tin and lead, which serve only minor purposes, there is an exception to the general penance for the sin of theft (*steya-upapātaka*).

Furthermore, this is the penance for stealing half-a-hundred-and-fifty *mūlya* units—which is the cause for a *Cāndrāyaṇa*—when stealing fifteen parts of that amount of tin, lead, or similar items, because that [general penance] consists of fifteen parts of a *Cāndrāyaṇa*.

Likewise, by means of the specific nature of the object, there is an exception to the vow obtained through the general category of *upapātaka*: "In the case of stealing food that may be eaten or chewed, and of vehicles, beds, and seats..."
"For flowers, roots, and fruits, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the purifier.
Thus it is said.
[Likewise for] the theft of edible foods, whether chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats.
For the theft of flowers, roots, or fruits, the purification is the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
This applies when one steals food or edibles sufficient for a single meal;
if the amount is sufficient for two or three meals, the purification lasts for three nights.

As Paiṭhīnasi has stated: "In the case of stealing enough food, whether hard or soft, to fill one's stomach, the penance is three nights or one night of subsisting on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Because of this association, this same penance applies to the theft of vehicles and other such items only when they are of a value equivalent to that amount.
In all cases, the lightness or heaviness of the penance must be determined according to the lesser or greater quantity of the stolen property.
Likewise, for grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
oil, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.
Thus: "For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
oil, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast for three nights."

And since this three-night penance consisting of eating [only] food-remnants (*bhakṣya*) and so forth is prescribed for these items, such as grass and the like, this same penance applies to those whose value is one-third of that [standard].
Likewise: "For gems, pearls, corals, copper, silver, iron, bronze, and stones, one must subsist on grain-particles (*kaṇānna*) for twelve days."
Thus:
for those who consume food consisting of grains for twelve days, there is purification from [the theft of] gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, bronze, and stones.
The state of eating broken grains.

In this case as well, since a twelvefold penance is observed—as in the case of edible items—this penance should be understood to apply to the theft of gems, pearls, and the like whose value is twelve times the value of that [stolen object]. Likewise: "For cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed and single-hoofed animals, birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must drink milk for three days."
Thus: For cotton, silk-worms, wool, cloven-hoofed animals, single-hoofed animals, birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must consume milk for three days.

Since even here a threefold penance is observed for items such as foodstuffs, this penance should be understood to apply specifically to the theft of goods whose value is threefold [that of the standard].
The lesser or greater severity of the penance must indeed be determined according to the deficiency or excess of the property being stolen.
Furthermore, this penance for theft is to be understood as applicable only after the stolen property has been restored.
As Viṣṇu has said: "Having returned the stolen property to its owner, one should perform the vow.
Having returned the stolen property to its owner, one should perform the vow.

Furthermore, it is ordained that "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons" regarding the clearing of debts; for its non-payment, as well as for the failure to perform sacrifices and other rites praised as "debts" by the Vedic statement, "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, is born [with three debts]," the fourfold set of penances prescribed generally for minor offenses (*upapātaka*)—beginning with "purification from a minor offense may thus be attained"—should be applied according to one's capacity. Another expiation has also been stated here by Manu: "One should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice at the end of each year for the sake of expiating the omission of animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed."
Thus:
"At the end of the year, one should indeed perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the sake of expiation for the omitted animal and Soma sacrifices, in case they cannot be performed."
"At the turn of the year" means at the end of the year.

Likewise, even if the person authorized [to perform the rite] has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), these same four vows are to be applied after a year in times of distress, according to one's capacity;
however, in the absence of distress, the three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.
However, Kārṣṇājini has stated a specific rule for the period prior to one year:
"A Brahmin, having established the sacred fires at the proper time, should perform the ritual acts according to the injunctions;
if he fails to do so, he becomes purified month by month by means of a three-night fast."
If a son intends to perform a sacrifice while his father or other ancestors have not maintained the sacred fires,
he should indeed perform a sacrifice with a *vrātya* animal as an expiation for that omission.
Thus it is said:
"A Brahmin, having established the sacred fires at the proper time, should perform the ritual acts according to the injunctions.
Failing to do so, he is purified by a three-night fast month after month."
If a son intends to perform a sacrifice while his father or other ancestors have not maintained the sacred fires,
he should indeed sacrifice with a *vrātya* animal as a means of expiation for that omission.
He has also stated a specific rule regarding even a single sacred fire:
"The eldest son who, having married, does not maintain the domestic *upāsana* fire in the home,
shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for a year, or else for one day every month."
Likewise, regarding the sale of articles that should not be sold, a specific penance is stated in another Smṛti.
As Hārīta says: "In the sale of molasses, sesame, flowers, roots, fruits, and cooked food, the penance is the Somapāna Saumya Kṛcchra.
In the sale of any one of lac, salt, honey, meat, oil, milk, curd, buttermilk, ghee, perfumes, skins, or garments, the penance is the Cāndrāyaṇa."

Likewise: for the sale of the *ūrṇā* hair, lions, cows, houses, stones, or weapons; and for the sale of edible meat, sinews, bones, horns, claws, or shells, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
For the sale of asafoetida, bdellium, yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, red ochre, alkali, salt, gems, pearls, coral, bamboo, or earthenware, one must also perform the *taptakṛcchra*.

"In the case of selling a grove, a pond, a well, or a lotus-pool, one becomes purified in a year by bathing at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, eating only at the fourth meal-time, and reciting [the Gāyatrī] ten thousand times. This also applies to the sale of deficient weights and measures, or of mixed and impure goods.

Thus, according to other statements by Śaṅkha, Viṣṇu, and others, where no specific penance is mentioned, the three-month penance prescribed by Manu—which applies generally to minor offenses (*upapātaka*)—is to be adopted in cases other than those involving mortal sin.
In times of distress, however, the fourfold set of vows prescribed by Yājñavalkya should be applied according to one's capacity.

Likewise, regarding the *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother), Vasiṣṭha has stated concerning the matter of penance: "The *parivividāna*, having performed the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances and having given [the bride] back to him, may marry again and wed that very same woman.
The term *parivividāna* refers to the *parivettṛ*;
its specific nature has already been explained above.

Having performed the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, he should give that woman whom he himself married to his elder brother; having offered her—like alms obtained through celibacy—for the sake of avoiding the humiliation of the elder, he should marry again. To the question "Whom? it is said: "He should marry her alone. He should marry that very same woman whom he had married, who was offered to the elder, and who has been approved by him.

As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "When the elder brother is unmarried, the younger brother who marries becomes a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother is the *parivitti* (the one superseded); the girl is the *parivedanī*; the giver is the *paridāyī*; and the officiating priest is the *pariyaṣṭṛ*; all of these are fallen (*patita*) and should purify themselves for one year by performing the *prājāpatya* penance," and also that which was stated by Śaṅkha: "The *parivitti* and the *parivettṛ* should subsist on alms at the houses of Brāhmaṇas for one year"—both of these refer to a case of marriage performed out of one's own will without the permission of the girl's father and others, because of the severity of the penance.
Furthermore, when one marries a maiden who has been given by her father or others out of mere desire, then the three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.
The previously mentioned *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra*, as well as the fourfold vow of Yājñavalkya, refer to cases where the act was committed unknowingly.

A specific rule regarding this matter has also been stated by Yama: "In the case of marrying a younger brother before the elder, there are two *kṛcchras* for the elder brother, and a single *kṛcchra* for the maiden."
The giver shall perform the *atikṛcchra* penance, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Thus:
"In the case of marrying a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, two *kṛcchra* penances are required; for the girl herself, a single *kṛcchra*;
the giver of the bride should perform an *atikṛcchra*, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*."
And this is the same for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*paryāhitāgni*) and so forth, because they are mentioned in a single grammatical construction.

As Gautama says: "For the elder brother whose younger brother marries first (*parivitti*), the younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), the one who has maintained the fires after his younger brother (*paryāhita*), the one who maintains the fires before his elder brother (*paryādhātṛ*), the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried (*agredidhiṣū*), and the husband of an elder sister whose younger sister is already married (*didhiṣūpati*), the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be observed for one year.

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha has prescribed this same penance for the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried and others: "The husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, having performed a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance, may marry her."
"The husband of a *didhiṣū* shall perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances and may marry again the woman who was given to him.

The definitions of the *agredidhiṣū* and others are stated in another Smṛti: "If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried, she is to be known as an *agredidhiṣū*, while the elder sister is remembered as a *didhiṣū*."
Thus it is said:
"If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried,
she is to be known as an *agredidhiṣū*, while the elder sister is remembered as a *didhiṣū*."

In that regard, the husband of an *agredidhiṣū* (the younger sister married before the elder) shall perform a *prājāpatya* penance and then marry that same elder sister after she has been married by another.

But the husband of a *didhiṣū* (the elder sister married after the younger) shall perform a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance, give his own wife—the elder sister—to the man who previously married the younger one, and then marry another woman.

Likewise, regarding both the teacher for hire and the student taught for hire, Viṣṇu has stated under the heading "one shall drink *brahmasuvarcalā* with milk": "Having performed the teaching for hire, as well as the one taught for hire..."
By providing instruction, one should certainly drink [the nectar] for three fortnights.
Thus:
"Having taught for hire, or having been taught by one who teaches for hire,
as well as by providing a false explanation, one shall drink [the decoction] for three fortnights under a strict vow."
"Anuyogapradāna" (the granting of an inquiry) is the interrogation of one who is studying for the sake of excellence, such as asking, "What are you reading? You have ruined it!
For this very reason, it is stated in another Smṛti: "Manu has declared that those who study after having been granted an inquiry [without permission] are outcasts."
In this case as well, there is an option between these and the previously mentioned vows, depending on one's capacity.
Thus concludes the section concerning those who teach for wages and those taught by such teachers.

Similarly, regarding adultery, although the three-month penance prescribed by Manu and the fourfold vows prescribed by Yājñavalkya are generally applicable to minor offenses (*upapātaka*), an exception has been stated for the case of the teacher’s wife and similar instances.
Likewise, elsewhere, Gautama and others have stated an exception based on the specific nature of adultery.

As Gautama says: "Two years for [adultery with] another's wife, three for [the wife of] a Śrotriya. Similarly, having introduced the standard one-year period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he has declared this very same rule regarding minor offenses (*upapātaka*): "And it is the same in the case of minor offenses."

In this regard, the established rule is as follows: for intentionally approaching a Brāhmaṇī who is merely by birth during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), one must observe the standard vow of celibacy (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*) for one year; for approaching a Brāhmaṇī possessing qualities such as being the instrument of ritual action during that same period, the standard vow of celibacy lasts for two years; and for approaching the wife of a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) of that same kind, the standard vow of celibacy lasts for three years. Alternatively, the rule is that for a virtuous Brāhmaṇī who is the wife of a *śrotriya*, the penance is three years; for a Kṣatriya woman of the same description, it is two years; and for a Vaiśya woman of the same description, it is one year. Such is the settled rule.
By the same principle, for one who has violated his vow with a Śūdra woman, a period of ordinary *brahmacarya* lasting six months should be prescribed.

For this very reason, Śaṅkha has shown a reduction according to the order of castes: "One who has spilled his seed with a Vaiśya woman should observe *brahmacarya* for one year, performing the three daily ablutions; with a Kṣatriya woman, for two years; with a Brāhmaṇa woman, for three years; and with a Śūdra woman married to a Brāhmaṇa, [the penance is] as prescribed for a Vaiśya.

In the same way, for a Kṣatriya also, in the case of women of the Kṣatriya and other castes respectively, penances of two years, one year, and six months should be applied to the same aforementioned subject matter.
For a Vaiśya, [the penance] toward a Vaiśya woman or a Śūdra woman is one year or six months respectively.
For a Śūdra, toward a Śūdra woman who is the wife of another, it is exactly six months.

As for the rule of Āpastamba—"In the case of a single encounter with a woman of the same caste who has not belonged to another, there is a quarter-penance; thus, for repetition, a quarter for each instance, and at the fourth time, the whole"—that refers to the same subject matter as the three-year penance prescribed by Gautama.

However, since a twelve-year penance is prescribed for the practice [of intercourse] four times with a woman who has not belonged to another before, this penance does not apply when there is repeated intercourse with the same woman; rather, a penance one-quarter less than that should be assigned for each instance of going.
All of this refers to cases of intentional action (*kāmakāra*).
In the case of unintentional action (*akāmataḥ*), however, this very same penance should be applied to the previously mentioned subject matter by reducing it to half.

However, for sexual intercourse out of desire with a woman who is merely a Brāhmaṇī by birth during a time other than her fertile period (*anṛtukāla*), the three-month penance prescribed by Manu applies.

Furthermore, in this same case, regarding women who are merely Kṣatriyas and so forth, their respective penances—the two-month Cāndrāyaṇa and the one-month [Cāndrāyaṇa]—should be applied; and for Kṣatriyas and others having intercourse with Kṣatriya and other women, the two-month and subsequent penances apply respectively.

Moreover, for the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) having intercourse with these women unintentionally, the following should be observed in order: the gift of eleven cows including a bull (*ṛṣabhaikādaśagodāna*) according to Yājñavalkya, subsisting on the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month, and performing the Prājāpatya penance for one month.
But in the case of approaching a Śūdra woman intentionally, the very vow prescribed for a month should be applied by halving it.
For this very reason, Saṃvarta says:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Śūdra woman [should observe] for a month or even for half a month."
Subsisting on cow urine and barley gruel, one should remain in this state for the sake of liberation from that sin.
Thus:
"But a Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Śūdra woman shall remain for a month or even half a month subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel (yāvaka) for the sake of liberation from that sin."
It is intended that for unintentional [intercourse], the penance is half-monthly.

If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally approach the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, then for one who has desisted from such unrighteous acts, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; for one who has not desisted, it is an *atikṛcchra*. This should be understood to apply to the case of a Śūdra woman who is the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, or to twice-born women who have been married by him and have strayed two or three times, or in the case of approaching them unintentionally.
And so says Saṃvarta:
"Having approached a Brahmin woman who is not a blood relative, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Thus it is said.
Having approached a Brahmin woman who is not a blood relative, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.

But if it is out of desire, one should perform two *kṛcchra* penances for approaching a queen, a female ascetic, a nurse, a virtuous woman, or even a woman of the highest caste, as well as for approaching a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*).
Thus, the two *kṛcchra* penances mentioned by Yama are to be understood.
However, in the case of repeated transgression with a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) or a *vṛṣalī*, one who has spilled his seed shall bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa.
If it is with a Vaiśya woman, he should eat only at every fourth meal-time, feed Brāhmaṇas, and give a load of fodder to the cows.
If one has had sexual intercourse with a Kṣatriya woman, he should fast for three nights and give a vessel of clarified butter;

if with a Brāhmaṇa woman, he should fast for six nights and give a cow. If he has discharged his semen among cows, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance. If he has discharged his semen in an unmarried woman, he should give a load of straw and a māṣaka of lead; this is to be understood as stated by Śaṅkha.

Furthermore, its applicability to the practice [of penance] beginning with the fourth year is understood from another Smṛti: "In the fourth year she is called a *svairiṇī* (wanton woman); in the fifth, she is considered a *bandhakī* (unchaste woman).
Regarding this very subject, it is also stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "Having approached a Brāhmaṇa *bandhakī*, one should give something to a twice-born man."
If he has approached a Kṣatriya woman, he should give a bow; but having approached a Vaiśya woman, he should give a garment.
If a Brahmin has approached a Śūdra woman, he should give a water-pot to a twice-born man;
or, having fasted for a day, he should provide a meal to a Brahmin.
Having approached an unchaste Brāhmaṇa woman, one should give something to a twice-born man;
if she is a Kṣatriya woman, one should give a bow; but having approached a Vaiśya woman, one should give a garment.
If a Brahmin has approached a Śūdra woman, he should give a water-pot to a twice-born man;
or, having fasted for a day, he should provide a meal to a Brahmin.
This collection of expiations pertains to the non-conception of a fetus.

However, when conception has occurred, one should perform that specific expiation which has been prescribed for that particular case, but doubled; for, as the Smṛti of Uśanas states: "But whatever vow there may be for sexual intercourse, one should perform that same vow doubled in the case of a fetus."

Regarding one who conceives a child with a Śūdra woman, a specific rule is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "But one born of a Vṛṣalī woman should eat only at night during the fourth meal-time for three years.
As for the statement of Manu: "A Brāhmaṇa who mounts a Śūdra woman goes to a low state;
having fathered a son upon her, he falls away from Brāhmaṇahood itself."
Thus, that [passage] is primarily intended to proclaim the gravity of the sin;

however, in the case of sexual intercourse in the reverse order (prātilomya), there is always only the death penalty for the man, according to the statement: "In the reverse order, there is death for the man and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the woman."
As for the statement of Vṛddhapracetas: "If a Śūdra, out of delusion, approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman and desires purification, this full vow must be imposed upon him, for she is indeed his mother."
For one who approaches women of other castes, there is a loss of one quarter for each successive lower caste.

Thus, this extension of the twelve-year penance is to be understood as applying to one who approaches [the woman] under the delusion that she is his own wife, because of the inclusion of the qualification "through delusion" (*mohāt*).
As for the statement of Saṃvarta: "If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should somehow approach a Brāhmaṇī woman, the penance for purification shall be either a *Kṛcchra* or a *Sāntapana*."
If a Śūdra, however, should somehow approach a Brāhmaṇa woman, being deluded by lust,
he becomes pure after one month, subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
That [penance] refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇī woman with whom one has had absolutely no prior sexual intercourse.

Regarding sexual intercourse even with women of the lowest castes (*antyajā*), a penance has been stated by Bṛhatsaṃvarta: "A Brāhmaṇa who has approached these women—the washerwoman, the hunter, the actress, and those who live by bamboo-work or leather-work—should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
Thus:
"If a Brāhmaṇa has sexual intercourse with women who subsist as washermen, hunters, actors, or by means of bamboo and skins, he shall perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
This refers to the case of a Brahmin approaching [these women] once out of desire;
however, for Kṣatriyas and others, it should be calculated as reduced by one-quarter for each successive class.
On this very point, Āpastamba has stated: "The Mlecchī, the Naṭī, the leather-worker woman, the washerwoman, and likewise the Buruḍī..."
Having had sexual intercourse with these women, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Thus:
"Having had sexual intercourse with a Mlecchī woman, an actress, a leather-worker's wife, a washerwoman, or a Buruḍī woman, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
And the outcastes (antyajas) have been shown by that very same [author]:
the washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
the fisherman, the Meda, and the Milla— these seven are indeed remembered as the outcastes.
Thus: the washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
the fisherman, the Meda, and the Milla— these seven are indeed remembered as the Antyajas (outcastes).

However, regarding those such as Cāṇḍālas who are outcastes (antyāvasāyins), a heavier penance for sexual intercourse with their women has been shown in the section on violating the Guru’s bed (gurutalpa). Among these women of the lowest castes, whatever penance is prescribed for intercourse with one applies to all of them, because they are all equal in status.
As Uśanas said:
When a single property is predicated of many things that possess that same property,
it must belong to all of them, for they are remembered as being of one and the same form.
Thus:
"When that which is predicated of even one among many things possessing a single property is stated, it must be the effect of all of them; for they are remembered as being of a single form."
But if one approaches women unintentionally— those of the Caṇḍāla, Meda, Śvapaca, or those who observe the Kāpālika vow—
one should perform the Parāka penance.
This should be understood as stated by Āpastamba.

And as for the statement of Saṃvarta: "When a Brahmin approaches the wives of washermen, hunters, actors, or those who subsist on bamboo-work or leather-work, he shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
Thus, that [previous rule] also refers to unintentional cases.

As for what was stated by Śātātapa: "One is purified from [intercourse with] a Kaivarta woman, a Rajaki woman, or one who subsists on bamboo and leather, by means of a single Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance."
Thus, that [penance] refers to cases prior to the emission of semen.

As for what was stated by Uśanas: "For those who eat the food of *kapālika*s, and likewise for those who have sexual intercourse with their women, a year-long *kṛcchra* is prescribed if done intentionally;
if done unintentionally, two *aindava*s."
Thus, that refers to the case of repeated practice.
However, when a conception occurs from approaching a Caṇḍālī or similar women, then, having caused a conception in a Caṇḍālī, one should perform the penance for violating the Guru’s bed;
this should be understood as the twelve-year penance prescribed by Uśanas.
As for that which states: "No expiation is prescribed for one born of a woman of the lowest caste;
he must undoubtedly be banished after having been branded."
This statement of Āpastamba refers to cases of intentional action (*kāmakāra*).

Regarding women as well, in the case of sexual intercourse with a man of the same caste (*savarṇa*) or a lower caste (*anuloma*), the same penance that was prescribed for the man—such as a three-year term (*traivārṣika*) and so forth—applies to her as well; for Manu records: "Whatever penance is prescribed for a man in regard to the wives of others, he should cause her to perform that very vow."
The distinction in penance for a man and a woman of another caste occurs specifically in cases of intercourse in the reverse order.

As Vasiṣṭha says: "If a Śūdra approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in vīraṇa grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇī's head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a donkey and cause her to be led along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known."

Likewise, it is traditionally taught: "If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red darbha grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī's head and having anointed her with clarified butter, she should be led naked along the high road mounted upon a donkey; thus she becomes purified."

Likewise, it is declared: "If a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇī's head and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a bull and a donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road; thus she becomes purified. Similarly, [the rule applies] for a Vaiśya with a Kṣatriya woman, and for a Śūdra with a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman.

By the statement "she becomes purified," it is shown that being paraded along the royal road is itself the form of punishment and a means of purification, independent of any other expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*).

Regarding sexual intercourse with members of the twice-born castes in the reverse order of classes, Saṃvarta has stated another penance for a Brāhmaṇī: "If a Brāhmaṇī should unintentionally have intercourse with a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, she is purified by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel for one month and for half that time respectively."
Thus:
"If a Brāhmaṇī woman should go to a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya against her will,
she is purified by subsisting on cow's urine and barley-gruel for one month and half a month, respectively."
However, if it is done intentionally, double that must be performed, according to the statement: "If done intentionally, it shall be double.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* as well: "A Brāhmaṇa woman, upon serving a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, should perform an Atikṛcchra, a Kṛcchra, and an Atikṛcchra respectively.
A Kṣatriya woman, upon serving a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya, [should perform] half a Kṛcchra, a Prājāpatya, and an Atikṛcchra respectively."
For a Vaiśya woman, in the case of service to a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, the penance is a quarter-kṛcchra, a half-kṛcchra, and a prājāpatya respectively.
For a Śūdra woman, in the case of service to a Śūdra, the penance is a prājāpatya;
however, for service to a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, it is a day and night, three nights, and a half-kṛcchra respectively.
Regarding service to a Śūdra, however, a specific rule has been stated by Bṛhat-Pracetas:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman has sexual union with a Śūdra and does not give birth from him, an expiation is prescribed for her:
a Kṛcchra penance and three Cāndrāyaṇas."
This should be understood to apply when she does not desire it or when there is a mistake regarding her husband.
For a Brahmin woman’s service to a Vaiśya, two Cāndrāyaṇas and one Kṛcchra are prescribed;
for her union with a Kṣatriya, a Kṛcchra and a Cāndrāyaṇa should be performed.
A Kṣatriya woman who has had contact with a Śūdra must perform a Kṛcchra penance and two Cāndrāyaṇas;
one who has united with a Vaiśya must perform a Cāndrāyaṇa and a Kṛcchra.
Having approached a Śūdra, a Vaiśya woman should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by a Cāndrāyaṇa;
in the case of approaching one of a lower caste (ānulomya), she should perform the Kṛcchra reduced by one quarter.
Thus:
for a Brahmin woman’s service to a Vaiśya, there shall be two Cāndrāyaṇas and one Kṛcchra;
for her union with a Kṣatriya, there shall be a Kṛcchra and a Cāndrāyaṇa.
A Kṣatriya woman, through contact with a Śūdra, shall perform a Kṛcchra and two Cāndrāyaṇas;
but one who has united with a Vaiśya shall perform a Cāndrāyaṇa and a Kṛcchra.
A Vaiśya woman, having gone to a Śūdra, should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance followed by a Kṛcchra;
in the case of approaching [a man] of a lower caste in the natural order (ānulomya), she should perform a Kṛcchra reduced by one-quarter.
Regarding a woman who has given birth, it is stated in the twenty-fourth chapter on doubtful cases:
"In the case of the fetus of a Brāhmaṇa, there shall be a Parāka penance; likewise for a Kṣatriya, an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa);
