and for a Vaiśya, both an Aindava and a Parāka, if the act was unintentional."
If there is an abortion from the womb of a Śūdra, one is born as a Caṇḍāla;
therefore, in the case of a miscarriage due to defects of the bodily humors (dhātus), one should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Thus:
"In the case of a Brahmin embryo, there shall be a Parāka penance; likewise for a Kṣatriya, an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa);
and for a Vaiśya, both an Aindava and a Parāka, when the act was unintentional."
If there is an abortion from the womb of a Śūdra, one is born as a Caṇḍāla;
therefore, in the case of a miscarriage due to defects of the bodily constituents (dhātus), one should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Because of the inclusion of the qualification "without her own consent," if she acts with her own consent, one should perform the *parāka* and other penances twice as much.

However, when she gives birth after remaining pregnant for ten months without having previously miscarried, there is no penance; for it is said: "The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived, but not otherwise."

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Vasiṣṭha. However, when a woman who has already conceived subsequently commits adultery with Śūdras and others, she should perform the penance only after the birth, due to the fear of causing an abortion; for it is said: "A pregnant woman who has been approached by a lustful man need not perform penance as long as the fetus has not emerged."
Once the child is born, one should thereafter observe the vow of eating barley-gruel for one month;
there is no defect caused by the womb for him, and he is to be consecrated according to the prescribed rule.
This is because of the observation of another Smṛti text.

However, it should be understood that when they do not perform penance due to arrogance, then there shall be the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the women. Furthermore, regarding sexual intercourse with those born of the lowest castes (antyaja) and others, a penance for women is also shown in another Smṛti text.

If a Brāhmaṇī should unintentionally have sexual intercourse with these— washermen, hunters, actors, or those who subsist by bamboo-work or leather-work— she must observe the Aindava penance for three nights.
Thus:

"If a Brāhmaṇī should unintentionally have sexual intercourse with these— a washerman, a hunter, an actor, or one who lives by bamboo-work or leather-work— she must perform the Aindava penance for three days."

Likewise, even regarding sexual intercourse with outcaste women such as Cāṇḍālas and others, [it is said]: "If a Brāhmaṇī unintentionally approaches a Cāṇḍāla, a Pulkasa, a Mleccha, a Śvapāka, or one who has fallen from his caste, she must perform four Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
Thus:
"A Brāhmaṇī woman who has unintentionally approached a Cāṇḍāla, a Pulkasa, a Mleccha, a Śvapāka, or likewise one who has fallen from his caste, must perform four Cāndrāyaṇa penances."
Because of the statement "if unintentionally," it should be understood that if done intentionally, the penance is double.
Likewise: "If one should somehow come into contact with a Caṇḍāla, he should perform a tonsure including the top-knot and eat barley-gruel."
One should observe a fast for three nights and dwell for one night in water within a well that is equal in size to oneself and filled with the mud of cow-dung and water.
Having remained there without food for three nights, she should then cast [the plant] away;
she should then drink the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper,
having boiled it with milk mixed with gold.
Thereafter, she should eat only one meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
and she should dwell outside for as long as she performs that vow.
Once the penance has been performed, one should then provide a feast for Brahmins;
Svāyambhuva declared that two cows should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of purification.
Thus it is said: "If one should somehow come into contact with a Cāṇḍāla,
he should have his hair shaved, including the top-knot, and eat only boiled rice mixed with barley."
One should fast for three nights and dwell for one night in water within a well that is equal in size to oneself, filled with mud made of cow dung and water.
Having remained there for three nights without food, she should then cast it away.
She should then drink milk mixed with gold after boiling it with the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper.
Thereafter, she should eat only one meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
and she should dwell outside as long as she performs that vow.
Once the penance has been performed, one should then provide a feast for Brahmins;
Svayambhuva declared that two cows should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of purification.
This [penance] also applies only to cases where there was no desire, because of the statement, "if she should somehow go [to him].
Furthermore, another penance for sexual intercourse with an outcaste (antyaja) was stated by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"If a woman has become defiled by outcastes, she should perform a Kṛcchra for one year."
Thus:
"If she has become united with the outcastes, she shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
This [penance] applies to a single instance of intentional intercourse.
But when a woman who has already conceived is subsequently defiled by intercourse with a Cāṇḍāla or similar person, a specific rule for that case has been stated:
"A young woman who is pregnant and defiled by one of the lowest castes shall not perform penance until the fetus has emerged."
She should not move about within the house, nor should she adorn her limbs;
she should not sleep with her husband, nor eat together with her kinsmen.
When the fetus has been lost, one should perform the expiation consisting of the Kṛcchra penance for one year;
or else, one should give gold or a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Thus it is said:
"A young woman who is pregnant, even if she has had sexual intercourse with one of the lowest castes,
shall not perform penance until the fetus has been delivered."
She should not move about within the house, nor should she adorn her limbs;
she should not sleep with her husband, nor eat together with her kinsmen.
When an embryo has perished, one should perform the penance of a Kṛcchra for a year;
alternatively, one should give gold or a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.

But when she engages in excessive sexual intercourse out of desire, then, "If she has had contact with an outcaste—whether in eating or in sexual union—she shall enter a blazing fire; through death she is purified."

Thus the statement of Uśanas is to be understood. However, when she does not perform the prescribed penance, then she should be marked with a brand or executed as a male; for it is recorded in the Smṛti of Parāśara: "She who has been enjoyed by a man of a lower caste should be branded or else executed."

Likewise, the determination of the penances for the elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (*parivitti*) should be understood to be analogous to those for the younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*).
However, there is this distinction:

whereas for the *parivettṛ* there are the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances in a given case, for the *parivitti* there is the *prājāpatya*. For Vasiṣṭha records: "The *parivitti*, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, may marry again and take that very same woman as his wife."

Regarding usury and the purchase of salt, however, the penances for general minor offenses (upapātaka) prescribed by Manu and Yājñavalkya should be applied in consideration of caste, capacity, qualities, and other factors. 3.265.

Immediately after [the section on] the purchase of salt, "the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya" is recited among the minor offenses (upapātaka); regarding that, he states another penance as well: "For the killing of a Kṣatriya, a man should give one thousand cows plus one bull, or he should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for three years."
A slayer of a Vaiśya shall perform this for one year and give one hundred cows;
a slayer of a Śūdra shall perform this for six months, or else give ten cows.

That which has one more than a thousand is "one-thousand-plus" (*ekasahasra*); that which completes such a number is "the one-thousandth" (*ekasahasra*). Those cows for whom there is a bull as the one-thousandth are "those with a bull as the one-thousandth" (*ṛṣabhaikasahasrāḥ*); these he should give upon killing a Kṣatriya.
Alternatively, he should perform the extensive penance, the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa, for three years.
Furthermore, one who kills a Vaiśya should observe this same vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for one year.
Or he may give one hundred and one bulls among cows.
But a killer of a Śūdra shall perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for six months;
or else, he may give ten cows that have recently calved, together with their calves.

This refers to the killing of a *kṣatriya* or others who are *jātimātra* (by birth alone) without intention (*akāmataḥ*), because these same penances are prescribed in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra] following the introduction: "But having unintentionally caused the downfall of a *rājanya*... The application of gifts and austerities is determined according to one's capacity. However, regarding a *vaiśya* or a *śūdra* who slightly abides by their conduct, [the following applies]: "A fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin is ordained for the killing of a *kṣatriya*."
In a Vaiśya established in his proper conduct, it should be known as an eighth part; but in a Śūdra, it is a sixteenth part.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Manu.
However, in the case of a Kṣatriya who abides in good conduct (*vṛttastha*), a penance of four and a half years should be prescribed.
By the word "conduct" (*vṛtta*) here, qualities and so forth are meant: "Veneration of the guru, compassion, purity, truthfulness, and restraint of the senses."
And the promotion of beneficial things—all that is called conduct (vṛtta).
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Manu.
As for the statement of Vṛddha-Hārīta: "A Brāhmaṇa, having killed a Kṣatriya, shall observe the vow for six years;
having killed a Vaiśya, the twice-born man shall likewise observe that vow for three years."
Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform penance for one year and give ten cows with a bull as the eleventh.
Thus, that [penance] refers to cases where the act was committed intentionally.
However, regarding the killing of a learned Kṣatriya and others, it is said: "In the case of killing a Kṣatriya, one should perform a penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa reduced by one-fourth;
in the case of killing a Vaiśya, one should perform half; but in the case of a Śūdra, one-fourth."
Thus should the statement of Vṛddha-Hārīta be understood.

As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha—"A Brāhmaṇa, having killed a Kṣatriya, shall observe the vow for eight years; six years for a Vaiśya; and three years for a Śūdra"—that too refers to the same subject matter as that of Hārīta.
The only distinction is that in the case of a Kṣatriya, he is slightly inferior in qualities.

But when he is both learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in good conduct (*vṛttastha*), then the twelve-year penance prescribed by Āpastamba for killing a student of the Veda belonging to either of the two higher castes should be observed. However, if a Kṣatriya or another who has not studied the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) kills one who has commenced a sacrificial rite, it should be understood that the rule applies: "One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the vow [prescribed] for Brahman."

Furthermore, regarding a *śrotriya* Kṣatriya or others engaged in a sacrifice, for the killing of such a person by a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the standard six-year period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh; for the killing of a Vaiśya, one should perform three years of it and give a hundred cows with a bull as the eleventh; for the killing of a Śūdra, one should perform one year of it and give eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh. This combination of gift-giving and austerity mentioned by Gautama is to be understood as applying to cases where the act was not intentional.
This [penance] refers to a situation where the act was unintentional.

As before, having killed [a Brahmin] unintentionally among the four castes, one should prescribe penances of twelve years, six years, three years, and one year respectively; at the conclusion of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, half of that again, and half of that once more, for all of them in due order, according to the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha.
And this twelve-year penance is to be understood as applying specifically to a Kṣatriya who is slightly inferior in qualities, while it applies to a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who possess superior qualities.

Since the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya is specifically enumerated among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), it does not fall within the scope of the maxim regarding general rules and exceptions (*utsargāpavādanyāya*); therefore, the penances generally prescribed for minor offenses must also be applied here.

In that regard, when a wicked Kṣatriya or similar person is killed intentionally, the penances prescribed by Manu—lasting three months, three years, two months, and the *cāndrāyaṇa*—should be applied according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*).

But for unintentional killing, the following prescribed by the Lord of Yogins should be applied in due order: a fast for three nights accompanied by the gift of eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh, subsisting on *pañcagavya* for one month, and the monthly milk-vow (*payovrata*).
Furthermore, this aforementioned collection of vows is to be understood as applying to the killing of a Kṣatriya or others when committed by a Brāhmaṇa.
"But having unintentionally slain a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born..."
Likewise,
O Brāhmaṇa, for the killing of a Rājanya, the penance lasts for six years;
likewise, a Brāhmaṇa having killed a Kṣatriya [must perform it].

In these and other such statements by Manu, Gautama, Hārīta, and Vasiṣṭha, because of the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," it should be understood that when the act is committed by a Kṣatriya or others, the penalty is reduced by one quarter for the killing of a Kṣatriya and so forth. As it is said: "The full amount is to be given for a Brāhmaṇa; for a Kṣatriya, it is recorded as being one-quarter less; for a Vaiśya, half; and for those of the Śūdra caste, one quarter is prescribed."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti of Vṛddha-Viṣṇu:
"The assembly for Brāhmaṇas is as prescribed; for Kṣatriyas, it is considered to be double that;
for Vaiśyas, it is declared to be triple. And the penance is remembered to be in accordance with the assembly."
Such is the statement of Aṅgiras; it was stated in the section on cow-slaughter that this refers to cases of verbal or physical cruelty committed in a contrary manner.

This collection of penances does not apply to the killing of Mūrdhāvasikta and others, because they lack the status of being Kṣatriyas and so forth. Therefore, in their case, the increase or decrease of the aforementioned set of observances must be determined solely in accordance with the punishment.

Furthermore, the increase and decrease of punishment have been shown in the rule that "the infliction of punishment must be carried out according to the higher or lower status of the caste and class" (3.266–267).
He states the penance for killing a woman:
"Having killed women of the Brahmin, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly,
one should give, respectively, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep for the sake of purification."

Having killed wives of Brahmins and others who are ill-behaved and unchaste, one should give, in order, a water-skin (a leather pouch for holding water), a bow, a goat, a sheep, and a ram for the sake of purification. This refers to the unintentional killing of Brahmin women and others born of the reverse order of castes (*prātilomya*). However, regarding intentional killing, Brahmagarbha says:
For women born of inverse unions (pratiloma), a period of one month is prescribed;
for those of intermediate origin, such as Sūtas and others, it is four, two, and six months respectively.
Thus it is said:
for women born of inverse unions (pratiloma), the period of impurity is prescribed as one month;
for those of intermediate origin, such as Sūtas and others, it is four, two, and six [months respectively].

In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇī and so forth, the connection is according to the actual status: six months for a Kṣatriyā, four for a Vaiśyā, and two for a Śūdrā. However, when one kills a woman who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśyā, then "something" must be given, because of the Smṛti of Gautama: "In the case of a Vaiśyā, nothing [is required]. When she who lives by the occupation of a Vaiśyā (vaiśika) is killed, only something small should be given, and that is water; as it is said: "One should offer a water-pot or a well to a Brāhmaṇa, or [the same] for a Brāhmaṇī."
For killing a Kṣatriya woman, a cow is prescribed; for killing a Vaiśya woman, a goat is traditionally ordained.
Having killed a sheep, a man should give water as an offering for killing one born of a Śūdra woman or a Vaiśya woman.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Aṅgiras;

furthermore, when Brāhmaṇas and others who have been violated by Kṣatriyas and others through inverse order (prātilomya) are slain, then the penances for cow-slaughter should be applied as appropriate. 3.268.
He states a specific rule regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa woman or others who have slightly deviated [from chastity]:
"Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the vow for killing a Śūdra.
When one kills a Brāhmaṇa woman or another such woman who is not excessively corrupt—that is, one who has slightly deviated—then one should perform the six-month vow for killing a Śūdra.
Or else, one may give ten cows;
this [penance] lasting six months is to be understood as applying to the intentional killing of a Kṣatriya woman, whereas it applies to the unintentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa woman.
For the intentional killing of a Vaiśya woman, one should give ten cows.
In the case of intentionally killing a Śūdra woman, one must consume *pañcagavya* for one month, as this is the general penance prescribed for minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
However, when one intentionally kills a Brāhmaṇa woman, the penance lasts for twelve months.
But in the case of unintentionally killing women of the Kṣatriya and other castes, the penances are three months, one and a half months, and twenty-two and a half days respectively.
As Pracetas has stated: "Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who has not reached her menses, one should perform a Kṛcchra for one year or for six months;
having killed a Kṣatriya woman, for six months or for three months;
having killed a Vaiśya woman, for three months or for a month and a half."

"Having killed a Śūdra woman, [one shall observe penance] for one and a half months or twenty-two and a half days. As for that which was set forth by Hārīta—having established that "for a Kṣatriya, the basic period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) is six years; for a Vaiśya, three; and for a Śūdra, one and a half"—and then stating, "as in the case of a Kṣatriya woman, so for Brāhmaṇa women; as for a Kṣatriya woman, so for a Vaiśya woman; as for a Vaiśya woman, so for a Śūdra woman; having killed a Śūdra woman, [one shall observe penance] for nine months," that too should be understood to apply to the intentional killing of women who possess qualities such as being instrumental in religious rites.
But in all cases where it is unintentional, half [of the penance] should be prescribed;
however, regarding an Ātreyī woman, that which was stated previously applies.

In connection with the expiation for violence, he now states the expiation even for the killing of living beings that constitutes a minor offense (*anupapātaka*), which is designated under the category of miscellaneous rules (*prakīrṇaka*):
"But [the expiation is] for a thousand vertebrate animals, and likewise for a cartload of boneless ones."

Having killed a thousand vertebrate creatures such as lizards for which no specific expiation has been mentioned, and having killed a cartload—that is, just enough to fill a cart—of boneless creatures such as lice, bedbugs, gadflies, and mosquitoes, one should observe the six-month vow of celibacy prescribed for killing a Śūdra, or else give ten cows.
Because of the restriction on the quantity by the word "thousand," if more than that number are killed, an additional penance must be determined.

On the other hand, for killing fewer than that, he will state that for each individual killing involving bones something should be given, while for boneless creatures it is a breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Likewise, the rule "anaḥ" (a cartload) regarding boneless creatures refers to very minute animals;

however, for the killing of larger boneless creatures such as wood-boring insects (*ghuṇa*) and the like, one should refer to Manu’s statement following the passage beginning with "Having killed worms, insects, or birds," which describes them as causes of defilement (*malinīkaraṇīya*), and specifically the rule: "For acts causing defilement, one should subsist on *yāvaka* for three days. (3.269)
Furthermore:
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance.

Cats and the like are well known; as for birds, they include the blue jay (*caṣa*), the crow (*kāka*), and the owl (*ulūka*). Having killed these, one should drink milk for three nights or perform a *pādakṛcchra* penance.
By the use of the word "or" (*vā*), one may also undertake such acts as traveling a *yojana*.
As Manu has said:
One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana*,
or touch the waters of a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the waters (*ab-daivata*).
Thus it is said:
"One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana,
or touch the waters of a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the Waters."
And this refers to the case of killing each [animal] individually.
However, in the case of killing them together, having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
and a frog, as well as a dog, a monitor lizard, an owl, and a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra.
Thus, what was stated by Manu should be understood as referring to a six-month penance.

Furthermore, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a snake, a small mouse, or a rat, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and give some gift"—is to be understood as applying to cases of intentional repetition. "Dahara" means a small mouse or a muskrat (chuchundarī). (3.270)
Furthermore: for an elephant, five blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for donkeys, goats, and rams, a bull should be given; and for a crane, a three-year-old [bull].
When an elephant is killed, five blue bulls must be given;
for a parrot bird, a two-year-old calf;
and for each of an ass, a goat, or a ram being killed, one bull each.
In the case of a crane, a three-year-old calf is to be given;
the phrase "is to be given" is to be supplied everywhere. A specific rule regarding this has also been stated by Manu.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; for killing a goat or a sheep, an ox; and for killing a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Thus [ends verse] 3.271.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; and for killing a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Furthermore:

Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous animal, a peacock living on land or water, or a vulture, one should give a cow; however, for killing a non-carnivorous bird, one should give a heifer.
A "kravyāda" is a specific type of wild animal, such as a tiger or a jackal, that eats raw meat (*kravyam*); this is understood from its association with the monkey.
Likewise, from its mention alongside the *haṃsa* and the *śyena*, it also includes specific types of birds such as the *kaṅka* and the vulture.
By the word "water" (*jala*), water-dwelling creatures such as the *baka* crane and others are included.
By the word *sthala* (land), land-dwelling creatures such as cranes (*balākā*) and others are meant;
*śikhaṇḍin* is a peacock;
and *bhāsa* is a particular species of bird.
The remaining [terms] are well known.
For the killing of each of these, one should give a single cow.
However, having killed non-carnivorous animals such as the *hariṇa* deer and specific birds such as the *khañjarīṭa*, one should give a heifer.
And so Manu says:
"Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or a peacock,
as well as a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should cause a cow to be touched by a Brāhmaṇa."
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; and for killing a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
having killed non-carnivorous ones, a heifer; but having killed a camel, a kṛṣṇala of gold.
Thus [ends verse] 3.272.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock,
as well as a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should present a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; for killing a goat or a sheep, an ox; and for killing a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
having killed non-carnivorous ones, a heifer; and having killed a camel, a kṛṣṇala of gold.
Furthermore: For a snake, an iron rod; for a eunuch, tin and lead; for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a *guñjā* seed; and for a horse, a fine cloth.
When reptiles have been killed, an iron staff with a sharp point should be given [as compensation].

When a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) or neuter person has been killed, one should give a *māṣa*-weight of tin and lead, or a load of straw; for it is seen in another *Smṛti* text that "having killed a *paṇḍaka*, one should give a load of straw, or tin, or lead.
Even though it is said: "A *paṇḍaka* may be devoid of sexual organs, yet he is not at all fit for sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*)."

Although Devala’s statement thus indicates [the object] in a general sense as being devoid of masculine or feminine gender, nevertheless, there is no intention here to refer to the form of cows and Brahmins. This is because the prohibition against killing cows and Brahmins operates by way of delimiting the genus (*jāti*), and since the inherence of that genus is no different in a eunuch (*paṇḍa*) who lacks gender, it is for that reason alone that a light penance has been prescribed.
Therefore, only wild animals and birds are intended, both because of this [statement] and because of their mention in conjunction with wild animals and birds.
When a boar or a pig has been killed, a jar of ghee should be given;
for a camel, a *guñjā* seed should be given;
and when a horse has been struck down, a fine garment should be given.
And so Manu says:
"Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead."
Thus [ends verse] 3.273.
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.
Furthermore:
If one is unable to give a drona of sesame seeds for each [animal] beginning with the partridge and ending with the elephant as a gift,
one should perform a kṛcchra penance for the purification of each individual case.
When a winged partridge has been killed, one should give a *droṇa* of sesame seeds.
The word *droṇa* denotes a specific measure of capacity:
eight handfuls make a *kiñcit*, and eight *kiñcit*s make a *puṣkala*.
Four *puṣkala*s, however, are proclaimed to be one *āḍhaka*.
Four āḍhakas make one droṇa; such is the definition of these measures.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.

Upon killing the aforementioned elephants and other animals, one who is unable to perform the gift of five blue bulls and so forth due to poverty should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each in order to achieve purification.
Furthermore, the word *kṛcchra* here should be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to any austerity whatsoever that is accomplished through hardship.

And the penances (*tapas*) have been shown by Gautama: "The time [of penance] consists of one year, six months, four, three, two, or one month; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, or a day and night.
These very [periods] should be performed optionally when no specific rule is given—severe ones for a grave sin and mild ones for a light sin.
If the primary meaning were taken by the word *kṛcchra*, then in the case of either an elephant or a parrot, there would specifically be only the *prājāpatya* penance.
And that is not logical;

for if one were intent on austerity alone, then even within austerity, the distinction between what is heavy and what is light would be appropriate based on the consideration of the gravity or lightness of the gift [offered].
Consequently, there would be a two-month penance of drinking barley-gruel for an elephant, whereas for a parrot, it would be a simple fast.
In the same way, elsewhere as well, penance should be determined according to the nature of the gift. || 3.274 ||
Furthermore, he says:
"In the case of killing living beings produced in fruits, flowers, food, and liquids, one should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Regarding fruits such as the *udumbara*, flowers such as the *madhūka*, food such as boiled rice or parched flour that has stood for a long time, and liquids such as molasses—in the destruction of those living beings and creatures that are born therein, the consumption of clarified butter is the means of purification."

And this consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*) is prescribed specifically for the purpose of eating, because expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are of the nature of austerity (*tapas*). This nature as austerity has been demonstrated in the *Āṅgirasa* [text] under the guise of etymologizing the term "expiation": "Austerity (*prāya*) is said to be heat; 'mind' (*citta*) is called determination."
That which is joined with the resolve for austerity is called expiation (prāyaścitta).
Thus it is said.
*Prāya* is said to mean austerity (*tapas*), and *citta* is called determination (*niścaya*). That which is joined with both austerity and determination is called *prāyaścitta*.

Since there is an infinity of expiations for each individual living being, and because it would be impossible to state them even by questioning ten million times, he states the expiation in general terms:
"Something should be given for the killing of a creature with bones; however, for a boneless creature, a breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is required."
For the killing of each of up to one thousand vertebrate creatures, such as lizards and the like, a small amount of grain, gold, or other goods should be given.

However, for a boneless creature, there is a single *prāṇāyāma*. Regarding the phrase "a small amount," when gold is to be given, it should be exactly one *paṇa*, because of the traditional teaching of Sumantu: "In the case of killing a vertebrate creature, one *paṇa* should be given."
But when grain is to be given, then eight handfuls (muṣṭi) should be given, according to the traditional rule that "eight handfuls shall constitute 'something'.
And this applies to cases of killing animals for which no specific expiation has been mentioned;
however, where a specific expiation is heard in the scriptures, that very one prevails.
As Parāśara has said: "One who kills a swan, a crane, a ruddy goose, a curlew, or a cock, as well as one who kills a peacock or a ram, becomes pure by eating only one meal [a day]."
Having killed a water-crow, a lapwing, a parrot, a pigeon,
a gallinule, or a crane, one is indeed purified by eating only at night.
One who kills blue jays, crows, pigeons, sarīs,
or partridges is purified by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water at both twilights.
One who kills vultures, hawks, birds, or owls,
and eats uncooked food, shall remain standing during the day and subsist on air alone for two meal-times.
Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a water-snake,
one should feed Brahmins individually, and an iron staff is the sacrificial fee.
A killer of porcupines, tortoises, iguanas, rabbits,
or hedgehogs is purified by eating eggplant and guñjā seeds for a day and night.
One who kills deer, roe-deer, boars, sheep, goats, and rams,
as well as wolves, jackals, bears, and hyenas;
He should subsist on air for three days and give a measure of sesame seeds as a gift for the killing of an elephant, a ram, a horse, a camel, or a gayal.
The expiation for one who kills a donkey, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger is a fast of one day and night and immersion in water at the three junctions of the day.
One attains purity after three nights and by feeding Brāhmaṇas.
Thus [it is said].
One who kills swans, cranes, ruddy geese, curlews, or wild cocks,
as well as peacocks and rams, is purified by eating only one meal a day.
Having killed a water-crow, a lapwing, a parrot, a pigeon,
a gallinule, or a crane, one is indeed purified by eating only at night.
One who kills blue jays, crows, pigeons, sarīs,
or partridges is purified by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water at both twilights.
One who kills vultures, hawks, other birds, or owls,
and eats uncooked food, shall remain standing during the day and subsist on air alone for two meal-times.
Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a water-snake, one should feed Brahmins individually; and an iron staff is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
A killer of iguanas, tortoises, and lizards, or of rabbits and porcupines,
is purified in a day and night by eating eggplants and guñjā fruits.
One who kills deer, roe-deer, boars, sheep, goats, or rams,
as well as wolves, jackals, bears, and hyenas;
However, for the killing of an elephant, a ram, a horse, a camel, or a gayal, he should subsist on air for three days and give a measure (prastha) of sesame seeds as a gift.
The expiation for one who kills a donkey, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger is a fast of one day and night, along with immersion in water at the three junctions of the day.
One attains purity after three nights and by feeding Brāhmaṇas.
In this way, for other statements of the Smṛti as well, the determination of their scope should be understood by taking into account factors such as place and time. (3.275)

The cutting down of trees for the sake of fuel is indeed listed among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*). However, because it was recited out of sequence due to its connection with violence and greed, [the author] extracts it and prescribes the penance there:
"For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred *ṛc* verses should be recited;
for the useless cutting of medicinal herbs, one should subsist on milk and follow cows for a day."

If one cuts trees that bear fruit, such as mangoes and jackfruit trees, or shrubs and the like, for any purpose other than sacrifices and other rites for unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), one must recite the *gāyatrī* and other Vedic verses (*ṛc*) one hundred times.
However, if one cuts cultivated or wild herbs in vain, one must follow cows for the entire day for the sake of their service and, at the end, drink only milk while abandoning all other food.
But there is no fault if it is for the sake of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*).

And this should be understood as applicable to useful trees by way of their fruit and so forth; however, for the cutting down of fruit-bearing trees, one hundred *ṛc* verses are to be recited, as well as for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Manu. Even though it serves a visible purpose, there is no fault in its being for the sake of the plow and other implements that are auxiliary to cultivation; for Vasiṣṭha’s traditional teaching states: "One should not harm trees laden with fruit and flowers, yet one may destroy them for the purpose of performing cultivation.
However, where the punishment is increased due to a particular location, an increase in penance must also be inferred there.
Thus it has been said: "In the case of trees grown at a shrine, a cemetery, a boundary, a holy place, or a temple, as well as in the case of a tree renowned for its fame, the fine is double."

Thus, this recitation of one hundred Ṛgvedic verses pertains to the twice-born classes and not to Śūdras and others, because they lack the qualification for such recitation. Therefore, for them, a penance of two nights or more should be determined in accordance with the severity of the punishment.

In order to avoid the redundancy of its specific mention among the minor offenses (upapātaka), the penance generally applicable to minor offenses also applies here; however, due to the gravity of this offense, that penance should be understood as pertaining to cases of repeated practice. (3.276)

In connection with the penances for killing unchaste women, monkeys, and so forth, he states the penance occasioned by being bitten by them: "One who is bitten by unchaste women, monkeys, or donkeys, or by dogs, camels, and crows... [repeated].
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) in water and consumed clarified butter (ghṛta), one becomes purified.
Prostitutes and the like are well known; a man bitten by these, having performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water and having consumed ghee, becomes purified.
By the inclusion of the word "and the like" (ādi), jackals and others are included.
As Manu has said:
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus: "One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma)."

This consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśa*) should be understood as a substitute for a meal, because expiations, being of the nature of austerity (*tapas*), are intended to cause heat in the body.
This refers to cases where one lacks the capacity [to perform other penances].

As for the statement of Sumantu—that for those bitten by a dog, a jackal, a deer, a buffalo, a goat, a sheep, a donkey, a camel, a mongoose, a cat, a mouse, a water-fowl, a crane, a crow, or a human, there shall be bathing with the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses and three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*)—that applies to cases of slight bites below the navel region.
As for the statement of Aṅgiras: "A student who has been bitten by a dog should drink milk in the evening for three days;
if he is a householder, then for two nights; but if he maintains the sacred fires, for one day."
For one bitten above the navel, that same [penance] shall be doubled;
it shall be tripled for a bite on the face, and quadrupled on the head.
Thus, that refers to the case of one who has seen [the truth] correctly.
For a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, however, it should be calculated as reduced by one-quarter and one-quarter respectively.
But for a Śūdra: "The purification of Śūdras is through fasting or else through giving."
Or one should give a cow or a single bull to a Brahmin for the sake of purification.

Thus it should be understood as stated by Bṛhad-Aṅgiras. As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "A Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog becomes pure by going to a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and consuming clarified butter."
Thus, that refers to the region of the head.
But in the case of women: "A Brāhmaṇī woman bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a wolf becomes pure immediately upon seeing the risen planets and stars."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Parāśara.
Furthermore, a specific rule for a woman observing vows such as the Kṛcchra has been shown by that same author:
"A woman of virtuous vows who has been bitten by a dog should fast for three nights."
Having eaten barley gruel with ghee, one should complete the remainder of the vow.
Thus it is said:
"A woman of good vows who has been bitten by a dog should fast for three nights;
having eaten barley-gruel with ghee, she should complete the remainder of her vow."
A specific rule regarding a woman in her menses has also been shown by Pulastya:
"When a woman in her menses is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey,
she becomes pure after fasting for five nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
Above the navel it is double, at the mouth likewise triple, and it is recorded as quadruple at the head; if bitten elsewhere, there shall be immersion [in water].
Thus:
when a woman in her menses is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey,
she becomes pure after fasting for five nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Above the navel it is double [the size], at the mouth likewise triple, and at the head it is remembered as fourfold; if bitten elsewhere, there shall be immersion [in water].
Except in the case of being in one's menstrual period;
however, regarding one who is defiled by dogs and the like through smelling and so forth, a specific rule has been stated by Śātātapa:
"For one who has been smelled by a dog, or scratched by its claws..."
Purification consists of washing with water and heating with fire.
Thus it is said:
"For that which has been licked by a dog, scratched with its claws,
or defiled by water, purification is achieved by washing with water and by warming over fire."
"Upacūlana" means heating.
However, when worms arise in a wound produced by the bite of a dog or the like, or by a blow from a weapon and so forth, a specific rule has been stated by Manu:
"When pus and blood appear in the opening of a Brahmin's wound..."
If worms arise within one's body, what should the expiation be?
One should perform a bath with the urine and dung of cows at the three junctions of the day;
by consuming the five products of the cow for three nights, one is purified even if the defilement is below the navel.
If a worm arises in a wound produced between the navel and the throat,
it is prescribed in the Smṛti that one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for six nights or three days.
In that regard, for a wound caused by the bite of a dog or similar animal, this [following rite] must be performed immediately after the penance for that specific bite.
However, in the case of a wound produced by a weapon or other such means, the remainder of the rule is that one must consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth for three days.
For Kṣatriyas and the other castes, however, a reduction of one-quarter for each successive class should be applied. (3.277)

In connection with the penance for biting that severs the bodily element of skin, he now states the penance for emission that severs the final bodily element: "With these two verses, *yan me 'dya retaḥ* and so forth, one should consecrate the emitted semen;
with the ring finger, one should touch the space between the breasts and the middle of the eyebrows."

If, somehow, even without sexual intercourse with a woman, the final element (semen) is emitted, then one should consecrate that spilled semen with these two mantras: "The semen which today has been spilled by me upon the earth; may my faculty return to me. With that consecrated semen, one should touch the middle of the breasts and the eyebrows with the ring finger. Others, however, explain that because the spilled semen is impure and thus unfit for the act of touching, the word "with that" (*tena*)—due to its association with the ring finger—refers to the thumb present in one's own mind.
The claim that "tena" (by that) was specified [instead of "anāmikayā"] because using the term "aṅguṣṭhapada" (the word 'thumb') would result in a metrical break is incorrect;
for the thumb is not present in the mind [at that point].
Nor is it logical to connect something present in the mind through the sense of the passage while abandoning what is directly presented by the words.
Thus it has been said:
"No qualification of an object currently being understood is ever observed,
whether by means of other words or by case-endings, as in the expression 'this smoke is burning.'"
Thus:
"An implied meaning is never seen to be qualified by other words or by case-endings, as in the expression 'this smoke is burning'."
Nor is semen unfit for touch due to its impurity;
for it is understood from the injunction itself that it is fit for touching in the form of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), just as liquor is fit for drinking in the form of an expiation.

And this expiation applies only to a householder who has unintentionally emitted [semen], because a heavy expiation is seen prescribed for a religious student (*brahmacārin*) in cases of emission during sleep or while awake.

As for the statement of Yama—which the NSP edition reads as a statement of Manu: "If a householder should intentionally cause the emission of semen upon the ground, he should recite [the Gāyatrī] a thousand times along with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma)."
Thus, that refers to the case of acting according to one's own will. (3.278)
Furthermore:
"And if one sees one's own reflection in water, thinking 'there is fire in me,' one should mutter the Sāvitrī;
likewise when seeing something impure, or when acting with fickleness, or even when speaking untruth."
If one sees one's own reflection in water, then one should mutter this mantra: "The sensory faculty of light is in me.
Furthermore, upon seeing an impure substance, one should mutter the *Sāvitrī*—the verse dedicated to the deity Savitṛ beginning with "tat savituḥ.
Likewise, in the event of engaging in the restlessness of speech, hands, feet, and so forth, as well as in speaking untruth, one should mutter that same verse.
This should be understood as applying when done intentionally.
But in the case of what is done unintentionally: "Having slept, having eaten, having sneezed, having spat, and after speaking untruths;
and after drinking water, one who is about to study should sip water (ācamana), even if he is already pure."
Thus, the sipping of water (ācamana) mentioned by Manu is to be observed.

As for the statement of Saṃvarta: "Upon sneezing, upon spitting, likewise when food is stuck between the teeth, upon speaking untruth, and upon conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear."
Thus, this should be understood as applying to cases where the purpose is minor or when there is a lack of water.

Following the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya, "living by reprehensible means" is mentioned; in that regard, the penances for secondary sins (upapātaka) prescribed by Manu and Yājñavalkya are to be understood according to considerations of caste, capacity, virtue, and so forth.

Even in the case of atheism (*nāstikya*), those same penances (*prāyaścitta*) are to be applied in that very manner. By the word "atheism," the reviling of the Vedas is meant; by that, living [in such a state] is expressed. Regarding both of these, Vasiṣṭha has also stated another penance: "An atheist, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism; but one who follows the conduct of an atheist [must perform] the *atikṛcchra*. And this refers to the case of a single occurrence.
The penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), however, refer to cases of repeated practice.

As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha—"An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who brings false accusations—these shall beg alms at the house of a Brāhmaṇa for five years"—and that which was stated by Hārīta, beginning with "An atheist, one who lives like an atheist," and continuing, "They shall perform the penance of the five fires, sleeping under the open sky, and lying in water during the summer, the rainy season, and the winter respectively"—both of these refer to cases involving a firm adherence to [heretical] views and prolonged practice. (3.279)
It was stated that the violation of a vow follows immediately after atheism.
Since the term *avakīrṇin* is not well-known, he states the penance for such a person after first providing its definition:
"A religious student (*brahmacārī*) becomes an *avakīrṇin* by having sexual intercourse with a woman."
By sacrificing an ass as an animal offering to Nirṛti, he becomes purified.

The religious student (*brahmacārin*) is of two kinds: the *upakurvāṇaka* (the temporary student) and the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong student). If either of these approaches a woman, he becomes an *avakīrṇin* (one who has spilled his seed).

"Spilling" (*avakīrṇa*) refers to the emission of the final element; one who possesses this is an *avakīrṇin*. He is purified by performing a sacrifice with a donkey as the sacrificial animal, which has Nirṛti as its presiding deity.

Although the status of the donkey as the sacrificial animal is already established, the word "animal" (*paśu*) is repeated here in order to ensure the application of the ritual rules for animals (*paśudharma*) as prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras* of Āśvalāyana and others, such as those beginning with "Now follows the ritual procedure for the animal."

And this [penance] is to be performed in the forest at a crossroads before the common fire; for Vasiṣṭha records in his Smṛti: "If a religious student should approach a woman, he shall sacrifice an ass as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣas deity in the forest at a crossroads before the common fire."
Likewise, at night, one who has violated his vow of celibacy (avakīrṇin) should perform the sacrifice with a one-eyed, black, four-footed animal at a crossroads;
thus says Manu:
"But the avakīrṇin [should sacrifice] with a one-eyed, black [goat] at a crossroads."
One should worship Nirṛti at night according to the procedure for the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
Thus it is said:
"But one who has broken his vow of chastity shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed, tawny-colored goat, according to the procedure for a *pākayajña*."
In the absence of an animal victim, one should sacrifice with an oblation (*caru*); or one should offer an oblation to Nirṛti.
Regarding this, one should sacrifice [reciting]: "To Kāma, svāhā! To Kāmakāma, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities who are Rākṣasas, svāhā!"—according to the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha.
And this applies to the case of one who is incapable [of performing the full rite].
Furthermore, one who is capable [of performing the penance] but has committed the *avakīrṇin* offense should sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a donkey.

Having put on its skin with the hair facing upward and carrying a red vessel, he should beg for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his deed; according to Gautama, he is purified after a year. This should be understood as a sacrificial animal offering (*paśuyāga*) or a cooked oblation (*caru*), combined with the aforementioned year-long austerity. Likewise, bathing three times a day and eating only once a day should be observed. When this sin has been incurred: "Having worn the donkey-skin... [and so forth].
He should go for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own past deeds.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day,
and performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu. Furthermore, this [penance] lasting for one year should be understood to apply in the case of a non-learned (*aśrotriya*) Brāhmaṇa woman or a Vaiśya woman who is the wife of a learned (*śrotriya*) man. However, when one discharges semen in a virtuous Brāhmaṇa or Kṣatriya woman who is the wife of a learned man, then penances lasting for three years and two years respectively should be observed.
As Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated: "One who has emitted semen in a guarded Vaiśya woman shall perform penance for one year, bathing at the three sessions of the day;

in the case of a Kṣatriya woman, for two years; and in the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman, for three years. As for the statement of Aṅgiras: "On account of the emission [of semen], however, one should perform the vow prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa."
But one who wears rags for six months shall likewise be freed from sin.

Thus, this [penance] refers to a case of unintentional [intercourse] with a woman of the Mānava class for one year, or with a woman who has committed a slight transgression. However, in the case of women who have completely strayed—such as a wanton woman (svairiṇī) or a Śūdra woman—one who has had seminal emission (avakīrṇin) shall bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa.
In the case of a Vaiśya woman, having fasted for three nights, he shall give a vessel of clarified butter.
Having approached a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should fast for six nights and give a cow as a gift.
One who has discharged semen among cows should perform a Prājāpatya penance.
Regarding one who has discharged semen among a eunuch, it should be understood that Śaṅkha and Likhita have declared: "He shall give a load of straw and a māṣaka of lead."

And this expiation for an *avakīrṇin* applies equally to a student (*brahmacārin*) of any of the three twice-born classes: "A twice-born man who has broken his vow of chastity—whether he be a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya—is purified after a year by performing the *Iṣṭi* sacrifice, eating only alms, and remaining constantly composed."

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śāṇḍilya. When one intentionally emits the vital fluid (caramadhātu) without sexual intercourse with a woman—whether during the day or in a dream—then only the sacrifice to Nirṛti (nairṛtayāga) is to be observed; for Vasiṣṭha has extended this very sacrifice alone to cases where semen is emitted through effort during the day or in a dream. Furthermore, when emission occurs during other vows (vrata), such as the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa, which entail the observance of celibacy (brahmacarya), this same sacrifice alone applies; for he has likewise extended [this rule] to other vows with the words, "and so it is in other vows."
Regarding emission during sleep, however, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:
"A twice-born student who has involuntarily emitted semen in a dream shall bathe,
worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with 'punar mām'."
Thus:
"If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should involuntarily emit semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with 'punar mām'."

For forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and others, if there is a breach of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), this very vow of the *avakīrṇin* becomes augmented by three *kṛcchra* penances; for when a forest-dweller or an ascetic (*yati*) emits semen intentionally, he should perform the vow of the *avakīrṇin* conjoined with three *parāka* penances.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śāṇḍilya.
When one has fallen away from renunciation by taking up the life of a householder, then that which was stated by Saṃvarta should be observed:
"If some evil-minded person, having renounced, should return to worldly life..."
He should perform the *kṛcchra* penance without weariness for six months immediately thereafter.
Thus it is said:
"If some evil-minded person, having renounced, should return to the worldly life,
he must perform the *kṛcchra* penance without weariness for six months immediately thereafter."
"Return" means the resumption of the householder's life.
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"But he who, having become a renunciant, should again indulge in sexual intercourse..."
For sixty thousand years, one is born as a worm in ordure.
Thus it is said: "But he who, having become a renunciant, should again indulge in sexual intercourse,
shall be born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years."

And so Parāśara says: "If a Brahmin who has fallen away from his status, having departed from the life of renunciation, and having desisted from fasting unto death, desires to enter the state of a householder again..."
He shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances and three *cāndrāyaṇa* observances;
once consecrated by all the sacraments beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), he shall attain purification.
Thus:
"If a Brahmin who has fallen from his status, having emerged from the life of renunciation, and having desisted from fasting unto death, desires to enter the householder's state again..."
He shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances and three *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts;
once consecrated by all the sacraments beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), he shall attain purification.

In this regard, the settled rule is that for a Brāhmaṇa there is a six-month *kṛcchra* penance followed by the rite of re-initiation (*saṃnyāsasaṃskāra*), for a Kṣatriya three *cāndrāyaṇas*, and for a Vaiśya three *kṛcchras*. Alternatively, these three types of penances should be understood as being prescribed specifically for a Brāhmaṇa, determined according to his capacity and whether the act was committed once or repeatedly.
Likewise, Yama has also declared a penance for those who have renounced the world (*saṃnyāsins*) at the time of death.
Those who have perished by water or fire, by hanging, or by wandering as ascetics;
those who have died through fasting, or by falling from a precipice, by poison, or by the stroke of a weapon.
These nine, having fallen from their status and being excluded from all society,
are purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
Thus:

"Those who have perished by water, fire, or hanging; those who have fallen from the mendicant life or through fasting unto death; and those who have perished by poison, leaping [from a cliff], or by the stroke of a weapon."
These nine, having fallen from their status and being excluded by all the world,
are purified either by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
This pair of penances—the Cāndrāyaṇa and the two Taptakṛcchras—should be understood as being determined according to one's capacity and other such factors.

However, when the reading is *śastraghātahatāś ca* ("and those killed by the stroke of a weapon"), then this instruction for the son or others should be seen as applying to cases caused by death through unscriptural means such as suicide.

Furthermore, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"One who attempts suicide while still living shall perform a Kṛcchra for twelve nights and fast for three nights"—that too should be understood as applying specifically to one who has resolved upon an unscriptural death but somehow remains alive, depending on his capacity.
Alternatively, the rule is that for one wounded by a weapon or similar means, the penance lasts three nights if it was merely an intent, but twelve nights if the act was committed.

Furthermore, this expiation for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) applies to cases of approaching women who should not be approached (*agamyā*) other than the wife of a guru or those equal to her, because more severe expiations have been shown for those specific cases.
Nor is it appropriate that the minor vow of an *avakīrṇin* should remove the taint of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), such as that which must be expiated over twelve years.

Nor is it correct to say that the prescription of a light penance is conditioned by the status of being a *brahmacārin*, because in the section on the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), an increase [in penance] such as doubling has been shown for the other stages of life (*āśrama*).

Furthermore, a separate penance for sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman (*agamyāgamana*) need not be performed here, because for a *brahmacārin*, the lapse of celibacy with a woman is necessarily concomitant with sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman. Therefore, in other cases as well, when one occasion necessarily entails another occasion that is equal or lesser, one does not apply a separate occasional rite (*naimittika*) for that [secondary] occasion.
For example: "If one threatens [to strike], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance;
if one actually strikes, the *atikṛcchra*; if blood flows, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and if the blood is internal, the *kṛcchra*."

In this case, regarding the cause of producing blood, the two causes characterized by threatening and falling do not, by virtue of their inevitability, entail their respective effects—the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances; thus it should be inferred in other cases as well.
However, where there is no rule of inclusion among the causes, the effects are applied separately.
Examples of such causes are: when one goes on a festival day to another's wife who is menstruating, being anointed with oil, during the daytime, or into water.

Now, it might be argued that for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), the failure of his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) with respect to a woman does not necessarily entail the offense of approaching a forbidden woman (*agamyāgamanāntarīyakatva*). This is because there is no fault of approaching a forbidden woman in the case of approaching a *putrikā* (appointed daughter). To explain: a *putrikā* is certainly not an unmarried girl (*kanyā*), since her virginity is intact; nor is she the wife of another, as she has not been given away in marriage; nor is she a courtesan, as she does not follow that profession; nor is she a widow, as her husband has not died.

Therefore, since a *putrikā* is not included in any of these categories, she is not prohibited [as a forbidden woman]. Consequently, one who commits an emission of semen with her incurs only the penance of an *avakīrṇin*.

However, for one who has transgressed otherwise, because of the convergence of another cause (*nimittāntara*), it is argued that both the vow of the *avakīrṇin* and another occasional rite (*naimittika*) must be performed.
That is incorrect, because a daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*) is included among the wives of others;
even in the absence of the formal giving away (*pradāna*), she is consecrated by the marriage sacrament (*vivāhasaṃskāra*), just like a woman wedded through the Gāndharva or other forms of marriage.
Furthermore, a wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother or whose father is unknown, for fear of violating the law regarding an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).

Because of this prohibition, it must be stated that wifehood does not arise [in the case of such women] just as it does not with those of the same *gotra*, since the prohibition has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), like the prohibition against marrying women who are deformed or have missing limbs.
And its having a visible purpose is due to the mention of the reason "because of the suspicion of the practice regarding an appointed daughter" (*putrikā-dharma-śaṅkā*).
Furthermore, marriage is not solely for the sake of obtaining a son, but also for the sake of fulfilling religious duty (*dharma*).
Therefore, for one who has fathered a son and whose wife has died, what contradiction is there in marrying a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) for the sake of dharma?
This has already been explained in detail previously; so, enough with this digression.

Thus, it is well said that since the lapse of celibacy by a student (*brahmacārin*) with a woman is immediately followed by the sin of approaching a forbidden woman (*agamyāgamanānantarīyakatva*), no separate expiatory rite (*naimittika*) need be performed. (3.280)
In connection with the penances for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), he states another penance for a minor offense (*anupātaka*):
"But having neglected the begging of alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill,
one who has emitted semen through lust should offer two oblations with these two [verses] beginning with *kāmāvakīrṇaḥ*."
Then he should perform the ritual attendance with the verse, "May they sprinkle me together with this.

However, if one who is not ill—a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*)—continuously neglects begging for alms or the fire-ritual for seven nights, he should offer two oblations with these two mantras: "I am one whose vow is violated by desire;

I am violated, to the one who desires desire, svāhā! I am one who has fallen through desire; I have fallen, to the one who desires desire, svāhā! Having offered these oblations, he [should recite]: "May the Maruts sprinkle me together, may Indra, may Bṛhaspati."
With this mantra, "May this Agni sprinkle me with glory and Vedic luster," he should worship the fire.
And this [exemption] is to be understood as applying when one fails to perform [the duties] due to being preoccupied with more weighty tasks, such as service to the guru.

However, when one who is not so preoccupied neglects both the begging for alms and the fire-ritual, then: "If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*."
Thus it should be understood according to the *Mānava*.

Regarding the loss of the *yajñopavīta*, Hārīta has stated the following expiation: "Having offered four oblations of clarified butter with the *manovrata* and *patī* verses, one should resume one's duties as before. One should likewise offer these same oblations in the event of eating improper alms-food, at sunrise or sunset, upon vomiting, sleeping during the day, seeing a naked woman, sleeping naked, stepping upon a cremation ground, riding horses and other such animals, or neglecting those worthy of worship. For killing stationary beings, reptiles, and the like, or for failing to kindle the sacred fire, one should offer clarified butter with the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses. Upon accepting gifts such as jewels, garments, or cows, one should mutter the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times."

"By those [verses] containing the marks of *manas* (mind) and *vrata* (vow)" means by those containing the marks of *manas*, such as "The light of the mind," and so forth, and by those containing the marks of *vrata*, such as "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," and so forth.
"One should perceive according to the purpose" means one should receive [the sacred thread] with the accompanying mantras according to the procedure prescribed for the initiation (*upanayana*).

However, regarding the performance of eating and other acts without the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), [it is said]: "If one eats, or otherwise voids excrement or urine, without the *brahmasūtra*..."
One is purified by eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī mantra accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus it should be understood as spoken by Marīci. 3.281.
Furthermore: "In the case of consuming honey or meat, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance and the remaining vows."
Having acted contrary to the teacher's wishes, one becomes pure only after propitiating him.
If a student unintentionally consumes honey or meat, he must perform the *kṛcchra* penance;
thereafter, he should complete the remaining vows.

And this refers to the consumption of the meat of hares and other animals fit for the food of the learned (*śiṣṭa*); for the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha states: "If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should eat meat fit for the food of the learned, he shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and then complete the remainder of his vow.
The mention of "twelve nights," however, is intended to include even the *atikṛcchra*, *parāka*, and other such penances, depending on whether the act was intentional and habitual.

But when one is overcome by a disease that can be cured only by meat, then meat may be eaten after making it the leavings of the teacher; for it has been stated by that very [author]: "If he is ill, he may at will eat everything as the leavings of the teacher for the sake of medicine.
The inclusion of the word "everything" is intended to include all forbidden substances such as meat, garlic, and so forth.
Having been freed from the disease by eating that, he should worship the Sun.
And so Baudhāyana says: "If one wishes to treat [a disease], when he has recovered from his illness, he should then rise and worship the sun with the verse, ‘The swan dwelling in purity...
There is no fault even in the unintentional consumption of honey, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "Honey that comes unawares does not cause defilement in the Vājasaneyaka.
However, we shall discuss the expiation for eating food during a period of impurity (*sūtaka*) and similar matters in the section on expiations for eating what is forbidden.

By acting contrary to the teacher through such means as disobeying his commands and so forth, one becomes purified by propitiating the teacher with prostrations at his feet and other such acts. (3.282)
In connection with the penances for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), he now states the penance even for the teacher (*guru*):
"If one sent on a mission dies, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances."

However, if a teacher sends a disciple for the sake of some business to a region agitated by fears of thieves, snakes, tigers, and the like, during the occasion of the dead of night thickened by dense darkness, and that disciple, being sent by the teacher, dies by chance, then that teacher should perform three *prājāpatya* and other such *kṛcchra* penances.
It does not mean three separate *prājāpatyas*; for if that were the case, the number [three] would be untenable as it would reside in distinct entities.
Nor is it correct to argue that the number refers to repetition, as in the case of "he performs eleven *prayāja* offerings."

Since the distinctness of their own forms (*svarūpa-pṛthaktva*) is possible, it is improper to rely on repetition (*āvṛtti*). If this number were attached to what has already arisen, then perhaps some reliance on repetition might be justified; however, this number pertains to the act of origination itself. Therefore, as in the case of "one offers three oblations of clarified butter," it is logical that the formation of the number three depends precisely upon the distinctness of their own forms. (3.283)
He states an exception to the general penance for all forms of injury:
"But when a Brahmin dies while receiving assistance, there is no sin;
likewise in the case of bulls during the ripening of crops, or during medical treatments and fire-rites."

If a Brāhmaṇa or anyone else for whom medical assistance—consisting of the administration of medicine, wholesome food, and so forth—is being performed in accordance with the instructions of Āyurveda, should die by some chance, no sin whatsoever accrues to the practitioner. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate all living beings in general. For this very reason, it is said: "In restraining [an animal], in treating cattle, and in dislodging a hidden fetus..."
If misfortune should occur despite effort having been made, one is not tainted by sin.
Thus and so forth has been stated by Saṃvarta and others;
and this has already been explained in detail previously.
With the intention of explaining the expiation for one who brings a false accusation, he first states an explanatory passage (arthavāda) relevant to that purpose:
"The guilt of one who brings a false accusation is twice as great as that of one who speaks of what actually occurred;
furthermore, by speaking falsely, he takes upon himself the guilt of the person falsely accused."

However, for one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is defiled by anger born of envy toward another’s excellence, and who falsely imputes a charge such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) against that person in the presence of others, that very sin becomes doubled for him.
Furthermore, for one who publicly reveals an existing fault that was previously unknown to the world, he too incurs a fault equal to that of the sinner.
Thus says Āpastamba: "Having learned of a fault, one should not be the first to proclaim it to others regarding one who has fallen; rather, one should exclude him from religious duties."

It is not only that the one who brings a false accusation incurs double the guilt; rather, this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) for the penance to be prescribed later, stating that he also takes upon himself whatever other collection of evils belongs to the one falsely accused. However, the intention here is not to establish a doubling of sin and so forth, because the occasion [for the offense] is light and a light penance will be taught, and because otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequences of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). (3.284)
Regarding this, he states the penance:
"He who falsely accuses another of a great sin (mahāpātaka) or a minor sin (upapātaka) shall subsist on water for one month, reciting [the sacred texts] with his senses restrained."

But he who falsely accuses another of a great sin such as the killing of a Brahmin, or of a minor sin such as the killing of a cow, shall subsist on water for one month, remain devoted to recitation (*japa*), and keep his senses under control.

This recitation should be performed with the *Śuddhavatī* verses, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime involving loss of caste or a minor offense, one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the *Śuddhavatī* verses, or go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse-sacrifice.
The mention of "great sins" and "minor sins" is an elliptical expression intended to include other categories as well, such as "heinous crimes" (*atipātaka*).
And this should be understood to apply only when a Brāhmaṇa has made a false accusation against another Brāhmaṇa.

But when a Brāhmaṇa makes an accusation against a Kṣatriya or others, or when a Kṣatriya or others makes an accusation against a Brāhmaṇa, then: "In cases of accusations against those of inverse order, the fine shall be double or triple;
for those of the castes in the direct order, it shall be reduced by half and half again from that."

Thus, the increase or decrease of the penance should be determined in accordance with the punishment. However, for one who falsely accuses another of a mortal sin (*bhūta-abhiśaṃsin*), it should be determined as half of that [penance] in accordance with the previously mentioned explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the punishment. Likewise, for one who falsely accuses another of a most heinous crime (*atipātaka*), this same vow is reduced by one-quarter; for one who falsely accuses another of a major sin (*pātaka*), it is reduced by one-half; and for one who falsely accuses another of a minor sin (*upapātaka*), it is reduced by one-quarter. Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛtis that a fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa applies to the killing of a Kṣatriya.

Thus, because a fourth part of the penance for a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) is seen [to apply] to the killing of a Kṣatriya or others who have committed a minor offense (*upapātaka*), in the same way, for one who falsely accuses another of miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇa*), a penance less than that for a minor offense should be prescribed. "Having considered the capacity and the nature of the sin, one should determine the penance. "Having considered the capacity and the nature of the sin, one should determine the penance."
Thus it is from the Smṛti.

As for the heavy penance stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita—"An atheist, an ungrateful person, one who practices fraud, one who destroys the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas, and one who makes false accusations—these six shall subsist on alms at the houses of Brāhmaṇas for six years; they shall eat only washed alms-food for one year; or they shall follow cows for six months"—that should be applied according to the degree of repetition [of the offense]. (3.285)
In connection with the penance for one who falsely accuses another, he states the penance for the accused:
"One who has been falsely accused should perform a *kṛcchra* penance or an *āgneya* [rite];
or he should offer a *puroḍāśa* cake to Vāyu, or indeed a sacrificial animal to Vāyu."
Furthermore, he who has been falsely accused shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance;
or he shall sacrifice with a *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni;
or he shall sacrifice with a *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Vāyu.
Or [one may perform penance] with an animal dedicated to Vāyu.
The application of these alternatives is determined by one's capacity and circumstances.

As for the statement by Vasiṣṭha that "one who has been falsely accused is explained by this same rule," that should be understood to apply to one who has been falsely accused but has not yet performed penance for a short period; for one who has been falsely accused for a year, the fine is double.

Thus, because an excessive penalty is observed [in other cases], as for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi—"One falsely accused of a sin should perform a *kṛcchra* for one month; in the case of mortal sins (*pātaka*), two months"—that too refers to the same subject matter as the rule of Vasiṣṭha.

As for that which was stated by Baudhāyana—"For one who accuses another of a mortal sin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; for the one accused, it is half of that"—that refers to the subject matter of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and the like, or to the case of one who is incapable [of performing the heavier penance].
In this manner, the determination of other penances—whether high or low—as applicable to those accused of offenses, should be understood as depending on factors such as time and capacity.
As Manu says:
"Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*..."
And the Śākala oblations performed daily are the purification for those excluded from the company at meals.
Thus:
eating only at the sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
and daily *Śākala* oblations— these are the purification for those excluded from the company at a meal (*apāṅkta*).
Among those excluded from the company at a meal (*apāṅkta*), persons such as the falsely accused (*abhiśasta*) are enumerated.
