Although no actual performance of a prohibited act is observed in the case of the falsely accused here, nevertheless, this penance—based on the *apūrva* (unseen merit/demerit) resulting from prohibited conduct in a previous birth, which is inferred from the mark of being falsely accused—is like that for those bitten by worms; thus there is no contradiction. (3.286)
Furthermore:
"One who approaches his brother's wife without being appointed should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
That is to say, he who approaches the wife of either an elder or a younger brother without a formal appointment (niyoga) must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa.
And this [penance] should be understood to apply to a single instance where the act was unintentional;

however, as for the statement of Śaṅkha—"The elder brother who has married before his younger brother and the younger brother who marries before his elder brother shall both subsist on alms at the houses of Brāhmaṇas for one year; likewise, he who approaches the wife of an elder brother without authorization, and he who approaches the wife of a younger brother"—that refers to a case of intentional action.
And what does it say?
"Having consumed clarified butter at the end of three nights and having approached a woman in her courses, one becomes pure."
Furthermore, he who approaches a woman in her courses, even if she is his own wife, becomes purified by fasting for three nights and consuming clarified butter at the end;
this refers to a single instance of unintentional intercourse.
In that same case, for repeated practice of approaching a woman in her courses, the rule stated by Śātātapa—namely, "for seven nights"—should be observed.
Even in the case of approaching her once out of desire, this same penance applies.

As for that which was stated in the *Bṛhatsaṃvarta*: "He who approaches a woman during her menses, or one who is pregnant, or likewise one who is fallen—*atikṛcchra* is the purification for the sake of cleansing his sin."
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of intentional habitual practice.

Furthermore, as for the three-year penance stated by Śaṅkha— "But a quarter [of the penance] applies to the killing of a Śūdra and likewise to approaching a woman in her courses"— that refers to the case of intentional, continuous, and extreme habitual practice.
Regarding the touch of one woman in her menses by another woman in her menses, the expiation prescribed in other Smṛtis should be observed.
Thus says Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha:
"When two women in their menses, who are of the same caste and have the same husband, touch each other..."
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, one is purified immediately by bathing.
Thus:
when two women of the same caste who have their husbands living touch each other while in their menses,
whether intentionally or unintentionally, they are both purified immediately by bathing.
However, for two women of the same caste who have no husband, there is merely bathing if it occurs unintentionally.
But if a woman in her courses is touched by another woman in her courses who is of the same caste,
she undoubtedly attains purification by bathing on that very day.

Thus it is from the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa*. As for the statement of Kaśyapa: "If a Brahmin woman who is menstruating is touched by another Brahmin woman, she becomes pure after fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."
Thus, that [rule] refers to cases where one acts according to one's own will.
However, regarding the touching of a woman of a different caste, a specific rule has been shown by Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman and even a Śūdra woman, both being in their menses, touch each other..."
A Śūdra woman of the first type is purified by a penance (kṛcchra), while a Śūdra woman [of the second type] is purified by giving gifts (dāna).

"By means of a gift" means she is purified by giving a gift equal to one-fourth of a *niṣka*, which serves as a substitute for a quarter-*kṛcchra* penance. Regarding the rule: "If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their menses, touch each other, the former shall perform a quarter-*kṛcchra* less [than a full *kṛcchra*], and the latter likewise a quarter-*kṛcchra*."
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified by half a Kṛcchra penance, and the latter by half of that.
If a Kṣatriya woman and a Śūdra-born woman touch each other while in their menses,
the former is purified by three days of fasting, and the latter by one day and night.
If a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman who have both reached their menses touch one another,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified after one day and night.
If a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified after two days.
This is the ancient rule for purification when there is intentional contact with members of the various castes.
Thus:
if a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former shall perform a three-quarter Kṛcchra penance, and the latter likewise a quarter Kṛcchra.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified by half a Kṛcchra penance, while the latter is purified by half of that.
If two women— one a Kṣatriya and the other born of a Śūdra— touch each other while in their menses,
the former must fast for three days and the latter for one day and night.
If a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman who have both reached their menses touch one another,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified after one day and night.
If a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified after two days.
This is the ancient rule for purification when there is intentional contact with members of the [lower] castes.

However, regarding unintentional contact, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu has stated that there is merely a bath: "If a menstruating woman touches another menstruating woman of a lower caste, she shall not eat until she becomes pure;
but having touched one of the same or a higher caste, she is purified immediately after bathing.
Regarding contact with a Caṇḍāla or similar outcastes, however, a specific rule has been stated by Bṛhad-Vasiṣṭha.
If a woman in her courses is touched by one who has fallen from his caste, by an outcaste, or by a horse-slaughterer,
she should perform the penance after those days have passed.
On the first day, there should be a three-night fast; on the second, a two-day fast;
on the third day, a single day and night; and thereafter, one should practice eating only at night.
If one is touched by a Śūdra woman who has not washed after eating, or by a dog, one should observe the penance for two days.
Thus:
"If a woman in her menses comes into contact with an outcaste, one of the lowest castes, or a dog-cooker,
she should perform the penance after those days have passed."
On the first day, there should be a three-night fast; on the second, a two-day fast;
on the third day, a single day and night; thereafter, one should observe eating only at night.
If one is touched by a Śūdra woman who has not washed after eating, or by a dog, one should observe the penance for two days.

"Having passed those days by fasting"—that is to say, having spent them without food. This refers to a case where the contact was intentional; however, in the case of unintentional contact, [the text says]: "But a menstruating woman who has been touched by a Cāṇḍāla, an Antya, a dog, or a crow..."
She shall remain without food for as long as it takes for her to be purified.

Thus it should be understood as stated by Baudhāyana. Furthermore, he [Baudhāyana] himself has stated: "But a menstruating woman who has been touched by village cocks, pigs, or dogs shall bathe and remain [without food] until the appearance of the moon."
Thus, that [rule] refers to a case where [the woman] is unable [to stop].
However, when a dog or similar creature touches a woman while she is eating, a specific rule is stated in another Smṛti:
"If a menstruating woman, while eating, should be touched by a dog, an outcaste, or the like..."
One who subsists on cow’s urine and barley gruel is purified in six nights.
If one is unable [to do so], one should give gold or even food to the Brahmins.
Thus [it is said].
If a menstruating woman, while eating, should touch a dog, an outcaste, or the like,
she becomes pure after six nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
If one is unable [to provide these], one should give gold or even food to the Brahmins.

But when there is mutual contact between two persons who are both impure from food remnants, then: "If a woman in her menses is ever touched by one who is impure from food remnants, the former is purified by a *kṛcchra* penance, while a Śūdra woman is purified by gifts and fasting."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Atri.

But when a woman in her courses touches twice-born men who have food remnants [on them], then: "If one standing in her menses should somehow touch twice-born men who have food remnants, she should fast for a day and a night if the remnants were below [the navel], and for three days if the remnants were above."
Thus it should be understood as spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya.

Thus, having explained certain penances for secondary sins (*anupātaka*) by way of the occasion of the penance for an *avakīrṇin*, we shall return to the subject at hand. In that regard, immediately after the *avakīrṇin*, it was stated: "and likewise the sale of one's own children. Concerning this, the penances prescribed by Manu and Yājñavalkya, such as those lasting three months and so forth, are to be determined as before, depending on whether the act was intentional or unintentional, the caste involved, the capacity of the offender, and other such factors.

As for the statement of Śaṅkha, "Having sold a temple, a shelter, a garden, a grove, an assembly hall, a water-station, a tank, a meritorious bridge, or one's own son, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance," and that which was stated by Parāśara, "Having sold a daughter or a cow, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance"—both of these should be understood to apply to cases where the act is committed unintentionally during times of distress (*āpad*).
However, in the case of intentional action, [one should follow]: "Having sold women, one should observe the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow."
The wise have declared that the vow for a male is indeed twofold.
Thus it should be understood as stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*.

As for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi—"In the case of selling a grove, a pond, a well, a lotus-pool, or a virtuous son, one becomes purified in a year by bathing at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at the fourth meal-time"—that refers to the case of having only one son. Immediately following that, the theft of grain, base metals, and cattle has been mentioned, and the penances for those have been explained in detail in the section on theft (Chapter 3, Verse 287).

Immediately after it was stated that officiating at sacrifices for those who should not be sacrificed for is [a sin], he now declares the penance for that: "One who performs sacrifices for *vrātyas*, even if performing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances;
likewise one who causes the Veda to be forgotten, one who eats barley for a year, and one who abandons a person who has come for refuge."
He who performs a sacrifice for those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī should perform three Kṛcchra penances beginning with the Prājāpatya.
And among these Kṛcchras, which vary in severity, the specific penance must be determined according to the gravity or lightness of the cause.
Likewise, one practicing malevolent magic (abhicāra) should also perform this very same expiation.

And this applies with the exception of those who are *ātatāyin* (aggressors), such as arsonists and the like, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "One does not fall [from his caste] by performing malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) against these six.
The word "api" (even/also) is intended to include those who sacrifice for unworthy persons and those who perform the *antyeṣṭi* (funeral rites) for them.
For this very reason, it was stated by Manu:
Having performed sacrifices for Vrātyas, funeral rites for others,
malevolent magic, or an Ahīna sacrifice, one removes the taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
Thus:
"By performing the sacrifice for Vratyas, the funeral rites for others,
malevolent magic, or an Ahina sacrifice, one removes [the taint] through three Krichchhra penances."

The phrase "the funeral rites for others" refers either to those performed with extreme frequency or to the funeral rites for *śūdras* and outcastes (*antyajas*), because of the severity of the penance required.
An *ahīna* sacrifice is a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa-yāga*) lasting from two nights up to twelve days.

As for what was stated by Śātātapa—"One should not initiate, teach, or officiate at sacrifices for those whose *sāvitrī* has been lost; he who initiates, teaches, or officiates for them shall perform the Uddālaka-vow"—that refers to cases of intentional action.

The Uddālaka vow has already been shown previously. These three *kṛcchra* penances constitute exceptions to the general expiation for minor offenses (*upapātaka*); therefore, the general expiation for minor offenses applies specifically to officiating at sacrifices for those from whom one should not accept gifts, such as Śūdras. In that case, if done intentionally, the penance lasts for three months.
However, for one who acts unintentionally, the penance prescribed by Yājñavalkya, such as the month-long vow (*māsavrata*), applies.

As for that which was stated by Pracetas after enumerating those who sacrifice for Śūdras and others—"they should perform the five-fold austerity (*pañcatapa*), sleeping in the open air, and lying in water;
they should eat cow-urine and barley-gruel for a month during the summer, the rainy season, and the winter respectively"—that refers to the case of intentional repetition.

As for that which was stated by Yama: "If a Brahmin who serves as a domestic priest for a king of noble lineage acts [unrighteously] out of affection or through attachment to wealth, the Kṛcchra penance is his means of purification."
Thus, that [rule] refers to the case of incapacity.

And as for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi—"One who officiates at sacrifices for Śūdras becomes pure by the renunciation of all property after performing a thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) ten times"—that too refers to the case of repeated practice committed unintentionally. However, as for what was stated by Gautama—"In the employment of forbidden mantras, one should perform a thousand prostrations"—whereby ordinary studenthood (brahmacarya) is prescribed for the repeated and habitual employment of mantras consisting of officiating at sacrifices or teaching for those who are forbidden, such as the outcastes (patita), that refers to the case of repeated practice committed intentionally.

Likewise, he who causes his own Veda to be lost, and he who, though capable of protection, neglects one who has come for refuge—provided that person is not a thief—is purified by eating barley-gruel for one year.
In this context, "causing loss" (*viplava*) means studying during forbidden times (*anadhyāya*), such as on festival days, in the presence of a *caṇḍāla*, or within earshot of one;
or it is called causing loss when, to one studying for the sake of excellence, one subjects him to interrogation such as, "What are you reading? You have ruined it!"
Therefore, it has been stated in another Smṛti:
"Manu declared those who do not study after having been urged to do so to be outcasts."
Manu declared that those who do not study when the instruction has been given to them are outcasts (*patita*).

As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"Upon hearing [the sound of] an outcast, a *caṇḍāla*, or a corpse, they should remain silent and fasting for three nights; it is known from tradition that by reciting [the Veda] a thousand times at most, they become pure"—by this very rule, teachers of censured subjects and officiating priests are explained; and it is known from tradition that "they become pure by abandoning their fees," which refers to cases where the act was intentional.

As for what is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*—"If one recites the *Śruti* or *Smṛti* within earshot of a Cāṇḍāla, there shall be fasting for one night"—that refers to cases where the act is unintentional.
When there is merely the passing of a snake or similar creature between [the teacher and pupil], but no study takes place therein, the penance has been declared by Yama:
"In the case of a snake, a mongoose, a goat, or a cat..."
Of the mouse, the camel, and the female frog.
Listen now to this immediate expiation for when a man [intercourse] occurs with a human woman, a ewe, a dog, a horse, or a donkey.
One must fast for three nights and perform ablutions three times a day;
or else one must go to another village on one's knees—of this there is no doubt.
Thus [it is said].
Of the serpent and the mongoose, as well as of the goat and the cat,
of the mouse and the camel, and of the frog and the woman.
Listen now to this immediate expiation for the case of a man who has sexual intercourse with a human woman, a ewe, a dog, a horse, or a donkey.
One must fast for three nights and perform ablutions three times a day;
or else one must travel to another village on one's knees—of this there is no doubt.

Regarding the abandonment of father, mother, or son, and the sale of tanks or gardens, the penances prescribed by Manu and Yājñavalkya for common minor offenses (*upapātaka*) should be applied as before, taking into account caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth.

Among these, because the abandonment of father, mother, and others is included among those excluded from the *pākṣa* (those unworthy of sitting at the same sacrificial row) in the passage: "One who has abandoned mother, father, or guru without cause," a penance on that account is also required.
As Manu said:
"Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
and daily *Śākala* oblations— these are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals."
Thus:
eating only at the sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
and daily *Śākala* oblations— these are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkta*).

Those excluded from the *pāṅkta* (the company of those worthy of sitting in a row) have been shown in the section on *śrāddha* by such statements as, "those who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs," and so forth.
Regarding the sale of tanks and groves, certain specific two-month penances along with their respective scopes were mentioned during the discussion of the penance for selling one's son.

Immediately following that, the "defiling of a maiden" was mentioned; in that case, the three-month, two-month, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other penances are to be applied according to the castes involved when the maiden is of the same caste (*savarṇā*).

Furthermore, regarding the inverse order (*ānulomya*), there is the consumption of milk for one month or the *prājāpatya* penance; however, there is no fault when [the woman] is of the same caste (*anuloma*) and willing, but otherwise there is a fine (*dama*).
This is because a smallness of punishment is observed [in such cases].

As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha—"One who defiles a maiden and one who sells Soma should perform the Kṛcchra penance while subsisting on water"—and that statement of Hārīta—"One who defiles a maiden, a seller of Soma, the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who abandons a wife from childhood, a drinker of spirituous liquor, a priest for Śūdras, one who strikes back at his teacher, an atheist, one who lives as an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, one who destroys the livelihood of Brāhmaṇas, a false accuser, one who associates with outcasts, a betrayer of friends, a killer of those seeking refuge, and one who lives by forgery—these shall undergo the penances of five fires, exposure to the open air, and lying in water during the summer, rainy, and winter seasons respectively; for one month they shall eat barley-gruel with cow's urine"—both of these [penances] are to be applied in the case of defiling [a maiden] through the inverse order (prātilomya) by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.

But for a Śūdra, there is indeed death [for causing injury]; however, for defilement, there is the cutting off of the hand, and likewise death in the case of the highest caste woman—such is seen from the mention of death. For officiating at a sacrifice for one who has married before his elder brother, for giving away a daughter to such a man, for deceitfulness, for the violation of vows not prohibited by the learned, for undertaking the act of cooking for one's own sake, and for associating with women who drink liquor, the penance for common minor sins (upapātaka) should be established as previously described.

Regarding the first two [cases], specific penances have already been shown in the context of explaining the penances for marrying before an elder brother (*parivedana*) and officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy of sacrificing (*ayājya-yājana*).

Immediately after, it was stated: "the abandonment of Vedic study, the sacred fires, and one's son. In that regard, if the abandonment occurs due to addiction or incapacity, a penance equal to that for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) has been prescribed, based on the principle that "there is the destruction of what has been studied.

However, if the abandonment occurs because of being distracted by listening to the scriptures and other such pursuits, then the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as those lasting three months, should be applied according to considerations of caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth.

As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha—"One who has abandoned the Veda (brahmojjha), having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, may again receive the Veda from his teacher"—that refers to a situation of extreme distress.

Regarding even the abandonment of the sacred fires (agnityāga), a specific rule was shown by that same author: "He who neglects the fires, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, shall have them re-established.
The mention of "twelve nights" is intended to include heavier or lighter Kṛcchras, such as the Prājāpatya and others, depending on the duration for which the fires were neglected.

In that regard, for an interruption of two months, the *prājāpatya* penance is prescribed; for four months, the *atikṛcchra*; for an interruption of six months, the *parāka*. Beyond six months, the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) mentioned by Yogīśvara should be applied according to the circumstances of time and other factors. However, beyond one year, the rule is the three-month or two-month penance prescribed by Manu. This applies specifically to cases of abandonment due to atheism (*nāstikya*). Thus says Vyāghra:
"A twice-born man who abandons the sacred fire out of atheism should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Thus it is said:
"A twice-born man who abandons the sacred fire out of atheism should perform the Prājāpatya penance."

But when one neglects [the observance] through negligence, then a specific rule is stated in the *Bhāradvāja-gṛhya*: "Up to three nights, there shall be a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*); up to twenty nights, there shall be fasting; beyond that, up to sixty nights, one should fast for three nights; beyond that, up to a year, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance; and beyond that, as the duration increases, the gravity of the fault increases."

But when one abandons [the fire] due to laziness or other such reasons, a specific rule for that case has also been stated by him: "If twelve days have passed, there shall be a fast for three days; if a month has passed, a fast for twelve days; if a year has passed, a month-long fast or subsisting on milk. Regarding the period beyond a year, a specific rule has been stated by Vṛddha-Hārīta: "If the *agnihotra* has been neglected for a year, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance and then re-establish the fires.
If it has been neglected for two years, one should perform both the *cāndrāyaṇa* and the *somāyana*."
"If the [sacred fire] has been extinguished for three years, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year and then re-establish it.
The *Somāyana* will be described in the section on *kṛcchra* penances.
A specific rule has also been stated by Śaṅkha: "One who has let the fires go out should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance for one year and give a cow as a gift."
In the case of intentionally abandoning one's wife or abandoning a kinsman, the penance for killing a cow (*govadhavrata*) is to be observed for three months.
However, in the case of unintentional abandonment, the fourfold set of penances mentioned by Yogīśvara should be applied according to one's capacity and other relevant factors.
Regarding the cutting down of trees, the expiation has been stated previously.

For making a living through the killing of women or animals, subjugation spells (*vaśīkaraṇa*), and so forth, as well as for operating oil-presses and sugarcane mills, those same penances (*prāyaścitta*) are to be applied in exactly the same manner.
And regarding vices such as gambling and hunting, those same vows (*vrata*) are likewise to be applied.
As for that which was stated by Baudhāyana: "Now, the causes of impurity..."

Gambling, performing malevolent magic, living by gleaning for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, and begging for alms by one who has returned home from his teacher’s house—as well as his continued residence in the teacher’s household beyond four months, teaching him [the Vedas] during that time, and the pointing out of constellations—these constitute the enumeration of causes of impurity.

For twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, three days, and one day—this is the enumeration of the acts causing impurity. Regarding gambling, the annual vow (*vārṣikavrata*) has been prescribed; that refers to the case of habitual practice.

As for that which was stated by Pracetas—"A liar, a thief, a king's servant, one who subsists by planting trees, a poisoner, an arsonist, one who subsists by riding horses, chariots, or elephants, a stage-player, a keeper of dog-fights, a teacher of Śūdras, the husband of a Śūdra woman, a maker of musical instruments, one who subsists by astrology, one who lives like a dog, one who lives as a Brāhmaṇa [without Vedic study], a physician, a temple-priest, a domestic chaplain, a gambler, a drunkard, a forger, a seller of offspring, and a seller of human beings or cattle—one should rescue them by assembling [the community] according to justice through the settlement of Brāhmaṇas. Having renounced all their property, they shall eat at every fourth meal-time for a year, perform ritual ablutions three times a day, and at the end of that period, perform libations to the gods and ancestors and provide daily fodder for cows; thus they become fit for social intercourse"—that also pertains to the same subject matter as Baudhāyana.

A *śvāgaṇika* is one who lives by means of a pack of dogs. A *bhāṇḍika* is one who awakens kings with the sounds of musical instruments and the like, distinct from a *bandin*, as indicated by the separate mention of the *bandin*.
A *śvavṛtti* is a servant.

A *brahmajīvī* is one who serves for a fee in the affairs of Brāhmaṇas. Even the penances for those excluded from the *paṅkti* (the company at a meal) mentioned by Manu—such as eating only at the sixth meal-time for a month and so forth—are to be applied according to considerations of caste and other factors, because even among those excluded from the *paṅkti* mentioned by him, those addicted to vices such as gambling are included. For the sale of oneself and for service to a Śūdra, the general penances are to be applied exactly as before.

As for that which was stated by Baudhāyana: "Sea-voyage, the misappropriation of a deposit, trading with all kinds of merchandise, lying regarding land, service to a Śūdra, and he who is born of a Śūdra woman—along with whatever offspring he has—regarding these, the rule is as follows:
they shall eat sparingly at every fourth meal-time; they shall enter the water according to the ritual of the *savana* [ablutions];
and by alternating between standing and sitting, they remove that sin in three years."
This [penance] refers to the case of long-term association.
However, in the case of friendship with those of lower caste, only the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) apply.

As for that which was stated by Pracetas—"Having caused a breach of friendship, one should fast for a day and night, perform an oblation, and drink milk"—that refers to the breach of friendship with those who are not of lower status.
Even in the case of associating with those of low birth, the general expiations for minor offenses (upapātaka) should be applied.

As for that which was stated by Śātātapa—"A Brāhmaṇa who has previously married a Kṣatriya girl should perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance and then marry her; one who has previously married a Vaiśya girl should perform the *taptakṛcchra*; one who has previously married a Śūdra girl should perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. If a Kṣatriya has previously married a Vaiśya girl, he should perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* and then marry her; if he has previously married a Śūdra girl, he should perform the *atikṛcchra*. If a Vaiśya has previously married a Śūdra girl, he should perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* and then marry her"—in this context, the phrase "he should settle down and marry her" means that after the completion of the *kṛcchra* penance, and subsequent to marrying a woman of his own caste (*savarṇā*), he may then marry that Kṣatriya or other woman.
And this refers to cases of ignorance;
however, when there is knowledge [of the act], it should be understood that the general expiation for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) is indeed established.

Furthermore, regarding sexual intercourse with common women, it has been stated that "resorting to a base womb" is included therein; in that context as well, it is ordained that a *Prājāpatya* penance is required for approaching cattle or prostitutes.
Thus it should be understood that what was stated refers to unintentional [offenses].

However, regarding intentional offenses, that which was stated by Yama should be observed: "The twice-born remove the sin arising from sexual intercourse with a prostitute by drinking boiled water infused with *kuśa* grass once each day for seven nights."
Thus,
the twice-born remove the sin arising from approaching a prostitute by drinking boiled water infused with *kuśa* grass once every day for seven nights.

The general expiations for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) are to be applied according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and with regard to its repetition. In that regard, since the principle holds that "for every cause, the occasional rite recurs," when the recurrence of the occasional rite for each instance of the cause would follow, Laugākṣi has stated a specific rule: "For repetition, an increase by a factor of the number of days is prescribed before a month;
beyond that, the increase is by a factor of the number of months, up to one year."
Then, for as long as he commits sin, it is multiplied by a factor of one year.
Thus:
"In the case of repeated transactions, interest calculated by the day is prescribed for a period less than a month;
beyond that, interest calculated by the month shall apply until one year has passed."
Then, for as long as he commits sin, it is multiplied by the factor of one year.
This refers to cases where the act was intentional.
Regarding unintentional repetition, a specific rule is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "But that which is prescribed for a single instance becomes tripled after three days;
it is said to become fivefold after a month, and tenfold after six months."
For a year, it is fifteenfold; for three years, it becomes twentyfold. Beyond that, it should be calculated in the same manner, according to the words of Śātātapa.
Thus [it is said].
That which is prescribed for a single performance is said to be tripled over three days;
it is said to be fivefold after a month, and after six months it becomes tenfold.
For fifteen years it becomes twentyfold;
beyond that, it should be calculated in the same manner, according to the word of Śātātapa.

Furthermore, as for the rule stating that "one should perform double [the penance] on the second [occasion] from this first injunction," which prescribes repetition for every occasion, it has already been stated previously that this refers specifically to the case of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).

As for Yama’s extension of the vow prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*) to the case of approaching a common woman: "Some prescribe the vow of the violator of the Guru’s bed, some the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow;
some desire it for the killer of a cow, and some for the student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*)."
Thus, this refers to the case of one whose habituation [to non-dharma] has been continuous and uninterrupted since birth.

Immediately thereafter, it was stated that "one may likewise dwell without a stage of life" (*anāśrama*); regarding that, Hārīta has specified an exception: "One who remains without a stage of life for a year should perform the *prājāpatya* penance and then enter a stage of life;
for a second year, the *atikṛcchra*; for a third year, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and beyond that, the *cāndrāyaṇa*."
This refers to cases where [the specific causes] are impossible.
However, when they are possible, the general penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) should be applied according to whether the act was intentional or unintentional.

Furthermore, regarding those who take pleasure in cooking for others, studying false scriptures, serving in mines, and selling one's wife, the general penances for minor offenses set forth by Manu and Yājñavalkya should be determined in accordance with the caste, capacity, qualities, and other factors of the individual. (3.289)

Regarding the phrase "and the sale of their wives," it has been stated that the word "and" (ca) is intended to include—as illustrative examples—the acceptance of improper gifts, the eating of forbidden food, and so forth, as mentioned by Manu and others.
In that regard, he states a specific penance for the acceptance of improper gifts:
"Dwelling in a cow-pen, a student observing celibacy shall perform the milk-vow for one month."
One who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts.

However, he who accepts an improper gift—that is, a gift from one for whom acceptance is forbidden—becomes purified by observing a month-long vow of subsisting on milk, while remaining celibate, dwelling in a cow-pen, and being devoted to and habituated to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*.
The "impropriety" (*asattva*) of a gift is based on the caste and conduct of the giver, such as in the case of a Caṇḍāla or an outcaste;

likewise, it is based on place and time, such as at Kurukṣetra or during an eclipse; and it is also based on the nature of the object to be accepted, such as liquor, a ewe, a bed used by a corpse, or a two-faced cow.

However, when one accepts a ewe or similar property from an outcast (patita) or the like, this heavier penance should be observed, because the occasion for it is grave due to the observation of two transgressions.

Regarding the recitation (japa) in that case, a specific number has been stated by Manu: "Having concentrated his mind and recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times, and having drunk only milk in a cow-pen for a month, one is released from the sin of accepting gifts from the unworthy."
Thus, it should be understood that there is a recitation of three thousand [times] every day;
for by the use of the accusative case in the word *māsam* ("for a month"), it is understood that the recitation numbering three thousand is to be performed throughout each day.

However, when one accepts forbidden items such as sheep from a righteous Brāhmaṇa or the like, or even unforbidden land and so forth from an outcaste (*patita*) or similar person, then that which is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* should be observed: "All terrible types of acceptance are purified by the *Pavitreṣṭi* sacrifice."
By means of the Aindava rite, the Mṛgāreṣṭi, or sometimes the Mitravindā,
or simply by one hundred thousand recitations of the Goddess [Gāyatrī], they are purified from the acceptance of improper gifts.
Thus it is said: "By the Pavitreṣṭi, all terrible acceptances of gifts are purified;
likewise by the Aindava, the Mṛgāreṣṭi, or sometimes by the Mitravindā."
By reciting the mantra of the Goddess one hundred thousand times, they are purified from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
As for the statement of Bṛhaddhārīta: "Having accepted a gift from a king, one should always dwell in the waters for a month;
subsisting on milk at every sixth meal-time, one becomes purified when the month is complete."
Having constantly gratified the twice-born with their desires, he remained ever firm in his vows.
Thus, this should be understood as referring to the practice mentioned previously;
or else, it concerns the acceptance of a black antelope skin and so forth from outcasts and others during events such as the solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra.
Likewise, due to the smallness of the substance to be accepted, there is a corresponding smallness of the penance.
As Hārīta says: "Upon accepting gems, garments, cows, and so forth, one should mutter the Sāvitrī eight thousand times.
Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "When even a mere alms-meal has been accepted, one should recite a meritorious mantra;
for all types of acceptance, one should assign a sixth part [of the merit] [to the donor]."
Thus, this entire collection of penances is to be understood as applying to the time following the relinquishment of wealth—namely, when Brahmins acquire property through censurable actions;
they become purified by its renunciation, by the recitation of sacred texts, and indeed by austerity.
Thus, according to the recollection of Manu;
in this manner, other Smṛti passages as well are to be applied to specific cases based on the smallness or greatness of the value of the substance.

Now, however, [the practice] is being elaborated upon, which avoids food that is censurable due to defects such as its species or source, and which is so by its very name, and which consists of the multitude of vows taught by the Lord of Yogins.

In that regard, regarding the intentional and single instance consumption of onions and other such substances inherently defiled by their species (*jātiduṣṭa*), the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed by the rule beginning with "an onion and a village-pig.
However, in the case of intentional repetition, the penance equal to that for drinking liquor is prescribed by the rule beginning with "eating forbidden food, dishonesty," and so forth.

For unintentional single consumption, the *Sāntapana* penance applies; for repetition of the same in that context, the *Yaticāndrāyaṇa* applies, according to the rule: "Having unwittingly eaten these six, one should perform the *Kṛcchra-Sāntapana*."
Or he may perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [offenses], he should fast for a day.
Thus it is from the recollection of Manu.
As for that which was stated by Vṛddha-Yama: "Those produced from bedsteads, eggplants, gourds, and cuttings;
bhūtṛṇa, śigruka, khukhaṇḍa, and mushrooms."
Having consumed these, a twice-born man should perform the Prājāpatya penance.

Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of intentional repetition; for the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) has stated a three-day period for eating fish intentionally once: "Having eaten fish intentionally, one should spend three days fasting.
*Khaṭvā* is a type of bird; others say it is *kusumbha*.
*Kavaka* refers to the vegetable known as *rājasarṣapa*;

*khukhaṇḍa* is mentioned as a specific variety of it, according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). As for that which was stated by Yama: "Likewise, those produced from *tandulīyaka*, *kumbhīka*, and *vraścana*..."
The nālikā, the nārikela, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka;
Having eaten bhūtṛṇa, śigruka, that which is called khaṭvā, and likewise kavaka, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Thus, that [penance] also refers to cases where the act is intentional and habitual.

*Nālikā* and *nārikelī* are specific types of leafy vegetables, as is the one called *khaṭvā*. However, regarding eating these once unintentionally, one should observe the rule stated by Manu: "In the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day."

In that same case, if there is repetition, a repeated penance should be prescribed. But in the case of extreme repetition: "Having unintentionally eaten food that is defiled by contact, defiled by the mode of preparation, or naturally defiled, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance."

Thus it should be understood as stated by Pracetas. Regarding the unintentional single consumption of indigo, however, there is a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance: "If a Brāhmaṇa should ever consume indigo through negligence, purification occurs through the *cāndrāyaṇa*; so said the sage Āpastamba."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba;
and in the case of intentional repetition, a repeated performance should be inferred.
Furthermore, that which has been stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "Hemp-flower, silk-cotton tree [flower], curd churned by hand..."
Having eaten the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) outside the altar, one should not eat for a day and a night.
Thus, that [penance] also refers to an unintentional case.

As for what was stated by Sumantu—"Upon eating garlic, onion, leek, or mushroom, one should pour eight thousand oblations of the Sāvitrī mantra over the head"—that refers to a case of eating against one's will due to force, or it should be understood as referring to eating for the purpose of curing a disease that can only be treated by that means.
For this very reason, he stated immediately thereafter: "These same things are not forbidden for one who is ill, when used under the direction of a physician."
And regarding those things of this kind, there is no fault;
one should bring them together by pouring drops of water.

Now, the expiation for drinking the milk of animals defiled by birth, such as a *saṃdhinī* cow, and so forth: regarding that, if one drinks it once unintentionally— namely, the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, camel’s milk, the milk of one-hoofed animals,
sheep’s milk, the milk of a *saṃdhinī*, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died.
And among all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo, the milk of females must be avoided; likewise, all substances that have turned sour (śukta) are to be shunned.
Among sour substances, curd is edible, as is everything produced from curd.
Having said this, regarding the remaining cases, the fast for one day as stated by Manu should be observed;
however, in the case of intentional consumption, the three-night fast stated by Yājñavalkya should be observed.

As for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi—"Upon consuming the milk of a camel, a female donkey, or a human woman, there is the Taptakṛcchra penance and a second initiation"—[this applies to specific circumstances].
For consuming the milk of a cow or a buffalo within ten days of calving, there shall be fasting for six nights.

This same rule applies even to drinking the milk of all animals that have only two teats, with the exception of the goat. And as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha: "When a wise man consumes the products of those milks which are themselves forbidden to be consumed..."
One should diligently observe this vow for seven nights with a concentrated mind.

Thus has the barley-meal vow (*yāvakavrata*) been described; both of these refer to cases of intentional and repeated consumption. As for the fortnight-long vow (*pakṣavrata*) prescribed by Śaṅkha regarding the drinking of milk from a cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*) or the consumption of impure substances, stating: "Having eaten [milk] from a cow in heat or having consumed impurities, one should perform the fortnight-long vow"—that too refers to repeated practice. Regarding a single instance of drinking, one should fast after consuming any milk except that of cows, goats, and buffaloes.

For Viṣṇu has declared that fasting is required for these [milk products] within ten days of calving, as well as for the milk of a cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*), one yielding milk while in heat (*yam asūsyandinī*), one whose calf has died (*vivatsā*), and the milk of those who eat impure food.

Likewise, there is a prohibition based on caste: "Whether he be a Kṣatriya established in his duty, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra—whoever drinks the milk of a *kapilā* cow, there is no doer of evil greater than he."

In cases such as these, where no specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is seen to be prescribed, one should observe the general expiation stated by Manu: "In the remaining cases, one should fast for a day. This is how it should be understood.
Now, the expiation for eating meat and other substances that are inherently defiled has been stated.

In that regard, for eating such things once intentionally, the general expiation prescribed by Manu—“in the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day”—should be understood to apply.
However, regarding intentional consumption of the following: “blue jays, birds with red feet, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat (*vallūra*);”
And having eaten fish intentionally, one should dwell for three days observing a fast.
Thus, the statement by the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya) is to be observed.
However, in the case of intentional repetition, the statement by Manu is to be observed: "Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights."

And this refers to meat other than that of village pigs and the like; for the consumption of the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks, as well as that of humans, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
Thus, because Manu has prescribed specific penances according to the particular species [of animal],

this same [penance] applies even to the consumption of their urine and excrement: "And for boars, single-hoofed animals, as well as crows and cocks, and for all carnivorous animals, and those which have been declared unfit for food."
Having consumed meat, urine, and feces, as well as beef,
and the flesh of dogs, jackals, and monkeys, the Taptakṛcchra penance is prescribed.
Or, having fasted for twelve days, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.

Thus, according to the *Bṛhadyama-smṛti*, the rule is as follows: for intentional consumption, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance; however, in the case of repetition, the *parāka* penance accompanied by the *kūṣmāṇḍa* oblations is prescribed. Likewise, Pracetas has also stated: "In the case of eating the flesh of a dog, jackal, crow, cock, hyena, monkey, leopard, blue jay, carnivorous animal, donkey, camel, elephant, horse, village pig, cow, or human being, one should prescribe the *taptakṛcchra*; but in the case of eating their urine or excrement, one should prescribe the *atikṛcchra*."
And this refers to cases where one has eaten intentionally.
As for the statement of Uśanas: "Having eaten human flesh, dog flesh, cow flesh, or even horse flesh, or the flesh of five-toed animals, one should perform the Mahāsāntapana penance."
Thus [it is stated], and that refers to unintentional contact.
As for the statement of Aṅgiras: "Having seen a crane, a vulture, a hawk, a mouse, a donkey, a monkey, or a pig, and having touched their impurities, one becomes pure by sipping water."
Having intentionally consumed these impure substances, the twice-born should perform the Sāntapana penance;
if unintentionally, they should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra.
Thus, that refers to the case of poison that has been swallowed and then vomited up;

and here, by the word *sāntapana*, the *mahāsāntapana* is intended, because the *prājāpatya* penance is prescribed for unintentional [consumption]. Furthermore, as for the statement of Aṅgiras: "Having eaten the flesh of hell-beings, crows, donkeys, horses, and elephants..."
A twice-born man who consumes the urine or feces of these shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus, as for that which was stated by Bṛhadyama— "A Brahmin who eats dried meat should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow"—
both of these refer to the case of intentional repetition.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha— "Having eaten [the flesh of] animals with two rows of teeth, and likewise those with uncloven hooves..."
Having eaten the meat of a camel or a cow, one should likewise perform the vow for six months.
Thus [it is said]; that refers to the case of intentional and extreme repetition.

As for what is stated in another Smṛti: "Having eaten the flesh of humans, as well as that of the village pig, the donkey, and likewise all five-toed animals such as cows, horses, elephants, and camels..."
One should observe the vow for a year regarding a carnivorous cock or a domestic fowl.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of repeated practice that is absolutely uninterrupted.
In this context, the mention of urine and feces is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for fat, semen, blood, and marrow.
Regarding the six impurities beginning with earwax, however, half [of the penance] should be prescribed.

Furthermore, regarding hair and other such things, a specific rule is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "In the case of intentionally eating the raw flesh of goats, sheep, buffaloes, or deer, or consuming hair, nails, or blood, the penance is three nights; if done unintentionally, it is a fast.

As for that which was stated by Pracetas—"Purity is attained through fasting for a day and night after consuming nails, hair, earth, or clods"—that also refers to the case of a single instance of consumption done unintentionally.
Furthermore, there is a statement from another Smṛti: "Having consumed hair, insects, or nails, as well as fish-bones..."
By drinking ghee heated with blood, one is purified at that very moment.
Thus, that [rule] refers to the case of food entering only the mouth.

However, when food placed in a vessel becomes defiled by hair or the like, then: "But when food at the time of eating is defiled by flies or hair, one should subsequently touch water and touch that food with ashes."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Pracetas.
This verse is incidental.

Furthermore, regarding the consumption of very minute worms, insects, bones, and so forth, Hārīta has stated a specific rule: "Upon consuming worms, insects, ants, leeches, moths, or bones, one becomes pure after three nights by subsisting on cow urine and cow dung."
The leech, fish, and so forth [are examples].

Thus, the expiations for consuming the flesh of domestic animals, birds, aquatic creatures, humans, and so on, have been shown in brief; they are not written out for every individual case here for fear of excessive length.
Now, regarding the expiation for consuming food touched by impurity, first the expiation for eating the leavings of others or forbidden food will be stated.
On this point, Manu says: "Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog, or a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink *brahmī* and *suvarcalā*."
Thus, because no specific duration of time is mentioned, it refers to a single night;
and this should be understood as applying to intentional cases.
As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "In the case of a large quantity of food or liquid that has been pecked or gnawed by birds or beasts of prey..."
Even for one who is free from ritual preparation, eating [at such a time] incurs the Kṛcchra-pāda penance.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of intentional action (*kāmakāra*).

Furthermore, the purification (*saṃskāra*) should be understood as stated in the section on the purification of substances in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], beginning with "in a sacrificial shed for the gods" (*devadroṇyām*).

As for what was stated by Śātātapa—"In the case of eating what has been licked by dogs, crows, and the like, or the leavings of a Śūdra, however, there is an *atikṛcchra* [penance]"—that refers to the case of repeated unintentional action.
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha: "Having eaten the leavings of dogs, one should observe the vow for one month;
having eaten the leavings of crows or what has been smelled by a cow, one should observe the vow for a fortnight."
Thus the vow of barley-gruel (*yāvakavrata*) has been described; that refers to the case of intentional repetition.

Regarding the consumption of the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) of a Brāhmaṇa and others, however, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu states: "A Brāhmaṇa, upon eating the leavings of a Śūdra, shall drink *pañcagavya* for seven nights; upon eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, for five nights; upon eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya (*rājanya*), for three nights; but upon eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, for one day. This refers to the case of intentional action. As for the statement of Yama: "Having eaten together with a Brāhmaṇa, one is purified by the *Prājāpatya* penance."
Having eaten food together with a king, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Having eaten food together with a Vaiśya, one is purified by an Atikṛcchra penance;
having eaten food together with a Śūdra, one should perform a Cāndrāyaṇa.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of intentional repetition.

Furthermore, as for the statement of Śaṅkha—"In the case of eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, one should drink water consecrated with the Mahāvyāhṛtis; in the case of eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, one should subsist on milk boiled with the juice of the *brāhmī* plant for three days; in the case of eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, one should fast for three nights and drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*; in the case of eating the leavings of a Śūdra, there is a fast for six nights"—that refers to the case of unintentional [consumption]. In those cases, a doubling of the penance and so forth should be prescribed for repeated practice.

And this [prohibition] applies with the exception of one's father and others, because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "The leavings (ucchiṣṭa) of a father and of an elder brother are fit to be eaten.
As for the statement of Bṛhadvyāsa: "One should not eat together with a mother, a sister, a wife, or other women; having so eaten, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Thus, that refers to the subject of eating together.

However, regarding the eating of mere leavings, one should observe what was stated by Āpastamba: "In the case of eating the leavings of a Śūdra, there shall be a fast for seven nights, as well as for women.
As for the statement of Aṅgiras: "He who should ever eat together with a Brāhmaṇī woman, or eat her leavings..."
In that regard, all wise men indeed consider it to be a fault.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the context of marriage or to a state of distress.

However, regarding the eating of the remnants of food from those of the lowest caste (*antyajātīya*), the rule is: "If twice-born men eat the leavings of those of the lowest caste, the ordinance for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya is respectively the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Kṛcchra, and half of that."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Āpastamba.
Here, *cāndram* refers to the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Regarding the consumption of the leavings of those who dwell at the extremities, that is, the eating of the food-leavings of Caṇḍālas, outcasts, and so forth.
A Brahmin shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; a Kṣatriya shall perform the Sāntapana penance.
And for the two castes, [the penances last] six nights and three nights respectively.

Thus has the *sāntapana* been described by Aṅgiras; here, the *mahāsāntapana* is to be understood [as the corresponding penance]. But in times of distress: "If food has been eaten by a Brahmin in the house of a Śūdra during a time of distress, he shall be purified by mental remorse and by reciting the *drupadāḥ* one hundred times."

Thus it should be understood as stated by Parāśara. However, that which was stated by Bṛhacchātātapa—"Whatever remains after being drunk, or whatever has been poured from the mouth into a vessel, one should know that to be unfit for consumption; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance"—[is also to be considered].
This refers to cases of repeated practice, because the cause is extremely slight.
Furthermore, if a Brāhmaṇa should ever drink water that has been left over after someone else has drunk from it,
or water held in the left hand, he should observe a vow for three nights.
This refers to cases where the act is intentional;
however, if done unintentionally, half the penance should be prescribed.
Regarding the remains of a lamp: "As for the oil remaining from a lamp, and that which has been brought [to the house] from the street at night..."
And having eaten what remains after an oil massage, one becomes pure by eating only at night.
Thus, it should be understood as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Now, regarding the expiation for consuming food touched by impure substances:

on this point Saṃvarta says: "Having eaten food into which hair or insects have fallen, which has been tainted by indigo or lac, or which has come into contact with sinew, bone, or skin, one should fast for a day."
Thus it is said:
"Having eaten food contaminated by hair or insects, tainted by indigo or lac, or touched by sinew, bone, or skin, one should fast for a day."

Thus says Śātātapa: "In the case of eating food contaminated by hair or insects, or blood, or meat, or that touched by an untouchable, or looked upon by a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan), or licked by a bird, or smelled by a dog, a pig, or a cow, or that which is sour, stale, cooked for no sacred purpose, or the food of the gods (devānna) or sacrificial oblation (havis)—for such eating, there shall be a fast followed by the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Both of these [penances] apply to cases where the act was unintentional. However, if done intentionally: "Having consumed earth, water, flowers, and so forth, or fruits, tubers, sugarcane, and roots defiled by feces or urine, one should perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance."
If the offense is proximate, it shall be only half; a Kṛcchra penance shall be the purification for such impurity.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Viṣṇu:
"In the case of minor contact, a quarter [of the penance]; in the case of major contact, half a Kṛcchra.
As for that which was stated by Vyāsa: "Food defiled by contact, and food defiled by the manner of its preparation, [if consumed] intentionally..."
And having eaten that which is inherently defiled, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.

This should be stated in the case of perceiving the taste of something mixed with impure substances and the like. However, regarding contact with a woman in her menses and others, Śaṅkha has said: "Having eaten food touched by those who are impure, outcasts, Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, women in their menses, Avadhūtas, those with elephantiasis, lepers, or those with deformed nails, one should perform a Kṛcchra penance."
A *kuṇi* is one whose hand is deformed; this refers to cases of intentional action. In the case of unintentional action, it is half [the penalty].
Having eaten food defiled by untouchable persons, or by those in a state of impurity, or by hair and insects,
one becomes purified by drinking a decoction of kuśa grass, udumbara, bilva, and so forth, along with jackfruit leaves, lotus leaves, śaṅkhapuṣpī, suvarcā, and other such ingredients.

Thus, that which was stated by Viṣṇu pertains to cases involving those who are incapable [of purification] or to food touched by washermen and the like. However, in the case of contamination by a Śūdra and so forth, that which was stated by Hārīta should be understood: "Food defiled by a Śūdra, or by insects that frequent impure things;

or where a Śūdra touches those while they are eating because of his unworthiness; or where one rising from among those eating gives them leavings or sips water; or where they give food after reviling—in these cases, the penance is a day and a night."

The same applies even to eating from a row where food has been left over: "But that twice-born man who ever eats from a row where food has been left over becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."

Thus it is from the *Kratu-smṛti*. Regarding eating food released by the left hand, however, [the *Viṣṇu-smṛti* states]: "He who eats while standing up, or he who eats from a discarded vessel—having eaten thus, Vaivasvata has declared that one should perform the Sāntapana penance."
Thus it should be understood as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Likewise, Parāśara has also said here:
"When Brahmins seated in a single row eat together..."
If even one person should leave his bowl, one should not cause the remaining food to be eaten.
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, should eat the leavings of food in that row,
he must perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Sāntapana penance.
Thus [it is said].
When Brahmins are seated in a single row eating together,
if even one should set aside his vessel, the remaining food must not be eaten.
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, should eat there in that row as one who eats leavings,
he must perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Sāntapana penance.

Regarding the drinking of water from wells or similar sources contaminated by corpses and the like, Viṣṇu says: "Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-nailed animal, or one that is extremely defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three days, a Kṣatriya for two days, a Vaiśya for one day, and a Śūdra for one night.
At the conclusion, all of them shall drink the *pañcagavya*.
By the phrase "or one that is extremely defiled," it is intended that this refers to contamination by urine, feces, and so forth.
But when a corpse in that very place has become bloated and burst open, Hārīta states a specific rule:
"If one should drink the water situated there when the corpse is wet and burst open,
one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for purification, or else the Taptakṛcchra."
If any excellent twice-born man should bathe there through negligence,
he becomes pure by reciting [mantras] and bathing at the three periods of the day for one full day and night.
Thus it is said:
"If one should drink water situated there where a corpse is moist or decomposed,
for the sake of purification one should perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Taptakṛcchra penance."
If any best of the twice-born should bathe there through negligence,
he becomes pure by reciting [mantras] and bathing at the three periods of the day for one full day and night.
And this Cāndrāyaṇa penance applies to the case of intentionally drinking water from a well defiled by a human corpse;

however, if done unintentionally, it is for six nights. But if a wet or decomposed corpse is seen within the well, one should drink milk for three nights; if it is a human corpse, it is remembered that the penance is doubled.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Devala.
And when one drinks water found in a well or vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla, then that which was stated by Āpastamba should be observed:
"If a man should intentionally drink water situated in a well or vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla..."
How should one prescribe the expiation in each respective caste?
A Brahmin shall perform the Sāntapana penance, and a Kṣatriya the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya shall perform half of that, and for a Śūdra, one quarter is prescribed.
Thus:
"If a man should drink water out of desire from a well or vessel belonging to a Cāṇḍāla,
how should one prescribe the expiation for that in each respective caste?"
A Brahmin shall perform the Sāntapana penance, and a Kṣatriya the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya shall perform half of that, and for a Śūdra, one quarter is prescribed.
And this refers to cases where one acts intentionally;
however, if one unintentionally drinks water from a well or a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he shall be purified in three days, whereas a Śūdra is purified in one day.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Devala:

"Even in small reservoirs of water connected to outcasts (*cāṇḍāla*) and others, purification is like that of a well; for small, stationary reservoirs on the surface of the earth, purification is declared to be like a well, but in large ones, there is no defilement."

Thus, from the recollection of Viṣṇu: "Furthermore, regarding lotus ponds and the like: having drunk water from [the hands of] Mlecchas and others, the water in a lotus pond or even a lake is to be known as pure up to the depth of the knees; it is declared impure below that."
Whatever Brahmin should drink that water, whether intentionally or even unintentionally—if unintentionally, he should eat only at night; but if intentionally, for a day and a night.

Thus it should be understood as stated by Āpastamba. Regarding water contained in the vessels of washermen and others, [Āpastamba says]: "If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should, through negligence, drink water, curd, or milk situated in the vessels of those of the lowest castes (antyaja)," [he must undergo penance].
For the twice-born, however, expiation is achieved through the Brahmakūrca fast.
And for a Śūdra, it is likewise through fasting and by giving gifts according to his ability.

Thus it should be understood as stated by Parāśara. However, if done intentionally, the penance is double: "Wells, tanks, or large ponds dug by those of the lowest castes (antyaja)—having bathed in or drunk from these, one is purified by the Prājāpatya penance."
This statement by Āpastamba should be understood as referring to cases of repeated practice.

As for what was stated by Āpastamba regarding the drinking of water from tanks, wells, and the like belonging to Caṇḍālas and others—that one should consume only *pañcagavya*—and his further rule: "Having drunk water from roadside stalls (*prapā*), in the forest, from a small jar (*ghaṭaka*), from a leather bag (*saura*), from a wooden trough (*droṇī*), or from water emerging from a well, or having drunk water from places maintained by *śvapākas* and Caṇḍālas, one becomes pure by consuming *pañcagavya*."
This refers to a situation where [water] is unavailable.
One who, having gone to a water-shed (*prapā*), sprinkles his body without water,
shall perform a fast for one day and then bathe with his clothes on.
Having drunk water from a vessel containing liquor, or from a waterfall, or likewise from water used for a boat,
one should fast for a day and night and then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus [it is said].
He who goes to a water-station and sprinkles his body with no water at all should perform a fast for one day and carry out a ritual bath along with his clothes.
Having drunk water from a vessel containing a jar of liquor, or likewise water from a boat,
one should fast for a day and night and then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Now, the expiation for consuming that which is defiled by intention (*bhāvaduṣṭa*).

That which is called "defiled by intention" refers to that which, by its color or shape, produces a sense of loathing due to its dissimilarity, such as the impression of bodily impurities, or when there is suspicion of poison administered by an enemy.
Regarding this, Parāśara says:
If a Brāhmaṇa eats food that is defiled by speech or defiled in intention from a person whose disposition is corrupt, he becomes purified after three nights.
Thus it is said:
"Having eaten food from one who is corrupt in speech and corrupt in disposition, or from a vessel defiled by such dispositions, a Brāhmaṇa is purified after three nights."
This refers to the case of intentional action.

As for the penance stated by Gautama—having previously recited "that which is merely defiled in its nature" and so forth up to "before the five-toed animals," stating "vomiting and the consumption of clarified butter before the five-toed animals"—that refers to the case of unintentional action.
But regarding doubt: "When a ground for suspicion has arisen concerning that which is designated as unfit to be eaten or consumed..."
I shall speak of the purity of food; listen as I declare it to you.
A Brāhmaṇa should drink the dry *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*, free from alkaline salt, for three nights; or he may drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* together with milk.
Having boiled the leaves of the palāśa and bilva, kuśa grass, lotus, and udumbara,
along with water, one becomes purified after three nights by drinking it.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Vasiṣṭha.
Manu also has stated regarding the suspicion of eating what is unfit to be eaten:
"The best of the twice-born should perform even a single Kṛcchra penance once a year."
For the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly, and especially for that which was known [to be impure].
Thus [it is said].

The best of the twice-born should perform at least one *kṛcchra* penance during the course of a year for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, this must be done with particular care in the case of what was known [to be impure].

Now, regarding the expiation for consuming food that is "vitiated by time" (*kāladuṣṭa*). Food vitiated by time includes such things as milk from a cow within ten days of calving or milk that has been kept overnight. In that regard, one should understand what was stated by Manu: "In the case of unintentional consumption of the remaining [forbidden items], one should fast for a day."
But if one intentionally eats only fermented sour substances, as well as food that has stood overnight,
or food cooked in a vessel containing dregs, one must observe the vow for three nights.
Thus it should be understood that this was stated by Śaṅkha.

These alone have been mentioned without reference to oiliness (sneha). Regarding the milk of cows that have not passed ten days since calving and so forth, the penance has already been demonstrated previously.

Upon drinking new rainwater, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); having drunk new rainwater from vessels made of horn, bone, or ivory, or from conch shells, mother-of-pearl, or cowrie shells, one becomes pure by consuming pañcagavya.
Thus, according to the *Bṛhadyājñavalkya-smṛti*:
"If one drinks new water intentionally, one must fast; for that [water] is pure at the [proper] time, but one should not drink it for three days.
If, however, one drinks it at the wrong time, the impurity lasts for ten days; having drunk it, one should not eat for a day and a night."
This is because of the observation of another Smṛti text:

"But for eating at the time of a formal reception (grahaṇaka), one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; likewise for eating the food of a Navaśrāddha, the food of a village priest, or during an eclipse.
Having eaten after the first pregnancy of women, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śātātapa. But when one eats at a prohibited time other than during an eclipse, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"O Bhārgava, on whichever day there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun..."
But in that case, there would be grasping [of the object], yet not prior to the act of eating.
One should not eat during an eclipse, nor likewise when [the sun] has set;
one should certainly not eat until its re-appearance.
Likewise, there may be an eclipse of the moon from the first watch of the night;
one should eat before the sun's turning [at midday] during the first [watch], and below the first [watch] during the first [eclipse].
Likewise, one should eat in the afternoon, not at midday, nor in the evening, but rather during the *saṅgava* period;
for if one were to eat during *saṅgava*, there would have been no prior act of eating.
Thus:
one should eat in the afternoon, not at midday, nor in the evening, but rather during the *saṅgava* period;
for if the meal were taken during *saṅgava*, there would have been no prior act of eating.

Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu: "One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor too early, nor too late," and so forth; and that which was stated by Bṛhat-Śātātapa: "One who desires prosperity should avoid parched grain, curd, and flour at night, as well as food mixed with sesame and bathing, O wise one."

In cases such as these where no specific penance has been prescribed— for all types of minor offenses (upapātaka) and indeed for those for which no penance is enjoined— one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) should be performed for the removal of all sins.
Thus, the hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) mentioned by the Lord of Yogins (Yogīśvara) should be observed;
however, for unintentional acts among the remaining [offenses], the fast for one day mentioned by Manu—namely, "one should fast for a day"—should be observed.
Now, regarding the expiation for consuming substances that are spoiled by defects, such as fermented liquids:
on this matter, Manu says:
"Having drunk fermented liquids, astringent decoctions, or even impure substances, a twice-born man..."
One remains unrestrained only so long as that [evil] does not descend into the lower realms.
Thus:
"Even after drinking fermented acids and decoctions, or even impure substances, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that [substance] has not passed downward."
In this context, regarding the remaining cases, one should observe a fast for a day when the act was unintentional;
however, if done intentionally, having eaten only fermented acids, as well as stale food,
or food cooked in a vessel that still contains dregs, one must remain under a vow for three nights.
This statement by Śaṅkha is to be understood as referring to cases other than sour gruel (kāñjika) and the like that contain fruits such as the *āmalaka*. It means:
"In those houses where a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) containing fruit is kept."
From that [cow], however, the sour gruel (kāñjikā) should be taken, and never from any other.
This is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*).

Regarding foods from which the oil has been extracted and so forth, after stating, "One should not eat things such as oil-extracted [foods], melted butter-residue (*vilayana*), oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), and products of churning that have lost their potency," one should observe what was stated by Gautama: "In the case of [eating] animals with five claws, there shall be vomiting and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
*Vilayana* refers to the dregs of clarified butter and the like.
Regarding the eating of food that has not been offered as an oblation and so forth, Likhita says:
"That which is not offered into the fire and the first portion of which is not given away should not be eaten by the twice-born; having eaten it, one should fast for a day."
A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, having eaten kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, or śaṣkulī in vain, shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Thus [it is said].
That which is not offered in the fire and that of which no portion is first given—such food is not to be eaten by the twice-born; and having eaten it, one should fast for a day.
If a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires eats kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, or śaṣkulī in vain, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Regarding those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), however, one should observe a fast for a day on the remaining occasions; thus, fasting is to be understood as the rule.
Regarding eating from broken vessels and the like, Saṃvarta has stated:
"Having eaten from the vessel of Śūdras, or having eaten from a broken vessel..."
Having fasted for a day and night and then eaten, one becomes pure by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus:
Having eaten from the vessel of Śūdras, or having eaten repeatedly from a broken vessel,
one becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Likewise, it is also stated in another Smṛti:

"Having eaten from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *arka*, and *aśvattha* trees, or from the leaves of the *kumbhī* and *tinduka*, or from the *kovidāra* and *kadamba* trees, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
Thus:

having eaten from the leaves of the banyan, the arka, and the aśvattha, or from the leaves of the kumbhī and the tinduka, or from the kovidāra and the kadamba trees, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Likewise, if a householder eats from the leaves of the *palāśa* or *padma* trees, he must perform the *aindava* penance;
whereas a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and an ascetic (*yati*) incur the fruit of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
Thus [it is said].
A householder who eats from palāśa or lotus leaves must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, a forest-dweller and an ascetic incur the fruit of a Cāndrāyaṇa.
Now, the expiation for eating forbidden food resulting from actions such as giving with the hand:
regarding this, Parāśara says:
"Honey, molasses, vegetables, milk products, salt, and ghee..."
Having eaten food given by hand, one must fast for one day.
Thus: Having eaten honey, molasses, vegetables, cow's milk products, salt,
or ghee that have been offered by hand, one must fast for one day.

However, regarding intentional acts: Hārīta has stated that for eating food given by hand, eating in the presence of a non-Brāhmaṇa, eating in a defiled row (duṣṭapaṅkti), eating at the head of a row, voiding urine or excrement while anointed with oil, or eating the food of one who has undergone a death or birth impurity or a Śūdra—along with sleeping together with Śūdras—the penance is fasting for three nights; this should be understood. Regarding food rendered impure by being given in exchange: "A Śūdra giving the food of a Brāhmaṇa, or a Brāhmaṇa giving the food of a Śūdra—both of these are unfit to be eaten; having eaten either, one should fast for a day."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya:

"But regarding eating from the hand of a Śūdra: 'He who eats from the hand of a Śūdra, or drinks water from such a hand at any time, becomes purified by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).'"
Thus it should be understood as stated by Kratu.
