Furthermore, even in the case of food blown upon with the mouth: "If one has blown upon food with the mouth while having a foot placed on a seat, or even while half-covered by a garment, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance."
Thus it was said by him:
"If one eats food offered for the sake of a father or other ancestors during a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, he should perform six *prāṇāyāmas*;
fasting is prescribed for periods ranging from three months up to a year."
In the case of an increase [in the number of rites], three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) are prescribed; at the Sapindana rite, it is one day and night;
for a dissimilar rite, a night-fast is ordained, and likewise at the conclusion of a vow.
This [penance] is doubled for eating the food of a Kṣatriya, tripled for eating the food of a Vaiśya,
and it is recorded as being fourfold when eating the food of a Śūdra.
If those twice-born who drink water while a guest stands at the door should consume that water, it becomes blood; having consumed it, they must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Bhāradvāja. Hārīta has also said:
"Having eaten food on the eleventh day, and likewise having eaten at the *saṃcayana* (the gathering of the bones),"
Having observed the fast according to the rules and bathed, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
Thus it is said:
"Having eaten food on the eleventh day, or likewise having eaten at a funeral feast (*saṃcayana*),
one should fast, bathe according to the rules, and offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras."
Viṣṇu has also said: "For a *navaśrāddha*, the penance is that of a *prājāpatya*; for the first monthly *śrāddha*, it is three-quarters of that;
for the three-fifths-month (*traipakṣika*), half of that; and for the second-month *śrāddha*, the consumption of *pañcagavya*."
Thus:
for a *navaśrāddha*, the penance is a *prājāpatya*; for the first monthly *śrāddha*, it is three-quarters of that;
for the tri-monthly (*traipakṣika*), it is half of that; and for the second monthly, it is the consumption of *pañcagavya*.
This refers to cases of emergency;
however, in non-emergency situations, it is prescribed that one should perform a Cāndrāyaṇa for a *navaśrāddha*, a Prājāpatya for a *miśraka* (mixed) śrāddha,
a single-day fast for *purāṇa* (ancient) śrāddhas, and a Prājāpatya for [other] ancient śrāddhas.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Hārīta.
As for the statement, "But the *prājāpatya* [penance] applies to the *miśraka*," this should be understood as referring to the first monthly *śrāddha*.
However, regarding the second and subsequent months, [Hārīta says]: "The *prājāpatya* applies to the *navaśrāddha*, and a quarter less than that to the first monthly *śrāddha*."

In the case of three fortnights, it shall be half of that; likewise, in the case of two months, it is a quarter. For six months and for a year, a *kṛcchra* less a quarter is prescribed. For other months, it is three nights; if [the period] is daily, one day is ordained.
Thus it should be understood as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Regarding the consumption of food at a *śrāddha* for Kṣatriyas and others, however, when not in a state of distress, it is stated in that very same work:
"A *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is prescribed for eating at a *navaśrāddha*, and a *parāka* is remembered for a monthly (*māsika*) *śrāddha*."
For three fortnights, the Sāntapana penance is prescribed; for two months, the Kṛcchra is traditionally taught.
This vow has been declared for a Kṣatriya at a *navaśrāddha*;
however, the wise have stated that for a Vaiśya it is half more than that of a Kṣatriya.
For a Śūdra, however, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇas for a *navaśrāddha*;
for a monthly rite, one and a half Cāndrāyaṇas; and for a three-fortnightly rite, an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa) is prescribed.
For two months, the Parāka penance is prescribed; beyond that, the Sāntapana is traditionally taught.
Thus it is said: "For a *navaśrāddha*, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed; for a monthly (*māsika*) rite, the Parāka;
for a three-fortnightly (*traipakṣika*) rite, the Sāntapana; and for a two-month rite, the Kṛcchra is prescribed."
This vow has been declared for a Kṣatriya at a Navaśrāddha;
however, the wise have stated that for a Vaiśya it is one and a half times that of the Kṣatriya.
For a Śūdra, however, at a *navaśrāddha* (a funeral rite for a recently deceased), he should perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
at a monthly rite, one and a half *cāndrāyaṇas*; and at a three-fortnightly rite, an *aindava* (*cāndrāyaṇa*) is prescribed.
For two months, it shall be a Parāka penance; beyond that, it is recorded as a Sāntapana.
As for the statement of Śaṅkha: "The Cāndrāyaṇa is prescribed for the Navaśrāddha; the Parāka is remembered for the monthly (Māsika);
the Atikṛcchra should be performed for the third fortnight; and the Kṛcchra indeed for the six-month [anniversary]."
For an annual rite, there shall be a quarter-pādakṛcchra; for a subsequent annual rite, a single day.
Beyond that, there shall be no fault, according to the statement of Śaṅkha.

Thus, that [rule] refers to those killed by snakes and the like, or to those excluded from the company at meals (apāṅkteya), such as thieves, outcasts, and eunuchs. "Death from a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a snake, from a Brāhmaṇa, or even from lightning,
as well as from fanged beasts and wild animals, [is the fate] of evildoers."
A twice-born man who has eaten at the sixteen-fold śrāddha of those who have died by falling, by destruction, or likewise by poison or hanging, should perform the moon-vow (induvrata).
Thus it is said: "Death from a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, from lightning,
or from fanged beasts— these are the deaths of those who have committed evil deeds."

A twice-born man who has eaten at the sixteen śrāddhas performed for those who have died by falling [from a cliff], by destruction [of the body], or likewise by poison or hanging, should observe the lunar vow (induvrata).
Likewise, if a Brāhmaṇa eats food at a Śrāddha performed on the eleventh day for those excluded from the company (apāṅkteya), he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus:
"If a Brāhmaṇa eats food at a Śrāddha performed on the eleventh day for those excluded from the company (apāṅkteya), he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Having eaten at an *āmaśrāddha* (a funeral rite with raw food), one is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
likewise, having eaten at a *saṃkalpita* (an intended or informal) rite, there should be a fast for three nights.
Thus, because Bharadvāja has stated that the penance is generally [the same as] for a teacher,
Bṛhadyama states a specific rule regarding the student (brahmacārin):
"If a twice-born who has not completed his vow should eat at [funeral feasts] such as those monthly [śrāddhas], [he must perform penance]."
A fast for three nights is prescribed as his penance.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consumed clarified butter, one becomes purified.
Thus:
"If a twice-born man who has not completed his vow should eat at a monthly śrāddha or similar rites,
a three-night fast is prescribed as his penance."
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and consumed clarified butter, one becomes purified.
This concerns the subject of ignorance;
for he himself has also stated regarding desire:
"He who eats honey or meat at a śrāddha, or during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka)..."
One should perform the Prājāpatya penance and complete the remainder of the vow.
Thus:
"He who should eat honey or meat at a śrāddha, or during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka),
shall perform the Prājāpatya penance and complete the remainder of his vow."

"In the case of an *āmaśrāddha*, however, [the penance] is half in all instances; in an *āmaśrāddha*, it is half of that, but a *prājāpatya* is always required," because this is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
As for that which was stated by Uśanas: "A twice-born who has partaken in a *śrāddha* should drink water ten times with the *gāyatrī* mantra."
Then one should perform the twilight devotions; immediately thereafter, one shall become pure.
Thus, that [rule] refers to the subject of *śrāddha* for which no expiation has been stated.
However, regarding the eating at a *śrāddha* that is an auxiliary part of a sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), a specific rule has been stated by Vyāsa:
"But when the *cūḍā-homa* has been performed, as well as prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*)."
Indeed, having eaten at a birth ceremony, one should perform the Sāntapana penance.
But after eating food at the rites of others, O best of the twice-born,
one is purified from the sin of consuming forbidden food by fasting at the command of his superior.
Thus [it is said].
If one has eaten after the cūḍā-homa has been performed, but before the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa),
as well as after the birth-rite (jātakarman), one must indeed perform the sāntapana penance.
But for other refined foods, O best of the twice-born, having eaten them,
one is purified by fasting at the command [of the teacher] when they consist of censurable food.
Furthermore, regarding the parting of the hair and other such rites, Dhaumya stated a specific rule:
"In the case of the *brahmaudana*, the *soma* sacrifice, the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*),
a birth-śrāddha, and a new-śrāddha, a twice-born man shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
Thus:
"In the case of the *brahmaudana*, the *soma* sacrifice, the *sīmantonnayana*,
as well as at a birth-śrāddha and a new-śrāddha, a twice-born man shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
In this context, the rite called *brahmaudana* is a constituent part of the *ādhāna*, because of its association with the *soma*.
Now, the penance for eating food that is unfit to be eaten due to its ownership:

that which, though not forbidden by its own nature, is declared unfit to be eaten because it belongs to a specific person, is "impure due to ownership. Regarding this, the Lord of Yogins [Yājñavalkya] stated: "In times of non-distress, one should not eat the food of one who has not given it, nor of one who is devoid of the sacred fires."
Beginning with these words, those whose food should not be eaten have been set forth in five and a half verses.
Manu has also set forth those same persons, with a few additions:
"Nor at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor likewise at one performed by a priest for an entire village."
A Brahmin may, on some occasions, eat when the offering has been made by a woman or a eunuch.
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor the food of a group, nor the food of a prostitute, nor that which is despised by the wise.
One should not eat the food of a thief or a singer, nor that of a carpenter or a usurer; nor that of one who has been consecrated for sacrifice, a miser, or one who is bound in fetters.
[The food] of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman,
of a hypocrite, of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, and of one who eats the leavings of others.

The food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, that over which someone has sneezed before eating, food from within ten days of a death, food offered without respect, meat not intended for sacrifice, and the food of a woman who lacks a husband or sons— these one should avoid.
The food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of one who has fallen, and that which is sneezed upon;
likewise, the food of a slanderer, a liar, and a seller of sacrificial rites.
The food of an actor, a tailor, an ungrateful person,
a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, and one who enters the stage for performance;
[The food] of a goldsmith, of a bamboo-worker, of a seller of weapons,
of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, and of a washerman [is forbidden].
The washerman, the cruel man, he in whose house a paramour resides,
those who tolerate a paramour, and those who are entirely dominated by women— all these go to hell.
And food offered to the deceased within ten days of death is indeed unsatisfying.
Thus it is said.

A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one performed by a priest who officiates for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch.
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted, nor the food of a group, nor the food of a courtesan, nor that which is despised by the wise.
The food of a thief and a singer, of a carpenter and a usurer, of one who has been consecrated for sacrifice, of a miser, and of one who is bound in fetters, [should not be eaten].
[The food] of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman,
of a hypocrite, of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, and of one who eats the leavings of others [is forbidden].

The food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, that over which someone has sneezed before eating, food from within ten days of a death, food offered without respect, meat not intended for sacrifice, and the food of a woman who lacks a male relative— these one should avoid.
The food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of one who has fallen, and what is sneezed upon;
likewise, the food of a slanderer, a liar, and a seller of sacrifices.
The food of an actor, of a tailor, and of an ungrateful person; as well as the food of a blacksmith, of a Niṣāda, and of one who enters the stage [as a performer].
[The food] of a goldsmith, of a bamboo-worker, of a seller of weapons,
of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, and of a washerman [is forbidden].
The washerman, the cruel man, he in whose house a paramour resides,
those who tolerate a paramour, and those who are entirely ruled by women— all these go to hell.
And food offered to the deceased within ten days of death is indeed unsatisfying.
In this context, the substances [prohibited] have been explained in the section on forbidden foods and the section on ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
Here, he states the expiation:
"Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days."
Having consumed semen, feces, or urine intentionally, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Thus:
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.

Paiṭhīnasi has also stated that for one who does so unintentionally, the penance lasts exactly three nights: "One with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who quarrels with his father, one conquered by women, one afflicted with leprosy, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, a merchant, a priest for a village, one accused of a crime, one who has begotten a child on a Śūdra woman, a younger brother who marries before his elder, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, the husband of a *didhiṣū* woman, the son of a remarried woman, a thief, a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, and a servant—these are persons whose food should not be eaten, who are excluded from the row at a meal, and who are unworthy of the *śrāddha*. Having eaten or given [food] to these through ignorance, one must fast for three nights."
But Śaṅkha, having recited these very same [acts] with a slight addition, prescribed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; that refers to the case of habitual practice.

Furthermore, Gautama, having enumerated those whose food is not to be eaten—beginning with "those who eat leavings, unchaste women, those accused [of crimes]," and so forth—stated the penance as "vomiting before the five-toed animals and consuming clarified butter. That, however, refers to a situation of distress (*āpad*).
But regarding one who is forced to eat by compulsion, a specific rule has been stated by Āpastamba:
"Those who have been forcibly enslaved by Mlecchas, Caṇḍālas, or Dasyus..."
They have committed impure deeds, such as the killing of living beings like cows and others.
Wiping away food-leavings, as well as eating the leavings of others,
and the devouring of the flesh of donkeys, camels, and village pigs.
Likewise, association with their women and eating together with them [constitutes an offense];
for a twice-born man who has lived thus for a month, the Prājāpatya penance is the means of purification.
For one who has maintained the sacred fires, however, there shall be either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penance;
or, having lived [in that state] for a year, he should perform both the Cāndrāyaṇa and the Parāka.
A Śūdra who has resided [as a guest] for one year should drink barley-gruel for half a month;
a Śūdra who has resided for one full month is purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
After one year, the expiation should be determined by the best of the twice-born;
indeed, after three years, he attains that very state [of purity].
Thus:
"Those who have been forcibly enslaved by Mlecchas, Caṇḍālas, or bandits,
and compelled to perform inauspicious acts such as the slaughter of living beings like cows and the like..."
Likewise, wiping away food-leavings, eating the leavings of others,
and consuming the flesh of donkeys, camels, mules, and pigs.
Likewise, association with their women and eating together with them requires the Prājāpatya penance as a means of purification for a twice-born man who has resided [among them] for a month.
For one who has maintained the sacred fires, however, there shall be either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Parāka penance;
having lived [in this manner] for a year, he should perform both the Cāndrāyaṇa and the Parāka.
A Śūdra who has resided [as a guest] for one year should drink barley-gruel for half a month;
a Śūdra who has resided for one full month is purified by a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
After one year, an expiation should be prescribed by the best of the twice-born;
after three years, he indeed attains the same state as that [sin].
Regarding the consumption of food taken from one who is under ritual impurity (*āśauca*), Chāgaleya says:
"If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*),
they become pure by performing a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), provided it is the birth-impurity of a Śūdra."
For a Vaiśya it shall be sixty days, for a Kṣatriya twenty, and for a Brāhmaṇa ten;
[the penance consists of] fasting for one day, three days, five days, and seven nights respectively.
Then their purification occurs; thereafter, they should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus it is said:
"If Brahmins eat during a period of impurity caused by birth or death out of ignorance,
they become pure by performing one hundred *prāṇāyāmas* in the case of the impurity caused by a Śūdra's birth."
For a Vaiśya it shall be sixty days, for a King twenty, and for a Brāhmaṇa ten;
[the penance consists of] fasting for one day, three days, five days, and seven nights respectively.
Then their purification occurs; after that, they should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One-day, three-day, and other penances should be applied according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇa and so forth.
This refers to cases where the act was unintentional;
however, regarding intentional acts, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
Having eaten during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a twice-born man shall perform the Sāntapana penance;
having eaten during the period of impurity of a Kṣatriya, a Saptakṛcchra is prescribed.
Having eaten during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya, one should perform the Mahāsāntapana penance;
likewise, having eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, one should observe the vow for three months.
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha: "Having eaten at a birth-impurity (sūtaka) of a Śūdra, one should perform a vow for six months;
likewise, having eaten at that of a Vaiśya, one should perform a vow for three months."
Likewise, having eaten [the food] of a Kṣatriya, one should observe a vow for two months;
and having eaten during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, one should observe a vow for one month.
Thus, this refers to the subject of repeated practice.

Furthermore, this expiation (prāyaścitta) is to be understood as occurring after the period of impurity (āśauca); for according to the Smṛti of Viṣṇu: "If one eats food even once during the period of impurity of Brāhmaṇas and others, his own impurity lasts as long as theirs; however, upon the cessation of their impurity, he should perform the expiation."
Regarding the eating of food from those such as a sonless man, Likhita says: "Having eaten the food of a usurer, of one who does not observe vows, of one who has no son,
and likewise having eaten the food of a Śūdra, one must fast for three nights."
Likewise:
"A twice-born man who eats the food of one who abstains from cooking for others, yet delights in cooking for others, or of one who does not cook at all, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Thus it is said:

"A twice-born man who eats the food of one who has desisted from cooking for others, of one who delights in cooking for others, or of one who does not cook at all, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
And this refers to the subject of practice (*abhyāsa*).
The definition of one who has desisted from cooking for others and so forth was stated by that same [author]:
"Having taken up the sacred fire and performed the ritual of internalizing it (*samāropa*), one should not perform the five sacrifices."
He who has desisted from cooking for others is thus proclaimed by the sages.
But he who, having performed the five sacrifices, subsists on the food of others,
is one who constantly rises at dawn and is devoted to the cooking of others.
He who gives while remaining detached from the conduct of a householder’s duty is proclaimed by the sages, who know the essence of dharma, to be one who does not cook for himself (an *apaca*).
Thus it is said:

having taken up the sacred fire and performed the internal installation (samāropa), one should not fail to perform the five great sacrifices; such a person is proclaimed by the sages as one who has desisted from relying on the food cooked by others.
He who, having performed the five sacrifices, subsists on the food of others,
always rising early in the morning, is one who is devoted to the cooking of others.
He who gives while avoiding the conduct of the duties of a householder is proclaimed by the sages, who know the essence of dharma, to be an "apaca."

Regarding the eating of food from one who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) and others, Vriddha-Yajnavalkya says: "Both the ascetic (*yati*) and the student of sacred knowledge are the owners of cooked food;
the food of these two must not be eaten, and having eaten it, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
Thus [it is said].
Both an ascetic and a celibate student are the rightful owners of cooked food;
one must not eat the food of these two, and having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

Regarding the eating of food belonging to one who does not perform the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and other rites, Bharadvāja says: "If the deities do not eat [the offerings] of one for a fortnight or even a month, a twice-born man who eats the food of that evil-minded person shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."
Thus, both of these refer to the subject of habitual practice.

However, regarding the eating of the food of those whose conduct is prohibited—those who exceed the previously enumerated [categories] and are habitually engaged in forbidden acts—it is said: "A twice-born man, having eaten the food of a Brahmin who lacks proper conduct and who practices what is forbidden, shall fast for one day."
Thus it should be understood as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Regarding the repeated practice of this very [offense] for a year, it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* itself:
"For one who is joined with a minor offense (*upapātaka*), [the penance lasts] continuously for one year."
Having eaten such food, a twice-born man should perform the Parāka penance as a means of purification.
Thus:
"A twice-born man who has eaten the food of one guilty of a minor offense (upapātaka) shall perform the Parāka penance for one continuous year as a means of purification."
Furthermore, this collection of vows prescribed without distinction in the section on penance for eating forbidden food applies specifically to the foremost of the twice-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
For Kṣatriyas and the others, however, there is a reduction by one-quarter at each stage: "The whole [penance] is to be given to a Brāhmaṇa; it is recorded as one-quarter less for a Kṣatriya;
half for a Vaiśya; and only one quarter is recommended for those of the Śūdra caste."
Thus, from the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
At the time of enumerating the specific causes [of sin], those acts that cause loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) and so forth were enumerated immediately after the minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Regarding those, the penances are now stated.
On this point, Manu says:
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāntapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness of receiving alms, purification is by the lunar penance (*aindava*) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should consume hot barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for three days.
Thus:
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra; if unintentionally, the Prājāpatya.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness to receive alms, purification is achieved by the lunar penance (Cāndrāyaṇa) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.
The phrase "any one of these" applies everywhere.
Furthermore, a specific rule regarding Yama has been stated here:
"Having committed an act that causes mixture [of castes], one should eat barley-gruel for a month."
Or else, one should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance as an expiation.
Having committed an act that renders one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), one becomes pure by performing the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Purification for acts causing defilement is achieved through the Śītakṛcchra or the Mahāsāntapana penance;
for acts causing loss of caste, the Taptakṛcchra is the means of purification.
Thus [it is said].
Having committed an act that causes confusion of castes, one should eat barley-gruel for a month,
or else perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance as an expiation.
Having committed an act that renders one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), one becomes pure through the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Purification for acts causing defilement is achieved by either the Śītakṛcchra or the Mahāsāntapana penance;
for acts causing further corruption, the Taptakṛcchra is the means of purification.
Bṛhaspati has also stated a specific rule regarding acts that cause loss of caste:
"Having inflicted a wound upon a Brāhmaṇa, having killed a donkey or similar animal,
or having accepted wealth from censurable persons, one should perform half of the Kṛcchra penance."
Thus:
"Having caused pain to a Brāhmaṇa, having killed a donkey or similar animal,
or having accepted wealth from censurable persons, one should perform the Kṛcchrārdha vow."

The scope of these penances for acts causing loss of caste and so forth, as stated by Manu and others, must be distinguished according to considerations such as the caste and capacity [of the offender].
Thus, the penance for consuming forbidden food and similar acts, as held in the heart of Yogīndra, has been shown in brief. (3.289)
Now we shall follow the subject at hand.
Five types of sin have been mentioned: mortal sins (mahāpātaka), heinous sins (atipātaka), secondary sins (anupātaka), minor sins (upapātaka), and miscellaneous sins (prakīrṇaka).
Having described the fourfold penance for those [other categories], the author now states the penance for the miscellaneous sins that follows in the sequence.

One who practices breath control (prāṇāyāma) after bathing in water, one who travels in a vehicle drawn by a donkey or a camel, one who bathes naked, and one who eats or has sexual intercourse with a woman during the day— [these must perform penance].
A vehicle yoked with donkeys is a "donkey-vehicle" (*kharayāna*);

a vehicle yoked with camels is a "camel-vehicle" (*uṣṭrayāna*), such as a chariot or a cart. Having traveled by these on a road, one who is naked (*digambara*) becomes pure after bathing, eating, enjoying the company of his own wife during the day, and plunging into a pond or river while performing breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
And this refers to the case of intentional action; for having mounted a camel-vehicle or a donkey-vehicle intentionally—
Having immersed oneself in water while still wearing one's clothes, one becomes purified by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu, if the act is unintentional, mere bathing is to be prescribed.
However, in the case of actually riding a donkey, a double repetition [of the penance] is to be prescribed, because of its greater gravity. (3.290)
Furthermore: Having addressed a guru with "huṃ," or having addressed a brahmin as "thou," or having defeated him in debate,
or having bound him with a garment, one must quickly propitiate him and fast for a day.

Having rebuked one’s teacher, father, or others by addressing them with the word "thou" (*tvam*), saying "you said this," or "this was done by you alone," using the singular form of the pronoun *yuṣmad*; or having angrily insulted a Brahmin—whether senior, equal, or junior—by saying "Hum! Be silent! or "Hum! Do not speak so much!"; or having defeated a Brahmin through frivolous debate (*jalpa*) or destructive disputation (*vitaṇḍā*), both of which result in victory; or having bound him around the neck even with a soft cloth; one should quickly appease him by prostrating at his feet and other such means, cause him to abandon his anger, and fast for a day.
One should spend the entire day without eating.
As for that which was stated by Yama: "Having defeated a Brāhmaṇa in debate, one who desires to perform an expiation should fast for three nights, bathe, prostrate, and seek his favor."
Thus, that refers to the object of practice. 3.291
Furthermore:
"In raising a staff against a Brahmin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if he strikes him down, it is an *atikṛcchra*;
if blood flows, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and if the blood is internal, it is a *kṛcchra*."
If one raises a staff or other weapon with the intent to kill, the *kṛcchra* penance is the means of purification;
if one strikes or causes it to fall, the *atikṛcchra*;
and if blood flows—that is, if there is a discharge of blood—the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
Even when internal blood is shed, the *kṛcchra* penance is the cause of purification.
Bṛhaspati has also stated a specific rule in this regard:
"Having struck [someone] with wood or other such objects, one should perform the *kṛcchra* if there is no wound."
If the bones are broken, it shall be an Atikṛcchra penance; but if a limb is severed, it is a Parāka.
Thus it is said:
"Having struck [another] with wood or similar objects, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance if no wound is made;
if a bone is broken, it shall be the *atikṛcchra*; but if a limb is severed, it is the *parāka*."
Regarding the striking with the foot, Yama said:
"Having touched a Brāhmaṇa with the foot,
one who desires to perform the penance should fast for a day, bathe, prostrate, and seek his favor."
Thus.
Having touched a Brahmin with one's foot,
one who desires to perform the penance should fast for a day, bathe, prostrate, and seek his favor.
But Manu has shown other penances for miscellaneous offenses:
"If one who is afflicted, having discharged bodily waste either without water or even in water,
becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow."
Thus:
"If one who is afflicted, having performed a bodily evacuation without water or even in water,
becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow."
"Without water" means even when water is not present.
"Bodily [impurity]" refers to urine, feces, and so forth.
This applies to cases where there is no intentional desire [for such acts].
But if one, out of desire and having fallen into distress, partakes of human excrement when water is unavailable,
he shall fast for one day and enter the water along with his clothes.
Thus it should be understood as stated by Yama.

As for the statement of Sumantu, "For one who urinates in water or fire, [the penance is] the Taptakṛcchra," that refers to cases where one is not afflicted by distress or to cases of habitual practice.
Regarding the omission of obligatory Śrauta and other rites, however, Manu says:
In the event of the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas,
and upon the violation of the vows of a Snātaka, the penance is fasting.
Thus:
"In the case of the transgression of obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda,
and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting."

In the case of Śrauta rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Smārta rites such as the occasional (anitya) homas, there is a combination of fasting with the specific expiations (prāyaścitta) prescribed for each, such as the iṣṭi sacrifice. Furthermore, the vows of a Snātaka, such as "one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes if one has the means," and others previously mentioned, must also be observed.
Concerning the observances of a *snātaka*, Kratu has also stated: "If one omits even a single one of these practices, one becomes purified by reciting the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times."

Regarding the non-performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), Bṛhaspati says: "The householder who, while not being ill and possessing wealth, eats every day without having performed the great sacrifices, is purified by half a *kṛcchra* penance."
He who maintains the sacred fires but fails to perform the ritual worship on the festival days,
or he who does not approach his wife during her season, shall likewise perform half a *kṛcchra* penance.
Thus:
"A householder who, being free from illness and possessing wealth, eats every day without having first performed the great sacrifices, is purified by half a *kṛcchra* penance."
He who maintains the sacred fires but fails to perform the ritual worship on the festival days,
or he who does not approach his wife during her season, shall likewise perform half a *kṛcchra* penance.

Regarding the death of a second wife while the first is still living, Devala says: "If one should cremate a deceased second wife with the Vaitānika fires while the first wife is still alive, that act is indeed equal to the drinking of liquor."
Thus it is said:
"If a man should cremate a second wife with the sacrificial fires while the first is still living,
that act is indeed equal to the drinking of liquor."
Regarding the false accusation against one's own wife, Yama said: "When a man,
out of anger, says of his own wife, 'She is unapproachable,' a Brahmin should perform the Prājāpatya penance, and a Kṣatriya for nine days."
A Vaiśya, however, should observe it for six nights, while a Śūdra should observe it for three nights.
Thus [it is said].
If a man, out of anger, should call his own wife "unapproachable," a Brahmin must perform the Prājāpatya penance, and a Kṣatriya for nine days.
A Vaiśya should observe this for six nights, while a Śūdra should observe it for three nights.
Regarding not bathing before eating and other such matters, Hārīta says:
"Carrying an empty water-pot while not having bathed and while eating food,
one's purification shall occur after a day and night, as well as through the recitation [of mantras] for a full day."
Thus:
"Carrying an empty water-pot, and eating food without having bathed,
one's purification shall occur after a day and night, as well as by means of recitation performed during that day."
Regarding the unequal distribution of gifts and so forth out of affection or other motives among those seated in a single row, Yama says:
"One should not give unequally in a row, nor should one beg, nor should one cause others to beg.
The beggar, the one who causes begging, and the giver—none of these indeed go to heaven."
One is liberated from that [sinful] act by performing the Prājāpatya penance;
this applies also to one who destroys a bridge over a river and to one who creates an obstacle to a maiden's marriage.
And no atonement is possible for one who commits an act of inequality; yet,
for all three of these [offenses],
if they seek restoration, the twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance while subsisting on food obtained through alms.
Thus:
"One should not give unequally in a row, nor should one beg, nor cause others to beg;
the beggar, the one who causes begging, and the giver do not indeed go to heaven."
One is liberated from that deed by performing the Prājāpatya penance;
this applies also to one who destroys a bridge over a river and to one who creates an obstacle to a maiden's marriage.
Furthermore, no atonement is possible for one who commits an act of injustice against an equal; yet,
for all three of these [offenses],
if they seek restoration, the twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance while subsisting on food obtained through begging.
A *saṃkrama* is a path for descending into water.
Regarding making what is level uneven for the purpose of worship and so forth,
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said in the context of seeing a rainbow and similar phenomena:
If one should point out a rainbow or a fire in a *palāśa* tree to another person,
the penance is a fast for a day and night, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a bow and a staff.
Regarding conversation with those who have fallen [from their status] and so forth, Gautama says: "One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous.
Having conversed, one should mentally meditate upon those who perform meritorious deeds, or one should converse with a Brahmin."
"Regarding the loss of a bed, food, or wealth, there are separate years.

This means that for the destruction—that is, the creation of an obstacle—to the acquisition of a wife, food, or wealth, one must observe the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year each.
Likewise, another Smṛti text prescribes a penance for voiding feces or urine and so forth without the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*).
If a twice-born man becomes impure while without his sacred thread,
the expiation is either a fast for a day and night or the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.

In that regard, the rule is as follows: for one who has been defiled by food from above, there is a fast; for one defiled by food from below, there is the recitation of the Gāyatrī during the drinking of water and so forth.

However, in the case of unintentional acts: "For one who drinks, urinates, or eats while not wearing the sacred thread, there shall be three, six, and nine sets of *prāṇāyāmas* respectively, followed by eating at night."
Thus it should be understood as stated in another Smṛti:
"If one rises after eating without having performed purification and sipping water, or if one rises from a fast without having sipped water..."
One should perform an immediate bath; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
Thus it should be understood as stated in another Smṛti.
Regarding the release of thieves and others, Vasiṣṭha says: "Upon the release of one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night, and the domestic priest for three nights;
upon the punishing of one who does not deserve punishment, the domestic priest shall perform a Kṛcchra penance and the king shall fast for three nights."

One with deformed nails and one with black teeth should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then undergo the purificatory rite; thus said Mārkaṇḍeya: "If any excellent twice-born man eats in the row of one who is unfit to sit in the row, he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
Thus [it is said].
If any excellent twice-born man eats in the company of one who is unworthy of the row,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Regarding the subject of indigo, Āpastamba says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa wears a garment dyed with indigo on his limbs,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
If the juice of any indigo plant should enter through the pores of the skin,
the common purification for all three castes is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
The keeping, the selling, and living by that trade as one's livelihood—these constitute a fall for a Brahmin; he removes it by three *kṛcchra* penances.
If one should pierce the body of a Brāhmaṇa with indigo wood,
or wherever blood is seen, the twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the case of women, there is no fault in sexual enjoyment for the sake of play upon a bed.
Thus:
"If a Brāhmaṇa wears a garment dyed with indigo on his limbs,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
If the juice of indigo should enter anyone through the pores of the skin,
the common purification for all three castes is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
The keeping, the selling, and living by that trade as one's livelihood—these constitute a downfall for a Brahmin; he removes it through three *kṛcchra* penances.
If one should pierce the body of a Brāhmaṇa with indigo wood,
and blood is seen there, the twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the case of women, there is no fault in sexual enjoyment for the sake of sport upon a bed.
Bhṛgu also said:
"Wearing indigo on a bed does not defile a Brāhmaṇa;
for a King it is permitted during times of prosperity, and for a Vaiśya it may be worn except on festival days."
Thus it is said:
"Indigo worn by a woman on a bed does not defile a Brāhmaṇa;
for a king, its wearing is permitted during prosperity; and for a Vaiśya, its wearing is allowed except on festival days."
Likewise, there is a counter-exception regarding specific types of clothing; for it is stated in the Smṛti: "The indigo dye does not cause defilement on woolen blankets or silk thread.
Regarding the act of ascending a bedstead or similar object made from the wood of the Brahma-tree, Śaṅkha says:
Having used a bed, a vehicle, a seat,
or sandals made from the Palāśa tree, a twice-born man shall observe a vow for three nights.
A Kṣatriya who, intent on saving his own life, turns his back in battle,
or one who cuts down a fruit-bearing tree, shall perform a vow for one year.

If one should pass between two Brahmins, or between a Brahmin and the sacred fire, or between a husband and wife, or between a cow and an eminent twice-born, he shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
If a twice-born man passes between [a woman and her husband] during the time of a fire sacrifice, milking, Vedic study, or taking a wife, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus:
Having used the bed, vehicle, seat,
or sandals of a *palāśa* tree, a twice-born man shall observe a vow for three nights.
But a Kṣatriya who, intent on saving his life, turns his back in battle,
or one who cuts down a fruit-bearing tree, shall perform a vow for one year.

If one should pass between two Brahmins, or between a Brahmin and the sacred fire, or between a husband and wife, or between a cow and an excellent twice-born man, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
If a twice-born man passes between [a woman and her husband] during the time of a fire sacrifice, milking, Vedic study, or the taking of a wife, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
The two *doha* [verses] are ancillary to the *sānnāyya* and other rites;
this refers to the subject of repeated practice.
Regarding the sight of ill omens such as the sun with a hole in it, Śaṅkha says: "Upon seeing bad dreams, ill omens, and the like, one should give ghee and gold."
Regarding travel to certain specific regions as well, Devala says: "Having gone to Sindhu, Sauvīra, and Saurāṣṭra, as well as those dwelling in the borderlands,
and to Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and Andhra, one deserves a purificatory rite."
And this should be understood as applying except during a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*).
Regarding looking at one's own excrement and so forth, Yama says:
"One should not urinate facing the sun, nor should one look at one's own feces."
Having seen [an impurity], one should look at the sun, a cow, fire, or likewise a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus:
one should not urinate facing the sun, nor should one look at one's own excrement;
having seen it, one should gaze upon the sun, a cow, fire, or a Brāhmaṇa.
Śaṅkha also said:
"Having repeatedly washed his feet and likewise having applied fire [to them],
and having wiped his feet with *kuśa* grass, one should observe the vow for one day."
Thus [it is said].
Having performed the *pādapratana* (stretching out the feet) and likewise having placed fire beneath them,
one should wipe the feet with *kuśa* grass and observe the vow for one day.

Regarding the salutation of Kṣatriyas and others, Hārīta says: "Upon saluting a Kṣatriya, one should fast for a day and a night; upon saluting a Vaiśya, for two nights; and upon saluting a Śūdra, there shall be a fast for three nights.

Likewise, there shall be a fast for three nights for saluting someone who is reclining on a bed, or whose feet are placed in sandals or shoes, or who is impure from eating, or who is in darkness, or who is performing a Śrāddha, or who is engaged in recitation (japa) or the worship of deities; and likewise, even for one invited elsewhere, there is a three-night fast for eating at another place.

The same applies even when one who holds sacrificial fuel, flowers, and so forth in his hand offers a salutation: "One should certainly not salute a twice-born man who is holding sacrificial fuel, flowers, *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, water, clay, food, or unbroken grains (*akṣata*) in his hand, nor one who is performing silent recitation (*japa*) or a fire-oblation (*homa*)."
Thus, according to Āpastamba, because this is mentioned in conjunction with silent recitations (*japa*) and other such acts;

this same expiation applies even to one who offers a salutation, for Śaṅkha prohibits him as well: "One should not offer a salutation while holding a water-pot, nor while wandering for alms, nor while holding flowers, clarified butter, or the like, nor while impure, nor while performing silent recitation, nor while performing rites for the gods or ancestors, nor while lying down.
Other similar statements should be sought from other *smṛtis*, but they are not written here for fear of excessive length. (3.292)

Because causes (nimitta) are infinite and it is impossible to state an expiation for every individual case, this [verse] is spoken in order to provide knowledge of specific expiations regarding both those cases where they have been taught in general and those where they have not been taught:
"Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the sin,
an expiation should be prescribed where no atonement has been stated."

Whatever collection of penances has been mentioned or will be mentioned hereafter should be applied to specific cases after considering the location and other factors, in such a way that no loss of life occurs for the performer; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cessation of the primary rite.
And so he will say:
"Subsisting on air, standing during the day, having passed the night in water while gazing at the sun..."
Thus it is said.

In that regard, if dwelling in water near the Himavat mountains, or during seasons such as the winter when one is overwhelmed by extreme cold, is prescribed, then since death might occur, the practice of dwelling in water should be arranged by avoiding such places and times.

Likewise, even due to differences in age, if a twelve-year penance is prescribed for someone who is ninety years old or younger than twelve, then since their life might perish, that penance should be assigned to those of a different age.
For this very reason, in another Smṛti, a reduction in penance is prescribed for the elderly and others, being half in some cases and a quarter in others;
this has already been explained in detail.

Likewise, [the penance] depends on one's capacity for giving wealth, performing austerities, and so forth; for it is not possible for a person without wealth to give sufficient wealth to a worthy recipient, and so on.
Likewise, one who has an excess of bile (pitta) and so forth should not perform *parāka* and other such penances; nor should women, Śūdras, and others perform *japa* and the like.
For this very reason, one who is unable to give gifts to elephants and other beings should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for the purification of each individual [offense].
Thus it has been stated. Likewise, in another Smṛti, a reduction of the penance is prescribed for one incapable of austerity, stating: "Women and the sick deserve only half of the expiation."

Likewise, having carefully examined the nature of the sin—whether it be a mortal transgression (*mahāpātaka*) or the like, and whether it was committed intentionally (*sapratyaya*), unintentionally (*apratyaya*), once, or habitually—one should determine the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) through a thorough investigation of all the *Dharmaśāstras*.

In this regard, whatever is prescribed for an unintentional act should be doubled for an intentional one, and quadrupled for intentional repetition; thus it should be determined in accordance with other *Smṛtis*.
Similarly: "He who falsely accuses another of a mortal transgression or a minor offense..."

It is stated: "One should subsist on water for a month. Since it is improper for the same penance to apply equally to both a major sin (*mahāpātaka*) and a minor offense (*upapātaka*), a reduction of the one-month vow must be prescribed for the minor offense in comparison to the major sin. Furthermore, regarding cases where one might act impulsively through laughing, yawning, crying out, or clapping, as well as [the rule]: "One should not bathe in the waters of the ocean, nor should one have one's beard and so forth shaved."
A husband who has intercourse with a pregnant woman will certainly remain childless.

In such cases, no expiation has been prescribed; even there, an expiation must be determined with regard to the location and other factors. Now, is there not some collection of causes for which no atonement is mentioned? [The answer is: "A hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed for the removal of all sins, indeed for all classes of minor offenses (upapātakas) and for those for which no specific rule has been taught."
Thus, since an expiation will be prescribed even for those cases where no specific atonement has been mentioned,
Gautama has also established that in the absence of a specific instruction, these very one-day penances (*ekāha*) and others should be performed as alternatives.
It is said in reply:

It is true that there is indeed a general instruction regarding expiation; nevertheless, because factors such as place and time must be taken into account in every case, there is certainly room for adaptation.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to prescribe one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) in all instances of laughing and so forth, because the cause [the offense] is minor.
Therefore, a reduction should be determined in proportion to the sin, or another form of expiation should be prescribed.
Now, one might ask: how can there be lightness of sin such that a reduction in the penance could be prescribed?
Nor should it be said that this is due to the smallness of the penance itself, for [the sin] is precisely of a kind for which no expiation has been stated.
True.

However, the relative gravity or lightness of a fault is easily understood through the mention of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and by considering factors such as whether the act was intentional or unintentional, along with its consequences;
likewise, the relative gravity or lightness of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is determined by the corresponding decrease or increase in the punishment.

Just as penances such as the *prājāpatya* have been prescribed for acts like threatening a Brāhmaṇa when the victim belongs to the same caste, so too, when such acts as threatening are committed in the direct order (*anuloma*) or the inverse order (*pratiloma*), or when they are committed against those such as the *mūrdhāvasikta*, the gravity or lightness of the penance must be determined by inferring the smallness or greatness of the fault from the very observation of the graduated scale of punishment. And this graduated scale of punishment has been shown [by the text] in such passages as: "In cases of verbal abuse involving the inverse order, the fine shall be double or triple," and so forth.

Thus has the expiation for one who has fallen due to mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like been declared. Now, as to what should be done with one who, out of arrogance, does not wish to perform this, he says:
"His own kinsmen should carry a jar of water outside the village;
they should exclude the fallen man from all social functions."

While the outcaste is still alive, his own kinsmen and relatives on the father’s and mother’s side shall all assemble and, together with female slaves and servants sent by those sapinda-relations and others, carry outside the village a jar or pot filled with water brought by them. This rite of offering water for the outcaste must be performed on an inauspicious lunar day such as the fourth, during the fifth part of the day, in the presence of elders and other authorities; for it is said: "The sapinda relatives and kinsmen should perform the water-rite for the outcaste outside [the village], on a censured day, in the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and elders."
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Manu.
Alternatively, a female slave herself, directed by the sapinda relatives and others, may pour out the water;
as Manu has said:
A female slave should overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a deceased person;
the impurity shall last for a day and a night, shared by the kinsmen.
Thus [it is said]:
"A female slave should overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a deceased person;
they, together with their kinsmen, shall observe impurity for a day and a night."
The phrase "like a *preta*" is intended to establish that [the performer] should face south and have the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

Furthermore, that pouring of water (*ninayana*) should be understood as occurring after the *preta*-rites, such as the offering of water-clods (*udakapiṇḍa*) and so forth; for it is said: "His teachers in knowledge and those related by birth, having assembled, shall perform all the *preta*-rites beginning with the water-offering.
And they shall overturn his vessel."

A slave or a servant, having brought a vessel from the refuse heap and filled it from the pot of a female slave, should overturn it with his foot while facing south, uttering the name [of the deceased] and saying, "I deprive so-and-so of water.
All [the relatives], wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and with their topknots loosened, should touch that [vessel].
The teachers of the Veda and those related by birth should look upon it.
For there is a traditional teaching (smṛti) of Gautama stating: "Having touched water, they should enter the village.

Furthermore, this abandonment is to be understood as occurring if, even when urged by his kinsmen, he does not perform penance; for Śaṅkha’s traditional teaching states: "In the presence of his elders, kinsmen, and the king, having proclaimed and repeatedly declared his faults, [the king] should say, 'Obtain proper conduct once again. If, even after this, his mind remains unsettled, then one should overturn his vessel."
Then, once he has received water and fallen [from his status], they should exclude him from all activities, such as conversation, sitting together, and so forth; they should avoid him.
And thus says Manu: "They should desist from conversing with him and from sitting together."
The inheritance, the giving away [of a daughter], and even the worldly journey of one whose [time] has come.
Thus it is said: "Therefore, one should desist from conversation and sitting together with him,
as well as from the giving of an inheritance and even ordinary social intercourse."
If he converses with him out of affection or similar motives, then an expiation must be performed.
Beyond that, having conversed with him, he should remain for one night reciting the Sāvitrī if it was done unintentionally; if it was done intentionally, however, for three nights. (3.294)
But when he has become disenchanted through the abandonment of his kinsmen or otherwise, and has performed the penance, then what should be done? To this he says:
"When he has completed his vow and returned, they should pour out a new jar [of water] for him;
they should not despise him, nor should they live with him in every respect."

When the one who has performed the penance has returned to the presence of his kinsmen, his *sapiṇḍas* and others, together with him, should pour out a new, undamaged jar filled with water. This pouring out is to be understood as occurring after bathing in a sacred pool or similar place; for it is said: "But when the penance has been performed, they should, having bathed in a holy reservoir, cast a new jar full of water along with him."

Thus it is from the Smṛti of Manu. However, Gautama has stated a specific rule: "But he who is purified by penance—once he is purified, they should fill a vessel made of gold with water from a most sacred pool or from flowing rivers, and then cause him to touch those waters.
Then they should give that vessel to him."

Having accepted that [gift], he should mutter: "Peaceful is heaven, peaceful is earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; that which is luminous, that I accept here. With these Yajus formulas, with the Pāvamānī verses, the Taratsamandī verses, and the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, he should offer clarified butter into the fire, give gold, and a cow to the teacher.
He for whom the penance ends in death becomes pure upon dying; this same water of pacification (śāntyudaka) applies to all minor offenses (upapātaka).
Then, once he has performed the penance, they should not despise him;
likewise, in all affairs such as buying and selling, they should carry on transactions with him. (3.295)
He states the extension of the previously mentioned rule regarding the abandonment of outcasts and so forth:
"This very same rule for men who have become outcasts is proclaimed for women as well;
they should be given a dwelling at the edge of the house, food, clothing, and protection."

The same rule regarding the rite for offering the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*) upon the exclusion of men, as well as the rule for their readmission after they have performed penance, should be understood to apply to women who have become outcasts (*patita*) as well.
However, there is this distinction:
even for those women who have become outcasts, once the rites such as the offering of water have been performed, a small hut made of grass and leaves should be provided near the main house.
Likewise, food sufficient merely to sustain life and even soiled clothing should be given, provided that it is accompanied by measures to prevent its use by another person. (3.296)
Now, one might ask: "Who are those who have fallen for whom this rule of abandonment is prescribed? To this, he says:
"Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming her husband—these also are certainly specific causes of loss of caste for women."

"Approaching a man of inferior caste, causing an abortion, and the killing of a husband—even if he is not a Brāhmaṇa—or the killing of a non-Brāhmaṇa husband: these are the causes of loss of caste (*patana*) that are specific to women.

By the use of the word 'even' (*api*), those causes of loss of caste for a man—namely, the *mahāpātakas*, *atipātakas*, *anupātakas*, and the repeated practice of *upapātakas* and so forth—also certainly and definitively become causes of loss of caste for women.

For this very reason, Śaunaka says: 'Those very things which are causes of loss of caste for a man are also [causes] for women; however, a Brāhmaṇa woman falls even further by serving a man of inferior caste.'"
As for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins for a woman in this world:
the murder of her husband, the killing of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of her own fetus."

Thus, the mention of "killing an embryo" (*bhrūṇahatyā*) was made for the sake of illustration, and not to exclude other major sins (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth from being causes of loss of caste (*patana*). Furthermore, as stated by that same [author]: "But four [wives] are to be abandoned: she who goes to a pupil, she who goes to a teacher, she who especially kills her husband, and she who has approached a degraded man (*juṅgita*)."

Thus, it has been stated that there is a renunciation of only four [types of women]. The intention is that even among those for whom no penance is prescribed, one should effect the renunciation of only four—namely, the female disciple (*śiṣyā*) and the others—by severing their means of livelihood, such as clothing, food, and residence in the house, and not that of others.
Consequently, it is understood that for other fallen women for whom penance is not performed, one must still perform duties such as providing them with lodging near one's own house. (3.297)
"They should not despise him, nor should they cohabit with him in any way"— this is the exception he states:
"One should not dwell even for a moment with those who harm one who has sought refuge, children, or women, nor with those who are ungrateful, even if they have completed their vows."

This prohibition is based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*): one should not engage in social intercourse with those who have committed the murder of those who have sought refuge and so forth, nor with the ungrateful, even if their faults have been diminished by penance. Why should one not follow the scriptural word? For there is no such thing as an excessive burden for a scriptural injunction; and therefore, although the penance for killing unchaste women is indeed very slight, nevertheless, this prohibition against social intercourse remains a matter of scriptural mandate. (3.298)

Having thus explained the specific rule regarding women by way of digression, he now states the specific rule for the actual procedure of completing the vow: "When the water-pot has been discarded, he who stands in the midst of his kinsmen should first give fodder to the cows; for this is the act of honoring one who has already been honored by the cows."
When the jar has been removed from the pond and another full jar has been brought down, he who has completed his vow, standing amidst the sapindas and others, should give fodder to the cows.
After he has first been honored—that is, worshipped—by them, the honoring by the kinsmen should then take place;
and the honor shown to him by the cows consists precisely in their eating the fodder given by him.
If the cows do not accept the fodder given by him, then he should perform the penance again.
As Hārīta says: "Taking the fodder with his own head, he should give it to the cows; if they accept it, then he may proceed [with the rite], otherwise not"—this is the intended meaning. (3.299)
Having described the collection of specific penances for each of the five classes of faults beginning with the *mahāpātaka*s, he now states the dharma common to all penances:
"One whose fault is well-known should perform a penance approved by an assembly (*parṣad*).
This means that one whose fault—whatever it may be and however great it may be—is known and recognized by others, should perform the penance prescribed by the assembly.

Even if one is personally adept at investigating the meaning of all the scriptures, nevertheless, having approached an assembly and deliberated with it, one should act only with their approval. Regarding such an approach, Aṅgiras has stated a specific rule:
"When a sin has been committed that is beyond doubt, one should not eat without being present [before the assembly]."
One who eats increases their sin as long as they do not confess it before an assembly.
Having bathed with his clothes on, restrained in speech, wearing wet garments, and composed in mind, a man, with the approval of the assembly, should confess all the truth; then,
having undertaken the vow once more, he should perform the rite after bathing again in that same manner.
Thus [it is said].
When a sin has been committed and is beyond doubt, one should not eat while remaining present;
for by eating, one increases the sin as long as it is not confessed before the assembly.
Having bathed with his clothes on while maintaining silence, wearing wet garments and being composed in mind,
a man, with the approval of the assembly, should proclaim the entire truth;
then, having again taken up the vow, he should perform the penance after bathing in that same manner.
And the public proclamation [of the penance] should be performed immediately after the presentation of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the assembly.
As Parāśara says:
"The sinner, having given a cow and likewise a bull, should proclaim his sin."
Thus:
"A sinner, having given a cow and likewise a bull, shall proclaim his sin.
And this refers to the category of minor offenses (upapātaka).

In the case of the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and others, a more severe penance should be prescribed. As for that which was stated: "Therefore, a twice-born man who has incurred sin, having bathed once in water and having confessed his sin to the assemblies (*parṣad*), shall perform a vow after giving something."
Thus, that refers to the subject of miscellaneous cases (*prakīrṇaka*).
And the nature of the assembly (*parṣad*) has been shown by Manu:
"One who is learned in the three Vedas, a dialectician, a logician, an etymologist, and a reciter of the Dharma..."
And the three preceding stages of life—this assembly consists of at least ten members.
A *haituka* is one who knows the reality of the meaning of the *Mīmāṃsā* and so forth;
a *tarkī* is one skilled in the science of logic (*nyāya*).
Likewise, he has shown two other types of assemblies as well.
One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this should be understood as the secondary assembly for the determination of doubts regarding dharma.
Thus:
"One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this is to be known as the secondary assembly for the resolution of doubts regarding dharma."
Likewise, even if he is alone, whatever dharma a knower of the Vedas may determine with a concentrated mind—
that should be known as the supreme dharma, not that which is proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant.
Thus:

"Even if it be but one person learned in the Veda who, being composed, determines a duty— that is to be known as the supreme dharma, not that which is proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant."
The establishment of these assemblies is based on the nature of the case, or on the gravity of the offense, such as a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth.
As for that which is stated in another *Smṛti*: "For mortal sins, the assembly shall consist of one hundred; for great sins and the like, one thousand;
for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), fifty; and for very slight offenses, it should be accordingly small."

Thus, that [statement] as well is intended to demonstrate the gravity or lightness of the assembly (*parṣad*) according to the severity of the faults, such as the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), and not for the purpose of fixing a specific number, because that would result in a contradiction with the great *smṛtis* of Manu and others.
Likewise, Devala has shown a distinction in this regard:
"The Brahmins themselves shall pronounce the expiation in cases of minor faults."
Both kings and brahmins have tested him in great matters.
Thus it is said:
"In cases of minor offenses, the Brahmins themselves shall declare the expiation;
but in cases of major offenses, both the king and the Brahmins shall determine the expiation after due investigation."

And that assembly must certainly prescribe vows and penances for those twice-born who, though knowing them, do not grant them to the distressed who are seeking them; they become equal to those [sinners].
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Aṅgiras:

"The assembly must instruct the penance only after having ascertained [the facts]. He who bestows a penance without knowing the Dharmaśāstras becomes purified by the penance himself, while the guilt falls upon the assembly."
Thus it is from the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*.
However, regarding the specific rule for instructing those of the Kṣatriya and other castes who have committed sins, Aṅgiras has shown:
"A Brāhmaṇa may, according to justice, quickly [instruct] a Kṣatriya or others who have committed sins."
Having placed the Brāhmaṇa in between, one should prescribe the entire vow.
Having approached a Śūdra, she should always provide expiation preceded by the Dharma, but excluding recitation and burnt offerings (japa and homa).
Thus,
according to the rule, for a Kṣatriya or others who have committed an offense, a Brāhmaṇa should quickly prescribe the entire penance by interposing himself between the offender and the penance.
Having approached a Śūdra, she should always provide expiation preceded by the Dharma, but devoid of recitation and burnt offerings.
And in that regard, for those whose habit is the performance of sacrifices and the like, recitation (*japa*) and so forth should be prescribed; for others, however, austerity (*tapas*).
Those devoted to ritual action and those devoted to austerity may at times fall into sin;
to them, recitation, fire-oblations, and the like are specifically granted.
To those Brahmins who merely bear the name, who are ignorant and destitute of wealth,
one should especially give the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances.
Having explained the series of vows that destroy well-known sins,
the sage spoke further, describing those which remove the multitude of transgressions committed in secret.
In this regard, he first states the dharma common to all secret vows:
"But one whose fault is not publicly known should perform a secret vow."
One whose offense is unrecognizable by others other than the perpetrator himself should perform a secret, non-public penance (*prāyaścitta*).
Therefore, since she too is an agent in cases such as sexual intercourse with a woman, it should be understood that for one whose fault is unknown to others, there is a secret vow.
In this regard, if the perpetrator is himself skilled in the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), he should then perform the appropriate penance for his own cause without making it known to another.

However, one who is himself ignorant [of the secret penance] may learn—under some pretext from another—what the secret expiation is for a deed such as the killing of a Brahmin committed in secret, and then perform that secret vow (*raho-vrata*).
For this very reason, women and Śūdras also attain the qualification [for secret rites], since the knowledge of the secret vows is established through this same method.

Nor should it be argued that because secret vows consist primarily of recitations (*japa*) and the like, and because women and Śūdras lack Vedic knowledge, they are ineligible; for [the requirement of Vedic knowledge] does not apply here.

Since the primacy of recitation (*japa*) and other such practices for those observing secret vows (*rahasya-vrata*) is not absolute— given that giving (*dāna*) and other acts are also taught, and because practices such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) mentioned by Gautama are also possible—

the mere knowledge of the mantra, deity, seer (*ṛṣi*), and meter (*chandas*) is what is useful for eligibility (*adhikāra*) even for others, and not knowledge concerning other subjects. For indeed, an understanding pertaining to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices is of no use in the construction of a reservoir (*taḍāga*) and similar works.

However, a thorough knowledge of the deity and so forth must certainly be relied upon; for it is said: "He who teaches or even recites [the Veda] without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity, and the application, becomes a sinner."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching of Vyāsa.

Here too, since no specific food is mentioned, milk and the like [are to be understood]; since no specific time is mentioned, years and the like; and since no specific place is mentioned, mountains and the like—these should be sought out as prescribed by Gautama and others, just as in the case of public penances (prakāśaprāyaścitta). 3.300.

Having thus stated the common rules applicable to all secret penances, he now describes the secret expiations for killing a Brahmin and other such crimes, following the same order as the public expiations:
"A slayer of a Brahmin, having fasted for three nights and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while submerged in water,
shall be purified after giving a milch cow."

Having fasted for three nights and, while submerged in water, having recited the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* hymn seen by the great seer—the triplet beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*), composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, dedicated to the deity Bhāvavṛtta—and having given a milch cow at the end of the three nights, a killer of a Brahmin is purified.
This recitation must be performed three times while submerged in water.
As Sumantu has said: "A slayer of gods, twice-born men, or a guru, being submerged in water, should repeat the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* hymn three times."

"Having approached one's mother, sister, maternal aunt, daughter-in-law, female friend, or having committed any other forbidden sexual act, one becomes purified from that by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water. This [rule] applies to cases where the act was committed unintentionally. As for that which was stated by Manu: "Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava..."
Even those who have committed the murder of an embryo are purified within a month by these [rites] performed day after day.
Thus, that [penance] also should be understood to apply to this same subject for one who is unable to give the gift of a cow.

As for what Gautama stated after describing the thirty-six-night vow—namely, "In the case of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, or violating the Guru’s bed, one should, while observing that very vow, bathe with breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn"—that refers to the case of a single act of killing committed unintentionally.
As for what Baudhāyana has stated:

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, bathed, pure, and wearing clean garments, he should smear a sacrificial mound at the water’s edge; then, wearing a garment moistened once, with his hand purified by cow-dung, facing the sun, he should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* as a private Vedic study.
He should recite it one hundred times in the morning, one hundred times at midday, and one hundred times in the afternoon; and when the stars have risen, he should eat a handful of barley-gruel.

"One is released from minor offenses (*upapātaka*) committed intentionally or unintentionally after seven nights; from major sins (*mahāpātaka*), excluding the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and the theft of gold, after twelve nights; and even those [three] are overcome after twenty-one nights. This refers to cases of intentional action, or to the case of unintentionally killing a learned *śrotriya*, a teacher, or one engaged in a sacrifice.

As for that which was stated by Manu: "Or, having purified himself with three *parāka* penances, one who is self-restrained recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest; he is released from all sins."
Thus, that [penance] refers to the intentional killing of a *śrotriya* or similar person; otherwise, it refers to intentional repeated practice.

As for what was stated by Bṛhad-Viṣṇu—"Having committed the murder of a Brahmin, one should go out from the village toward the east or north, kindle a fire with abundant fuel, and offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter with the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn; thereafter, one becomes purified from this"—that refers to the killing of one who lacks [distinguished] qualities, or to the case of an accessory. As for what was stated by Yama—"One should fast for three days, being disciplined, and entering the water three times a day..."
By reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa three times, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, that [penance] refers to a virtuous slayer who kills one devoid of virtue, or to the instigator or the consenter.

As for what was stated by Hārīta—"When any one of the great sins (mahāpātaka), extreme sins (atipātaka), secondary sins (anupātaka), or minor sins (upapātaka) occurs, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times"—that refers to the agent who acts under such a specific cause.
In this manner, other Smṛti passages as well should be sought out and distributed according to their respective subjects; they are not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous.

This very same collection of penances is to be performed—reduced by one-fourth—in the case of killing a woman engaged in a sacrifice, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, as well as an Ātreyī, the wife of one who has established the sacred fires, or a pregnant woman, provided the pregnancy was unknown at the time of the offense. (3.301)
He states another expiation:
"Or else, subsisting on air for a day,
one should stand in water and offer forty oblations of clarified butter with the mantra 'To the body hairs, svāhā!'"

Alternatively, having fasted for a day and night and having stayed in the water during the night, one should emerge from the water in the morning and offer forty oblations of clarified butter—five oblations with each of the eight mantras beginning with *lomabhyaḥ svāhā*—thus making forty oblations in total. This [rite] has the same scope as the previously mentioned one, because staying in the water involves a great deal of hardship. (3.302)
He states the penance for drinking liquor, which follows in sequence:
"Having fasted for three nights and offered ghee with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses, one becomes pure.
For a drinker of *surā*, "forty oblations of ghee" is understood to follow.
