Having fasted for three nights and offered forty oblations of clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses—beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods" (*yad devā devaheḷanam*) and so forth—which were seen by Kūṣmāṇḍa, composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and addressed to deities indicated by the mantras' internal signs (*mantraliṅga*), one becomes pure.

Thus it has also been stated by Baudhāyana: "Now, one who considers himself impure should offer oblations with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses; he is released from whatever sin he has committed up to and including the murder of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*). This applies also to having discharged semen in a non-vaginal place, except in a dream."

As for that which was stated by Manu: "By muttering the *kautsa* hymn beginning with *apaḥ*, the *vasiṣṭha* verse beginning with *pratīty ṛcam*, the *māhitra* hymn, and the *śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of *surā* becomes purified."

Thus, it is prescribed that one should mutter daily for a month sixteen times any one of these [hymns]: *apano śośucad agham*, *prati stomair uṣasam vāsiṣṭham*, *mahitrīṇām avo astu*, or *tad indraṃ stavāma*. This should be understood as applicable for one who is unable to perform the three-night fast (*trirātropavāsa*) and the *kūṣmāṇḍa* oblations. Furthermore, this applies to the unintentional single consumption of *paiṣṭī* liquor, and to the repeated consumption of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* liquors.

And as for that which was stated by Manu: "A twice-born man, having offered clarified butter for a year with the Śākala-homa mantras, destroys even a heavy sin by reciting the verse beginning with 'namaḥ'."

Thus, for one year, the performance of an oblation with the eight mantras beginning with "devakṛtasyainasaḥ" each day, or the recitation of the verse "nama id ugram nama āvivāse," has been prescribed; that refers to cases of intentional action (*kāmakāra*).
As for the statement: "One who is joined with a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the *pāvamānī* verses for a year, subsisting on alms, he is purified."
Thus, this refers either to the case of repeated practice or to the case of the commission of all the great sins (mahāpātaka) together.
He states the expiation for stealing gold:
"But one who has stolen the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, standing in water, shall recite the Rudra-mantras."

Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa who has stolen gold, having fasted for three nights and remaining in the midst of water while reciting the *Śatarudriya* with the mantra "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, [and] to Manyu," becomes purified. A specific rule regarding this has been stated by Śātātapa:
"Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of a guru, having committed theft, and having committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa..."
Covered in ashes, lying on a bed of ashes, and reciting the Rudrādhyāya, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, having drunk liquor, gone to the wife of a guru, committed theft, and even perpetrated the murder of a Brahmin—
one who recites the Rudrādhyāya, covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes, is liberated from all sins.
The recitation should be performed eleven times, or the knower of dharma should repeat the Rudra hymns eleven times;
even one touched by great sins is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Thus it is stated in the *Atri-smṛti*.
As for that which was said by Manu: "Having recited even once the *Asyavāmīya* and the *Śivasankalpa*, one becomes stainless in an instant, even after having stolen gold."

Thus, the single recitation of this hymn consisting of fifty-two verses beginning with "Of this lovely, unaging Hotṛ," or likewise of the six-verse hymn seen by Śivasankalpa beginning with "That divine [light] which rises far from the waking state," has been prescribed; however, that should be understood to apply to a virtuous thief who steals gold belonging to a master who is absolutely devoid of qualities.
It concerns cases where the quantity of gold is less than a Suvarṇa, or where the offender is an abettor or an instigator.
But in the case of repetition, one should refer to what is stated in such passages as: "One joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) should follow [the cow]," and so forth. (3.303)
He states the penance for one who violates the Guru’s bed, which follows in sequence:
"One who violates the Guru’s bed is liberated by reciting the *Sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn];
at the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow must be given separately for each of these [offenses]."

But one who has violated the teacher's bed is freed from that sin by muttering the sixteen-verse hymn beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā," which was seen by Nārāyaṇa, has Puruṣa as its deity, is in the Anuṣṭubh meter, and ends in Triṣṭubh.
From the suffix denoting habit in the expression "one who is habitually a mutterer of the *sahasraśīrṣā*," repetition is understood. For this very reason, it was stated by Yama:
"By reciting the Puruṣa-sūkta, one is liberated from all sin.
Thus it is said:
"By reciting the Puruṣa-sūkta, one is liberated from all sin."
And since a number is required for the repetition, the number forty found in the preceding verse is inferred here as well;
in this case too, the phrase "having fasted for three nights" from the previous verse is connected.
For this very reason, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu states: "A man who has violated the Guru’s bed is purified by fasting for three nights along with the recitation and fire-offerings of the Puruṣasūkta."
And for these three—the drinker of spirits, the thief of gold, and the violator of the guru’s bed—separately at the conclusion of this three-night vow, a cow yielding much milk should be given.
This refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally.
As for that which was stated by Manu: "Having practiced the *Haviṣyāntīya* and the *na tamaṃ ha* [hymns]..."
Having recited the Puruṣasūkta, however, one who has violated the preceptor’s bed is liberated from that sin.
Thus:

"The protector of the oblation, ageless, finder of heaven; neither distress nor misfortune [reaches him]"—or "thus is my mind"—or "the thousand-headed," etc.; it is prescribed that one of these should be recited sixteen times every day for a month, and that too applies only to cases where there is no intentional desire.
However, in the case of intentional action, one should look to what was stated by Manu: "with the mantras belonging to the Śākala-homas."

As for that which is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "A twice-born man should perform an oblation with sesame seeds accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis, numbering one thousand, for the sake of purification from minor offenses (*upapātaka*)."
One who is joined with a great sin (mahāpātaka) is purified by a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma).
Thus [it is said]; that refers to the subject of repetition.
As for what was stated by Yama: "Or one may recite the *Asyavāmīya*, or the *Pāvamānī* hymns, or the *Kuntāpa*, the *Vālakhilyas*, the *Nivits*, the *Praishas*, and the *Vṛṣākapi*."
Having recited the Hotṛ Rudras once, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of approaching a woman who is an adulteress.

However, regarding those cases which are subject to the extension of the rule for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*), or which are equal to it, and which are designated by the terms *atipātaka* (near-sin) or *upapātaka* (minor sin), it should be understood that the penance is respectively reduced by one-fourth or by half.

Or, when any one of the *pātaka* (sin), *atipātaka*, *upapātaka*, or *mahāpātaka* (great sin) occurs—whether individually or in combination—one should observe what was stated by Hārīta: "One should simply mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times."

And because of the scriptural statement, "One who associates with a perpetrator of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall perform the very same vow as that person," the penance is that of the one with whom the association occurred.
Nor should it be argued that secrecy is untenable here because association through teaching and so forth is accomplished by multiple agents;
for even though there are multiple agents, secrecy exists simply by the fact that no third party other than the agents is aware of it, just as in the case of adultery with another's wife.
Therefore, secret penance indeed exists.

In this same way, it should be understood that even for one who associates with those guilty of mortal sins (*atipātaka*) and so forth, the penance belonging to that very person [with whom he associated] is to be prescribed. (3.304)
Now, in due order, he states the expiation for the fifty-six minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as the killing of a cow:
"One hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should be performed for the removal of all sins,
indeed for those belonging to the class of minor offenses and for those for which no specific penance has been prescribed."

For the removal of all minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as the killing of a cow—numbering fifty-six—as well as those for which no specific secret penance has been prescribed, and those causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) and so forth, one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should be performed.
Likewise, for the removal of all major sins (*mahāpātaka*) and others, ranging from heinous crimes (*atipātaka*) down to miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*), breath-restraints must be performed;
in this regard, an increase in the number of repetitions should be calculated as follows: four hundred for major sins, three hundred for heinous crimes, and two hundred for minor offenses.

Since it is observed that in the penances for manifest sins (*prakāśa*), a fourth part of the penance for mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) is prescribed for minor sins (*upapātaka*), a reduction must be inferred for miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇaka*).
For this very reason, Yama has stated:
"By four hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) joined with ten *praṇavas*..."
One is liberated from the murder of a Brahmin; how much more so from other remaining sins!
Thus:
"By four hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) joined with ten *praṇavas*, one is released from the murder of a Brahmin; how much more so from other sins?"
Baudhāyana has also stated a specific rule here: "Furthermore, in cases of transgression involving speech, sight, hearing, touch, smell, or the mind, one is purified by three *prāṇāyāmas*.
In cases of sexual intercourse with a *śūdra* woman or eating the food of a *śūdra*, one should perform seven *prāṇāyāmas* for each instance over a period of seven days.

In cases of consuming forbidden food, inedible substances, or impure matter; likewise in the sale of merchandise that is unfit for sale—excluding honey, meat, ghee, oil, lac, salt, liquids, and cooked food—and in whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve *prāṇāyāmas* for each instance over the course of half a month."

Except for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and those leading to loss of caste (*patanīya*), whatever else may be similarly constituted, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) each month for twelve months.
Except for other mortal sins (*pātaka*), whatever else is similarly constituted, one should perform twelve breath-restraints each half-month for twelve half-months.
Now, regarding mortal sins, one should perform twelve breath-restraints each month for one year.
In this context, the triad of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) beginning with "speech," "eye," and so forth, is intended for miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*).

The forty-nine breath-restraints mentioned in the passage beginning with "intercourse with a *śūdra* woman" and "eating forbidden food" are intended for specific minor offenses (*upapātaka*). Likewise, the one hundred and forty-four breath-restraints mentioned in the passage beginning with "eating what should not be eaten" are also intended specifically for minor offenses.

Now, the one hundred and eighty breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) mentioned in the passage beginning with "excluding the *pātaka* and *upapātaka* sins" are intended for those acts that cause loss of caste (*jāti-bhraṃśakara*) and the like.

Next, the three hundred and sixty breath-restraints mentioned in the passage beginning with "excluding the *pātaka* and *patanīya* sins" are intended for minor offenses such as the killing of a cow (*govadha*).

Finally, the two thousand two hundred and sixty breath-restraints mentioned in the passage beginning with "excluding the *pātaka* sins" are intended for the major transgressions (*atipātaka*) and the secondary offenses (*anupātaka*).

Now, the four thousand breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) consisting of three hundred and twenty [repetitions], as stated in the passage beginning with "In the case of mortal sins" (*atha pātakeṣu*), pertain to the category of great sins (*mahāpātaka*).

Furthermore, this pentad of expiations mentioned in the passage beginning with "In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten" (*abhakṣyabhojya*) pertains to cases of extreme repetition or to cases where [the offenses] are combined.
As for that which was stated by Manu: "Desiring to remove even gross and subtle transgressions..."
One should recite the *avetya-ṛc* for a year, or [the verse] beginning with "whatever this is."

Thus, for up to a year, the muttering (*japa*) of the verse "avate heḍo varuṇa," or of "yat kiṃcedam," or of "itimemanaḥ," every day at times not inconsistent with other purposes, has been prescribed; that too is a matter of practice. (3.305)
He states an exception to the hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) generally prescribed for minor offenses (*upapātaka*):
"Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, the best of the twice-born should drink the purifying Soma-liquid consecrated with the syllable *Oṃ*."
A twice-born man, having consumed semen, feces, or urine, shall drink the juice of the *soma* plant consecrated with the syllable *oṃ* as a means of purification;
this applies to cases where the act was committed unintentionally.

However, Sumantu has stated that after intentionally consuming semen, feces, or urine; after eating garlic, onions, leeks, mushrooms, and other forbidden foods; and after eating the flesh of swans, village cocks, dogs, jackals, and so forth—one should descend into water reaching up to the neck, perform breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Śuddhavatī* verses, and drink water from the chest upward while reciting the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*; by this, one becomes purified from that.
Manu also has prescribed another penance for the consumption of the seven kinds of forbidden foods.
Having accepted what should not be accepted or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
Thus:
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
That which is unfit to be accepted includes poison, weapons, liquor, and so forth, as well as the property of outcasts and others.
Furthermore, when one discharges bodily impurities such as semen, feces, or urine into water, it has been stated by that same [author]:
"But having performed an improper act, one should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water."
Thus [ends verse] 3.306.
But having committed an unpraiseworthy act, one should subsist on alms for a month while staying in water.
Regarding the penance for miscellaneous offenses (prakīrṇaka) and minor mental transgressions (upapātaka) committed unintentionally, he says:
"Whether by night or by day, whatever has been done unintentionally..."
By performing the twilight devotions at the three periods of the day, all that [evil] is utterly destroyed.

Whatever miscellaneous minor offense (*upapātaka*) committed through negligence—whether mental or verbal—during the night or the day, all of that is destroyed by the performance of the obligatory daily twilight worship (*nitya-saṃdhyopāsana*) prescribed for the three times of morning, midday, and so forth.
And thus says Yama: "Whatever sin one commits during the day by deed, mind, or speech..."
Seated during the evening twilight, he destroys that [sin] by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Thus it is said:
Whatever sin one commits during the day by deed, thought, or speech,
one destroys that by sitting for the evening twilight prayer and performing breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*).
Śātātapa has also said: "The twilight worship performed outside purifies one from falsehood, the smell of liquor, sexual intercourse during the day, and the food of a Śūdra."
Thus [ends verse] 3.307.
The twilight worship performed outside purifies one from falsehood, the smell of liquor,
sexual intercourse during the day, and the food of a *vṛṣala*.
Now he states the purifying mantras common to all major sins and the like:
"The recitation of the Śukriya and the Āraṇyaka, and especially that of the Gāyatrī—
these indeed remove all sins, as does the eleven-fold Rudra."

The *Śukriya*, a specific portion of the *Āraṇyaka* beginning with "O God Savitṛ, all... is recited in the *Vājasaneyaka*; furthermore, the *Yajur-āraṇyaka* passage beginning with "I take refuge in the Ṛc, the speech; I take refuge in the Yajus, the mind" is recited in that very same place. The chanting (*japa*) of these two removes all great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the like. Likewise, for the *Gāyatrī*, a specific chanting of one hundred thousand times removes great sins; ten thousand times removes secondary sins (*atipātaka*) and minor sins (*upapātaka*); one thousand times removes minor sins; and one hundred times removes miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇaka*). Thus, such specific chanting removes all sins.
And likewise, a verse concerning the Gāyatrī has been spoken by Śaṅkha:
"The Sāvitrī, when recited a hundred times, destroys great sins;
when recited a thousand times, it likewise liberates one from all sins."
Recited ten thousand times, she destroys all sins;
recited one hundred thousand times, that Goddess destroys even the most heinous crimes.

A Brahmin who has stolen gold, a killer of a Brahmin, one who has violated the teacher’s bed, and a drinker of liquor—all these are purified by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; of this there is no doubt.
Thus it is said:
"The Sāvitrī, when recited one hundred times, destroys even the great sins;
when recited one thousand times, it likewise liberates one from all transgressions."
Recited ten thousand times, she destroys all sins;
when recited one hundred thousand times, that goddess destroys even the greatest of crimes.

A Brahmin who has stolen gold, a killer of a Brahmin, one who has violated the teacher’s bed, and a drinker of liquor—these are purified by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; of this there is no doubt.
As for that which is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "By reciting the Gāyatrī ten million times, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
he who recites it eighty lakh times is liberated from the drinking of liquor."
Seventy lakhs of recitations of the Gāyatrī purify one who steals gold;
sixty lakhs of the Gāyatrī, however, liberate one who has violated the teacher’s bed.
Thus, because of its gravity, that refers to the subject of illumination (*prakāśa*).
Likewise, the *rudraikādaśinī* is the collection of the eleven *rudrānuvākas*;
when specifically recited, it removes all sins.
Or, by reciting the eleven Rudras eleven times, the knower of dharma is liberated from great sins; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, since an elevenfold repetition is observed for the great sins (mahāpātaka), a reduction by one-fourth for each successive quarter should be applied to the heinous sins (atipātaka) and so forth. The word "ca" (and) serves to include the Aghamarṣaṇa and other such rites.
As Vasiṣṭha has said:
Henceforth, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas, by whose recitations and burnt offerings people are purified; of this there is no doubt.
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍyas, the Pāvamānyas, and likewise the Durgā-sāvitrī.
The *abhīṣaṅgas*, the *padastomas*, the *sāmans*, as well as the *vyāhṛtis*;
the *bhāradaṇḍas*, the *sāmans*, the *gāyatra*, and likewise the *raivata*.
The Puruṣavrata, the Bhāsa, and likewise the Devavratas;
the Ārtvija, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and the Madhucchas.
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Trisuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta, the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans known as Indraśuddha;
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agner Vrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these songs purify living beings when one desires to attain the recollection of past lives.
Thus [ends the verse]. 3.308.
Henceforth, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas, by whose recitations and burnt offerings one is purified; of this there is no doubt.
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses, the Pāvamānī hymns, and likewise the Durgā-Sāvitrī;
The *abhīṣaṅgas*, the *padastomas*, the *sāmans*, as well as the *vyāhṛtis*;
the *bhāradaṇḍas*, the *sāmans*, the *gāyatra*, and likewise the *raivata*.
The Puruṣavrata, the Bhāsa, and likewise the Devavratas;
the Ārtvija, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and the Madhvṛcas.
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Trisuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta, the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans known as Indraśuddha;
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agner Vrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—these songs purify living beings; one obtains the memory of past births if one so desires.
Furthermore:
In whatever place a twice-born man considers himself defiled,
in that very place there should be an oblation of sesame seeds and likewise the recitation of the Gāyatrī.

In whatever case a twice-born man considers himself defiled and overwhelmed by the mass of impurity produced by such acts as the killing of a Brahmin, in each such instance an oblation of sesame seeds with the Gāyatrī mantra must be performed.

Among the great sins (mahāpātakas), the oblation should be performed one hundred thousand times; for it is recorded in the Smṛti of Yama: "By a hundred-thousand-fold oblation of the Gāyatrī, one is liberated from all sins."
In cases such as the *atipātaka* (most heinous sins) and others, a reduction of one-quarter [of the penance] for each degree should be calculated.
Likewise, the recitation and the giving of sesame seeds (*tila*) should be performed.
And so says Vasiṣṭha in the section on secret penances (*rahasyādhikāra*).
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should cause five or seven Brāhmaṇas to recite [the mantra],
using black sesame seeds mixed with honey, or otherwise with other [seeds].
"May Dharmarāja be pleased," or whatever else dwells in one's mind—
whatever sin has been committed throughout one's life perishes in that very instant.
Thus:
on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should cause five or seven Brāhmaṇas to recite [the mantra] while offering black sesame seeds mixed with honey, or otherwise [with other substances].
"May the King of Dharma be pleased"— whatever such thought dwells in one's mind,
even the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes in that very instant.
Likewise, he has stated that giving may also occur at an indefinite time:
"He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds."
Thus:
"He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds."
Likewise, it has been stated by Vyāsa as well:
"He who, with self-restraint, gives a sesame-cow to a twice-born man, is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt."
Thus:
"He who, with self-restraint, gives a sesame-cow to a twice-born man, is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this."

This collection of gifts and so forth, as declared in the Rahasyakāṇḍa, is to be understood as applicable to unlearned twice-born men, as well as to women and Śūdras. As for that which was stated by Yama: "He who gives sesame seeds in the morning, touches sesame seeds, eats them, bathes with sesame seeds, and offers oblations of sesame seeds—such a person overcomes all evil deeds."
Likewise: the two eighth days of the month, as well as the two fourteenth days, the new moon, the full moon, the seventh day, and the two twelfth days.
He who, having constantly subdued his senses, abstains from food for a year,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.
Thus it is said.
And as Atri has stated: "Hari reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk on the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
he abandons sleep on the full moon of Kārttika. One should worship Hari during those two [periods]."
It swiftly dispels sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.

All such passages as these are to be established as referring to the practice of those devoid of knowledge, whether performed with desire or without desire, and either repeatedly or not repeatedly. (3.309)
Moreover:

"Sinful acts, even those arising from the great transgressions (mahāpātaka), do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and who is intent upon the performance of the five sacrifices."
First, the acquisition of the Veda, then its investigation, its practice, its recitation,
and its impartation to disciples— thus, indeed, the study of the Veda is fivefold.

In the manner thus described, sins arising even from the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, endowed with forbearance, and intent on the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*).

What need is there to mention those arising from miscellaneous acts (*prakīrṇaka*), or the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) produced by speech and mind? This is the intended meaning indicated here by the word "even" (*api*). And this applies to cases where the act was committed unintentionally (*akāmakāra*).
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha said: "Even if more than a hundred forbidden acts have been committed, if the Veda is retained, the fire of that Veda burns them all away, just as fire consumes fuel."
Having spoken thus with reference to miscellaneous matters and the like, it was stated: "One should not take pleasure in evil deeds by relying on the power of the Veda;
for through ignorance and negligence, one is consumed by [the results of] action, and not otherwise."
Thus [ends verse] 3.310.
One should not take delight in evil deeds by relying on the power of the Vedas;
for it is through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by karma, and not otherwise.
Furthermore:
Subsisting on air, standing during the day and spending the night in water while gazing at the sun,
one is purified from all sins— even the killing of a Brahmin— by reciting the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times.

Fasting during the day while seated, and spending the night dwelling in water, one who recites the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times immediately after sunrise is liberated from the entire collection of sins, including the great mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) with the exception of killing a Brahmin.

Furthermore, this [penance] should be understood to apply to minor sins (*upapātaka*) in cases of repeated practice or the accumulation of multiple offenses, because it is improper to treat unequal subjects as equivalent.
For this very reason, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha has prescribed specific vows for major and minor sins according to the distinction of time.

As it is said: one should consecrate with the mantra "You are barley, the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey. You are the cleanser of all sins, remembered as a purifier by the seers" either the handful or the palmful of barley while it is being cooked or once it is cooked.
[The mantra continues: "Barley is ghee, barley is honey, barley is a purifier, barley is nectar."
Or else, with the words, "May they purify all my sins arising from speech, mind,
and body," one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) and likewise offer the oblation to the spirits (bhūtabali).
One should not abandon the first portion [of food], nor alms, nor hospitality, nor the remnants of food.

"May those gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, and whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they favor us; obeisance to them, svāhā to them!"—with this, one should offer oblations into oneself for three nights for the increase of intelligence and the destruction of sin, for twelve nights in cases such as the killing of a Brahmin, and likewise for one born of an outcaste. Following this general direction, other Smṛti passages should also be analyzed accordingly. 3.311.

Now, since the specific distinctions among the various forms of the multitude of prescribed vows are desired to be known— asking "of what nature are they?"— their definition shall be stated here in brief.
In that regard, he first states the dharmas which constitute the limbs of the vow of the secret of all the illuminations:
"Celibacy, compassion, patience, generosity, truthfulness, sincerity,
non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-restraint— these are known as the *yamas*."
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, restraint of the generative organ,
service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas).

Brahmacarya is the restraint of all the sense organs. The control of the genitals is specified as the control of the sexual organ according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull. Akalkatā is the absence of crookedness.
The rest is well known.

Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Manu: "One should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness," that too is merely an illustration of these [virtues] and not an exhaustive enumeration.

And here, although compassion, patience, and so forth are already established as ends of human life (*puruṣārtha*), they are enjoined again for the purpose of being auxiliary to expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

In some cases, there is also a specific distinction; for example, the injunction of truthfulness is intended to prevent false speech, even though such speech might be permitted in certain contexts like marriage ceremonies.
The injunction of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is for the purpose of ensuring that even one's sons, disciples, and others are not to be struck; such is the meaning of these verses (3.312–3.313).
In this regard, he first describes the vow known as Sāntapana:
"Having consumed cow's urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with Kuśa grass, one should fast on the following day while performing the Sāntapana Kṛcchra."

On the previous day, having abandoned other food and having mixed and drunk the five substances of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)—namely cow urine and so forth—along with *kuśa* water, one should fast on the following day; this is the two-night *sāntapana* *kṛcchra*.
Furthermore, that they are to be combined is understood from their being prescribed separately in the subsequent verse.
And the term *kṛcchra* is an etymological designation, because it is to be accomplished through hardship due to its nature as ascetic austerity (*tapas*).
The measurements of the cow’s urine and the other ingredients will now be stated.

Furthermore, when one fasts on the previous day and, on the following day, consumes the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) after mixing them together with the recitation of mantras—and indeed drinks it while still accompanied by those mantras—it is then designated as the *brahmakūrca*.
As Pārāśara has said:
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
these are specified as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), each serving to purify the body.
The urine of a copper-colored cow, the dung of a white cow,
the milk of a golden-colored cow, and likewise the curd of a blue cow.
And for ghee, that from a black cow or from a Kapila cow is prescribed;
in the absence of all these colors, this is the rule regarding the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Cow's urine is eight māṣakas; cow dung is sixteen;
milk is said to be twelve; and curd is proclaimed to be ten.
The quantity of ghee is desired to be like that of cow urine, while the water of *kuśa* grass is half of that.
Taking the cow urine with the *gāyatrī*, the cow dung with "gandhadvārā," the milk with "āpyāyasva," and the curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."

One should offer into the presence of the fire clarified butter with the mantra "Tejo 'si śukram," Kuśa-water with the mantra "Devasya tvā," and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) purified by the [appropriate] Ṛgvedic verse.
And with those seven-bladed *darbha* grasses that have uncut tips and pure luster,
one should offer the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) after drawing it out, according to the prescribed rule.
With the hymns "irāvatī," "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "mānastoke," and the "śaṃvatī" verses, the twice-born should offer oblations; he should then drink the remainder of what has been offered.
Having stirred it with the *praṇava*, having consecrated it with the *praṇava*,
and having drawn it up with the *praṇava*, one should drink it with the *praṇava*.
One should drink [the water] with a cup of medium size made of *palāśa* wood or a lotus leaf,
or again, with a vessel of gold or silver, using the *brāhma-tīrtha*.
Whatever sin resides within a human body, having reached even the skin and bones,
the fast of the Brahmakūrca consumes it like fire consumes fuel.
Thus it is said: Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
these are specified as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), each of which purifies the body.
The urine of a copper-colored cow, the dung of a white one,
the milk of a golden-colored one, and likewise the curd of a blue one.
The ghee from a black cow and all that from a Kapila cow [are preferred];
in the absence of cows of all these colors, this is the rule regarding the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Cow’s urine is eight māṣakas; cow dung is sixteen;
milk is said to be twelve; and curd is proclaimed to be ten.
The quantity of ghee is desired to be like that of cow urine, while the water of *kuśa* grass is half of that.
Taking the cow urine with the *gāyatrī*, the cow dung with "gandhadvārām," the milk with "āpyāyasva," and the curd with "dadhikrāvṇo."

With the mantra "Tejo 'si śukram," one should offer clarified butter; with "Devasya tvā," water from *kuśa* grass; and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), purified by the *ṛc*, one should offer as an oblation in the presence of the fire.
With seven-bladed *darbha* grasses that have uncut tips and pure luster,
one should offer the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) after drawing them up, according to the prescribed rule.

With the verses beginning with *irāvatī*, *idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*, *mā naḥ stoke*, and those that are auspicious (*śaṃvatī*), the twice-born should offer oblations; he should then drink the remainder of what has been offered.
Having stirred it with the *praṇava*, having consecrated it with the *praṇava*,
and having drawn it up with the *praṇava*, one should drink it with the *praṇava*.
One should drink [the water] with a cup made of the middle leaf of the *palāśa* tree, or with a lotus leaf,
or again with a vessel of gold or silver, using the *brāhma-tīrtha*.
Whatever sin resides within a human body, even reaching the skin and bones,
the fast of the *brahmakūrca* burns it away like fire consumes fuel.

When this very mixture of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is practiced for three nights, it receives the designation of *yatisāntapana*; for it is stated in the Smṛti of Śaṅkha: "This same [mixture], when practiced for three days, is known as *yatisāntapana*. However, Jābāla has described a *sāntapana* that is to be accomplished over seven days.
Having drunk each of these daily— cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass— and fasting for one day and night,
this is the penance named *Sāntapana*, which destroys all sins.
Thus: having drunk cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
one by one, every day, followed by a fast for a day and night.
The penance known as Sāntapana is the destroyer of all sins.
The determination of these heavy and light penances (kṛcchra) should be understood as depending on one's capacity and other such factors;
in this same way, the determination is to be understood in subsequent cases as well. 3.314.
He describes the penance known as the Mahāsāntapana:
"With separate Sāntapana substances for six days, followed by a day of fasting—
this seven-day penance is remembered as the Mahāsāntapana."
The penance known as the *mahāsāntapana* is to be understood as one completed in seven days.

To address the question of how this is done, it is stated that one should pass each of the first six days with one of the individual substances beginning with cow’s urine, and the seventh day with fasting.
However, by Yama, a *mahāsāntapana* to be accomplished in fifteen days has been described.
One should drink cow’s urine for three days, and indeed drink cow dung for three days;
then for three days curd, for three days milk, and for three days ghee—thereby one becomes pure.
For this Mahāsāntapana is indeed the destroyer of all sins.
Thus:
one should drink cow urine for three days, and indeed drink cow dung for three days;
[then] curd for three days, milk for three days, and ghee for three days; thereafter, one is purified.
He is pure in every respect.
For this Mahāsāntapana indeed destroys all sins.
Jābāla, however, has described a Mahāsāntapana penance to be completed in twenty-one nights:
"One should employ each of these six [substances] for three nights;
they know that the final three-night period of fasting constitutes the Mahāsāntapana."
Thus: one should employ each of these six for three nights.
They know that the Mahāsāntapana consists of fasting for the final three days.
But when each of the six substances of the *sāntapana* penance is consumed for two days, then it is the *atisāntapana*.
As Yama says:
"These very same [substances] should be drunk in that manner, one by one, for two days each."
The *atisāntapana* penance is said to purify even a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*).
Thus it is said:
"These very same [substances] should be drunk in that manner, each for two days at a time;
this is called the *atisāntapana*, which purifies even a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*)."
"He should purify even a dog-cooker"—this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). || 3.315 ||
He describes the vow known as Parṇakṛcchra:
"The Parṇakṛcchra is declared to consist of drinking, day by day, the juices of the leaves of the parṇa, udumbara, rājīva, and bilva trees, along with kuśa-water, each one separately."

One should drink water boiled with each leaf individually—of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aravinda*, and *śrīvṛkṣa* trees—every day; and on one day, water boiled with *kuśa* grass. This *parṇakṛcchra* is accomplished in five days.
However, when a decoction made from all these leaves combined is drunk at the end of three nights, it is called *parṇakūrca*.
As Yama has said:
"Having fasted for three nights and being pure, one should boil all these [leaves] together and drink them with water; this is called the *parṇakūrca*."
Thus:
"Having fasted for three nights and being pure, one should boil all these together and drink them with water; this is called the *parṇakūrca*."
However, when fruits such as the *bilva* and others are each boiled and drunk for one month, they then receive the designation of "fruit-kṛcchra" and so forth.
As Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The wise declare that when [fruits] are boiled for a month, it is the 'fruit-kṛcchra'."
The Śrī-kṛcchra is said to be performed with śrī-phalas, and another likewise with lotus seeds.
In this same manner, another [type of] Śrī-kṛcchra is prescribed using *māsa* and *āmalaka* fruits;
*patra*-kṛcchra is considered to be performed with leaves, and that kṛcchra is said to be performed with flowers.
The *mūlakṛcchra* is known to consist of roots, while the *toyakṛcchra* consists of water.
Thus [ends verse] 3.316.
The wise have declared that the *phalakṛcchra* consists of boiling fruits for one month;
the *śrīkṛcchra* is said to be performed with *śrīphala* fruits, and another is likewise performed with lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*).
In this same manner, another [type of] Śrīkṛcchra is prescribed using *māsa* and *āmalaka* fruits;
*Patrakṛcchra* is considered to be performed with leaves, and that [other] *Kṛcchra* is said to be performed with flowers.
The *mūlakṛcchra* is known to consist of roots, while the *toyakṛcchra* consists of water.
He describes the *taptakṛcchra*: "One should drink each of these—hot milk, ghee, and water—on successive days, followed by a fast for one night; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra*."
Having consumed each of these—milk, clarified butter, and water—when heated, one day after another, one should fast on the following day.
This is the *mahātaptakṛcchra*, which is accomplished in four days.
By consuming all three together with the fasting day, as in the *sāntapana* penance, the *taptakṛcchra* is accomplished in two nights.
But by Manu, a twelve-night rite is prescribed:
"A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily with a concentrated mind."
Thus:
"A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed."
The specific quantities of milk and so forth should be understood as stated by Parāśara:
"One should drink three *palas* of water, two *palas* of milk, and one *pala* of clarified butter;
this should be done for three nights while consuming only warm air."
Thus:
one should drink three *palas* of water, two *palas* of milk, and one *pala* of clarified butter;
this regimen for three nights [should be followed] while remaining in the warm air.
The meaning is that for the completion of the *trirātramāruta* [penance], one should drink the steam of hot water.
However, when cold milk and such are drunk, then it is the *śītakṛcchra*: "For three days one should drink cold water; for three days one should drink cold milk;
having drunk cold ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for the final three days."
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama (3.317).
He describes the *pādakṛcchra*:
"By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for, and by fasting— this is proclaimed as the *pādakṛcchra*."
"By eating once" means by eating only once during the day, since "at night" is mentioned separately.
Therefore, one should pass the entire day and night by eating only once during the day alone.
In this context, the word "day" serves to exclude the night.
The phrase "once" excludes [eating] two or more times;
"with food" excludes fasting.

Since these [penances] such as the *kṛcchra* are of the nature of a vow (*vrata*), this prescribes eating—which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *kṛcchra*—by way of excluding ordinary eating for the sake of personal ends.
And likewise Āpastamba says: "For three days he should not anoint himself and should eat only at night; then for three days [he follows the same];
for three days he observes the vow of not asking for anything, and for three days he eats nothing at all."
Thus:
for three days he should eat only what is un-anointed and not during the day;
then for three days he observes the vow of eating only what is unasked for; for three days he does not eat anything at all.

And here, by the suffix *ṇini* prescribed for a vow in the expression "one who does not eat at night" (*anaktāśī*), he demonstrates a restriction on eating during the day through the exclusion of eating at night.
This very point has been made explicit by Gautama: "Having eaten sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) at the morning meal, one should not eat for three nights.
The same applies to the injunction regarding eating only at night.

That food in which nothing is requested is called *ayācita* (unasked). Since no specific time is prescribed, this may be done once either by day or by night; for since these are of the nature of ascetic penance (*tapas*), a second meal would be inconsistent with them.

By the term *ayācita*, there is not only a prohibition against requesting the food of others, but one must also not request even one's own food from servants, wives, and so forth, because the act of requesting is common to both sending and entreating.

Therefore, even in one's own home, if servants, wives, and others offer food without being commanded, then it may be eaten, but not otherwise. With this very intention, Gautama stated: "Then for another three days, one should not beg from anyone. And regarding the restriction on the number of mouthfuls in this context, Parāśara has shown it as follows:
Twelve mouthfuls are prescribed for the evening meal, fifteen for the morning;
twenty-four are prescribed for the "begging" meal, and beyond that is known as fasting.
Thus it is said: "Twelve mouthfuls are prescribed for the evening meal, fifteen for the morning;
twenty-four are prescribed for the *āyācita* (begging) meal, and beyond that, fasting is prescribed."

Āpastamba, however, has stated otherwise: "Twenty-two mouthfuls are prescribed for the evening meal, twenty-six for the morning, and twenty-four for the day of fasting; beyond that are three days of total abstinence. The mouthfuls should be the size of a hen's egg, such that they enter the mouth with ease."
Thus.
Twenty-two mouthfuls are prescribed for the evening meal, twenty-six for the morning;
twenty-four are for the "unasked" (āyācya) meal, followed by three days of total fasting.
These mouthfuls should be the size of a hen's egg, so that they enter the mouth with ease.
Between these two alternatives, there is an option depending on one's capacity.

Āpastamba, however, having divided the *prājāpatya* penance into four parts and established them as four *pādakṛcchra*s, has shown their application according to the respective social classes (*varṇa*):
"Three days without food is one quarter; three days of eating only what is unasked for is another quarter."
Three days in the evening, and likewise one quarter for three days in the morning.
A Śūdra should perform service for one day in the morning; for a Vaiśya, he should be made to do so in the evening;
for a Kṣatriya, it is for an unasked favor; and for a Brāhmaṇa, it is traditionally held to be for three nights.
Thus:

three days without eating constitutes one quarter; likewise, three days of eating only what is unasked for constitutes another quarter; three days of eating only in the evening constitute another quarter; and three days of eating only in the morning constitute yet another quarter.
A Śūdra should perform service for one quarter of the day in the morning; for a Vaiśya, one should cause it to be given in the evening;
for a Kṣatriya, it is requested without prior solicitation; and for a Brāhmaṇa, it is prescribed for three nights.
When, however, one performs two sets of three days consisting of fasting without soliciting food, that is known as an *ardhakṛcchra* (half-kṛcchra).

But when one performs three other sets of three days excluding the evening meal, it should be understood as a *pādona* (three-quarters); for it has been stated by that same author: "Without the morning and evening meals, it would be half; without the night meal, it is three-quarters."
Another variety of the *ardhakṛcchra* has also been shown by that same author:
"One [meal] in the evening and one in the morning, likewise for two days [of eating] unasked-for food,
and for two days one should not eat at all— that is prescribed as the *ardhakṛcchra*."
Thus [ends verse] 3.318.
In this manner, eating once in the evening and once in the morning for two days,
and fasting for two days— this is prescribed as the *kṛcchrārdha* penance.
He describes the *prājāpatya* penance:
this *prājāpatya* is said to consist of three times [the basic unit] in whatever manner.

This very same thing is a *pādakṛcchra*. Whether by repetition like a "measuring-stick" (*daṇḍakalita*) or by extension in its own place (*svasthānavivṛddhi*), and whether in direct order (*ānulomya*) or reverse order (*prātilomya*), as well as with or without the recitation (*japa*) to be mentioned later—when practiced three times in such a way, it is designated as a *prājāpatya*.
In this regard, Vasiṣṭha has demonstrated the method of rotation like the swinging of a staff:
one day in the morning, one day at night, one day with food obtained unasked, and one day the Parāka penance;
thus two further four-day periods follow.
For the sake of favoring the brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma,
likewise prescribed the Śiśukṛcchra for children, the elderly, and the sick.
Thus:
one day at dawn, one day and night, one day of unasked food, and one day of the *parāka* penance; in this manner, there are two further sets of four days.
For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma,
likewise prescribed the Śiśukṛcchra for children, the elderly, and the sick.
However, the method for increasing the penance in its own place according to the direct order (*ānulomya*) has been shown by Manu:

"A twice-born man performing the *Prājāpatya* penance should eat in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, eat food obtained unasked for three days, and fast for the final three days."
Thus:

for three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, for three days he should eat what is unasked for, and for the final three days he should not eat at all; this is the Prājāpatya penance performed by a twice-born man.
But Vasiṣṭha has shown the procedure for the reverse order:
"A Brahmin who acts in the reverse order shall perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa."
A Brahmin who has committed an offense against the inverse order (prātilomya) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa.
However, regarding the case of women, Śūdras, and others, Aṅgiras has shown a rule that excludes the recitation of mantras (japa) and so forth:
"Therefore, having approached a Śūdra who always stands upon the path of dharma..."
An expiation should be administered, excluding recitations, burnt offerings, and the like.
Thus it is said:
Therefore, having approached a Śūdra who always stands upon the path of dharma,
a penance should be prescribed that is devoid of recitation, fire-oblations, and the like.
The alternative involving recitation (*japa*) and so forth, however, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and by its suitability, pertains to the three *varṇas*.
And this has been shown by Gautama and others: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the *kṛcchra* penances. Having eaten sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) for breakfast, one should not eat for three nights."
Then for another three days he should eat only at night;
then for another three days he should not beg from anyone;
then for another three days, fasting, he should stand during the day and sit during the night if he desires speed.
One should speak the truth;
one should not converse with those who are ignoble;
and one should constantly employ the recitation of the *raurava* and *yodhā* mantras.

At each *anusavana*, he should perform the touching of water and purify himself with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* accompanied by the *pavitra* mantra, and with the eight verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*.
Then follows the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*):
"Homage to Ahamā, Mohamā, Mahamā, Dhanvan, Tāpasa, and Punarvasu; homage to Mauñjya, Aurmya, Vasuvinda, and Sarvavit."

Homage to Pāra, Supāra, Mahāpāra, Pāradā, Parapāra, and Pārayiṣṇu! Homage to Rudra, Paśupati, the Great God, Tryambaka, the Solitary Wanderer, the Overlord, Hara, Śarva, the Destroyer of Sin, Ugra, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, the Compassionate One, and Kapardin! Homage to Sūrya, the Āditya!
Salutation to the blue-necked one, to the white-throated one; salutation to the black one, to the tawny one;
salutation to the eldest, to the most excellent, to the ancient, to Indra, to the golden-haired one, to the one whose vital energy flows upward.
Salutation to the True One, the Purifier, the one of purifying color, the one of singular color, the Desire, the one who takes form at will!
Salutation to the Blazing One, the one of blazing form! Salutation to the Sharp One, the one of sharp form!
"Salutation to the gentle one, to the good person, to the great person, to the middle person, to the supreme person, to the celibate student;
salutation to the moon-browed one, to the one clothed in animal skin.
This indeed is the ritual attendance upon the sun.
These indeed are the oblations of clarified butter.
At the end of the twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial porridge (caru), one should offer it to these deities:
"Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! To Agni and Soma! To Indra and Agni! To Indra! To the All-gods! To Brahman! To Prajāpati! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! Thus [he offers].
"Before the feeding of the Brahmins":
the meaning of this is that one who desires speediness should stand during the day and sit during the night.

He, however, who desires to be quickly liberated from even great sin by means of a single *kṛcchra* penance alone, should stand at times not incompatible with his duties during the day and sit during the night.

Thus, one who desires swift results should perform the recitation of the *sāman* known as the *Raurava-yodha*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with "Namo hamāya" and so forth, the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*), and the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (*caruśrapaṇa*), even if not mentioned by the *Yogīśvara* and others.

Therefore, in place of the two *Prājāpatya* penances mentioned by the *Yogīśvara* and others, that which is prescribed in the *Gautamīya* together with its various procedures (*itikartavyatā*) should be observed.
In this same manner, other particulars mentioned in different *smṛtis* should also be specifically sought out.
Homage to the destroyer of sin, the fierce one, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the compassionate one with matted hair;
homage to Sūrya, the Āditya;
homage to the blue-necked one, the white-throated one.
Salutation to Kṛṣṇa, to Piṅgala.
Salutation to the Eldest, the Best, the Ancient, Indra, the Golden-haired, the One with Upward Vital Energy.
Salutation to Truth, to the Purifier, to the Fire-colored, to the Single-colored, to Desire, to the One who takes any form at will.
Salutation to the radiant one, to him whose form is radiant;
salutation to the sharp one, to him whose form is sharp;
salutation to the gentle one, to the excellent person, to the great person, to the intermediate person, to the supreme person, and to the celibate student.
"Salutation to the one with the moon on his forehead, the wearer of the skin-clothing.
This indeed is the worship of the Sun;
these are the very oblations of clarified butter.
At the end of twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial oblation (caru), one should offer it to these deities:
"Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! To Agni and Soma! To Indra and Agni! To Indra! To the Viśve Devas! To Brahmā! To Prajāpati! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!
At the conclusion, there is the feeding of Brāhmaṇas; this he calls the Atikṛcchra penance.
This indeed would be the Atikṛcchra penance, consisting of eating only as much food as fills the hollow of the hand.
The *atikṛcchra* penance would consist of these very same characteristics, joined with the duties of the *prājāpatya* such as eating a single meal per day;
however, there is this distinction:
during the first three sets of three days, one should eat only as much food as fills the palm of the hand, and not twenty-two or more morsels.
And here, since the filling of the hand with food is prescribed as a restatement of the meal already obtained, the fasting that is extended by analogy to the final three days remains uncontradicted.

In this case as well, the distribution into quarters should be understood to be exactly as before. As for what was stated by Manu: "For three [periods] of three days each, one should eat a single morsel, as previously described."
A twice-born man performing the Atikṛcchra penance should fast for the final three days.
Thus, because it is smaller than that which is measured by a handful of food, this [rule] pertains to those who have the capacity [to eat more]. (3.319)
He describes the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*:
"The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of twenty-one days of subsisting on milk.
One should understand that the vow known as *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* is the practice of living on milk for twenty-one nights.

Gautama, however, has stated that subsisting on water for twelve nights constitutes the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; the third [type], subsisting on water alone, is also the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. Therefore, the application of these two is determined according to one's capacity.
Regarding the *parāka*, he says: "The *parāka* is proclaimed to consist of fasting for twelve days."
The meaning of this half-verse is straightforward. (3.320)
He describes the Saumya-kṛcchra:
"The consumption of oil-cake, rice-scum, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, each on successive days,
followed by a fast for one night— this is called the Saumya-kṛcchra."

Having consumed each day one of these five—oil-cake, sesame-rice from which the oil has been extracted, the scum of boiled rice, whey, or water-gruel—and fasting on the sixth day, this is called the *saumya* penance (*kṛcchra*).
However, the quantity of the substances should be understood as being restricted only to what is necessary for the maintenance of life.
By Jābāla, however, the *saumya-kṛcchra* is described as lasting for four days.
Oil-cake, barley meal, buttermilk, and fasting on the fourth day;
one should give a garment as the sacrificial fee—this is called the Saumya Kṛcchra.
Thus [ends verse] 3.321.
Oil-cake, barley meal, buttermilk, and fasting on the fourth day;
one should give a garment as the sacrificial fee—this is called the Saumya Kṛcchra.
He describes the penance known as the *tulāpuruṣa*:
"By practicing each of these for three nights in succession,
this [penance] lasting fifteen days is to be known as the *tulāpuruṣa*."
The penance known as *tulāpuruṣa* should be understood as lasting fifteen days, consisting of the sequential three-night practice of each of these five items beginning with oil-cake.
And because a fifteen-day duration is prescribed here, fasting (*upavāsa*) is excluded.
However, by Yama, a twenty-one-night *tulāpuruṣa* has been described.
Then, consuming gruel, oil-cake, buttermilk, and water-mixed barley-meal for three days each, and subsisting on air alone for two sets of three days;
The Tulāpuruṣa vow is said to last for twenty-one nights.
Thus: "Then,
consuming only water for rinsing, oil-cake, buttermilk,
and barley-meal for three days each, he should subsist on air alone for two periods of three days."
The Tulāpuruṣa vow is said to last for twenty-one nights.
The procedure for this, as stated by Hārīta and others, is not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. (3.322)
He describes the Cāndrāyaṇa:
"One performing the Cāndrāyaṇa should eat morsels of food the size of a peacock's egg, increasing them by one each day during the bright fortnight,
and decreasing them by one each day during the dark fortnight."

Performing the vow known as *cāndrāyaṇa*, one should consume food-balls (*piṇḍa*) the size of a peacock’s egg during the waxing fortnight of the bright moon, increasing them according to the lunar days (*tithi*).

Just as there is an increase of one digit of the moon each day from the first day (*pratipad*) until the half-month, so too should one consume the food-balls, increasing them by one each day—eating one on the first day, two on the second, and so on—until the full moon.

Then, having eaten fifteen morsels on the fifteenth day, one should eat fourteen on the first day of the dark fortnight, thirteen on the second, and so on, decreasing the morsels by one each day until the fourteenth day. Then, having consumed one morsel on the fourteenth day, one should fast when the moon has vanished (on the new moon). Thus says Vasiṣṭha:

One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight; one should not eat at all when the moon has waned—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus:

"One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight; one should not eat at all when the moon has waned. This is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa."
The term *cāndrāyaṇa* refers to a ritual course (*āyana*) in which the movement (*caraṇa*) follows the course of the moon, characterized by decrease and increase;
the vowel is lengthened as a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
This practice is called *yavamadhya* ("middle like a barley grain") because it is narrow at both ends and thick in the middle, like a barley grain.

When this very vow is undertaken on the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and performed according to the previously mentioned sequence, it is called "ant-shaped" (*pipīlikamadhyama*), because it becomes thinnest in the middle like an ant.
For instance, following the aforementioned sequence, one should eat fourteen morsels on the first day of the dark fortnight and then reduce the intake by one morsel each day until the fourteenth day.
Then, having consumed one morsel on the fourteenth day and fasted on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), one should consume only a single morsel on the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).

Then, as the remainder of the fortnight is completed by increasing the food intake by one morsel at a time, fifteen morsels are reached on the full moon day; thus, the "ant-middle" (pipīlikāmadhya) form is indeed appropriate.
And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels."
Eating while gradually reducing his morsels, he should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In the same way, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, he should eat another morsel;
eating while increasing the number of morsels, he should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
Thus:
at the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels;
eating while gradually reducing the number of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In the same way, one should eat another morsel at the beginning of the bright fortnight;
eating while increasing the number of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.

However, when in one fortnight there are sixteen days or fourteen days due to the increase or decrease of the lunar dates (*tithi*), then an increase or decrease of the morsels (*grāsa*) must also be understood, according to the rule: "One should consume the food-balls (*piṇḍa*) in accordance with the increase of the lunar dates. Gautama has shown a specific detail here: "Now, therefore, the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Its procedure has been stated [in the Kṛcchra]; one should perform the shaving and observe the vow."
When the full moon day has arrived, one should observe the fast.

With the verses "āpyāyasva," "saṃ te payāṃsi," and "navo nava," he should perform the libation, the oblation of clarified butter, the consecration of the sacrificial food, and the worship of the moon. He should offer clarified butter with the four verses beginning with "yad devā devaheḍanam" and at the end with "devakṛtasya. Then, with three fuel-sticks, he should consecrate each morsel of food with the formulas "oṃ bhūḥ," "bhuvaḥ," "svaḥ," "mahaḥ," "janaḥ," "tapaḥ," "satyam," "yaśaḥ," "śrīḥ," "ūrj," "iṭ," "ojaḥ," "tejaḥ," "puruṣaḥ," "dharmaḥ," and "śivaḥ. With each mantra, he should mentally utter "namaḥ svāhā," or he may consume all the morsels using these very formulas.

The measure of that mouthful is such that it can be taken without distorting the mouth; sacrificial oblations consisting of cooked rice, alms-food, barley-meal, grains, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, or water are increasingly meritorious in the order mentioned.
Having eaten fifteen mouthfuls on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight by decreasing the amount by one mouthful each day.

Having fasted on the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the amount by one mouthful each day; according to some, this Cāndrāyaṇa month is performed in the reverse order.

Regarding what was stated here—that the measure of a mouthful (*grāsa*) is according to the unaltered capacity of the mouth—that refers to the intention of the ignorant (*bāla*), because they lack the capacity to consume fifteen mouthfuls measured by a cock’s egg (*śikhyaṇḍa*).
However, in the case of sacrificial foods such as milk and the like, the measurement of a cock’s egg may be achieved by means of leaf-cups and similar vessels.

Likewise, other measures of a mouthful mentioned in different Smṛtis—such as a chicken’s egg, a fresh *āmalaka* fruit, and so forth—are intended for those who have the physical capacity, since these are smaller than the measure of a cock’s egg.

Furthermore, regarding the statement here that one should fast on the day after the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), which prescribes fasting on the fourteenth day and then eating fifteen morsels on the full moon day and so forth—thereby describing the *cāndrāyaṇa* as consisting of thirty-two days—that is intended to show an alternative method and is not universal, since a version consisting of thirty days has been demonstrated in accordance with the words of the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya).
If this were universal, then the performance of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance continuously for a year would be impossible, as would the following of the moon's course. 3.323.
He now describes another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa: "Alternatively, one may consume two hundred and forty morsels in a single month; this is another Cāndrāyaṇa."

One should consume two hundred and forty morsels of food in a month. This may be done by eating eight morsels every day at midday; or four each during the day and night; or four on one day and twelve on the next; or likewise, having fasted for one night, eating sixteen on the following day, and so forth. One should eat according to whichever of these methods suits one's capacity and other circumstances. This is another form of *candrāyaṇa*, distinct from the two previously mentioned types of *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Therefore, for these two, there is no fixed rule regarding the number of morsels; rather, the number is precisely two hundred and twenty-five.
And these methods have been shown by Manu:
"One should eat eight morsels when the sun is at midday."
With self-restraint, one should perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa using sacrificial food (haviṣya).
A self-controlled Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set; thus he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance.
By eating, with a concentrated mind, eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever for one month, one attains the same world as Candra.
Thus:
"With self-restraint, one should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food at midday; this is how one should perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa."
A composed Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set; thus he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance.
By eating, with a concentrated mind, eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever throughout a month, one attains the same world as the Moon.
Likewise, there is the inclusion of the term "others" (para) for the purpose of encompassing even that which is accomplished by a number of morsels less than two hundred and forty;
as Yama says:
"With self-restraint and firm in his vow, he should eat three morsels at each meal."
Eating sacrificial food for a month is traditionally known as the Ṛṣicāndrāyaṇa.
Thus it is said:
"One who is self-restrained and firm in his vow should eat three morsels at each [meal] for a month, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya);
this is known as the Ṛṣicāndrāyaṇa."
Furthermore, in these practices such as the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* and others, it is not required to follow the actual movement of the moon.

Therefore, when performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* continuously using a common month consisting of thirty days, there is no fault even if the commencement occurs on the fifth lunar day or later due to the increase or decrease of lunar days (*tithi*). As for the monthly vow called *saumāyana* mentioned by Mārkaṇḍeya: "One should drink cow's milk from four teats for seven nights."
For seven nights from three breasts, and for seven nights from two breasts.
For six nights or three nights, one should subsist on air while consuming [milk] from only one breast;
this is the vow called Somāyana, which destroys all impurities.

Thus, in another *smṛti* it is said: "And for seven days [one should consume] the entire udder of a cow; then one may do so from three udders, then two, and likewise one; and if there are three fasts, then that is the *somāyana* within a month. This too is indeed a form of the *cāndrāyaṇa* rite, because Hārīta, after describing the *cāndrāyaṇa* along with its procedural requirements beginning with "Now, therefore, we shall describe the *cāndrāyaṇa*," states by way of extension: "The *somāyana* is exactly like this. As for the *somāyana* which he further described as beginning on the fourth day of the dark fortnight and ending on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight—

For three nights with four breasts beginning from the fourth [lunar day], for three nights with three breasts, for three nights with two breasts, and for three nights with one breast; thus, starting again from one breast up to four breasts, [he recites]: "O Soma, that which is your fourth body, protect us with it; obeisance to it, svāhā! O Soma, that which is your fifth, your sixth," and so on—these are the *tithi*-offerings for the sake of sacrifice. Having praised in this way, purified from sins, he attains equality, co-residence, and union with the Moon. Thus the twenty-four-day *somāyana* has been described; it is intended for those who are unable [to perform the full lunar fast]. 3.324.
Now he states the procedure common to both the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances:
"One who bathes at the three periods of the day should perform the Kṛcchra and likewise the Cāndrāyaṇa;
one should recite purificatory mantras and consecrate the morsels of food with the Gāyatrī."

One should perform the *kṛcchra* penance, such as the *prājāpatya* or the *cāndrāyaṇa*, accompanied by bathing at the three periods of the day (*triṣavaṇa*). This applies with the exception of the *taptakṛcchra*, because Manu specifies a particular rule for that: "In that case, one who is composed should bathe only once. Furthermore, Śaṅkha states regarding the *kṛcchras*: "Three times during the day and three times during the night, one should enter the water wearing one's clothes."
Thus, that [rule] refers to one who is incapable [of performing it].

Furthermore, as for what was stated by Vaiśampāyana— "The bath for the twice-born should be at two times, or indeed at three times"— that is to be understood as referring to one who is unable to perform the bath at the three daily junctures (*triṣavaṇa*).

Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Gārgya—"One should wander for alms wearing a single garment, and having bathed, one should not wring out the garment"—that too applies only to one who is capable [of such austerity], because Śaṅkha describes even the state of wearing a single garment as being optional, stating: "Wearing a single garment or a wet garment, eating light food, sleeping on the bare ground... and so forth.

Regarding bathing, a specific rule has been stated by Hārīta: "Having bathed at least three times with the *śuddhavatī* verses and having muttered the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn while submerged in water, one should put on washed or new (unwashed) clothing and worship the sun with the *saumya* Sāman.
Furthermore, after bathing, one should mutter purificatory prayers (*pavitrāṇi*).

One should mutter within the water during times not incompatible with one's purpose any of the purificatory texts (*pavitrāṇi*) taught by Vasiṣṭha and others—such as the *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *devakṛta*, the *śuddhavatyaḥ*, the *taratsamāḥ*, and so forth—or else the *sāvitrī*. For Manu records: "One should constantly mutter the *sāvitrī* and the purificatory texts according to one's ability.

As for what was stated by Gautama—"One should always employ the *raurava* and *yaudhā* [hymns] in one's muttering"—that too was stated precisely because of their purificatory nature, and not as a restrictive rule; for if it were so, it would entail the undesirable consequence of having to postulate a basis in another Śruti text.

Therefore, one who has not studied the Sāmaveda should recite only the *gāyatrī* and other such mantras. As for the statement that after reciting "Obeisance to Haṃma, to Mohamma," and so forth, "these indeed are the offerings of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*)," that too is not mandatory; rather, the oblation must be performed daily by oneself with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, because Manu has prescribed the performance of the oblation with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"If any rite such as recitation (*japa*) or fire-oblation (*homa*), or whatever is prescribed for a *kṛcchra* penance, cannot be performed,
one should perform it all with the *vyāhṛtis*, the *gāyatrī*, and the *praṇava*."
Thus: whatever recitations, fire-offerings, and so forth prescribed for the *kṛcchra* penance may not be possible,
one should perform them all with the *vyāhṛtis*, the *gāyatrī*, and the *praṇava*.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the offering of water libations (tarpaṇa), the worship of the sun (ādityopasthāna), and so forth are included.
For this very reason, Vaiśampāyana says:
"Having bathed, one should worship the sun with verses addressed to Sūrya, with palms joined in reverence."
Thus:
"Having bathed, one should worship the Sun with verses addressed to the Sun, with palms joined in reverence.

In this manner, regarding other conflicting items as well, an option (*vikalpa*) should be adopted; however, where there is no conflict, there is a combination (*samuccaya*), because—according to the principle of the section on different Vedic branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*)—the ritual act is based upon the authority of all Smṛtis.
The specific rule regarding the number of recitations has been shown by that very [author]:
one should recite the *Ṛṣabha*, the *Viraja*, and likewise the *Aghamarṣaṇa*,
or else recite the divine *Gāyatrī*, the purifier and mother of the Vedas.
One should satisfy the ancestors and the deities either one hundred times, or eight hundred times, or even a thousand times, or at most, by means of whispered recitation or even mentally.
Then, having bowed his head to both men and all living beings, he [proceeded].
Thus:
one should recite the *Ṛṣabha*, the *Viraja*, and likewise the *Aghamarṣaṇa*,
or else the divine *Gāyatrī*, the purifier and mother of the Vedas.
One should satisfy the ancestors and the deities either one hundred times, or one hundred and eight times, or even a thousand times, or at most, by means of whispered recitation or even mentally.
Then, having bowed his head to both men and all living beings, he [proceeded].
Likewise, one should consecrate each morsel (*piṇḍa*) with the *Gāyatrī* mantra;
for a specific rule has also been stated by Yama:
"The morsel held at the tips of the fingers should be consecrated with the *Gāyatrī*."
Having consumed it and sipped water, one should again perform the consecration for another as well.
Thus:
Having consumed the morsel held at the tip of the finger while consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra,
and having sipped water (ācamana), one should again perform the consecration for another [morsel].
Therefore, an option is stated for this [rite] with the consecration mantras beginning with *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* as taught by Gautama.

As for the consecration of the oblation (*havis*) prior to the forming of the balls (*piṇḍa*), which is taught with the mantras beginning with *āpyāyasva* and *saṃ te payāṃsi*, that is to be combined [with the former], because they belong to different contexts.

And when these vows, such as the *kṛcchra*, are performed for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), they must be undertaken preceded by the shaving of hair and so forth, according to the traditional teaching of Gautama: "One should perform the vow after shaving."
However, there is no shaving at all for the sake of *abhyudaya* (prosperity).

Vasiṣṭha has also stated a specific rule in this regard: "In the case of *kṛcchra* penances performed as vows, one should shave the beard, hair, and so forth, with the exception of the hair on the belly and the top-knot (*śikhā*)."
Regarding the *kṛcchras* in the form of vows:
the remainder [of the sentence] is that the constituent parts (*aṅgas*) in the form of vows, such as shaving the hair and so forth, will be described.
Furthermore, the undertaking of the vows as instructed by the assembly (*parṣad*) should be performed on the evening preceding the day of the vow's performance.
As Vasiṣṭha has said:
"I shall fully explain the undertaking of all the vows according to the prescribed rule for all sins, when an expiation is desired to be performed."
At the end of the day, having removed the nails, hair, and other such [impurities], one should perform a bath prepared with ashes,
cow dung, earth, water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and so forth.
The removal of impurities should be performed for the sake of accomplishing external purification,
preceded by the cleansing of the teeth and accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The vow should be undertaken at the beginning of night when the stars are visible outside;
thereafter, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should remain silent, meditating upon one's own misdeeds.
One should ultimately bear even intense mental anguish and grief.
Thus:
I shall now fully explain the formal undertaking of all vows according to the prescribed rules for every sin, when one intends to perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
At the end of the day, having removed the nails, body hair, and so forth, one should perform a bath prepared with ashes,
cow dung, earth, water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and other such substances.
The removal of impurities must be performed for the sake of accomplishing external purification,
preceded by the cleansing of the teeth and accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The vow should be undertaken at the beginning of night when the stars are visible outside;
thereafter, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should remain silent while meditating upon one's own misdeeds.
One will ultimately experience intense mental anguish and carry deep sorrow.
