"Outside" means having gone out from the village; even for a woman, the undertaking of the vow (vrata) must be performed in this very same way.

However, there is no shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, or the nails, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Baudhāyana: "In the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such observances, this same procedure applies to a woman, with the exception of shaving the hair."
However, for one who does not desire shaving, a specific rule has been stated by Hārīta:
"Whether it be a king, a prince, or a learned Brāhmaṇa,
having performed the shaving of the hair, he should perform the penance."
For the sake of protecting one's hair, however, one should observe a vow that is double [the usual duration];
when that double vow has been performed, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall likewise be double.
Thus:
whether it be a king, a prince, or a learned Brahmin,
having performed the shaving of the hair, one should carry out the expiation.
For the sake of preserving one's hair, however, one should observe a vow that is double [the usual duration].
When that double vow has been performed, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall be double.

And this should be understood as referring specifically to the particular faults such as the *mahāpātaka* (great sins); the shaving of the hair is not prescribed for learned Brahmins, kings, or women, nor for one who has committed a *mahāpātaka*, a killer of a cow, or an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) during the performance of a vow.
Thus it is from the recollection of Manu.
Jābāla also has stated a specific rule in this regard:
"At the commencement of all kṛcchra penances, and especially at their conclusion..."
And with that very food, one should offer the Vyāhṛtis individually into the domestic fire.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should perform a śrāddha ceremony, with cows, gold, and other such items as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus it is said:
At the commencement of all *kṛcchra* penances, and especially at their conclusion,
one should offer oblations of food alone into the domestic fire (*śālāgni*), reciting each of the *vyāhṛtis* separately.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should perform a śrāddha ceremony, offering cows, gold, and other such gifts as dakṣiṇā.
In this regard, a specific detail has also been stated in the *Yama*:
"Remorse, desistance, and bathing are declared to be constituent parts (*aṅga*) of all occasional rites (*naimittika*), as well as their recitation."
Likewise, one observing a vow should avoid anointing the body, anointing the head, betel, ointments,
and everything else that produces strength or passion.
Thus:
"One observing a vow should avoid anointing the limbs, anointing the head, betel, unguents, and everything else that produces strength or passion."
The collection of such duties should be sought from other Smṛti texts.
Having thus undertaken the vow according to this rule, it must necessarily be brought to completion;
otherwise, however, there is a transgression: "But having previously taken the vow, one who is deluded by desire does not practice it."
While living he is a Cāṇḍāla, and when dead he is born as a dog.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Chāgaleya; enough of this elaboration. 3.325.
Having thus stated the nature of the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances whose application has been described, he now states their application to other matters that arise incidentally:
"Purification from unspecified sins is achieved by the Cāndrāyaṇa;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon."

That which is prescribed is called *ādiṣṭa* (prescribed penance); there is no [other] penance for those sins for which a specific one has been ordained. For such sins, purification is achieved through the *Cāndrāyaṇa*.

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), purification may also be attained through the *Prājāpatya* and other *Kṛcchra* observances, either in conjunction with the *Aindava* (Cāndrāyaṇa) or independently of it.
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Whatever sins there may be, even those more grievous than the grave, are purified by the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and Cāndrāyaṇa penances; so Manu has declared.
Thus, the combination of these three is established.
Uśanas, however, has stated the combination of both:
"For misfortunes, ill-performed rites, and sins— even great ones—
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are the destroyers of all evil."
Thus:
For misfortunes, ill-performed rites, and even great sins,
both the *kṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances are the destroyers of all evil.
*Duritam* refers to a minor offense (*upapātaka*),

while *duriṣṭam* refers to a major sin (*pātaka*). However, by employing a non-compound construction in the statement "the *kṛcchra*, the *atikṛcchra*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa* constitute the universal expiation" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*)— namely, *kṛcchrātikṛcchrau cāndrāyaṇam*— Gautama indicates that the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* are independent of the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
The independence of the *cāndrāyaṇa* is indicated by the word "iti," and there is a combination of the three [penances].
However, the independent performance of the *prājāpatya* alone has been stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"But when a minor offense is not specifically prescribed, one should perform the *prājāpatya*."
Thus [it is said].
However, when a minor offense has been committed that was not specifically prescribed, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
Gautama also stated the independence of the *prājāpatya* and other such penances: "Having performed the first [penance], one becomes pure, purified, and fit for ritual action."
Having performed it a second time, one is liberated from whatever sin one commits other than the great sins (*mahāpātaka*);
having performed it a third time, one is liberated from all transgression—by which it is intended that this applies even to the great sins.
This has also been stated by Manu:
"This penance called Parāka is the remover of all sins.
Thus [it is said]: "This penance called Parāka is the remover of all sins."
Hārīta has also said:
"The Cāndrāyaṇa, the barley-meal penance, the Tulāpuruṣa,
and likewise following after cows— these destroy all sins."
Likewise: Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, water infused with *kuśa* grass, and a fast for one night—even these purify a dog-eater (*śvapāka*).
Likewise, with reference to the *taptakṛcchra*, it has been stated by that same author:
"This *kṛcchra* penance, when performed twice, shall liberate one from mortal sins (*pātaka*);
when performed three times according to the rule, it removes even the murder of a Śūdra."
Thus,
this Kṛcchra penance, when practiced twice, shall liberate one from mortal sins (pātaka);
when practiced three times according to the rule, it removes even the sin of killing a Śūdra.
And it was said by Uśanas:
"Whether it be mentioned or not mentioned as a destroyer of great sins (mahāpātaka), one should purify oneself by means of the Prājāpatya penance; there is no doubt in this matter."
Thus it is said:
"Whether it has been mentioned or not mentioned as a destroyer of great sins (mahāpātaka), one should purify oneself by means of the Prājāpatya penance; of this there is no doubt."

These penances, beginning with the *prājāpatya*, are to be applied—either individually or collectively—to the minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and others that are not specifically prescribed, depending on whether they are committed once or repeatedly.
Likewise, they are also to be applied to the major sins (*mahāpātaka*) and others among those for which specific vows are prescribed, depending on the degree of repetition.
For this very reason, Yama stated: "Where it has been said," and so forth.
Gautama also employed the term "all penances" (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) for the purpose of summarizing those expiations that had not been specifically mentioned.

Likewise, although he stated: "Having performed the second [penance], one is released from whatever sin other than the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) one commits," and further, "Having performed the third, one is released from all sin (*enas*)," this too is intended with reference to great sins and not minor sins (*upapātaka*).
Moreover, it is impossible for a great sin to exist without a prescribed expiation.
Therefore, even in cases where specific expiations have been prescribed, penances such as the *prājāpatya* should be applied.

In that regard, regarding the twelve-year vow (*dvādaśavārṣika-vrata*), if one calculates by assigning one *prājāpatya* for every twelve days, then three hundred and sixty *prājāpatyas* constitute the optional performance required for the twelve-year vow. In the event of inability to perform that, an equal number of cows should be given as gifts.
In the absence of that, three hundred and sixty niṣkas should be given.
Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"If one is unable to perform the Prājāpatya penance, a wise person should give a cow."
In the absence of a cow, its equivalent value must undoubtedly be given.
"Or half the value, or a *niṣka*, or half of that, according to one's capacity;
in the absence of cows, it shall be a *niṣka*, or half of that, or even a quarter," so says the Smṛti.
If one is unable even to pay the prescribed fine, one should perform as many water-fasts (udavāsas) as there are [units of the fine].

If one is unable even for that, one should perform thirty-six lakh recitations of the Gāyatrī mantra. As it is said: "A Kṛcchra penance, ten thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, likewise an udavāsa, and the gift of a cow to a Brahmin—these four are equal."
Thus it is from the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Parāśara.
As for that which has been stated in the Caturviṃśatimata: "By reciting the Gāyatrī ten million times, one removes the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa;
he who recites it eighty lakhs is liberated from the drinking of liquor."
Seventy lakhs of the Gāyatrī purify one who steals gold;
sixty lakhs of the Gāyatrī liberate one who has violated the Guru’s bed.
Thus, that [penance] is stated as having rules identical to those of the twelve-year penance, and not as being intended for those who are incapable; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Likewise, others [are prescribed]: "A *kṛcchra* penance, ten thousand recitations to the Goddess (*devī*), two hundred *prāṇāyāmas*, a thousand oblations of sesame seeds, and likewise the complete recitation of the Vedas (*vedapārāyaṇa*)."
These and other substitutes, as declared in the twenty-four Smṛtis, are to be understood as being multiplied three hundred and sixty times for the great sins (mahāpātaka).
For the heinous sins (atipātaka), two hundred and seventy Prājāpatya penances must be performed,
or an equal number of substitutes such as cows and the like.
For major sins (*pātaka*), however, there are one hundred and eighty *prājāpatya* penances, and the substitutes such as cows and so forth are likewise that same number.
Thus it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"From birth onwards, there are many various sins."
Having committed an act short of Brahman-murder, one should perform the vow for six years.
In lieu of the cows, a wealthy person should give one hundred and eighty;
or else, the wise man should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one million eight hundred thousand times.
Thus:
"Having committed many various sins from birth onwards,
even prior to the murder of a Brahmin, one should perform the vow for six years."
In lieu of the cows, one hundred and eighty coins should be given by the wealthy;
or else, the wise man should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one million eight hundred thousand times.
This very point is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the arrangement of each *prājāpatya* penance over twelve periods of twelve days within the twelve-year vow.

Likewise, in the case of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) that fall under the scope of a three-year penance, there are ninety *prājāpatyas* and an equal number of substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*). Furthermore, regarding those offenses subject to a three-month penance, there are seven and a half *prājāpatyas*, and an equal number of substitutes such as cows, water-vows (*udavāsa*), and so forth.

Regarding matters concerning the monthly vows (*māsika-vrata*), the substitute penance (*pratyāmnāya*) is two and a half *prājāpatya*s, or exactly that same amount. Furthermore, regarding secondary sins (*upapātaka*) that fall within the scope of the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, the penance is three *prājāpatya*s;
for one unable to perform that, the substitute penance is exactly that same amount.

Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "In the rule for the substitute (*pratyāmnāya*), eight [cows] are always to be given for a *cāndrāyaṇa*," that too refers to the substitute for a *cāndrāyaṇa* such as the *pipīlikāmadhya* for one who possesses wealth. However, regarding minor offenses (*upapātaka*) that fall under the category of a month-long *kṛcchra*, there are seven and a half *prājāpatyas* as substitutes, and the same number of cows and so forth; specifically, "for a *prājāpatya* one should give one cow, and for a *sāntapana*, two."
In the Parāka, Taptakṛcchra, and Atikṛcchra penances, one should likewise give three cows for each.

This is because it is stated thus in the *Caturviṃśatimata*. Furthermore, this should be understood to apply to the alternative of eating each mouthful the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, according to the rule "one should eat each single mouthful. However, in the case of eating a mouthful that fills the hand, there are only two cows [to be given], because a *prājāpatya* penance is equivalent to six fasts, and an *atikṛcchra* is twice that.

Even though one eats a handful of food during the nine days, nevertheless, because of the excessive hardship involved in performing it continuously for twelve days, it is indeed equal to two *prājāpatya* penances, which are equivalent to six days of fasting.
And it is entirely appropriate that a *prājāpatya* is equal to six fasts;
for instance, when the three evening meals are omitted during the first three days, the accomplishment of one full fast is achieved.
In the second three-day period, for one intent on abstaining from the three meals of the morning time,
and likewise in the next three days of not begging, for another who avoids the three evening meals— thus there are three fasts over nine days;
and again, in the final three days, there are three fasts, so that the equivalence to six fasts is logically established.

In the penance for cow-slaughter consisting of a three-night fast accompanied by the gift of eleven cows including a bull (*ṛṣabha*), there are eleven and a half *prājāpatya* penances, as well as an equal number of substitutes such as water-dwelling and so forth. In the month-long milk-vow (*payovrata*), however, there are two and a half *prājāpatyas*.

In the penance for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) consisting of a *parāka*, one should perform three *prājāpatyas*; in place of a *parāka* or a *taptātikṛcchra*, one should perform three *kṛcchras*, or three and a half *sāntapanas*. One should perform the vow in this manner if one is incapable [of the original penance].
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.

However, the *cāndrāyaṇa*, *parāka*, *kṛcchra*, and *atikṛcchra* penances, which consist of three *prājāpatyas* each, amounting to one hundred and twenty in total, are to be performed in place of the twelve-year vow.
The substitutes for these, such as cows and other items, are likewise tripled.
For the ninety types of *atipātaka* (grave sins), there are ninety *cāndrāyaṇa* penances and so forth;
for those equal to them, which are designated by the term *pātaka* (sins), there are sixty;
and for the *upapātaka* (minor sins) that require a three-year penance, there are thirty.
In the case of the three-month vow for cow-slaughter, because of the multiplicity of duties such as bathing with cow-urine and so forth, there are three *cāndrāyaṇas* (as prescribed by Yājñavalkya).
However, in the one-month vow, there is only one *cāndrāyaṇa* as stated by Yogīśvara; yet, in all cases, the substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*) such as the gift of cows or fasting in water must be tripled.

Furthermore, regarding miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*), a *prājāpatya* penance should be applied according to the specific expiation prescribed for each, by calculating it as a quarter and so on.
Regarding repetition, however, there shall be the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances; following this direction, one should make similar calculations for other cases as well.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Bṛhaspati: "Whatever sin or minor offense (upapātaka) has been committed since birth, one should repeat the Kṛcchra penance until it becomes sixtyfold."

Thus, Gautama’s statement that "the two [penances] apply to another's wife" refers to the same subject matter as the two-year penance; or it may refer to cases of repeated commission of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) such as those lasting three months; or it may refer to the case of a double repetition of approaching women of the *caṇḍāla* class and others, who are designated by the term "sinful" (*pātaka*). In this regard, since it is ordained that "for intentional [action] a year-long *kṛcchra* is prescribed, and for unintentional [action] two *aindava* [penances]"—and because a year-long *kṛcchra* is thus prescribed for a single intentional approach, it is entirely appropriate to prescribe sixty *kṛcchras*, which is equivalent to two years, for its repetition.

As for that which was stated by Sumantu: "Even a great sin committed intentionally and repeated many times is purified by a year-long *kṛcchra* penance, except in the case of a mortal transgression (*mahāpātaka*)."

This [penance] also refers to the repetition of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and the like; likewise, the statement by Yama that "for two *aiṇḍava* [fasts] due to ignorance" refers either to the repetition of those specific sins for which two *aiṇḍava* fasts are prescribed.

However, one who is incapable of performing such ascetic penances (*tapas*) but possesses an abundance of grain should accomplish the vows of *kṛcchra* and so forth by means of giving food to the foremost of the twice-born.

For thus says another Smṛti: "In a *kṛcchra*, five [mouthfuls]; in an *atikṛcchra*, three times that; every day in the third [type], thirty; and forty in the *taptakṛcchra*; in a *parāka*, twenty multiplied by three."

In the penance called *sāntāpana-kṛcchra*, there are twenty-six [meals]; that same number, reduced by two, would apply to the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. In this austerity, one whose strength is diminished should feed the most eminent Brahmins. The phrase "day after day" (*aharahar*) is to be connected with every instance. The third is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
In this context, by calculating the day of Prajāpati, there is a feeding of sixty learned Brahmins.
As for that which has been stated in the Caturviṃśatimata: "Twelve Brahmins should be fed, as well as the Pāvakeṣṭi;
or some other purificatory rite—so the wise have declared."
Thus, the feeding of twelve Brahmins in place of a *prājāpatya* penance has been prescribed; that refers to the case of one who is destitute.

Furthermore, regarding the *cāndrāyaṇa*, a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) and so forth have been stated in that very same context: "The *cāndrāyaṇa*, the *mṛgāreṣṭi*, the *pavitreṣṭi*, likewise the *mitravindā*, the *apaśu*, and the three-month *kṛcchra*."
In the absence of regular (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, as well as of iṣṭis and animal sacrifices, sacrificial porridges (carus) are prescribed.
Thus, that [penance] as well is for one incapable of performing the *cāndrāyaṇa*.

As for the eight *kṛcchras* prescribed as a substitute by the rule "likewise three months of *kṛcchra*," that too concerns those who are aged or dull-witted, since it has been shown that a *cāndrāyaṇa* is equivalent to three *kṛcchras*; so enough of this elaboration.
Let us return to the subject at hand.

However, he who, desiring prosperity (*abhyudaya*), performs this *cāndrāyaṇa* for the sake of merit—that is, for the purpose of fulfilling optional injunctions (*kāmya-niyoga*)—and not for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), attains the same world as the Moon (*candrasālokya*), which is a particular region of heaven. And this is with reference to its repetition for a year, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "Having performed it once, one becomes free from taint and sin; having performed it a second time, one purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first; and having completed a year [of performance], one attains the same world as the Moon.
Furthermore:
One who performs the kṛcchra penance while desiring dharma shall attain great prosperity;
being well-composed, he obtains the fruit of a major sacrifice.
However, he who desires worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and performs the *kṛcchra* penances such as the *prājāpatya* experiences great fortune and power characterized by sovereignty and the like.

Just as the performer of major sacrifices (*gurukratu*) such as the *rājasūya* obtains the great fruit characterized by self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) and so forth, so too this person, being well-concentrated and performing the entire collection of constituent parts without omission—this citation of the example of the sacrifice is for the purpose of illuminating the majesty of the result.

By the phrase "well-concentrated" (*susamāhita*), the author speaks of the unimpaired performance of the scripture, thereby indicating that when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) due to its being a rite for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*), the fruit is not attained.

Therefore, one need not accept the performance of as many auxiliaries as possible—as is the case with expiations (*prāyaścitta*)—and thus the recourse to substitutes (*pratyāmnāya*) is ruled out from the start. However, regarding the repetition of the performance of *kṛcchra* and other such rites, the repetition of the fruit for the qualified agent is already established by the principle that "in a ritual action, the result is to be brought about by the commencement [of the act]"; thus, this point is certainly not unintended. (3.327)

Under the guise of summarizing all the matters previously mentioned, [the author] speaks in order to set forth, along with their explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the injunctions for the memorization of the *Dharmaśāstra* and so forth, in the form of a request and the granting of a boon:
"Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya,
the great-souled sages spoke thus to that lord of yogis, who possessed immeasurable luster."

For here, six types of duties distinct from those pertaining to caste, stage of life, and so forth, have been expounded; having heard all these words spoken by the Lord of Yogins, the sages, their eyes blossoming with great joy, addressed him—who is endowed with majesty and virtue and possesses inconceivable power and splendor—with the following words that are about to be related. 3.328.
Those who, free from sloth, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain fame in this world and go to the third heaven.
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; likewise, one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
similarly, one desiring long life shall obtain long life, and one desiring prosperity shall obtain great prosperity.
For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard at a śrāddha ceremony, the ancestors of that person shall attain imperishable satisfaction; of this there is no doubt.
By the retention of this scripture, a Brāhmaṇa attains the state of being a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth.
Thus, through verses of straightforward meaning, Sāmaśravas and others made their requests in many ways. (3.329–3.332)
He states another prayer as well:
"O Wise One, may you grant your approval for the fruit of a horse-sacrifice to accrue to that learned man who causes this to be heard by the twice-born on every sacred festival day."

"He who shall cause the twice-born to hear this treatise on Dharma at every festival-parvan shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice"—this is the explanatory praise (arthavāda) for the injunction regarding recitation.
Therefore, may you grant your approval everywhere for this very purpose which we have requested. (3.333)
Regarding the granting of the boon, it is said:
Having heard this speech of the sages, Yājñavalkya, with a delighted soul, said,
"So be it," after bowing to the Self-born One.

Having heard this spoken by the sages, even the Lord of Yogins, his lotus-face blossomed with the desire for the fruits of upholding the Dharma-śāstra composed by himself; having paid homage and bowed to the Self-born Brahmā, the Blessed One indeed spoke thus: "May everything requested by you be so. (3.334)

Thus ends the third chapter, on Expiation (*prāyaścitta*), in the *Ṛjumitākṣarā*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Vijñāneśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, the son of the venerable Bhāradvāja Padmanābha Bhaṭṭopādhyāya.

This commentary on the Dharmaśāstra is the work of the yogin Vijñāneśvara, a disciple of the one whose name begins with the syllable *Uttama*. (1)
Thus, this commentary on the treatise of the sage Yājñavalkya is not without purpose for any learned man;
though concise in its syllables, it is rich in vast meaning and sprinkles nectar upon the ears. (2)
I have composed this commentary using words that are profound yet clear, concise in syllables yet not lacking in meaning, and brief in length. (3)
There has never been, nor is there now, nor will there ever be on the surface of the earth a city equal to Kalyāṇakalpa, nor a sovereign king like the illustrious Vikramārka, seen or even heard of;
and as for the scholar Vijñāneśvara, he has no peer at all. May this triad—resembling a wish-fulfilling creeper—remain for a short while.

May the Lord of the Knowledge of Reality, the creator of words whose forms are sweet and which stand as the limit of wonder for the learned; the giver of objects of exceeding excellence to the multitude of supplicants through their prayers; and the meditator upon the form of the Conqueror of Mura—may he live as long as the sun and moon, a victor over his enemies who are born of his own body.

May King Vikramāditya—whose feet shine with the luster of the crest-jewels of bowing monarchs—protect this entire world until the moon and stars cease to exist; he whose fame extends from the Setu bridge to the king of mountains, and from the western ocean with its high, dancing waves stirred by schools of playful dolphins to the eastern sea. 6.
If the cavities [of the senses] are turned inward, what is the use of austerity? If the cavities are not turned inward, what is the use of austerity?
If Hari is both within and without, what is the use of austerity? If Hari is neither within nor without, what is the use of austerity? (7)
